items.question_content: A 41-year-old completely edentulous woman who is a hepatitis B carrier is being rehabilitated with maxillary and mandibular complete dentures using strict infection-control measures and incorporation of a laminated QR code containing her identification and medical information into the maxillary denture. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, fig_06.jpg, and fig_07.jpg, and select all correctly paired stage-procedure statements.

question_options.text: Primary impressions were made in stock trays using alginate before fabrication of the custom tray.
Sectional border molding with low-fusing compound preceded a monophase addition-silicone final impression.
Both primary and secondary impressions were immersed in 2% glutaraldehyde for 10 min.
The master cast was disinfected by sodium hypochlorite spray left in contact for 10 min.
Jaw relation was recorded by Niswonger's physiologic method and later verified at try-in for esthetics and phonetics.
The laminated QR code was incorporated during conventional packing and heat curing, so no post-deflasking fixation stage was needed.
The metal stock tray was managed only by surface wiping with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
After insertion, the denture was rinsed, debris was removed with an ultrasonic cleaner, and the prosthesis was then immersed in alkaline glutaraldehyde.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Correct pairings are A, B, D, E, and H. The secondary impression, unlike the primary, was disinfected in 2% glutaraldehyde for 1 hour, not 10 minutes. The QR code was not heat-cured in place; it was added after deflasking with autopolymerizing resin. The metal stock tray was autoclaved, not merely wiped.

items.answer_explanation: Correct pairings are A, B, D, E, and H. The secondary impression, unlike the primary, was disinfected in 2% glutaraldehyde for 1 hour, not 10 minutes. The QR code was not heat-cured in place; it was added after deflasking with autopolymerizing resin. The metal stock tray was autoclaved, not merely wiped.

items.question_content: A 64-year-old man has a 10-month history of progressive swelling in the anterior mandible that later became painful. Odontogenic keratocyst

items.question_content: A 41-year-old systemically healthy woman presents with 2 months of redness and bleeding from the lower front gums. The site is painless. A small growth in the same mandibular anterior labial gingiva was removed 6 months earlier and again 1 year earlier, with recurrence after each procedure. Oral hygiene is good and she has no systemic symptoms. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. She does not want another operation. Is the current clinicopathologic information sufficient to justify non-operative management, or would you recommend immediate further tissue diagnosis despite her reluctance? Give your leading diagnosis, name the single alternative diagnosis that would most change your threshold for intervention, and justify your decision from the figures and history. Also state the exact clinical or microscopic change that would make you switch to repeat biopsy or definitive treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis is localized juvenile spongiotic gingival hyperplasia (LJSGH), despite the patient's age. The current information is sufficient to support a clinicopathologically concordant working diagnosis and justify non-operative management now rather than immediate repeat biopsy.

The reasoning comes from integrating the history and figures. fig_01.jpg shows a sharply localized erythematous gingival lesion with a characteristic velvety/papillary surface in the anterior gingiva. The lesion has recurred after prior excisions and the patient has good oral hygiene, which makes routine plaque-induced inflammation less convincing. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show an epithelial-predominant process: nonkeratinized epithelial hyperplasia/acanthosis with spongiosis and inflammatory exocytosis, rather than dysplasia, invasion, or a stromal pattern typical of common reactive masses. fig_04.jpg suggests rapid persistence/reappearance after biopsy, which is compatible with the known recurrent behavior of LJSGH.

The single alternative diagnosis that would most change my threshold for intervention is epithelial dysplasia/erythroplakia or early squamous cell carcinoma, because a persistent red gingival lesion in an adult can occasionally represent a premalignant or malignant process and would warrant repeat tissue diagnosis or definitive excision/referral. It is less favored here because the biopsy figures do not show cytologic atypia or invasion, and the clinical history lacks pain, induration, destructive change, or systemic warning signs. Common reactive lesions such as pyogenic granuloma remain broader differentials, but the clinicopathologic pattern shown is less supportive.

Management now should be conservative and documented: explain the benign but recurrent nature of the lesion, confirm clinicopathologic concordance if needed, remove any local traumatic/irritational factors, maintain meticulous plaque control, consider low-risk supportive measures such as an SLS-free toothpaste, and review with standardized photographs/measurements. Immediate re-excision is not preferred because prior surgery has not been durable and the patient declines another operation.

I would switch to repeat biopsy, wider excision, or specialist referral if the lesion enlarges, becomes indurated, ulcerates, becomes painful, shows disproportionate or persistent bleeding, develops fixation, destructive or bony change, cervical lymphadenopathy, or systemic features, or if further histology shows dysplasia, invasion, or other clinicopathologic discordance.

items.question_content: A 32-year-old woman has a long-standing, painless mass on the posterior tongue that became more raised over recent months. The lesion has now been excised. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, you are asked to advise the surgeon on the pathologic diagnosis and whether any further treatment is needed. What diagnosis would you render, and what postoperative management and follow-up would you recommend? Justify your plan from the history and the microscopic pattern, including why other clinically plausible entities do not require the same management in this case.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best diagnosis is gastric mucosal choristoma (heterotopic gastric mucosa) of the tongue. The slides show squamous mucosal lining with focal surface erosion and a deep, organoid proliferation of closely packed glands that resemble gastric-type mucosa rather than a destructive invasive carcinoma. The clinical history also fits a benign choristoma: a long-standing posterior tongue nodule with slow change rather than a rapidly progressive painful ulcerative mass. The key management implication is that complete local excision is definitive treatment if the lesion has been fully removed. No wider oncologic resection, neck treatment, or adjuvant therapy is indicated. Postoperative care should be routine clinical follow-up to confirm healing and detect the uncommon event of residual or recurrent lesion; re-excision would be considered only if there is documented incomplete removal or persistent mass/symptoms. Important alternatives before final sign-out include salivary gland lesions and malignant epithelial tumors that may present as a posterior tongue mass, especially when surface erosion is present, but those would be expected to show different architecture and/or cytologic atypia, destructive invasion, or other malignant features not evident here. Prognosis is excellent after adequate excision.

items.question_content: A man in his 20s presents with a 1-month history of an asymptomatic 1 x 0.5 cm nodular lesion on the lingual gingiva adjacent to the mandibular left lateral incisor and canine. It bleeds mildly, the surface is intact, radiographs show no bony change, medical workup is unremarkable, and there is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, state the most likely diagnosis and the definitive management you would choose now. Justify your plan by explaining which clinical-pathologic features make this lesion biologically different from more common reactive gingival enlargements, and how that should affect the extent of excision, prognosis, and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is a localized gingival lymphangioma, i.e., a superficial oral lymphatic malformation. The key evidence is the microscopic pattern in fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg: multiple enlarged endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces immediately beneath the epithelium, containing proteinaceous fluid with lymphocytes and a few RBCs. That is not the vascular granulation tissue expected in pyogenic granuloma, not the multinucleated giant-cell lesion of peripheral giant cell granuloma, not the calcifying fibrous stroma of peripheral ossifying fibroma, and not a simple fibroma. The normal radiograph and lack of cervical nodes support a soft-tissue process confined to the gingiva rather than an aggressive destructive lesion.

Definitive treatment is conservative but complete surgical excision of this localized lesion, with removal to clinically uninvolved soft tissue at the base while preserving the adjacent teeth because there is no evidence of osseous involvement. Histopathologic confirmation is essential because, unlike common reactive gingival enlargements, lymphangioma is a developmental lymphatic malformation with a non-encapsulated, infiltrative growth pattern. That biologic behavior means a limited shave or incomplete removal risks persistence or recurrence even when the lesion appears small and superficial. For a small accessible gingival lesion, excision is the best definitive option; nonexcisional modalities are more relevant when lesions are diffuse, extensive, or difficult to access.

Prognosis is generally favorable in this patient because the lesion is small and localized, but recurrence remains the main concern if excision is incomplete. I would therefore plan long-term clinical follow-up for several years, with early postoperative review and periodic recall to look for regrowth at the surgical site.
