levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a realistic prognosis and explains what follow-up is intended to detect, such as local recurrence or unexpected later evidence suggesting incomplete excision or a different diagnosis.

items.question_content: A 39-year-old woman underwent superficial parotidectomy for a 3-year mobile left parotid mass; FNAC was Milan IVb and CT had suggested a benign superficial-lobe tumor. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg only. At tumor board you must decide whether to sign out a specific malignant salivary neoplasm now, issue only a qualified “favor” diagnosis with recommended molecular confirmation, or defer classification pending fusion testing. State which path you choose, give the report wording you would use, and justify that confidence level from the figures. Then provide a rank-ordered differential of the two strongest alternatives and explain which figure-based findings push each alternative down. Identify the single unrevealed pathologic feature from the resection report that would most change postoperative management after an otherwise complete excision, and why. Finally, if DOG1 were convincingly supportive of acinic differentiation while mammaglobin became only focal/weak, how would your report wording and use of molecular testing change?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would sign the case out now as a specific entity: “Secretory carcinoma of the parotid gland (formerly mammary analog secretory carcinoma), conventional/low-grade.” A brief comment could state that the morphology and immunophenotype are concordant and sufficiently classic that immediate molecular confirmation can be deferred in a resource-limited setting.

Why this confidence level is justified from the figures: fig_01.jpg shows a lobulated, predominantly circumscribed neoplasm with a small infiltrative edge, built largely of microcystic/secretory spaces with additional cystic, solid, and cribriform or follicular-like areas. The lumina contain colloid-like secretory material highlighted on PAS/ALPAS images. The cells are bland polygonal cells with eosinophilic to vacuolated cytoplasm, without necrosis, marked pleomorphism, or obvious high-grade transformation in the material shown. fig_02.jpg shows a classic secretory phenotype: CK7 positive, diffuse S100 positive, diffuse mammaglobin positive, focal GCDFP-15 positive, with p63 negative, CEA negative, HER2/neu negative, and DOG1 only nonspecific/non-supportive rather than convincingly acinic. Ki67 is only moderately increased at about 12%. Taken together, that is strong enough for a definitive diagnosis rather than only “favor” or deferral.

Ranked differential:
1) Zymogen-poor acinic cell carcinoma. This is the closest mimic because architecture can overlap, especially microcystic and cystic patterns. It is pushed down by the strong diffuse S100 and mammaglobin expression, absence of convincing acinic differentiation, and DOG1 not showing a clearly supportive pattern.
2) Low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. It is considered because of cystic change and luminal mucin-like material, but it is pushed down by p63 and CEA negativity, diffuse S100/mammaglobin positivity, and the lack of a convincing triphasic squamoid-intermediate-mucinous population.

The single unrevealed pathologic feature that would most change postoperative management after an otherwise complete excision is margin status. In a small, apparently low-grade salivary carcinoma without high-grade transformation on the figures, close or positive margins would be the most immediately actionable finding for re-excision or consideration of postoperative radiotherapy. Perineural invasion, nodal disease, and final stage also matter, but margin status is the key missing datum most likely to alter escalation after this surgery.

If DOG1 became convincingly supportive of acinic differentiation while mammaglobin were only focal or weak, the case would no longer be a classic concordant secretory carcinoma. I would lower my confidence and change the report to a qualified diagnosis, for example: “Salivary carcinoma, favor secretory carcinoma over zymogen-poor acinic cell carcinoma; recommend ETV6 rearrangement/fusion testing if feasible,” or similar wording. In that discordant setting, molecular confirmation becomes much more important and I would not be as comfortable issuing an unqualified definitive sign-out based on morphology and IHC alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg in a coherent way, gives an incorrect diagnosis, or relies mainly on generic textbook statements unrelated to the figures.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses specific findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to justify the leading diagnosis, including secretory-pattern architecture, luminal secretions, low-grade cytology, and the supportive CK7/S100/mammaglobin profile with negative or non-supportive comparator stains.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a tightly reasoned confidence-tiered sign-out from the figures, explicitly integrating the focal infiltrative border, multiple architectural patterns, secretory material, concordant immunophenotype, DOG1 non-supportive nature, and absence of shown high-grade features to justify why a definitive sign-out is appropriate rather than only a qualified or deferred diagnosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not provide plausible alternatives, misidentifies major competing diagnoses, or cannot distinguish the lesion from unrelated entities.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a reasonable rank-ordered differential that includes the strongest competing entities, especially zymogen-poor acinic cell carcinoma and low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and distinguishes them using figure-based findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the differential in a clinically persuasive way, showing why acinic cell carcinoma is the closest mimic, why mucoepidermoid carcinoma is secondary, and exactly which findings in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg most strongly weaken each alternative.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses an inappropriate sign-out confidence level or identifies a postoperative decision factor that is not materially relevant to management in this case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a generally reasonable sign-out path or mentions a relevant missing pathologic feature, but does not explain why that feature would be the most management-changing after excision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a defensible sign-out confidence level and identifies a high-impact unrevealed pathologic feature, most commonly margin status, with a clear explanation of how it would influence postoperative escalation or follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Demonstrates clear prioritization by linking the chosen report confidence and the selected high-impact missing feature to real postoperative consequences, while appropriately acknowledging other adverse features such as perineural invasion, nodal disease, or stage without losing focus on the single most actionable datum.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: States that molecular testing is always required or never useful, or does not adjust reasoning when the hypothetical DOG1/mammaglobin pattern changes.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the hypothetical altered IHC would reduce confidence, but does not clearly change report wording or explain why molecular confirmation becomes more important.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that the hypothetical DOG1-supported, weak/focal mammaglobin profile creates a discordant case in which a qualified diagnosis is more appropriate and molecular confirmation should be sought if feasible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly contrasts the current concordant case with the hypothetical discordant one, revises the report wording appropriately, and balances resource limits, diagnostic confidence, and potential future therapeutic value of confirming an ETV6/NTRK-related fusion.

items.question_content:
A previously healthy 65-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal pain, emesis, chronic constipation, significant weight loss, and normal CEA/CA19-9. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg from a resection of a deep mesocolic mass. You are also asked how you would advise an oral/maxillofacial surgeon if an analogous deep head-and-neck lesion yielded only core-biopsy material comparable to fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg.

Write a concise consult note that identifies the lesion's most defensible biologic classification and preferred sign-out for the resection, reconciles the aggressive appearance in fig_01.jpg with the pathology data, ranks the 2 most consequential alternatives that still require exclusion, and states whether you would support immediate ablative surgery for the head-and-neck analogue or choose 1 different next action first. End by naming 1 later clinicopathologic development that would most strongly force reclassification and why.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Most defensible biologic classification on the resection is a reactive fibroinflammatory lesion, best signed out as inflammatory pseudotumor (IPT), with a comment that the principal neoplastic exclusion is inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). On the resection I would be comfortable using a named diagnosis such as "inflammatory pseudotumor / reactive fibroinflammatory lesion" because the architecture, inflammatory background, and immunophenotype are available. If the same pattern were seen only on a deep head-and-neck core biopsy, I would use more qualified wording, for example: "fibroinflammatory spindle-cell lesion, favor IPT, but IMT and other locally aggressive spindle-cell processes are not fully excluded on limited tissue."

fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg are discordant in a clinically important way. fig_01.jpg shows a large aggressive-appearing deep mass with adjacent organ involvement and nearby nodes, so imaging alone could suggest malignancy. However, fig_02.jpg shows a bland lesion composed of histiocytes and spindle/myofibroblastic cells in a prominent lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory background without overt malignant cytology, and fig_03.jpg supports that pattern with CD68 positivity in histiocytes, SMA positivity in myofibroblasts, and lack of ALK and CD34 expression. That combination supports IPT more than a clearly malignant spindle-cell neoplasm, while the infiltrative radiology prevents overconfidence.

The 2 most consequential alternatives to rank are: first, IMT, because it is a true neoplastic process with recurrence potential and possible kinase-fusion implications; second, a locally aggressive spindle-cell neoplasm such as desmoid-type fibromatosis. IMT remains the key exclusion because morphology overlaps and ALK-negative IMT exists, so ALK negativity does not fully rule it out. Desmoid-type fibromatosis is less favored because this lesion is conspicuously inflammatory and histiocyte-rich rather than a relatively monotonous long-fascicular fibromatosis; CD34 negativity also makes some other spindle-cell mimics less likely.

For the analogous deep head-and-neck core biopsy, I would not support immediate ablative surgery. My single next action would be to obtain more representative tissue for expert clinicopathologic review; if tissue adequacy were already assured, targeted molecular testing aimed at excluding IMT would become the highest-yield next step. The reason is to avoid irreversible overtreatment of a lesion that still sits on the reactive-versus-neoplastic border on limited sampling.

A later development that would most strongly force reclassification would be recurrence or progressive destructive behavior after excision, especially if accompanied by demonstration of an ALK or other kinase fusion. That would argue against a purely reactive IPT framework and would reopen classification toward IMT or another neoplastic spindle-cell lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misclassifies the lesion as a definite malignant spindle-cell neoplasm or another unsupported primary diagnosis, or does not recognize the reactive-versus-neoplastic classification problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a fibroinflammatory/reactive process but remains overly vague, or favors another overlapping entity as the primary sign-out without adequately justifying why IPT is not preferred.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies inflammatory pseudotumor/reactive fibroinflammatory lesion as the leading diagnosis for the resection, with generally appropriate calibration of certainty.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies IPT as the best-supported resection diagnosis, explicitly frames it as reactive rather than overtly neoplastic, and appropriately lowers confidence for an analogous limited core biopsy while retaining IPT as the leading interpretation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully, or misinterprets the imaging, morphology, or immunophenotype.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the imaging or the pathology/immunohistochemistry, but does not convincingly reconcile their discordance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg with fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg and explains that the aggressive radiology is concerning but not sufficient to override the bland fibroinflammatory pathology.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically identifies the aggressive deep/infiltrative appearance in fig_01.jpg as the main source of uncertainty and the bland histiocyte-myofibroblastic lymphoplasmacytic pattern in fig_02.jpg plus CD68+/SMA+/ALK-/CD34- profile in fig_03.jpg as the main support for IPT, explaining how these data together support the final interpretation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible management-relevant alternatives, or names alternatives that are not clinically credible from the available data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists alternatives but does not rank them, or gives limited case-specific reasoning for why they remain in or fall down the differential.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Ranks 2 plausible consequential alternatives and gives case-based reasons for why they still merit consideration but are less favored than the leading diagnosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Ranks IMT first as the key management-altering alternative, explains why ALK negativity and sampling limitations do not fully exclude it, and provides a second plausible management-relevant alternative with case-specific reasons it is less favored on the current morphology and immunophenotype.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Supports immediate ablative/wide surgery for the analogous limited-biopsy head-and-neck lesion, or gives no meaningful next step.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that more workup is needed but does not choose and justify a single next action, or omits a clear trigger for later reclassification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Does not endorse immediate ablative surgery on limited tissue and prioritizes either broader sampling/expert review or targeted ancillary testing, while naming at least one later finding that would prompt reclassification.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes one highest-yield action before irreversible surgery—most often more representative tissue with expert review, or targeted molecular testing if tissue is already adequate—justifies that choice over immediate ablation, and identifies a concrete reclassification trigger such as recurrence after excision, progressive destructive behavior, metastasis, or discovery of an ALK/other kinase fusion.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Supporting immediate ablative surgery for the analogous limited-biopsy head-and-neck lesion without first addressing the unresolved reactive-versus-neoplastic differential.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is the most likely presumptive clinicogenetic diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_02.jpg suggests a hypoplastic enamel defect because the enamel is reduced/irregular while overall crown contour is preserved. fig_01.jpg shows vertical transmission affecting both sexes, supporting autosomal dominant inheritance. Together, the best presumptive clinicogenetic diagnosis is autosomal dominant hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta.

items.question_content:
A 54-year-old man has a slowly enlarging 1.2-cm sessile nodule on the dorsal tongue. A separate midline erythematous/fissured change improved with cleaning and topical antifungal therapy. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg as if you are signing out the excision for the surgeon.

1) Using fig_01.jpg only, give your provisional line diagnosis and a prioritized differential of 2 other entities that would materially change management. State the single best next ancillary study or study set, and explain why a routinely positive adipocytic marker would not solve the key diagnostic problem.
2) After adding fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, issue the final diagnosis. Identify the 4 highest-value figure findings supporting it: 2 morphologic findings and 2 immunohistochemical findings. Also name 1 stain result in fig_03.jpg that could mislead an overcaller and explain why.
3) Give a brief surgeon-facing management comment: whether re-excision, molecular escalation, or routine follow-up is most appropriate now, and why.
4) If the only changed result were focal weak nuclear MDM2 and CDK4 staining, with the rest of fig_01.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg unchanged, what would you do next and how would your diagnostic wording change?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
1) fig_01.jpg alone: provisional impression is an atypical/deceptive lipomatous lesion of the dorsal tongue, with benign lipoma showing reactive/degenerative change favored but not yet secure. The 2 management-altering entities to prioritize are atypical lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma (ALT/WDL) and dysplastic lipoma. The best next ancillary workup is an MDM2/CDK4-centered panel, ideally interpreted with Rb and p53; if immunostains are equivocal, the most decisive escalation test is MDM2 amplification analysis. A positive routine adipocytic marker such as S100, vimentin, or FASN would only confirm adipocytic/mesenchymal nature, not distinguish benign degenerative change from ALT/WDL or dysplastic lipoma.

2) Final diagnosis after fig_02.jpg-fig_04.jpg: lipoma with reactive/degenerative changes of the tongue.

Highest-value supportive findings:
Morphologic:
- fig_01.jpg shows variably sized adipocytes with ring-like/vacuolated pseudo-lipoblastic cells and Lochkern change, but without the classic pattern of broad atypical fibrous septa populated by conspicuous atypical stromal cells expected for ALT/WDL.
- The lesion is accompanied by fibrous stroma with numerous stromal histiocytes, supporting degenerative/reactive change rather than true malignant lipoblastic differentiation.
Immunohistochemical:
- fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show nuclear MDM2 negativity and CDK4 negativity, strongly arguing against ALT/WDL.
- fig_03.jpg shows retained Rb expression, which argues against dysplastic lipoma; fig_04.jpg also shows only rare Ki-67-positive cells, reinforcing low proliferative activity.

Potentially misleading fig_03.jpg result: p16 positivity (CD10 also acceptable). p16 is not specific for malignant adipocytic tumors and can be seen in benign adipocytic lesions, so overinterpreting it could drive an unjustified sarcoma diagnosis.

3) Surgeon-facing management comment: Findings support a benign lipoma with reactive/degenerative atypia. If the lesion has been completely excised and clinicopathologic findings are concordant, routine follow-up is appropriate. I would not recommend automatic wider re-excision or routine molecular escalation now. Re-review or additional testing would be reserved for recurrence, residual disease, clinical-pathologic discordance, or equivocal ancillary results.

4) If the only change were focal weak nuclear MDM2 and CDK4 staining, I would not immediately reclassify the lesion as ALT/WDL, because weak expression can occur in benign lipomatous lesions with degenerative change. My next step would be confirmatory MDM2 amplification testing and/or expert soft tissue pathology review. Diagnostic wording should become more cautious, such as: 'Atypical adipocytic neoplasm with degenerative change; ALT/WDL not excluded pending confirmatory molecular correlation.' If amplification is absent, the lesion remains best classified as benign lipoma with reactive/degenerative changes; if amplified, the diagnosis shifts toward peripheral ALT/WDL and management escalates to margin-oriented re-review, consideration of local re-excision, and closer surveillance.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates at least 2 relevant morphologic findings and 2 relevant immunohistochemical findings from fig_01.jpg-fig_04.jpg into a coherent benign interpretation.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains that weak focal MDM2/CDK4 positivity alone is insufficient for definitive reclassification, prioritizes confirmatory MDM2 amplification testing or expert review before escalation, and revises the wording to a cautious provisional atypical adipocytic diagnosis rather than an immediate ALT/WDL sign-out.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending immediate wider tongue resection or definitive ALT/WDL sign-out based only on pseudo-lipoblasts, p16 positivity, or weak equivocal MDM2/CDK4 staining without confirmatory correlation

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Using the Ben Salem morphological classification, what type of fusion is shown?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The mandibular lateral incisor-canine complex shows two fused crowns with fused roots radiographically, which corresponds to Ben Salem Type IV. This differs from Type III, where the crowns are fused but the roots are double conical rather than fused.

items.answer_explanation: The mandibular lateral incisor-canine complex shows two fused crowns with fused roots radiographically, which corresponds to Ben Salem Type IV. This differs from Type III, where the crowns are fused but the roots are double conical rather than fused.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old man presents with a 6-month painless, firm upper-lip mass and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg from the excisional specimen. The lesion is reported as circumscribed, with no invasive growth or other malignant features on routine sections. What is your most defensible diagnosis and management plan at this stage? Justify your answer from the clinical setting and microscopy, explain why competing salivary gland tumors are less likely, and state whether any further workup or follow-up is needed.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best diagnosis is a benign myoepithelioma of a minor salivary gland in the upper lip, with mixed myoepithelial morphology dominated by spindle/plasmacytoid cells and focal clear-cell change. This is supported by the clinical pattern of a slow-growing, painless, well-circumscribed lip mass and by the histology showing a circumscribed/encapsulated salivary neoplasm composed of myoepithelial-type cells in multiple forms rather than an infiltrative destructive lesion. The absence of malignant cytology or invasion argues strongly against myoepithelial carcinoma.

Pleomorphic adenoma is less likely because myoepithelioma is more purely myoepithelial and lacks the characteristic chondromyxoid/fibromyxoid stromal component; occasional limited ductal structures do not necessarily exclude myoepithelioma if they are sparse. Basal cell adenoma is less favored because it more typically shows a basaloid, duct-forming architecture rather than this broad myoepithelial spectrum. Clear cells alone do not make the lesion malignant if invasion, necrosis, marked atypia, and brisk mitoses are absent.

Management is complete local excision with histologically clear margins; if the excisional biopsy already achieved this, no additional radical surgery, neck treatment, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy is indicated. Routine imaging, FNA, molecular testing, or immunohistochemistry is not mandatory after a small superficial lesion has been excised and routine histology is convincing. Those tests would be reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, margin concern, unexpected deep extension, or features raising suspicion for carcinoma.

Prognosis is generally favorable, but the patient still needs follow-up because local recurrence is possible and rare malignant transformation has been described. I would advise periodic long-term clinical review of the upper lip/surgical site, especially during the first few years, with re-evaluation if any new swelling, firmness, or rapid change appears.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated features such as painless swelling or one cell type, but does not integrate circumscription, mixed myoepithelial morphology, and lack of invasion into a coherent argument.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the slow-growing upper-lip presentation with the circumscribed histology and mixed spindle/plasmacytoid/clear-cell morphology to support a benign myoepithelial salivary tumor.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a clear, logically sequenced interpretation from both clinical and figure-based findings, correctly emphasizing why the lack of invasion/malignant features limits the need for further staging or aggressive therapy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differential diagnosis or relies on irrelevant alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a plausible alternative such as pleomorphic adenoma or carcinoma but gives little or incorrect reasoning for exclusion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately weighs at least two key alternatives and rules them out using features such as stromal pattern, duct formation, invasion, and cytologic malignancy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows nuanced distinction between myoepithelioma and pleomorphic adenoma, myoepithelial carcinoma, and/or basal cell adenoma, including the point that sparse ducts or focal clear cells do not automatically reclassify the lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as a non-salivary process or as a malignant tumor without support.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign minor salivary gland neoplasm but does not arrive at myoepithelioma or gives an equivocal label without justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the lesion as a benign myoepithelioma of a minor salivary gland.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies benign myoepithelioma and accurately characterizes the mixed myoepithelial morphology seen in this lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management such as observation alone despite a salivary neoplasm, or aggressive oncologic therapy despite benign noninvasive histology.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests excision in general terms but does not address margin adequacy, the limited role of additional tests, or the absence of indication for adjuvant therapy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends complete local excision with clear margins as definitive treatment, with no routine need for radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or extensive additional workup if histology is convincing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan that distinguishes what is needed now versus what would only be indicated if margins were involved, deeper extension suspected, or morphology became equivocal.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Notes follow-up vaguely but does not connect it to recurrence or transformation risk.

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content:
A healthy 10-year-old has a 6-week painless enlarging mass in the right mandibular premolar region with delayed eruption after loss of the primary teeth. No trauma is reported; cervical nodes are normal and labiomental sensation is intact. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.
Before any pathology is available, decide whether this is more likely a superficial soft-tissue lesion secondarily interfering with eruption or a primary intraosseous/tooth-associated process presenting through the mucosa. Commit to one interpretation, justify it with the figures, and state your first operative plan. Your plan must explain how mixed dentition changes the safe extent/depth of surgery and what single new finding would make you abandon that plan and escalate.
Now review fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg. Additional stains: desmin, S100, CD34, beta-catenin, ALK-1/CD246, cytokeratin, and CD163 are negative; Ki67 is about 22%.
Give the single best final diagnosis. Defend it against two spindle-cell mimics you choose: one benign/reactive and one malignant. For each, cite one morphologic or immunophenotypic reason it is less likely here. End with the follow-up message you would give the family regarding recurrence and what would warrant urgent reassessment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is more plausibly a superficial gingival/supracrestal soft-tissue lesion that is secondarily delaying eruption, not a primary central jaw lesion. fig_01.jpg shows a lobulated exophytic sessile mass arising from the crest/gingiva and projecting into the oral cavity, with surface trauma/bleeding from occlusion, which fits a superficial soft-tissue process. fig_02.jpg shows mixed dentition and developing premolars without convincing bone lysis, cortical destruction, or an expansile intraosseous radiolucent lesion driving the presentation. Delayed eruption can therefore be secondary to local soft-tissue occupation rather than proof of an odontogenic or central bony tumor.

The best-supported first operative plan is a conservative excisional biopsy because the lesion is clinically accessible, localized, and appears superficial; this can be both diagnostic and therapeutic in a child while avoiding multiple procedures. The excision should remain tissue-sparing and superficial/supraperiosteal, avoiding ostectomy, deep curettage, or bone trimming that could traumatize the developing premolar follicles/tooth germs. A tightly limited incisional biopsy could be acceptable only if the clinician had substantially higher suspicion for malignancy, but definitive aggressive surgery would still be inappropriate at baseline. A finding that should make me abandon simple local excision and escalate is clear evidence of aggressive deep disease, such as cortical destruction on imaging, new labiomental hypoesthesia, or fixed deep invasion; that would shift management first to cross-sectional imaging and planned biopsy/specialist sarcoma-style workup before deciding surgical extent.

The single best final diagnosis is oral nodular fasciitis (pseudosarcomatous fasciitis). fig_03.jpg shows a spindle-cell/myofibroblastic proliferation arranged in long sweeping/interlacing bundles beneath ulcerated reactive gingival mucosa, with mitotic activity but without the marked pleomorphism or atypical mitotic pattern expected in sarcoma. fig_04.jpg shows diffuse SMA positivity, supporting myofibroblastic differentiation. The negative panel (desmin, S100, CD34, beta-catenin, cytokeratin, CD163) helps exclude muscle, neural, vascular/fibroblastic, epithelial, histiocytic, and fibromatosis-type mimics, and ALK negativity argues against inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Ki67 around 22% and the presence of mitoses indicate proliferation but do not by themselves prove malignancy.

Acceptable benign/reactive mimics include inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor or myofibroma. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is less likely because ALK-1/CD246 is negative. Myofibroma is less favored because the classic biphasic zoning and hemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern are not the dominant features in fig_03.jpg. A key malignant mimic is fibrosarcoma or low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma; that is less likely here because the histology lacks convincing cytologic atypia/marked pleomorphism and the clinical-radiographic picture does not show destructive bony or neurosensory behavior.

Family counseling: this is a benign lesion with very low recurrence risk after conservative excision, so no radical surgery is indicated now. The child should have clinical follow-up for healing and eruption surveillance. Urgent reassessment would be needed if there is rapid regrowth, new pain, persistent bleeding, fixation/deeper expansion, labiomental numbness, new radiographic bone destruction, or ongoing eruption disturbance.

items.question_content: A 63-year-old woman who works outdoors presents with a 1-year, asymptomatic, nonhealing crusted plaque on the left lower vermilion with mild induration and no regional lymphadenopathy. Serology for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C is negative. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend now, and why is it preferable to other reasonable approaches in this patient? Base your answer on the clinical appearance, histology, and immunophenotype, and include the main elements of follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would manage this as localized plasma cell cheilitis with complete local surgical excision of the involved lower-lip lesion and submission of the specimen for full histopathologic review. The diagnosis is supported by the clinical setting of a persistent lower-lip vermilion lesion in an older, chronically sun-exposed patient, plus fig_02.jpg showing a dense band-like infiltrate of mature plasma cells without features of invasive carcinoma, and fig_03.jpg showing CD138-positive plasma cells with both kappa and lambda expression, indicating a polyclonal reactive process rather than a monoclonal plasma-cell neoplasm. That immunophenotype lowers concern for plasmacytoma/lymphoma as the primary process, so routine oncologic treatment is not indicated unless systemic features or monoclonality emerge.

Excision is preferable here because the lesion is localized, persistent, clinically overlaps actinic cheilitis and early squamous cell carcinoma, and medical therapies for plasma cell cheilitis are variably effective with documented persistence or relapse. Excision provides both definitive treatment and complete tissue assessment, avoids prolonged empiric topical or systemic immunosuppressive therapy on a sun-exposed lower lip, and removes a lesion from a site where rare malignant transformation has been reported.

Follow-up should be long-term: early reviews for wound healing, infection, scarring, lip competence, and sensation, then periodic surveillance of the vermilion for recurrence, new ulceration, increasing induration, dysplastic change, or SCC. I would also reinforce strict sun protection and avoidance of local irritants.

items.question_content: A 7-year-old girl has a recurrent, asymptomatic gingival mass in the maxillary left canine-incisor region; an earlier excision 18 months ago had been diagnosed as pyogenic granuloma. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. Based on the clinical appearance, microscopy, and immunostains, what definitive management would you choose now, and how do the findings determine the appropriate treatment intensity and follow-up?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This should be managed as a hobnail hemangioma with Dabska tumor-like (papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma-like) features: a benign/very low-grade superficial lymphatic vascular neoplasm that still merits complete local control. My definitive treatment would be complete local excision of the lesion with adequate margins, or re-excision if margins are uncertain, while preserving adjacent developing teeth and periodontal tissues as much as possible. Because the lesion has already recurred after a prior limited procedure and was previously misclassified, I would also request review of the prior specimen and ensure the current specimen is adequately sampled and margin-assessed by oral pathology.

The reason not to escalate to sarcoma-type therapy is the clinicopathologic pattern: the figures show superficial dilated irregular vascular channels with hobnail/plump endothelial cells and intraluminal papillary tufts with fibrous/hyaline cores. CD31 and ERG confirm endothelial differentiation, D2-40 supports lymphatic phenotype, and low MIB argues against a high-grade malignant vascular tumor. There is no convincing marked atypia, brisk mitotic activity, or destructive deep invasion to justify angiosarcoma-type management. Pyogenic granuloma is also less favored because the lesion lacks the classic lobular capillary architecture.

Follow-up should be more careful than for an ordinary reactive gingival overgrowth because of prior recurrence and the Dabska-like component: regular clinical review for at least 2 years, with earlier reassessment for any bleeding, color change, or regrowth. Imaging is not routine for every benign gingival vascular lesion, but if examination suggests deeper extension or if recurrence occurs again, targeted imaging would be reasonable. The key is to avoid both undertreatment and unnecessary radical surgery.

items.question_content: A 48-year-old woman receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV (CD4 357) has a 5-month enlarging painful pigmented lesion of the anterior maxillary labial mucosa/vestibule with ipsilateral palpable submandibular nodes. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, fig_06.jpg, and fig_07.jpg; only an incisional biopsy is available. What is the single best pathologic diagnosis, what is the most important competing interpretation you must exclude, and which specific morphologic and IHC findings from the figures decide between them? Based on that diagnosis, should the multidisciplinary team initially plan this case more as melanoma or as conventional SCC, and why? Then give the first 3 management priorities before any definitive dental procedure, explicitly addressing the palpable node and the friable bleeding lesion. Finally, explain how your interpretation would change if the pigmented cells were AE1/3-positive but S100/HMB45-negative.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best diagnosis is a combined malignant tumor composed of oral malignant melanoma and invasive squamous cell carcinoma, i.e., a combined/collision or squamomelanocytic-type lesion, rather than melanoma alone.

The key competing interpretation to exclude is pigmented squamous cell carcinoma (including SCC colonized by melanocytes). The decisive evidence is biphasic. Morphology in fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg shows invasive squamous epithelial islands with keratin pearl formation, consistent with SCC. fig_04.jpg shows numerous atypical melanocytes in the connective tissue, scattered in a cord-like pattern and of variable size and shape, supporting a true malignant melanocytic component rather than incidental pigmentation. IHC confirms two distinct malignant populations: AE1/3 positivity in infiltrating squamous cells and keratin pearls in fig_06.jpg, and diffuse S100 and HMB45 positivity in atypical melanocytes in fig_05.jpg and fig_07.jpg. In pigmented SCC, the neoplastic cells would be cytokeratin-positive without a true HMB45/S100-positive malignant melanocytic population.

At the MDT stage, this should be planned primarily along melanoma principles while recognizing the concurrent invasive SCC. The reason is that the prognosis of this rare combined tumor is uncertain, the melanocytic component carries major metastatic concern, and available guidance is to treat/measure such lesions as malignant melanoma. Incisional biopsy establishes the diagnosis but does not fully stage the lesion.

The first 3 priorities before any definitive dental procedure are: (1) urgent referral to a head-and-neck oncology MDT for staging of local, regional, and distant disease; (2) formal assessment of the palpable submandibular node as possible metastatic disease, typically with imaging-guided nodal workup and tissue sampling such as FNA/core as appropriate; and (3) management of the friable bleeding oral mass with supportive hemostatic measures and prompt surgical planning for oncologic resection if operable, with careful margin assessment and detailed examination of the excision specimen. HIV with CD4 357 does not reduce the cancer urgency, though medical coordination is appropriate.

If the pigmented cells were AE1/3-positive but S100/HMB45-negative, the interpretation would shift away from a combined melanoma-SCC lesion and toward pigmented SCC or SCC with melanocytic colonization, because a separate malignant melanocytic component would no longer be demonstrated.

items.question_content: A 75-year-old woman taking amlodipine for long-standing hypertension presents with a painless, slowly enlarging sessile mass in the maxillary interdental papilla between 22 and 23. The adjacent teeth are vital, firm, noncarious, and periodontally sound; oral hygiene is poor with generalized bleeding on probing, and no regional lymph nodes are palpable. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend for this lesion, and why? Justify your plan by identifying the diagnosis most supported by the combined findings, explaining why the main competing diagnoses are less likely, and stating the follow-up intensity warranted by its biologic behavior.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The lesion is most consistent with a non-odontogenic soft tissue fibromyxoma of the gingiva. The strongest synthesis is the slow painless localized enlargement, the fact that 22 and 23 are vital and clinically sound, fig_02.jpg showing no periapical or intraosseous involvement, and fig_03.jpg/fig_04.jpg showing fibrous tissue admixed with abundant myxoid stroma that is Alcian blue positive, supporting a mucopolysaccharide-rich myxomatous lesion rather than a purely reactive vascular overgrowth. Amlodipine-related gingival enlargement is less likely because that is typically more generalized, not a solitary papillary mass. Pyogenic granuloma is a reasonable provisional diagnosis clinically, but it is less convincing after histology because the lesion shows fibromyxoid/myxoid stroma rather than predominantly granulation tissue with a lobular capillary pattern. Central or odontogenic myxoma is weakened by the absence of bone involvement on fig_02.jpg. Definitive management is complete local excision of the soft tissue lesion with submission for histopathologic confirmation, ideally including a small cuff of adjacent normal tissue to reduce incomplete removal; the adjacent teeth and supporting bone should be preserved. Initial plaque control is appropriate to reduce inflammatory confounding and improve healing. Laser excision is reasonable in an elderly hypertensive patient because of hemostasis and postoperative comfort, but the key principle is complete removal and diagnosis, not the instrument itself. Prognosis is generally favorable after complete excision, but recurrence is possible if removal is incomplete, so periodic clinical follow-up beyond early healing is warranted, with re-evaluation or further imaging/referral if the lesion recurs or any bone change appears.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A 68-year-old man has had 3 months of painful swelling in the right posterior maxilla. fig_01.jpg shows the intraoral mass. CT of the paranasal sinuses reports a destructive lesion arising from the right maxillary sinus with local extension and bony erosion. Biopsy with immunostains is shown in fig_02.jpg. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, and what definitive management strategy would you recommend now? Explain why the local treatment should be as extensive or conservative as you think appropriate, whether neck treatment is indicated at presentation, and which case features most influence prognosis and surveillance.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma arising in the right maxillary sinus with oral extension. The key reasoning is a malignant, locally destructive sinus mass plus fig_02.jpg showing a biphasic salivary-type tumor: duct-like luminal cells and an abluminal clear/spindle myoepithelial layer, with myoepithelial markers such as p63 and alpha smooth muscle actin and S100 positivity supporting dual differentiation. This pattern is more consistent with EMC than pleomorphic adenoma, myoepithelial carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, or a clear-cell mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

Definitive care should be oncologic resection with negative margins, at a maxillectomy-level extent determined by the full local spread, rather than limited intraoral excision, because the lesion originates in the maxillary sinus and already shows bone erosion and local extension. Management should be coordinated in a head-and-neck team with pathologic review and planning for reconstruction or obturator rehabilitation. Neck dissection is not routine at presentation unless there is clinical or radiologic nodal disease, because EMC has a relatively low rate of nodal metastasis; the main priority is local control. Adjuvant radiotherapy should be considered if margins are close or positive or if other adverse features are found on the resection specimen.

Prognosis is driven more by local behavior than by nodal spread. Adverse features here include bone-destructive local extension plus necrosis and mitotic activity on histology; final margin status and any perineural or lymphovascular invasion would further affect risk. Long-term follow-up with clinical and imaging surveillance is important because local or regional recurrence can occur even in a generally low-grade tumor.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A 57-year-old man has a 3-year, minimally symptomatic ulcero-proliferative mass in the floor of mouth. Incisional biopsy H&E and immunostains are shown in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg; additional epithelial markers are negative. Based on these findings, what is the most defensible integrated diagnosis, and what immediate management pathway would you recommend before and after definitive local treatment? Justify your answer from the morphologic and immunophenotypic clues visible.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best integrated diagnosis is a malignant granular cell tumor of non-neuronal origin (an S100-negative/non-neural granular cell tumor) in the floor of mouth. fig_01.jpg supports a malignant granular cell neoplasm because it shows sheets of polygonal cells with abundant granular cytoplasm together with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, pleomorphism, spindle-cell change, necrosis, and mitotic activity—features consistent with malignant behavior rather than a routine benign granular cell tumor. fig_02.jpg shows vimentin, NSE, and CD10 positivity with S100 negativity, favoring non-neural granular cell differentiation rather than the conventional Schwannian granular cell tumor; the stated negative epithelial markers make an ulcerated squamous carcinoma mimic less likely.

Management should proceed as for a malignant head-and-neck soft-tissue tumor: urgent referral to a head-and-neck oncology/multidisciplinary team, staging to define local extent, nodal status, and distant spread, then complete surgical excision with clear margins if resectable. Final pathology should guide whether adjuvant radiotherapy and/or systemic therapy is considered, especially for high-risk, recurrent, unresectable, nodal, or metastatic disease, recognizing the rarity of this lesion and limited evidence base. The patient should be counseled that prognosis is guarded compared with benign granular cell tumor because malignant granular cell tumors can recur and metastasize, so long-term close surveillance is required.

items.question_content: A 55-year-old man who smokes half a pack per day has had asymptomatic white papules on the upper and lower lips for several years, without pain, itching, or constitutional symptoms. Biopsies were taken from lesions on both lips. Using fig_02.jpg_clinical and fig_02.jpg_histopathology, provide the most likely clinicopathologic diagnosis and justify it from both figures. In your reasoning, discuss at least one plausible alternative diagnosis and the most important dysplastic or malignant process to exclude in this smoker. Then outline appropriate management and follow-up for the current lesions, including the specific later changes that should prompt repeat biopsy or urgent referral.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely clinicopathologic diagnosis is glycogenic acanthosis involving the lips/vermilion, a benign lesion.

Justification: The clinical figure shows multiple discrete white papules on both the upper and lower lips, including the wet-dry vermilion border and mucosal lip, with a chronic asymptomatic course. The histopathology shows acanthotic squamous epithelium with hyperkeratosis and enlarged pale-clear keratinocytes. PAS positivity with diastase sensitivity indicates intracytoplasmic glycogen. The biopsies do not show epithelial dysplasia or invasion. Together, the multifocal white papules plus glycogen-rich, non-dysplastic squamous epithelium support glycogenic acanthosis.

A plausible alternative diagnosis is verruca, lichen planus, leukoplakia/keratinizing dysplasia, or another white papular keratotic lesion, but these are less consistent with the biopsy findings. The most important process to exclude in this smoker is epithelial dysplasia or early squamous cell carcinoma. That concern is reduced here because biopsies from upper and lower lip lesions show no dysplasia or invasion.

Management should be conservative: reassure the patient that the biopsied lesions are benign, document baseline appearance, and review periodically. Treatment is usually unnecessary unless lesions become symptomatic or the patient desires treatment for cosmetic reasons. Smoking-cessation counseling is appropriate.

Repeat biopsy or urgent referral is warranted if a lesion later shows rapid enlargement, induration, ulceration, bleeding, pain, fixation, persistent crusting, marked change in color or surface texture, or if a new dominant lesion appears that does not match the previously biopsied pattern.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: An 18-year-old man has a 1-year painless swelling in the anterior mandible, a retained deciduous mandibular right canine, and a clinically missing permanent mandibular right canine. fig_01.jpg shows the preoperative orthopantogram, and fig_02.jpg shows the histopathology after enucleation of the lesion with removal of the impacted tooth. Based on the clinical setting and the features visible in the figures, identify the lesion and describe the key radiographic and microscopic findings that support the diagnosis. What is the clinical significance of finding focal epithelial dysplasia in the cyst lining, and what broad follow-up implication does this suggest?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The lesion is a parakeratinized odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) associated with an impacted mandibular right canine, with focal epithelial dysplasia in the lining.

Radiographically, fig_01.jpg shows a well-defined unilocular radiolucency with corticated border in the anterior mandible, extending around the region of the impacted canine. This supports an odontogenic cystic lesion.

Microscopically, fig_02.jpg shows features typical of OKC: a thin parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelial lining, surface corrugation, a palisaded hyperchromatic basal layer, and a flat epithelial-connective tissue interface. Additional findings visible in the sections include basal budding and daughter cysts. Focal dysplastic change is supported by loss of basal cell polarity, cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, nuclear hyperchromatism, altered nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, dyskeratosis, and suprabasal mitotic activity.

The dysplastic lining does not by itself establish malignant transformation, but it is an unusual finding in OKC and is clinically important because it may indicate potential for altered biologic behavior, including concern for recurrence or possible malignant change. Therefore, the main management implication supported by this case is the need for close periodic follow-up after treatment rather than routine discharge.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify the lesion as odontogenic keratocyst or gives a diagnosis inconsistent with the radiographic and histologic findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the lesion as parakeratinized odontogenic keratocyst with focal epithelial dysplasia in the lining.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides little or no accurate support from the figures, or cites features that do not fit the lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Describes the essential supporting features: a well-defined unilocular corticated radiolucency associated with the impacted canine, and typical OKC histology such as thin parakeratinized lining, surface corrugation, palisaded hyperchromatic basal cells, and flat interface.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets dysplasia as definite carcinoma, or ignores its significance entirely.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States the broad implication of close periodic follow-up after treatment because of OKC behavior and the presence of dysplasia, without overclaiming specific re-interventions or prognosis.

items.question_content: A 6-year-old girl presents with a soft, darker swelling of the left posterior maxilla extending buccally and palatally. An incisional biopsy was performed. Examine fig_01.jpg. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what definitive management pathway would you recommend now? Justify your plan using the histologic and immunohistochemical pattern visible in fig_01.jpg, and explain the main factors that shape prognosis and follow-up in this child.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is synovial sarcoma of the maxilla, specifically a monophasic spindle-cell type. fig_01.jpg shows a malignant spindle-cell proliferation with brisk mitotic activity and a high Ki67 proliferative index (~40%). The immunoprofile supports synovial sarcoma: TLE1, Bcl-2, and vimentin are positive, while myogenic, neural, vascular, and epithelial-associated markers shown here are negative (myogenin, SMA, SOX10, CD34, EMA), making rhabdomyosarcoma, smooth-muscle tumors, neural-sheath tumors, and solitary fibrous/other spindle-cell lesions less likely. This requires urgent multidisciplinary sarcoma management, not local dental excision. The next steps are oncologic staging of the primary site and metastatic workup, then complete surgical resection with histologically negative margins as feasible. Because maxillary/head-and-neck anatomy often limits wide margins, adjuvant radiotherapy is reasonable to improve local control when margins are close or other high-risk features are present. Care should involve maxillofacial surgery, pediatric oncology, radiation oncology, pathology, and later prosthetic/reconstructive support. Prognosis is influenced by local control, difficulty achieving clear margins in the maxilla, and the high proliferative index; recurrence and distant metastasis remain concerns, so long-term clinical and imaging surveillance beyond 1 year is essential, along with monitoring growth, dentofacial development, and late radiation effects.

levels.title: Partial

items.question_content: A 64-year-old man presents with right parotid swelling and facial palsy. MRI shows a locally invasive parotid mass with suspected soft-tissue and mandibular infiltration. On resection, fig_01.jpg shows an atypical biphasic basaloid salivary carcinoma with partial duct formation; Ki-67 is about 70%. Immunophenotype: CK AE1/AE3, CK7, p40, DOG1, and p63 positive; S-100, alpha-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, androgen receptor, HER2, CD56, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and beta-catenin negative. Based on fig_01.jpg and these data, what is your most defensible final diagnostic approach? State your favored diagnosis, the single ancillary molecular test you would prioritize before final sign-out, how a positive versus negative result would shift your differential, and the implications for prognosis and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: My favored diagnosis is epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (EMC), most likely a high-grade EMC or EMC with high-grade transformation, rather than a conventional low-grade biphasic salivary tumor. The key reasoning is the biphasic architecture in fig_01.jpg with duct formation plus abluminal/basal-type marker expression, but with distinctly aggressive features: facial palsy, radiologic invasion, marked atypia, and a very high Ki-67. The single ancillary molecular test I would prioritize is HRAS mutation analysis, especially codon 61. In this setting, a codon 61 HRAS mutation would strongly support EMC and make EMC-spectrum carcinoma the most defensible final diagnosis, while still recognizing that HRAS is supportive rather than absolutely specific in all salivary carcinomas. A negative HRAS result would not completely exclude EMC, but it would substantially weaken that diagnosis and push me to re-weigh other biphasic/basaloid salivary carcinomas using morphology and targeted ancillary studies guided by the leading mimic. Prognostically, this should be considered high risk despite EMC often being low grade: the facial nerve dysfunction, locally invasive behavior, marked atypia, and Ki-67 around 70% imply increased risk of recurrence and possible metastasis. Follow-up should therefore be close and long term, with multidisciplinary head-and-neck surveillance and interval imaging rather than minimal follow-up appropriate for a typical low-grade EMC.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. Besides the MIH-type opacities, what developmental defect term best classifies the maxillary incisor/canine enamel changes?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The maxillary anterior teeth show a reduced enamel thickness with groove-like defects and a smooth transition to normal enamel. That pattern is hypoplasia, and because the defects are groove-like, the most specific term is linear enamel hypoplasia rather than demarcated opacity.

items.answer_explanation: The maxillary anterior teeth show a reduced enamel thickness with groove-like defects and a smooth transition to normal enamel. That pattern is hypoplasia, and because the defects are groove-like, the most specific term is linear enamel hypoplasia rather than demarcated opacity.

items.question_content:
A 61-year-old woman presents with burning and swelling of the right cheek and a mobile buccal submucosal nodule. No cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic abnormalities are reported. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. You are the pathologist, and the requisition says only: "right buccal soft-tissue mass." The surgeon wants to know whether today’s pathology should trigger wider oncologic work-up/referral or be managed as a localized reactive process.

State the single sign-out category you would use now and draft 2–3 sentences of report wording. Defend that threshold by integrating one imaging clue from fig_01.jpg and two separate histologic/immunologic clues from fig_02.jpg–fig_04.jpg that pull in different diagnostic directions. Name the most consequential alternative diagnosis you still must account for, and explain exactly what feature keeps you from overcalling it. Finally, identify the one missing history item that would most change your confidence, and explain how your recommendation would differ if that history remained unavailable versus if it were later confirmed.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Most defensible sign-out category now: a descriptive diagnosis favoring foreign-body granulomatous inflammation/exogenous material reaction, not an immediate oncologic sign-out and not yet a fully specific named hyaluronic-acid diagnosis without corroborating history.

Example report wording:
"Right buccal soft-tissue mass, excision: Granulomatous inflammation with extracellular myxoid/Alcian blue-positive material, associated CD68-positive epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophil-rich chronic inflammation. Findings favor a foreign-material reaction; no definitive salivary epithelial neoplasm is identified in the examined sections. Correlation with prior cosmetic/procedural history is recommended before assigning a specific etiology."

Why this threshold is appropriate:
- fig_01.jpg supports a reactive soft-tissue process rather than immediate salivary-oncologic escalation because the lesion is in the buccal subcutaneous/muscular plane with surrounding inflammatory change and is not clearly centered in accessory parotid or a discrete minor salivary gland mass.
- fig_03.jpg provides the major tumor-mimicking clue: pseudoduct/pool-like mucinous spaces, which in this location could suggest a mucin-producing salivary neoplasm. However, the same figure also shows the stronger anti-neoplastic clue: the material is being surrounded and phagocytosed by CD68-positive epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells rather than forming bona fide epithelial-lined glands.
- fig_02.jpg further lowers concern for a gland-origin carcinoma because the process engulfs adjacent minor salivary gland and muscle instead of showing a convincing gland-centered epithelial proliferation.
- fig_04.jpg adds a dense eosinophil-rich, degranulating inflammatory reaction with peripheral T-cell infiltrates, which fits a foreign-body/delayed hypersensitivity-type reaction better than a low-grade salivary carcinoma.

Most consequential alternative diagnosis:
A mucin-producing minor salivary gland carcinoma, especially low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma (with accessory parotid/minor salivary origin as the clinically important anatomic concern).

What keeps this from being overcalled:
The apparent pseudoducts/mucin pools are not convincing true epithelial tumor structures. Alcian blue positivity alone is not specific, because both tumor mucin and hyaluronic-acid-related material can stain. The decisive restraint is the foreign-body pattern: macrophage uptake of the material, CD68-positive giant-cell/epithelioid cuffing, and eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation rather than an unequivocal epithelial neoplasm.

Single missing history item most likely to change confidence:
Targeted history of prior cheek cosmetic filler or other injected/implanted material, including timing, laterality, and if known the substance used.

If that history remains unavailable:
Keep the report descriptive and favor reactive/foreign-material etiology; do not recommend wider oncologic surgery solely on current morphology. Advise clinicoradiologic correlation and, if there is persistent discordance or a new discrete mass, additional workup such as deeper levels and epithelial-focused stains/re-review before a definitive benign dismissal.

If that history is later confirmed:
The diagnosis can be made more specifically as delayed foreign-body granuloma associated with hyaluronic-acid filler, with eosinophil-rich histiocytic/giant-cell inflammation. In that setting, localized follow-up is appropriate, and wider salivary-oncologic referral is unnecessary unless subsequent material shows a separate true epithelial salivary neoplasm.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. What impression technique is being demonstrated?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The figures show a preliminary impression first, then fabrication of a custom tray, followed by the definitive putty impression on that tray. That sequence defines a two-step impression technique, which is favored here because it reduces intraoral material volume and improves safety and control in a neonate.

items.answer_explanation: The figures show a preliminary impression first, then fabrication of a custom tray, followed by the definitive putty impression on that tray. That sequence defines a two-step impression technique, which is favored here because it reduces intraoral material volume and improves safety and control in a neonate.

items.question_content: A 3-year-old boy has a painful carious triple primary incisor in the maxilla, with poor cooperation for treatment. The periapical radiograph shows an apical radiolucency around the enlarged central component, and micro-CT later shows two pulp chambers in that component joining cervically, with the lateral component having a separate chamber/canal that communicates with the central canal. Which findings best explain why observation, sealing alone, or selective pulp therapy would be unreliable for retaining this tooth? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: fig_02.jpg shows periapical radiolucency at the enlarged central component, so preventive measures alone would not address established endodontic infection.
fig_03.jpg shows that the enlarged central portion contained two pulp chambers joining at the cervical area, rather than a simple isolated chamber pattern.

fig_03.jpg shows that the lateral component had a separate pulp chamber and root canal, but its root canal was connected to the enlarged central component’s root canal, making segmented treatment less straightforward.
The child’s age and poor cooperation reduced feasibility of technically demanding multistep endodontic treatment.
fig_03.jpg shows communication between the lateral component’s root canal and the enlarged central component’s root canal, weakening the logic of treating only the visibly more affected part.
The gingival laceration alone would have mandated extraction even if the triplication had been caries-free and noninfected.
Because developmental grooves were present, extraction would have been mandatory even without pulpal disease.
The absence of mobility after trauma made delayed review preferable to active treatment.
On fig_02.jpg, the pulp chamber of the enlarged central portion is not clearly defined because of the carious lesion, further reducing the predictability of pulp therapy.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Established apical infection, unclear radiographic anatomy, later-confirmed cervical joining of chambers, communication between canals, and poor cooperation all make conservative or segmental pulp therapy unreliable. Developmental grooves alone, lack of mobility, or gingival laceration alone are not decisive indications for extraction.

items.answer_explanation: Established apical infection, unclear radiographic anatomy, later-confirmed cervical joining of chambers, communication between canals, and poor cooperation all make conservative or segmental pulp therapy unreliable. Developmental grooves alone, lack of mobility, or gingival laceration alone are not decisive indications for extraction.

items.question_content: A 23-year-old man has a 2-week history of a slowly enlarging painless dark red-violaceous exophytic mass on the ventral/lateral tongue causing speech and swallowing difficulty. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show the clinical lesion, histology, and immunostains; HHV-8 is negative and routine infectious screening is unrevealing. What diagnosis best fits these findings, and what management would you recommend if the lesion is localized and surgically accessible? Briefly justify the plan from the clinicopathologic clues and state the main follow-up concern.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best diagnosis is oral hemangiolymphangioma, a mixed blood- and lymphatic-vessel malformation. The dark red-violaceous tongue lesion plus dilated vascular spaces containing erythrocytes and proteinaceous material beneath acanthotic/papillomatous epithelium, together with the mixed immunoprofile (CD34 positive, focal D2-40, some α-SMA) and HHV-8 negativity, support this diagnosis and argue against Kaposi sarcoma or an infectious mimic. If the lesion is localized and can be removed without major functional loss, the preferred management is complete/minimally invasive surgical excision after clinicopathologic confirmation, with follow-up focused on recurrence and recovery/preservation of speech and swallowing.

levels.title: Incorrect or absent
levels.description: Does not identify the lesion as oral hemangiolymphangioma or gives an unrelated diagnosis.

levels.title: Partially correct
levels.description: Identifies a vascular lesion but is nonspecific, incomplete, or confuses hemangiolymphangioma with a different entity.

levels.title: Correct
levels.description: Correctly identifies oral hemangiolymphangioma (or equivalent mixed hemangiolymphangioma/lymphangiohemangioma terminology).

levels.title: Minimal integration

levels.title: Basic integration
levels.description: Uses some clinical or pathologic findings, but does not connect the morphology with the immunoprofile and negative workup.

levels.title: Strong integration
levels.description: Integrates the tongue lesion appearance, histology, mixed endothelial/lymphatic markers, and HHV-8 negativity into a coherent clinicopathologic diagnosis.

levels.title: Inappropriate or absent plan
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate intervention, no plan, or ignores the need for definitive management in a localized accessible lesion.

levels.title: Reasonable but incomplete
levels.description: Suggests surgery or observation in vague terms without clearly stating localized excision as the preferred approach when feasible.

levels.title: Appropriate plan
levels.description: Recommends complete or minimally invasive surgical excision after clinicopathologic confirmation when the lesion is localized and surgically accessible.

levels.title: No meaningful risk-benefit reasoning
levels.description: Does not address functional risk, morbidity, or recurrence considerations.

levels.title: Partial risk-benefit reasoning
levels.description: Mentions excision but gives limited or generic rationale for why it is suitable in this patient.

levels.title: Balanced risk-benefit reasoning
levels.description: Explicitly weighs symptom relief and local control against tongue morbidity, preserving speech and swallowing, and the need for recurrence surveillance.

levels.title: Opaque reasoning
levels.description: Provides a conclusion without explaining how the findings support it.

levels.title: Some reasoning
levels.description: Gives a partial explanation, but the chain from findings to diagnosis and management is incomplete or disorganized.

levels.title: Clear reasoning
levels.description: Explains the diagnosis and management logically from the clinical appearance, histology, immunostains, and lesion accessibility.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommending extraction or other irreversible therapy without first establishing the correct clinicopathologic diagnosis is inappropriate for a localized tongue vascular lesion.
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Assigning a definitive diagnosis without accounting for the histology, immunostains, and HHV-8 negativity would be premature.
Misattributed Etiology: Attributing the lesion to an infectious process or Kaposi sarcoma despite unrevealing screening and HHV-8 negativity would misread the cause.

items.question_content: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for an incidental, painless right mandibular mass near the lower molars. Serum calcium, phosphorus, and PTH are normal. fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg are provided. Based on the clinical picture plus the images, what is the most likely diagnosis? Which findings are supportive versus mainly exclusionary against close mimics? If you had to choose between observation, limited excision/curettage, and wider resection, what would you recommend now, and why? Finally, if PTH were elevated, which diagnosis would move to the top of the differential and how would management change?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is mandibular non-ossifying fibroma (NOF). The key morphologic findings are the bland whorled/spindle-cell lesion with foam cells and scant multinucleated giant cells and no bone formation; the mandibular osteolytic lesion on fig_01.jpg supports this clinicopathologic impression. SATB2 and ER positivity are supportive but not diagnostic on their own. Negative USP6 rearrangement is mainly exclusionary, arguing against primary aneurysmal bone cyst. If H3.3G34W negativity is considered, that also helps exclude giant cell tumor of bone. The main mimics to keep in the differential are brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism, giant cell tumor of bone, aneurysmal bone cyst, and central giant cell lesion/granuloma. For this child, limited excision/curettage or diagnostic local removal with follow-up is more appropriate than observation alone or wider resection, because the lesion is benign but the mandibular site is rare enough that tissue confirmation is reasonable. If PTH were elevated, brown tumor would move to the top of the differential, and the first step would be endocrine evaluation and treatment of hyperparathyroidism before lesion-directed surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives an incorrect diagnosis or no clear diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a broad benign spindle-cell or giant-cell mandibular lesion but not mandibular non-ossifying fibroma.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies mandibular non-ossifying fibroma as the most likely diagnosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies mandibular non-ossifying fibroma and notes that the gnathic location is rare enough that tissue confirmation/local diagnosis is reasonable.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A 28-year-old woman has a recurrent, painless, mobile swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at level II; a similar swelling at the same site was removed 10 years ago without histopathology. FNAC yielded thick mucoid material. Examining fig_01.jpg and the smear in fig_02.jpg, what is the most likely nature and origin of this lesion, and what definitive management would you recommend now? Justify your plan from the site, recurrence history, and cytologic pattern, and explain how you would distinguish it from the main alternative causes of a lateral neck mass.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most likely a recurrent pleomorphic adenoma arising in heterotopic salivary gland tissue in the upper lateral neck. The key reasoning is the combination of an unusually placed but well-circumscribed level II mass on fig_01.jpg, prior excision at the same site, and fig_02.jpg showing a classic biphasic salivary neoplasm: bland epithelial cells with myoepithelial cells in abundant chondromyxoid/myxoid stroma. That pattern is much more consistent with pleomorphic adenoma than with reactive lymphadenopathy, keloid, or a simple cystic lesion.

Important alternatives for a lateral neck mass would include lymphadenopathy, branchial cleft cyst or other cystic lesions, scar/keloid from prior surgery, metastatic/cystic nodal disease, and other salivary tumors. These are less likely because the aspirate/cytology is salivary-type rather than inflammatory, keratinous, or overtly malignant, and the lesion is recurrent but still clinically bland and mobile.

Definitive management should be complete surgical excision as a salivary gland neoplasm, ideally en bloc with the capsule intact and a cuff of surrounding dispensable soft tissue to obtain clear margins. It should not be managed as simple lymphadenitis, drained, or treated by limited scar revision/enucleation alone, because incomplete removal and capsular rupture increase recurrence. The entire specimen must undergo histopathologic examination to confirm pleomorphic adenoma and exclude carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma or another salivary neoplasm. Because this is a recurrence after a prior uncharacterized excision, she needs counseling about higher recurrence risk and long-term follow-up for regrowth or malignant transformation. Neck dissection or adjuvant therapy is not indicated unless final pathology or clinical findings suggest malignancy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figure/stem data coherently; ignores either the unusual level II location, the recurrence history, or the salivary-type cytology, leading to an unsupported conclusion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign neck lesion or salivary lesion but integrates only limited evidence; may mention pleomorphic adenoma without linking it convincingly to heterotopic salivary tissue or recurrence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly synthesizes the lateral neck location, prior same-site excision, and biphasic chondromyxoid FNAC pattern to support pleomorphic adenoma in heterotopic salivary tissue.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains why the upper lateral neck along the SCM is compatible with heterotopic salivary rests and why prior surgery without histology strengthens concern for recurrent pleomorphic adenoma rather than a routine nodal or scar process.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that complete excision offers diagnosis and durable control, while incomplete excision/capsular rupture increases recurrence; notes need for long-term follow-up and awareness of malignant transformation.

levels.title: Exceeds
