golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is solitary circumscribed neuroma (palisaded encapsulated neuroma) of the upper-lip vermillion. At first presentation, the best management is conservative excisional biopsy/local excision rather than surveillance alone, because this is a persistent adult-onset papule with prior interval growth, bland but nonspecific clinical appearance, and a very small size that makes removal low morbidity while providing definitive diagnosis and treatment. It is appropriate but not an emergency.

The single most diagnostically weighty feature is the low-power architecture in fig_02.jpg panel A: a well-circumscribed benign spindle-cell fascicular proliferation with focal palisading in a loose collagenous stroma, bounded by a thin incomplete fibrous capsule/perineurial delimitation and lacking atypia or significant mitotic activity. That pattern is more decisive than the immunostain. If fig_02.jpg panel B were unavailable, I could still strongly defend solitary circumscribed neuroma on architecture alone. fig_02.jpg panel B is supportive because diffuse S100 positivity confirms Schwannian/neural differentiation, but it is not specific enough by itself to establish this exact entity.

The two closest alternatives to exclude are other benign neural spindle-cell lesions, especially schwannoma and neurofibroma (mucosal neuroma is also acceptable if well argued). Schwannoma is less favored because the figures do not show the classic Antoni A/Antoni B pattern or Verocay bodies expected in schwannoma, despite both lesions being S100-positive. Neurofibroma is less favored because it is usually more poorly circumscribed and unencapsulated, with a more haphazard/myxoid background rather than this neatly circumscribed fascicular lesion with focal palisading. If mucosal neuroma is raised, the argument against it is the solitary, small, circumscribed presentation without the typical broader syndromic context or the appearance of multiple enlarged nerve bundles.

The fig_01.jpg clue most likely to be site-related rather than tumor-specific is the superficial fingerprint-like pigmentation over the papule. On the vermillion, especially in skin of color, native physiologic pigmentation can be distorted by a raised subepithelial lesion, so this pattern should not be over-read as intrinsic tumor pigmentation. Over-interpreting it could misclassify the lesion as a pigmented surface process. It may also obscure or alter appreciation of vascular structures, so the absence of arborizing/telangiectatic vessels here does not exclude a lesion that may show vessels more readily on cutaneous skin.

No routine further systemic or syndromic evaluation is indicated after local treatment of a solitary circumscribed neuroma. Broader work-up would become appropriate if the presentation changed to multiple mucosal neuroma-like lesions or if associated syndromic features emerged, such as marfanoid habitus or findings concerning for MEN2B-related disease (for example, medullary thyroid carcinoma or pheochromocytoma), because that would suggest a generalized mucosal neuroma syndrome rather than an isolated sporadic lesion.

levels.title: Fails

Correctly treats fig_02.jpg panel B as supportive but not specific and indicates that the diagnosis can still be defended without it.

Acceptable reasoning includes, for example, absence of Antoni A/B areas or Verocay bodies against schwannoma, poorer circumscription/unencapsulated more myxoid architecture against neurofibroma, or multiplicity/syndromic context and nerve-bundle pattern against mucosal neuroma. Strongly justified non-neural alternatives are acceptable if the histology is used to rule them out.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Correctly states that routine broader work-up is not needed now, or identifies a possible trigger for expanded evaluation, but does so vaguely or without linking it to a specific syndrome-oriented concern.

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: A 6-year-old girl has a slowly enlarging dome-shaped nodule at the upper-lip commissure that was excised after 6 months. Review fig_01.jpg (clinical), fig_02.jpg (H&E), and fig_03.jpg, which includes CK, SOX10, synaptophysin, ERG-1, and MIB-1/Ki67 immunostains. Based on the clinicopathologic findings and these stains, what is your final diagnosis/sign-out, and what immediate management advice would you give the treating dentist? Margin status is not provided.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best final interpretation is a Spitz-spectrum melanocytic lesion, most appropriately signed out as a benign Spitzoid melanocytic nevus/Spitz nevus rather than squamous cell carcinoma. The H&E appearance is deceptive because pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and invasive-appearing nests can mimic SCC, but the overall clinicopathologic context favors a melanocytic lesion in a young child. The immunoprofile supports this: SOX10 positivity indicates melanocytic lineage; CK negativity argues against epithelial carcinoma; ERG-1 negativity argues against vascular differentiation; synaptophysin negativity argues against a neuroendocrine-type mimic; and weak/low MIB-1(Ki67) labeling supports low proliferative activity rather than an aggressive malignant process. A cautious comment that atypical Spitz-spectrum lesions can overlap histologically is acceptable, but the overall balance here favors a benign Spitzoid melanocytic nevus.

Immediate management advice: do not treat this as SCC and do not recommend oncologic lip resection or other cancer therapy on the basis of these findings. Because the lesion has already been excised and margin status is not provided, advise correlation with the excision report and clinical site to determine completeness of removal. If completely excised and there are no concerning residual clinical changes, conservative follow-up is appropriate, typically with periodic review such as every 3-6 months initially. Re-evaluation, possible re-biopsy, and/or specialist review should be recommended only if there is recurrence, rapid enlargement, ulceration, change in color/shape, or persistent diagnostic uncertainty.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Diagnoses the lesion as SCC, a vascular/neuroendocrine tumor, traumatic fibroma, or another clearly non-melanocytic process.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a melanocytic lesion but gives a vague answer or labels it definite melanoma without adequately rejecting carcinoma.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a Spitz-spectrum melanocytic lesion and rejects SCC, though the distinction between benign Spitz nevus and atypical Spitz lesion is only briefly addressed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly signs out a benign Spitzoid melanocytic nevus/Spitz nevus-spectrum lesion as the best final diagnosis and explicitly explains why SCC and melanoma are less likely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores major clinical, histologic, or immunohistochemical information.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely; for example, mentions age or SOX10 positivity alone without integrating the misleading H&E pattern and the non-supportive stains for other lineages.

Ignoring provided stain context: failing to use the named fig_03.jpg immunostains when justifying the diagnosis

items.question_content: A 25-year-old healthy man is referred after an incidental painless lesion is found in the left posterior mandible. Intraoral exam shows no buccolingual expansion or mucosal change, and teeth 36-38 are vital. Examine the panoramic image in fig_01.jpg and the biopsy photomicrographs in fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg. What diagnosis is most defensible, and what definitive management and surveillance strategy would you choose? Justify your plan by integrating the imaging and histology, and explain the main harms that could follow if this lesion were managed as an ordinary odontogenic radiolucency.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best diagnosis is an intraosseous angiolipofibroma (angio-lipo-fibroma/angiofibrolipomatous benign mesenchymal lesion) of the mandible. fig_01.jpg suggests a circumscribed benign intraosseous process rather than inflammatory endodontic disease: the lesion is incidental, painless, and associated teeth are vital, with no clinical expansion or destructive behavior. The photomicrographs show the key triphasic pattern needed to move beyond a nonspecific radiolucency: mature adipose tissue, numerous capillary-sized vascular channels, and fibrocollagenous stroma. That combination argues against a routine odontogenic cyst, a simple intraosseous lipoma, or a pure vascular lesion.

Management should be conservative complete excision/enucleation with histopathologic confirmation, preserving the vital teeth unless they are directly compromised. A radical resection is not justified by this small, well-defined, nonaggressive presentation. Routine preoperative embolization is also not required from the information shown, because there is no evidence here of a large high-flow vascular lesion; however, the surgery should still be planned with hemostatic readiness because the lesion has a vascular component. In comparable undiagnosed cases, aspiration and biopsy before definitive surgery are important because the radiographic appearance is nonspecific.

Surveillance should include periodic clinical and radiographic follow-up, at minimum around 6-12 months and longer if feasible, to ensure bony healing and detect persistence or recurrence.

If this were treated as an ordinary odontogenic radiolucency, the main harms would be unnecessary endodontic treatment or extraction of vital teeth, failure to anticipate operative bleeding, and possible overtreatment if the lesion were mistaken for a more aggressive tumor.

items.question_content: An 18-year-old woman presents before biopsy with a 1-year history of a painless gingival mass in the mandibular left incisor region that bleeds during brushing. Local plaque/calculus retention is present. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. This lesion does not fit a single textbook pattern cleanly. State the final clinicopathologic label you would use in your report and justify why that label is preferable to reclassifying the lesion as another reactive gingival proliferation. Your answer must identify the single strongest contradictory feature against your own diagnosis and explain why you still do not let that feature dominate. Then rank the two most plausible alternatives you would keep in reserve, giving one figure-based reason for not placing each first. Finally, propose the least aggressive definitive management that is still diagnostically responsible at this stage, and name one follow-up event that should make you formally re-open the diagnosis rather than simply assume uncomplicated recurrence.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Final clinicopathologic label: long-standing (chronic) pyogenic granuloma with reactive bone formation.

Why this label is preferable: the most important deciding factor is that fig_02.jpg is still fundamentally a vascular-inflammatory reactive lesion. The section shows hyperplastic surface epithelium over connective tissue with numerous capillary channels and inflammatory infiltrate, which fits a chronic pyogenic granuloma pattern better than a primarily fibro-osseous gingival proliferation. fig_01.jpg also supports a reactive gingival lesion associated with local irritants and a bleeding history.

Strongest contradictory feature: the mineralized component in fig_02.jpg (osteoid/bony trabeculae), together with the relatively mature pale clinical appearance in fig_01.jpg, argues strongly for peripheral ossifying fibroma. I would still not let that feature dominate because mineralization alone does not outweigh the overall capillary-rich inflamed architecture; in this case the ossification is best interpreted as secondary/reactive change within a chronic pyogenic granuloma rather than evidence that the whole lesion should be relabeled.

Ranked reserve alternatives:
1. Peripheral ossifying fibroma. It remains the closest alternative because the lesion is gingival, occurs in a young patient, and contains mineralized tissue. I do not rank it first because fig_02.jpg is not dominated by a fibrocellular/fibrous stroma with mineralization as the principal pattern; the vascular-inflammatory component is too prominent.
2. Peripheral giant cell granuloma. It stays in the differential because it is also a reactive gingival mass. I do not rank it first because fig_02.jpg does not show multinucleated giant-cell-rich hemorrhagic stroma, which is the expected key feature.

Least aggressive but diagnostically responsible management: eliminate local irritants and perform complete local excisional biopsy of the lesion including its base/attachment, with submission for histopathologic examination and clinicopathologic correlation. That is definitive enough to treat a small benign-appearing localized reactive gingival lesion while still securing tissue diagnosis; wider resection is not justified at this stage.

Follow-up event that should trigger re-opening the diagnosis: recurrence despite adequate irritant control and apparently complete excision. That should prompt review of the original histology and reconsideration of a peripheral ossifying fibroma-like lesion or another look-alike rather than assuming simple repeat pyogenic granuloma behavior. Repeat treatment would then require re-excision with careful inclusion of the base/attachment and closer surveillance.

items.question_content: A 51-year-old woman previously underwent parotidectomy for pleomorphic adenoma 5 years ago and now presents with a new right parapharyngeal mass. Staging 18F-FDG PET/CT (fig_01.jpg) shows the parapharyngeal lesion and multiple pulmonary nodules. Histology and immunophenotype from the current tumor are shown in fig_02.jpg. 68Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT of the same sites is shown in fig_03.jpg. Based on the history and figures, what is the most likely diagnosis and pattern of spread, and what is the most appropriate overall management approach at this stage? In your answer, address how the prior pleomorphic adenoma history and the FDG-FAPI discordance affect staging, theranostic suitability, and the roles of local versus systemic treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma arising in or from a prior pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), with locoregional recurrence in the parapharyngeal region and hematogenous pulmonary metastases. fig_02.jpg supports EMC by the classic biphasic pattern: inner ductal/luminal epithelial cells and outer myoepithelial cells, with luminal CK7/EMA positivity and abluminal p63, S100, and calponin expression. The history of prior pleomorphic adenoma makes malignant transformation in residual/recurrent salivary tissue highly plausible.

The FDG-positive parapharyngeal mass and lung nodules indicate metabolically active metastatic disease, whereas the absent/minimal FAPI uptake suggests low FAP expression and poor suitability for FAPI-based radionuclide theranostics. Therefore, FAPI PET is not useful here as a therapeutic selector and is less helpful than FDG PET/CT for disease mapping/follow-up in this tumor.

Because disease is already disseminated, management should be through a head and neck oncology multidisciplinary team with complete staging and histologic confirmation of metastatic disease if not already secured. Curative local surgery alone would not be appropriate. Systemic therapy is the main treatment direction; a platinum-based regimen such as cisplatin with capecitabine is reasonable in this setting, with surgery or radiotherapy reserved for diagnosis, symptom palliation, or selected local control. Follow-up should rely on FDG PET/CT or conventional CT rather than FAPI PET. Prognosis is guarded because distant metastases are present despite EMC often being histologically low grade.

Misattributed Etiology: Treating the current parapharyngeal mass and lung nodules as benign recurrent pleomorphic adenoma rather than metastatic salivary malignancy.

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, and based on the provided histology and immunostains from the retromolar trigone tumor, breast biopsy, and lung wedge, a woman had a 1.5 cm oral minor salivary gland neoplasm at age 34 that was variably diagnosed as polymorphous adenocarcinoma versus myoepithelial carcinoma. Fifteen years later, while being staged for ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative breast carcinoma, PET/CT showed multiple pulmonary nodules. As seen in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, the lung lesion shows more solid-cribriform growth than the oral tumor, focal necrosis, increased mitoses, Ki-67 about 35%, and is CK7/S100/SOX10 positive with patchy p63, but negative for p40, TTF1, mammaglobin, GATA3, ER, PR, HER2, DOG1, SMA/calponin, and GFAP. What is the most defensible diagnosis for the lung lesion and the prior oral tumor, which confirmatory diagnostic step should be prioritized before final sign-out, and what key surveillance implication should be communicated?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most defensible interpretation is metastatic microsecretory adenocarcinoma (MSA) to the lung arising from the prior retromolar trigone minor salivary gland primary, with retrospective reclassification of the original oral tumor as MSA rather than breast metastasis, primary lung carcinoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, or myoepithelial carcinoma. The strongest next step is molecular confirmation of the characteristic MEF2C::SS18 fusion on the lung lesion and/or archived oral specimen using targeted fusion testing or an expanded salivary gland panel. The reasoning is that the lung nodule matches the prior oral tumor better than the breast carcinoma: both salivary lesions show microcystic/solid-cribriform architecture with luminal secretions and a salivary-type immunophenotype of S100 and SOX10 positivity with patchy p63 but p40 negativity. The lung lesion is negative for breast markers (GATA3, mammaglobin, ER, PR, HER2) and for TTF1, arguing against metastatic breast carcinoma and primary lung adenocarcinoma. DOG1 and myogenic markers are not supportive of acinic or myoepithelial differentiation. Important differentials include polymorphous adenocarcinoma, secretory carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and myoepithelial carcinoma, but the fusion result would resolve the diagnosis in favor of MSA. The report should clearly state that although MSA is usually low grade, this case shows aggressive potential with very late distant metastasis and more adverse metastatic morphology, so long-term multidisciplinary surveillance is warranted even if the original tumor appeared bland.

items.question_content: An 80-year-old woman has had a painless gingival enlargement for 12 months in the interdental papilla between the maxillary left first and second molars. Periodontal therapy and chlorhexidine produced no regression. The teeth are vital, probing does not induce bleeding, and exam shows firm mucosa-colored exophytic nodules on both buccal and palatal aspects. fig_01.jpg shows only chronic horizontal periodontal bone loss without interval destructive change; fig_02.jpg shows the lesion clinically; fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg show the biopsy findings. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis, which alternative gingival lesions are less likely and why, and what definitive treatment and follow-up strategy are most appropriate?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is peripheral ameloblastoma of the maxillary gingiva. The key synthesis is a long-standing, painless, firm, nonbleeding gingival mass that failed periodontal/antiseptic therapy, with vital adjacent teeth and no destructive radiographic bone change, indicating a peripheral soft-tissue lesion rather than inflammatory periodontal disease or an intraosseous tumor. fig_03.jpg is consistent with ameloblastomatous odontogenic epithelium arising from the surface/basal epithelium, showing peripheral palisading columnar cells with reverse polarity and central loose stellate-reticulum-like areas; fig_04.jpg supports odontogenic epithelial origin, although immunostains are supportive rather than independently diagnostic. Pyogenic granuloma is less likely because the lesion is not friable or hemorrhagic and the histology is not that of lobular capillary granulation tissue. Peripheral giant cell granuloma and peripheral ossifying fibroma are also less likely because their characteristic giant-cell or calcified fibrous patterns are not present. Management is complete local supraperiosteal excision of all clinical disease with microscopic margin assessment; if the biopsy was excisional and complete, that may be definitive, with local re-excision/curettage of the underlying periosteal or superficial bony bed if margins are involved or recurrence appears. Tooth extraction or radical resection is not indicated without evidence of invasion. Prognosis is generally favorable, but long-term, ideally annual, follow-up is needed because recurrence usually reflects incomplete removal and rare malignant transformation has been reported.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully integrate the clinical history, radiographic findings, and biopsy figures; reasoning is absent or internally inconsistent.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Coherently integrates the persistent painless firm gingival mass, lack of bleeding, vital teeth, minimal radiographic change, and biopsy features of odontogenic epithelium with peripheral palisading and central reticulum-like areas to support the diagnosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, high-level synthesis that distinguishes a peripheral odontogenic neoplasm from reactive gingival lesions and from intraosseous ameloblastoma, correctly noting that immunostains support odontogenic epithelial origin but morphology and clinico-radiographic correlation establish the diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, a 14-year-old girl has a painless 1 × 0.5 cm gingival nodule at the maxillary right central incisor that has slowly enlarged over 4–5 years and recurred 18 months after a prior excision. It was clinically thought to be fibroma or pyogenic granuloma. fig_01.jpg shows no osseous involvement. Using the radiograph and histology, what is the most likely diagnosis, why is it favored over both common reactive gingival lesions and peripheral ameloblastoma, and what definitive management and follow-up would you recommend to avoid both undertreatment and unnecessary aggressive surgery?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is peripheral dentinogenic ghost cell tumor (peripheral DGCT, extraosseous DGCT). It is favored because this is a recurrent, long-standing gingival soft-tissue lesion with no radiographic intraosseous component on fig_01.jpg, while fig_02.jpg shows the defining combination of ameloblastomatous odontogenic epithelial strands/islands, ghost cells that may calcify, and adjacent dentinoid material; the special stain supports separation of dentinoid from ghost-cell keratinization. Reactive gingival lesions such as pyogenic granuloma, irritation fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, or nonspecific epulis do not show odontogenic epithelium with ghost cells and dentinoid. Peripheral ameloblastoma is a closer mimic, but it lacks the characteristic ghost cells and dentinoid/calcifying component seen here.

Management should be conservative but complete: perform/confirm complete local excision of the lesion with removal to the base, ideally including the periosteal attachment if involved, and submit all tissue for histopathologic evaluation with clinicoradiographic correlation. Because fig_01.jpg shows no bone involvement, aggressive osseous resection is not indicated; this should not be treated like a central/intraosseous DGCT. Given the prior recurrence, I would suspect incomplete previous excision and recommend careful margin-oriented excision if feasible, baseline documentation, and periodic long-term follow-up to detect local recurrence. Prognosis for the peripheral variant is generally good after adequate excision, but recurrence history justifies closer surveillance.

items.question_content: Examining fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, a 5-month-old male kitten has progressive dyspnea, dysphagia, and a steadily enlarging left oropharyngeal mass involving the buccal mucosa, palate, and pharynx. CT in fig_01.jpg shows a 4.5 × 6.5 cm multiloculated lesion filling the maxillary region, with ventral orbital wall destruction and dorsal globe displacement, but no intracranial extension. Using the imaging and histology shown, what is the most likely diagnosis, and what definitive management and follow-up are most appropriate? Briefly justify why complete excision is preferred over drainage, partial debulking, or adjuvant therapy.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is a mature extragonadal solid-cystic oropharyngeal teratoma (benign, grade 0). The diagnosis is supported by the combination of a congenital-age, progressively obstructive oropharyngeal mass and histology showing well-differentiated tissues from all 3 germ layers: ectodermal skin/adnexa and neural tissue, mesodermal cartilage, smooth muscle and adipose tissue, and endodermal respiratory/bronchial epithelium. This favors mature teratoma over dermoid/epidermoid cyst, inflammatory cyst, or immature teratoma. Definitive treatment is prompt complete surgical extirpation guided by CT-defined extent, because the patient already has airway and feeding compromise and recurrence is mainly due to residual tumor. The entire specimen should be submitted for histopathologic confirmation of maturity and exclusion of immature elements. Drainage or partial debulking is inadequate because it leaves pluritissue tumor behind and increases recurrence risk. Adjuvant therapy is not indicated when the lesion is mature, fully resected, and lacks intracranial extension. Follow-up should monitor oral healing, airway and feeding function, and local recurrence over time; prognosis is good after complete excision.

items.question_content: A 30-year-old woman has a painful 2-month history of a mobile 2 × 2 cm swelling of the right buccal mucosa/cheek. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and the immunostain panel in the Supplementary Figure, identify the most likely diagnosis. State the immunohistochemical pattern that supports this diagnosis while excluding the closest mimics, and give the definitive management and expected follow-up for this lesion.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The leading diagnosis is oral angioleiomyoma (vascular leiomyoma), likely the solid variant. This is supported by a painful but mobile, well-circumscribed buccal soft-tissue mass, a hypoechoic lesion on ultrasound, and H&E showing bland spindle smooth-muscle cells in intersecting fascicles/whorls concentrically related to vascular channels with extravasated RBCs and no significant atypia or mitotic activity. The confirming IHC pattern would be diffuse strong SMA positivity, vimentin positivity, variable or focal desmin positivity, and CD34 staining limited to endothelial cells rather than the tumor spindle cells; S-100 should be negative, helping exclude schwannoma/neurofibroma, and CD68 negative if a histiocytic lesion is considered. Leiomyosarcoma is excluded by the absence of cytologic atypia, necrosis, infiltrative behavior, and significant mitotic activity. Myopericytoma/myofibroma remain considerations but are less favored with mature smooth-muscle morphology and desmin positivity. Definitive management is complete conservative surgical excision, with the specimen fully submitted for histopathologic review and IHC confirmation when morphology is equivocal. No radical resection, neck treatment, or adjuvant therapy is indicated for a benign lesion without malignant features. Postoperative follow-up should monitor healing and look for rare local recurrence; prognosis after complete excision is excellent.

items.question_content: Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, an 18-year-old woman has an incidental, painless lesion in the right mandibular canine-premolar region. The teeth are vital, oral mucosa is normal, and there is no facial asymmetry. Imaging shows a well-circumscribed unilocular lesion lingual to the adjacent teeth, containing dense irregular tooth-like/calcified material, without cortical expansion, root resorption, or tooth displacement. What is the most likely preoperative diagnosis, which alternative diagnoses should be actively excluded, and what definitive treatment and follow-up strategy is most appropriate?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best preoperative diagnosis is a calcifying odontogenic cyst associated with a complex odontoma, specifically an odontoma-producing COC. This fits the patient’s age, the well-defined unilocular mandibular lesion, the internal irregular calcified/tooth-like material, its lingual position, and the benign behavior shown by vital adjacent teeth with no root resorption, displacement, or cortical expansion. Important alternatives to exclude are an isolated complex odontoma, cementoblastoma, adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor, and cemento-ossifying fibroma. Cementoblastoma is less likely because the mass is not fused to a root; AOT is less likely because the site and pattern are atypical; CEOT and fibro-osseous lesions usually have a different radiographic pattern and often more expansion. Definitive management is conservative complete enucleation/removal of the cystic lesion and calcified component, with curettage as needed, using CBCT to plan safe access and preserving adjacent vital teeth unless directly involved. All tissue must be submitted for histopathology to confirm ghost-cell cyst lining and odontoma. Follow-up should include clinical review and radiographic surveillance because recurrence is uncommon but depends on completeness of removal. Prognosis is generally favorable after complete excision.

items.question_content: A 54-year-old woman develops a painless tongue-tip mass over about 4 weeks. She reports repeated dressmaker-needle trauma to the area and has a remote history of intestinal adenocarcinoma treated 5 years earlier. On examination, there is a solitary ~1 cm well-circumscribed sessile/exophytic white lesion with soft-elastic consistency; adjacent benign migratory glossitis is present, and there is no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what is the most likely diagnosis, which competing diagnosis must still be actively excluded because of this presentation, and how should the lesion be managed to maximize diagnostic certainty while minimizing procedural risk?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The leading diagnosis is an ulcerated capillary angioma of the tongue, most likely a trauma-associated reactive vascular proliferation. This is supported by the rapid appearance after repeated needle trauma, the small exophytic soft lesion on the tongue tip, the white surface consistent with ulceration/pseudomembrane masking the usual red-blue vascular color, and the histology showing capillary vascular hyperproliferation with ulcerative change rather than invasive epithelial malignancy. The key competing diagnosis that must still be excluded is oral metastasis from the prior intestinal adenocarcinoma, because tongue metastases can be painless, rapidly appearing nodular or exophytic lesions and can mimic benign reactive lesions. Lesser differentials include pyogenic granuloma, traumatic fibroma, and squamous cell carcinoma; peripheral giant cell granuloma is less likely on the tongue. Management should not be simple observation or symptomatic treatment for glossitis. The lesion requires prompt tissue diagnosis, ideally biopsy with histopathology. If the lesion is small and clinically resectable, complete excision is reasonable; otherwise incisional biopsy is appropriate first. Because a vascular lesion may bleed heavily, the procedure should be planned with hemostatic precautions, such as vasoconstrictor-containing local anesthetic when appropriate, careful surgical technique, secure suturing, and consideration of hemostatic devices such as laser or electrosurgery if available. Follow-up is needed to confirm healing and detect recurrence. The migratory glossitis is an incidental coexisting finding unless symptomatic.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a painless, firm, well-circumscribed upper-lip submucosal swelling and no cervical lymphadenopathy. The small superficial lesion was excised under local anesthesia with an intact 5 mm rim. Histopathology from the intact specimen showed a benign-appearing encapsulated salivary gland neoplasm; the surrounding surgical margin was unremarkable, and there was no invasion or other malignant feature. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg, what is the most likely diagnosis, how would you distinguish it from its key salivary gland mimics, and is excision alone adequate or are further imaging, immunohistochemical/molecular tests, wider surgery, or adjuvant therapy indicated? Justify the follow-up plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is benign myoepithelioma arising in a minor salivary gland of the upper lip. The slides support a well-circumscribed myoepithelial neoplasm with mixed morphology—predominantly spindle and plasmacytoid cells, with focal clear-cell change—without invasive growth or malignant cytology. Pleomorphic adenoma is the main mimic, but it is less favored because there is no convincing chondroid or myxochondroid/fibromyxoid stromal component; any ductal differentiation appears only minimal. Myoepithelial carcinoma must be excluded by the absence of invasion, significant atypia, necrosis, and other malignant features. Basal cell adenoma is less likely because that tumor more typically shows a basaloid/duct-forming architecture rather than a dominantly myoepithelial mixed-cell pattern. Management is complete local excision with negative margins, which is already appropriate here. No routine radiotherapy or chemotherapy is indicated for a benign lesion with clear margins, and wider resection is unnecessary unless margins are involved or malignant transformation is suspected. Additional imaging, FNA, molecular studies, or even IHC are not routinely required after definitive benign histology in a small superficial lip lesion; they would be reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, suspected deep extension, or concern for malignancy. Prognosis is favorable, but periodic long-term clinical follow-up is still needed because local recurrence can occur and malignant transformation, while uncommon, is possible.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. Which findings from this case favor localized juvenile spongiotic gingival hyperplasia over common reactive gingival lesions and granulomatosis with polyangiitis-associated strawberry gingivitis? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: Adult age excludes the diagnosis because this lesion is confined to children.
A localized erythematous velvety gingival lesion in the setting of good oral hygiene.
Hyperplastic nonkeratinized epithelium with prominent spongiosis and inflammatory cell exocytosis.
Diffuse gingival involvement expected in association with systemic vasculitic disease.
Fibrocellular stroma with mineralized material as the key microscopic clue.
Recurrence after prior simple excisions is compatible with the lesion.
Lobular capillary proliferation of the connective tissue as the defining histology.
Painful ulceronecrotic change is a characteristic presentation.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: LJSGH may occur in adults, often recurs, and typically presents as a localized bright-red velvety gingival lesion despite good plaque control. Its main microscopic clue is epithelial: hyperplastic nonkeratinized epithelium with spongiosis and inflammatory exocytosis. Lobular vascular proliferation favors pyogenic granuloma, mineralization favors peripheral ossifying fibroma, and diffuse strawberry gingivitis with systemic features favors granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

items.answer_explanation: LJSGH may occur in adults, often recurs, and typically presents as a localized bright-red velvety gingival lesion despite good plaque control. Its main microscopic clue is epithelial: hyperplastic nonkeratinized epithelium with spongiosis and inflammatory exocytosis. Lobular vascular proliferation favors pyogenic granuloma, mineralization favors peripheral ossifying fibroma, and diffuse strawberry gingivitis with systemic features favors granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. The lesion is clinically verruciform. What specific microscopic invasive pattern in this specimen argues against a diagnosis of pure verrucous carcinoma?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Pure verrucous carcinoma typically shows broad pushing fronts with minimal infiltrative behavior. Single-cell infiltration/invasion indicates a more infiltrative conventional squamous cell carcinoma component rather than a pure verrucous carcinoma pattern.

items.answer_explanation: Pure verrucous carcinoma typically shows broad pushing fronts with minimal infiltrative behavior. Single-cell infiltration/invasion indicates a more infiltrative conventional squamous cell carcinoma component rather than a pure verrucous carcinoma pattern.

items.question_content: After identifying the tumor in fig_01.jpg, name the specific surgical-margin status associated with increased local recurrence in this tumor type.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: For polymorphous adenocarcinoma, local recurrence has been associated with positive or unknown surgical margins. This is distinct from focal papillary growth, which is the histologic feature linked to cervical lymph node involvement.

items.answer_explanation: For polymorphous adenocarcinoma, local recurrence has been associated with positive or unknown surgical margins. This is distinct from focal papillary growth, which is the histologic feature linked to cervical lymph node involvement.

items.question_content: After the initial biopsy favored a benign fibromyxomatous process, the resection specimen established the final diagnosis. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg, select all statements that are most defensible and together best explain why the lesion is peripheral ossifying fibroma rather than its closest differentials.

question_options.text: The first biopsy likely sampled a superficial/peripheral fibromyxoid zone, so absence of mineralized tissue in that specimen does not exclude the final diagnosis.
The excision shows a benign fibro-osseous pattern: trabecular bone with osteocytes in lacunae and osteoblastic rimming in fibrocellular stroma, without malignant cytology.
The overall clinicoradiologic pattern is that of an exophytic soft-tissue lesion with no convincing medullary origin or centrifugal intraosseous expansion.
Because calcification is present, pyogenic granuloma with secondary ossification is effectively excluded even without considering architecture or vascularity.
Peripheral odontogenic fibroma remains favored here even if odontogenic epithelium and dysplastic dentin are not identified.
A hard palatal mass containing bone should still be regarded as para-osteal osteosarcoma despite bland histology and lack of destructive bone involvement.
A lesion composed mainly of dense mature compact bone with little intervening fibrocellular stroma would fit soft tissue osteoma better than the sections shown.
The posterior palatal location by itself rules out peripheral ossifying fibroma because a periodontal-ligament origin is mandatory.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The resection resolves the discrepancy: the incisional biopsy likely undersampled a superficial fibromyxoid area, whereas deeper tissue shows benign trabecular bone with osteoblastic rimming in fibrocellular stroma. The lesion is exophytic and soft-tissue based rather than medullary/centrifugal. The sections are not those of a dense compact osteoma, and they lack the features needed for pyogenic granuloma, peripheral odontogenic fibroma, or osteosarcoma.

items.answer_explanation: The resection resolves the discrepancy: the incisional biopsy likely undersampled a superficial fibromyxoid area, whereas deeper tissue shows benign trabecular bone with osteoblastic rimming in fibrocellular stroma. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, counsel this couple in their next natural pregnancy at 11+6 weeks. The mother is clinically normal, but two prior fetuses carried the same pathogenic EFTUD2 deletion and fig_02.jpgC shows a faint maternal mosaic signal. In this pregnancy, the 12-week scan now shows definite micrognathia and a repeatedly small stomach bubble. She refuses IVF/PGT-M, wants no more than one invasive procedure if reasonably possible, and would consider termination only if the diagnosis is robust before 20+0. Your unit can obtain an early placental sample with maternal-cell-contamination controls but only targeted testing for the familial EFTUD2 variant, or perform later amniocentesis on fetal cells with CNV analysis plus broader sequencing. Choose the single best test now for this specific pregnancy and justify why it is better than the alternative. State which result patterns would or would not be enough for an irreversible decision, explicitly using the pedigree and the contrast in fig_02.jpg between clear fetal heterozygosity and faint maternal mosaicism. Then explain what diagnoses, complications, and referrals you must still pursue if familial EFTUD2 testing is negative despite the scan findings, and what you would do differently if the same pregnancy had a completely normal 12-week scan instead.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The figures support recurrent EFTUD2-related mandibulofacial dysostosis, Guion-Almeida type, with materially increased recurrence risk from maternal mosaicism: the same pathogenic frameshift recurred in two fetuses, and the mother shows only a faint mutant trace on Sanger, so a normal phenotype and previously normal early scans do not lower concern enough to dismiss recurrence. However, in this specific new pregnancy the key new fact is that the scan is already abnormal: definite micrognathia plus a repeatedly small stomach bubble broadens the differential beyond the known familial variant.

Because she strongly prefers one invasive procedure, I would recommend primary amniocentesis rather than early targeted placental sampling. The reason is not that CVS is wrong in general; it is that targeted placental testing is a good single-question test only when the main question is recurrence of the known familial variant. Here, if CVS were negative, the fetus would still remain high risk because the anatomy is abnormal and those findings are not specific for EFTUD2. That would likely force a second invasive test for CNV analysis and broader fetal sequencing, defeating her one-procedure priority. Amniocentesis samples fetal cells, avoids placental-confined ambiguity, and gives the best chance of a single decision-grade workup before 20 weeks, although the time window is tighter and results should be expedited.

Decision-grade results: a clean positive result from fetal-cell testing showing the same familial pathogenic EFTUD2 variant, with sample identity/contamination controls adequate, is sufficient for counseling that the fetus is affected by the familial disorder and can support an irreversible decision if the couple chooses. A trace, very low-level, or otherwise ambiguous result is not enough for irreversible action, because Fig2 shows that true maternal mosaicism can generate only a faint signal; weak findings may reflect contamination, technical artifact, or true fetal mosaicism and need orthogonal confirmation and phenotype correlation. A clean negative result for the familial variant alone is not enough in this abnormal fetus; it must be interpreted alongside normal CNV analysis, broader sequencing as indicated, and ongoing imaging.

If familial EFTUD2 testing is negative, I would actively pursue chromosomal aneuploidy/pathogenic CNV, other monogenic craniofacial disorders causing micrognathia, and structural foregut pathology including esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula. I would arrange detailed fetal anatomy review, serial assessment of stomach filling and amniotic fluid, fetal echocardiography, and genetics/MFM counseling. Oral-maxillofacial and neonatal implications that should be discussed include mandibular and malar hypoplasia, cleft or high palate, neonatal airway compromise, feeding/swallowing difficulty, and ear/hearing problems; if the pregnancy continues, delivery planning should involve a center able to manage airway and feeding issues.

If the same pregnancy had a completely normal 12-week scan instead, I would switch to early CVS with maternal-cell-contamination controls and targeted testing for the known familial EFTUD2 variant. In the normal-scan scenario, the dominant question is early exclusion or confirmation of the known recurrent variant before the patient’s 20-week decision limit. There, a clean positive targeted CVS would be decision-grade, a trace/low-level result would require confirmatory amniocentesis, and a clean negative targeted CVS would usually be sufficient to rule out this specific familial recurrence while continuing routine anatomic surveillance for unrelated anomalies.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses the significance of recurrent EFTUD2 disease or maternal mosaicism, or treats the findings as an isolated nonsyndromic jaw anomaly.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes recurrent familial craniofacial disease or mosaicism but does not clearly identify recurrent EFTUD2-related mandibulofacial dysostosis as the main diagnostic concern.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies recurrent EFTUD2-related mandibulofacial dysostosis with maternal mosaic recurrence and explains why a normal mother or previously normal early scans do not exclude substantial recurrence risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use the pedigree, ultrasound findings, and sequencing figures together.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case data but does not explicitly connect the recurrent pedigree pattern and Fig2 contrast between clear fetal heterozygosity and faint maternal mosaicism to test interpretation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates pedigree recurrence, current abnormal scan, and Fig2 signal patterns to distinguish robust fetal positivity from low-level maternal-like ambiguity and to justify the management pathway.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not choose a test now, or gives generic advice without prioritizing the one-procedure preference, abnormal scan, and pre-20-week decision constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a pathway but does not convincingly justify it against the competing option in this abnormal-scan pregnancy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses and defends a clinically reasonable pathway, incorporating timing and the one-procedure constraint, but incompletely addresses how the already abnormal scan changes the strategy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes broader fetal-cell testing as the best single-procedure strategy in the abnormal-scan scenario, and explicitly states that the strategy would change toward early targeted CVS if the 12-week scan were normal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores key trade-offs such as placental versus fetal-cell sampling, timing to result, or decision-grade versus non-decision-grade results.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions timing or sample-type trade-offs but does not clearly state which result patterns are sufficient or insufficient for irreversible action.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly weighs earlier targeted placental testing against later broader fetal-cell testing, explains why the abnormal scan changes the balance, and clearly classifies clean positive, clean negative, and trace/low-level results by decision-grade value.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not broaden the differential when scan abnormalities persist despite negative familial testing.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges that negative familial testing does not exclude disease but gives only vague alternatives.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically broadens to chromosomal/ pathogenic CNV causes, other monogenic craniofacial disorders causing micrognathia, and structural foregut pathology such as esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits clinically important fetal/neonatal complications relevant to oral and maxillofacial care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only facial abnormality or jaw smallness without linking to airway, palate, feeding, hearing, or swallowing concerns.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies likely oral-maxillofacial and neonatal consequences, including mandibular/malar hypoplasia, palate abnormalities, airway compromise, feeding/swallowing problems, and hearing/ear anomalies, and links small stomach findings to possible swallowing dysfunction or EA/TEF.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses coercive counseling, ignores informed consent, or recommends irreversible action on ambiguous data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Respects patient preference but does not clearly frame counseling as nondirective or does not address why ambiguous results cannot justify irreversible decisions.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nondirective counseling, explicitly ties recommendations to informed consent and the patient's procedural/time limits, and refuses to base irreversible decisions on low-level or poorly controlled results.

red_flags: Generic Textbook Management: Recommending early targeted placental testing purely because it is earlier, without addressing that an already abnormal scan plus a one-procedure preference makes a targeted-only placental approach a poor single-procedure strategy.

Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Treating a negative familial EFTUD2 result as sufficient reassurance despite persistent micrognathia and a small stomach bubble, without pursuing CNV analysis, broader sequencing, and evaluation for EA/TEF or other syndromic causes.

Premature Irreversible Treatment: Advising termination or definitive reassurance on the basis of a trace/low-level result that could reflect maternal-cell contamination, confined placental mosaicism, or unconfirmed fetal mosaicism.
Misattributed Etiology: Labeling the findings as isolated Pierre Robin sequence or benign facial variation without considering recurrent syndromic craniofacial disease and foregut pathology.

Severity Misjudged: Reassuring because the mother is phenotypically normal or because prior early scans were normal, despite recurrent transmission of the same pathogenic EFTUD2 variant and maternal mosaicism in Fig2C.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Oral hairy leukoplakia is classically confirmed by demonstrating EBV within lesional epithelium using EBER in situ hybridization. The superficial epithelial positivity in Fig2 fits this confirmatory study.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The tumor nests show classic ameloblastoma-like features, especially peripheral palisading and reverse nuclear polarity with subnuclear vacuolization. Those findings indicate ameloblastic differentiation, which is a key clue favoring ameloblastic carcinoma in this clear-cell intraosseous lesion.

items.question_content: A 56-year-old man has a rapidly enlarging right maxillary intraosseous lesion. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Biopsy showed a clear-cell epithelial neoplasm. Immunostains were AE1/AE3+, vimentin+, CD10+, CK19+, p63+, and CK5/6+, while CK7, CK20, RCC, and PAX8 were negative; PET showed no extragnathic primary tumor. Which diagnosis is most strongly supported?

question_options.text: Clear cell variant of ameloblastic carcinoma
Clear cell odontogenic carcinoma
Metastatic renal cell carcinoma
Central mucoepidermoid carcinoma

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Fig3 shows ameloblastoma-like architecture with peripheral palisading, reverse polarity, and subnuclear vacuolization, supporting ameloblastic differentiation. CK19/p63/CK5/6 positivity supports odontogenic epithelium. Negative RCC and PAX8 staining plus a negative PET make metastatic renal cell carcinoma unlikely. Central mucoepidermoid carcinoma lacks this ameloblastic pattern, and clear cell odontogenic carcinoma typically lacks the strong ameloblastic morphology seen here.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. Using the common three-tier histopathologic grading system for adenoid cystic carcinoma based on growth pattern, what grade best fits the dominant pattern shown?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The figure shows a cribriform-dominant adenoid cystic carcinoma with pseudocystic spaces and no evident dominant solid component. In the standard three-tier morphologic grading approach, tubular or cribriform patterns are classified as grade I, while tumors with increasing solid growth are graded higher.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What classic histologic growth pattern is shown by this spindle-cell proliferation?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Nodular fasciitis typically shows plump spindle myofibroblasts in short sweeping fascicles with a loose, feathery appearance, often described as a tissue culture-like pattern. Recognizing this clue helps distinguish it from true sarcoma when combined with the relatively bland cytology and supportive immunohistochemistry.

items.question_content: A 21-year-old woman has a 6-month, painless swelling of the left anterior maxilla with facial asymmetry, vestibular expansion with eggshell crackling, retained #63, and an unerupted #23. Aspiration yields straw-colored fluid. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, determine the most appropriate definitive management strategy and justify it from the available evidence. Explain why your plan fits this lesion better than other reasonable approaches and what postoperative surveillance is necessary for this patient.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most appropriate diagnosis is an intraosseous calcifying epithelial odontogenic cyst/calcifying cystic odontogenic tumor (CEOC/CCOT), and the preferred treatment is conservative surgical enucleation with curettage of the lesion, removal of the pathologic lining for complete histopathologic assessment, and management of associated teeth according to their restorability and relation to the lesion; the retained primary tooth would usually be removed, while adjacent permanent teeth should be preserved if structurally and functionally maintainable. This choice is supported by the well-circumscribed cystic appearance on imaging, association with an impacted tooth, cystic aspirate, and the histology showing ameloblast-like basal cells, stellate-reticulum-like suprabasal cells, and ghost cells. These findings favor a cystic ghost-cell odontogenic lesion over a simple dentigerous cyst, AOT, or unicystic ameloblastoma. The absence of obvious radiographic calcification does not exclude CEOC. More aggressive resection is not first choice here because the lesion appears localized and cystic rather than frankly infiltrative or malignant; observation alone is inappropriate because there is expansion and root resorption. Postoperatively, the patient needs long-term clinical and radiographic follow-up to detect recurrence, assess bone fill, monitor adjacent teeth for vitality/stability and further resorption, and reassess the impacted #23 for eruption potential or later orthodontic/surgical management. Any recurrence or more solid/aggressive histologic features would justify escalation of treatment.

items.question_content: A 69-year-old man with well-controlled diabetes has 3 weeks of painful left facial and neck swelling, fever, throat pain, a prior choking sensation, and severe trismus after only slight improvement on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Intraoral examination is limited by mouth-opening restriction. Reviewing fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, determine the most likely odontogenic process and state the immediate management plan you would recommend now. Explain how the imaging changes the urgency, source-control strategy, antimicrobial approach, and need for broader medical or surgical involvement.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with Lemierre syndrome, or septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis of odontogenic origin, arising from an infected impacted maxillary third molar with contiguous maxillary sinus and deep neck space spread. fig_01.jpg supports a decayed impacted maxillary third molar as the likely source. fig_02.jpg shows that this is not a localized dental infection: there is extension from the maxillary region into deep facial and cervical spaces with pharyngeal mass effect and internal jugular vein thrombosis. That makes the case urgent and hospital-based because of airway compromise, ongoing sepsis, and risk of septic emboli.

Immediate management should include urgent admission, airway assessment, systemic workup, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with reliable anaerobic and oral flora coverage, and blood tests/cultures if feasible before antibiotics are changed. Source control is essential: drain any accessible collections and remove the causative maxillary third molar in a controlled setting once airway and overall status are secured; extraction should not be deferred if the tooth remains the nidus. Care should be coordinated with oral and maxillofacial surgery and ENT/head-and-neck teams, with medical/infectious-disease input and diabetic monitoring; chest evaluation is warranted if there are pulmonary symptoms or concern for septic emboli.

Anticoagulation should not be routine or automatic. It is controversial and should be considered case by case with the medical team, especially if thrombosis progresses, sepsis persists despite drainage and antibiotics, or there is extension toward major intracranial venous pathways, while balancing bleeding risk. The key decision is to treat this as a life-threatening deep neck infection with jugular thrombosis rather than a routine outpatient dental abscess or uncomplicated sinusitis.

items.question_content: A 58-year-old smoker has p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the right tongue/floor of mouth with poor intake, 12 kg weight loss, intermittent tumoral bleeding, and bilateral cervical adenopathy. He was initially being considered for curative treatment. During admission, a right ventricular lesion is detected; anticoagulation worsens the oral bleeding, and repeat cardiac assessment shows no improvement. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide whether you would change treatment intent without obtaining tissue from the cardiac lesion. In your answer, state: (1) the most likely nature of the ventricular lesion; (2) the strongest evidence for and against at least one competing diagnosis; (3) your immediate management priorities in order; and (4) what additional finding or change in results would be needed to keep curative resection on the table.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would change treatment intent away from curative surgery even without cardiac biopsy, because the right ventricular lesion is most consistent with cardiac metastasis from the oral SCC rather than a bland thrombus. The key imaging synthesis is interval change across the figures: fig_01.jpg shows the aggressive primary/regional disease but no abnormal cardiac metastatic focus, whereas fig_02.jpg shows a persistent right ventricular lesion on CT/echocardiography and a new intensely FDG-avid intracardiac focus on PET/CT. In addition, the lesion does not improve after anticoagulation, which argues against a bland thrombus. A competing diagnosis is thrombus: malignancy, venous compression, immobility, and hospitalization make thrombosis plausible, so it was reasonable to consider initially. However, thrombus becomes less favored because the lesion persists despite heparin, appears associated with right ventricular dysfunction, and is hypermetabolic on PET/CT. A primary cardiac tumor is much less likely than metastasis in a patient with known advanced SCC and interval systemic progression.

Immediate priorities are: first, stabilize hemorrhage and stop anticoagulation once thrombus is no longer the leading diagnosis, because it is causing harm without clear benefit; second, protect the airway if bleeding/tumor bulk threatens obstruction; third, maintain nutrition and supportive care; fourth, obtain coordinated cardiology-oncology-head and neck reassessment and restage the disease as metastatic unless another explanation is proven; fifth, proceed with noncurative systemic therapy and monitor for cardiac complications such as arrhythmia, right ventricular failure, obstruction, or embolic events.

Cardiac biopsy is not required before changing intent if the result would be unlikely to outweigh the procedural risk, treatment delay, and the already compelling imaging/clinical evidence in an unstable bleeding patient. Curative resection would stay on the table only if the distant lesion were convincingly excluded as metastasis—for example, if it regressed with anticoagulation, lacked malignant metabolic activity on further workup, or additional cardiac imaging/biopsy demonstrated a nonmetastatic process after stabilization.

items.question_content: A 78-year-old woman has a 15-year history of recurrent left submandibular sialadenitis/sialolithiasis treated with multiple transoral stone removals. She now has bilateral submandibular tenderness and a year of new right-sided swelling. Left duct cannulation is impossible because the papilla is completely scarred. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What management strategy would you recommend now, and why? Base your answer on the imaging-defined anatomy, which side should be prioritized, and the strengths and limits of the available imaging for guiding intervention.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The priority is the left side. The key problem is not simply duplicated anatomy, but chronic obstructive sialadenitis with distal/outlet obstruction: the left papilla cannot be cannulated because it is scarred, and fig_01.jpg/ fig_02.jpg show a markedly dilated left submandibular duct with inflammatory change/heterogeneity, supporting persistent poor drainage. I would recommend a gland-preserving left duct procedure—open ductoplasty/papilloplasty with sialendoscopic assistance if access can be established after opening the scarred orifice—rather than observation alone. The objective is to re-establish drainage of the main duct while accounting for the accessory left duct joining the main duct, so the accessory drainage pathway is not overlooked during surgery.

The right side does not need to be the first operative target. Conventional sialography has already defined a duplicated right duct/gland system with posterior duct irregularity/dilatation, but the immediate mechanical problem on the left is more advanced because the outlet is completely scarred and the duct is markedly dilated. The right side can be monitored or treated symptomatically unless its symptoms become dominant or obstructive episodes recur.

Imaging choice matters. Conventional sialography is superior when cannulation is possible because it maps ductal anatomy and smaller branches more clearly, as on the right. MR sialography is the appropriate alternative on the left because cannulation failed; it is less detailed for tertiary ducts but still shows the major obstruction pattern, accessory duct confluence, and inflammatory changes needed for surgical planning. Ultrasound is supportive for gland heterogeneity and duct dilatation but is not sufficient alone for detailed duct mapping.

I would counsel the patient about recurrence or persistent obstruction if the scarred outlet or accessory drainage pattern is incompletely addressed, postoperative restenosis, ongoing sialadenitis/stone recurrence, and floor-of-mouth complications including lingual nerve injury. Submandibular gland excision should be reserved as salvage if gland-preserving duct surgery fails or if the gland proves severely damaged/nonfunctional.

items.question_content: A 41-year-old woman has a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless left floor-of-mouth mass with leftward tongue deviation. She has no tongue numbness and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Reviewing fig_01.jpg, what management strategy would you defend from initial assessment through follow-up, including whether tissue diagnosis should precede definitive surgery? Justify how the imaging and pathologic findings in fig_01.jpg affect your estimate of malignancy risk, the extent of resection, and nerve management, especially whether tongue deviation should be treated as evidence of nerve-invasive salivary malignancy.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Tongue deviation makes malignancy a concern, but I would not treat it as proof of nerve invasion by itself. The long, painless course, mobility, absence of numbness or nodes, and fig_01.jpg imaging showing a circumscribed vascular lesion that displaces adjacent tongue musculature favor a localized neoplasm rather than obvious infiltrative adenoid cystic carcinoma. Before pathology, the differential would include a salivary gland tumor, a neurogenic tumor, and a mesenchymal spindle-cell tumor. fig_01.jpg F-K then strongly supports solitary fibrous tumor: a well-demarcated expansile spindle-cell lesion with alternating cellularity, collagen, staghorn vessels, diffuse nuclear STAT6, and CD34 positivity.

My management would be definitive transoral excision of the lesion with the involved sublingual gland, aiming for complete removal while preserving the hypoglossal and lingual nerves unless there is direct operative evidence of invasion. Preoperative needle biopsy is reasonable to consider in some floor-of-mouth masses, but here it is not essential because the lesion is small and resectable and appears vascular on ultrasound, so biopsy may add bleeding risk without clearly changing the need for excision. Frozen section can help determine whether wider resection is needed if unexpected malignancy is found, but routine nerve sacrifice or neck dissection is not justified without radiologic, clinical, or intraoperative evidence of invasion or nodal disease.

After complete excision, prognosis is favorable but not zero-risk because SFT has intermediate behavior. The provided sections look low aggression compared with infiltrative carcinoma, so I would recommend long-term surveillance for local recurrence and continued documentation of tongue/cranial nerve function. Persistent postoperative deviation would not, by itself, prove missed nerve invasion.

levels.title: Exceeds
