items.question_content: A healthy 42-year-old man seeks a fixed replacement for a long-standing missing mandibular right first molar after orthodontic treatment. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, the residual space is reduced, the adjacent teeth are mostly vital, oral hygiene is good, and the mandibular right second molar has a defective occlusal amalgam with recurrent caries. He wants the most conservative definitive option possible. What restoration would you recommend for this site, and how would you justify the abutment choice, pontic form/size, and retainer design using the patient-specific findings? Include the main biomechanical risks you would plan to control.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend a minimally invasive single-abutment resin-bonded inlay-retained cantilever fixed dental prosthesis, using the mandibular right second molar as the abutment. The key reasons are that the space visible in the figures is too narrow for a normal first-molar replacement, the patient wants a fixed solution, the neighboring teeth are largely sound and vital, and the second molar already needs operative treatment because of recurrent caries beneath a defective amalgam. Using that tooth for an inlay retainer preserves the other adjacent tooth rather than preparing multiple mostly healthy teeth for full-coverage retainers.

The pontic should not be a full first-molar form; it should be reduced to fit the available mesiodistal space, effectively a premolar-sized or narrowed posterior pontic with a smaller occlusal table to limit load. A cantilever design from a single abutment is preferable to splinting two abutments in this setting because differential tooth movement increases stress and failure risk in 2-retainer resin-bonded designs, and unilateral debonding may go unnoticed. The retainer should incorporate the restored inlay preparation in the second molar and, if enamel is available, auxiliary buccal and lingual adhesive wings or equivalent enamel-bonded extensions to increase bonding area and resist torsional forces on the posterior cantilever. A high-strength monolithic ceramic such as zirconia is reasonable for posterior loading.

The main risks to control are debonding, connector or ceramic fracture, recurrent caries at the abutment margins, occlusal overload on the cantilevered pontic, and possible pulpal consequences in a deeply restored abutment. Risk reduction includes maximizing enamel bonding, careful adhesive isolation and surface treatment, adequate connector dimensions, a light occlusal scheme with limited excursive contacts on the pontic, and periodic follow-up for margins, vitality, occlusion, and hygiene.

items.question_content: A 31-year-old woman has an endodontically treated maxillary first molar with a failed composite restoration and no apical pathology (fig_01.jpg). Before any milling, you must decide whether the preparation shown in fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg is acceptable for a definitive one-visit restoration or whether the design should be changed first. Using fig_05.jpg and fig_06.jpg as well, state the restorative concept you would choose, the material family you would favor, and the specific figure findings that support that choice. Then explain how you would handle the occlusal/proximal contacts and the block position to minimize remake risk and reproduce the adjacent tooth gradient. Finally, name the one clinical change that would most strongly make you rethink the plan, and say whether it mainly changes shade strategy or the entire restorative concept.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best plan is a conventional full-coverage monolithic crown, preferably in multilayer fourth-generation zirconia, not an endocrown or partial-coverage design. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg support that choice because the preparation is already a crown-type prep with rounded internal geometry and adequate occlusal reduction, and fig_04.jpg confirms a continuous finish line with no undercuts and sufficient space for a monolithic crown. fig_05.jpg argues for keeping occlusal contacts small before glazing while making the proximal contacts slightly more definite, because tight proximal contacts can be refined predictably after glazing, whereas weak contacts are harder to rebuild. fig_06.jpg supports positioning the restoration slightly below the block surface to exploit the built-in color gradient and better match the visible tooth anatomy of the neighboring teeth.

A high-strength glass-ceramic is the main alternative, but zirconia is favored here because the tooth is posterior and endodontically treated, the prep appears consistent with a conservative monolithic crown, and zirconia tolerates thinner sections while still fitting a same-visit workflow. The tradeoffs are that translucent zirconia can show stump color through thin cervical areas and long-term clinical data for these newer multilayer materials are still limited, so material selection and cementation should follow manufacturer guidance closely. The intaglio should be air-abraded with fine alumina and the crown luted with a self-adhesive resin cement.

If the stump were only moderately darker, I would mainly change the shade/masking strategy and block position while staying with zirconia. If the stump were markedly discolored or the cervical walls were too thin to mask it reliably, that would be the point at which I would reconsider the material family or overall restorative concept rather than relying only on shade adjustment.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old odontophobic woman wants a faster esthetic improvement with minimal tooth reduction. fig_01.jpg shows her pretreatment smile and maxillary anterior dentition; she also reports marked cervical sensitivity in the maxillary premolar region. What definitive management strategy would you recommend, and how would you sequence the key steps? Explain why your plan is preferable to other reasonable options for this patient, using the dental, gingival, occlusal, and perioral findings visible in fig_01.jpg, and identify the main risks that must be assessed before and after treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend a conservative interdisciplinary rehabilitation centered on additive bonded anterior restorations after diagnostic validation, rather than an extraction-first or prolonged orthodontic-first pathway. fig_01.jpg suggests bilateral maxillary lateral incisor agenesis with canine substitution, a retained primary canine, a midline diastema, disharmonious gingival levels, and a perioral asymmetry/lip incompetence component. In an adult who is odontophobic and wants rapid change, the best fit is an enamel-preserving plan that repurposes the existing teeth instead of removing them.

The sequence should be: full records and radiographs; occlusal and periodontal assessment, especially probing around the retained 53 before any gingival change; diagnostic wax-up and intraoral mock-up to test tooth proportions, smile width, phonetics, lip support, and patient acceptance; conservative management of the cervical erosive sensitivity and only minimal enamel/interproximal refinement if needed; limited gingival recontouring of 53 only if probing confirms a safe biologic situation; then definitive additive bonded restorations, preferably enamel-based ceramic veneers or equivalent additive restorations, to reshape the substituted canines as lateral incisors, reanatomize the retained primary canine as a canine, close the diastema, lengthen the incisals, and broaden the smile. After the dental framework is finalized, reassess lip support and use filler only as an adjunct for the residual lip incompetence, not as the primary solution.

This is preferable because it preserves tooth structure, suits her anxiety and desire for speed, offers strong esthetic control, and can address tooth form, gingival display, and lip support in a coordinated way. Other options such as orthodontic space redistribution with later replacement, direct composite-only treatment, or extraction-based prosthetic replacement are reasonable in some patients but are less aligned here with her minimal-invasive preference, existing anterior tooth positions, and need for immediate esthetic improvement.

Key risks to assess and monitor are: violating biologic width or creating recession when recontouring the gingiva around 53; uncertain long-term prognosis of the retained primary canine; bond failure or marginal problems when bonding to largely unprepared/aprismatic enamel; occlusal overload or altered anterior guidance after changing incisal length and canine form; persistent cervical sensitivity; and periodontal inflammation if contours or hygiene are unfavorable. Follow-up should check guidance, intercuspation, soft-tissue stability, restoration margins, hygiene access, and patient satisfaction.

items.question_content: Case 1: A 35-year-old man wants a fixed, aesthetic, tooth-preserving solution for his maxillary left central incisor after endodontic treatment. Use fig_01.jpg to decide whether the tooth is restorable and identify the single pre-definitive problem that must be solved before committing to any final prosthesis. Then recommend the definitive restoration you would choose and justify it with at least three findings visible in fig_01.jpg plus one mechanical principle. Finally, explain how your recommendation would change in each of these situations: (i) after soft-tissue healing, enough sound supragingival dentin is available to create a predictable ferrule; (ii) the patient refuses any procedure intended to expose additional tooth structure.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would judge the tooth conditionally restorable, not immediately ready for a definitive prosthesis. The key pre-definitive problem is that the remaining tooth structure is at a very cervical/subgingival level with soft-tissue encroachment, so sound margins and biologic width cannot be predictably managed until additional tooth structure is exposed and the site has healed.

My definitive choice for the case as shown would be a staged custom cast one-piece post-retained crown, i.e., a Richmond-type restoration, after periodontal/soft-tissue management and healing. The justification from fig_01.jpg is: (1) there is very little remaining clinical crown at the fracture level; (2) gingival tissue overlies or closely encroaches on the remnant, making margin control difficult; and (3) this is a maxillary central incisor in an obvious aesthetic zone with spacing/diastema, so contour, emergence, and angulation matter. The mechanical principle is that when coronal tooth structure is minimal, a custom one-piece cast design that follows canal anatomy provides more reliable retention and anti-rotation and avoids creating a very thin separate core that would be mechanically weak. The sequence would be: confirm restorability and endodontic adequacy, expose sound tooth structure with crown-length management, allow healing, prepare post space while preserving the apical seal, fabricate and try in the custom restoration with radiographic verification of passive fit, then cement and adjust occlusion.

If, after healing, enough sound supragingival dentin were available to create a predictable ferrule, my recommendation could shift toward a more conventional separate post-core-crown approach, often favoring a fiber post/core in the aesthetic zone, because the case would no longer depend so heavily on a one-piece cast design for retention and alignment.

If the patient refused any procedure to expose additional tooth structure, I would not proceed directly with definitive crowning. The risks of inadequate ferrule, biologic-width violation, poor periodontal response, decementation, and mechanical failure would be too high. I would discuss the worsened prognosis, consider orthodontic extrusion if acceptable, and reassess whether the tooth can be predictably retained; if not, replacement options would need discussion.

items.question_content:
A 56-year-old woman presents with impaired mastication related to missing mandibular left posterior teeth. The remaining mandibular dentition is extensively restored; no tooth mobility is recorded and probing depths are under 3 mm. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg only.

You are authorizing the definitive data-capture visit for rehabilitation of the mandibular left posterior segment (#34-37). Propose the definitive restorative architecture you would prescribe and justify it against the strongest competing design that a reasonable prosthodontist might still consider. Then give a risk-ranked record and verification workflow that separates: data you would trust from a routine IOS pass, data that require localized recapture or independent verification, and any relationship you would not accept unless it is re-proved clinically at the chair. Tie each decision to specific visual findings in the figures, including the opposing arch. Finally, name one finding that would make you convert only part of the case away from a fully digital pathway, and one finding that would make you defer definitive fabrication entirely.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible architecture is biologically separate tooth-supported and implant-supported restorations: individual crowns on #34 and #37, plus an implant-supported restoration for #35-36. I would not rigidly connect natural teeth to implants across #34-37 because the figures show a mixed-support posterior segment with natural abutments adjacent to implants; the different mobility and load behavior make a tooth-implant-connected fixed segment the weaker choice for maintenance, fit, and long-term biomechanics. A reasonable competing design is a connected #34-37 prosthesis, because it simplifies CAD design and may seem attractive when multiple adjacent units are being fabricated together, but in this patient it is less appropriate than maintaining support independence. Within the implant portion, splinting #35 and #36 is reasonable if passive fit is verified and retrievability is preserved; separate implant crowns could also be defended if access, fit, and occlusion are favorable.

The figures define the workflow. fig_01.jpg shows the opposing arch is a maxillary complete denture, so the highest-risk relationship is not the mandibular geometry alone but the validity of the jaw record against a removable tissue-borne antagonist. fig_02.jpg shows a unilateral posterior edentulous span in a heavily restored mandibular arch, so this is not a routine single-unit digital crown case. fig_03.jpg shows prepared natural teeth adjacent to implant abutments/scan bodies, meaning the tooth margins and the implant positions are being captured under different technical conditions. fig_04.jpg shows a combined digital record is feasible, but it should not be treated as a single uncritical scan event.

Risk-ranked workflow:
1. First, verify the opposing denture can seat fully and repeatably; without that, the occlusal record is unreliable even if the mandibular scan is excellent.
2. Confirm scan-body seating and peri-implant soft-tissue health clinically before scanning; implant geometry is acceptable from IOS only if the components are unquestionably seated.
3. Obtain a full-arch IOS to capture the stable arch form and implant positions.
4. Do not accept the tooth preparation margins from that routine pass if the finish lines are unclear. For #34 and #37, use gingival displacement and localized cut-out/rescan to capture the cervical finish lines without overwriting accepted implant data.
5. Record the maxillary denture separately as the antagonist and obtain the interocclusal record only with the denture in its verified seated position.
6. Before final fabrication, independently verify the implant relationship if there is any doubt about passive fit, for example with a verification jig, printed prototype, or other clinical fit check.

What I trust from a routine IOS pass: overall mandibular arch form and, if clearly seated, implant scan-body geometry. What I would not trust from a routine pass alone: subgingival or equivocal finish lines on #34 and #37, because the figures show prepared natural teeth adjacent to implants and those margins are the deformable boundary in this case. What I would not accept unless clinically re-proved at the chair: the occlusal relationship against the maxillary complete denture, because fig_01.jpg shows a removable opposing prosthesis whose seating can vary.

A finding that would make me convert only part of the case away from a fully digital pathway is unreadable or bleeding tooth margins after retraction; I would keep the implant portion digital if reliable, but use a conventional elastomeric impression for the tooth-supported crowns or a hybrid workflow for those preparations. Another partial-conversion trigger would be uncertainty about scan-body seating, in which case I would switch the implant portion to a verified implant impression or additional verification step while keeping the tooth data digital if sound.

A finding that would make me defer definitive fabrication entirely is non-repeatable seating or closure with the maxillary complete denture. In that situation the entire mandibular definitive occlusal plan is unstable, so even accurate tooth and implant records would be mounted against an unreliable antagonist. I would correct, reline, or remake the denture as needed, or otherwise re-establish a repeatable jaw relation before authorizing definitive zirconia fabrication.

Main complications to prevent are inaccurate tooth margins, misregistered implant position from an unseated scan body, passive-fit error across the implant units, and an occlusal scheme that destabilizes the complete denture. Delivery checks should therefore confirm crown seating and margins on #34 and #37, implant restoration fit and retrievability, radiographic or equivalent confirmation of implant seating as indicated, controlled centric contacts, limited excursive overload on the implant segment, and hygiene access for periodontal and peri-implant maintenance.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes some risks but does not rank them clearly or does not distinguish routine acceptance, independent verification, and deferment thresholds.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a logical, risk-ranked sequence that distinguishes what can be accepted from routine IOS, what needs localized or separate verification, and what must be clinically re-proved before proceeding.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly prioritizes competing vulnerabilities in this case, especially occlusal validity against the removable antagonist versus margin capture and implant transfer accuracy, and gives clear thresholds for partial workflow conversion versus full deferral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully compare benefits and drawbacks of the chosen plan and alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions tradeoffs only generically or without linking them to this patient's findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with a plausible competing design using case-specific tradeoffs such as tooth-implant biomechanics, digital efficiency versus record reliability, retrievability, and occlusal risk against the opposing denture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison that explains not only why the chosen plan is preferable here, but also under what clinical conditions the competing design or a more conventional record pathway could become reasonable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses major technical or biologic failure modes relevant to the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies some complications but without connecting them to prevention, verification, or management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies likely failure modes such as unclear finish lines, uncertain scan-body seating, passive-fit error, unstable denture-based occlusion, overload, or hygiene difficulty, and links them to appropriate prevention or verification steps.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates implant-specific, tooth-specific, and occlusal complications into the plan, including targeted fallback actions for unreliable data and concrete criteria for when definitive fabrication should be postponed.

items.question_content: A 45-year-old woman reports repeatedly loose maxillary anterior crowns and wants a fixed esthetic solution. After removal of the existing restorations, the four maxillary incisors are found to be non-restorable and both canines remain usable abutments. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg. At the stage when the tissue architecture in fig_04.jpg has been created and the digital plan in fig_05.jpg is available, would you proceed with this implant-based reconstruction, modify it, or change the definitive strategy altogether? Defend one choice. Your justification should identify the figure findings that matter most, explain how the non-mirror-image implant distribution affects prosthetic design and papilla expectations, and state why your surgical access should or should not preserve the sculpted tissue exactly as shown. Then describe the provisional/restorative sequence you would use if you proceed, naming the single highest-risk biologic failure in this case and how your design reduces it. End by stating one case-specific threshold that would make you abandon the implant plan for another fixed option.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would proceed with an implant-based reconstruction, but only after confirming that the fig_05.jpg plan remains prosthetically acceptable; I would not accept or reject it on symmetry alone. fig_01.jpg shows a low smile line, which lowers the visibility of small gingival discrepancies but does not remove esthetic risk in the anterior maxilla. fig_02.jpg shows a failed restored incisor segment with posts, recurrent breakdown, and clinical compromise consistent with the incisors being non-restorable, while the canines remain valuable abutments. fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg show that the soft tissue has already been intentionally shaped into stable ovate receiving sites with papillary form and adequate contour. That changes the next decision: preserving this tissue architecture becomes a major priority. fig_05.jpg shows a bone-driven two-implant plan that is not mirror-image; one implant is positioned more laterally on the right and the other more centrally on the left. fig_06.jpg shows access designed to avoid cutting directly through the customized facial tissue margin.

I would accept that non-mirror-image implant pair only if restorative validation shows that the final prosthesis can still have cleansable contours, acceptable emergence, and no excessive cantilever or facial overbulking. In other words, available bone can justify asymmetry, but only within a prosthetic envelope that preserves papilla expectations and hygiene. If the bone-driven positions in fig_05.jpg force an obvious esthetic compromise, such as unstable papillae, overcontoured facial surfaces, or a biomechanically poor span, then I would change course rather than place implants in the wrong positions.

The single most important step for preserving papillae is the tooth-supported provisional phase before implant insertion. That phase allows gradual molding of the pontic sites, testing of cleansability, and stabilization of the scallop before the implants are asked to support the tissue. It is more critical here than rushing to immediate implant provisionalization.

If proceeding, my sequence is: atraumatic extraction of the hopeless incisors, ridge/socket preservation and seal, immediate fixed canine-supported provisional with light initial ovate contact and open cleansable embrasures, then serial refinements until the soft tissue reaches the stable architecture seen in fig_04.jpg. Only after that would I place the implants in the validated fig_05.jpg positions. I would not immediately load the implants; I would keep the canine-supported provisional during osseointegration so the developed tissue form is not lost. After integration, I would transfer that established contour to a screw-retained implant provisional and then to the definitive implant prosthesis. The canines should remain restored separately rather than splinting natural teeth to implants.

For surgical access, I would favor a conservative open-flap approach like fig_06.jpg rather than a routine punch or a blind flapless approach. Once the tissue has been sculpted, simply choosing the least invasive-looking approach is not automatically best. A tissue punch would discard the customized scallop, and flapless placement could jeopardize implant position or damage the shaped tissue if visualization is inadequate. An incision placed away from the prepared facial margin better protects the contour while still allowing direct control of osteotomy position and irrigation.

The highest-risk biologic failure is loss of the sculpted soft-tissue architecture through inflammation and collapse, driven by overpressure, plaque-retentive provisional contours, premature loading, or surgical injury to the prepared margin. I would reduce that risk with light initial pontic pressure, progressive rather than aggressive reshaping, highly polished and cleansable provisional contours, maintenance of the tooth-supported provisional during healing, delayed implant loading, and screw-retained implant provisionalization to avoid subgingival cement.

My threshold to abandon the implant plan would be this: if the validated fig_05.jpg positions require a final prosthesis with clearly overcontoured facial emergence, poor papilla predictability, or an unacceptable cantilever/implant span for the four-incisor replacement, I would stop and select another fixed strategy, most likely a canine-supported bridge, because that would be more esthetically and biologically predictable in this patient.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic answer or misreads major figure-based findings. Does not meaningfully use the figures to support the recommendation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figure details but incompletely or in isolation. May mention smile line, tissue contour, or implant planning without correctly linking fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg/fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg to the final recommendation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the key figure findings into the decision: fig_01.jpg low smile display as an esthetic modifier, fig_02.jpg as evidence of a compromised incisor segment with usable canines, fig_03.jpg/fig_04.jpg as evidence of matured pre-implant tissue architecture, fig_05.jpg as a non-mirror-image bone-driven implant plan, and fig_06.jpg as tissue-conscious surgical access.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes those findings into a single patient-specific rationale, including why the established tissue form changes surgical priorities and why the fig_05.jpg asymmetry may be acceptable only if the prosthetic envelope, papilla expectations, and hygiene remain favorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not make a clear proceed/modify/abandon decision, or bases the decision on superficial factors such as symmetry or speed alone.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Makes a choice but gives only generic justification, or does not define a concrete threshold for changing to another fixed strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Makes and defends a clear go/no-go decision that prioritizes esthetic predictability, biologic stability, and prosthetic feasibility. States one case-specific threshold that would justify abandoning the implant plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows nuanced prioritization by distinguishing acceptable from unacceptable compromise in the fig_05.jpg plan, such as when asymmetry is tolerable versus when emergence, papilla support, or span biomechanics become unacceptable and should trigger a change in strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate or incomplete sequence that omits major phases or would not realistically preserve the esthetic result.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for staged care and provisionalization but gives an incomplete sequence or weak rationale for timing and transfer of tissue contour.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a coherent stepwise plan from extraction-site preservation and canine-supported provisional sculpting through implant placement after tissue maturation, maintenance during osseointegration, transfer to an implant provisional, and definitive restoration. Avoids splinting implants to natural teeth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds clear progression logic and explains why the pre-implant provisional phase is the critical step for papilla control, tissue testing, and hygiene validation before implant loading.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh meaningful case-specific tradeoffs, or gives one-sided claims unsupported by the figures and case facts.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general pros and cons of implants or provisionals but does not analyze the important tradeoffs in this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances at least two relevant tradeoffs, such as accepting the fig_05.jpg support distribution versus changing strategy, or conservative open-flap access versus flapless or punch approaches after tissue sculpting.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced appraisal showing why low smile display slightly widens esthetic tolerance without eliminating risk, and why protecting the created tissue may still favor a conservative open approach over apparently less invasive alternatives.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses important biologic complications or proposes steps that would predictably jeopardize tissue stability or implant success.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists complications in general terms but does not identify the main biologic vulnerability in this case or how the plan specifically addresses it.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the main biologic vulnerability as loss of the sculpted tissue through inflammation, plaque retention, overpressure, premature manipulation, or surgical injury, and gives concrete preventive measures.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates how provisional contour, cleansability, incision placement, delayed loading, and screw-retained provisionalization work together to preserve papillae and reduce peri-implant soft-tissue complications.

items.question_content:
A 53-year-old woman seeks replacement of an intolerable maxillary single complete denture. Routine radiography shows severe maxillary resorption without other pathology. Surgical management is not being pursued. fig_01.jpg shows the current arches, fig_02.jpg the previous opposing prosthetic arrangement, and fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg the tray/impression system.

You have only one chance to make the definitive maxillary impression today if you judge the tissues suitable. Based on the figures and case details, choose your next step and justify it.

In your answer, state: whether you would complete the definitive impression today or stage tissue management first, and the specific finding that controls that timing decision; how you would differentially record the stable and mobile maxillary tissues, including the figure-based design features that make this method preferable here but still technique-sensitive; the single most important non-impression factor that must be corrected in the opposing arch/prosthetic plan to protect prognosis; and how your definitive impression strategy would change if the anterior flabby tissue were absent but the maxilla remained severely resorbed.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not commit to the full definitive maxillary impression today unless the anterior vestibular tissues are first made reproducible. fig_01.jpg shows anterior vestibular soft-tissue redundancy/epulis fissuratum adjacent to the mobile premaxillary ridge. If that tissue is still inflamed or distorted, recording it definitively today risks building a distorted labial flange into the denture. My priority would be tissue rest with relief of the existing prosthesis and, if needed, tissue conditioning, then a return visit for the final border capture. If the posterior tissues were healthy, they could potentially be assessed or preliminarily recorded, but I would avoid finalizing the anterior flange under distortion.

Once the tissues are suitable, I would use a two-stage custom double-tray differential-pressure impression. The firm posterior palate and non-flabby ridge are recorded first with a rigid custom tray and border molding while the mobile anterior segment is relieved/excluded from compressive capture. Before reseating, any excess first-stage material over the flabby area must be removed so it cannot drag or preload the mobile tissues. The first tray is then reseated on the stable tissues, and the keyed second tray is positioned. The feature that makes fig_03.jpg-fig_05.jpg different from a simple unsupported window is the supported second tray keyed to the first, creating an even space over the flabby ridge; the perforations vent excess material. That allows light-body VPS to be injected through a controlled, tray-supported gap, reducing displacement of the flabby ridge and reducing distortion of the wash during seating, removal, and cast pouring. It is still technique-sensitive because inaccurate keying, residual excess material, or overfilling can mis-seat the assembly or compress the tissue.

The most important factor outside the impression is the opposing arch biomechanics: this is a maxillary single denture opposing remaining mandibular teeth and a mandibular prosthesis. If posterior support is not properly re-established and anterior contacts are not controlled, the new denture remains at risk of anterior tipping and premaxillary overload, similar to combination-syndrome-type mechanics. The planned mandibular RPD should restore posterior support, and jaw relations and occlusal scheme should minimize destabilizing anterior loading.

If the anterior flabby tissue were absent but the maxilla were still severely resorbed, I would not use the windowed double-tray recording of a separate mobile segment. I would switch to a conventional rigid custom-tray selective-pressure impression for the whole arch, with careful border control and uniform material thickness suited to an atrophic maxilla. Severe resorption alone still requires excellent tray support and controlled extension, but it does not require separate mucostatic capture of a flabby anterior ridge when that mobile tissue is no longer present.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures or case details meaningfully, or misreads the clinical problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the soft-tissue findings or the tray/impression figures, but does not connect them coherently to timing and design of the definitive impression.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg with fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg by linking the anterior mobile/distorted tissues to a staged, two-part impression approach and identifying the keyed second tray/supported space or venting features.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly interprets the clinical and figure-based evidence together, including the timing implication of the anterior vestibular tissue condition and the roles of key/keyway seating, controlled uniform space, perforation venting, and first-stage versus second-stage recording in minimizing displacement and distortion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate conventional compressive impression, stock-tray approach, or no workable definitive plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a low-pressure concept but provides incomplete sequencing, does not clearly separate recording of stable and mobile tissues, or does not address how the plan changes if flabby tissue is absent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides an appropriate staged plan: manage distorted anterior tissues before definitive capture if needed, record stable tissues first, then record the flabby segment separately with low-viscosity material through the supported second stage; also states an appropriate simpler approach if flabby tissue is absent.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a clear, stepwise plan that includes tissue rest/relief or conditioning when indicated, avoidance of definitive distorted flange capture, removal of excess first-stage material before reseating, accurate use of the keyed double tray for the flabby segment, and a justified switch to a conventional rigid custom-tray selective-pressure impression when the flabby tissue is absent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not make or justify a decision about whether the definitive impression should be completed today.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Makes a timing decision but supports it only with generic rules or without identifying the controlling clinical finding.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the condition of the anterior vestibular tissues in fig_01.jpg as the key determinant of timing and makes a defensible decision to delay full definitive capture or narrowly limit what is recorded that day.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes tissue health and reproducible border anatomy over same-day completion, explicitly explaining what should not be definitively recorded while distorted and, if relevant, what stable areas could still be managed safely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no case-specific rationale for the chosen design or for changing the plan when the scenario changes.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States only generic advantages such as 'less pressure' without explaining the supported-space benefit or the altered scenario.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a tray-supported, vented, uniform-thickness low-viscosity recording is advantageous in this case and how the strategy would appropriately simplify if the flabby tissue were absent.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Weighs benefits and limitations of the double-tray approach in this patient, including residual technique sensitivity such as mis-seating, overfilling, or drag, and contrasts those risks with the more conventional whole-arch approach appropriate when the mobile anterior segment is absent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify a major non-impression threat to the long-term result.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions vague risks such as instability or sore spots without tying them to the opposing dentition/prosthetic arrangement.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies maxillary single-denture biomechanics against the remaining mandibular teeth/prosthesis as the main threat and links this to anterior tipping or premaxillary overload.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies the major biomechanical threat and pairs it with concrete preventive measures such as restoring posterior mandibular support with the planned RPD, recording accurate jaw relations, and minimizing destabilizing anterior contacts.

items.question_content: Patient 1 is a 50-year-old woman with chewing difficulty and sensitivity from worn mandibular right posterior teeth after a long history of frequent pickle intake; medical history is unremarkable. Patient 2 is a 58-year-old woman with cold sensitivity and impaired chewing at a mandibular right molar; she has hypertension controlled with atenolol and frequently eats pineapple. In both patients, the likely erosive habit has been addressed, the symptomatic tooth/teeth are vital, periodontally healthy, radiographically free of apical disease, and there is little restorative space. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide the definitive management you would provide for each patient. In your answer, identify the figure-based features that make the two cases require different restorative designs, state whether you would use a localized supra-occlusal definitive restoration or a different space-gaining strategy, specify the key tooth/restoration-surface modification needed before placement, reject one reasonable alternative for each case, and explain how your plan for the fig_02.jpg tooth would change if there were minimal remaining enamel and a clear nocturnal parafunction history. Also name the main early complication(s) you would monitor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Patient 1 is best managed with adhesive indirect metal onlays on the worn mandibular right molars, used as definitive restorations in localized supra-occlusion (a one-stage Dahl approach). fig_01.jpg shows a more extensive posterior problem than a simple isolated cup: there is advanced structural loss across the mandibular right posterior segment, short clinical crowns, and limited restorative space. In a high-load posterior segment with substantial loss, indirect metal is more predictable than a large direct build-up because it works reliably at thin section, preserves tooth tissue, and avoids the higher risk of bulk fracture, wear, polymerization shrinkage stress, and marginal leakage associated with a large supra-occlusal direct composite. The key surface modification is minimal enamel-preserving preparation with supragingival enamel margins and adhesive retention rather than aggressive mechanical retention. A reasonable alternative I would reject here is a large direct multi-tooth composite build-up, because the defect size and posterior load make long-term marginal and bulk failure more likely.

Patient 2 is best managed with a direct bonded composite occlusal onlay/build-up placed in localized supra-occlusion as the definitive restoration. fig_02.jpg shows a single mandibular right first molar with moderate occlusal cupping and a proud existing amalgam rather than the extensive multi-tooth breakdown seen in fig_01.jpg. The remaining enamel rim makes adhesive direct restoration realistic and conservative for an isolated defect. The key modification before placement is to remove the proud amalgam rather than bonding around it, so the bonded surface area can be improved and the additive build-up can be shaped predictably. A reasonable alternative I would reject here is a conventional full-coverage approach or any more extensive occlusal intervention for a localized, vital tooth, because it would remove additional tooth structure to solve a space problem that can be managed more conservatively.

A localized supra-occlusal definitive restoration is appropriate in both cases because the wear is localized, symptoms justify treatment, the etiologic habit has been addressed, the teeth are vital and periodontally sound, and there is no apical disease; the key issue is limited restorative space rather than generalized occlusal collapse.

If the fig_02.jpg tooth had minimal remaining enamel and clear nocturnal parafunction, direct composite would become less predictable. I would shift toward an indirect adhesive restoration better suited to high load and reduced bonding substrate, or I would defer/modify the localized supra-occlusal plan until parafunction is managed and the bonding prognosis is reassessed. If the substrate were too compromised, I would reconsider whether this tooth is an appropriate direct additive Dahl case at all.

Main early complications to monitor are tolerance of the altered bite, delayed or absent re-establishment of occlusal contacts, restoration fracture/debonding/wear, postoperative sensitivity or pulpal symptoms, and TMJ/muscle or periodontal symptoms. Lack of progressive occlusal re-establishment or worsening symptoms should prompt reassessment of the design and case selection.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the history and figures to distinguish the two cases, or misreads the visual findings in a way that undermines the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant information, but the answer relies mostly on generic wear-management points and misses major figure-based differences that affect substrate, extent, or loading.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the key non-visual findings with the figure-based difference between extensive multi-tooth posterior structural loss in fig_01.jpg and an isolated moderately cupped molar with an existing standing restoration in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes history, vitality, periodontal/apical status, limited space, and the figure-based differences into a coherent rationale that explicitly links defect extent and bonding substrate to restoration design and suitability for localized supra-occlusal management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not provide a defensible definitive plan for one or both patients, or proposes essentially the same generic restoration for both without case-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes conservative localized management but mismatches the restoration type to the case, omits whether supra-occlusal management is intended, or fails to state the key surface/preparation modification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects adhesive indirect metal onlays for the worn mandibular right molars in fig_01.jpg and a direct bonded composite occlusal build-up/onlay for the fig_02.jpg molar, using a localized supra-occlusal definitive approach, with broadly correct rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the correct patient-specific plans and clearly specifies the execution details that make them appropriate: enamel-preserving supragingival adhesive preparation for fig_01.jpg and removal of the proud amalgam to improve the bonding substrate before direct additive restoration in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh meaningful risks, benefits, or alternatives for the proposed interventions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives generic advantages or disadvantages without tying them to defect size, occlusal load, substrate, or conservatism in these specific patients.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why the chosen approach is preferable to at least one reasonable alternative for each case, using patient-specific reasoning about tooth preservation, defect extent, bonded substrate, posterior loading, repairability, or durability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: In addition to case-specific comparison of alternatives, correctly changes the fig_02.jpg plan when remaining enamel is minimal and parafunction is present by recognizing that direct composite becomes less predictable and that a different indirect or deferred strategy with risk control may be needed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits meaningful early complications or follow-up concerns.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions follow-up in vague terms but does not identify the main early failure modes relevant to localized supra-occlusal treatment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies at least two relevant early concerns, such as altered-bite intolerance, fracture or debonding, restoration wear, sensitivity, or delayed occlusal contact re-establishment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a focused monitoring plan that includes altered-bite or TMJ/muscle symptoms, failure or delay of occlusal re-establishment, restoration fracture/debonding/wear, and pulpal or periodontal symptoms, and states that these findings should trigger reassessment of the plan.

items.question_content: A 52-year-old fit and healthy woman has a maxillary central incisor with repeated crown dislodgement over 7 years and tenderness on palpation and percussion. fig_01.jpg shows the pre-operative appearance/radiograph, and fig_02.jpg shows the fabrication concept. The tooth is considered non-restorable and will be extracted before later implant rehabilitation. What immediate provisionalization would best preserve esthetics and function without loading the healing site? State how it should sit in occlusion, name one pre-delivery cast/lab verification step, and give two arch/occlusal situations where this approach should be avoided or reconsidered.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Choose a bonded acrylic tooth splint: an acrylic denture tooth trimmed on the cast to the post-extraction contour, then splinted to the adjacent teeth with wire and composite on the palatal/lingual surfaces. It should be kept completely out of centric and excursive occlusion, with no premature contacts.

Before delivery, verify on the cast that the pontic fits the edentulous space and that the wire/composite assembly can be adapted with enough clearance for static and dynamic occlusion.

fig_01.jpg supports a hopeless prognosis: repeated crown failure, severe mobility, infection/pus, deep localized pocketing, periapical/endodontic pathology, and fracture/failure of the root-support complex. This option should be avoided or reconsidered in deep overbite, crowded or malaligned adjacent teeth, limited palatal/lingual space, or parafunction, because these increase interference, overload, and debonding risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg or fails to recognize the tooth as non-restorable.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes extraction/provisionalization but cites only generic symptoms or only one figure finding.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the history with fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg to support a hopeless prognosis and the need for pre-fabricated immediate provisionalization; notes several relevant findings such as severe mobility, infection/pocketing, periapical or root-fracture pathology, and the cast-based design shown in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends no clear provisional plan or an unrelated/removable option without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a fixed temporary tooth replacement but omits a key design feature such as palatal/lingual fixation, cast adaptation, or occlusal clearance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Selects a bonded acrylic tooth splint or equivalent fixed acrylic pontic splinted to adjacent teeth, with preoperative cast adaptation and placement out of centric and excursive contacts to preserve esthetics while protecting the healing site.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not explain why this option is prioritized in this patient.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one benefit such as esthetics or function but does not connect it to healing-site protection or chairside practicality.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why this fixed provisional is preferred for immediate esthetics/function while avoiding loading the extraction site and minimizing chairside time before or at the extraction visit.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not name a valid limitation or names an unrelated issue.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names one limitation but does not explain the mechanism of failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies deep overbite, crowded or malaligned adjacent teeth, limited palatal/lingual space, or parafunction and links these to interference, overload, or dislodgement risk.

items.question_content:
A 24-year-old healthy woman is referred after root canal treatment of maxillary tooth 17. She wants to keep the tooth if the long-term trade-off is reasonable and prefers to avoid surgery or extraction unless they clearly improve predictability. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg only; do not assume the definitive treatment that was later provided.

From these figures, rank the case's 3 main restorability constraints from greatest to least: occlusal clearance/restorative thickness, ferrule or maintainable margin access, and root-level prognosis. Justify the ranking with specific figure findings.

Then recommend your first-choice definitive restoration and name the single most credible alternative that another experienced clinician might reasonably select for this tooth. Compare the 2 approaches in terms of tooth preservation, retention/resistance, likely failure mode, and periodontal consequences.

Finally, state 1 specific chairside finding that would make you escalate to a margin-gaining procedure, 1 that would make you extract, and 1 unverified datum at the preparation appointment that is most decisive for whether your preferred plan remains acceptable.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The dominant constraint is occlusal clearance/restorative thickness. fig_01.jpg shows very limited space to the opposing dentition in the posterior segment, so a conventional full crown would require reduction that is difficult to obtain without further weakening the remaining tooth or compromising restorative thickness. The second constraint is ferrule/maintainable margin access. fig_02.jpg shows a severely broken-down maxillary second molar with minimal residual axial wall height and broad coronal loss, making a predictable circumferential ferrule for a conventional crown doubtful and leaving adhesive margin quality dependent on what is found chairside after cleanup. The least important of the three is root-level prognosis. fig_03.jpg shows a root-treated tooth whose roots appear maintainable, without obvious periapical disease or a radiographic reason to judge the tooth hopeless; the problem is mainly coronal biomechanics and restorability, not root prognosis.

My first-choice definitive restoration is non-surgical chamber-retained cuspal coverage, preferably a cast metal endocrown/endocoronal metal restoration. It best fits a very short molar with minimal clearance because thin-section metal can function predictably where ceramics are thickness-sensitive, and chamber retention avoids unnecessary post preparation in a pulpless molar. The design should provide complete cuspal coverage, a flat supracervical butt-joint margin where sound tooth structure permits, rounded internal line angles, retention from the pulp chamber rather than intraradicular posts, internal correction of undercuts with bonded resin if needed, adhesive or self-adhesive resin cementation, and careful occlusal adjustment.

The most credible alternative is a margin-gaining procedure, typically crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion, followed by a conventional full-coverage crown with a core. That alternative may improve ferrule and traditional resistance form, but it costs more tissue, may worsen crown-root ratio, can create posterior periodontal and cleansability problems, and in a molar may risk furcation-related compromise. Its failure pattern is more likely to involve further biologic and structural sacrifice; adding a post may also introduce radicular risk without strengthening the tooth. By contrast, the endocoronal metal option is more conservative and better matched to the clearance problem, although its main vulnerability is adhesive/interface failure if isolation or margin quality is poor.

A finding that would shift me toward a margin-gaining procedure is inability to obtain a continuous, maintainable, isolatable cervical margin on sound tooth structure after removal of the temporary material and caries. A finding that would shift me to extraction is a crack or structural defect extending into the furcation/root, or another non-restorable subgingival defect that cannot be predictably exposed without destroying prognosis. The single most decisive unverified datum at the preparation appointment is whether a circumferential bonded margin can be established and isolated predictably; that determines whether a conservative adhesive endocoronal plan is feasible at all.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use the provided figures, or bases the answer on generic endocrown principles without case-specific visual evidence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses limited figure information and identifies only one broad problem area, or misranks the major constraints without linking them to specific visual findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the figures to identify severe coronal compromise and a radiographically maintainable root/endodontic status, with a mostly plausible ranking of the major restorability constraints.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly ranks occlusal clearance/restorative thickness and ferrule or maintainable margin access ahead of root-level prognosis, and justifies that ranking with specific observations from both the clinical image and the radiographs.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends a clearly unsuitable definitive plan, or does not provide a workable restorative strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends cuspal coverage or an endocoronal approach only in generic terms, with little case-linked rationale or inappropriate material selection for the observed constraints.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a non-surgical chamber-retained cuspal-coverage restoration and links it to conservative retention of a severely broken-down root-treated molar.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically justifies a thin-section cast metal endocoronal restoration as the preferred plan for this short, clearance-limited molar and describes the key preparation and bonding features needed for it to succeed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify a credible alternative or compares options inaccurately.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative plan but compares it superficially or without patient-specific trade-offs.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the preferred plan with one plausible alternative using at least two relevant dimensions such as tooth preservation, periodontal cost, retention/resistance, radicular risk, or expected failure mode.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies a credible competing plan, such as a margin-gaining procedure followed by a conventional crown, and clearly explains why its biologic and mechanical trade-offs are less favorable now, including posterior periodontal or furcation consequences and differing failure patterns.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not state when management should change, or gives unsafe or irrelevant triggers.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides vague or incomplete thresholds for changing to surgery or extraction, or does not identify a decisive missing chairside datum.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions without a traceable rationale.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some reasoning, but key links between figure interpretation, ranking, and treatment choice are missing or inconsistent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a generally logical progression from figure findings to ranking of constraints, restorative choice, and threshold findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a clear, internally consistent chain of reasoning from figure-based interpretation to prioritization of constraints, preferred restoration, competing alternative, and contingency thresholds.

items.question_content: An 18-year-old woman with bilateral complete cleft of the primary and secondary palate presents after completion of surgical and orthodontic care. She is dissatisfied with her removable partial denture and requests a fixed rehabilitation. Bone quantity/quality in the premaxillary region is inadequate for implants, while the remaining posterior maxillary teeth are serviceable as abutments. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg, formulate the most defensible definitive prosthodontic plan. Use figure-derived findings to explain why this anatomy is unfavorable for a conventional fixed solution, what specific design modification makes a fixed approach acceptable here, how the prosthesis should replace both tissue and tooth loss while preserving biomechanics, and how you would protect it occlusally. Also identify the major design-specific failure that must be excluded before final cementation and state how your recommendation would change if the anterior segment could not be kept out of functional contact.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible plan is a custom tooth-supported fixed prosthesis that replaces the missing premaxillary teeth plus the lost hard and soft tissue, built on a lightweight hollow metal substructure rather than a solid long-span bridge. fig_01.jpg shows a large anterior cleft-related premaxillary deficiency with only posterior teeth available for support, so a conventional solid fixed prosthesis would create excessive weight and leverage on a limited number of abutments while still needing to restore lip support and palatal contour. fig_02.jpg shows the amount of ridge/tissue replacement required; fig_03.jpg and especially fig_04.jpg demonstrate the key modification that makes a fixed option biomechanically acceptable: a hollow intaglio/substructure to reduce mass. fig_05.jpg shows that this hollow compartment must be sealed; fig_06.jpg shows the palatal replacement and final fixed configuration.

The prosthesis should restore the anterior teeth, premaxillary bulk, labial support, and palatal form needed for esthetics, phonetics, and mastication, while using the healthy posterior teeth as abutments. The reason to hollow the prosthetic premaxillary segment is to reduce weight, improve retention biomechanics, and decrease cantilever-like stress on the abutments. Occlusion should be protective: stable posterior support, reduced incisal loading, minimal or no functional contact on the prosthetic anterior segment, and avoidance of heavy horizontal forces; keeping the incisors out of occlusion is ideal in this case.

Before final cementation, the major design-specific failure that must be excluded is leakage into the hollow segment from an inadequate seal or porosity. In addition, passive fit, clearance, phonetics, esthetics, and hygiene access should be checked. Follow-up should monitor soft-tissue health, retention/debonding, abutment overload, fracture/chipping, and evidence of fluid ingress.

If the anterior segment could not be kept out of functional contact, I would be much less willing to proceed with this tooth-supported fixed design because anterior guidance and horizontal loading would markedly increase the risk of overload, debonding, and material failure. In that altered situation, a removable or combined prosthetic approach would become more appropriate despite the patient's fixed preference.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Selects an inappropriate definitive approach or gives only a generic prosthesis label without a workable plan for this defect, tissue loss, and abutment pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a broadly plausible prosthetic option but does not show how it would replace the missing premaxillary tissues and teeth while remaining mechanically feasible.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a patient-specific fixed tissue-replacing prosthesis supported by the remaining posterior teeth and explains the need for protective occlusion and controlled loading.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly recommends a custom lightweight hollow fixed tissue-replacing prosthesis, explains why hollowing is the key modification that makes a fixed plan feasible in this anatomy, and appropriately changes the plan if anterior functional contact cannot be avoided.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is disconnected from the clinical history and figures, or does not use the available evidence to support the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts or figure details, but misses important implications of the defect extent, tissue loss, or figure sequence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the patient's preference, implant limitation, serviceable posterior abutments, and figure-based defect morphology into a coherent justification for the chosen prosthesis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg with the history to explain the extent of tissue replacement needed, the hollow design rationale, the palatal/labial support requirements, and the occlusal strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh patient-specific tradeoffs or ignores major constraints affecting definitive treatment choice.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some advantages or disadvantages but gives a shallow analysis of why the selected approach is preferable in this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances patient preference, implant infeasibility, remaining tooth preservation, and the biomechanical burden of the defect when defending the plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced judgment that explains why a fixed approach is acceptable only with weight reduction and protective occlusion, and correctly shifts toward a removable or combined option if anterior loading cannot be controlled.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major foreseeable technical or biologic complications and provides no meaningful verification or follow-up plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only generic risks or monitoring points without linking them to this prosthesis design.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recognizes relevant complications such as poor fit, occlusal overload, hygiene-related inflammation, debonding, or material failure, and includes sensible checks before delivery and during follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
