items.question_content: A 50-year-old woman seeks functional rehabilitation with limited esthetic demands. She declines implant surgery and has financial constraints. Clinical records show maxillary Kennedy class II edentulism (#14-17, #22-23, #27), mandibular Kennedy class II edentulism (#36-37), a satisfactory existing bridge replacing #46, and no need to increase OVD. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, then state the definitive prosthodontic plan you would choose and outline the key digital and clinical steps needed to fabricate distal-extension RPDs that will fit accurately with the fixed restorations. In your answer, justify the abutment/restoration design and explain the main limitation of a scan-only digital workflow for the edentulous saddle areas.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would choose a combined fixed-removable rehabilitation rather than implants because the patient refuses surgery and has cost limits, while the remaining teeth can still serve as strategic abutments. No OVD increase is indicated because restorative space is adequate. In the maxilla, I would restore the anterior segment with splinted metal-ceramic crowns/FDP from #13 to #21 and place an extracoronal attachment on #13 to provide esthetic retention for the maxillary RPD without a visible clasp. The posterior maxillary abutments would receive splinted monolithic zirconia crowns. Because the maxillary abutments are endodontically treated, teeth with insufficient coronal structure should receive CAD/CAM anatomic post-and-cores before definitive crowns. In the mandible, I would retain the satisfactory #46 bridge, perform limited coronoplasty of #44 if needed to harmonize the occlusal plane, and fabricate a mandibular Kennedy II RPD for #36-37. The key digital step is not to rely on IOS alone for distal-extension saddles. I would use the virtual patient workflow for wax-up and occlusion, then reline the interim or well-fitting RPDs intraorally with impression material to capture functional tissue displacement and border molding. After a validation period, I would scan the arches with and without the prostheses, record the MMR, scan the relined RPDs extraorally, and merge the datasets using stable palatal landmarks so the edentulous ridge areas on the virtual cast are replaced by the relined intaglio surfaces. Definitive FDPs are designed first; then those FDPs are rescanned on the cast so the RPD framework, teeth, clasps, and attachment housing are designed to the definitive fixed contours and occlusion. A scan-only saddle workflow risks failure to record functional mucosa and extension, causing poor support, retention, and stability, tissue soreness, altered occlusion or MMR errors, misfit between RPD and fixed components, and greater maintenance or remake risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes a plan fundamentally inconsistent with the case, such as extraction-based or implant-centered treatment despite stated preferences/constraints, or fails to coordinate fixed and removable components. Omits management of the endodontically treated maxillary abutments and the distal-extension saddle problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects a broadly mixed rehabilitation but with important flaws or omissions, such as no clear abutment strategy, no rationale for attachment use, incorrect sequencing of FDP/RPD fabrication, or unnecessary OVD change.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses an appropriate combined FDP/RPD plan that matches the patient's constraints, preserves the satisfactory #46 bridge, avoids unnecessary OVD change, and includes an esthetic retention strategy for the maxillary RPD plus appropriate restoration of compromised maxillary abutments.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a fully coherent stepwise plan: maxillary fixed segment with extracoronal attachment, posterior splinted crowns, mandibular Kennedy II RPD, post-and-core use when coronal structure is inadequate, interim validation, and definitive RPD design only after definitive fixed contours are established.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or none of the case data or misreads the radiographic/workflow information.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Incorporates some case facts but misses several major planning drivers, such as the endodontically treated maxillary dentition, Kennedy II distal-extension anatomy, or the preserved OVD.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the key findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg and the scenario: multiple endodontically treated maxillary teeth, distal-extension edentulism, adequate restorative space, existing serviceable mandibular bridge, and patient preference/cost constraints.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the above with the digital workflow logic, including stable landmarks for merging, preservation of MMR across stages, and the role of dynamic occlusal records in coordinating the fixed and removable prostheses.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores patient-specific benefits and drawbacks.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers only superficial justification, such as stating implants are expensive or that RPDs are cheaper, without discussing esthetics, conservation, or abutment implications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a fixed-removable solution is preferable here versus implants, why an extracoronal attachment is advantageous over a visible anterior clasp, and why maintaining the existing OVD is appropriate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds nuanced trade-offs, such as prerequisites and limits of the digital altered-cast approach, options if no well-fitting interim RPD existed, and material/abutment-loading considerations for the definitive restorations.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses the principal complications relevant to distal-extension digital prosthodontics and abutment protection.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic fit or soreness issues but does not connect them to the missing functional impression data or fixed-removable interface.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the main risks of a scan-only workflow for extension bases: failure to capture tissue displacement and border molding, over- or underextension, poor support/retention/stability, mucosal soreness, occlusal discrepancy, and misfit against the fixed units or attachment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also recognizes longer-term issues such as attachment/clasp wear or retightening, hygiene and periodontal maintenance around crowned endodontically treated abutments, and overload risk if the saddle does not provide adequate support.

items.question_content: A 55-year-old woman on anticoagulants with hyperthyroidism needs a single-unit PFM crown on an endodontically treated maxillary molar. The tooth is asymptomatic, has adequate remaining structure, and the periapical radiograph shows satisfactory obturation with no periapical pathology. The gingiva is delicate and accurate recording of the finish line is a concern. Examining fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, what impression strategy would you choose for this preparation, and why is it the best option in this patient? Justify your plan using the clinically important design features visible in the figures and explain how the approach improves both tissue safety and marginal accuracy compared with other reasonable options.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would use a customized provisional-crown impression technique rather than routine traumatic gingival displacement. This patient has two important risk modifiers: anticoagulant use increases bleeding risk, and hyperthyroidism makes adrenergic chemicomechanical retraction less attractive. An atraumatic pressure-based approach is therefore preferable if the tooth is otherwise restorable, which it is: the molar is asymptomatic, has adequate coronal structure, and the endodontic result is acceptable with no apical disease.

Using the preformed provisional shell as a custom matrix, I would trim and adapt it to the prepared tooth, then modify it as shown in fig_02.jpg with a buccal guiding groove for repeatable seating and retention/control of the wash, plus an occlusal vent so excess light-body PVS can escape rather than hydraulically preventing full seating. I would load the shell with light-body silicone, seat it firmly to create gentle sulcular displacement and carry the material around the finish line, then make a pick-up impression with putty/heavy body.

This is the best choice here because it minimizes cord packing, chemical exposure, and surgical trauma, so it reduces bleeding, postoperative recession risk, and patient discomfort. It also improves accuracy because the provisional shell functions like a custom tray, limiting the bulk of light-body material, which reduces distortion and shrinkage and helps produce a clearer marginal record, as the cast in fig_03.jpg suggests. Other reasonable options such as conventional cord, paste, or digital scanning may be possible in some patients, but in this patient they are less attractive because they either increase tissue trauma/bleeding risk or may not expose and control the sulcus as predictably when the tissue is fragile.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not choose an appropriate impression approach for this patient, or proposes a generic/invasive plan without a coherent sequence. Omits the core concept of using a customized provisional shell to carry the wash and obtain the final impression.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a plausible impression method but the plan is incomplete, poorly sequenced, or misses key procedural elements such as customizing the provisional shell, loading it with light-body material, or using a pick-up impression.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a provisional-crown/customized shell impression strategy and gives an appropriate stepwise rationale: fabricate/adapt shell, place light-body material, seat it to displace tissue and record the margin, then use a pick-up impression.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, case-appropriate plan and clearly explains the functional purpose of the shell modifications, material sequencing, seating control, and how the technique acts as an atraumatic custom-tray approach for a single prepared tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the significance of anticoagulant use and hyperthyroidism, or recommends methods with avoidable bleeding or systemic risk without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the patient is medically higher risk but discusses the implications superficially or incompletely, with limited comparison to other reasonable approaches.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that a minimally traumatic method is preferred because of bleeding risk and tissue fragility, and notes that chemicomechanical approaches using adrenergic agents are less desirable in hyperthyroidism.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances safety, accuracy, comfort, and practicality; explicitly explains why the chosen pressure-based method is better suited than other reasonable options in this specific patient, not just in general.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Makes assertions with little or no use of the clinical facts or misinterprets the figures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical data or some figure information, but does not integrate them into a coherent justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the key case facts appropriately: restorable endodontically treated molar, adequate remaining tooth structure, no periapical pathology, and figure-based recognition of a customized shell and impression-related modifications.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the history, radiographic status, restorability, and the figure-derived features of the shell, groove, vent, and resulting cast into one clear argument for the selected approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful technical or biological risks associated with the impression procedure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one or two generic problems such as bleeding or distortion without linking them to prevention in this technique.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant risks such as incomplete seating, trapped excess material, marginal voids, wash overbulk, or tissue trauma, and gives practical preventive steps.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates both biologic and technical complications and explains how the groove, vent, seating pressure, moisture control, and post-impression inspection help prevent an inaccurate or traumatic result.

items.question_content: A 35-year-old woman has food lodgment between 44 and 45. A 25-year-old man has food lodgment involving 36, 37, 46, and 47. Radiographs show crown-confined caries without pulpal involvement; 45 is enamel-limited, whereas 44, 36, 37, 46, and 47 extend into dentin. Using fig_01.jpg, formulate the restorative plan you would carry out to recover function while keeping the approach as conservative as predictably possible. For each tooth group, state what you would use as the reference for final occlusal anatomy, which tooth you would restore first and why, and how proximal form/contact management would differ between the premolar pair and the molar groups. Your justification should rely on what fig_01.jpg shows about the remaining external anatomy, not only on lesion depth. Then state the intraoperative findings that would make a purely intracoronal composite no longer the most predictable option even without pulp exposure, and explain how your plan changes if 45 needs no dentin restoration after excavation but 37 shows functional cusp undermining.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The two groups should not be managed from the same anatomic reference. In fig_01.jpg panel a and fig_01.jpg panel c, 44 and 45 still retain usable occlusal morphology despite proximal disease, so their remaining external occlusal anatomy can serve as the reference for the final surface. In fig_01.jpg panel g, fig_01.jpg panel h, fig_01.jpg panel k, and fig_01.jpg panel m, the molars show deep cavitated occlusal loss, so the preoperative external surface is no longer a dependable template; copying it directly would reproduce a defect or distorted occlusal map rather than functional anatomy.

For 44 and 45, I would keep the plan adhesive and conservative, working one tooth at a time. The occlusal index/stamp should be made before preparation while the external anatomy is still intact enough to copy. Because these are proximal lesions with food lodgment, proximal form must be rebuilt first with a sectional matrix, wedge, and contact control; the index is used only on the final occlusal composite increment after the proximal wall and bulk of the restoration are established. A defensible sequence is to assess and, if needed, treat 45 first because it is radiographically shallower; if it proves minimal or non-restorative, preserving it gives the best natural reference while restoring 44.

For 36, 37, 46, and 47, I would not rely on the existing occlusal surface as the anatomy source. I would generate a new reference outside the cavity, such as an extraoral wax-up/cast reconstruction followed by a rigid or clear index, then restore tooth by tooth with adhesive composite. Proximal contact rebuilding is not the primary challenge here because these are Class I occlusal lesions; the priority is recreating posterior stops and cusp-fossa relationships without losing all remaining landmarks at once. I would stage by quadrant and usually restore the first molar before the adjacent second molar (36 before 37, 46 before 47), or otherwise restore the tooth with the most dependable remaining landmarks first. I would avoid preparing both teeth in a pair before one is definitively rebuilt, because sequencing is more critical when the native occlusal map is already lost.

I would stop pursuing a purely intracoronal composite, even without pulp exposure, if excavation reveals undermined or cracked cusps, excessive intercuspal width loss, very thin remaining walls, inability to achieve durable isolation, or margins extending to areas where bonding becomes unreliable. In that setting, the issue is not pulpal status alone but structural predictability; management shifts to cuspal coverage, either a bonded direct cusp-capping composite in selected situations or an indirect onlay/overlay when the tooth is too weakened or isolation is less predictable.

If 45 requires no dentin restoration after excavation, I would de-escalate: avoid enlarging the preparation, use sealant/infiltration or a very small enamel restoration only if cavitation or contour demands it, and preserve 45 as a reference tooth if possible. If 37 shows functional cusp undermining, I would escalate in the opposite direction: a simple intracoronal anatomy-transfer composite is no longer enough, because reproducing anatomy on a structurally weak shell does not address fracture risk. That tooth would need cuspal coverage rather than only occlusal form reproduction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg meaningfully, or bases the plan mainly on enamel-versus-dentin depth without interpreting the remaining external anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the premolars and molars differ, but does not clearly connect specific fig_01.jpg findings to whether the existing occlusal surface is a reliable reference or why proximal demands differ between the groups.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg and the radiographic data to distinguish the preserved occlusal reference in 44/45 from the lost or unreliable occlusal morphology in 36/37/46/47, while also recognizing the non-pulpal crown-confined baseline.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg and the clinical data into a clear explanation that 44/45 chiefly require proximal reconstruction with preserved occlusal referencing, whereas the molars require a newly generated occlusal reference because direct copying would reproduce defective anatomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate or generic plan, such as using the same anatomy-generation workflow for all teeth or omitting how final anatomy and contacts would actually be produced.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a broadly conservative plan but does not specify when the anatomy reference is created, how it is used, or how contact/proximal form is handled in the premolars versus the molars.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives workable adhesive plans for both groups: preserved-surface indexing with matrix-assisted proximal rebuilding for 44/45, and staged reconstruction from a newly created occlusal reference for 36/37/46/47.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides precise stepwise planning, including creating the premolar index before preparation, using it only for the final occlusal increment after proximal form is rebuilt, and using extraoral reconstruction or an equivalent newly generated reference to guide tooth-by-tooth molar restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not state a treatment order, or recommends sequencing that needlessly destroys remaining references.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests an order, but the reasoning is generic and not tied to preservation of landmarks, contacts, or posterior stops.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses a defensible order for both groups and explains why one-tooth-at-a-time staging preserves reference anatomy better, especially in the molar group.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly prioritizes the least destructive or most informative reference tooth in the premolar pair and stages the molars by quadrant so that one rebuilt tooth helps guide the adjacent one, while explaining why simultaneous preparation would be more harmful in the molars.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers no meaningful thresholds for changing the restorative plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic concerns about large restorations or fracture risk without linking them to this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies valid structural or isolation-related thresholds for abandoning a purely intracoronal composite despite no pulp exposure, and balances conservation against durability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Separately analyzes the risk of reproducing defective occlusal anatomy and the risk of leaving weakened cusps under load, and uses those distinctions to justify escalation to cuspal coverage only when indicated.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: States conclusions without explaining how the plan changes when the intraoperative findings differ.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Explains only one of the two altered intraoperative scenarios, or gives a generic answer not clearly tied to the case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Clearly explains why management should de-escalate for enamel-limited 45 and escalate for structurally weakened 37.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows a logical, case-specific progression from fig_01.jpg findings to opposite management shifts: preserving or minimally treating 45 while converting 37 from intracoronal restoration to cusp-covering care.

items.question_content: A 16-year-old male presents with poor mastication and dissatisfaction with appearance. His mother reports recurrent hyperthermia since infancy, and two siblings have hypodontia/micro-shaped teeth. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg only; you are not told what treatment was eventually carried out. The father wants the most stable result, but the family can afford only one low-complexity intervention now, and any procedure that removes bone should be avoided unless clearly justified. Write the management note you would give today: identify the syndrome pattern and the 3 findings from the figures/history that most determine your prosthodontic decision; choose the current rehabilitation and the specific preprosthetic procedure you would request first; explain why a broader or more definitive alternative is not yet the better choice on the available evidence; and state the objective findings after skeletal maturity that would make you change to implant-based rehabilitation, including whether you would expect a fixed restoration to be automatically preferable.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with complete anodontia and marked alveolar underdevelopment, in a hereditary pattern supported by affected siblings. The findings that most influence treatment are: (1) fig_05.jpg shows complete absence of teeth/tooth buds, so tooth-supported prostheses, overdentures, and orthodontic/tooth-preserving options are unavailable; (2) fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg show underdeveloped ridges, especially a vertically reduced mandibular ridge, so denture support and stability will be limited, with the lower arch being the more difficult one; (3) fig_04.jpg shows a very adherent/high labial frenum that directly interferes with flange extension, while fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show reduced facial support consistent with the need to restore appearance and lower facial height. The hyperthermia history also means care should be delivered in short, cool, well-hydrated appointments.

My present-phase rehabilitation would be reversible complete dentures for both arches during growth, with planned review, adjustment, and likely future reline/remake. The first preprosthetic procedure I would request is localized frenectomy/release of the interfering labial frenum attachment visible in fig_04.jpg, prioritizing the mandibular site if only one area can be treated. That choice is best supported by the actual figure because it is a specific, surgically modifiable soft-tissue obstacle to border extension and stability, can be done with relatively low complexity and cost, and does not sacrifice bone.

A broader alternative such as generalized vestibuloplasty/sulcoplasty is not yet the best choice on the available evidence: the records clearly show an adherent frenum, but they do not prove that a more extensive soft-tissue procedure would add enough benefit to justify the additional morbidity at this stage. Immediate implant rehabilitation is also not first-line now because the patient is still growing, bone appears limited, cost is constrained, and advanced imaging/planning would be needed. Alveoloplasty or other bone-removing surgery should be avoided because the patient already has deficient ridges and that bone may be critical for future implant options.

After skeletal maturity, I would switch to implant-based rehabilitation only if growth completion is confirmed, imaging (ideally CBCT) shows adequate bone volume/quality or augmentable sites, the patient still has functional dissatisfaction or poor denture stability despite optimized removable prostheses, and financial/surgical acceptance improves. Even then, a fixed restoration would not automatically be preferable. In ectodermal dysplasia with severe hard- and soft-tissue deficiency, an implant-supported overdenture may better restore flange bulk, lip support, and facial soft-tissue contours than a fully fixed prosthesis; a fixed option would be considered only if the tissue deficiency, implant distribution, and esthetic demands made it appropriate.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either ectodermal dysplasia or severe tooth absence, but the diagnosis remains incomplete or poorly specified.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare alternatives or ignores major harms and constraints.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A 28-year-old woman presents with food lodgement in the maxillary left posterior region and requests an aesthetic tooth-colored restoration. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, which show the preoperative clinical view, the preoperative radiograph, and the cavity after caries removal. For tooth 26, what definitive restoration would you choose now, and why is that option better suited to this tooth than other reasonable restorations? Base your justification on the structural and radiographic findings visible here, state the key preparation and bonding conditions required for long-term success, and identify the specific intraoperative findings that would make you change to a different restorative plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best definitive restoration for tooth 26 is a bonded indirect ceramic inlay, provided the cavity remains an intracoronal defect after caries removal. The figures support that choice: the lesion is proximal and causing food impaction, but the tooth appears restorable, the preparation in fig_03.jpg preserves the external tooth form rather than requiring cusp replacement, and the radiograph does not show obvious periapical disease or gross structural destruction that would push this toward endodontic treatment or extraction. A ceramic inlay is preferable here because it preserves more sound tooth structure than a full-coverage restoration while offering better proximal contact, contour, wear resistance, and color stability than a large direct posterior composite in a cavity of this size. It is also less affected by polymerization shrinkage than a direct placement in a broad proximal preparation.

For success, the case must remain within classic inlay indications: intact and sufficiently supported cusps/walls, smooth expulsive preparation without sharp internal angles, adequate material thickness, margins that are accessible and ideally in enamel or at least bondable and isolatable, reliable moisture control, accurate fit, and adhesive luting with material-appropriate ceramic surface treatment. Occlusion and proximal contact must be verified carefully because thin ceramic or high occlusal loading increases fracture risk.

I would abandon the inlay plan if excavation revealed pulpal exposure or symptoms suggesting irreversible pulpal disease, major cusp undermining or flexure requiring cuspal coverage, margins extending too far subgingivally or onto poorly controllable dentin/cementum, inability to isolate for adhesive cementation, or a heavy parafunctional risk that would reduce prognosis. Follow-up should focus on marginal adaptation, contact tightness, postoperative sensitivity, occlusion, hygiene, and recurrence of food impaction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses a clearly inappropriate definitive restoration for the findings, or gives no defensible plan for tooth 26.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a potentially acceptable restoration but the rationale is generic, weakly tied to this tooth, or does not explain when the plan should change.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a bonded indirect ceramic inlay and justifies it as a conservative intracoronal solution for a restorable proximal posterior defect with preserved external tooth structure; identifies at least some findings that would require a different restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Selects a bonded indirect ceramic inlay and gives a patient-specific comparison with other reasonable options, clearly explaining why tissue preservation, contact/anatomy control, wear behavior, and restoration size favor this choice here, while defining clear thresholds for switching plans.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or invents unsupported clinical findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one source of information or cites visible findings vaguely without linking them to the decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg to identify a proximal carious defect causing food impaction, a restorable intracoronal preparation, preserved surrounding tooth structure, and no obvious radiographic periapical alarm.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the clinical and radiographic views into a coherent indication analysis, explicitly linking preserved cuspal/wall structure, cavity form, and absence of gross pulpal or periapical compromise to the suitability and limits of an indirect inlay.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful weighing of benefits, risks, and alternatives, or ignores the patient's aesthetic preference.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions isolated pros or cons, such as esthetics alone, without tying them to this preparation or to competing restorative options.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances key benefits of a ceramic inlay in this case, such as tooth preservation, proximal form/contact control, color stability, wear resistance, and lower polymerization shrinkage than a large direct composite, against relevant risks such as brittleness, technique sensitivity, cost, and dependence on bonding conditions.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced, case-specific tradeoff analysis and names decisive risk modifiers that would alter the recommendation, such as cuspal undermining, deep subgingival margins, inability to isolate, heavy occlusal load/parafunction, or pulpal involvement.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses major foreseeable complications or proposes unsafe management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists possible complications but gives little prevention strategy or follow-up relevance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies likely complications such as marginal gap/microleakage, postoperative sensitivity, open or deficient proximal contact, secondary caries, fracture, or debonding, and links them to prevention through proper preparation, fit, isolation, bonding, and occlusal adjustment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds targeted postoperative surveillance priorities, including margins, contact tightness, occlusion, symptoms, and recurrence of food impaction, with appropriate implications for early correction if problems are detected.

items.question_content: A healthy 20-year-old woman with high esthetic expectations seeks correction of an unattractive smile. The maxillary lateral incisors are vital and not discolored. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg only. Formulate the definitive management pathway for these teeth. Your answer must decide whether this case should be managed with restoration alone or whether tooth position should be changed before definitive restoration, and justify that decision from the figure-based morphology and position. If you would restore now, identify the key design features required to correct form and version without losing the biologic advantages of adhesive dentistry. Then state the specific findings at mock-up or reduction planning that would make you stop and choose a different pathway instead.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This case can be managed restoratively now; I would not make tooth movement the first step based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg alone. The figures show peg-shaped, undersized maxillary lateral incisors with form disharmony and rotational/version discrepancy, more pronounced on 22. In a 20-year-old with vital, non-discolored teeth, the main problem is esthetic reshaping with limited correction of apparent alignment while preserving enamel and pulp. Because the malposition is rotational rather than a simple undersized facial deficiency, a purely facial additive approach or conventional facial veneer risks either bulky contour/emergence or excessive reduction to obtain proper line angles, symmetry, and seating.

The best definitive restoration is a bonded ceramic three-quarter crown, or equivalent palatally extended partial-coverage ceramic restoration, for each lateral incisor. It is preferable to full crowns because it is more biologically conservative in a young patient, and preferable to facial-only veneer/composite approaches because the palatal extension helps correct the version discrepancy while preserving useful enamel for bonding.

If restoring now, the essential design features are: enamel-dominant preparation; enough incisal reduction to shorten the laterals and provide ceramic thickness; a sloping palatal preparation that compensates for the rotation and creates a favorable path of insertion; and a palatal finish line positioned away from centric and excursive contacts rather than at a loaded dentoprosthetic junction. Occlusally, these teeth should have at most light static contact and should be excluded from protrusive and lateral functional guidance so shear is not concentrated at the palatal margin.

I would stop and change the pathway if mock-up or reduction planning showed that the desired contour correction could not be achieved without broad dentin exposure, gross facial/proximal overcontour, or a palatal margin remaining in functional contact. Under those conditions, the adhesive and biologic advantages of this partial-coverage ceramic plan are reduced. The preferred next step would be pre-restorative tooth movement to create a more enamel-friendly restorative situation; full coverage would be a later fallback only if conservative options could not meet the esthetic goal and the patient accepted the biologic tradeoff.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg meaningfully, or ignores the key morphologic/positional findings that determine management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only a general esthetic problem or only one key finding, such as peg shape without explaining the positional significance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the clinical facts with the figures to identify peg-shaped, undersized, vital, non-discolored lateral incisors with positional discrepancy relevant to treatment selection.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies the figure-based combination of peg form, relative form/length disharmony, and rotational/version discrepancy, especially on 22 in fig_02.jpg, and explains why these findings make a simple facial-only solution less predictable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends a clearly unsuitable plan, such as routine full-coverage crowns or a purely additive/facial restoration without addressing the positional problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects a plausible conservative option but does not clearly match the restorative design or sequencing to the specific anatomy shown.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a defensible conservative pathway linked to age, vitality, color, and esthetic demand, with some explanation of when tooth movement might be needed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly recommends immediate palatally extended bonded partial-coverage ceramic restoration (three-quarter crown or equivalent) as the best current-case balance of contour correction, enamel preservation, retention, esthetics, and pulp safety, while reserving tooth movement for loss of enamel-dominant feasibility.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison of management pathways or ignores major tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives only generically, without relating their advantages and disadvantages to this patient's figures and biologic constraints.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares at least two clinically plausible alternatives with relevant pros and cons for this patient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison of plausible pathways, explicitly linking figure-based malposition to overcontour or excessive reduction risk with facial-only approaches, biologic cost with full coverage, repairability/esthetic tradeoffs with composite, and the role of tooth movement when adhesive goals cannot be preserved.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not state when the original plan should be abandoned, or prioritizes esthetic correction over enamel and pulp preservation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes enamel preservation as important but gives only vague or incomplete thresholds for changing course.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly states that broad dentin exposure, unacceptable overcontour, or a palatal margin in functional contact should trigger a change away from restorative-only veneer-style management toward tooth movement first, or only then more invasive coverage with informed consent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify relevant failure risks or occlusal hazards.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general risks such as debonding or fracture but gives limited case-specific prevention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important adhesive or biomechanical risks and gives reasonable preventive design or occlusal measures.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains that enamel-dominant preparation, palatal extension on usable enamel, finish-line placement away from centric and excursive contacts, and minimizing functional guidance on the restored laterals are the key protections against debonding, chipping, and overload.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending routine full-coverage crowns as first-line treatment in this 20-year-old without justifying why a more conservative bonded option cannot meet the case goals

Generic Textbook Management: recommending a standard facial veneer or additive approach without addressing the rotation-related path-of-insertion problem and the risk of overcontour or excessive enamel loss

items.question_content: A 19-year-old man presents 8 months after resection of an odontogenic myxoma with a healed acquired maxillary defect. He reports difficulty eating and drinking, indistinct speech, and major distress about the change in his appearance. The remaining maxillary teeth are clinically sound. Using fig_01.jpg, determine the defect pattern and the main biomechanical problems a definitive prosthesis must overcome. Then propose your definitive prosthodontic rehabilitation, stating whether you would provide the lost cheek/lip support within the same prosthesis or as a separate component, and justify that choice against at least one other reasonable prosthodontic approach. Base your reasoning on retention, rotational control, weight, hygiene, adjustability, and the patient's psychosocial goals. Finally, explain how your plan would change if the posterior abutments on the dentate segment later showed reduced periodontal support.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg is compatible with a large acquired maxillary defect that crosses the midline with loss of anterior dentoalveolar/labial support and a single posterior dentate segment, i.e., a pattern compatible with Aramany class IV. The key biomechanical problems are: (1) restoring separation between the oral cavity and the maxillary/sinonasal space so speech and swallowing improve, while preventing rotation of the prosthesis into the defect; and (2) replacing major cheek/lip volume without creating a heavy lateral cantilever on the remaining abutments.

My definitive choice is a cast metal removable partial obturator supported by the remaining teeth and available tissues, with broad palatal support, well-distributed rests/bracing/clasping on the remaining segment, and as much indirect retention as the remaining teeth permit. I would first make the obturator functionally acceptable for seal, comfort, speech, and occlusion. Because the facial volume loss is substantial, I would not incorporate all of the cheek/lip bulk into the same prosthesis as a solid flange or extra row of teeth. Instead, I would provide the facial support as a separate lightweight hollow detachable cheek-lip plumper attached to the obturator once the base prosthesis is stable; a detachable attachment such as magnets is reasonable if the patient accepts the maintenance needs.

This is preferable to a one-piece bulky plumper because a single-unit design adds weight and rotational leverage, can fatigue the musculature, may reduce retention/stability, and is harder to clean or refine. A detachable component is lighter, easier to clean, independently adjustable, removable if sore or socially inconvenient, and still addresses the patient's strong psychosocial need for facial fullness. Compared with more invasive reconstruction, this is conservative, reversible, and rapidly restores function in a healed defect.

If the posterior abutments later showed reduced periodontal support, my priority would shift to protecting those teeth. I would reassess prognosis and fit, reduce tooth loading, modify or simplify clasping/rest design as needed, consider relining or remaking the obturator or using a lighter interim design, and reduce, defer, or redesign the detachable plumper if it increased leverage. Follow-up should monitor leakage/hypernasality, pressure areas, plaque/caries/periodontal breakdown of abutments, and attachment wear/corrosion if detachable retention is used.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic answer with little or no use of fig_01.jpg, or misinterprets the defect pattern in a way that undermines the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a maxillary defect or facial asymmetry but does not clearly derive the major biomechanical consequences from fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg to identify a large acquired maxillary defect with loss of anterior/labial support and a remaining dentate segment that must provide most support and retention, and links these findings to the need for obturation and control of rotation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also characterizes the defect as crossing the midline with a single posterior dentate segment (compatible with Aramany class IV) and explicitly connects that pattern to leverage, limited indirect retention options, and the challenge of restoring facial support without destabilizing the prosthesis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not recommend an obturator-based definitive rehabilitation, or proposes a plan incompatible with the remaining abutments and functional deficits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests an obturator or an esthetic augmentation device, but the plan is incomplete, poorly sequenced, or does not explain how function and facial support will be balanced.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a definitive tooth-and-tissue-supported obturator with appropriate emphasis on seal, support, retention, and stability, and explains that facial support must be added without overloading the remaining segment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Recommends a staged definitive cast-framework obturator plus a separate lightweight detachable cheek-lip support rather than a bulky one-piece extension, and clearly explains why the facial support should be refined only after the obturator is functionally stable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers no meaningful comparison of options, or recommends an approach likely to worsen stability, hygiene, or patient adaptation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons but does not compare the chosen plan against a realistic alternative for this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the proposed plan with at least one plausible alternative, such as a one-piece bulky plumper, additional tooth bulk, or other integrated facial support, and explains the effects on weight, rotational control, hygiene, and adjustability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also weighs reversibility, maintenance burden, likely attachment wear, and the psychosocial benefit of improved facial contour in this young patient, and justifies why the chosen conservative prosthetic approach is preferred at this stage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address how the plan should change if posterior abutments become periodontally compromised.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions recall or monitoring but gives no concrete change in priorities or design if abutment support worsens.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that preservation of the remaining abutments becomes the priority and proposes reasonable changes such as reducing tooth loading, reassessing fit/support, and considering relining, redesign, or remake.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also explains that the detachable facial support may need to be reduced, deferred, or redesigned if it increases leverage, and presents a logical sequence of reassessment, stabilization, and maintenance decisions.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. A 45-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea refuses CPAP and is treated with the depicted intraoral appliance. Which statement best describes how this device is intended to improve airway patency during sleep?

question_options.text: It passively helps maintain the tongue within the physiologic free orolingual space without advancing the mandible.
It primarily protrudes the mandible to tension the suprahyoid and pharyngeal soft tissues.
It delivers overnight electrical stimulation to the tongue through incorporated intraoral electrodes.
It acts as a maxillary palatal lift that elevates the soft palate away from the posterior pharyngeal wall.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The appliance shown is a lingual elevator, designed to occupy the free orolingual space and support a more favorable tongue posture while remaining passive and not repositioning the jaw. That distinguishes it from mandibular advancement devices. The TENS shown elsewhere was used during fabrication, not as nocturnal therapy, and the device is not a palatal lift.

items.answer_explanation: The appliance shown is a lingual elevator, designed to occupy the free orolingual space and support a more favorable tongue posture while remaining passive and not repositioning the jaw. That distinguishes it from mandibular advancement devices. The TENS shown elsewhere was used during fabrication, not as nocturnal therapy, and the device is not a palatal lift.

items.question_content: A 25-year-old man seeks maxillary re-rehabilitation after failure of a previous full-arch implant prosthesis placed without augmentation. He is medically fit, lost his teeth from aggressive periodontitis, has severe esthetic/functional concerns, refuses extraoral bone harvesting, and wants to avoid a prolonged treatment course. Examine fig_01.jpg and the postoperative soft-tissue problem illustrated in fig_02.jpg. What definitive maxillary rehabilitation strategy would you recommend now, and why is it the most defensible option for this patient? Justify your choice from the imaging and history, then explain the planning and maintenance decisions that are most important to reduce recurrence of failure and to manage the soft-tissue risk.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend a customized, prosthesis-driven maxillary subperiosteal implant supporting a fixed full-arch prosthesis. The key reason is that fig_01.jpg shows a severely resorbed maxilla after failure of prior endosseous implants from peri-implant disease, so repeat conventional implant placement would not be predictable without major augmentation. Because he refuses extraoral bone harvesting and wants to avoid a long staged reconstruction, graft-based reimplantation is a poor fit for his anatomy, preferences, and timeline. A removable option would be less invasive, but it would not address his strong concern about function, speech, and appearance as well as a fixed solution. A patient-specific SPI can use the remaining basal maxillary support without rebuilding the alveolar ridge first.

Success depends on reverse planning from the intended tooth position. The radiographic stent visible on fig_01.jpg should be used with CBCT to determine abutment emergence and angulation in relation to the planned occlusion, because these are difficult to change once the framework is inserted. The framework should be digitally designed for intimate passive fit and verified on a printed model to minimize misfit, micromovement, soft-tissue trauma, and recurrent infection. Occlusion should distribute forces evenly and avoid overload or long cantilevers. I would allow early soft-tissue healing before provisionalization/loading rather than contaminate a fresh wound.

Maintenance is critical because trans-mucosal components are plaque-retentive and soft tissues may be vulnerable, as suggested by the dehiscence in fig_02.jpg. I would prescribe strict hygiene measures and close follow-up to monitor exposure/dehiscence, mucosal inflammation, infection, pain, mobility, and mechanical complications. A small, clean, non-progressive dehiscence can be managed conservatively with hygiene reinforcement and observation, but progression, suppuration, or loss of stability would require active intervention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not provide a coherent definitive rehabilitation plan, or recommends routine repeat endosseous implants without addressing the severe atrophy and the patient's refusal of extraoral grafting.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a plausible treatment direction but the plan is incomplete, poorly sequenced, or not well matched to the patient's anatomic limitations and preferences.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a customized subperiosteal implant-supported fixed maxillary restoration and gives an appropriate stepwise rationale, including prosthesis-driven planning and avoidance of major graft-dependent reconstruction.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-prioritized SPI plan with clear sequencing, emphasizes passive fit verification, abutment emergence planning, load control, and shows how the plan specifically reduces the chance of repeating the prior failure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is generic and does not use the history or figures in a meaningful way.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts but misses major links between anatomy, prior implant failure, patient refusal of grafting, and treatment choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the severe maxillary bone loss on fig_01.jpg, prior peri-implant-related implant failure, refusal of extraoral grafting, and the patient's desire to avoid prolonged treatment into a coherent justification.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: In addition to the above, uses the radiographic stent in fig_01.jpg to justify prosthesis-driven abutment positioning and links the soft-tissue vulnerability illustrated by fig_02.jpg to the maintenance strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives, or presents a one-sided recommendation without acknowledging trade-offs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general pros and cons but does not compare options in a patient-specific way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why the chosen plan is preferable to other reasonable approaches because it better fits the patient's anatomy, consent limits, morbidity tolerance, and fixed-restoration goals, while acknowledging SPI limitations.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced appraisal of benefits and drawbacks, including the technical sensitivity of SPI therapy, difficulty of revision, and the dependence of long-term success on hygiene and accurate fit.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores likely complications or proposes unsafe management of the soft-tissue problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic complications but gives limited prevention or follow-up strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important risks such as dehiscence/exposure, recurrent infection, mobility or misfit, plaque-related inflammation, and occlusal overload, with an appropriate monitoring plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds practical prevention and management details, including timing to protect early wound healing, the rationale for observing a small stable dehiscence, and clear triggers for intervention if progression occurs.

items.question_content: A 36-year-old man seeks retreatment of an unaesthetic maxillary anterior fixed prosthesis involving 11, 21, and 22. He wants the midline diastema preserved. Review fig_01.jpg. Before naming a procedure, identify the key esthetic and biologic constraints visible in this patient and propose 2 clinically plausible ways to manage the problem while honoring that request. Select the approach you would recommend and justify why the other is less suitable here. In your justification, state the site of the interproximal soft-tissue defect, explain how an unfavorable soft-tissue result would influence your definitive prosthetic design, and describe the main maintenance and phonetic trade-off you would discuss with the patient.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg shows a combined pink-and-white esthetic problem rather than a simple bridge remake. The key constraints are: a midline diastema that the patient wants to preserve, a black triangle in the interproximal area between the pontic and tooth 22, and recession associated with 22. Because this is in the esthetic zone, remaking the prosthesis alone risks reproducing the embrasure defect or forcing bulky, disproportionate contours.

Two clinically plausible management pathways are:
1. Interdisciplinary soft-tissue-first treatment: initial periodontal therapy, soft-tissue site development to improve papillary fill and address the recession at 22, healing, then a definitive fixed prosthesis designed to preserve the midline diastema.
2. Prosthetic camouflage/compromise: remake the prosthesis while preserving the diastema, modifying contours and accepting a residual black triangle or using pink restorative camouflage if needed.

The preferred approach is soft-tissue-first interdisciplinary management because the main esthetic failure involves both tissue architecture and the restoration. Since the diastema must remain, prosthetic camouflage alone offers limited ability to hide the defect and is more likely to leave a visible black triangle or require overcontoured, less cleansable cervical form.

The specific soft-tissue defect is the black triangle between the pontic and 22. If soft-tissue augmentation is not satisfactory, the definitive prosthesis should still preserve the patient's requested midline diastema, avoid excessive cervical overcontouring, and use only limited camouflage of any residual defect as needed. A loop-connector fixed partial denture is an appropriate diastema-preserving design after soft-tissue management.

The main maintenance trade-off is that loop connectors and pontic contours can retain plaque, so meticulous oral hygiene and maintenance are necessary. A palatal loop connector may also affect tongue comfort and phonetics, especially linguopalatal sounds, if it is too bulky; therefore it should be kept rounded and close to the tissues.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg to identify the problem as a combined soft-tissue and restorative esthetic issue, or ignores the requirement to preserve the diastema.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies some relevant visible constraints from fig_01.jpg, but incompletely or without explaining why routine prosthesis replacement alone may be inadequate.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the visible findings in fig_01.jpg—preserved midline diastema, a black triangle between the pontic and 22, and recession at 22—and explains that these create a pink-and-white esthetic problem not predictably solved by a routine remake alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides only one approach, or compares alternatives that are not clinically plausible for this patient.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides two plausible approaches but gives only a generic comparison, with limited patient-specific justification for the preferred option.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares two clinically plausible diastema-preserving strategies, recommends soft-tissue site development before definitive prosthodontics, and clearly explains why the alternative is less suitable because it would likely leave a visible defect or require unnatural contouring with poorer cleansability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits the key site-specific defect, proceeds directly to definitive prosthodontics without justification, or proposes unrealistic changes such as simply closing the diastema.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions the relevant defect site or a phased plan, but incompletely explains how an unfavorable soft-tissue result should influence the definitive prosthetic design.

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: A 24-year-old man presents 6 months after road-traffic trauma requesting a definitive fixed restoration for the maxillary anterior region. Orthodontic space redistribution is not feasible because of post-traumatic bone loss. Tooth 22 is Grade II mobile and out of occlusion. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, write a sequential definitive design map from 14 to 24: identify which existing teeth you would prepare as retainers, which tooth would be excluded from the definitive design, and what tooth form each unit of the final prosthesis should represent. Justify the design from the space pattern and migrated tooth positions visible in the figures, not just from the history. Then compare your plan with two other plausible fixed definitive strategies for this arch and explain why they are less suitable here. Finally, if 22 improved to Grade I mobility after stabilization but space redistribution still remained impossible, would that change whether you include 22 in the definitive prosthesis? Defend your answer.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg indicate a space-compromise, tooth-supported fixed prosthesis rather than an anatomically literal site-for-site replacement. The key figure-derived finding is that 13 has migrated mesially into the lateral-incisor region, leaving a separate residual space between 13 and 14 that corresponds to the canine position. The total mesiodistal space across the anterior segment is reduced and asymmetrically distributed, while 22 is periodontally compromised, mobile, and out of occlusion, so it should not be part of the definitive load-bearing design.

Sequential design map from 14 to 24:
- 14: full-coverage retainer, maintained in premolar form
- space between 14 and 13: canine-form pontic
- 13: full-coverage retainer, recontoured to lateral-incisor form
- 11 position: pontic in central-incisor form
- 21 position: pontic in central-incisor form
- 22 position: pontic in lateral-incisor form after excluding/extracting the compromised 22 from the definitive design
- 23: full-coverage retainer in canine form
- 24: full-coverage retainer in premolar form
This is therefore a long-span 14 to 24 space-compromise FDP with retainers on 14, 13, 23, and 24. fig_02.jpg supports that the definitive arrangement should be verified digitally with diagnostic wax-up/CAD and provisional assessment to confirm proportions, connector placement, phonetics, occlusion, and pontic cleansability.

Why other fixed strategies are less suitable:
1. A site-for-site tooth-supported design is unsuitable because the existing spaces and tooth positions no longer correspond to normal positions for 13, 12, 11, 21, and 22; forcing a literal replacement would create distorted tooth proportions, overcontoured or undersized units, and poor emergence.
2. A shorter-span bridge that incorporates 22 as an abutment is less suitable because 22 is Grade II mobile, out of occlusion, and periodontally weak after trauma, making it an unreliable definitive abutment with risk of differential mobility and overload.
3. Implant-based or more anatomically ideal fixed replacement would require site development and more favorable space/bone relationships; in this case post-traumatic bone loss and the inability to redistribute space make such positioning less predictable without additional major intervention.

If 22 improved to Grade I mobility after stabilization but space redistribution still remained impossible, I still would generally not include 22 in the definitive prosthesis. Improved mobility alone does not solve the space-compromise layout, prior periodontal compromise, or the biomechanical concern of adding a questionable tooth into a long anterior FDP. I would reassess whether 22 could be retained temporarily or monitored independently, but unless both its prognosis and the space relationships became favorable, it should remain outside the definitive load-bearing design.

items.question_content: A 39-year-old woman wants a fixed replacement for the missing maxillary left second premolar, which now occupies a first-premolar position because both maxillary first premolars are congenitally absent and the space has changed after long-standing tooth loss. Disease control and replacement of defective restorations have already been completed, oral hygiene has improved, and she refuses implant surgery. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, decide which definitive fixed restoration you would actually deliver. Defend the abutment you would use, the retainer/preparation design, connector strategy, occlusal scheme, and material choice from figure-based findings rather than generic rules. In your reasoning, identify at least two other fixed approaches that are plausible here and explain why they are less favorable in this specific mouth. Finally, state the main failure modes you would monitor and one realistic change in the clinical situation that would make you switch to a different material or overall plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The restoration I would deliver is a posterior single-retainer mesial cantilever fixed partial denture supported by the maxillary left first molar, using an onlay/overlay-like adhesive retainer and a single premolar pontic. The crucial decision is the abutment: the first molar is the most defensible abutment for a posterior mesial cantilever in this mouth, whereas the canine may serve only as a slight enamel support area, not as the primary retainer. fig_01.jpg shows a shortened bounded space between canine and molar and a restored molar that can be incorporated conservatively; fig_02.jpg shows that an onlay-type preparation on the molar is feasible; fig_03.jpg shows a design in which connector height/cross-section can be maximized and pontic contacts can be controlled; fig_04.jpg shows why slight enamel-only modification of the distal canine can help disperse stress but does not make the canine the main abutment.

Design priorities are posterior biomechanics: mesial rather than distal cantilever; limited disinsertion axes; an onlay-like retainer on the first molar with enough reduction to create bulk; lowered mesial finish line and maximized connector height/cross-sectional area; broad, smooth embrasure radii; no heavy occlusal contact on margins; and only controlled static intercuspal contact on the pontic, with protrusive, working, and non-working excursive contacts minimized or eliminated. Because the missing tooth visually occupies a first-premolar position, esthetics matter. In this specific case, a reinforced glass-ceramic is defensible because the edentulous span is short and the connector can be made large, with height particularly important; a more mechanically conservative zirconia-based option would be preferable if connector dimensions or loading were less favorable.

Less favorable fixed alternatives include a canine-retained cantilever resin-bonded prosthesis, which places posterior premolar loading on an anterior abutment; a two-abutment adhesive or conventional bridge between canine and molar, which is more invasive and/or susceptible to differential tooth movement and debonding; and implant replacement, which the patient declines and which would also be complicated by reduced mesiodistal space and bone loss/site development.

Main failure risks to monitor are debonding, connector or pontic fracture/chipping, marginal leakage and recurrent caries at the molar abutment, plaque retention and periodontal inflammation around the pontic/connector, abnormal probing or mobility, and development of new excursive contacts or occlusal overload over time. If the connector could not be made sufficiently tall/bulky, if parafunction or heavier excursive loading were present, or if occlusal clearance were inadequate, I would switch away from reinforced glass-ceramic toward a stronger zirconia-based posterior cantilever; if the fixed cantilever still remained biomechanically unfavorable and the patient accepted surgery, implant therapy after site development would then become the preferred overall plan.

items.question_content: A 26-year-old man presents 1 year after left decompressive craniectomy for a gunshot-related injury, with a large healed frontoparietotemporal contour defect causing facial asymmetry. As the prosthodontist on the team, examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg and justify the prosthetic plan for fabricating a custom heat-polymerized polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) cranial prosthesis. In your answer, discuss the dental-maxillofacial prosthodontic principles involved in making the facial impression and cast, the purpose of blocking out the defect and refining the wax pattern to restore normal craniofacial contour, and the design features of the processed prosthesis that support acceptable fit, tissue adaptation, hygiene, and esthetic rehabilitation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Yes. From a maxillofacial prosthodontic standpoint, a custom heat-polymerized PMMA cranial prosthesis is an appropriate plan for this patient because he has a large healed frontoparietotemporal defect with visible loss of cranial contour and associated facial asymmetry. The prosthodontic goal is to restore external craniofacial form accurately and produce a prosthesis that can be seated securely by the surgical team with close adaptation to the bony margins.

The impression approach is consistent with dental maxillofacial prosthetic practice. A special tray adapted over the defect and face with impression compound helps support the impression material over a broad irregular surface. An irreversible hydrocolloid facial impression is suitable for recording the defect and surrounding facial contours, and pouring the impression in dental stone provides a working cast on which the margins and contour can be planned precisely.

Blocking out the central portion of the large defect on the cast is important to control the bulk and thickness of the final prosthesis so it is not unnecessarily heavy. The wax pattern is then the key prosthodontic step: it must be viewed and adjusted from frontal, lateral, superior, and inferior perspectives to reproduce the native cranial convexity, blend smoothly with the adjacent skull, and improve facial symmetry. This contouring is not only esthetic but also essential for normal external head form.

Heat-polymerized PMMA is a reasonable material because it is dimensionally stable, readily shaped on the cast, modifiable, relatively economical, and capable of accurate reproduction of the planned contour. The processed prosthesis should have smooth beveled edges for a gradual transition over the bony margins and reduced edge show-through. The multiple perforations are useful because they reduce dead space, permit fluid egress, and can support soft-tissue adaptation. Finishing, polishing, and disinfection are also important prosthodontic steps to improve tissue compatibility and cleanliness before placement.

Overall, this is a sound prosthodontic plan because it uses familiar dental materials and laboratory steps to create a patient-specific craniofacial prosthesis that restores contour, improves facial balance, and supports functional and esthetic rehabilitation.

items.question_content: A 42-year-old woman presents mainly for esthetic correction of a long-standing discolored maxillary left central incisor after remote trauma. She is ASA I, has excellent oral hygiene, no symptoms, no mobility, normal responses in the adjacent anterior teeth, and tooth #21 is non-responsive to cold and electric testing. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management strategy would you recommend now, and why? Justify your choice using the clinical and radiographic findings, explain why it is preferable to other reasonable options for this patient, and state the prognosis of #21 and the follow-up or contingency advice you would discuss before treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend a conservative but comprehensive esthetic rehabilitation rather than treating #21 as an isolated discoloration problem. The best plan is to retain #21 for now, because it is asymptomatic and stable, and use adhesive ceramic restorations—most appropriately porcelain laminate veneers in the visible maxillary smile zone—to harmonize color, shape, and smile proportions after diagnostic wax-up/mock-up and occlusal assessment.

The key reasoning is that fig_02.jpg is consistent with advanced replacement resorption/ankylosis of #21 after trauma, with loss of normal root/canal architecture, so the tooth has little biologic potential for endodontic rescue and discoloration management by conventional endodontic/bleaching approaches is unlikely to be predictable or meaningful. Clinically, #21 is non-vital by sensibility testing, but there is no pain, mobility, or periodontal breakdown, so immediate removal is not mandatory. fig_01.jpg also shows that the patient’s complaint is not only color; there is broader anterior smile disharmony, so a single-tooth restoration would make matching more difficult and may leave the smile proportions unattractive.

This plan is preferable because it is minimally invasive, preserves existing hard and soft tissues in the esthetic zone, and can mask severe intrinsic discoloration while improving the overall smile. The main drawback is that #21 has a guarded to poor long-term biologic prognosis because replacement resorption may progress; however, the short-term restorative prognosis can still be acceptable if the tooth remains symptom-free and stable.

Before treatment, I would explain the uncertainty clearly and obtain informed consent that this is a salvage/esthetic plan, not reversal of the underlying resorption. Follow-up should include periodic clinical and radiographic review for symptoms, mobility, infraocclusion, cervical breakdown, fracture, or progressive resorption. If any of these develop, the treatment plan should be reconsidered and transition to extraction and replacement may become necessary.

items.question_content: A healthy 34-year-old woman with high esthetic expectations needs definitive restoration of endodontically treated tooth 36; the endodontic result is acceptable. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. The tooth has been prepared and a chairside CAD proposal has been generated, but you must decide whether to authorize manufacture, alter the plan, or redirect the case. What definitive restoration strategy and material class would you support for this tooth today, and why? Make the argument from the figures, not from a generic CAD/CAM workflow: identify the preparation-design feature that is truly rate-limiting for predictability, explain why the most plausible competing concern is secondary, describe the least invasive correction that would let you proceed if the current proposal is not yet acceptable, and state the specific substrate or geometry change that would make you abandon your chosen plan for a different definitive strategy.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would keep tooth 36 in a conservative cuspal-coverage adhesive partial-coverage plan rather than automatically convert it to circumferential full coverage, but I would not authorize manufacture from the current proposal without clinician validation. The most defensible choice today is a chairside etchable glass-ceramic onlay/overlay; in this case a leucite-reinforced glass ceramic is acceptable if the preparation and CAD proposal are validated.

fig_01.jpg and especially fig_02.jpg support that choice because the tooth appears restorable, the preparation is conservative, and the margins appear largely accessible for bonding rather than forcing a crown by default. The rate-limiting issue is not simply that the tooth is endodontically treated, and it is not the fact that software has already produced a morphology. The real limiter is the preparation-design interface shown in fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg: margin capture, insertion path, ceramic thickness in functional areas, and contact intensity. Those are the variables that can look acceptable on screen or even at try-in yet still lead to early fracture, debonding, or marginal breakdown if a thin area or misread finish line is approved.

The most plausible competing concern is the endodontically treated status itself or the biogeneric morphology. Both matter, but they are secondary here: the root filling is acceptable, and morphology can be edited. An unreadable margin or inadequate bulk is less forgiving than a merely imperfect autogenerated shape.

The least invasive correction is to stay with partial coverage but re-check the scan in monochrome, clinically verify the entire finish line, confirm insertion path, and re-evaluate the contact and thickness maps. If needed, I would make selective preparation refinement to improve clearance or smooth internal form, improve soft-tissue control, redraw the margin, and rescan before milling. I would abandon this plan if the cervical substrate proved predominantly circumferential dentin/cementum or became non-isolatable/subgingival, if a crack or fracture reduced predictable adhesive control, or if adequate ceramic bulk could not be achieved without weakening the remaining tooth; then a more retentive core-supported full-coverage restoration becomes the better definitive strategy.
