items.question_content: A 62-year-old edentulous man with severe microstomia from perioral scarring is treated with a sectional collapsible complete denture. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. In this patient, the definitive maxillary prosthesis was made in 2 segments, and the mandibular prosthesis was stabilized by ridge form and tongue pressure rather than ball attachments. Select ALL statements that are correct about the definitive maxillary prosthesis.

question_options.text: It was fabricated as separate anterior and posterior segments.
A custom Co-Cr hinge was incorporated at the midline as far posteriorly as possible.
Two ball attachments were placed in the posterior segment to retain the anterior segment after assembly.
The same ball-attachment mechanism was used to stabilize the mandibular prosthesis.
A stepped butt joint served as the definitive intersegmental joint of the maxillary denture.
The hinge made the maxillary prosthesis collapsible in the vertical plane.
A dental surveyor was used to establish parallel paths of insertion on both sides.
The female housings for the ball attachments were incorporated into the posterior segment.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The maxillary denture was sectional, with anterior and posterior segments, a posteriorly positioned midline Co-Cr hinge, and two ball attachments on the posterior segment. A surveyor was used to create parallel paths of insertion. The mandibular prosthesis did not use ball attachments; its stability depended on ridge form and tongue pressure. A stepped butt joint was used for sectional custom trays, not the definitive denture, and the female housings were in the anterior segment.

items.answer_explanation: The maxillary denture was sectional, with anterior and posterior segments, a posteriorly positioned midline Co-Cr hinge, and two ball attachments on the posterior segment. A surveyor was used to create parallel paths of insertion. The mandibular prosthesis did not use ball attachments; its stability depended on ridge form and tongue pressure. A stepped butt joint was used for sectional custom trays, not the definitive denture, and the female housings were in the anterior segment.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Select ALL statements that are fully accurate for the reported management and outcomes; each option may combine details from history, surgery, endodontics, and restoration.

question_options.text: In fig_01.jpg, a pre-existing intracanal metal post was removed before the buccal transverse fracture could be confirmed and bonded; the bonded fragment then facilitated the subsequent endodontic phase.

In fig_02.jpg, the labial sinus tract that appeared 1 month after initial repair was managed as evidence of inadequate prior root canal treatment, so nonsurgical retreatment preceded further stabilization.
In fig_02.jpg, full-coverage crowning was ultimately avoided: after periodontal stabilization, the intact labial aspect was preserved and the palatal side was completed with composite resin.
In fig_01.jpg, foundation reinforcement was achieved with three equal-diameter main fiber posts surrounded by sleeves because the canal was flared and had no previous post material.

In fig_01.jpg, flap reflection revealed a vertical labial bony defect at the fracture level, and the exposed fracture surface was covered with MMA-based resin cement before regenerative periodontal management.
In both cases, orthodontic extrusion was used before surgery to obtain ferrule and improve the restorative prognosis.
In fig_02.jpg, flap elevation confirmed the fracture to be 2 mm above the alveolar bone margin, and reinforcement used three 1.0-mm main fiber points with additional sleeve modification.
In fig_01.jpg, definitive zirconia restoration was placed immediately after foundation construction because periodontal stabilization had already been achieved at that appointment.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Correct choices are A, C, E, and G. Case 1 involved post removal, bonding, endodontic treatment, labial flap access, resin sealing, regenerative periodontal therapy, delayed zirconia restoration, and no orthodontic extrusion. Case 2 had adequate prior endodontics, sinus tract interpreted as refracture at the bonded interface, three 1.0-mm fiber points with sleeve modification, fracture 2 mm above bone margin, and final palatal composite with the labial surface preserved.

items.answer_explanation: Correct choices are A, C, E, and G. Case 1 involved post removal, bonding, endodontic treatment, labial flap access, resin sealing, regenerative periodontal therapy, delayed zirconia restoration, and no orthodontic extrusion. Case 2 had adequate prior endodontics, sinus tract interpreted as refracture at the bonded interface, three 1.0-mm fiber points with sleeve modification, fracture 2 mm above bone margin, and final palatal composite with the labial surface preserved.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. In the provisional-crown impression technique, select all statements that correctly explain the purpose of the two modifications shown before the shell is loaded with light-body silicone.

question_options.text: The buccal modification helps orient the shell reproducibly during seating on the prepared tooth.
The buccal modification provides an undercut that helps retain the light-body silicone within the shell.
The occlusal perforation acts as a vent, allowing excess light-body silicone to escape and reducing the risk of incomplete seating from trapped material.
The occlusal perforation is primarily intended to carry a hemostatic medicament into the sulcus.
The buccal modification is designed to secure a retraction cord around the finish line during the pickup impression.
These modifications are intended to increase the bulk of wash material around the preparation to improve dimensional stability.
The modifications convert the provisional shell into a reservoir for chemicomechanical gingival displacement paste.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The buccal groove functions as a seating guide and provides an undercut to help retain light-body silicone. The occlusal hole vents excess silicone so the shell seats fully instead of being hydraulically displaced by trapped material. Together, they support controlled mechanical sulcular displacement without cords or chemicals.

items.answer_explanation: The buccal groove functions as a seating guide and provides an undercut to help retain light-body silicone. The occlusal hole vents excess silicone so the shell seats fully instead of being hydraulically displaced by trapped material. Together, they support controlled mechanical sulcular displacement without cords or chemicals.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. A 32-year-old woman has recurrent loss of a facial restoration on a maxillary central incisor. The defect is limited to enamel, and parafunction is absent. Which statements best justify the definitive restoration that was actually delivered? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: Preserving an enamel substrate is advantageous because adhesive durability is generally better to enamel than dentin.
Prior loss of direct composite makes a full-coverage crown the biologically preferred next step.
Feldspathic porcelain offers superior control of translucency and color for an anterior facial veneer.
Lithium disilicate offers higher strength, but feldspathic porcelain is generally more translucent because of its glassy matrix.
A refractory-die technique is especially suitable when very thin margins are desired in unprepared or minimally prepared veneers.
A margin placed above the gingiva can still blend acceptably when an ultrathin feldspathic veneer is used.
Intentional additional reduction to expose dentin would be expected to improve long-term survival of this veneer.
This restoration depends mainly on ceramic bulk strength and only minimally on resin-luting support.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Enamel preservation was central because bonding is more predictable to enamel than dentin. Feldspathic porcelain was chosen for superior optical control in an anterior facial veneer, and the refractory-die method is well suited to ultrathin restorations with delicate margins. A supragingival margin can still blend because of feldspathic translucency. Prior composite failure alone did not justify a crown, lithium disilicate is less translucent, dentin exposure would weaken the adhesive rationale, and ultrathin veneers rely on bonded support.

items.answer_explanation: Enamel preservation was central because bonding is more predictable to enamel than dentin. Feldspathic porcelain was chosen for superior optical control in an anterior facial veneer, and the refractory-die method is well suited to ultrathin restorations with delicate margins. A supragingival margin can still blend because of feldspathic translucency. Prior composite failure alone did not justify a crown, lithium disilicate is less translucent, dentin exposure would weaken the adhesive rationale, and ultrathin veneers rely on bonded support.

items.question_content: A 74-year-old woman presents 4 hours after her porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on tooth 11 dislodged exactly as a brain MRI began. The crown was made overseas 8 years ago; the alloy is unknown, she has had no prior symptoms, and she does not consent to destructive testing of the crown. Examination shows a sound preparation with only a small distal marginal carious area. She will need serial brain MRIs for tumor surveillance. What management strategy would you recommend now and for her ongoing care, and what clinical reasoning makes that strategy preferable to other reasonable options in this patient?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would manage tooth 11 conservatively today if the tooth and crown are still clinically restorable: remove the small marginal caries, repair the margin, assess crown fit and retention, and recement as an interim measure after informed consent. Immediate irreversible treatment is not justified because the preparation is largely sound and the event does not prove the tooth is unrestorable. However, I would not present recementation as a definitive long-term solution because she needs repeated MRIs and the crown alloy is unknown.

The most likely mechanism is magnetically induced displacement of a ferromagnetic component overcoming already weakened retention from aged cement and minor marginal breakdown; radiofrequency heating is a less likely explanation because clinically important temperature rise is expected to be minimal. The timing of dislodgement at MRI start strongly supports an MRI-related event rather than routine cement failure alone, although existing caries and 8-year service likely reduced retention.

For ongoing care, I would recommend planning replacement with a restoration/material of known and more MRI-compatible behavior once medically and logistically appropriate. I would document the event, explain the risks of recurrent loosening, swallowing/aspiration, and possible imaging artefact, and communicate with the MRI team that the crown composition is unknown. Before and after future scans, retention should be checked; if stability becomes doubtful again, definitive replacement should be prioritized before further MRI where feasible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management, such as extraction or other irreversible treatment without establishing unrestorability, or proposes simple recementation as a complete long-term plan while ignoring the need for serial MRI.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only an immediate or only a long-term plan, or gives a vague plan that does not clearly address the marginal caries, the crown's current restoratability, and the implications of repeated MRI exposure.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends conservative immediate management if clinically restorable, including treating the marginal caries and recementing as an interim measure, while advising that a more definitive replacement should be considered because ongoing MRI surveillance creates recurrent risk.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan that includes reassessing crown fit/retention before reuse, conservative interim restoration today, informed consent about limitations of recementation, and planned later replacement with a restoration/material of known MRI behavior timed around the patient's medical needs.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the MRI-related risk, denies the likely relationship to the scan, or attributes the event solely to heating without considering magnetic displacement and existing retention compromise.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes some MRI relevance but gives superficial or one-sided reasoning, with little comparison of the benefits of rapid conservative care versus the risks of recurrent dislodgement and unknown alloy behavior.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies magnetically induced displacement of a possibly ferromagnetic crown as the more plausible mechanism, acknowledges that aged cement and marginal caries may have reduced retention, and balances the benefit of prompt interim recementation against recurrent loosening, artefact, and safety risks during future MRI.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced analysis that also incorporates the patient's need for serial brain MRI, refusal of destructive testing, absence of prior symptoms, and the rationale for avoiding unnecessary irreversible treatment while still moving toward a lower-risk definitive solution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the case facts to justify the diagnosis of the problem mechanism or the management plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated facts from the scenario, with weak linkage between history, examination findings, and management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Synthesizes the key facts: dislodgement exactly at MRI startup, unknown overseas alloy, 8-year service life, no prior symptoms, small marginal caries with otherwise sound preparation, and the need for serial MRI.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all major data into a coherent explanation of why MRI-triggered displacement is likely but probably acted on a crown with already reduced retention, and why that supports interim conservation followed by a more definitive future solution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits clinically important complications and monitoring needs related to future MRI exposure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a generic risk but does not connect it to practical prevention or follow-up in this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant complications such as recurrent loss of retention, swallowing/aspiration risk, and possible image artefact, and recommends checking crown retention before and after subsequent MRI scans.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds clear prevention/monitoring steps, including documenting the event, informing the MRI team that the alloy is unknown, and escalating to definitive replacement if retention becomes questionable again before further scans.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old patient presents after bicycle trauma with fractured maxillary incisors, and a 13-year-old patient presents after baseball trauma with a fractured maxillary left central incisor. Both families want maximal preservation of sound tooth structure and do not want routine full-coverage crowns. Using the attached figures, write a definitive planning note for the 15-year-old's teeth #8 and #9 and the 13-year-old's tooth #9. For each injured tooth, decide whether management should stay mainly additive or should involve bonded partial-coverage preparation, and justify that choice from the figures. Then identify (1) the tooth at greatest risk of iatrogenic overtreatment if additional intact enamel is removed, and (2) the tooth at greatest risk of visible long-term compromise if treatment is kept entirely direct/additive; explain how those judgments change your preparation boundaries and incisal management. Before any irreversible preparation, name the two trauma-related findings that should be confirmed and state exactly how each could change the plan. Finally, if heavy protrusive guidance is found after delivery, explain how your occlusal adjustment, protective appliance advice, and recall intensity would differ between the two patients.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg shows that the 15-year-old patient's case is not uniform. Tooth #8 has a limited mesio-incisal/line-angle defect with most of the facial surface and cervical third preserved, so management should stay mainly additive; a direct bonded composite is the most conservative definitive choice. Tooth #9 in the same patient has a broader facial-incisal-mesial loss affecting the visible form of a maxillary central incisor. fig_02.jpg shows that enough structure remains for bonded partial coverage rather than circumferential preparation, but some controlled preparation is justified. My plan for the 15-year-old's #9 is an indirect bonded ceramic restoration with minimal preparation.

fig_03.jpg shows that the 13-year-old patient's #9 has a localized fracture with substantial cervical and midfacial enamel still intact. fig_04.jpg and fig_05.jpg show a guided, very conservative preparation: mostly creating seating and restorative space rather than reducing the entire tooth or shortening it routinely. Even though this fracture is more localized than the 15-year-old's #9, it still involves a central incisor in the esthetic zone where contour, symmetry, surface texture, and incisal form matter. I would therefore choose an indirect bonded ceramic restoration for the 13-year-old's #9 as well, but with a more additive, length-preserving geometry than the 15-year-old's #9.

The tooth at greatest risk of iatrogenic overtreatment if additional intact enamel is removed is the 15-year-old's #8, because the defect is small and localized; turning that tooth into a broadly prepared indirect case would sacrifice intact enamel for little benefit. The tooth at greatest risk of visible long-term compromise if treatment is kept entirely direct/additive is the 15-year-old's #9, because the defect is larger and more visible, making long-term control of form, gloss, translucency, and contralateral symmetry harder with a purely direct repair.

These judgments should shape preparation boundaries differently. The 15-year-old's #8 should remain essentially additive with no unnecessary facial or cervical reduction. The 15-year-old's #9 can justify limited incisal involvement/edge smoothing and a defined cervical or gingival seating margin to control path of insertion, thickness, and margin placement while still remaining conservative. The 13-year-old's #9 should preserve tooth length, avoid routine intentional incisal shortening, and keep the cervical facial enamel largely untouched; preparation should be only what is needed to seat and blend the bonded restoration.

Before any irreversible preparation, two trauma-related findings must be confirmed. First is pulpal status: symptoms, vitality testing, and whether there is any pulpal involvement. If the pulp is compromised or there is an unrecognized complicated crown fracture, priority shifts to pulp therapy or endodontic management and definitive indirect bonding may need to be delayed. Second is periodontal/radiographic trauma status: mobility, percussion sensitivity, displacement/luxation, root or alveolar fracture, and whether the fracture extends subgingivally. Positive findings here could change the sequence entirely toward splinting and observation, or toward a different restorative access strategy such as orthodontic extrusion or other measures rather than proceeding directly with routine adhesive restoration.

If heavy protrusive guidance is found after delivery, I would not leave a restored central incisor as a point stop. In both patients I would redistribute protrusive and excursive contacts, smooth and repolish adjusted surfaces, and reinforce protective appliance use at night. The difference is emphasis. In the 15-year-old I would review more closely because there are two restored traumatized anterior teeth with different restorative demands: I would monitor the indirect restoration on #9, the direct restoration on #8, edge symmetry, and whether guidance is being shared across the anterior segment. In the 13-year-old I would be especially intolerant of any concentrated point load on the restored incisal segment of #9; if guidance cannot be fully lightened, recall should remain close to monitor chipping, debonding, marginal deterioration, and delayed pulpal or periapical sequelae.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the visible fracture or preparation patterns, or does not use the figures to distinguish the three injured teeth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses the figures only generically; recognizes that conservative bonded treatment is preferable but does not clearly distinguish the limited defect on the 15-year-old's #8 from the broader defect on the 15-year-old's #9, or does not interpret fig_02.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg meaningfully.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly interprets fig_01.jpg and fig_03.jpg as showing different defect extents and uses fig_02.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg to support that the 15-year-old's #9 requires more defined preparation control than the 13-year-old's #9. Correctly identifies the small 15-year-old's #8 defect as most vulnerable to overtreatment and the 15-year-old's #9 as most vulnerable to visible compromise if kept entirely direct/additive.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the initial and preparation figures into a coherent continuum: the 15-year-old's #8 remains largely additive, the 15-year-old's #9 needs controlled indirect reconstruction, and the 13-year-old's #9 is an intermediate situation where preserved cervical/facial enamel justifies a markedly more conservative geometry than the 15-year-old's #9 while still supporting an indirect bonded approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no clear definitive plan, or recommends clearly inappropriate management such as extraction, routine full-coverage crowns, or non-conservative circumferential reduction.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes generally conservative care but does not commit to tooth-specific plans, or does not explain how preparation extent should differ among the 15-year-old's #8, the 15-year-old's #9, and the 13-year-old's #9.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a tooth-specific plan that keeps the 15-year-old's #8 mainly additive, treats the 15-year-old's #9 with indirect bonded partial coverage, and treats the 13-year-old's #9 with indirect bonded partial coverage that is more conservative than the 15-year-old's #9.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: In addition to the correct tooth-specific plans, clearly defines preparation logic: the 15-year-old's #8 should avoid unnecessary reduction; the 15-year-old's #9 may justify limited incisal involvement and a defined seating/cervical margin; the 13-year-old's #9 should preserve tooth length and keep preparation largely defect-limited without routine intentional incisal shortening or unnecessary cervical reduction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Finalizes irreversible restorative treatment without identifying key trauma findings that still need confirmation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic additional tests or trauma review but does not identify two high-priority findings or does not explain how positive findings would alter the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies two key pre-restorative trauma findings not shown in the figures—typically pulpal status and periodontal/radiographic trauma status—and explains how they could change the restorative sequence or delay definitive treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the missing trauma findings explicitly before irreversible preparation and distinguishes how each could alter management, for example shifting first to pulp therapy/endodontic care, splinting/observation, or a different restorative access strategy such as managing subgingival extension rather than proceeding directly with the planned bonded restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits postoperative overload management or follow-up implications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic occlusal adjustment or recall but does not explain how heavy protrusive guidance should change management, or does not distinguish the two patients.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that protrusive load should be reduced or redistributed, recommends protection, and identifies relevant follow-up risks such as chipping, debonding, marginal problems, and delayed pulpal sequelae.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a patient-differentiated overload response: monitoring for the 15-year-old includes both the larger #9 reconstruction and the adjacent #8 direct restoration with shared anterior guidance; the 13-year-old is especially intolerant of concentrated point loading on the restored incisal segment and links successful load redistribution to the intensity of subsequent recall.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending routine full-coverage crowns or other aggressive circumferential reduction for these restorable adolescent incisors without first exhausting conservative bonded options
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: finalizing irreversible restorative treatment without accounting for trauma-related pulpal status and periodontal/radiographic injury

items.question_content: An 86-year-old woman taking rivaroxaban, who requires an escort for appointments, presents with a detached mandibular anterior 3-unit FPD. The prior abutment teeth are hopeless. Maximum intercuspation is stable and reproducible. She refuses a removable prosthesis and declines preparation of additional teeth. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, formulate the definitive plan you would defend at case conference. Commit to 2 implant sites and identify 1 anterior site you would explicitly avoid, justifying those choices from both the figure-based anatomy and the restorative trajectory. Then choose the record-making workflow that best reduces visit burden in this patient and explain why one reasonable alternative workflow is inferior here. Finally, state what single part of your plan would change first if, on the day of surgery, either anticoagulation management remained unresolved or one implant did not achieve adequate primary stability.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The defensible definitive treatment is a fixed implant-supported anterior mandibular prosthesis after removal of the hopeless abutment teeth; reusing those teeth or recruiting additional teeth would be biologically unsound and conflicts with the patient's wishes.

I would commit to implant placement in the left central incisor and right lateral incisor regions. fig_02.jpg supports those sites as compatible with the planned prosthetic envelope while avoiding regenerative surgery. I would explicitly avoid the right canine region because fig_02.jpg shows apical buccal cortical fenestration there, making that site less safe and less predictable for a prosthetically driven implant. A right central site could be considered by some clinicians, but the left central plus right lateral combination better matches the restorative span and support distribution shown in the planned contour.

The most efficient record strategy is a hybrid workflow: obtain rapid preliminary conventional impressions to create casts, use the detached prosthesis position or a wax-up on the cast to define the desired tooth form, digitize that cast/wax-up for CBCT-based prosthetically driven planning, and then, at surgery, capture only a localized implant-level digital record of the operated segment rather than repeating the entire arch. This works here because intercuspation is already stable and the unchanged parts of the arch do not need to be rescanned intraorally. A reasonable alternative such as a full conventional definitive implant impression is inferior because it adds chair time, impression discomfort, and management of sutures and undercuts in a frail elderly patient. A full-arch intraoral scan on the surgical day is also less efficient because most of the arch information is already available and rescanning it would unnecessarily prolong the visit.

If anticoagulation management remained unresolved, the first change would be to postpone elective implant surgery until physician-coordinated perioperative management and local hemostatic planning were clarified; the surgery should not proceed on assumptions. If one implant failed to achieve adequate primary stability, the first change would be the healing/loading strategy: abandon any thought of accelerated loading or restorative progression dependent on that stability, use a more protected healing approach, and defer the definitive implant-level restorative phase as needed. In other words, the site selection and overall prosthetic goal can remain the same, but the timing and invasiveness of the surgical-restorative sequence become more conservative.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, or the patient history, or proposes site choices that are unsupported by the presented anatomy and constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case data but gives vague or weak figure-based justification for implant site selection, or does not clearly connect stable intercuspation, frailty, and patient preferences to the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg with the clinical history to support fixed implant rehabilitation, selects the left central and right lateral regions as the preferred sites, rejects the right canine region, and links the workflow choice to stable intercuspation and reduced visit burden.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows precise figure-based reasoning for why the chosen sites fit both the available bone and restorative trajectory, explicitly explains why the avoided anterior site is less defensible, and synthesizes anatomy, occlusion, patient preference, and logistics into a coherent argument.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate definitive approach or provides no coherent treatment sequence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects a broadly plausible fixed solution but gives an incomplete or inefficient clinical sequence, or does not explain how records would be obtained.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a coherent plan for implant-supported fixed rehabilitation with a hybrid record workflow that includes preliminary cast-based information, prosthetically driven planning, and limited definitive implant record capture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, efficient, prosthetically driven plan that clearly minimizes appointments and chair time without sacrificing accuracy, and explains why the sequence is especially suitable for this patient.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses or mishandles the priority decisions created by unresolved anticoagulation or inadequate primary stability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the contingencies matter but gives generic or poorly prioritized changes to the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes postponing elective surgery if anticoagulation management is unresolved and shifting to a more conservative healing/loading sequence if primary stability is inadequate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly identifies the first plan element that must change in each contingency, explains why that priority comes before other adjustments, and preserves the overall restorative objective while adapting the sequence safely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare meaningful alternatives or ignores the trade-offs relevant to this patient's frailty, anticoagulation, and treatment preferences.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions benefits or risks of the chosen plan but does not adequately compare it with a reasonable alternative workflow or site choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why the chosen workflow is preferable to a reasonable alternative in terms of patient comfort, visit reduction, surgical efficiency, or prosthetic predictability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced trade-off analysis that balances bleeding risk, operative burden, accuracy of records, prosthetic control, and patient autonomy when defending both the chosen and rejected approaches.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Lists conclusions with little or no explanation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some reasoning, but the links from findings to site choice, workflow, and contingency planning are incomplete or hard to follow.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a logical progression from findings to plan, including why the selected sites, workflow, and contingency responses fit this case.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Maintains clear, case-specific reasoning throughout, with each major decision explicitly tied to the figures or the patient's medical, prosthetic, and logistical constraints.

items.question_content:
A 42-year-old woman with nocturnal GERD taking omeprazole has completed endodontic treatment for 45. The implant at 46 has remained uncrowned for 6 months. She wants a tooth-colored result and asks to have 45 finalized before 46 is restored.

Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, decide whether 45 should receive a definitive restoration now or only a transitional restoration until 46 is crowned. If you proceed definitively, state your preferred restoration and the strongest reasonable alternative you would not choose today; justify that choice from the figures, including restorative height, remaining tooth structure, substrate quality, and the effect of the future implant crown. State the single chairside finding that would make you abandon your preferred plan. Then describe the distal contour and occlusal contact scheme you would create on 45 before 46 is restored, and give the 2 GERD-specific appointment modifications that matter most during delivery of this restoration.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Definitive restoration of 45 before 46 is crowned is reasonable only if clinical inspection confirms that 45 is truly restorable with a predictable circumferential ferrule on sound dentin and margins that can be isolated without violating the supracrestal tissue attachment. If that cannot be achieved, I would not force a definitive restoration; I would place only a well-sealed transitional restoration/build-up and discuss options such as orthodontic extrusion, selective crown lengthening, or extraction/replacement depending on feasibility and patient preference.

If restorability is confirmed, my preferred definitive option is a space-efficient custom post-supported full-coverage tooth-colored restoration for 45, ideally a cast/monoblock post-crown with ceramic coverage. fig_01.jpg shows a severely worn posterior occlusal scheme with bite collapse and limited restorative height, and also shows extensive coronal destruction of 45 rather than a small contained lesion. fig_02.jpg supports that the tooth is endodontically treatable and single rooted without periapical disease, but it also shows that retention must be generated efficiently from the remaining radicular/cervical dentin because coronal structure is reduced. In that setting, a separate core plus crown or an adhesive-only posterior cuspal-coverage restoration is less predictable because it either consumes more vertical space or depends more heavily on remaining bonded substrate than the figures suggest is available. A tooth-colored full-coverage result also matches the patient's esthetic request and avoids leaving exposed metal adjacent to an implant in an acid-challenged mouth.

The strongest reasonable alternative I would reject today is an adhesive indirect cuspal-coverage restoration over a bonded core. Its advantages are tooth preservation and esthetics, but in this specific case the generalized erosive wear, reduced axial height, extensive wall loss, and the fact that 45 will function next to an uncrowned implant make debonding, fracture, and overload more concerning. I would switch toward an adhesive cuspal-coverage strategy only if chairside assessment after cleanup showed substantially more circumferential supragingival sound tooth structure, reliable isolation, and a more favorable bonded substrate than the figures imply.

The single chairside finding that would make me abandon the preferred plan is inability to obtain a predictable ferrule on sound dentin with maintainable margins. Without that, prognosis falls sharply and definitive treatment should be reconsidered rather than disguised with a more heroic restoration.

Before 46 is restored, 45 should not be shaped as a surrogate molar. The distal contour should be cleansable and moderately convex, leaving space for the future mesial emergence profile and contact of the 46 crown rather than creating a broad distal platform. Occlusally, 45 should receive light centralized centric contact only, avoiding heavy distal incline contact and avoiding excursive contacts that would make it the terminal posterior stop. After 46 is crowned, occlusion must be reassessed because the implant will not have periodontal ligament mobility and should typically receive slightly lighter centric loading with no lateral interference.

The 2 most important GERD-specific delivery modifications from fig_03.jpg are: keeping the chair/head elevated and avoiding prolonged supine positioning, and actively managing reflux-related contamination risk with pre-procedure timing/antacid measures plus water or sodium bicarbonate rinsing if reflux occurs before or during cementation. Generic anti-erosion advice alone is insufficient here because GERD affects not only long-term tooth wear but also immediate patient tolerance, moisture control, and contamination of the restorative field during delivery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg meaningfully, or gives a generic post-endodontic answer that could apply to many posterior teeth.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not decide between definitive versus transitional management now, or proposes a plan that ignores restorative height, remaining tooth structure, or the future restoration of 46.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

The strongest answer recognizes why a space-efficient custom post-supported full-coverage tooth-colored design is particularly persuasive here, while allowing another plan only if it is justified equally rigorously against the same constraints.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare the preferred plan with a credible alternative, or ignores major case-specific risks.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the preferred plan with a strong self-generated competing approach and explains why it is not chosen today, linking benefits and failure risks to this specific case, including substrate loss, short preparation height, implant-neighbor effects, erosive environment, and the implications of proceeding without predictable ferrule.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify the key chairside switch-point, or does not explain how 45 should be contoured and loaded before 46 is restored.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Addresses either the chairside switch-point or the pre-46 contour/occlusal design, but not both clearly or specifically.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: A skeletally mature woman underwent childhood partial left maxillary resection for juvenile ossifying fibroma, followed by two failed scapular bone grafts and prolonged use of a removable prosthesis. She now asks for a fixed, lower-maintenance solution because repeated clasp repairs and altered appearance remain frustrating. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, what is your preferred long-term rehabilitation strategy now, and how would you justify it to the patient? Use the visible anatomy, prior treatment history, and the lesion’s behavior to explain both your choice and the follow-up priorities that should shape care.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My preferred plan is a definitive adult removable obturator/partial maxillary prosthesis, ideally a refined hollow-bulb design, rather than immediate conversion to a fixed reconstruction. The figures show a large unilateral left maxillary defect with extension into the sinus/nasal space, healed but unsupported tissues on the resected side, and preserved contralateral teeth that can provide mechanical retention and stability. That anatomy favors a lightweight prosthesis that obturates the defect, restores facial support, speech, and mastication, and remains adjustable and repairable. The history of two failed bone grafts makes another reconstructive attempt less predictable, and a fixed implant-supported solution would be limited by deficient support on the resected side and would require fresh multidisciplinary assessment and imaging before being considered.

I would explain that juvenile ossifying fibroma is benign but locally aggressive with substantial recurrence risk, so lifelong clinical and radiographic surveillance is part of treatment. A removable prosthesis is advantageous because it is noninvasive, reversible, easier to modify, and does not compromise surveillance of the site. Follow-up should monitor recurrence, clasp fatigue or loosening, pressure areas and mucosal irritation, hygiene, occlusion, phonetics, and facial support. Retention also depends on adequate salivary flow, so xerostomia risks should be reviewed. Because of the communication with the sinonasal space, impression and repair procedures must protect the airway and avoid aspiration. If, after sustained recurrence-free follow-up and informed counseling, the patient still cannot tolerate the prosthesis functionally or psychosocially, secondary reconstructive options can be reconsidered with prosthodontic, maxillofacial surgical, and psychological input.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an implausible or unsafe plan, or gives no coherent rehabilitation strategy. Does not address restoration of function/esthetics and ignores the need for long-term surveillance.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a rehabilitation approach but gives mostly generic reasoning, weak sequencing, or little explanation of why it fits this patient better than other reasonable paths.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends an appropriate current strategy, typically a definitive removable obturator/partial maxillary prosthesis or a clearly staged reassessment before invasive reconstruction, with rationale tied to the defect, prior graft failure, and functional goals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced staged plan: optimize a definitive adult removable prosthesis now, reserve secondary reconstruction only if recurrence-free reassessment and anatomy support it, and clearly links the plan to function, esthetics, maintainability, and surveillance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads or ignores the figures and history, or bases the answer on unsupported assumptions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated facts from either the history or one figure but does not synthesize them into a coherent justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the clinical history with the figures to recognize a unilateral maxillary resection defect, preserved contralateral dentition for support, healed defect margins, and prosthesis-dependent restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes multiple figure-based findings and history into a strong argument, including the asymmetry of available support, the role of adult skeletal maturity in definitive planning, and the challenge of fixed support in the resected side anatomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh meaningful risks and benefits, or makes unsafe assumptions about predictability of treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic advantages or disadvantages but does not apply them well to this defect or history.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a removable approach offers important benefits here, such as reversibility, lower biologic burden, repairability, and easier surveillance, while acknowledging limitations such as clasp wear, hygiene burden, and esthetic concerns.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances current prosthetic benefits against the uncertainty of invasive reconstruction in this patient, and explains that any future fixed option would require informed expectations, updated imaging, and multidisciplinary candidacy review.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses important risks or follow-up issues relevant to the defect and prosthesis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only one limited complication or follow-up concern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies several important issues such as recurrence, mucosal irritation, clasp fatigue or loss of retention, hygiene problems, and the impact of reduced salivary flow on prosthesis performance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds practical prevention and management priorities, including surveillance intervals, repair/reline needs, and protection against aspiration or sinonasal contamination during impression procedures.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits the need for other specialties where clearly relevant.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions referral in vague terms without linking it to decision-making.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately involves maxillofacial surgery and at least one other relevant discipline, such as radiology or psychological support.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly assigns roles across prosthodontics, maxillofacial surgery, imaging follow-up, and psychological support to sustain long-term function, surveillance, and quality of life.

items.question_content: A 23-year-old man lost the left maxillary central and lateral incisors in a motorbike accident and has a thin gingival biotype. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg; do not assume the photographed sequence is automatically the best plan. Recommend one fixed definitive approach for this defect. First, identify the two most decisive drivers from the case and figures: the finding that makes full biologic re-creation of the lost dentogingival complex least predictable, and the finding that makes prosthetic tissue replacement most acceptable. Then state where you would concentrate implant support within the span, which tissue dimensions you would still try to improve surgically before restoration, and which parts you would intentionally replace prosthetically. Defend the trade-off you are accepting versus another fixed design a reasonable clinician might choose. Finally, specify the design and maintenance features that are essential for long-term success, list the minimum additional clinical information you would still need before finalizing the plan, and explain how your recommendation would change if the smile showed the tissue-restoration junction.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The strongest argument against trying to biologically recreate the entire lost dentogingival complex is the defect itself in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg: this is a severe combined height-and-width anterior ridge deficiency across two adjacent teeth in a thin phenotype, so recreating stable cervical volume and papillae around separate implant emergence profiles is unlikely to be predictable. The strongest finding that makes prosthetic tissue replacement acceptable is fig_06.jpg, which shows that the smile does not expose the tissue-restoration junction. That hidden junction changes the esthetic threshold substantially.

My preferred fixed plan is limited implant support concentrated toward the distal, less visually critical part of the span, consistent with fig_03.jpg, while using pontic-driven esthetics and pink prosthetic replacement to control the more demanding central portion of the defect. I would therefore use one implant toward the lateral-incisor/canine side rather than placing support under both missing teeth. This preserves restorative freedom for the central zone, where papilla illusion and cervical contour are hardest to achieve around an implant abutment in a thin biotype.

Surgically, I would improve the site only enough to create a stable horizontal and soft-tissue foundation for the prosthesis, as supported by fig_04.jpg. I would not make the plan depend on full vertical biologic reconstruction. The residual vertical deficiency, papilla simulation, and part of the cervical soft-tissue form are better replaced prosthetically. fig_05.jpg also implies an important limit: once pink replacement is used, the contour must stay shallow and cleansable rather than steep or bulky.

The main trade-off is that this plan accepts some biomechanical compromise in exchange for better esthetic control. A reasonable competing fixed design would be either two adjacent implants or a single implant placed more centrally under the larger crown. Another clinician might choose one of those to place support under the tooth load more directly or to avoid a mesial pontic/cantilever effect. I would still rank them lower here because they reduce restorative freedom in the papilla-critical zone and increase the risk of black triangles, recession, or an unnatural cervical outcome in a thin biotype with severe ridge loss.

Essential design features are a concealed transition line, controlled transmucosal emergence, a non-steep pink contour to minimize food trapping, cleansable embrasures, and retrievability if possible. Long-term risks are plaque accumulation beneath the pink component, food impaction, phonetic or lip-interference from excessive bulk, and peri-implant inflammation if hygiene access is poor. Maintenance should include explicit instruction for cleaning under the restoration, regular professional review, and radiographic monitoring of crestal bone.

Before finalizing the plan, I would still need CBCT-based 3D bone volume and adjacent-root position, interarch restorative space, occlusal scheme and anterior guidance, more precise smile dynamics and phonetics, and confirmation of the patient's hygiene ability and esthetic expectations. If the smile showed the tissue-restoration junction, I would be much less willing to rely on visible prosthetic gingiva, would raise the priority of biologic reconstruction of facial and vertical tissues, and would reconsider whether this fixed implant design could meet the esthetic demand at all.

levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or gives a generic anterior implant answer that could fit many cases.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings only, such as ridge loss or smile line, without linking fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg into a coherent case-specific argument.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the severe combined ridge deficiency, thin phenotype, and hidden smile junction into a coherent rationale for limited implant support with selective site development and prosthetic tissue replacement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly synthesizes fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg as severe combined height-and-width loss, fig_03.jpg as support concentrated away from the most demanding esthetic zone, fig_04.jpg as foundation improvement rather than full vertical re-creation, fig_05.jpg as a contour/cleanability constraint, and fig_06.jpg as the reason a concealed transition line is feasible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not commit to a clear fixed definitive plan or proposes a plan that ignores the ridge-defect problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a plausible fixed restoration but is vague about support location, or does not distinguish what should be improved surgically versus replaced prosthetically.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends an appropriate fixed plan with limited implant support, selective horizontal hard- and/or soft-tissue development, and deliberate prosthetic replacement of the residual defect.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise plan that concentrates support toward the distal or less visually critical part of the span, preserves pontic-driven control in the central esthetic zone, and clearly separates biologic foundation-building from prosthetic replacement of the remaining dentogingival deficiency.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare alternatives or ignores the trade-offs of the chosen design.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative fixed design but gives only generic advantages or disadvantages.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with another reasonable fixed design using patient-specific reasoning that includes esthetic control, tissue behavior, biomechanics, or hygiene burden.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a balanced comparison that acknowledges why a more central or more extensive implant plan could improve direct support while worsening papilla or cervical control in this case, and correctly explains how a visible tissue-restoration junction would shift the threshold toward greater biologic reconstruction or away from visible pink prosthetic replacement.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major design-dependent complications, maintenance needs, or essential missing information before finalization.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions hygiene or follow-up only generally, or lists additional information without showing why it matters to the decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant design-dependent complications such as plaque retention, food trapping, esthetic mismatch, phonetic or lip-interference, or peri-implant inflammation; links prevention to contour and hygiene access; and names key missing data before finalizing the plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes what can be decided now from the figures versus what still requires workup, including CBCT/root relationships, occlusion, interarch space, smile dynamics or phonetics, and hygiene capacity, and ties the maintenance schedule directly to the chosen pink-prosthetic design.

items.question_content: A 25-year-old man with Papillon-Lefevre syndrome is being planned for definitive oral rehabilitation after prior preprosthetic surgery and implant placement. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg before answering. Without repeating the captions, interpret the support available in each arch and the status of the questionable maxillary site at review. Based on that, describe the prosthodontic plan you would choose for long-term function: when would you load, what type of definitive prosthesis would you favor, and which design features would you insist on to reduce failure risk? If the suspect implant were clinically immobile but still radiographically equivocal and the patient refused any further grafting or re-entry surgery, what would change in your plan?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: fig_01.jpg indicates that the maxilla has already been augmented, while the mandible has limited remaining bone support, so the plan should be conservative and load-controlled. fig_02.jpg should be read as an early compromised maxillary implant site at the review stage. If the implant is mobile or clearly failing, I would remove it, allow healing, and continue only with the stable implants after delayed loading rather than forcing immediate replacement or re-grafting when the patient refuses more surgery. The preferred definitive restoration is a fixed full-arch hybrid prosthesis on the remaining osseointegrated implants, with short cantilevers, tissue clearance for hygiene, careful occlusion, and strict maintenance/recall. If the implant were clinically immobile but radiographically equivocal, I would not immediately load it; I would monitor closely with serial clinical and radiographic review and proceed only if stability is confirmed, removing it if mobility or progressive bone loss appears.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg correctly, or misstates the support/bone status.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one image or gives an incomplete interpretation of the arch support or implant status.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly interprets fig_01.jpg as showing augmented maxillary support with limited mandibular bone and fig_02.jpg as early compromise of a maxillary implant, then links both to the management plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends immediate loading, ignores the compromised site, or proposes an unrelated rehabilitation plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for caution but does not clearly specify delayed loading, the definitive prosthesis type, or how the compromised site is handled.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Recommends removal or non-loading of a failing implant when indicated, healing before loading, and completion with a fixed full-arch hybrid prosthesis on the remaining stable implants.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores PLS-related failure risk, limited bone, or refusal of further grafting.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions risk but does not clearly balance why re-grafting, immediate replacement, or immediate loading is less attractive.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly weighs PLS failure risk, limited support, morbidity/refusal of re-entry surgery, and functional benefit to justify conservative delayed loading and retention of stable implants.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits relevant complications or suggests a plan that increases failure risk.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a complication but does not describe meaningful prevention or monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates recurrent mobility, peri-implant bone loss, and plaque-retention problems, and recommends hygiene access, occlusal control, and close clinical/radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes the wrong next step, such as immediate replacement or loading before stability is established.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Sequences some steps but does not explain how the refusal of further grafting changes management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly sequences image interpretation, stability assessment, removal or observation of the questionable site, healing, delayed loading, definitive prosthesis delivery, and long-term maintenance; if the site remains equivocal but stable, it is monitored rather than forced into immediate replacement.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, as well as fig_04.jpg and fig_05.jpg: a 45-year-old man has long-span posterior tooth loss in both arches with several remaining teeth of mixed restorative status. What definitive prosthodontic strategy would you select for this patient, and which patient-specific factors shown or implied in the records make that choice the most defensible? Include the pre-insertion checks you would use to protect the remaining abutments.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: Choose a maxillary distal-extension cast partial denture retained with extracoronal precision attachments on splinted terminal abutments, with fixed prosthetic rehabilitation in the mandibular arch. This is defensible because the patient has a long bilateral posterior edentulous span, retained abutment teeth with prior restorative/endodontic treatment, and a clear need to maximize retention, esthetics, and stress distribution while preserving tooth structure and controlling cost and invasiveness. Before insertion, verify abutment parallelism, periodontal/endodontic soundness, adequate interarch space, and a harmonious occlusal plane on the mounted casts; use the facebow/Broadrick records to avoid occlusal interferences. Long-term, monitor attachment wear, retention loss, plaque control, and abutment overload with regular recalls.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not propose a coherent arch-specific prosthodontic plan or gives a plan that ignores the distal-extension problem and remaining abutments.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a plausible prosthesis but omits either the arch-specific design, the attachment concept, or the sequence/verification steps.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a combined fixed-removable approach, including a precision-attachment-retained maxillary distal-extension prosthesis and fixed mandibular rehabilitation, with a reasonable rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives the correct arch-specific plan and also addresses parallelism, occlusal verification, and follow-up/maintenance planning to support long-term function.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or no case-specific information; the answer could apply to any edentulous patient.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some findings but does not connect the arch pattern, remaining teeth, or mounted records to the treatment choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the bilateral distal-extension pattern, remaining abutments, restorative/endodontic status, and mounted occlusal records into the plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all available clinical, radiographic, and mounted-record findings to explain why the chosen design is feasible and stable in this specific patient.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores trade-offs, maintenance burden, or preservation of remaining teeth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions benefit(s) such as esthetics or retention but gives little attention to meaningful risks or limitations.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances retention, esthetics, stress distribution, affordability, and preservation of remaining teeth against the long-term maintenance burden.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also addresses attachment wear, plaque retention, torque on abutments, and the need for periodic adjustment/reline or insert replacement.

items.question_content: An edentulous adult in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, fig_06.jpg, and fig_07.jpg was restored with fixed prostheses within 72 hours. Using only what the figures show, write an accept/modify/reject audit of that decision. Decide separately for the maxilla and mandible whether the observed implant distribution and framework geometry are sufficient for true immediate function, citing image-based features rather than generic implant theory. Identify the single image-based concern that most threatens the plan and explain whether the change from fig_06.jpg to fig_07.jpg increases or decreases your confidence. State the minimum additional examination or imaging you would require before definitive delivery. Then explain how you would manage the case if, at day 11, the framework remains rigid but the patient develops localized mandibular pain on loading with no obvious loosening on plain radiography. Briefly contrast your approach with one other realistic pathway of your own choosing and name the trade-off that decides between them.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
On the figures alone, I would accept the concept in the maxilla and only conditionally in the mandible.

The maxillary reconstruction is biomechanically defensible because fig_02.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_06.jpg show multiple nonparallel supports distributed across the arch with posterior support rather than an obvious small anterior cluster, and fig_04.jpg/fig_05.jpg show rigid metal cross-arch frameworks. That geometry is more consistent with a load-sharing unit than with a long crest-dependent cantilever. The immediate and 6-month radiographs do not show obvious loss of support, gross new radiolucency, or framework failure.

The mandible is the less forgiving arch, but the reason is not a generic textbook statement about mandibular flexure. fig_01.jpg shows a right mandibular body/inferior border contour abnormality most consistent with old fracture callus or another prior osseous change. fig_03.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg still show broad implant spread and a rigid splinted design, so the prosthetic mechanics are not obviously poor; however, host-bone stability at that abnormal body region is the main unresolved issue. If that site were clinically quiet and stable, I could accept immediate mandibular function cautiously. If it were tender, mobile, or suspicious for active pathology, I would not sign off the lower immediate-load plan.

The single concern most threatening the plan is therefore the mandibular body abnormality visible on fig_01.jpg. fig_06.jpg to fig_07.jpg is moderately reassuring: the arch reconstructions remain intact, there is no clear implant displacement or obvious progressive peri-implant halo, and the inferior mandibular contour appears smoother/less bulky, which fits remodeling of callus rather than worsening disease. Even so, the serial radiographs do not prove that the mandible was mechanically stable at delivery.

Before definitive delivery, the minimum additional information I would require is direct clinical assessment of the mandibular body abnormality: palpation for tenderness, segmental mobility, pain on loading, and correlation with occlusion. If any doubt remained, targeted cross-sectional imaging and surgical input would take priority over prosthetic completion. Passive framework fit and lack of implant mobility are necessary, but they do not override uncertainty about the basal bone itself.

If day 11 brings localized mandibular pain on loading while the framework is still rigid and the plain radiograph shows no obvious loosening, I would not dismiss it as routine postoperative discomfort. The main possibilities are overload concentrated on one support implant or stress transfer through the previously abnormal mandibular body. My first management change would be to unload the mandible: reduce or remove functional occlusal contacts, examine each implant and the abnormal body region for tenderness or mobility, and obtain targeted imaging. If the pain localizes to the body abnormality or any segmental mobility is detected, I would stop immediate mandibular function and stage the lower arch rather than waiting for overt radiographic failure.

A realistic alternative is staged mandibular management with a transitional removable or nonfunctional provisional while confirming mandibular stability, with the maxilla proceeding only if its support is independently sound. That becomes the stronger pathway when the fig_01.jpg abnormality is symptomatic or uncertain because it protects the weak link. The fully immediate two-arch plan is stronger only when the mandibular body change is demonstrably stable; an under-supported or diagnostically unresolved immediate lower arch is weaker than either principal option.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg-fig_07.jpg meaningfully, or answers with generic immediate-loading principles that could fit almost any case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions multiple implants, framework rigidity, or atrophy, but links the figures to management only superficially and misses or misreads the dominant mandibular concern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the figures to infer strategic nonparallel implant distribution, rigid cross-arch splinting, and a serially stable overall construct, and identifies the mandibular body contour abnormality on fig_01.jpg as the chief issue requiring caution.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates fig_02.jpg-fig_05.jpg with fig_06.jpg and fig_07.jpg to make an arch-specific judgment, explicitly separating what the serial images reassure about from what they cannot resolve, and explains why the geometry appears load-sharing rather than simply describing 'many implants'.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides an inappropriate single yes/no answer or endorses immediate function without meaningful conditions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a plan but does not decide separately for the maxilla and mandible, or does not tie the decision to the figure-based biomechanics and mandibular host-bone concern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a defensible arch-specific accept/modify/reject plan: the maxilla may proceed if support is truly posterior and rigidly splinted, whereas the mandible is conditional on proving stability of the abnormal body region.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds a coherent fallback if the mandibular risk remains unresolved, such as staging or unloading the lower arch while preserving only an independently defensible maxillary plan, and avoids forcing a compromised immediate lower fixed reconstruction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not prioritize further assessment of the dominant concern before definitive delivery.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Requests more information, but only in a generic way such as 'more scans' or 'more follow-up' without identifying the minimum decisive step.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes direct assessment of mandibular stability at the fig_01.jpg abnormality, including tenderness or segmental mobility, and escalates to targeted imaging if abnormal findings are present.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why verifying mandibular host-bone stability outranks routine implant checks alone and clearly states what finding would abort or stage the mandibular immediate-load plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully address day-11 localized mandibular pain, or treats it as trivial without changing management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the pain as concerning but gives only generic follow-up advice without a likely mechanism or a clear first management change.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies plausible early causes of pain despite a rigid framework and unrevealing plain radiography, such as occlusal overload, an unstable support implant, or stress through the previously abnormal mandibular body, and recommends unloading with targeted reassessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Distinguishes implant-level overload from basal-bone instability and links each to an appropriate escalation pathway, including temporary cessation of lower immediate function or conversion to a staged plan if mandibular instability is suspected.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare the plan with any realistic alternative.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative pathway but does not weigh it against the anatomy, figure-derived uncertainty, and treatment goals in this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with a realistic self-generated alternative, such as staged mandibular management or delayed augmentation-based treatment, using patient-specific trade-offs including morbidity, time, fixed-function goals, and uncertainty about mandibular stability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly states when the alternative becomes preferable and why an under-supported or diagnostically unresolved immediate lower arch is weaker than either principal pathway.

items.question_content: A 67-year-old man, fully independent and taking clopidogrel after an ischemic stroke, returns for definitive maxillary rehabilitation after healing from extractions. Four maxillary implants are present. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, determine the maxillary overdenture attachment architecture you would prescribe. Do not just name an attachment type: explain which region is space-limiting, how the implant spread and the full abutment-bar-attachment vertical stack constrain the design, where the retentive elements should be positioned relative to the implants, and whether you would aim for reduced palatal coverage or broader palatal support. Identify one reasonable alternative design you would reject and why. Then state how your plan would change if one side did not have enough vertical space for the planned stack, and list the main maintenance complications you would anticipate.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would prescribe a maxillary implant overdenture retained by two short bar segments, each splinting the implants on one side, with low-profile stud attachments incorporated into the bars rather than relying on a single continuous bar or four unsplinted studs.

The key figure-derived issue is not whether any space exists, but where space is most limited. fig_01.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg indicate that restorative space must be assessed as a total stack from the implant platform upward: intermediate abutment height, bar height, stud attachment/housing height, and then enough remaining room for acrylic base and tooth arrangement. The critical limitation is the anterior/central incisor region. Although overall space is adequate for a bar-based overdenture, a single transarch bar crossing that anterior zone would risk excessive bulk, altered tooth position, phonetic problems, weak acrylic around the teeth, and poor cleansability.

fig_02.jpg supports splinting in the maxilla because the implants are distributed across the arch but still benefit from load sharing and improved stability. For that reason, I would use two unilateral bar segments rather than independent attachments. Each segment would carry two low-profile stud attachments, positioned where prosthetic space and path of insertion are favorable, not necessarily directly over the implant positions. That is one major advantage of incorporating studs into a bar: the retentive elements can be moved to more favorable sites while the implants remain splinted.

I would aim for reduced palatal coverage, not an unnecessarily bulky palate, because the splinted design improves retention and stability; however, I would not sacrifice rigidity or tissue support simply to make it completely palateless. The superstructure should have passive fit, parallel attachment paths, hygienic relief beneath the bars, and enough acrylic thickness around the housings.

One reasonable alternative I would reject is a single continuous bar with conventional clip retention. In this patient, the anterior space limitation makes that design more likely to become bulky and less hygienic in the incisor region. Another rejectable alternative would be four unsplinted maxillary studs, because that would give less splinting and potentially more rotational instability and maintenance in the maxilla. Either rejection is acceptable if justified from the figures.

If one side lacked enough vertical space for the full abutment-bar-attachment stack, I would not force the same bar-stud design asymmetrically. I would step back and redesign the whole maxillary attachment concept toward the lowest-profile option that preserves tooth position, acrylic strength, and cleansability—most commonly unsplinted low-profile stud attachments with greater palatal/tissue support, or another simpler space-efficient attachment design. The principle is that inadequate vertical space is a reason to simplify, not to accept a bulky, weak, or unhygienic overdenture.

Main maintenance risks are plaque accumulation under the bars, mucosal inflammation or hyperplasia, stud insert wear with loss of retention, screw loosening, fracture of acrylic or denture teeth around the housings, and peri-implant tissue or bone changes from overload or poor hygiene. Prevention and monitoring include passive fit verification, cleansable contour design, hygiene instruction and reinforcement, regular recalls, replacement of worn retentive inserts, occlusal review, and periodic clinical/radiographic monitoring.
