items.question_content: A 70-year-old woman with diabetes and several other chronic conditions has a healed mandibular All-on-4 planned for a fixed complete denture. The posterior implants already use angled multi-unit abutments and the anterior implants use straight multi-unit abutments. Four months after placement, digital design of the provisional prosthesis shows that the 2 anterior screw access holes will emerge facially in the esthetic zone (see fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg). She cannot tolerate a removable prosthesis, wants a fixed solution, and minimizing extra appointments is important. What definitive restorative strategy would you choose, and why is it better suited to this patient than other reasonable ways of managing the facial access problem? Base your answer on the figures and clinical context, and include the main maintenance or biologic liabilities you would discuss before delivery.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would keep the existing multi-unit abutment configuration and use an abutment-level, screw-retained splinted full-arch framework, but design the 2 anterior facial-access sites as separate crowns that are cemented onto the framework after the framework is screwed in. This addresses a localized esthetic problem while preserving the main advantages of a screw-retained full-arch prosthesis.

This is the best fit because fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show that the problem is limited to the 2 anterior implants in a highly visible zone, not a generalized full-arch trajectory problem. A localized crown-over-framework solution masks the facial access holes without converting the whole prosthesis to cement retention. I would avoid replacing the healed straight anterior multi-unit abutments with angled ones in this patient because that would add visits, require reworking the prosthetic workflow, and may disrupt the established soft-tissue seal around the abutments. I would also avoid a fully cement-retained definitive full-arch prosthesis because it compromises retrievability and increases the risks of residual cement, peri-implant inflammation, and seating/misfit across multiple abutments.

The main trade-off is maintenance: if the prosthesis ever needs retrieval, the 2 individual anterior crowns may need to be removed or sacrificed, but that is a limited and replaceable complication compared with damaging or remaking the entire arch prosthesis. Before delivery I would discuss meticulous cement cleanup at those 2 sites, possible debonding or fracture of the individual crowns, future retrievability, peri-implant tissue monitoring, passive fit, occlusion, and screw-maintenance needs.

question_options.text: Integrate early preventive dental care into diabetes follow-up, with fluoride toothpaste, caregiver-assisted brushing, dietary counseling, and regular recalls.
Begin preventive dental intervention early despite inconclusive evidence for a higher ECC burden, because salivary and gingival vulnerability can still be present in T1D.
Recognize that gingival inflammation may occur in young children with T1D even when dmft is similar to peers, and address periodontal and salivary risk alongside caries prevention.
Acknowledge that medical follow-up and diet supervision may not fully offset oral vulnerability in T1D, so preventive dental care should be integrated early.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Although evidence does not conclusively show higher ECC prevalence in preschool children with T1D, consistent findings include reduced salivary flow, lower pH, reduced buffering capacity, gingival inflammation, and irregular preventive care. Poorer glycemic control is also often linked to worse oral findings. Gingival inflammation may occur even when dmft does not differ from peers, so management should not focus only on existing caries severity. The most appropriate approach is early integrated preventive dental care rather than delaying intervention or relying on medical monitoring and diet control alone.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old boy presents 24 hours after motorcycle-related facial trauma. The avulsed teeth, including one primary tooth, were brought dry in an empty box. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg to decide which teeth are realistically salvageable and to formulate the dental management plan at this visit. Explain what you would do for the injured teeth, how you would stabilize or replace missing teeth in this growing child, and which biologic risks most strongly influence your decisions and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, I would try to preserve only teeth that are still present and have a salvageable socket. The two mandibular incisors that are luxated but remain in the arch should be gently repositioned and stabilized with a flexible splint. The mandibular incisor that is disarticulated from a fractured socket should be removed rather than replanted or retained because the socket and cortical plates are disrupted, so periodontal support is not realistically restorable. I would not reimplant the avulsed maxillary permanent teeth: the images show severe maxillary dentoalveolar fracture/socket loss, and the teeth have been dry for 24 hours, so functional periodontal healing is extremely unlikely and the risks of contamination, ankylosis, and inflammatory or replacement resorption are high. The avulsed primary tooth should also not be replanted because of the risk of damage to the permanent successor.

Initial care should include soft-tissue debridement/assessment, occlusal check, oral-hygiene instructions with antiseptic rinsing, soft diet, analgesia, and infection control as clinically indicated, followed by close review. After soft-tissue healing, I would provide a removable interim prosthesis for the maxillary defect because the patient is still growing and needs restoration of esthetics, speech, and mastication without compromising eruption or committing to definitive fixed treatment. Follow-up should monitor the retained mandibular teeth and injured sites for loss of vitality, infection, mobility, periodontal healing, inflammatory or replacement resorption/ankylosis, radiographic healing of the alveolus, occlusal disturbance, and the need to adjust the prosthesis as eruption continues.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures or key history to inform decisions; misses major determinants such as prolonged dry storage, alveolar/socket destruction, mixed dentition, or which teeth remain potentially retainable.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely; recognizes either trauma severity or avulsion timing, yet does not clearly connect imaging findings and dentition stage to feasibility of salvage.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the 24-hour dry time, the alveolar fracture/socket loss visible on fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, and the distinction between luxated retained mandibular teeth versus avulsed/disarticulated teeth to guide management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes history, clinical status, and figure-based imaging into a coherent rationale that also accounts for developing dentition and future eruption/growth when judging salvageability and rehabilitation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Management is unsafe or largely inappropriate, such as blanket reimplantation, no stabilization of salvageable teeth, or no coherent plan for the missing maxillary segment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Includes some correct elements but mismanages major decisions about which teeth to retain, remove, or not reimplant, or omits short-term rehabilitation in the growing child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately repositions and flexibly splints the luxated mandibular incisors, removes the disarticulated mandibular incisor with a destroyed socket, does not reimplant the maxillary avulsed teeth, avoids reimplanting the avulsed primary tooth, and plans interim removable prosthetic replacement after soft-tissue healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan from acute management through stabilization and transitional prosthetic rehabilitation, with sound sequencing, growth-sensitive decision-making, and practical supportive care.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers little or no justification, or justifies choices with incorrect or generic reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives limited pros/cons but does not tie them well to this patient's dry storage time, alveolar injury, or developmental status.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that reimplantation into fractured or absent sockets after prolonged dry storage has very poor prognosis because of periodontal ligament death and high risks of ankylosis/replacement resorption, while retaining repositionable mandibular teeth may preserve function and support; recognizes why a primary tooth should not be replanted.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances immediate function, esthetics, biology, and growth in a nuanced way, including why transitional removable rehabilitation is preferable to definitive fixed solutions at this age and why conservative retention of viable mandibular teeth is advantageous.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No meaningful follow-up plan or complication monitoring.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions follow-up only vaguely, with few specific complications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key complications to monitor: pulpal necrosis/loss of vitality, infection, mobility, periodontal breakdown, inflammatory or replacement resorption/ankylosis, radiographic healing, occlusal disturbance, and prosthesis adjustment needs.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how these complications would alter prognosis and subsequent rehabilitation, and links surveillance to the evolving mixed-dentition stage and eruption changes.

red_flags: Contraindication Ignored: recommending reimplantation of the avulsed primary tooth despite mixed dentition and risk to the permanent successor
Generic Textbook Management: recommending routine reimplantation of the dry-stored maxillary avulsed teeth despite fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg showing major alveolar socket destruction

items.question_content: Examine fig_01.jpg only. A 12-year-old boy with prematurity, congenital chronic intestinal pseudoobstruction, chronic diarrhea/metabolic acidosis, and later somatic mitochondrial disease presents with his father because the lower front teeth have looked abnormal since eruption; the boy reports chewing sensitivity from the lower back teeth. You do not yet have radiographs or orthodontic records. Write the consultation note you would defend today: identify the likely diagnosis for each visible tooth group, making clear which findings you would group under MIH and which you would not, and why; choose the single most important initial treatment objective and justify it against the strongest reasonable competing priority in this case; then give two specific later findings that would move your long-term first permanent molar plan in opposite directions—one that would strengthen continued restoration and one that would make retention hard to defend. Use the medical history only insofar as it changes risk, durability, or prevention.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is a mixed developmental enamel-defect pattern rather than one diagnosis for every visible tooth. The first permanent molars show severe MIH: demarcated yellow-brown/brown opacities with posteruptive enamel breakdown, and the mandibular molars are symptomatic, which fits severe molar involvement. The mandibular incisors are most consistent with incisor involvement of MIH because they show demarcated white/cream to yellow-brown opacities with clear borders. In contrast, the maxillary anterior defects are better classified as enamel hypoplasia or another non-classic developmental enamel defect rather than typical MIH, because the visible pattern is linear grooving/localized loss of enamel thickness with a smoother transition to surrounding enamel, not mainly demarcated opacity.

My single most important initial objective is to stabilize and protect the symptomatic first permanent molars, not to start with anterior cosmetic treatment. The strongest competing priority is the father’s concern about anterior appearance, but posterior symptom control and prevention come first because the molars are functionally compromised and at risk of further rapid breakdown, caries, and repeated retreatment. The medical history does not prove a single cause for all defects, but it supports a prevention-first, durable, low-maintenance strategy in a medically burdened child. I would begin with risk reduction and desensitization, then provide durable protection for restorable severely affected molars. Full coronal protection is generally more predictable than small adhesive repairs in severely broken-down MIH molars because the enamel is porous and brittle and margins tend to fail. Anterior care can be delayed and individualized: opacity-dominant mandibular incisors may be monitored or managed conservatively for esthetics, whereas grooved/thinned maxillary anterior teeth would need additive resin restoration rather than microabrasion alone if treatment is desired.

A later finding that would strengthen continued restoration would be radiographic and clinical evidence of adequate remaining tooth structure, no pulpal/periapical disease, good symptom control after protection, and an orthodontic situation that does not favor loss of the first permanent molar. A later finding that would make retention hard to defend would be poor restorability, persistent pain or breakdown despite coverage, pulpal/periapical involvement, repeated failure, or later orthodontic assessment showing that sacrificing a poor-prognosis first permanent molar would be strategically favorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misdiagnoses the presentation as generalized caries, fluorosis, or amelogenesis imperfecta, or applies a single label to all affected teeth without recognizing a mixed defect pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes MIH or developmental enamel defects in general, but fails to separate the maxillary anterior grooved/thinned defects from classic MIH or misses the severity of posteruptive molar breakdown.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies severe MIH of the first permanent molars with mandibular incisor involvement and distinguishes the maxillary anterior defects as a different developmental enamel defect such as hypoplasia.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately characterizes the mixed pattern from fig_01.jpg and explicitly justifies it with figure-visible features such as demarcated opacities/posteruptive breakdown versus linear grooves or localized reduction in enamel thickness with smoother borders.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic answer not anchored to fig_01.jpg, symptoms, or medical history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the figure, the symptom history, or the medical history, but does not synthesize them into a coherent explanation of risk, durability, or prevention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg, posterior sensitivity, and the systemic history to justify a prevention-focused, durable plan and explains that the history increases maintenance burden or risk.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, symptoms, and medical history while also recognizing causal uncertainty: the history supports developmental vulnerability and the need to minimize repeated treatment, but the diagnosis still depends on the specific defect morphology seen clinically.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not establish a defensible first priority, or prioritizes anterior esthetics without addressing the symptomatic molars.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that molars matter first but does not justify this against the main competing priority in the case or does not sequence care clearly.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes symptom control and protection of the severely affected molars over anterior esthetic treatment and gives a logical order of care.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly identifies the esthetic concern as the strongest competing priority, explains why it is deferred relative to function/pain/breakdown, and shows how later anterior management would differ by defect type rather than treating all anterior teeth the same.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers a one-size-fits-all plan for all teeth, omits preventive/desensitizing care, or recommends irreversible molar loss without adequate workup.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Includes some appropriate measures but is vague about restorative strategy, does not match treatment to defect type, or gives nonspecific future reassessment triggers.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends prevention/desensitization followed by durable coverage for restorable severely affected molars, with more conservative or additive anterior treatment tailored to morphology; names one later finding favoring continued restoration and one making retention hard to defend.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly explains why limited adhesive repairs are less predictable than full coverage in severely broken-down MIH molars and gives specific opposite-direction future findings, such as adequate restorability/symptom control versus non-restorability, pulpal disease, repeated failure, or orthodontic timing that strategically favors molar removal.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending immediate extraction of a first permanent molar without assessing radiographs, restorability, pulpal status, and orthodontic timing.

items.question_content:
A 6-year-5-month boy returns after 2.5 years without review because of cold sensitivity in the maxillary incisors. His father and 8-year-old sister are also affected, and no molecular diagnosis is available. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg.

You have two short visits, and after preventive care there is time for only one operative procedure per visit. Write the brief consultant note that defends your sequence. Identify the most likely working diagnosis and why the pedigree and tooth morphology support it, name one plausible competing explanation that is less likely, identify the exact fig_04.jpg finding that changes urgency despite the chief complaint, choose what you would do first and second, explain one seemingly reasonable intervention you would defer at this age, and state what new clinical or radiographic development would make you reverse the order.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The strongest working diagnosis is hereditary generalized amelogenesis imperfecta affecting primary and erupting permanent teeth, with a hypoplastic phenotype favored. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show generalized rough, irregular, pitted/thin enamel with crown contours still identifiable rather than a primarily color-change pattern alone, which supports hypoplastic AI. fig_01.jpg supports likely autosomal dominant inheritance because the condition is seen across successive generations, affects both sexes, and includes male-to-male transmission. This is still a working diagnosis; definitive subtype confirmation would require genetic/molecular assessment.

A plausible competing explanation is a nonhereditary developmental enamel defect such as molar-incisor hypomineralization or generalized acquired enamel hypoplasia, but that is less likely because the defect is generalized, involves both dentitions, and follows a clear family pattern rather than a sporadic distribution.

The fig_04.jpg finding that changes urgency is not infection or a need for extraction; it is the misfitting preformed metal crowns on the maxillary second primary molars that are mechanically interfering with eruption of the first permanent molars. That posterior problem is more time-sensitive than the anterior chief complaint because delayed interception can alter eruptive path and future occlusal development.

Under the one-procedure-per-visit limit, my preferred order is:
Visit 1: behavior guidance, hygiene reinforcement, fluoride varnish/desensitizing prevention, then correct the eruption-interfering posterior problem by revising/removing/replacing the maladapted primary-molar crowns to clear the eruptive path while preserving the primary teeth if feasible.
Visit 2: provide conservative protective restoration/coverage of the symptomatic maxillary incisors to reduce cold sensitivity and protect defective enamel, for example with adhesive direct composite or other age-appropriate interim coverage. If, at reassessment, an erupted first permanent molar is showing greater immediate structural risk than the incisors, an alternative defensible second visit would be protective management of that molar, but only if the anterior sensitivity has at least been temporized non-operatively.

A seemingly reasonable intervention to defer is definitive indirect esthetic/prosthodontic rehabilitation or comprehensive orthodontic/open-bite correction. In a 6-year-old with mixed dentition, ongoing eruption, and compromised enamel substrate, these are poorly timed, more irreversible, and likely to need repeated revision. Premature extraction of the asymptomatic posterior primary teeth simply to eliminate the interference should also be avoided unless the teeth are otherwise non-restorable, because it may create unnecessary space-management problems.

I would reverse the order if new information showed that the fig_04.jpg posterior interference was no longer truly present or clinically significant, or if the anterior segment worsened to severe pain, rapid breakdown, or pulpal involvement, making the incisors the more urgent first operative target.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives an implausible diagnosis, does not identify amelogenesis imperfecta, or misclassifies the condition in a way inconsistent with the figures and history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies amelogenesis imperfecta or hereditary enamel disease but does not commit to a supported phenotype or likely inheritance pattern, or states the diagnosis with unwarranted certainty.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies generalized hereditary amelogenesis imperfecta with a plausible phenotype and inheritance pattern, and frames this appropriately as a working diagnosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies generalized amelogenesis imperfecta most consistent with a hypoplastic phenotype and likely autosomal dominant inheritance, explicitly supported by fig_01.jpg pedigree interpretation including male-to-male transmission and by fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg morphology showing generalized rough/pitted/thin enamel with preserved crown contours.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful differential diagnosis, or the alternative offered is clinically implausible.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a plausible alternative diagnosis but does not explain why it is less likely in this child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides at least one plausible competing explanation and rules it down using case-specific features such as generalized distribution, involvement of primary teeth, or family history.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically contrasts the working diagnosis with a plausible nonleading alternative such as a nonhereditary developmental enamel defect, and explains why the pedigree plus generalized involvement of both dentitions make that alternative less likely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully, or misreads the key radiographic finding on fig_04.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses one data source or figure in a general way, but the linkage to diagnosis or urgency is weak or incomplete.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates at least three relevant data sources among history, fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg to support diagnosis and management sequence.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately synthesizes fig_01.jpg pedigree findings, fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg clinical morphology, the symptom history, and the specific fig_04.jpg radiographic finding of misfitting crowns on maxillary second primary molars interfering with eruption of first permanent molars, and uses that synthesis to justify urgency and sequencing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides an unsafe or incoherent priority order, or ignores the key time-sensitive issue.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses an order of care but does not adequately weigh the asymptomatic posterior urgency against the symptomatic anterior complaint.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a coherent two-visit order under the stated constraint and explains the trade-off between posterior eruption risk and anterior sensitivity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly prioritizes the eruption-interfering posterior problem first because delayed interception risks altered eruptive path/occlusal development, while clearly justifying the second target based on symptom burden and structural risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Plan is generic, infeasible in two short visits, or does not specify what would actually be done.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Outlines a phased plan but remains vague about the specific operative procedures or does not fit the one-procedure-per-visit limit.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a feasible two-visit plan with preventive care and a specific operative action in each visit, including management of the posterior interference in one visit and an appropriate next target in the other.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a concrete, age-appropriate sequence in which visit 1 relieves the fig_04.jpg eruption interference by correcting the maladapted primary-molar crowns, and visit 2 addresses the next highest-risk target with explicit justification and temporary management of what is deferred; the plan is conservative and preservation-focused.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify any intervention to defer, or recommends an unnecessarily irreversible or harmful first-phase approach.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Defers an intervention only with generic statements about age or growth, without case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Defers a reasonable intervention with case-specific reasons related to mixed dentition, eruption stage, or compromised enamel substrate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly explains why apparently reasonable options such as definitive indirect rehabilitation, comprehensive orthodontic correction, or premature extraction/other irreversible treatment are not appropriate first-phase choices and how they could worsen prognosis or create avoidable retreatment or space-management problems.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives conclusions without a clear chain of reasoning, or omits the condition that would change the visit order.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some logic but the rationale for sequencing or the trigger to reverse the order is vague.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a logical progression from findings to diagnosis to sequence, and states a plausible development that would change the order.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides an internally consistent, figure-anchored rationale from diagnosis to prioritization to treatment sequence, and names a specific new clinical or radiographic development that would credibly reverse the first-two-visit order.

items.question_content: A healthy 10-year-old boy in mixed dentition presents with repeated cheek biting from a pedunculated left buccal lesion. Using the preoperative clinical and radiographic findings in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, explain the management you would recommend for the symptomatic maxillary left posterior sextant. Specify which teeth should be removed at this stage, which teeth may be left in situ for follow-up, and how the clinical appearance and imaging support that plan. Then state what fig_03.jpg represents in follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Active treatment is indicated because the child is symptomatic: the crowded, buccally displaced erupted molars are causing cheek trauma and have produced a traumatic/irritation fibroma at the line of occlusion. Preoperative assessment in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg shows multiple supplemental maxillary left molars, with three erupted and three unerupted teeth in that sextant.

The recommended management is surgical excision of the buccal fibroma together with extraction of all three erupted molars and one unerupted molar that is the most accessible and displaced, specifically the unerupted molar distal to the last erupted molar. This matches the aim of relieving current trauma and crowding while also avoiding a later second operation for the most surgically accessible displaced impacted tooth.

The remaining unerupted molars may be left in situ initially and monitored radiographically, because the immediate symptomatic problem is caused by the erupted crowded teeth and not every impacted tooth must be removed at the same time if it is not the most accessible or currently causing additional damage. Imaging supports this plan: panoramic radiography identifies the presence of six molars in the left maxillary sextant, while CBCT helps define the exact three-dimensional position of the supernumerary teeth and their relationships to adjacent teeth and nearby structures, which is important for deciding surgical access and which impacted tooth can be removed safely during the same procedure. In a child, CBCT should be justified and dose-optimized.

A single procedure under general anesthesia is reasonable here because multiple extractions and soft-tissue excision are required. The excised soft-tissue lesion should be submitted for histopathologic examination.

Follow-up should monitor the retained impacted molars and the developing occlusion for eruption changes, root effects on adjacent teeth, cystic or follicular change, and future space or orthodontic issues. fig_03.jpg is the 2-year postoperative OPG used for follow-up after the extractions and fibroma excision, not a preoperative image for the initial treatment decision.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation alone despite active trauma, or gives no clear plan for management of the symptomatic erupted teeth and soft-tissue lesion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that intervention is needed but gives a vague extraction plan, omits the fibroma, or does not distinguish between teeth removed now and impacted teeth left for follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends excision of the traumatic buccal lesion plus removal of the three erupted molars and one unerupted molar that is most accessible and displaced, while indicating that the remaining impacted molars can be monitored.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent stepwise plan that clearly links symptoms, crowding, and surgical accessibility to extraction of the three erupted molars and one distal unerupted molar, with justified follow-up of the remaining impacted molars and appropriate use of a single operative session.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figures or relies only on generic knowledge about supernumerary teeth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either symptoms or imaging, but not both; limited connection between the clinical and radiographic findings and the proposed plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to link cheek biting, posterior crowding, and the presence of three erupted plus three unerupted molars to the surgical plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how panoramic imaging demonstrates the number of teeth while CBCT clarifies three-dimensional position and accessibility for selecting the impacted tooth to remove, and correctly identifies fig_03.jpg as postoperative follow-up rather than part of baseline decision-making.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not balance benefits and harms, or recommends clearly disproportionate treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers generic pros and cons of surgery without applying them to this child's symptoms and developing occlusion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why intervention now relieves trauma and crowding, and why limiting removal among impacted teeth to the most accessible displaced one can reduce the need for later surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also justifies indication-based, dose-minimized CBCT and discusses why one operative episode under general anesthesia may be preferable in this child.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Mentions no relevant complications or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only immediate postoperative issues such as pain or infection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important follow-up issues for retained impacted molars and the developing dentition, such as eruption disturbance, adjacent root effects, recurrent trauma, caries/periodontal problems, or cystic/follicular change.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds histopathologic confirmation of the excised lesion and the need for orthodontic or space-management review if occlusion remains compromised.

red_flags: Chronology error: treating fig_03.jpg as a preoperative image for the initial surgical decision rather than a 2-year postoperative follow-up OPG.

Plan inconsistent with the presented management: failing to identify that treatment involved extraction of all three erupted molars and one displaced accessible unerupted molar, with the remaining impacted molars observed.

items.question_content: A 5-year-old boy presents with failure of eruption since 6-7 months of age. Medical and family history are non-contributory; routine blood/biochemical tests are normal, and pediatric/orthopedic assessment found no syndromic or generalized bony disorder. Chewing is impaired, but there is no facial asymmetry. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, state the most likely diagnosis, the single most important alternative diagnosis you would still keep before tissue confirmation, and your management recommendation at this visit while the parents decline an operation. In your justification, identify the imaging and clinical features that make the case non-emergent yet unsuitable for simple discharge. Then explain how your plan would change if follow-up later showed a new radiolucent/cystic area around part of the lesion with increasing localized jaw expansion.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely provisional diagnosis is multiple odontomas/odontomatosis, most consistent with a compound or compound-composite pattern. The strongest competing diagnosis before histology is another mixed odontogenic lesion such as ameloblastic fibro-odontoma; it stays in the differential because the child is very young and has eruption failure, but it is less likely because fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show numerous discrete tooth-like radiopaque structures across multiple quadrants rather than a more localized mixed lesion. fig_01.jpg supports marked eruption disturbance with only a few erupted primary teeth and bony fullness.

This is not an acute emergency: there is no facial asymmetry, infection, pain, or systemic/syndromic clue. However, it is not suitable for discharge because the lesion burden is extensive, mastication is already compromised, and the imaging suggests obstruction/displacement of multiple developing teeth with limited spontaneous eruptive potential. While parents decline surgery, I would arrange active co-management by pediatric dentistry and OMFS, document informed refusal, reinforce oral hygiene and caries prevention, advise a soft diet and monitor nutrition/growth, and schedule structured clinical and radiographic review. If consent is later obtained, the preferred definitive approach is CBCT-guided, staged, tooth-preserving removal/enucleation of the most obstructive segments, with histopathologic examination of removed tissue; one-stage total clearance would be unnecessarily morbid in a 5-year-old.

If follow-up shows a new radiolucent/cystic component with increasing localized expansion, my threshold for surgery becomes much lower. That change suggests progression/secondary cystic change, so I would recommend prompt OMFS intervention with operative exploration/biopsy and staged removal of the involved area, while reassessing adjacent developing teeth and the need for subsequent orthodontic input.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses the diagnosis or gives a clearly implausible diagnosis that does not fit the clinical and radiographic presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an odontogenic calcified lesion or odontoma in general terms but does not identify the multiquadrant provisional diagnosis or misclassifies the pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies multiple odontomas/odontomatosis as the most likely diagnosis, with appropriate caution that confirmation is histopathologic if tissue is obtained.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies multiple odontomas/odontomatosis as the most likely provisional diagnosis and accurately notes that the numerous tooth-like radiopacities favor a compound or compound-composite pattern involving both jaws.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible alternative diagnosis or lists alternatives that are clinically inconsistent with the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a broad or weak differential without explaining why an alternative remains possible or less likely.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies at least one plausible competing mixed odontogenic lesion and gives a reasonable explanation for why it is less favored than multiple odontomas.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes a single most important competing diagnosis and clearly explains why the multiplicity and tooth-like architecture across multiple quadrants make it less likely than odontomatosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or none of the provided history and figure information to support conclusions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts but remains generic, with limited reference to figure-based distribution or the child-specific clinical context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the child's age, severe eruption delay, impaired mastication, absence of facial asymmetry/systemic disorder, and figure-based evidence of extensive tooth-like calcified structures with impacted or obscured teeth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly interprets fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg to show sparse erupted dentition with bony fullness and a heavy multiquadrant burden of tooth-like radiopacities, including superimposition that complicates identification/preservation of developing teeth, and uses these findings to justify both diagnosis and management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends discharge only, indefinite unstructured observation, or unjustified radical one-stage surgery that ignores the child's age and developing dentition.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers either observation or surgery in general terms but does not provide a workable plan adapted to parental refusal and lesion extent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends active specialist follow-up while parents decline surgery, including documented informed refusal, preventive/functional support, and scheduled review; also states that definitive treatment, if accepted, should be conservative and tooth-preserving with histopathology of removed tissue.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear current plan and future definitive strategy: pediatric dentistry plus OMFS follow-up, preventive and nutritional support, structured imaging surveillance, and later CBCT-guided staged removal of the most obstructive segments with preservation of developing teeth where feasible, explicitly rejecting routine one-stage total clearance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misjudges the present case as either requiring immediate radical intervention without justification or needing no active follow-up, and/or fails to recognize that the hypothetical change would alter urgency.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for follow-up but does not clearly distinguish the current non-emergent state from findings that should prompt escalation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the current presentation as non-emergent but requiring active surveillance, and explains that new radiolucent/cystic change with increasing expansion would justify escalation to operative assessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly explains why the current case can be monitored despite lacking acute red flags, yet why later cystic change/localized expansion would warrant prompt OMFS intervention because it raises concern for progression, secondary pathology, and further compromise of tooth preservation and function.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending one-stage clearance with routine removal of all impacted or unerupted teeth in this 5-year-old rather than tooth-preserving staged specialist planning.

items.question_content:
A 4-year-old girl with diagnosed microcystic lymphangioma of the tongue is referred while receiving sirolimus. She has tongue pain/burning, dysphagia, speech difficulty, recent weight loss, two prior PICU admissions for bacterial pneumonia, and tolerates only very brief chairside care. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg for the oral/radiographic findings.

You can provide only noninvasive care today because current laboratory results and the medical team's reply are still unavailable. After acceptable medical clearance, you will get one short definitive visit and then review appointments only.

Set out a tooth-level management sequence for this case. Identify the exact tooth or teeth to be treated during that single definitive visit, the order in which they should be managed, what procedure each should receive, and why the other visible problems are not the best use of that visit. Base the justification on the figures, not on general principles alone. Also state: the one missing medical issue most likely to change the treatment setting rather than just the timing; one clinical change that would make you abort office-based care immediately; and the follow-up milestone that should be reached before attempting anterior rehabilitation or bite correction. Finally, explain what would change in your sequence if the tongue volume later decreased markedly but the dentition remained otherwise unchanged.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Today’s visit should remain noninvasive and brief: focused assessment, caregiver counseling, plaque-control/toothbrushing coaching adapted to the painful tongue, diet advice, and professional prophylaxis with topical fluoride only if tolerated. No irreversible or bleeding procedure should be done before medical clearance.

After acceptable medical clearance, the single definitive visit should include both conservative and surgical source control in the sequence actually supported by the figures and clinical description: first restore tooth 64 after local anesthesia, isolation, caries removal, and placement of glass ionomer cement; then extract the non-restorable maxillary primary incisors 51, 52, 61, and 62. fig_02.jpg shows the separate active cavitated lesion on 64 in addition to the extensively carious maxillary incisors. fig_04.jpg supports poor prognosis of the incisors by showing extensive caries with root resorption, so those anterior teeth are not good restorative candidates and are best extracted in the same cleared visit. The visit therefore addresses both the localized posterior cavitated lesion conservatively and the grossly destroyed anterior teeth surgically. fig_03.jpg’s anterior open bite is secondary to macroglossia and is not the best use of that short definitive visit, and no treatment of the tongue lesion itself is part of the dental visit.

The missing medical issue most likely to change treatment setting, not merely timing, is current airway and respiratory stability, including whether office-based local-anesthetic care is safe given the macroglossia, swallowing difficulty, breathing difficulty, and prior pneumonia history; this could shift care to a hospital-based setting. A clinical change that should abort office care immediately is worsening airway compromise such as increasing dyspnea or stridor, inability to manage secretions, or rapidly enlarging tongue swelling.

Anterior rehabilitation or bite correction should wait until there is a clear and stable reduction in tongue bulk and lesion activity, with improved function, so that prosthetic planning is feasible. In this patient, follow-up should confirm meaningful shrinkage of the tongue lesion before attempting anterior rehabilitation; once the tongue volume later decreases markedly and the dentition is otherwise unchanged, the sequence would not change for untreated teeth because the source-control visit already included restoration of 64 and extraction of 51, 52, 61, and 62. What changes later is that anterior prosthetic rehabilitation or space-maintaining replacement of the incisors can be considered, while bite correction remains deferred until tongue size is sufficiently reduced and stable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, or misinterprets the major findings in a way that leads to an unsupported plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes general findings such as macroglossia and caries but does not make a tooth-level interpretation from the figures, or does not use the radiograph to comment on prognosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the figures to identify both the active cavitated lesion on tooth 64 and the grossly destroyed maxillary primary incisors, and recognizes that the anterior open bite is not the priority for the single definitive visit.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly identifies tooth 64 for conservative treatment and 51, 52, 61, and 62 for extraction during the same definitive visit, using fig_02.jpg to distinguish the separate posterior cavitated lesion and fig_04.jpg to support severe destruction with root resorption of the incisors, while also using fig_01.jpg and fig_03.jpg to explain why tongue-related malocclusion correction is deferred.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent staged plan, or proceeds to irreversible treatment despite the stated lack of current medical clearance.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Separates today from later care in general terms but does not give a clear tooth-level sequence or specific procedures for the definitive visit.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Outlines an appropriate staged plan: noninvasive care today, definitive disease-control after clearance, and deferral of lower-priority findings until follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stage-based sequence that fits the short-session constraint: preventive/palliative care today; after clearance, restoration of tooth 64 with glass ionomer cement followed by extraction of 51, 52, 61, and 62 in the same definitive visit; then review visits with delayed anterior rehabilitation only after the tongue condition becomes sufficiently reduced and stable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes the wrong problem, such as malocclusion correction, tongue lesion manipulation in the dental office, or another lower-yield target, without defensible justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses reasonable treatment targets but does not clearly explain why the other visible problems are not the best use of the single definitive visit.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a defensible use of the single definitive visit and explains why at least the major competing visible problems should be deferred.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Demonstrates strong prioritization under the one-short-visit constraint by identifying that the definitive visit should address both tooth 64 and the non-restorable maxillary incisors, while explicitly rejecting spending that visit on open-bite correction, tongue lesion treatment in the dental office, or anterior rehabilitation before tongue reduction, and adapts the later plan appropriately if the tongue shrinks markedly.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the implications of sirolimus, macroglossia, feeding difficulty, or respiratory history for treatment safety and setting.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions medical complexity but does not explain which missing issue could change office versus hospital management, or does not identify a clinically appropriate reason to stop treatment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why airway/feeding vulnerability and immunosuppression limit office care and identifies at least one appropriate trigger for aborting office-based treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies current airway/respiratory stability as the missing issue most likely to change treatment setting, not merely timing, and gives a specific immediate stop trigger such as inability to manage secretions, worsening dyspnea/stridor, or rapidly increasing tongue swelling.

items.question_content: A 5-year-old girl presents 4 months after a fall onto her chin with pain on chewing in the left mandibular posterior region. Extraoral laceration has healed, mouth opening is normal, and medical history is noncontributory. Examine fig_01.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend for the injured primary molars at this visit? Justify your choice using the history and the clinical/radiographic findings visible in fig_01.jpg, explain why other plausible approaches are less appropriate in this child, and state the specific clinical or radiographic changes that would make you change course during follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most appropriate plan is conservative retention of the injured primary molars, provided they are restorable and can be adequately sealed. The history and fig_01.jpg support delayed complicated vertical crown-root fractures from indirect chin trauma: the child is now symptomatic on chewing, two adjacent primary mandibular molars are involved, and the radiograph suggests remaining root support without obvious gross furcal/periapical destruction or advanced pathologic resorption. At age 5, losing two primary molars early would risk loss of function and arch length and likely create a space-maintenance problem, so extraction should not be the default if the teeth can be predictably maintained.

Definitive care would be to stabilize the fractured segments and provide durable full coronal coverage/splinting to obtain a seal, then perform pulpectomy because these are complicated fractures with pulpal involvement and symptoms. A simple bonded restoration or pulpotomy-only approach is less suitable because the fracture extends onto the root and the crown is structurally unstable, making long-term sealing unreliable.

I would abandon retention and move to extraction if the teeth prove nonrestorable, the fracture extends too far subgingivally to achieve a seal, mobility is severe, isolation/cooperation is inadequate, or follow-up shows failure: persistent pain, swelling, sinus tract, abnormal mobility, gingival inflammation, furcal/periapical radiolucency, pathologic internal/external resorption, or any adverse effect on the permanent successors. Success would be an asymptomatic child, intact restoration, no infection, and continuation of normal physiologic root resorption and eruption.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No definitive plan, or recommends clearly inappropriate care for painful complicated crown-root fractures, such as observation alone or simple restoration without addressing structural instability and pulpal involvement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a plan but with major omissions or poor sequencing; may default to extraction without case-specific assessment of restorability/space consequences, or propose retention without definitive pulpal management and coronal stabilization.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a coherent definitive plan centered on conservative retention because the teeth appear restorable: stabilize/splint the fractured segments, provide durable full coverage and seal, perform pulpectomy, and arrange follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: As above, and explicitly defines practical thresholds for switching to extraction with space management if the teeth are nonrestorable, unstable, infected, impossible to isolate, or cannot be monitored reliably.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets the case or ignores the image and history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated facts; recognizes trauma or pain but not both, or misses the significance of two adjacent primary molars and the radiographic appearance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates delayed post-traumatic chewing pain, chin-impact mechanism, age 5, and fig_01.jpg evidence of crown-root fracture in two adjacent primary molars with retained root support and no gross destructive pathosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also explains how these combined findings support strategic value of retention despite the delay and why the current image does not by itself mandate extraction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No weighing of options; generic or one-sided reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only limited benefits or risks, or gives textbook statements without linking them to this child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances benefits of retention (mastication, arch length, alveolar development, avoiding premature loss of two primary molars and likely space management) against risks (endodontic failure, infection, effect on successors, need for compliance), and explains why simpler restorative or pulpotomy-only approaches are less suitable for an unstable complicated crown-root fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Individualizes the balance to restorability, subgingival extent, cooperation/isolation, and the clinical burden of extracting two molars at age 5.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No follow-up strategy or failure criteria.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Says only to review or monitor, with vague or nonspecific complications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key failure signs: persistent pain, swelling or fistula, abnormal mobility, gingival inflammation, loss of coronal seal, furcal/periapical radiolucency, pathologic internal or external resorption, or abnormalities affecting the permanent successors.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also distinguishes desired success findings such as symptom-free function, intact restoration, and continuation of normal physiologic resorption and eruption, and links failure findings to changing the treatment plan.

items.question_content: A healthy 14-year-old girl presents with caries in retained mandibular primary molars. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What management strategy would you choose now for tooth 75 and the rest of the posterior dentition, and how do the clinical and panoramic findings justify that choice? Explain how the radiographic pattern should change your decision making from routine management of a carious primary molar and what you would monitor over time.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The key radiographic diagnosis is generalized taurodontism, severe enough in several molars to be consistent with hypertaurodontism, with delayed eruption/dental development. That matters because 75 is a retained primary molar in a dentition where the permanent successors are not erupting on a routine timetable, so management should favor preservation if the tooth is restorable and there are no signs of irreversible pulpitis, swelling, sinus tract, or furcation/periapical pathology. For 75, I would choose conservative vital pulp therapy such as indirect pulp treatment and a well-sealed definitive restoration rather than immediate extraction or elective canal treatment. The deep lesion is close to the pulp, but taurodont teeth have elongated pulp chambers and an apically displaced pulpal floor, so aggressive caries removal/access increases the chance of exposure, difficult hemorrhage control, and technically complex endodontics. Retaining 75 also preserves function and space while the delayed permanent dentition continues developing. The rest of the posterior plan is caries control and prevention: restore other cavitated primary molars as indicated, seal susceptible permanent molars, topical fluoride, and reinforce hygiene/diet. Follow-up should be closer than routine: assess symptoms, restoration seal, any pulpal/periapical changes, eruption progress of successors and second molars, physiologic resorption of retained primary molars, and whether delayed eruption begins to affect occlusion or referral needs. Extraction or more invasive pulp therapy becomes appropriate only if the tooth becomes non-restorable, symptomatic, infected, or interferes with the developing permanent dentition.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or ignores the significance of generalized taurodontic morphology and delayed eruption when planning care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either unusual tooth morphology or delayed eruption, but integrates the findings incompletely or links them weakly to management of 75.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the clinical caries presentation with the panoramic pattern of generalized taurodontism and delayed eruption to support a preservation-focused plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg coherently, identifying generalized severe taurodontic change with developmental delay and explaining precisely why these findings alter immediate and longitudinal management of a retained primary molar.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes inappropriate management that is not supported by the case findings, or omits a workable plan for 75 and the posterior dentition.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a partially appropriate plan but with major omissions, such as not addressing the need to preserve a restorable retained primary molar or not including preventive/restorative care for the remaining posterior teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a reasonable conservative plan for 75 based on a restorable deep carious lesion and includes appropriate restorative/preventive management for the rest of the posterior dentition.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan: preserve 75 with conservative vital pulp therapy and a durable seal when no signs of irreversible disease are present, treat other posterior lesions appropriately, institute prevention, and define conditions that would justify escalation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks of conservative versus more invasive management in this developmental context.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some risks or benefits, but discussion is generic and not clearly tied to taurodontic anatomy or delayed eruption.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that preserving 75 helps maintain function/space during delayed eruption and that taurodontic anatomy increases the difficulty and risk of aggressive pulp intervention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances patient-specific advantages of retention against the anatomical hazards of exposure, hemorrhage, and complex endodontic treatment in taurodont teeth, while also stating when extraction or escalation would become preferable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify relevant complications or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only one complication or gives vague follow-up advice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key complications such as pulp exposure/endodontic difficulty and includes reasonable follow-up for symptoms, restoration failure, and eruption monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates the main taurodont-specific procedural pitfalls and outlines focused surveillance for pulpal/periapical change, pathologic resorption, restoration integrity, and developing eruption/occlusal problems.

items.question_content: A 12-year-old boy sustained complicated crown fractures of 11 and 21. Both teeth were root-canal treated and the fragments reattached, but 11 fractured again 1 week later after another fall while 21 remained serviceable. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg only. State your provisional definitive strategy for 11 and justify it using one finding from each figure plus the history. Then identify the main competing approach you rejected and why it is less suitable in this child. Do not assume findings that are not shown: name the single most important missing clinical feature or measurement that must be confirmed before you commit to the plan, and explain how your plan would change if that prerequisite is unfavorable. End with the most likely early failure mode you would monitor during follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Using the information available, I would provisionally favor a bonded chamber-retained adhesive restoration for 11, i.e., an endocrown-type restoration, rather than moving first to an intraradicular post-retained build-up. In a 12-year-old with repeat trauma, an indirect composite endocrown is especially attractive because it is conservative and more repairable if another fracture occurs, although the material choice remains secondary to restorability.

Figure-based support: fig_01.jpg shows extensive coronal loss of the maxillary central incisors but retained roots, so the problem is mainly coronal reconstruction rather than a non-restorable root. fig_02.jpg shows 11 is already endodontically treated with no obvious periapical pathology or obvious root fracture on the provided image, so retention can potentially be obtained adhesively from the remaining cervical tooth structure and pulp chamber rather than by further radicular preparation. fig_03.jpg shows the tooth was initially restorable enough for fragment reattachment, but the history of rapid re-fracture after another fall makes repeating a simple adhesive fragment/direct build-up less predictable as the definitive solution.

The main competing approach I would reject at this stage is a post-retained composite core/crown strategy. A fiber post can be clinically reasonable in some children, but here it is less attractive because it requires additional intraradicular intervention in a previously traumatized young incisor, removes radicular dentin, adds interfaces, and shifts failure toward root-level problems that are harder to manage. By contrast, a chamber-retained bonded restoration better preserves biomechanics if sufficient coronal substrate remains.

The single most important missing prerequisite to confirm before committing is whether there is adequate circumferential cervical tooth structure with an accessible, isolatable adhesive margin; this is effectively the restorability threshold for a chamber-retained restoration. Chamber form also matters, and if chamber depth is inadequate or the cervical margin is too limited, the plan changes. If the margin is deep/subgingival, remaining circumferential structure is insufficient, or chamber retention is inadequate, I would not force an endocrown. I would first address the restorability problem and reassess, with a post-retained build-up becoming a secondary option only if chamber-retained adhesive retention is not feasible.

The most likely early failure mode to monitor is debonding or chipping/re-fracture of the restoration; I would also review marginal leakage/discoloration, occlusal contacts, and periapical status during follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the case or does not use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg meaningfully.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated facts (for example, that 11 fractured and was root-canal treated) without linking the figures and history into a coherent restoration argument.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the key available evidence: major coronal loss/restorable root context from fig_01.jpg, endodontically treated status with no obvious radiographic contraindication from fig_02.jpg, and initial restoratability plus subsequent failure of simple repair from fig_03.jpg and the history.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes one relevant finding from each figure with the history, and explicitly distinguishes what is shown from what is still unknown rather than inventing unshown findings.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management or offers no defensible definitive strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a plausible restoration, but the plan is weakly justified or defaults to a more invasive approach without explaining why conservative adhesive rehabilitation is unsuitable.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a defensible conditional plan centered on conservative adhesive rehabilitation, recognizing that a chamber-retained endocrown-type restoration is preferred if adequate chamber form and cervical bonding substrate are confirmed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes a chamber-retained bonded restoration/endocrown for the currently available evidence, explains why this better preserves radicular dentin and biomechanics in a child, and gives an appropriate child-specific material rationale or contingency if prerequisites are not met.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify any missing decision-critical clinical feature or measurement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions that more examination is needed, but not which missing feature matters most or how it would alter management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a key prerequisite such as adequate circumferential cervical tooth structure/isolatable adhesive margin or adequate chamber depth, and explains that an unfavorable finding would preclude or delay a chamber-retained restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the most decision-changing prerequisite and states a concrete management redirection if it is unfavorable, such as addressing the restorability/margin problem first and reserving post-retained reconstruction for cases where chamber-retained retention is not feasible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison with a competing approach.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative but compares it only generically or without case-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a main competing approach and explains why it is less suitable here, such as poorer predictability of repeat direct repair or greater invasiveness/stress concentration with a post-retained option.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nuanced tradeoff analysis, including when the rejected option could become more appropriate if the preferred chamber-retained plan proves unworkable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address likely failure modes or follow-up concerns.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic review without identifying the likely early failure pattern for the proposed restoration.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies appropriate early risks such as debonding, marginal leakage/discoloration, chipping or re-fracture, or endodontic/periapical concerns.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the most likely early failure mode for the chosen plan and links follow-up to prevention or management, such as occlusal adjustment and trauma-prevention counseling.

items.question_content: A 4-year-old girl with severe early childhood caries returns 2 months after rehabilitation of the maxillary primary incisors. Pain has resolved; the parents are now concerned about appearance. Oral hygiene remains poor and cost is a concern. Use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to determine the current status of the anterior primary incisors. Among the teeth still present, which one is the poorest candidate for any further post-retained coronal rebuild, and what would you do today for each anterior tooth that still requires a management decision? Give a prioritized plan that separates immediate treatment from review only, state the specific findings that would make you change observation to extraction, and explain briefly how your decision for the failed tooth would change if fig_01.jpg instead showed minimal physiologic resorption and a substantially longer remaining lifespan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_02.jpg shows that the two central incisors remain coronally restored and serviceable, one lateral incisor is absent, and the opposite lateral has lost its coronal restoration with very little remaining tooth structure. fig_01.jpg shows a treated primary anterior segment with physiologic root resorption and developing permanent successors, so the remaining service life is finite. Among the teeth still present, the failed lateral incisor (52) is the poorest candidate for another post-retained rebuild.

My priority today would be: (1) do not disturb the asymptomatic, functioning central incisors except for clinical review and preventive maintenance; (2) for 52, avoid another aggressive intracanal/post-retained reconstruction because retention has already failed, coronal tooth structure is minimal, hygiene is poor, and additional post-space manipulation in a resorbing primary incisor offers limited benefit and may jeopardize normal resorption/exfoliation; (3) if the 52 remnant is asymptomatic and can be made smooth, cleansable, and sealed, manage it conservatively with smoothing/resealing if needed and observe rather than re-posting; (4) intensify prevention for the whole mouth with oral-hygiene instruction, dietary counseling, topical fluoride, and close recall. No routine replacement is required for the absent primary lateral in this high-caries-risk setting.

Observation would change to extraction if any treated anterior tooth developed pain, swelling, sinus tract, tenderness, recurrent infection, pathologic mobility, noncleansable plaque-retentive root remnant, soft-tissue irritation, loss of seal with recurrent caries, radiographic pathology beyond expected physiologic resorption, or interference with normal exfoliation/eruption of the successor.

If fig_01.jpg instead showed minimal physiologic resorption and a clearly longer remaining lifespan, a limited repeat coronal rebuild for 52 could be more defensible, but only if adequate tooth structure and moisture control were achievable and the parents understood the guarded prognosis. Even then, I would still avoid deep intracanal extension and keep any retentive approach as conservative as possible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, or misreads the anterior segment in a way that undermines the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes only isolated facts, such as that one tooth is missing or one restoration is absent, without integrating the radiographic implications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg that the central incisors remain restored, one lateral is absent, the opposite lateral has lost coronal retention with minimal remaining structure, and the radiograph shows a resorbing primary anterior segment with developing successors.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses the figure findings to explain not just what is present but why the failed lateral differs prognostically from the retained centrals, explicitly linking resorption and successor development to limited remaining service life.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends routine re-posting of the failed lateral or blanket extraction of teeth without a biologically sound, case-specific rationale.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a plausible plan for part of the segment but lacks a clear today-versus-review strategy or ignores prevention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a stepwise plan: leave the asymptomatic retained centrals under review, avoid aggressive retreatment of the failed lateral, use conservative local management if the remnant can be kept smooth/sealed, and reserve extraction for pathology or problematic mobility.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides an actionable segment-wide plan that also addresses prevention/recall and appropriately declines unnecessary replacement of the absent lateral in this high-risk setting.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions multiple possible actions but without clear prioritization or tooth-by-tooth decision making.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Clearly identifies the failed lateral as the poorest candidate for further post-retained rebuilding and separates immediate conservative care from review-only management of the stable centrals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes biologic safety and prevention over cosmetic retreatment, explicitly justifying why stable crowned centrals should not be unnecessarily disturbed while the failed lateral is managed conservatively.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh risks and benefits, or seriously misjudges them.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only one side of the tradeoff, such as esthetics or retention, while overlooking major case-specific risks.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances esthetic wishes against poor hygiene, cost, short remaining lifespan, repeat retention failure, and the biologic risk of further intracanal procedures in a resorbing primary incisor.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also addresses the counterfactual: explains that minimal resorption and longer lifespan could justify a more active rebuild attempt if isolation and remaining structure were favorable, while still limiting intracanal intervention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful follow-up criteria for changing management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests generic review but gives vague triggers for extraction or reintervention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies specific triggers such as pain, swelling, sinus tract, tenderness, pathologic mobility, radiographic pathology, or disturbance to eruption/exfoliation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds practical monitoring points such as loss of coronal seal, recurrent caries, plaque-retentive or sharp root remnants, soft-tissue irritation, and distinguishes pathologic mobility from expected physiologic mobility near exfoliation.

red_flags: Generic Textbook Management: recommending repeat or deeper intracanal post build-up for the failed resorbing primary lateral without accounting for the biologic limits seen in fig_01.jpg.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old girl is seen at her first dental visit during a school screening. She has no pain, systemic disease, or prior dental treatment. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show an unusual mandibular eruption pattern. Based on the clinical history plus the images, what is the most likely diagnosis, and what key image features support it? Then outline your initial management in this asymptomatic child. Specify which new clinical or radiographic changes would make you switch from observation to surgery, and in what circumstance extracting the developing successor would become reasonable.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is reverse dentition: a severely impacted/ankylosed primary mandibular second molar with a very delayed-forming second premolar. The images support this by showing an abnormal vertical relationship on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, with the successor developing in a follicular space above the impacted primary molar and appearing much less mature than expected for the child’s age.

Initial management should be conservative: document baseline clinical and radiographic findings and follow the child periodically, because she is asymptomatic and the successor is still immature. I would change to surgery if serial review shows progressive infraocclusion/ankylosis, failure of eruption or loss of progression, pain, infection, space loss, or follicular enlargement/cystic change. Extraction of the developing successor would only be reasonable if it becomes pathologic or nonviable, or if combined pathology makes removal of both teeth necessary, with space maintenance and orthodontic planning as needed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Relies on one data source only or gives an answer that does not connect the history with fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some relevant findings but does not clearly integrate the asymptomatic presentation with the radiographic relationship.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the child’s age and lack of symptoms with the fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg relationship to support an abnormal eruption/development pattern.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
