levels.description: Defines the intended tooth movement and acceptable reciprocal effects clearly, explains why those effects are tolerable, states concrete review triggers for anchorage redesign or plan change, and adapts the plan logically if 45 were absent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits meaningful risks, benefits, or patient-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic appliance pros and cons without tying them to this child's caries risk, cooperation limits, extraction difficulty, or successor eruption concerns.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a fixed, low-profile, compliance-independent approach is advantageous here and identifies relevant tradeoffs such as plaque retention, appliance failure, extraction difficulty, and the need for follow-up of 45.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the benefits of restoring access and eruption space against plaque, anchorage, and relapse risks, and correctly explains how the absence of 45 would materially shift the extraction-versus-retention balance for 85.

items.question_content: A 5-year-old boy has had several painless oral swellings for 3 months, first noticed during a febrile illness and slowly enlarging since. Medical, dental, and family histories are noncontributory, and there are no extraoral abnormalities. Examining fig_01.jpg, what management strategy would you recommend now, and why is that approach most appropriate for this child?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading working diagnosis is focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck disease). fig_01.jpg shows multiple soft, sessile papules on the lower lip and ventral tongue in a young child, which is a typical age group and distribution for FEH. The multifocal, painless, slowly enlarging pattern is less consistent with a mucocele or solitary squamous papilloma. Condyloma acuminatum remains an important mimic because it can also present as multiple HPV-related papules, so appearance alone is not enough for a definitive diagnosis. Goltz-Gorlin syndrome is less likely without extraoral or syndromic findings.

I would recommend tissue confirmation rather than observation alone: excisional biopsy of a representative lesion, or excision of all small accessible lesions if feasible, with histopathology as the key test and HPV typing/PCR as a useful adjunct when available. Because these lesions have persisted and enlarged over 3 months in visible, trauma-prone sites, establishing a diagnosis and removing them is more appropriate than simple reassurance. A child-friendly soft-tissue approach such as diode laser excision is reasonable because it offers hemostasis and operative comfort while still yielding tissue for diagnosis.

I would document lesion number and sites, review for any immunocompromising or syndromic features, use careful infection-control precautions because HPV is implicated, and arrange follow-up to confirm healing and monitor for recurrence or new lesions. If histology showed atypia or the lesions changed rapidly, the plan would need escalation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not integrate the child’s age, multifocal distribution, lesion morphology, and clinical course into a coherent interpretation; conclusion is unsupported or inconsistent with fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical features but reasoning is incomplete, superficial, or misses major figure-based clues such as the multifocal lower-lip and ventral-tongue pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly synthesizes age, painless multifocal soft sessile papules, typical oral sites, persistence, and absence of extraoral findings to support a benign HPV-related lesion, especially FEH.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a tightly reasoned synthesis of history and fig_01.jpg, explicitly showing why the distribution and morphology favor FEH over common reactive or solitary papillary lesions while preserving diagnostic uncertainty until tissue confirmation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differential diagnosis, or cites diagnoses that are clearly incompatible with the presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one or two plausible alternatives but gives little or no case-specific reasoning for why they are more or less likely.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Considers key alternatives such as squamous papilloma, condyloma acuminatum, and mucocele, with brief case-based reasoning for why they are less likely than FEH.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the differential well, including the significance of condyloma as a close mimic and the reduced likelihood of syndromic or reactive lesions given the absence of extraoral findings and the multifocal oral pattern.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management, omits diagnostic confirmation entirely, or proposes a plan that does not fit the child’s presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests either observation or removal but without a clear diagnostic pathway, inadequate justification, or poor adaptation to a young child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends biopsy-based confirmation, preferably excisional biopsy of a representative or accessible lesion, with histopathology and optional HPV testing/PCR as adjunctive support; justifies intervention because the lesions are persistent and enlarging.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a stepwise, child-appropriate plan that includes lesion documentation, tissue diagnosis before definitive labeling, excision of accessible lesions when indicated, and a justified technique choice such as laser for operative control and comfort, while recognizing that observation would be reserved for clearly regressing or trivial lesions.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh risks and benefits, or ignores clinically relevant follow-up and infection-control issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons of treatment but does not connect them to this child’s lesion behavior, age, or lesion sites.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benign/self-limiting nature of FEH against persistence, enlargement, visibility, potential trauma, and the value of diagnosis; includes follow-up for healing and recurrence/new lesions.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds nuanced discussion of child comfort, hemostasis/scarring considerations, HPV-related infection-control counseling, and the need to escalate if atypical change or dysplastic histology emerges.

items.question_content: A healthy 10-year-old boy presents a few days after a fall with pain on mastication from tooth 11. No treatment has yet been provided; the other teeth are normal and there is no periodontal disease. Use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Based on the fracture configuration in fig_01.jpg, choose the single management strategy you would recommend if the main goal is to retain the tooth through growth without sacrificing anterior esthetics. Explain which feature visible in fig_01.jpg makes your plan biologically and restoratively feasible, and why the strongest competing strategies are less suitable for this child. Then interpret fig_02.jpg: would you judge that 3-year result as a success or failure, and what residual problem is still present? Finally, name one preoperative finding that would make you reject your preferred plan and state the alternative direction you would take.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The preferred plan is intentional replantation of the remaining root with slight coronal repositioning and 180-degree rotation, using equivalent terminology such as surgical repositioning only if the same biologic concept is clearly described. fig_01.jpg shows an oblique complicated crown-root fracture with pulp exposure in which the deepest margin is on the palatal subgingival/subcrestal side. That specific orientation is what makes rotation useful: after removal and rotation, the previously deep palatal margin can be brought to a more accessible labial/supragingival position, improving isolation, restorability, and respect for biologic width while preserving the tooth and papilla in a growing child.

This is better suited than the main competing strategies because crown lengthening/osteotomy in the anterior maxilla risks loss of crestal bone, gingival asymmetry, papilla compromise, and an unaesthetic long clinical crown; orthodontic extrusion can preserve the tooth but is slower, compliance-dependent, and may bring gingiva and bone coronally, sometimes creating a need for additional periodontal reshaping; extraction with definitive replacement is undesirable during growth, and immediate implant placement is especially inappropriate in a 10-year-old.

A strong answer may add that the procedure should be atraumatic, extraoral time minimized to protect periodontal ligament viability, the tooth stabilized briefly if needed, and definitive pulpal/endodontic and coronal restorative management completed after initial periodontal healing.

fig_02.jpg should be judged an overall long-term success rather than failure. The tooth is retained, and the radiograph does not show obvious periapical pathology or clear evidence of root resorption/ankylosis. The residual problem is a marginal gingival contour abnormality/hyperplastic soft tissue on the labial aspect. That is primarily an esthetic soft-tissue issue, not by itself proof of biologic failure.

A preoperative finding that would make me reject intentional replantation would be an unfavorable root form such as a dilacerated or markedly divergent root, or another factor making atraumatic extraction unrealistic; established periodontal disease would also be a contraindication. In that situation, if the tooth remained restorable and the periodontium/root length were otherwise favorable, I would shift toward orthodontic extrusion. If tooth preservation were no longer feasible, I would extract and provide an interim child-appropriate replacement until growth is complete.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg meaningfully, or misreads the fracture/outcome in a way that undermines the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only part of the available evidence, such as recognizing a crown-root fracture but not the relevant orientation in fig_01.jpg, or noticing a late gingival issue in fig_02.jpg without integrating its significance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly interprets fig_01.jpg as a complicated deep crown-root fracture with a restorability problem and interprets fig_02.jpg as a retained tooth with a residual soft-tissue contour abnormality and no obvious radiographic failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates both figures into one coherent rationale, explicitly linking the fracture orientation in fig_01.jpg to why rotation/repositioning can improve access and biologic width, and distinguishing the residual soft-tissue change in fig_02.jpg from biologic failure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends a clearly inappropriate plan such as simple restoration/reattachment alone, immediate implant replacement, or extraction without a sound child-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a tooth-preserving strategy but not the best-matched one for this presentation, or gives an incompletely justified plan that does not resolve restorability and biologic width concerns.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends intentional replantation with slight coronal repositioning and 180-degree rotation, or an equivalent description of the same approach, and explains why it best preserves the tooth and esthetics in this child.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced plan centered on intentional replantation/rotational repositioning, including atraumatic handling, short stabilization as needed, and appropriate downstream pulpal/endodontic and restorative considerations.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides generic pros and cons that are not specific to this child, fracture location, or esthetic zone.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions limited advantages of the preferred plan or only briefly critiques one competing option.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the preferred plan against at least two plausible competing approaches and explains why they are less suitable in a growing child with an anterior esthetic concern.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a nuanced comparison that includes growth status, papilla/bone preservation, treatment speed and compliance, and the esthetic liabilities of tissue-sacrificing surgery in the anterior maxilla.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not name a meaningful preoperative finding that would alter the plan, or proposes an unsafe or illogical alternative.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a vague limiting factor such as 'bad anatomy' without explaining why it matters or how the treatment direction would change.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a concrete finding such as dilacerated/divergent root form, periodontal disease, or inability to extract atraumatically, and changes the plan appropriately.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links the contraindicating finding to loss of feasibility or periodontal ligament risk and selects a coherent alternative pathway based on whether tooth preservation remains possible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misclassifies the long-term result in fig_02.jpg or ignores the residual clinical problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Correctly calls the result a success or failure but does not identify the residual issue, or identifies the residual issue without a justified overall judgment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Judges fig_02.jpg as an overall success and identifies the remaining marginal gingival contour abnormality or hyperplastic soft tissue.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly distinguishes an esthetic soft-tissue irregularity from biologic failure by referencing the absence of obvious radiographic pathosis or destructive sequelae in fig_02.jpg.

red_flags: Generic Textbook Management: recommending implant placement as the definitive immediate replacement for this maxillary central incisor in a 10-year-old child.

items.question_content: An 8-year-old girl presents 2 days after a fall. Tooth 21 has a complicated crown-root fracture; the coronal two-thirds is mobile and sensibility testing is negative. She is otherwise healthy, and her family hopes the tooth can be retained if the prognosis is acceptable. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, decide which tooth-preserving pathway you would commit to at this visit and justify that choice from the visible fracture pattern, root development, and timing of the injury. Do not just list options. In your answer, state: (1) your first clinical priority before definitive restoration, (2) the strongest reasonable alternative plan you are not choosing and the case-specific reason you reject it, and (3) the single change in pulp findings after access or fragment removal that would make you switch to a different pathway.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would commit at this visit to a tooth-preserving pathway of immediate contamination control and restorability assessment, followed by canal-based management of the immature tooth and later orthodontic extrusion before definitive restoration.

This choice is justified by the visible fracture pattern and timing. The figures indicate a complicated crown-root fracture with a large mobile coronal fragment and a fracture line extending palatally below the gingival margin. That makes simple rebonding or immediate definitive restoration unreliable because the margin is contaminated and difficult to isolate. fig_03.jpg shows incomplete root development with an immature apex. Although the negative sensibility test at 2 days does not by itself prove necrosis after trauma, the combination of a deep subgingival fracture, marked fragment mobility, and compromised isolation makes immediate vitality-preserving pulp therapy less predictable than a canal-based approach in this specific case.

My first clinical priority before definitive restoration is contamination control and assessment of restorability. If the coronal fragment can be repositioned stably, I would use it temporarily as a biologic cover to limit crevicular contamination while gaining access. If it cannot be stabilized, I would remove it, control bleeding, expose the fracture extent, and create a temporary supragingival seal. After that, I would disinfect the canal and manage the open apex with apexification or an apical barrier approach, then complete obturation once the tooth is endodontically stabilized.

After endodontic stabilization, I would use orthodontic extrusion with light forces to bring sound tooth structure to an equigingival or supragingival level so the tooth can be restored predictably. Retention after extrusion is important, and circumferential fiber release may be considered to reduce relapse before the final restoration, using the fragment if serviceable or composite if not.

The strongest reasonable alternative plan is vitality-preserving partial pulpotomy followed by later extrusion. I am not choosing it because this case has a deep subgingival fracture configuration and contamination/isolation problems, so the predictability of maintaining pulp vitality is reduced despite the immature apex and the known unreliability of a negative sensibility test only 2 days after trauma.

The single pulp finding that would make me switch pathways is exposure of healthy pulp after fragment removal or access, with bright red bleeding that is readily controllable and isolation achievable. In that situation I would switch to partial pulpotomy/apexogenesis rather than continue with canal-based treatment, and then monitor closely for later signs of necrosis or apical pathosis.

Important prognostic concerns to acknowledge are periodontal attachment loss or gingival ingrowth if the margin is not managed well, relapse after extrusion, external resorption or ankylosis, and a potentially unfavorable final crown-root ratio that could limit long-term retention.

levels.title: Incorrect or non-committal plan
levels.description: Does not commit to a specific tooth-preserving pathway, recommends an implausible pathway for this case, or only lists options without choosing and defending one.

levels.title: Partially appropriate plan
levels.description: Commits to a pathway but the sequence is incomplete, poorly justified, or misses a key step such as contamination control, canal-based management versus vitality preservation, or the role of extrusion before definitive restoration.

levels.title: Appropriate case-specific plan
levels.description: Commits to a coherent tooth-preserving pathway that fits this case, with immediate contamination control/restorability assessment, appropriate endodontic or vital pulp strategy, and later extrusion/restorative planning explained in a logical sequence.

levels.title: Minimal integration
levels.description: Provides a generic trauma answer or uses only isolated facts without meaningfully connecting the fracture pattern, root development, and timing of injury.

levels.title: Partial integration
levels.description: Uses some relevant findings, such as the immature apex or mobile fragment, but does not clearly synthesize the subgingival fracture extension, unreliable sensibility result at 2 days, and implications for isolation and prognosis.

levels.title: Strong integration
levels.description: Synthesizes the visible fracture configuration, fragment mobility, immature root development, and early post-trauma timing into a coherent rationale for the chosen pathway, including why a negative sensibility test at 2 days is limited evidence on its own.

levels.title: No meaningful alternative considered
levels.description: Fails to identify a reasonable alternative tooth-preserving plan, or rejects alternatives with a generic statement not tied to the case.

levels.title: Alternative identified but weakly analyzed
levels.description: Identifies a plausible alternative plan, such as partial pulpotomy/apexogenesis, but does not clearly explain the case-specific reason for not choosing it.

levels.title: Alternative plan critically appraised
levels.description: Identifies the strongest reasonable alternative tooth-preserving pathway and rejects it using case-specific reasoning, such as contamination, isolation difficulty, fracture extent, or reduced predictability of vitality preservation in this presentation.

levels.title: Reasoning unclear
levels.description: Answer states conclusions without explaining the logic, omits one or more of the requested elements, or does not clearly identify the trigger that would change management.

levels.title: Reasoning partly explicit
levels.description: Shows some logical progression and addresses most requested elements, but the first priority, rejected alternative, or pulp finding that would trigger a switch is vague or incompletely linked to management.

levels.title: Reasoning explicit and complete
levels.description: Clearly explains why the chosen pathway is preferred, states the first clinical priority before definitive restoration, identifies the best alternative not chosen with a case-specific reason, and specifies the single pulp finding after access or fragment removal that would justify switching pathways.

red_flags: Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Commits to definitive extraction or irreversible treatment without first addressing fragment removal/repositioning, contamination control, and restorability assessment.
Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommends extraction despite the stem explicitly asking for a tooth-preserving pathway and the family wishing retention if prognosis is acceptable.
Misattributed Etiology: Treats the negative sensibility test at 2 days as definitive proof of pulpal necrosis without accounting for post-traumatic testing unreliability.
Generic Textbook Management: Recommends partial pulpotomy or simple rebonding as a routine immature-tooth protocol without addressing the deep subgingival fracture extension and isolation problem.
Severity Misjudged: Underestimates the significance of the mobile coronal fragment and subgingival palatal fracture in determining contamination risk and restorability.

items.question_content: A 2-year-old girl has had three painless bluish, fluctuant lower-lip nodules for 3 weeks that intermittently enlarge and shrink. She is afebrile, eating normally, has no cervical lymphadenopathy, and her parents report a habit of rolling or biting the lower lip behind the maxillary incisors. Examining fig_01.jpg, what management would you recommend now, and why? Justify your choice using the lesion pattern, likely mechanism, the child’s age/cooperation, and the measures you would take to reduce recurrence while avoiding treatment-related lip deformity.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is multiple lower-lip mucoceles, probably traumatic/extravasation lesions related to repetitive lip biting or rolling into the interdental spaces seen in fig_01.jpg. Because the lesions have persisted for weeks, fluctuate in size, and are multiple discrete lesions in the classic lower-lip location, observation or simple drainage is less appropriate than definitive removal. I would recommend excision of each lesion together with the adjacent minor salivary glands, with each lesion removed separately rather than one large combined excision. The child’s age matters: in an older cooperative child, habit elimination might be tried first, but at 2 years old reliable behavior modification is limited, so definitive treatment is reasonable now. fig_01.jpg suggests small, spatially separated lesions, so individual conservative closures should help preserve lip contour and reduce deformity risk. Tissue should be sent for histopathology. To reduce recurrence, the feeder glands should be removed, parents should receive guidance to limit the lip-biting habit as development allows, and follow-up should assess healing, contour, and recurrence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management or no coherent plan; may rely on aspiration/incision alone, ignore the need for definitive lesion management, or propose unnecessarily destructive treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests a plausible approach but with major omissions or weak rationale; may recommend excision without addressing the multiple separated lesions, associated minor salivary glands, age-related cooperation issues, or follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends appropriate definitive management, typically individual excision of each lesion with adjacent minor salivary glands, and gives a reasonable stepwise justification based on persistence, typical appearance, and recurrence tendency.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-justified, patient-specific plan: definitive individual excision with gland removal, conservative closure to preserve lip contour, histopathologic confirmation, and follow-up; explicitly explains why habit-only management is less reliable at this age and why drainage/observation alone is not preferred now.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not synthesize the clinical findings or misinterprets the figure; reasoning is disconnected from the presented history and exam.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely; may mention lower-lip location or bluish fluctuant appearance without integrating fluctuation over time, absence of infection, or the distribution in fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the key data: painless bluish fluctuant nodules, waxing and waning course, lower-lip location, lack of systemic/infective signs, and parental report of lip-biting habit.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly links the discrete lesion distribution in fig_01.jpg to repeated mechanical trauma from lip positioning against spaced primary incisors and uses that synthesis to support both diagnosis-level reasoning and management choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No meaningful weighing of options, or analysis is unsafe or clearly illogical.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions benefits or risks superficially but does not relate them to this toddler’s age, lesion behavior, or the pattern seen clinically.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the low urgency of a painless lesion against persistence and recurrence; explains why definitive treatment is favored over waiting alone in a very young child with limited capacity for habit control.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Thoughtfully weighs recurrence risk, cooperation limits, procedural morbidity, and preservation of lip form/function; justifies separate conservative excisions as the best compromise between definitiveness and minimizing deformity.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits clinically important complications or prevention strategies.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only one issue, such as recurrence or wound problems, without explaining prevention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recognizes recurrence risk and potential postoperative contour change or wound complications, with basic prevention measures.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies recurrence from residual feeder glands or persistent habit, and lip deformity from overly broad excision/closure; proposes prevention through gland removal, separate conservative closures, parental counseling, and follow-up monitoring.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. In a short phrase, name the anatomic discrepancy exploited by 180° rotation to convert the deep palatal fracture margin of the central incisor into a more favorable restorative position.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The maneuver relies on the difference in CEJ position/contour between the labial and palatal aspects. After 180° rotation, the previously deep palatal fracture margin can be repositioned more coronally and become easier to restore while preserving periodontal support.
objective_exact_answers: difference in labial and palatal CEJ levels

items.answer_explanation: The maneuver relies on the difference in CEJ position/contour between the labial and palatal aspects. After 180° rotation, the previously deep palatal fracture margin can be repositioned more coronally and become easier to restore while preserving periodontal support.

items.question_content: A healthy 5-year-old boy has had a small gingival lesion between primary mandibular teeth #Q and #R for more than a year. The parent reports little to no change and minimal symptoms. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. At this visit, what is your leading diagnosis and definitive management plan? Defend your plan by explaining how the lesion’s location, appearance, duration, and the subtle radiographic finding shape your differential, why tissue diagnosis is needed, what surgical extent/setting is appropriate for this child, and what follow-up you would discuss with the parent.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My leading diagnosis is a developmental gingival odontogenic cyst, most specifically a gingival cyst of the adult presenting unusually in a child. It should be strongly considered despite the age because the lesion is a small, circumscribed, persistent gingival nodule in the anterior mandible/canine-incisor region, and fig_01.jpg shows only a slight superficial radiolucency consistent with pressure-related cortical/alveolar change rather than a primary periapical or deep intraosseous process.

Reactive lesions remain in the differential, such as fibroma, pyogenic/peripheral giant cell lesions, or less likely a vascular lesion, but the long stability, limited symptoms, and subtle underlying bony change make a developmental cyst more likely than a purely inflammatory or traumatic lesion. I would not continue observation alone because the lesion has persisted for over a year and untreated gingival cysts can cause pressure necrosis of alveolar bone.

Definitive management is complete excisional biopsy, planned to remove the lesion in toto and address any superficial cortical component with a small full-thickness flap and curettage as needed, while preserving adjacent primary teeth and the developing permanent successor unless intraoperative findings indicate otherwise. Because the child is 5 and complete removal may require flap reflection and precise cooperation, I would use a controlled setting with sedation or general anesthesia if chairside cooperation is doubtful. This is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

I would counsel the parent that prognosis is excellent after complete excision, recurrence is rare, and follow-up should include early postoperative review plus periodic clinical, and if indicated radiographic, monitoring to confirm healing, no recurrence, no progressive bony change, and normal eruption development.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as primarily traumatic, infectious, endodontic, or vascular without recognizing a developmental odontogenic cyst as a serious possibility.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign gingival lesion and the need for biopsy but gives a vague or partly incorrect leading diagnosis without clearly favoring an odontogenic gingival cyst.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a developmental gingival odontogenic cyst as the leading diagnosis, even if subtype naming is imprecise.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically favors gingival cyst of the adult occurring in a child, while acknowledging that the age is unusual but the clinical pattern is characteristic.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully and ignores key case facts such as persistence, site, or the radiographic change.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but with weak synthesis; reasoning is mostly descriptive or omits why the radiograph changes the differential.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates lesion location, long duration, limited symptoms, circumscribed gingival appearance, and subtle radiolucency into a coherent explanation for the working diagnosis and the need for biopsy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains that the slight radiolucency can reflect superficial pressure atrophy from a gingival cyst and why the overall picture is less consistent with a tooth-based inflammatory lesion or a more aggressive deep cyst.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends continued observation only, empiric medication only, or an unspecified removal without biopsy principles or attention to surgical extent.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends biopsy or excision but does not make it clearly definitive, does not address likely superficial bony involvement, or omits preservation goals for adjacent/developing teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends complete excisional biopsy as definitive treatment, with flap access and curettage of the superficial defect if needed, while preserving adjacent primary teeth and developing dentition.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan that is both diagnostic and therapeutic, justifies the extent of excision from the imaging/clinical findings, and appropriately selects a controlled operative setting when a young child may not tolerate precise flap surgery chairside.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not discuss why observation or limited chairside management may be inadequate and gives no meaningful prognosis or follow-up.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either the benefit of excision or the need for follow-up, but the trade-offs of persistence, bone risk, and child cooperation are underdeveloped.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefits of definitive diagnosis and prevention of further bony change against procedure burden in a 5-year-old, and recommends follow-up with a realistic favorable prognosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly discusses parent counseling, the trade-off between observation and definitive excision, behavior/anesthesia considerations, rare recurrence, and monitoring for healing, recurrence, or eruption disturbance.

items.question_content: A 12-year-old boy presents 1 day after trauma with a fractured left maxillary central incisor. The detached fragment was recovered and kept in milk. On exam, the remaining coronal portion is mobile, there are no soft-tissue or supporting-tissue injuries, and the tooth is tender to percussion. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show an oblique complicated crown-root fracture with deep subgingival extension and a closed apex. The family strongly wishes to retain the tooth, and the patient is still growing. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what definitive management would you recommend now, and why is it the best choice for this patient over other reasonable options? Explain the critical treatment sequence needed to preserve esthetics and periodontal health. If follow-up resembles fig_03.jpg at 1 year and remains similar in fig_04.jpg at 2 years while the tooth stays asymptomatic and stable, how would that affect your prognosis and further management?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would aim to retain the tooth as an interim-to-medium term solution by endodontic treatment followed by intentional replantation with extraoral fragment reattachment, using the original fragment if it fits well and a fiber post only as reinforcement if needed. This is preferable because the patient is 12, still growing, and immediate extraction would sacrifice alveolar ridge and gingival architecture during a critical developmental period. The natural fragment offers the best esthetics. Simple intraoral reattachment is unlikely to be predictable because the fracture extends deeply subgingivally on fig_02.jpg, making isolation and margin control difficult. Crown lengthening/osteotomy would compromise bone and esthetics in the anterior zone, and orthodontic or surgical extrusion would be more prolonged and may not provide immediate esthetic recovery.

The key sequence is: keep the fragment hydrated; remove the mobile segment; complete root canal treatment because this is a complicated fracture with a closed apex; prepare any reinforcement conservatively; perform atraumatic extraction only if needed to gain access to the fracture margin; avoid touching or scraping the root surface; keep extraoral dry time as short as possible with the root moist; reattach the fragments extraorally; reimplant; then place a flexible short-term splint and review closely with radiographs.

The major risks are periodontal ligament injury, external surface/inflammatory or replacement resorption, ankylosis, attachment loss, mobility, and fragment debonding. If fig_03.jpg shows a localized coronal root resorptive change that is unchanged in fig_04.jpg and the tooth remains asymptomatic and stable, I would regard the prognosis as guarded but acceptable and continue monitoring rather than remove the tooth. A stable, nonprogressive defect is more consistent with transient/arrested resorption than aggressive replacement resorption. Worsening radiolucency, mobility, percussion changes suggesting ankylosis, symptoms, or loss of function would worsen the prognosis and prompt reconsideration of retention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate primary plan for this presentation, such as routine direct restoration or immediate definitive replacement, or omits the need to address pulpal involvement and deep subgingival fracture extension.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Advocates retention but gives an incomplete or poorly sequenced plan, such as fragment reattachment without solving access/isolation problems, or mentions replantation without essential operative steps.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends tooth preservation with endodontic management and intentional replantation with extraoral fragment reattachment, and outlines the main sequence: maintain fragment hydration, treat the canal, atraumatic extraction if needed for access, minimize extraoral dry time, reattach, reimplant, and flexible splint.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-prioritized, stepwise plan and clearly explains how the approach preserves esthetics, gingival architecture, and alveolar ridge until growth is complete, while using reinforcement judiciously rather than reflexively.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores major patient-specific factors such as age, ongoing growth, esthetics, and periodontal cost of different options.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some benefits of retention or some drawbacks of other options but the comparison is superficial or incomplete.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances retention against other reasonable options by explaining that deep subgingival fracture extension limits predictable intraoral restoration, crown-lengthening/osteotomy would harm esthetics and support, extrusion is slower and more demanding, and extraction risks ridge loss during growth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison that also weighs the biologic risks of intentional replantation itself, including periodontal ligament compromise, and justifies why those risks are acceptable in this specific child because the fragment is available, esthetics are urgent, and growth is incomplete.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives a generic trauma answer with little or no use of the clinical or radiographic findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as the patient's age or the diagnosis, but does not integrate the figures and follow-up information into the reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates key data: recovered fragment stored in milk, mobility of the coronal segment, complicated crown-root fracture, deep extension on fig_02.jpg, closed apex, lack of supporting-tissue injury, and stable asymptomatic follow-up context.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the initial findings and serial imaging into one coherent argument linking diagnosis, access limitations, treatment choice, and conservative follow-up of the later radiographic change.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications of intentional replantation/trauma or mismanages the stable follow-up defect by recommending unjustified aggressive treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies some complications but gives little prevention strategy or follow-up plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important risks such as periodontal ligament injury, external resorption, ankylosis, mobility, attachment loss, and fragment failure, and links them to prevention through atraumatic handling, moisture control, minimal extraoral time, flexible splinting, and serial review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly interprets a nonprogressive coronal root resorptive change over 1 to 2 years in an asymptomatic stable tooth as a guarded but monitorable finding rather than automatic failure, while stating the clinical/radiographic triggers that would worsen prognosis.

items.question_content:
A 6-year-old girl with limited cooperation presents with 1 week of spontaneous upper-right posterior pain, worse on chewing. Medical history is noncontributory, and she had dental treatment in that quadrant 1 year ago. Clinically, tooth 54 has a large existing restoration with recurrent caries, Grade I mobility, and tenderness to percussion. Tooth 55 has deep caries and is also tender to percussion. Both teeth are considered restorable if retained. Review fig_01.jpg carefully.

Formulate a quadrant management plan that aims to preserve arch length if reasonable, but does not assume the two teeth need the same pulp therapy. For each tooth, state the most likely pulpal/periradicular diagnosis, your preferred definitive treatment, and the main competing option you are rejecting. Your justification must cite one figure-based finding from 54 and one from 55. Then answer two constraints: if the child permits only one definitive procedure today, which tooth do you treat first and what interim care do you provide for the other? If the child is later found to be allergic to one antibiotic in any intracanal medicament you planned, how does your plan change?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The two teeth should be managed differently.

Tooth 54: The best working diagnosis is failed prior pulp therapy or necrotic pulp in a previously treated primary first molar, with furcal abscess/periradicular pathosis and inflammatory internal resorption. fig_01.jpg shows a prior-treatment appearance in 54 and a resorptive defect in the mesial root, with furcal radiolucency. Those findings make conventional canal debridement and especially predictable obturation less reliable. My preferred retention strategy is a non-instrumentation disinfection approach such as LSTR using triple-antibiotic paste, followed by a durable coronal seal and, if feasible, definitive full coronal coverage. The main competing option I would reject for 54 is conventional pulpectomy, because the internal resorption and prior-treatment failure pattern reduce the likelihood of predictable instrumentation and filling. Extraction is not first choice while the tooth remains restorable and space preservation is desirable, but it remains a fallback if retention becomes poor-prognosis.

Tooth 55: The best working diagnosis is chronic or symptomatic irreversible pulpitis in a restorable primary second molar; equivalent wording that recognizes it as endodontically involved but less structurally compromised than 54 is acceptable. fig_01.jpg shows deep caries approaching the pulp with only slight furcal change and no internal resorption or prior-treatment failure pattern. Therefore, the preferred definitive treatment is conventional pulpectomy with resorbable obturation and a durable coronal seal/full coverage. The main competing option I would reject for 55 is LSTR as first choice, because 55 is still a more conventional pulpectomy candidate and does not show the same obturation-compromising defect as 54. Extraction would be unnecessarily aggressive for a restorable tooth.

If only one definitive procedure can be completed today, I would treat 54 first because it has the greater disease burden and the less predictable conventional alternative. Interim care for 55 should stabilize the tooth rather than simply defer treatment: remove soft caries if tolerated, place a well-sealed temporary restoration, provide analgesic advice, and arrange prompt short-interval review for pulpectomy. The tooth should not be left open. Systemic antibiotics are not indicated unless there are signs of spreading infection or systemic involvement.

If the child is allergic to one antibiotic in the intracanal medicament, that antibiotic-containing LSTR regimen is contraindicated and should not be used. In that scenario, 54 must be reassessed: attempt conventional pulpectomy only if the tooth still appears technically manageable and likely to have a reasonable prognosis; otherwise extraction becomes the safer plan. The management of 55 remains conventional pulpectomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misdiagnoses both teeth, treats them as biologically equivalent, or gives diagnoses incompatible with the history, examination, and fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that 54 is more severely involved than 55 but incorrectly characterizes one tooth's pulpal/periradicular status or does not clearly distinguish the two disease patterns.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies 54 as a previously treated tooth with failed/necrotic pulp status, furcal periradicular disease, and internal resorption, and identifies 55 as irreversible pulpitis or equivalent endodontic involvement in a restorable tooth without the same resorptive defect.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides precise, tooth-specific diagnoses that clearly separate prior-treatment failure with internal resorption in 54 from the comparatively less structurally compromised 55; equivalent clinically sound wording is acceptable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg meaningfully, or relies only on generic textbook statements without linking radiographic findings to the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant information but cites figure-based support for only one tooth, or misses a key discriminator such as prior-treatment appearance/internal resorption in 54 or the absence of that pattern in 55.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Cites at least one relevant figure-based finding for each tooth and links those findings to different management choices.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a coherent figure-driven argument using the prior-treatment appearance, internal resorption, and furcal radiolucency in 54, and the deep caries approaching pulp with comparatively limited change and no internal resorption in 55, integrating these with the clinical findings and cooperation limits.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate therapy, gives the same unsupported definitive treatment for both teeth, or provides no clear tooth-specific plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects an appropriate definitive approach for only one tooth, or proposes tooth retention for both without a clear rationale for why the modalities differ.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a non-instrumentation disinfection approach such as LSTR with durable seal for 54 and conventional pulpectomy with durable seal for 55, with rationale tied to each tooth's disease pattern and technical feasibility.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a practical, tooth-specific plan that explains why 54 is better suited to LSTR or equivalent disinfection-based retention, why 55 remains the stronger pulpectomy candidate, and how behavior modifies execution without being the sole determinant.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify or address plausible competing options for the teeth, or bases the decision only on cooperation without discussing prognosis or technical predictability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a competing option for one or both teeth but gives weak, generic, or inconsistent reasons for rejecting it.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: For each tooth, identifies a plausible competing option and rejects it with case-specific reasoning, such as reduced obturation predictability in 54 or unnecessary departure from conventional pulpectomy in 55.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly weighs space preservation, disease burden, technical feasibility, and long-term predictability, showing why conventional pulpectomy is less defensible in 54 and why LSTR or extraction is less justified as first choice in 55.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not choose which tooth to treat first when limited to one definitive procedure, or leaves the other tooth without clinically adequate interim care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a treatment priority but with weak justification, or proposes interim management that is vague or incomplete.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes one tooth using a coherent rationale and provides reasonable interim stabilization for the other, including seal and follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes 54 first because of greater disease burden and less predictable conventional alternatives, and provides interim care for 55 that addresses contamination control, symptoms, and prompt review while avoiding unsafe deferral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Continues to recommend an antibiotic-containing intracanal medicament despite the stated allergy scenario, or ignores the scenario entirely.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the planned medicament should be avoided but does not revise the management plan appropriately.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Avoids the contraindicated antibiotic-based regimen and proposes a reasonable revised plan for 54, such as conventional pulpectomy if feasible or extraction if not, while preserving the plan for 55.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly explains why the allergy removes the preferred conservative option for 54, recalibrates the plan by weighing pulpectomy feasibility against extraction, and distinguishes this from the largely unchanged management of 55.

red_flags: Contraindication Ignored: Recommending an antibiotic-containing intracanal medicament despite the stated allergy scenario.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old healthy boy in mixed dentition complains of discomfort from the cervical area of #11. No trauma history is reported. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Before hearing anything about attendance, state the management pathway that is biologically safest for this tooth and explain which findings in the figures create that preference. The father then says repeated recall visits are unlikely. What plan would you actually carry out today, what operative endpoint are you aiming for, and what treatment would you intentionally avoid at this stage? Your justification must explicitly use the key radiographic features of #11. Also state the intraoperative finding that would make you abandon your initial plan and change immediately to a pulpal procedure, and how later loss of vitality would alter management.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The working diagnosis is a facial talon cusp on #11, with caries/deep plaque-retentive groove on the labial accessory cusp and associated local soft-tissue irritation. fig_02.jpg is the key management image because it shows pulpal extension into the cusp and an immature root with an open apex; there is no history suggesting trauma, and the tooth appears restorable without obvious periapical disease.

If attendance were reliable, the biologically safest approach would be gradual/serial reduction of the cusp with interim sealing/restoration. That approach best minimizes the chance of pulp exposure because the cusp contains pulp tissue, while preserving vitality for apexogenesis in a tooth with an open apex.

Once poor recall is disclosed, the plan I would actually carry out is cautious single-visit conservative reduction/removal of the accessory cusp with caries removal and immediate adhesive sealing/restoration under good isolation. The operative endpoint is not aggressive flattening at any cost; it is a cleansable, non-retentive labial contour with the lesion eliminated/sealed while preserving pulp vitality. I would intentionally avoid observation or sealant-only treatment, because active disease and the abnormal morphology would remain, and I would also avoid elective root canal treatment or extraction because this is a restorable young permanent incisor whose vitality is valuable for continued root development.

The intraoperative finding that should make me abandon simple reduction/restoration is pulp exposure or clear evidence that the remaining dentin thickness is no longer safely compatible with vitality preservation by restoration alone. At that point I would change immediately to vital pulp therapy in order to maintain vitality and allow continued root maturation.

If vitality is later lost, management should shift to an immature-tooth endodontic pathway rather than routine treatment for a mature incisor: regenerative endodontic treatment when feasible, or apexification/apical barrier as an alternative. Follow-up should assess symptoms, pulp status, restoration seal, periapical status, and continued root development/apical closure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the condition or proposes a diagnosis inconsistent with the figures and history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an accessory cusp/developmental anomaly but does not clearly identify facial talon cusp on #11 or does not relate it to the current lesion/symptoms.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies facial talon cusp on #11 with associated caries/plaque-retentive groove as the source of the local problem; stage 1 or equivalent description is acceptable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies facial talon cusp on a restorable young permanent incisor and appropriately excludes trauma-driven or primary periapical pathology as the main explanation of the presentation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or misreads the critical radiographic findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant data from the history or one figure, but omits a major figure-based finding that should drive management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explicitly integrates fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg by identifying the labial accessory cusp with a caries-prone/retentive defect and the radiographic pulpal extension into the cusp together with the immature root/open apex.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the clinical and radiographic findings into a coherent rationale that links pulpal extension and open apex to the priority of vitality preservation/apexogenesis while also recognizing the tooth as restorable and without obvious periapical disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan, such as no treatment despite active disease, immediate routine root canal treatment, or extraction of a restorable immature incisor.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests a broadly conservative approach but does not distinguish the ideal biologic pathway from the final plan under poor recall, or gives an incomplete operative plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that reliable recall would favor staged/gradual reduction with sealing/restoration, but that poor attendance justifies careful one-visit cusp reduction/removal with caries removal and immediate sealed restoration while preserving vitality.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise final plan tailored to the case, including the operative endpoint of a cleansable contour and sealed defect, while explicitly avoiding disproportionate irreversible treatment and unnecessary over-reduction that threatens the pulp.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no clinically sound comparison of management approaches.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions that alternatives exist but discusses them superficially or without explaining how the figures and recall issue change the decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that staged reduction is biologically safer because pulpal tissue extends into the cusp, but poor recall makes a single definitive conservative visit more reliable; also explains why observation/sealant-only or elective endodontic/extraction are less suitable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the short-term procedural risk of exposure against the long-term benefit of vitality preservation and apexogenesis, and clearly defends why attendance reliability changes the preferred approach in this specific tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores major complications or gives an inappropriate response to exposure/necrosis in an immature tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions pulp exposure or later necrosis but gives vague or nonspecific contingency planning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that pulp exposure or clear pulpal compromise during reduction should trigger vital pulp therapy, and that later loss of vitality requires an immature-tooth endodontic approach rather than routine treatment for a mature apex.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds appropriate monitoring and prevention concepts, including follow-up for symptoms, pulp status, restoration seal, periapical status, and continued root maturation/apical closure.

items.question_content: A 7-year-2-month-old boy is referred after several painful attempts to treat the maxillary right primary molars. He now has marked dental fear and pus discharge from the gingiva. Examine fig_01.jpg. What definitive management would you choose for this quadrant now, and why? Justify your plan from the clinical and radiographic findings, making clear how you would manage the two involved primary molars and what you would monitor over time.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My priority would be to control infection and complete definitive care in a way the child can tolerate. Because he is 7 years old and already fearful after painful treatment, I would use behavior guidance and, if needed, nitrous oxide to enable atraumatic treatment.

fig_01.jpg supports apical infection involving the maxillary right primary molars and shows a separated endodontic instrument in the mesio-buccal canal of the primary second molar. I would not extract both teeth automatically. The primary first molar appears poor-prognosis in this infected quadrant and would be extracted once acute inflammation is controlled. For the primary second molar, if it is restorable and root support is adequate, I would attempt retention: isolate, access, remove the accessible fragment as conservatively as possible, complete pulpectomy/root canal debridement, and place a good coronal seal. Retaining this tooth temporarily is valuable at this age because premature loss of primary molars can lead to space loss and later eruption problems.

If retrieval would require excessive dentin removal, risks perforation, or infection cannot be controlled, extraction becomes the safer alternative, with planning for space management if needed. Follow-up should be clinical and radiographic until the permanent successor erupts, monitoring symptom resolution, recurrent drainage, inflammatory root resorption, failure of the coronal seal/restoration, space loss or malocclusion, and developmental or eruption disturbances of the successor.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No coherent definitive plan, or proposes a clearly inappropriate plan such as ignoring the infection, restoring without addressing endodontic disease, or treating both teeth identically without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes need for definitive treatment but gives an incomplete or generic plan; may suggest extraction or pulpectomy without distinguishing between the two primary molars, without addressing the separated instrument, or without accounting for limited cooperation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a tooth-specific plan: control infection, use appropriate behavior support/sedation, extract the poorer-prognosis primary first molar, and attempt to retain the primary second molar if feasible by fragment removal followed by root canal treatment and a durable coronal seal; notes extraction as a fallback if conservation is not feasible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan with rationale and thresholds for changing course, including why temporary retention of the primary second molar is preferred at this age and when retrieval efforts should be abandoned in favor of extraction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figure or clinical findings appropriately, or misinterprets the key radiographic finding.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only general statements about infection or pediatric care, with weak linkage between symptoms, age, cooperation, and radiographic findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the child's pain/pus, severe dental fear, age, and fig_01.jpg's separated instrument with periradicular disease into a coherent management rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all relevant information and explains why the separated instrument specifically alters endodontic prognosis and why arch-space preservation and protection of the permanent successor influence management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful weighing of alternatives, or recommends a plan without considering major risks or benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either the benefit of retaining the tooth or the benefit of extraction, but does not balance both sides in this child's context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefit of retaining the primary second molar for function/space against the risks of fragment retrieval and endodontic failure, and balances extraction against premature space loss and possible eruption consequences.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nuanced decision thresholds, stating that retention is justified only if the fragment can be managed conservatively and infection controlled; otherwise extraction is safer with anticipatory space management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits follow-up needs and does not identify relevant complications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic review or pain recurrence without specifying important dental complications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the need to monitor for persistent or recurrent infection, drainage/pain, inflammatory root resorption or other pathologic change, and space loss or eruption disturbance if extraction occurs.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds long-term monitoring of coronal seal/restoration failure and developmental effects on the permanent successor, such as eruption disturbance or enamel defect, with clinical and radiographic follow-up until eruption.

items.question_content:
A 21-month-old boy with no significant medical history is brought to a pediatric dental clinic after waking irritable the morning after sleeping with a pacifier. His father reports that the pacifier was found attached over the left thumb and, when removed, the skin from the PIP distally changed from circumferential pallor to erythema. The child is afebrile and otherwise well. Review fig_01.jpg, which shows the thumb and the pacifier.

Using the history and fig_01.jpg, identify the most likely diagnosis and mechanism, and explain why another plausible mechanical explanation suggested by the device is less convincing. Include one nonmechanical alternative that should still remain in the differential at first assessment. Then decide whether conservative management in clinic is appropriate or whether same-day medical referral is needed, specifying the minimum examination findings that determine that disposition. Give your management and caregiver advice for a family reluctant to stop pacifier use, and state the single exam change that would most strongly overturn your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis is a pacifier-induced suction blister of the thumb, meaning a friction blister produced by prolonged negative pressure and soft-tissue entrapment against the pacifier during sleep. fig_01.jpg supports this: the lesion is a localized, intact, clear, oval distal thumb bulla rather than a deep circumferential wound, and the pacifier appears to be a soft one-piece silicone device whose compressible structure could form a seal around the thumb and maintain suction. The history that pallor changed to erythema after removal is consistent with transient pressure/suction followed by reperfusion.

A plausible competing mechanical explanation is simple ring-constriction/tourniquet injury from the thumb being trapped in an opening of the pacifier. That is less convincing because the morphology is more like a superficial suction/friction bulla than a fixed constriction injury: there is no described deep groove, persistent distal cyanosis, worsening edema, necrosis, or tissue loss, and the figure suggests a soft deformable device more likely to create a seal than act as a rigid strangulating ring. A nonmechanical alternative that should still be kept in reserve initially is an infectious blister such as herpetic whitlow or bullous impetigo/blistering distal dactylitis; those would become more likely with grouped vesicles or purulence, warmth, progressive tenderness/swelling, crusting, fever, or spreading erythema.

Conservative clinic management is appropriate only if a focused examination confirms normal perfusion and a benign local exam: pink color after release, brisk capillary refill, normal warmth, active use/movement of the thumb, no retained hair/thread or other circumferential constricting element, no progressive swelling, and no signs of infection, deep laceration, nail-bed injury, or necrosis. If those findings are present, same-day medical referral is not required.

Management is supportive: age-appropriate analgesia if needed, gentle cleansing with soap and water, leave the blister roof intact, and protect with a light nonadherent dressing if needed. The blister should not be routinely drained or deroofed, and antibiotics/antivirals are unnecessary unless new evidence suggests infection. If the blister ruptures, allow drainage, keep the superficial skin flap in place as a biologic dressing, continue local hygiene, and monitor for secondary infection.

For caregivers reluctant to stop pacifier use, explain that this device likely allowed prolonged suction/entrapment overnight. Preferred advice is discontinuation or active weaning given the child’s age, but if they continue use, counsel them to avoid unsupervised sleep use, use only intact age-appropriate one-piece pacifiers, inspect frequently for deformation, tears, or wear, replace worn devices promptly, and never tie a pacifier to the child or crib.

The single examination change that would most strongly overturn the plan is persistent delayed capillary refill or duskiness after device removal, because that suggests ongoing vascular compromise/ischemic constriction rather than a simple self-limited suction blister and warrants urgent medical/hand evaluation.

items.question_content:
A 20-month-old girl is seen in pediatric dentistry for missing and abnormal primary incisors. Since birth she has had minimal scalp-hair growth; review fig_01.jpg. Intraoral exam shows absent maxillary primary incisors and yellow, very small mandibular incisors. She has speech delay despite normal hearing evaluation, normal sweating, normal gross motor development, and no history of recurrent severe infections. Genetic testing has not yet returned.

As the pediatric dentist, provide a ranked differential of the 3 most plausible syndromic explanations for this hair-tooth presentation and justify the order from the available data, including at least one observation from fig_01.jpg. Then identify the lower-probability disorder you would still try to exclude early because missing it would change morbidity the most, and state the clinical or hair-shaft finding that would make you move it up your list. You may choose only one dental investigation before genetics returns: which one would most change your ranking once cooperation permits, and how would 2 different radiographic result patterns lead you to different counseling and recall pathways?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
A defensible ranking is: (1) tricho-dento-osseous syndrome (TDO), (2) a broader normohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia/oligodontia-hypotrichosis syndrome, and (3) a systemic hair disorder such as Menkes disease or trichothiodystrophy (TTD). TDO deserves strong early consideration because the phenotype is not just missing teeth: the mandibular incisors are yellow and miniaturized, suggesting tooth-structure abnormality, and fig_01.jpg shows marked congenital hypotrichosis with very sparse wispy lightly pigmented scalp hair and sparse brows, supporting a syndromic hair-tooth disorder. A broader ectodermal dysplasia pathway remains close because tooth agenesis/microdontia with hypotrichosis can occur in normohidrotic ectodermal conditions, and normal sweating does not exclude them. Menkes and TTD are lower probability from the current data because gross motor development is otherwise normal and there is no history of severe recurrent infections, but they remain important because of systemic morbidity. Chediak-Higashi or Griscelli syndrome are less favored without infectious or immunologic features.

The lower-probability disorder I would still try to exclude early is Menkes disease because delayed recognition risks progressive neurologic injury. Concern would rise with hypotonia, seizures, developmental regression, failure to thrive, or hair-shaft pili torti on microscopy. An acceptable alternative high-morbidity answer is TTD, which would move up with recurrent severe respiratory/GI infections, growth failure, or tiger-tail banding on polarized hair microscopy.

The single dental investigation most likely to change the ranking is age-appropriate radiographic assessment of the developing dentition once cooperation permits (occlusal/periapical views now or panoramic imaging later if feasible). The key questions are whether tooth germs are present, whether enamel/mineralization is broadly abnormal, and whether taurodontism is present.

If radiographs show taurodontism with generalized enamel defects, TDO moves clearly to the top. Counseling would shift toward a DLX3-related hair-tooth-bone disorder, close preventive/restorative surveillance for enamel breakdown, monitoring of feeding, speech, and eruption, and coordination with genetics and other pediatric services.

If radiographs instead show isolated tooth agenesis/microdontia without taurodontism or generalized enamel defects, a broader ectodermal dysplasia/oligodontia pathway becomes more likely. Counseling would emphasize long-term management of missing teeth, function, space maintenance/prosthetic planning as age permits, and continued surveillance for evolving ectodermal findings.

Regardless of final diagnosis, immediate dental priorities are a dental home, fluoride-based prevention, protection/monitoring of the abnormal incisors, diet/caries counseling, and avoidance of irreversible treatment before diagnostic characterization.

items.question_content: A 61-year-old woman with stage IV follicular thyroid carcinoma is taking lenvatinib. Four months after extraction of a right posterior maxillary molar, she has severe pain, persistent exposed bone, and fluid drainage despite chlorhexidine rinses and amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has bone metastases outside the jaws, no history of bisphosphonate or denosumab use, and prior radiotherapy did not involve the jaws. Examine fig_01.jpg. What is your preferred management strategy for this likely lenvatinib-related MRONJ at this visit, and why? In your justification, use the clinical and imaging findings to support the level of invasiveness you choose and state what changes would make you escalate or modify the plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with lenvatinib-related MRONJ, likely advanced/stage 3 disease: exposed bone has persisted well beyond 8 weeks after extraction in a patient receiving an antiangiogenic drug, with severe pain, drainage, and fig_01.jpg showing destructive change in the posterior maxilla with ipsilateral maxillary sinus involvement/opacification. The absence of jaw irradiation makes osteoradionecrosis less likely, and the medication/extraction history strongly supports MRONJ.

My initial approach would still be conservative but closely supervised rather than immediately aggressive surgery. I would continue local antiseptic care, optimize analgesia, reinforce meticulous oral hygiene and avoidance of further trauma, and use systemic antibiotics only if there is ongoing secondary infection or worsening purulence/pain rather than as indefinite empiric therapy. Low-trauma adjunctive care such as photobiomodulation is reasonable because the goal is pain control and mucosal healing while minimizing additional tissue injury. If loose sequestra are present, limited removal can be considered, but I would avoid major debridement or resection as the first step.

The reason to start conservatively is patient-specific: lenvatinib impairs angiogenesis and wound healing, the lesion arose after extraction, the maxilla is already compromised, and sinus involvement raises the risk of poor closure and oroantral/sinonasal complications after surgery. She also has advanced metastatic cancer, so symptom relief and preservation of quality of life matter greatly.

I would coordinate with the oncology team about whether any temporary lenvatinib interruption or dose adjustment is feasible, but only if oncologically acceptable. I would monitor pain, exposed bone size, mucosal closure, drainage, sinus symptoms, and radiographic progression. I would escalate to OMFS/surgical management if there is uncontrolled infection, progression of necrosis, persistent severe pain despite conservative care, fistula/oroantral communication, worsening sinus disease, or failure to stabilize/heal on close follow-up.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old girl presents with painful left mandibular swelling after extraction of an exfoliating sound primary molar. Teeth #35 and #36 are intact, tender to percussion, and nonresponsive to cold/EPT. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, decide whether these permanent teeth should receive irreversible dental treatment now, and state the overall management that best fits the jaw lesion. Defend your decision using the imaging and biopsy findings.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not perform endodontic treatment or extraction of #35 or #36 at this stage. The overall picture is most consistent with mandibular chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis (CNO), not primary pulpal disease. The key reasoning is that the teeth are clinically sound, while fig_01.jpg shows a diffuse expansile mixed lesion with ill-defined borders, cortical thinning, and layered periosteal new bone rather than a tooth-centered periapical process. fig_02.jpg supports active osseous involvement with loss of normal fatty marrow signal, bone marrow edema, periosteal new bone formation, and adjacent soft-tissue swelling. fig_03.jpg is more specifically described as showing multiple irregular viable bone fragments interspersed with abundant fibrous tissue, prominent peritrabecular clefting, predominant sclerosis, and lack of inflammation, with no bacterial colonies or sequestration. Together, these findings make altered sensibility of #35/#36 more likely secondary to the mandibular bone process than true pulpal necrosis.

Management should therefore be conservative and diagnosis-directed: preserve #35 and #36, provide symptomatic management with NSAIDs, and monitor clinically and radiographically with repeat pulp sensibility testing over time rather than proceeding to irreversible dental treatment. In this case, antibiotic courses were given, including prolonged clindamycin, and this was associated with clinical improvement, but the lesion was still diagnosed as CNO based on the overall clinical course, imaging, histopathology, and lack of sustained response to prior antibiotic therapy. Ongoing follow-up is important because recurrence can occur, and multidisciplinary coordination may be needed. The teeth should be preserved unless later objective evidence of true odontogenic disease appears.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly identifies mandibular CNO as the best working diagnosis and frames it appropriately as a non-odontogenic, nonbacterial inflammatory bone process in a child.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
