items.question_content: A healthy 3-year-old boy has had 2 months of oral soreness triggered by spicy food. Review only the initial-visit panels in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg and the pedigree in fig_03.jpg. On examination, the oral lesions are non-scrapable, non-indurated, and non-tender. Extraorally he has irregular hyperpigmented areas on the back and right arm; nails are normal. No medications or systemic disease are reported in the child or parents. Before any histology is available, give your provisional diagnosis and prioritized differential. Outline your first-visit management plan, making clear whether tissue diagnosis should be obtained now or after a short trial of symptomatic care, and justify that choice for a 3-year-old. Explain how fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg should influence your reasoning without over-interpreting them, including what they do and do not allow you to conclude about heredity. If you obtain tissue, name the lesion/site you would sample and the key pathology you would expect. Finally, state the single interval change on follow-up that would most strongly make you re-biopsy or escalate urgency.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading provisional diagnosis is pediatric oral lichen planus, or more cautiously an oral lichenoid interface mucositis most suggestive of OLP, with familial aggregation. From the initial panels in fig_01.jpg, the child has multifocal bilateral white reticular/papular change involving buccal mucosa, tongue, and lip, with erosive/pseudomembranous buccal involvement that fits the spicy-food pain. fig_02.jpg shows similar oral lesions in both parents, increasing suspicion for a shared predisposition. fig_03.jpg supports clustering in first-degree relatives, but it does not by itself prove a Mendelian inheritance pattern or allow a definitive diagnosis without histology, especially because age 3 is exceptionally young for OLP.

Prioritized differential diagnosis should include: (1) oral lichenoid reaction or another interface mucositis such as lupus-related oral disease, because these can clinically and histologically overlap with OLP, although the bilateral multifocal pattern and lack of medication history/local trigger make a reactive lichenoid lesion less likely; (2) hereditary childhood white-lesion disorders such as white sponge nevus and dyskeratosis congenita, because the age and family clustering are unusual, but the morphology here is more inflammatory/lacy with erosive change than diffuse folded plaque, and normal nails argue against dyskeratosis congenita; (3) candidiasis or frictional keratosis are lower-probability because the lesions are non-scrapable and multifocal. The skin pigmentation is nonspecific: it should be documented and correlated clinically, and dermatologic review is reasonable if lesions are progressive or otherwise suspicious, but it does not override the oral leading diagnosis.

My first-visit plan would favor obtaining tissue diagnosis at baseline rather than relying only on a short symptomatic trial. The reasons are the exceptionally early age, symptomatic erosive disease, and the need to exclude important mimics in a child with extraoral pigmentation. The parents’ similar lesions strengthen suspicion for familial OLP, but they should not substitute for confirming the child’s diagnosis. At the same time, I would begin conservative supportive care: avoidance of spicy/traumatic foods, gentle oral hygiene, elimination of local trauma, baseline photographs, and age-appropriate topical symptomatic care while awaiting pathology. I would not use systemic therapy initially.

If biopsying, I would sample a representative buccal mucosal lesion, preferably the right buccal mucosa, taking tissue from the edge of white striae with adjacent erythematous/erosive change rather than from only ulcer slough or pseudomembrane. Expected histopathology would be compatible with OLP: hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis, basal cell liquefactive degeneration, possible saw-tooth rete ridges/Civatte bodies, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate in the superficial lamina propria.

The interval change that would most strongly make me re-biopsy or escalate urgency is a persistent unilateral nonhealing indurated ulcer, especially with new verrucous or nodular thickening. That is more concerning for dysplasia, malignant transformation, or an alternative diagnosis than a routine inflammatory flare.

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: A 36-year-old man is being prepared for implants in the posterior maxilla. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg from his preoperative CBCT. What anatomic finding on these images most changes management, and what is your safest treatment strategy for this patient? Base your answer on the imaging and explain whether implant placement can proceed, which maneuver becomes highest risk if augmentation is considered, and how you would minimize and manage the main intraoperative hazard.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The critical finding is a bilateral, unusually large posterior superior alveolar artery coursing on the floor of the maxillary sinus rather than in the usual lateral wall position. fig_02.jpg shows a large caliber on both sides, with the right larger than the left, and fig_03.jpg shows the canal is about 15 mm from the crest on the right and 17 mm on the left. This means implant placement may still be feasible if the planned osteotomy remains safely coronal to the canal and does not violate the sinus floor; if vertical bone is limited, I would favor a modified implant plan such as shorter implants, altered position/angulation, or staged treatment rather than risking the vessel. The highest-risk maneuver is sinus augmentation, especially a lateral-window or sinus-floor-elevation step in the area of this floor-course artery, because it could directly injure the vessel. If augmentation is unavoidable, the access design must be altered to avoid the canal, and an experienced surgeon should use an atraumatic technique such as piezosurgery. The main complication is significant arterial bleeding with impaired visibility, possible membrane perforation, hematoma, and postoperative bleeding. I would counsel the patient about this increased risk, have suction, local pressure, hemostatic agents, and cautery/ligation readiness available, and proceed only with a plan that respects the vessel’s course.

items.question_content: An otherwise healthy 41-year-old nonsmoking woman has an isolated destructive periodontal lesion between teeth 25 and 26 despite excellent plaque control, regular maintenance, and only mild periodontal findings elsewhere. Prior scaling/root planing did not arrest progression. Tooth 25 has grade 3 mobility, probing depth to 10 mm with profuse bleeding, both teeth are vital, percussion is negative, and there is no furcation involvement. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. If flap exploration reveals firm granular tissue rather than typical soft granulation tissue, what management strategy would you choose for this site, and why?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would pursue a tooth-preserving exploratory periodontal surgery rather than repeat blind nonsurgical therapy or move directly to extraction. This lesion is atypical for routine plaque-driven periodontitis: it is highly localized, the patient is healthy and a nonsmoker with excellent oral hygiene, the rest of the dentition is relatively stable, and prior scaling/root planing failed. Vitality and negative percussion make a primary endodontic source less likely, while the isolated radiographic defect and severe mobility suggest a local destructive process that needs direct inspection.

My plan would be to stabilize the tooth first by reducing traumatic loading and splinting if needed, then raise a flap, thoroughly debride the defect, and inspect the root surfaces and surrounding hard tissues for vertical root fracture, cemental tear, or other local causes. The unusual firm granular tissue should be submitted for histopathology because it is not typical periodontal granulation tissue and raises concern for an atypical infectious or granulomatous lesion, including Actinomyces-associated disease. If the tooth is structurally maintainable and the defect morphology is favorable after debridement, I would retain the tooth and complete regenerative defect management. Antibiotics may be used only as an adjunct after obtaining tissue, not as sole treatment.

I would monitor closely for soft-tissue healing, reduction in bleeding and pocketing, mobility improvement, and radiographic stability/regeneration. Failure to improve or unexpected pathology would trigger reassessment of the diagnosis and escalation of the workup or treatment.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old nonsmoking woman wants a fixed esthetic replacement for two failing adjacent maxillary central incisors after trauma and prior periodontal breakdown. After initial periodontal therapy, probing is now ≤3 mm with no bleeding, but both incisors remain mobile, migrated, and discolored. Clinical exam shows a thick scalloped biotype with slight recession on one incisor and no acute infection. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive implant-restorative strategy would you choose to maximize papilla preservation and smile-zone esthetics, and how would you sequence it? Justify the plan using the figure-based anatomy and patient factors, and state the main complications you would specifically monitor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would avoid removing both central incisors at the same visit. fig_01.jpg shows a highly visible smile zone, so even small papilla loss or midfacial recession would be esthetically obvious. fig_02.jpg suggests a thin buccal plate and reduced interproximal bony support, which increases the risk of facial collapse and an unfilled interimplant embrasure if both adjacent sites are treated simultaneously. My preferred plan is staged, one-by-one immediate implant therapy: first stabilize periodontal health, then atraumatically and flaplessly extract one central incisor, place an immediate implant in a restoratively driven palatal position only if primary stability is sufficient, and provide a non-occluding provisional that supports the soft tissue contour; manage the facial gap/soft-tissue deficiency as needed to limit collapse. After soft-tissue maturation, treat the second central incisor in the same way while preserving the first restoration and maintaining adequate spacing between implants. This temporarily converts the most critical papilla from an implant-implant situation into a tooth-implant situation, preserving attachment and soft-tissue support during healing. Compared with simultaneous adjacent implantation or delayed healing without immediate support, this better fits the high esthetic demand, controlled periodontal status, and thin facial anatomy. I would monitor for loss of primary stability, buccal recession or plate resorption, papilla flattening/black triangle formation, overload from the provisional, and peri-implant inflammation.

items.question_content: A 24-year-old woman with recurrent hereditary gingival fibromatosis undergoes quadrant surgery for severe fibrotic gingival enlargement. Reviewing the intraoperative sequence in fig_01.jpg, in this buccal quadrant, the operative note states that after submarginal internal bevel and sulcular incisions with soft-tissue debridement, the surgeon raised a split-thickness flap from attached gingiva to the mucogingival junction, removed excess connective tissue until bone was exposed, performed osteoplasty of exostotic/non-supporting buccal bone with selective osteotomy and marginal bone recontouring where needed, positioned the buccal alveolar margin about 3 mm apical to the CEJ, and extracted residual roots encountered during curettage. Which steps were intended to create a maintainable surgical bed rather than simply reduce excess soft tissue? Select all that apply.

Removal of excess connective tissue overlying bone until the bone was exposed
Osteoplasty of exostotic/non-supporting buccal bone
Selective osteotomy with marginal bone recontouring where required
Positioning the buccal alveolar margin about 3 mm apical to the CEJ
Retention of residual roots because there was no radiographic bone resorption
Extraction of residual roots encountered during curettage
Guided tissue regeneration to preserve the buccal prominence
Full-thickness apically positioned flap as the principal exposure design
External bevel gingivectomy alone without osseous correction

Regenerative grafting, retaining roots, a full-thickness design, or soft-tissue trimming alone were not used.

items.question_content: A patient has a persistent interdental gingival overgrowth between teeth #24 and #25 after initial nonsurgical periodontal therapy. Review fig_01.jpg. The lesion is excised, a flap is reflected, and osseous recontouring is performed. After excision, an interproximal residual defect with exposed bone remains, and there is insufficient local tissue to obtain primary closure with flap advancement. Which reconstructive approach is most appropriate for this surgical defect?

question_options.text: Gingivectomy and gingivoplasty alone
Coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft
Free gingival graft
Gingival unit graft

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Fig4 shows an interproximal residual defect with exposed tissue that cannot be predictably closed primarily after excision and osseous correction. A free gingival graft is appropriate to cover the exposed area and recreate stable keratinized tissue. Gingivectomy alone would not reconstruct the defect, while CTG with CAF and gingival unit graft are more suited to root-coverage defects than this interproximal post-excisional situation.

items.question_content: A 65-year-old woman with erosive oral lichen planus had maxillary left premolar implants placed after the mucosal disease was brought under control with topical corticosteroid therapy. The site showed postoperative sloughing with delayed soft-tissue recovery
Thin tissue with cover-screw exposure developed before second-stage healing was completed
The mandibular implant placed in a healed ridge healed without abnormal tissue response
Implant surgery was performed while the erosive lesions were still untreated and symptomatic
The definitive restoration had already been in prolonged function before the radiograph in fig_03.jpg
Equivalent crestal bone loss was documented around the lower-right implant
Minimal flap manipulation at second-stage surgery is the most likely precipitating cause of early crestal bone loss in this case

items.question_content: A 31-year-old woman is planned for immediate implant placement at a retained maxillary primary canine site. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. After atraumatic extraction, the facial soft tissue and buccal plate were intact, and periodontal probing showed a thick gingival phenotype. In Elian's immediate extraction-socket classification, Class I indicates intact facial soft tissue and intact facial bone, Class II indicates intact soft tissue with partial loss of facial bone, and Class III indicates loss of both soft tissue and facial bone. What is the combined designation of this site? Provide both the socket class and tissue phenotype.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The site shows intact facial soft tissue and an intact buccal plate after extraction, which corresponds to Elian Type 1. The gingival phenotype is thick. Together, this is a favorable starting phenotype for immediate implant placement in the esthetic zone.
objective_exact_answers: Elian Type I with thick biotype

items.answer_explanation: The site shows intact facial soft tissue and an intact buccal plate after extraction, which corresponds to Elian Type 1. The gingival phenotype is thick. Together, this is a favorable starting phenotype for immediate implant placement in the esthetic zone.

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, formulate a site-specific mucogingival management plan for the mandibular implants in these two patients: a 65-year-old man being prepared for an overdenture at 33 and 43, and a 61-year-old woman with recurrent inflammation around a loaded overdenture implant at 33. For each site, identify the figure-based soft-tissue feature that most strongly drives treatment choice, select the augmentation approach you would use, and state whether any of the three sites can justifiably share the same approach. For each patient, compare your plan with one reasonable alternative you did not choose, focusing on vascularity, donor-site morbidity, color blend, and predictability of keratinized width versus thickness gain. Finally, answer both adaptations: (1) if the woman’s inflammation settled after hygiene instruction but the mucosal anatomy in fig_03.jpg was unchanged, would your plan change; (2) if, at surgery, the tissue over the man’s site 33 proved thinner than expected, what would you change and why?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
In the 65-year-old man, fig_01.jpg shows both implants are still tissue-covered and deficient in facial keratinized tissue, so both male sites can share the same biologic foundation: a local pedicled second-stage augmentation that redistributes existing peri-implant tissue. Site 33 is suitable for a modified roll-type pedicled flap if the overlying tissue is adequately thick, because this uses local vascularized tissue, avoids a second donor site, and gives good color and texture blending. Site 43 can still use the same base concept, but fig_02.jpg supports adding apical positioning of the buccal flap/pouch when a broader facial keratinized band or greater apical shift of the mucogingival complex is needed. The key point is that the two male sites do not require different sources of tissue; they can share the same local pedicled principle, with different execution.

In the 61-year-old woman, fig_03.jpg shows a loaded transmucosal implant with thin, mobile buccal mucosa and no useful tissue cap to recruit locally. That makes a roll-type pedicled approach unsuitable. The best choice is a connective tissue graft from the palate placed into a buccal or supraperiosteal pouch with apical positioning of the buccal flap, as illustrated in fig_04.jpg. This imports tissue where local tissue is inadequate and improves thickness plus a stable keratinized cuff around a functioning overdenture abutment.

Alternatives should be weighed differently in the two patients. For the man, an apically positioned flap alone would be less attractive if there is little keratinized tissue to reposition, and a free gingival graft or CTG would add donor-site morbidity that is unnecessary when thick local tissue is available. The pedicled option is biologically efficient because it preserves blood supply and usually blends better. For the woman, a free gingival graft is a reasonable alternative if maximal keratinized width is the top goal, but CTG is preferable here because it adds bulk, improves contour and color match, and is well suited to a loaded site with thin peri-implant tissue. Its trade-off is a second surgical site and greater technical demand.

If the woman’s inflammation improved after hygiene instruction but the anatomy in fig_03.jpg remained the same, my plan would not materially change. Plaque control may reduce inflammatory signs, but it does not create a stable, immobile peri-implant keratinized cuff; the anatomic deficiency would still matter, especially under overdenture function.

If the tissue over the man’s site 33 proved thinner than expected at surgery, I would not rely on a pedicled roll flap alone. I would change to a graft-based augmentation, most logically CTG if thickness and blending are priorities, with free gingival graft also defensible if maximal width is the main goal. The reason is that pedicled roll-type procedures depend on adequate local tissue bulk and coverage to be predictable.

items.question_content:
A female patient seeks esthetic correction of multiple maxillary anterior Miller class I recessions associated with cervical resin restorations. Use `fig_02.jpg`, `fig_03.jpg`, `fig_04.jpg`, and the anchored horizontal suture schematics in `fig_01.jpg`. You are planning a partial-thickness tunnel procedure for the upper right canine and the upper left central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine. Soft-tissue/root form is not uniform across the left side, and one candidate site has <2 mm of remaining gingiva preoperatively.

Build a site-specific plan rather than a generic tunnel protocol. Identify which involved teeth need only baseline suspended vertical fixation and which need added horizontal suspension, selecting the appropriate path from `fig_01.jpg` for each site and justifying it from defect geometry. Explain how you would manage the existing resin restorations before flap advancement, where connective tissue grafting is indicated, and which grafted site should be fully buried versus intentionally left partially exposed. Finally, state whether any involved tooth could reasonably be treated without added horizontal suspension, and how your graft-coverage decision would change if the upper left canine had at least 2 mm of remaining gingiva.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The plan should be individualized by defect shape, restorative surface, root form, and soft-tissue quantity.

Restorative/root-surface management: resin on root surfaces that lie within the intended coverage zone should be removed for soft-tissue compatibility. Where restorative material remains coronally, it should be recontoured to a smooth cemento-enamel-like reference line and polished so the advanced tissue can adapt to a biologically acceptable surface and the planned margin has a stable landmark.

Suturing logic: every involved tooth should first receive suspended vertical mattress fixation anchored at the splinted contact points to obtain baseline coronal traction and stabilization. However, none of the involved recession sites is well served by vertical fixation alone. Additional anchored horizontal suspension is needed at all involved recession sites because the defects are either broad/centered or asymmetric. The broad/symmetric horizontal path from fig_01.jpg should be used at the upper right canine, upper left lateral incisor, and upper left canine, because these sites need added central coronal support across the width of the recession. The asymmetric path from fig_01.jpg should be used at the upper left central incisor, where the recession axis is off-center and traction must be biased to harmonize the gingival collar.

Grafting: connective tissue grafting is indicated selectively at the upper left central incisor and upper left canine to compensate for root concavities/root-form deficiency. The graft at the upper left central incisor should be fully covered because the main goal is thickness and contour improvement under adequate tissue cover. The graft at the upper left canine should be left partially exposed because the remaining gingiva there is <2 mm and additional keratinized tissue is needed; partial exposure is therefore intentional, not a complication.

Adaptive change: if the upper left canine had at least 2 mm of remaining gingiva, the graft could still be used for concavity correction/thickening, but it would preferably be fully buried within the tunnel rather than intentionally exposed, because the need to create new keratinized tissue would be reduced.

So, no involved tooth should be managed with vertical suspension alone; the customization is in which horizontal design is added and how the graft is handled at each site.

items.question_content:
A 31-year-old woman, medically fit and nonsmoking, was referred for a 4-mm lingual recession on the lower right central incisor after orthodontic treatment in adolescence and again in 2017. Oral hygiene was fair. The mandibular central incisors were vital. Periapicals showed short roots, apically widened PDL space, and no interdental bone loss. Clinical crown inclination appeared neutral. A labial frenum with fiber pull and limited attached tissue was present in the mandibular anterior region.

Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, present a staged management plan for two time points: (1) the initial referral visit, before any surgery, and (2) the moment the finding in fig_02.jpg is encountered intraoperatively. Explain how the figure sequence changes your working diagnosis, threshold for intervention, and immediate priorities. For the established defect in fig_03.jpg, select the reconstructive strategy you judge most predictable and defend it against at least one other reasonable approach of your own choosing. Finally, state how your plan and prognosis would change if later 3D imaging showed the involved incisor root remained outside the facial alveolar envelope.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The key to this case is that the presenting complaint is a lingual recession on the lower right central incisor, whereas the preventive surgery and later complication concern the labial aspect of the other central incisor. fig_01.jpg shows a thin mandibular anterior phenotype with pathogenic frenal pull and very little attached tissue, but that alone does not make a broad prophylactic frenectomy automatically appropriate.

At the initial referral visit, my threshold for elective labial frenum surgery would be high. Prior orthodontic treatment, short roots, mandibular incisor location, and thin tissue raise suspicion that the roots may be close to or beyond a thin alveolar envelope despite apparently neutral crown inclination and intact interdental bone. I would first control modifiable trauma with atraumatic oral-hygiene instruction and monitoring. If surgery were still being considered because the frenum clearly destabilized the marginal tissue or interfered with hygiene, I would want targeted assessment of facial bone/root position, ideally limited-field CBCT or equivalent 3D assessment, because evidence of facial dehiscence would materially reduce my willingness to do a broad excision. If release were performed, it should be conservative: remove only the main frenal pull, keep the incisions close together, place them mainly in movable mucosa, and preserve as much attached gingiva as possible.

When fig_02.jpg is encountered, the operative goal should immediately change from prophylaxis to damage control. The figure implies an unrecognized labial bony dehiscence/root prominence has been exposed, and closure is already compromised because the coronal defect extends into attached gingiva. I would stop further marginal dissection, avoid additional stripping of lateral fibers in attached gingiva, preserve periosteum and the remaining tissue band, and obtain the most passive approximation possible rather than widening the wound to complete a textbook frenectomy. The patient should be informed that the main concern is now loss of marginal tissue and conversion to recession.

The mechanism of failure is not simply 'bone was exposed.' It is the combination of pre-existing anatomic vulnerability and operator-dependent incision design: a dehisced root was uncovered and left beneath a coronal wound in attached gingiva that could not be passively closed. Because attached gingiva cannot be advanced laterally and the remaining tissue has poor vascular support over a dehisced root, ischemia, marginal breakdown, and postoperative labial recession are highly likely. fig_03.jpg shows that this has become an established iatrogenic recession.

For the defect in fig_03.jpg, the most predictable reconstruction is an autogenous subepithelial connective tissue graft placed into an envelope/tunnel/pouch-type labial recipient bed after careful root debridement, without vertical releasing incisions. That approach best preserves blood supply in a thin mandibular anterior site, augments phenotype, increases the zone and thickness of keratinized tissue, and offers the best chance of durable root coverage.

A flap-only coronally advanced approach would be less predictable here because there is limited mobile tissue, a shallow vestibular situation, and high tension/relapse risk. A free gingival graft is a reasonable alternative if the main aim is phenotype conversion and durable keratinized tissue gain, but it is generally less favorable for complete root coverage and contour/color match at this site.

If later 3D imaging showed the involved incisor root remained outside the facial alveolar envelope, I would worsen the prognosis for stable long-term coverage and explicitly avoid promising durable complete correction with soft tissue surgery alone. If feasible, orthodontic repositioning/root torque back within the alveolar housing should be discussed before or in coordination with mucogingival reconstruction. If repositioning were not feasible, grafting could still be justified to improve tissue thickness and reduce future breakdown, but expectations should shift from ideal root coverage to biologic stabilization.

items.question_content: A 33-year-old woman with previously diagnosed aggressive periodontitis has a maxillary right first molar (#16) with severe periodontal destruction and initial class II–III mobility. After 10 months of non-surgical periodontal therapy and close maintenance, the tooth is asymptomatic, responds normally to vitality testing, and the surrounding tissues are clinically stable. She is systemically healthy, a nonsmoker, has no history of rhinitis or sinusitis, and strongly wants to avoid a prolonged posterior edentulous period. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management strategy would you recommend for #16 to achieve implant rehabilitation, and why is it the best choice now? Include the key prerequisites for choosing this route, how you would monitor the retained tooth/site before implant placement, and the findings that should make you stop this plan and change course.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend pre-extraction lateral sinus floor augmentation with temporary retention of #16, followed later by extraction and implant placement if the site remains favorable. This is not an attempt to save #16 long-term; it is a staged strategy to develop the implant site while preserving limited function.

The reason this is preferable now is that fig_02.jpg shows very limited residual bone beneath the sinus, so extraction alone would not make the site implant-ready and would likely lead to a long edentulous interval before implant restoration. fig_01.jpg supports that the periodontal condition has been brought into remission: the soft tissues look healthier, the tooth is asymptomatic, and vitality remains normal. In a healthy, nonsmoking, compliant patient with a clear sinus and a strong desire to avoid prolonged loss of posterior support, temporary retention can be justified while the sinus site is augmented in advance.

Key prerequisites are: controlled periodontal inflammation with good plaque control and no suppuration or active progression; a vital tooth without endodontic/apical disease; a healthy sinus; patient understanding that the tooth is only a temporary functional placeholder; and willingness to attend strict maintenance.

Monitoring should include supportive periodontal therapy at short intervals with probing/bleeding/plaque assessment, mobility, symptoms, pulp vitality, and any sinus complaints, along with radiographic review to confirm maturation and stability of the augmented bone. When adequate bone has formed, extraction should be atraumatic to preserve socket walls, and immediate implant placement should be considered only if socket integrity and primary stability are achievable.

I would stop this plan and change course if there is recurrent active periodontitis, suppuration, increasing mobility with loss of control, pain, loss of vitality or apical infection, sinus pathology, poor compliance/hygiene, graft-related complication, inadequate bone gain, or inability to obtain stable/safe implant placement after extraction.

items.question_content: A 22-year-old healthy nonsmoker presents with difficulty cleaning and fear of losing tooth #41. He has an isolated deep buccal recession on this mandibular central incisor, thin periodontal phenotype, prior orthodontic treatment, plaque accumulation, slight buccal prominence/linguoversion, and protrusive occlusal interference. The adjacent donor area has at least 2 mm of keratinized tissue and adequate vestibular depth. Examine fig_01.jpg, including the radiograph showing limited interproximal bone loss. What definitive periodontal management would you recommend for #41, and why is it preferable in this situation to other reasonable root-coverage options such as coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft or a free gingival graft? Include any treatment you would complete before surgery, the prognostic significance of the radiographic finding, and the key clinical or radiographic findings that would make you choose a different plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Initial management should address modifiable etiologic factors before mucogingival surgery: oral-hygiene instruction, supragingival debridement/plaque control, atraumatic brushing technique, and adjustment of the protrusive occlusal interference, followed by reassessment of tissue stability.

Based on fig_01.jpg, the recession is most consistent with an isolated mandibular incisor Cairo RT2 defect rather than RT1, because there is limited interproximal bone/attachment loss. This reduces the predictability of complete root coverage compared with RT1, but root coverage remains reasonable because the interproximal loss is limited and the tooth is still maintainable.

Definitive treatment would be a laterally positioned flap combined with a subepithelial connective tissue graft as a one-stage bilaminar root-coverage procedure. This is the best choice here because the recession is deep and isolated, the periodontal phenotype is thin, and the adjacent site provides sufficient keratinized tissue and vestibular depth to allow a tension-free donor flap. The CTG increases tissue thickness and vascular support, improves long-term stability and keratinized tissue gain, and lowers the risk of recession at the donor site compared with a laterally positioned flap alone.

This approach is preferable to a coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft in this mandibular incisor because local anatomy is less favorable for broad coronal advancement of tissue, whereas a suitable lateral donor site is available. It is preferable to a free gingival graft because the bilaminar LPF + SCTG approach offers better root coverage potential, better color/blend esthetics, and improved tissue thickness/stability for this isolated anterior defect.

Postoperatively, key priorities are passive flap mobility without tension, graft stabilization and vascularity, donor-site integrity, plaque control, and avoidance of recurrent traumatic occlusal loading.

I would choose a different plan if the defect were effectively Cairo RT3 because of extensive interproximal attachment loss, if the adjacent donor area lacked sufficient keratinized tissue or vestibular depth, or if the tooth were positioned too far outside the bony envelope for predictable coverage and donor-site safety.

items.question_content: Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A 58-year-old heavy smoker lost #11 and #21 to periodontitis 3 months earlier. The anterior maxilla shows severe horizontal/labial atrophy with U-shaped soft-tissue collapse; CBCT shows an extremely thin ridge; generalized periodontal breakdown is present. Tooth #22 has 7–9 mm probing depths, >10 mm attachment loss, grade 3 mobility, bleeding on probing, and 5 mm recession. He wants the fastest fixed implant result. Give one definitive plan and one fallback plan only. State exactly how many implants you would place in the anterior segment now, at which positions, whether the most deficient site should receive a basal cortical implant or a conventional implant, and whether #21 is better replaced by an implant or a pontic. Identify which augmentation steps are non-negotiable for an acceptable esthetic outcome versus which steps could be sacrificed for speed, and explain which refusal would change your plan more: continued heavy smoking or refusal of augmentation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
#22 is hopeless and should be extracted. The best definitive offer is a staged two-implant reconstruction, not three adjacent implants and not an immediate definitive fixed restoration simply to satisfy speed. After periodontal stabilization, hygiene reinforcement, and extraction of #22, place a conventional endosteal implant at #11 if prosthetically acceptable positioning is feasible in the healed site, and place a basal cortical implant at #22 because that site has the greatest labial deficiency and mesial-distal bone discrepancy; its advantage is better primary stability in the thinnest site, not elimination of augmentation. I would not place a separate implant at #21. In this ridge, #21 is better restored as a pontic because a third anterior implant would further challenge spacing, emergence profile, papilla support, and esthetics in an already collapsed thin ridge.

Non-negotiable steps are extraction of hopeless #22, periodontal disease control, and site development for contour: hard-tissue ridge contouring with particulate graft and membrane plus soft-tissue augmentation/thickening such as a VIP flap or equivalent, because the dominant esthetic problem is loss of facial volume and papillary support. A basal implant alone cannot recreate the missing labial contour. What may be sacrificed for speed is only the degree of esthetic refinement or the tempo of provisionalization, not disease control or augmentation if the goal is an acceptable anterior esthetic result.

The sequence should be: stabilize periodontal inflammation and plaque control, extract #22, place #11 conventional implant and #22 basal cortical implant with simultaneous contour augmentation, obtain primary closure/submerged healing, then perform second-stage soft-tissue management, customized abutments and provisionalization, followed by a definitive fixed prosthesis supported by #11 and #22 with #21 as a pontic, plus strict supportive periodontal maintenance.

If he continues heavy smoking, this markedly worsens prognosis and consent discussions and may justify deferral if compliance is poor, but smoking alone is more of a major risk modifier than the single absolute deal-breaker here. Refusal of augmentation changes the plan more decisively: if he declines hard- and soft-tissue augmentation, I would not offer fixed implant reconstruction in this anterior esthetic zone because neither a basal nor a conventional implant alone can predictably restore the lost contour and papillae. In that fallback scenario, I would defer implants and provide a non-implant provisional/alternative until risk factors and expectations become acceptable.

levels.title: Exceeds

Generic Textbook Management: Claiming that basal cortical anchorage alone removes the need for hard- and soft-tissue augmentation in this severely collapsed anterior esthetic defect.

Systemic Risk Overlooked: Proceeding to immediate definitive fixed implant treatment without materially adjusting timing, consent, or maintenance planning for heavy smoking and generalized periodontitis history.

items.question_content: A 62-year-old woman presents for restoration of 2 adjacent posterior maxillary implants at sites 2-5 and 2-6. The implants are osseointegrated, the peri-implant mucosa has fully healed around stock healing abutments, and the soft-tissue volume is adequate for contour modification without an additional mucosal graft. She wants fixed zirconia crowns with improved buccal contour and papillae. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, describe the most appropriate plan to condition the implant supracrestal complex before the definitive crowns, the clinical findings that indicate readiness to proceed to the final prosthesis, and the biologic and prosthetic risks that must be controlled to preserve peri-implant tissue stability and marginal bone.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The preferred approach is peri-implant soft-tissue conditioning with the X technique plus individualized emergence profile conformers, not immediate definitive crowns. This is appropriate because the implants are already osseointegrated and the peri-implant tissues are healed, so the existing mucosa can be redistributed rather than adding a graft if tissue volume is adequate and there are no major risk factors such as uncontrolled disease, untreated periodontitis, or heavy smoking. The sequence is: remove the stock healing abutments, inspect the mucosal tunnel and implant platforms, decontaminate the area/components, perform four oblique subperiosteal releasing incisions around each implant in an X pattern while preserving mesial and distal tissues, then screw in individualized conformers matching the intended cervical emergence profile. Use only slight progressive compression to laterally displace tissue buccally, palatally, and interproximally; sutures are not required. After healing, usually about 30 days, proceed only if there is a stable healthy muco-cervical imprint, improved buccal volume, preserved proximal tissues with papilla formation, no scarred or ischemic tissue, and no clinical/radiographic signs of peri-implant inflammation or bone loss. The final zirconia crowns should replicate that established emergence profile exactly so the definitive restoration does not disturb the ISC. Key risks are excessive compression causing ischemia/recession, damaging proximal tissues and losing papillae, repeated abutment changes that disrupt the soft-tissue seal, overcontoured restorations or cement excess causing peri-implant inflammation, and poor hygiene/decontamination increasing biologic complications and potential marginal bone loss.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.description: Pairs the major complications with prevention strategies such as preserving mesial/distal tissues, using only slight progressive compression, maintaining decontamination/hygiene, and ensuring the definitive crown precisely reproduces the conditioned emergence profile.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg panel b. What specific graft modification is shown?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The harvested graft in fig_01.jpg panel b shows an epithelialized coronal segment with an apical portion that has been de-epithelialized to connective tissue. That configuration is characteristic of a partly epithelialized free gingival graft, a modification intended to improve esthetics and limit apical displacement of the mucogingival junction.

items.answer_explanation: The harvested graft in fig_01.jpg panel b shows an epithelialized coronal segment with an apical portion that has been de-epithelialized to connective tissue. That configuration is characteristic of a partly epithelialized free gingival graft, a modification intended to improve esthetics and limit apical displacement of the mucogingival junction.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. Select all statements that accurately characterize the grafting approach shown.

question_options.text: The recipient site is prepared as a supraperiosteal tunnel extending at least one tooth mesial and distal to the recession defect.
This is a gingival unit graft that incorporates marginal and papillary gingiva to exploit a denser vascular plexus.
A small epithelial island is intentionally retained on an otherwise connective tissue graft so that the exposed portion better tolerates the oral environment.
Its main design principle is an apical de-epithelialized segment that permits spontaneous relocation of alveolar mucosa over the graft.
Compared with a conventional free gingival graft, it is intended to reduce mucogingival junction displacement and avoid vestibular flattening.
Donor-site morbidity is minimized because the donor wound heals entirely by primary intention.
The recipient sulcular incision is deliberately extended above the CEJ to allow coronal advancement of the overlying flap.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_01.jpg shows a partly epithelialized subepithelial connective tissue graft used with a tunnel approach. The recipient bed is a supraperiosteal tunnel, and the graft retains a small epithelial island to remain exposed while protecting underlying connective tissue. Reported advantages include avoiding MGJ displacement and vestibular flattening. The other statements describe the gingival unit graft, PE-FGG, or incorrectly state reduced donor-site morbidity or flap design.

items.answer_explanation: fig_01.jpg shows a partly epithelialized subepithelial connective tissue graft used with a tunnel approach. The recipient bed is a supraperiosteal tunnel, and the graft retains a small epithelial island to remain exposed while protecting underlying connective tissue. Reported advantages include avoiding MGJ displacement and vestibular flattening. The other statements describe the gingival unit graft, PE-FGG, or incorrectly state reduced donor-site morbidity or flap design.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The preoperative radiograph shows a scooped-out interproximal crestal defect localized between adjacent teeth, which is classically termed an interdental or osseous crater. Recognizing this morphology helps link the perforation to localized periodontal breakdown rather than generalized periodontal disease.

items.question_content: A 27-year-old woman developed a deep mesial periodontal defect at tooth #22 after orthodontic treatment and underwent root canal therapy followed by flap surgery. Review fig_01.jpg panel c through fig_01.jpg panel e. What is the name of the bony defect in which the denuded root surface communicates from the marginal periodontium to the apical area?

items.question_content: Two patients want single-stage, donor-site-free treatment of contiguous maxillary buccal recessions after initial periodontal therapy. Patient A is 27 years old with receding gums (fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, fig_10.jpg, fig_11.jpg, fig_12.jpg, fig_13.jpg). Patient B is 40 years old with receding upper gums and cold sensitivity (fig_06.jpg, fig_07.jpg, fig_08.jpg, fig_09.jpg, fig_10.jpg, fig_11.jpg, fig_12.jpg, fig_13.jpg). Using the figures as your main evidence, justify whether semilunar vestibular incision is an appropriate definitive pedicle procedure from the outset for each patient. For each case, identify the figure-derived feature that most supports added release and the feature that most threatens complete root coverage even if the flap remains vital. Name one tooth or zone where near-complete coverage is realistically expected and one where residual recession is most likely, and explain how the postoperative appearance supports that forecast. If both patients specifically want the least postoperative discomfort compatible with predictable coverage, which patient would you still most strongly recommend for semilunar vestibular incision at the initial surgery, and why? Finally, if flap mobilization cannot be positioned passively coronal to the CEJ across the whole segment, state the operative modification you would make next and the endpoint required before suturing.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Semilunar vestibular incision is an appropriate definitive pedicle procedure from the outset for both patients.

Patient A shows a strong indication for added release. From the preoperative and schematic figures, the recession spans a long contiguous segment from 21 to 25, with the deepest defects in the canine-first premolar region. The intraoperative figures and schematics show the value of the semilunar vestibular approach here: the vestibular semilunar incision is connected to the sulcular incision, permitting broad coronal mobilization while maintaining lateral blood supply, and the flap is stabilized by suturing to de-epithelialized papillae. The feature that most supports added release in Patient A is therefore the broad continuous anterior-premolar segment with substantial coronal advancement demand. The feature that most threatens complete root coverage is the deep canine-premolar zone, especially 23-24, where the initial recession is greatest and the required coronal displacement is largest.

For Patient A, near-complete coverage is most realistic at 22, and also favorable at 21 relative to the deeper posterior sites, because these teeth begin with less severe recession and the postoperative result shows better correction there. Residual recession is most likely at 24, with 23 also less favorable, because the postoperative figure still shows the greatest shortfall in the canine-premolar area despite overall improvement and good tissue blend. This matches the 3-month measurements, where residual recession remained greatest at 23 and especially 24.

Patient B was also managed with semilunar vestibular incision from the outset, and the figures support that this was an appropriate single-stage donor-site-free option for a contiguous multiple-recession segment. The involved segment is shorter than in Patient A, but it still includes multiple adjacent teeth from 22 to 25. The feature supporting added release is the presence of multiple contiguous recessions, especially with greater demand at the canine and premolars than at the lateral incisor. The feature that most threatens complete coverage is the canine-premolar zone, especially 23, because it begins deeper than 22 and requires greater coronal advancement. The postoperative figure supports that interpretation: coverage is best at 22, while the canine-premolar area remains the main site where small residual recession is most plausible. This is consistent with the 3-month findings of complete coverage at 22 and 1 mm residual recession at 23, 24, and 25.

So for Patient B, near-complete or complete coverage is most realistic at 22. The least favorable site is 23, with the adjacent premolars also less favorable than the lateral incisor because that zone starts deeper and is more mechanically demanding for complete coronal adaptation.

If both patients specifically want the least postoperative discomfort compatible with predictable coverage, I would still most strongly recommend semilunar vestibular incision initially for Patient A. Patient A has the wider and deeper recession complex, especially in the canine-premolar region, so the added vestibular release is more clearly justified by the extra coronal mobility needed across the whole segment. The technique also offers donor-site avoidance, gain in vestibular depth, and increased keratinized tissue. Patient B may also be appropriately treated with the same technique, as shown in the figures, but the initial need for the extra vestibular wound is most compelling in Patient A.

If flap mobilization cannot be positioned passively coronal to the CEJ across the whole segment, the next operative modification is to extend or complete the semilunar vestibular release with the described full-thickness followed by partial-thickness dissection so that the flap connects to the vestibular incision and gains additional mobility. The required endpoint before suturing is that the marginal flap can be positioned passively and stably coronal to the CEJ across all involved teeth, without visible tension or recoil, and then secured to the de-epithelialized papillary beds.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. Which findings explain why the initial surgery could be limited to arch-wise conventional external bevel gingivectomy without flap reflection or osseous recontouring? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: The enlargement is predominantly coronal soft tissue obscuring most clinical crowns
fig_03.jpg shows preserved alveolar bone height rather than periodontal bone loss
The increased probing depths expected here would mainly represent gingival pseudopockets
The case demonstrates infrabony defects that need direct surgical access
fig_03.jpg indicates tooth-position abnormalities requiring exposure instead of gingival excision
Scant plaque and little inflammation make debridement alone unlikely to reverse the enlargement
The problem is confined to a localized posterior tuberosity overgrowth
The dominant defect is true attachment loss extending apically, so pocket elimination by gingivectomy is inappropriate

golden_answer.subjective_directions: External bevel gingivectomy is suited to bulky suprabony fibrous enlargement with crown burial, preserved bone support, and pseudopocketing. Those features make flap access or osseous recontouring unnecessary initially. Minimal inflammation may explain why plaque control alone would not solve the problem, but it does not specifically justify a flapless excisional approach over flap surgery.

items.answer_explanation: External bevel gingivectomy is suited to bulky suprabony fibrous enlargement with crown burial, preserved bone support, and pseudopocketing. Those features make flap access or osseous recontouring unnecessary initially. items.question_content: A 38-year-old non-smoker with good oral hygiene presents with hypersensitivity and esthetic concern from mandibular anterior recession. Tooth 4.1 has a 5 mm recession, 2 mm buccal probing depth, thin phenotype, no keratinized tissue, and clear lip/muscle traction; 3.1 and 3.2 also have recession with 1 mm probing depths. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Cryopreserved human amniotic membrane (HAM) is available if you judge it useful. What definitive mucogingival management would you recommend for this segment, and why? Base your justification on the defect pattern and interproximal support visible, including the role—if any—of HAM and the prognosis you would give specifically for 4.1.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would use a site-specific plan rather than one technique for all three teeth. First, I would address the cause with atraumatic brushing instruction and plaque control. fig_01.jpg shows the deepest recession at 4.1, and fig_02.jpg indicates reduced interproximal support, so 4.1 is a reduced-predictability defect (Miller III-type behavior), further compromised by thin phenotype, absent keratinized tissue, and muscle/frenal traction. That tooth needs autogenous palatal tissue to create keratinized tissue and thickness—either an epithelialized epithelial-connective/free gingival component at 4.1 within a combined graft, or a staged autogenous augmentation if tension makes a single-stage approach less predictable. The smaller adjacent defects are more favorable and can be managed with a coronally advanced bilaminar approach over connective tissue, with release of the lip/muscle pull. HAM is useful as an adjunct on the palatal donor site to reduce morbidity, bleeding, pain, and accelerate epithelialization, but it should not replace the autogenous graft at 4.1 because HAM alone will not provide the fibrous keratinized tissue needed there. Prognosis is good for symptom relief and soft-tissue improvement overall, better for 3.1 and 3.2 than for 4.1. I would not promise complete root coverage at 4.1 because interproximal attachment loss lowers predictability, although increased keratinized tissue, coverage improvement, and long-term stability are realistic goals. Follow-up should assess recipient healing, donor-site epithelialization, persistence of traction, brushing habits, and relapse.

items.question_content: A 25-year-old ASA I woman reports sensitivity at the mandibular central incisors. Around #24-25, probing depths are 1-2 mm with no bleeding on probing; there is only 1 mm of keratinized tissue and no attached gingiva, and the incisors are mildly crowded. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, determine the best initial definitive periodontal management for this localized defect and justify why it should be the first intervention. Explain the dominant etiologic factor, how the interproximal support seen radiographically changes expectations for root coverage, and which healing outcomes would make you continue maintenance alone versus add another mucogingival surgery.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The first definitive local treatment should be a frenum-release procedure, preferably frenuloplasty, after basic plaque-control instruction and debridement. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show a high mandibular labial frenum exerting traction on the marginal/interdental tissues, with papillary loss and virtually no functional attached gingiva; this pull is the main modifiable cause of the localized recession and sensitivity, while mild crowding is contributory rather than primary. fig_03.jpg shows interproximal attachment/bone loss between #24 and #25, so this is an RT2/Miller III-type situation: complete root coverage from a root-coverage graft is not highly predictable because interproximal support is already reduced. Therefore a staged, cause-directed approach is preferable: eliminate the frenal pull first, improve tissue stability and cleansability, then reassess. I would continue maintenance alone if healing gives symptom resolution, no recurrent pull, stable or more coronal soft-tissue margin, improved papillary fill/vestibular depth, adequate function for oral hygiene, and no inflammation. I would add a second mucogingival/root-coverage procedure only if residual recession or sensitivity persists, attached gingiva remains inadequate, or the site remains unstable or inflamed despite good plaque control.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, sequenced plan tied to this case: control plaque/trauma, release frenal pull to reduce tension and improve vestibular function at #24-25, reassess tissue stability/sensitivity/attached gingiva after healing, and only then decide on further surgery if deficits persist.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content:
Use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. An 18-year-old nonsmoking male wants his teeth “fixed” and reports no current pain. He had been taking oral isotretinoin for acne, reports mouth breathing, usually chews on the right side, and does not brush or use other oral-hygiene aids. Full probing was initially impossible until limited gross debridement was performed. After that, FMPS and FMBS were both 100%, PD ranged 1–7 mm, facial recession on mandibular teeth was 1–2 mm, mean CAL was 3.5 mm, maximum CAL was 6 mm, and there was no mobility or furcation involvement. He also has multiple carious teeth, retained roots of #15 and #46, and tooth #26 has previously initiated endodontic access with asymptomatic apical periodontitis. Because of travel, you will have only 2 treatment visits before a 6-week reevaluation, yet he is asking to start visible corrective work immediately.

What is your most defensible patient-level periodontal diagnosis under the 2018 AAP/EFP system, and what makes this a gray-zone staging case? In your justification, include: one fig_01.jpg observation and one fig_02.jpg observation that materially affect either stage/grade assignment or confidence in the baseline; how you interpret the side distribution of deposits in light of his chewing history; what minimum disease-control tasks must be completed in those 2 visits, what you would deliberately defer, and why; and the reevaluation pattern that would make persistent 6-mm sites better managed without surgery.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible diagnosis is provisional generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B, with localized Stage III-level severity/features at isolated sites, plus generalized plaque-induced gingival inflammation. This is a gray-zone case because the single worst site reaches Stage III-level attachment loss, but the patient-level severity/complexity is lower. The overall case should not be escalated from the deepest site alone when most of the radiographic destruction is much milder and the baseline was obtained only after limited debridement in a heavily inflamed mouth.

A key fig_01.jpg finding is the massive generalized plaque/calculus burden, especially the heavier left-sided accumulation with severe gingival inflammation and plaque-retentive malposition/occlusal discrepancy. A key fig_02.jpg finding is the predominantly horizontal interproximal bone loss confined to the coronal third, reaching only about 15% of root length, despite affecting about 48% of the dentition. That pattern supports generalized Stage II overall rather than generalized Stage III, particularly since there is no periodontitis-related tooth loss, mobility, or furcation involvement. Grade B is more defensible than Grade C because the bone-loss/age ratio is about 15/18 = 0.83 and there are no stated smoking or diabetes modifiers; young age alone should not force Grade C.

The side distribution of deposits is interpretable as greater accumulation on the non-chewing side rather than evidence of unusually rapid progression. If he usually chews on the right, reduced self-cleansing on the left could help explain the heavier left-sided deposits seen in fig_01.jpg. Mouth breathing and plaque-retentive anatomy may further worsen local accumulation. These are etiologic/contextual modifiers, not staging or grading criteria by themselves.

With only 2 visits before reevaluation, the minimum acceptable disease-control objectives are: (1) reset expectations and establish effective home care/motivation immediately, making clear that visible corrective, orthodontic, prosthetic, and definitive restorative work must wait; (2) complete as much supra- and subgingival debridement/instrumentation as needed to create a valid reevaluation baseline and reduce inflammation; and (3) formally triage non-periodontal infectious/plaque-retentive foci that may confound healing. Clearly hopeless, nonmaintainable retained roots are reasonable to remove during the disease-control phase if feasible within the limited visits because they are active plaque traps and may distort reevaluation. Tooth #26 needs early restorability/endodontic assessment and should be treated during phase I if strategically retainable, or extracted if non-restorable. Gross caries can be stabilized if symptomatic or if they materially impair plaque control, but definitive correction should be deferred.

Persistent 6-mm sites are better managed without surgery if reevaluation still shows poor plaque control or generalized bleeding, unresolved local plaque-retentive factors or residual calculus, or unresolved endodontic/restorative confounders. In that situation, residual depth is more likely due to ongoing inflammation, pseudopocketing, or incomplete control of causative factors, so the next step is reinforcement, reinstrumentation, and continued supportive/nonsurgical care. Surgery becomes reasonable only if good overall control has been achieved and a small number of sites remain truly isolated, persistently deep and bleeding after confounders have been excluded.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Fundamentally misdiagnoses the case, such as calling it gingivitis alone or giving a classification clearly incompatible with the clinical and radiographic pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes periodontitis but materially misstates the overall stage or grade, or does not explain why this is a gray-zone patient-level staging case rather than a single-site staging exercise.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies generalized periodontitis with Stage II overall and Grade B, while recognizing isolated/localized Stage III-level severity or features and explaining that the single deepest site should not determine the whole-case stage.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately gives a provisional generalized Stage II, Grade B diagnosis with localized Stage III-level severity/features, and explicitly justifies it by contrasting the isolated deepest site with the overall pattern: coronal-third horizontal bone loss limited to about 15%, no periodontitis-related tooth loss, no mobility, and no furcation involvement; also avoids overcalling Grade C from age alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or ignores the effect of heavy deposits on baseline reliability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical or radiographic findings correctly but cites fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg only vaguely, inaccurately, or without linking them to diagnosis and sequencing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Cites at least one relevant observation from fig_01.jpg and one from fig_02.jpg and integrates them with the history and charting into a coherent explanation for diagnosis and early management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, history, and charting to explain both classification and baseline uncertainty; specifically interprets the side distribution of deposits in light of chewing history and local plaque-retentive factors, and uses the radiographic pattern of mainly horizontal coronal-third bone loss to constrain stage assignment, while treating mouth breathing and isotretinoin as contextual modifiers rather than grading criteria.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes visible corrective/elective treatment before disease control, or gives a generic plan that ignores the two-visit constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends initial periodontal therapy in general terms but does not define the minimum must-do disease-control tasks before reevaluation, or does not appropriately triage retained roots, #26, and caries.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Under the two-visit constraint, prioritizes expectation-setting/home-care improvement and comprehensive disease-control instrumentation, while appropriately triaging non-periodontal infectious or nonmaintainable foci and deferring definitive restorative, orthodontic, prosthetic, and esthetic treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes what must be completed before reevaluation from what can wait, and justifies the timing of retained roots and #26 by maintainability, restorability, plaque-control interference, and the risk of confounding periodontal reevaluation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no case-specific rationale for when persistent 6-mm sites should or should not be managed surgically.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions reevaluation or surgery only generically, without linking the decision to overall plaque control, local confounders, or generalized versus site-specific disease activity.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that persistent 6-mm sites should remain in nonsurgical/supportive management when plaque control is still poor, inflammation remains generalized, or obvious local causes have not been resolved; reserves surgery for isolated nonresponsive sites after good control.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Defines the no-surgery choice in case-specific terms by linking persistent 6-mm sites to unresolved inflammation, residual calculus, plaque-retentive anatomy, or endodontic/restorative confounders, and clearly distinguishes that situation from true isolated residual periodontal defects that may justify surgery after successful overall disease control.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending orthodontic, prosthodontic, or definitive restorative treatment before periodontal stabilization and reevaluation
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: giving a definitive long-term rehabilitation plan without acknowledging that the initial deposit burden limited reliable periodontal assessment

items.question_content: A healthy 22-year-old man presents after orthodontic treatment with recession at the mandibular left central incisor. Clinical measurements are: recession depth 6 mm, recession width 3 mm, and apicocoronal keratinized tissue width 0 mm. Use fig_01.jpg to assess the prognostically important anatomy. Would you attempt definitive root coverage in one surgery, stage soft-tissue augmentation first, or avoid a coverage procedure at this visit? Defend your choice by identifying the preoperative feature in fig_01.jpg that most limits predictability, explaining the flap-graft relationship you would intentionally create on the denuded root for this mandibular anterior site, and naming the main biologic/mechanical failure you are trying to prevent. Then state how your consent and plan would change if fig_01.jpg had shown clearly reduced interproximal support, and describe the 1-week postoperative appearance that would reassure you the graft is surviving versus indicate true necrosis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would still attempt definitive treatment in one stage rather than stage soft-tissue augmentation first. Based on fig_01.jpg and the measurements, this is a deep isolated mandibular incisor recession after orthodontics with no keratinized tissue. The periapical image suggests preserved interproximal hard-tissue support, while the clinical photo shows loss/reduction of papillary soft tissue. Prognostically, that fits a Miller class III / Cairo RT2-type situation, so the defect is not ideal for predictable complete root coverage even though the interproximal bone height is not severely compromised.

My preferred procedure would be an atraumatic supraperiosteal tunnel in the lower anterior region with a partially deepithelialized connective tissue graft (PE-CTG). I would not rely on a strongly coronally advanced flap here because the mandibular anterior region has thin tissue, shallow vestibular anatomy, and muscle/frenal pull; excessive coronal displacement risks tension, vestibular loss, mucogingival junction displacement, and relapse. I would also not stage a free gingival graft first unless other factors forced me to, because that adds morbidity and another surgery, whereas PE-CTG can simultaneously augment keratinized tissue and support root coverage.

The key flap-graft relationship is that the connective-tissue portion lies under the tunnel and papillary tissues for vascular support and thickening, while the epithelialized portion is intentionally designed to match the denuded root area and positioned over the exposed root as a butt-joint type coverage of the coronal exposed zone. This matters in a 6 mm defect because burying a conventional CTG completely would require greater coronal advancement than this site tolerates, while leaving a large conventional CTG exposed increases risk of desiccation and necrosis. The epithelialized portion can slough superficially while protecting the underlying connective tissue long enough for capillary ingrowth and later reepithelialization; the retained lamina propria/connective tissue also helps formation of stable keratinized gingiva.

The main failure I am trying to prevent is ischemic loss of the graft and relapse from an unfavorable blood-supply/tension balance: too much coronal advancement in the lower anterior site creates tension and vestibular distortion, while too much exposed conventional CTG risks necrosis because the coronal part is underperfused.

For consent in the current case, I would promise partial but clinically meaningful root coverage and increased keratinized tissue, not guarantee complete root coverage. Complete coverage may occur, but it should not be presented as the predictable outcome because papillary/interproximal soft-tissue loss limits coronal soft-tissue position. If fig_01.jpg had instead shown clearly reduced interproximal support, prognosis would worsen substantially. My consent would become more guarded, with goals shifting toward sensitivity reduction, tissue thickening, and stability rather than an esthetic expectation of complete root coverage; if the interproximal loss were marked, I would reconsider whether a coverage-focused procedure is appropriate at all or whether augmentation without strong root-coverage promises is the better plan.

At 1 week, reassuring findings would be superficial white/yellow sloughing of the exposed epithelialized surface with underlying red capillary ingrowth, maintained tissue volume, graft immobility, and no suppuration or progressive recession. Concerning findings would be gray-black progressive necrosis, collapse or shrinkage of the grafted area, mobility, foul odor, purulence, worsening recession, or increasing inflammatory destruction.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a deep lower incisor recession with preserved interproximal hard-tissue support but reduced papillary/interproximal soft tissue, and classifies it as Miller class III/Cairo RT2 or gives an equivalent prognostic description.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately interprets fig_01.jpg and explicitly explains that predictability is limited primarily by the papillary/interproximal soft-tissue deficiency despite relatively preserved interproximal bone support.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not integrate the history, measurements, and figure findings into a coherent rationale.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as recession depth or lack of keratinized tissue, without connecting them to the anatomy of this site.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the post-orthodontic history, 6 mm recession, 0 mm keratinized tissue, and fig_01.jpg findings into the decision about whether to treat in one stage, stage first, or defer.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all of the above and explicitly links the mandibular anterior anatomy (thin phenotype, shallow vestibular constraints, muscle/frenal pull) to the need to minimize coronal tension while augmenting tissue thickness and keratinized tissue.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Selects an inappropriate or unsafe plan, or provides no clear operative strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends a generic root-coverage or soft-tissue grafting approach without clearly explaining graft placement, vascular support, or stabilization.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a reasonable graft-based plan and explains how the recipient site and graft would be arranged to gain blood supply, increase tissue thickness, and improve coverage or stability.

levels.title: Exceeds
