levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison of risks, benefits, or case-specific trade-offs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons of grafting but does not relate them to this deep mandibular anterior defect.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with at least one plausible alternative the examinee derives and identifies the main failure mechanism that the plan is intended to avoid.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced, case-specific comparison showing why staging may add morbidity and may be unnecessary here, and why aggressive coronal advancement or a large exposed conventional CTG would raise the risks of ischemia/necrosis, vestibular loss or MGJ displacement, and relapse.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives an unrealistic prognosis, promises predictable complete coverage, or does not change the plan when interproximal support is hypothetically reduced.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a vague prognosis or mentions that prognosis worsens with reduced interproximal support but does not explain how consent or goals would change.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that the present case should be consented for partial but clinically meaningful coverage with increased keratinized tissue, not guaranteed complete coverage, and appropriately lowers expectations if interproximal support is reduced.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly reframes management when interproximal support is reduced: expectations are lowered substantially, goals shift toward stability/sensitivity control rather than cosmetic complete coverage, and the appropriateness of a coverage-focused procedure is reconsidered.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies normal early healing as failure, misses signs of graft loss, or omits postoperative assessment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that some sloughing can occur but cannot clearly distinguish reassuring healing from true necrosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly distinguishes acceptable 1-week superficial sloughing/revascularization from concerning features such as progressive necrosis, infection, or graft mobility.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifies reassuring findings (superficial epithelial sloughing with capillary ingrowth, maintained volume, immobility, no suppuration) versus true failure (progressive gray-black necrosis, collapse, mobility, purulence, worsening recession) and links these findings to the biology of PE-CTG healing.

items.question_content: A 55-year-old woman with stage IV grade C periodontitis presents with a maxillary central incisor in the esthetic zone that is extruded and pathologically migrated. After initial debridement and improved plaque control, the tooth still has grade III mobility, suppuration on probing, pockets up to 12 mm, no response to cold or electric pulp testing, and percussion tenderness. Examine fig_01.jpg. What definitive management strategy would you recommend for this tooth, and how would you sequence the key steps? Justify your plan from the clinical and radiographic findings, including why your priority order is appropriate despite the pulpal diagnosis and what findings would make you stop trying to retain the tooth later.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is a combined endo-perio lesion best interpreted as primary periodontal destruction with secondary pulpal necrosis. The decisive problem is the periodontal component: fig_01.jpg shows severe loss of support with pathologic migration/extrusion, and clinically there are suppurative deep pockets and grade III mobility. The non-vital pulp and symptomatic apical periodontitis also require treatment, but they do not by themselves explain the degree of attachment loss or mobility.

I would offer a guarded attempt at retention rather than treating this as routine endodontics alone or assuming extraction is mandatory. The patient has already shown improved plaque control after phase-I therapy, which is essential if regeneration is to be considered.

The sequence should be: first maintain inflammation control and confirm informed consent about guarded prognosis; then perform surgical periodontal management aimed at regeneration, not resective pocket elimination. During surgery the root surface should be thoroughly debrided, the extruded tooth repositioned into a more favorable occlusal position, and the tooth stabilized with a semi-rigid splint to reduce traumatic mobility and permit wound stability. A GTR-based regenerative approach is appropriate for the severe intrabony/peripheral defect, with primary closure. Definitive root canal treatment should then be completed once the tooth is adequately stabilized so isolation and instrumentation are more predictable. Occlusal trauma should be minimized, and the patient needs close supportive periodontal therapy.

The reason not to reflexively do endodontics first is that the extreme mobility and displacement make immediate RCT technically less predictable, while the main determinant of survival is the periodontal destruction. Stabilization and regeneration address the disease that threatens retention; RCT treats the secondary pulpal consequence.

I would reassess probing depth, BOP/suppuration, mobility, tooth position, and radiographic bone fill. I would stop trying to retain the tooth if plaque control becomes poor, suppuration or deep pockets persist, mobility remains uncontrolled, or healing shows progressive failure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends RCT alone, repeated nonsurgical therapy alone, or immediate extraction without a defensible management rationale; omits stabilization and periodontal regenerative management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes need for both periodontal and endodontic care, but the plan is generic or incomplete; sequencing is poorly justified and does not adequately address mobility/extrusion or wound stability.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends an attempted tooth-preserving plan centered on periodontal regenerative surgery with repositioning/stabilization of the tooth and definitive endodontic treatment once adequate stabilization is achieved, plus maintenance therapy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent, stepwise retention strategy and explains why regenerative rather than resective or purely nonsurgical care is appropriate in this severe attachment-loss case; also includes occlusal trauma control and explicit criteria for converting to extraction if the plan fails.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings or misinterprets the case; does not connect clinical and radiographic evidence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a combined lesion but incompletely links imaging, periodontal findings, mobility, and pulp test results to the proposed diagnosis and plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg and the examination findings to identify severe periodontal destruction with pathologic migration and secondary endodontic involvement, recognizing that the periodontal component drives the overall prognosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly synthesizes the figure, deep suppurative pockets, grade III mobility, non-vital pulp, and persistence after phase-I therapy to explain why this is a structural regenerative problem rather than unresolved plaque alone, and why lesion control must target both tissues.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores prognosis, patient-specific tradeoffs, or informed consent issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions guarded prognosis or alternatives superficially but does not meaningfully weigh retention against replacement or the patient's demonstrated compliance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that retention is reasonable but uncertain because the tooth is in the esthetic zone and the patient improved plaque control after initial therapy, while severe attachment loss and prior grade III mobility make prognosis guarded.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Frames prognosis as dynamic rather than fixed and explicitly defines later failure triggers such as recurrent suppuration, persistent deep pockets, poor plaque control, uncontrolled mobility, or radiographic/healing failure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent order of care or an order that ignores the impact of mobility/extrusion on treatment predictability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a sequence but with weak justification or without explaining why the order matters in this specific case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes control of inflammation/compliance, then surgical management that includes repositioning/stabilization and regenerative therapy, followed by root canal treatment once the tooth is stable, then close maintenance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains why the usual endo-first reflex may be reversed here: the extreme mobility and traumatic position reduce predictability of immediate RCT, whereas periodontal destruction is the main determinant of tooth survival.

items.question_content: A 14.7-year-old girl with Angle Class I malalignment and an impacted #11 is being planned for orthodontic arch expansion. Periodontal probing is 2–3 mm with moderate gingival inflammation but no established periodontitis. Examine fig_01.jpg for the mandibular anterior soft-tissue phenotype and alveolar housing. What periodontal-orthodontic strategy would you choose to enable safe tooth movement in this patient, and why? Explain why your plan is preferable to other reasonable approaches for these findings, when you would implement it relative to orthodontic activation, the biological basis for the soft-tissue change you would anticipate, and which short- and long-term findings would determine success.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would first control the gingival inflammation with oral-hygiene instruction and initial periodontal therapy, then use a combined phenotype-modifying approach rather than orthodontic expansion alone. Based on fig_01.jpg, the mandibular anterior segment has a thin scalloped phenotype, very limited keratinized tissue, and a thin labial alveolar plate; those features make routine labial expansion/high-incisor movement risky because the teeth can be moved outside the alveolar envelope, increasing the chance of dehiscence, fenestration, recession, and unstable soft tissue.

My preferred plan is corticotomy-assisted orthodontics/PAOO with buccal alveolar augmentation in the mandibular anterior region, performed shortly before orthodontic activation. That approach is preferable here because it addresses both deficiencies driving risk: the osseous housing and the soft-tissue phenotype. Orthodontics alone would not improve the thin labial bone envelope. A separate mucogingival graft could increase keratinized tissue, but by itself it would not correct the thin facial bone that makes expansion hazardous; it could be reserved if soft-tissue deficiency persists after combined therapy.

The soft-tissue response I would expect is not only maintenance of the gingiva but possible gain in keratinized tissue. Biologically, surgical exposure and healing can generate granulation tissue derived from periodontal ligament and adjacent connective tissue, which may re-epithelialize as keratinized tissue; added buccal support plus orthodontic mechanical stimulation may enhance this remodeling response.

Success would be judged by maintained shallow probing depths, resolution of inflammation, no new recession or attachment loss, increased or at least stable width of keratinized tissue in the mandibular anterior segment, and clinical/radiographic evidence that the labial bony housing is preserved or increased. Long term, I would look for stable tissue architecture after active movement, acceptable plaque control, and no signs of dehiscence, fenestration, or periodontal breakdown.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends orthodontic expansion without meaningful periodontal phenotype management, or gives a vague plan with no sequencing and no control of pre-existing inflammation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that periodontal support is needed but gives an incomplete, poorly sequenced, or one-dimensional plan, such as soft-tissue management alone without addressing the alveolar housing, or surgery with no timing relative to orthodontic activation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends initial inflammation control followed by a combined corticotomy-assisted/PAOO-type approach with buccal augmentation for the mandibular anterior segment, timed shortly before orthodontic activation, with a clear rationale tied to safer tooth movement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, patient-specific plan that clearly prioritizes inflammation control, phenotype modification, timing with orthodontics, and reserve use of secondary mucogingival grafting only if residual soft-tissue deficiency remains.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses or dismisses the major periodontal risks posed by the phenotype and planned tooth movement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic recession risk or generic pros/cons of surgery without linking them to this patient's thin labial bone, limited keratinized tissue, and planned expansion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that thin labial bone, scant keratinized tissue, and a thin scalloped phenotype increase the risk of dehiscence/fenestration/recession with orthodontics alone, and that combined augmentation improves the periodontal envelope while accepting surgical morbidity and maintenance needs.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced comparison of reasonable options, explaining why orthodontics alone is higher risk and why soft-tissue grafting alone may improve KT but not the osseous envelope, while acknowledging the benefits and tradeoffs of a combined regenerative approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides assertions with little or no use of the examination findings or fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the clinical findings or the figure findings, but not both in a coherent way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg findings with the clinical context: intact periodontium, shallow probing depths, moderate gingival inflammation, and planned expansion, to justify preventive phenotype modification rather than treatment of established periodontitis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes soft-tissue phenotype, alveolar housing, periodontal status, and orthodontic objectives into a clear causal chain showing why this mandibular anterior segment is vulnerable and why the selected approach best addresses that vulnerability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify key complications to prevent or relevant follow-up measures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only generic follow-up such as 'review healing' without specifying the periodontal or radiographic endpoints relevant to this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies appropriate monitoring: plaque/inflammation control, probing depths/bleeding, recession or dehiscence/fenestration, width/stability of keratinized tissue, and clinical or radiographic assessment of the facial bony housing over time.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds how management would change if monitoring is unfavorable, such as modifying tooth movement, intensifying maintenance, or considering secondary mucogingival augmentation if soft-tissue stability remains inadequate.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old man reports cold sensitivity from the lingual surface of #42. Medical history is noncontributory. After debridement and oral-hygiene instruction, review shows no mobility and 2-mm recorded probing depths on the labial/interproximal sites. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, fig_06.jpg, and fig_07.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend now, and why? Base your answer on findings you extract from the figures, not on a named recession classification alone. State any local factor you would still correct, what outcome would count as success, the main risk that would alter consent and early follow-up, how your plan would change if a palatal donor site were unacceptable, and briefly defend it against the strongest reasonable alternative for this site.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg shows an isolated narrow, deep lingual recession on #42 with very limited lingual keratinized/attached tissue and a thin phenotype; the tooth also appears somewhat labially inclined or root-prominent. fig_02.jpg shows preserved interproximal support without meaningful interproximal bone loss, with only slight PDL widening, so this is not behaving like generalized periodontal breakdown and remains a reasonable mucogingival root-coverage candidate once inflammation is controlled. fig_03.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg show the site-specific surgical design I would prefer: a minimally invasive full-thickness lingual tunnel/pouch extending onto adjacent teeth and beyond the mucogingival junction, placement of a subepithelial connective tissue graft, and coronal stabilization with sling/cross-mattress sutures. fig_04.jpg confirms the palatal donor-site component.

My recommendation would therefore be a tunnel-based bilaminar root-coverage procedure with autogenous CTG rather than flap-only therapy. Before or during surgery I would still address local traumatic factors, especially reassessing occlusal trauma/root prominence in light of the mild PDL widening, while ensuring plaque control remains excellent.

Success in this case is not synonymous with complete root coverage. A successful result would be relief of dentinal hypersensitivity, substantial root coverage, thicker and more stable lingual soft tissue, and increased keratinized tissue that is maintainable long term. I would not promise full coverage because the baseline defect is narrow and deep, the lingual mandibular anterior tissues are scant and mobile, and tooth position/root prominence limits the coronal ceiling. fig_07.jpg supports this expectation: major improvement with residual recession can still represent success rather than failure.

The strongest alternative is usually either a free gingival graft or a flap-only coronally advanced approach. I would reject flap-only therapy because this site lacks tissue thickness and reliable coronal mobility, so stability and predictability are weaker. I would reject a free gingival graft as first choice because although it can increase keratinized tissue and may reduce sensitivity, it is less predictable for root coverage, gives less favorable tissue integration, and lacks the bilaminar vascular advantages of CTG under a tunnel.

The main risk that most changes consent and early follow-up is lingual bleeding or hematoma in the floor of mouth with potential airway compromise. I would also discuss flap perforation, graft micromotion/necrosis, and palatal donor-site bleeding. That risk profile is why the procedure must remain minimally invasive and tension-free, with careful papillary undermining, secure graft stabilization, meticulous hemostasis, and early review for swelling, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth fullness, or breathing difficulty.

If a palatal donor site were unacceptable, I would not proceed with palatal CTG. I would explain that the most predictable option for simultaneous root coverage and phenotype augmentation is being declined, so expectations must be reset. Depending on the patient's priorities and available materials, I would consider a tunnel with a substitute interpositional graft material, or I would shift toward a more conservative goal of symptom control and tissue stability rather than maximal root coverage. In either case, expected root coverage and tissue-thickening predictability would generally be lower than with autogenous CTG.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the case as generalized periodontal disease, ignores the figures, or does not recognize an isolated lingual recession problem on #42.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses limited figure-based reasoning; identifies recession but does not adequately integrate interproximal support, soft-tissue deficiency, tooth position/root prominence, or the meaning of the mild PDL widening.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to identify an isolated lingual recession on #42 with preserved interproximal support and limited lingual soft tissue, and links these findings to candidacy for mucogingival surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg or fig_06.jpg, and fig_07.jpg into a coherent explanation: narrow/deep isolated lingual recession, minimal keratinized tissue/thin phenotype, likely tooth malposition or root prominence, slight PDL widening as a local traumatic/occlusal consideration rather than periodontal breakdown, and a realistic biologic ceiling on complete root coverage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no defensible definitive plan or recommends clearly inappropriate management such as extraction, observation alone despite ongoing symptoms, or a site-inappropriate procedure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends surgery in generic terms but does not specify an appropriate lingual site design, or omits necessary pre-surgical/local-factor correction.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a clinically appropriate definitive plan after initial therapy, correctly favoring a tunnel/pouch-based root-coverage approach with CTG and noting the need to control local etiologic factors such as plaque and possible traumatic occlusal influence.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, site-specific plan: confirm periodontal stability, address local traumatic or plaque factors, use a minimally invasive full-thickness lingual tunnel extending beyond the mucogingival junction and onto adjacent teeth, preserve papillary blood supply, place and stabilize CTG, and define success in functional and tissue-stability terms rather than complete coverage alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address a reasonable alternative, or ignores the scenario in which palatal donor-site harvesting is unacceptable.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions an alternative or donor-site refusal but gives only generic trade-offs not tied to the lingual mandibular anterior site.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with at least one plausible alternative of the respondent's choosing and explains relevant trade-offs such as root-coverage predictability, tissue-thickening potential, keratinized tissue gain, and donor-site morbidity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison grounded in this site: why a bilaminar tunnel plus CTG is preferred when maximal coverage and phenotype augmentation are both goals, why the strongest alternative is less suitable here, and how treatment goals and expectations appropriately shift if palatal harvest is refused.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits meaningful complications or mentions only routine postoperative discomfort.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic risks such as bleeding or infection without identifying the distinctive hazard profile of this lingual site.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies major complications including lingual bleeding or hematoma risk, flap perforation or graft instability, and donor-site bleeding.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links the complication profile to prevention and surveillance: atraumatic tunneling, papilla preservation, tension-free release beyond the mucogingival junction, secure stabilization, meticulous hemostasis, and early review for floor-of-mouth swelling, dysphagia, or airway compromise.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Promises certain complete root coverage or gives no realistic outcome assessment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a vague prognosis without defining what would count as success in this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Predicts significant improvement with possible residual recession and defines success as symptom relief plus soft-tissue improvement, not coverage alone.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly ties the likely residual recession pattern seen in fig_07.jpg to baseline anatomy and tooth position/root prominence, and explains that if palatal CTG is not an option, predictability for maximal root coverage drops further and expectations must be reset toward stability and symptom control.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction or replacement of #42 despite preserved periodontal support, no mobility, and a surgically treatable isolated recession defect

items.question_content:
A 45-year-old man presents with pain, bleeding, and severe mobility of tooth #21, 10 years after trauma. The tooth has had multiple previous endodontic attempts and is root-canal treated. He has a high smile line. Review fig_01.jpg.

What should the primary objective of treatment for #21 be at this visit, and why? Justify your choice from the history and the findings visible in fig_01.jpg, including why a different objective would be less suitable. Then outline the earliest priorities needed to make your plan biologically and mechanically sound. Finally, explain how your plan would change in two situations: first, if you cannot achieve infection control and a stable restorative foundation at the first visit because of access or bleeding; second, after extraction, if the site does not provide both socket integrity and primary implant stability.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The primary objective should be optimization of the future replacement site in the anterior esthetic zone, not long-term salvage of #21 as a definitive tooth. fig_01.jpg, together with the history, supports a hopeless restorative/periodontal prognosis for definitive retention: the radiograph shows severe external resorption involving the coronal third of the root, and the clinical image shows soft-tissue loss and contour asymmetry in a patient with a high smile line. When those findings are combined with severe mobility, bleeding, pain, prior trauma, and repeated endodontic intervention, the tooth is a poor candidate for predictable long-term retention. Immediate removal is a reasonable fallback, but making extraction the first objective risks further collapse of already compromised papillary, gingival, and vertical ridge architecture, which is especially problematic for a single maxillary central incisor.

Accordingly, if feasible, I would use the tooth only as a temporary biologic tool for site development. The earliest priorities are: remove pathologic coronal/root structure to sound margins; control contamination and isolate the communicating defect from the periodontal tissues with a durable deep seal; confirm that any remaining apical endodontic seal is satisfactory and there is no uncontrolled apical pathology; reinforce the tooth sufficiently to function as a provisional and tolerate orthodontic force; then proceed with slow orthodontic extrusion and a retention phase to encourage coronal migration of bone and gingival tissues before atraumatic extraction.

If I cannot achieve infection control and a stable restorative foundation because access is poor, bleeding cannot be controlled, or a durable seal cannot be obtained, I would abandon temporary retention early rather than persist with an unstable infected tooth. In that situation, I would move to atraumatic extraction and extraction-based site development, such as ridge preservation/augmentation and soft-tissue management, with implant timing determined later by healing and defect morphology.

Even after successful site development, immediate implant placement would only be appropriate if extraction is atraumatic, the socket walls and peri-implant soft-tissue architecture are adequate, and primary implant stability can be achieved in a restorative position. If either socket integrity or primary stability is lacking, I would stage treatment with preservation/augmentation and delayed implant placement rather than force an immediate implant into a compromised site.

During the temporary-retention phase, findings that should trigger conversion to extraction-based management include inability to maintain the seal, persistent inflammation or suppuration, progressive radiographic breakdown, fracture or inadequate remaining root support, uncontrolled mobility, or failure of patient compliance with the lengthy multidisciplinary plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Sets the wrong primary objective, such as definitive long-term retention of #21 despite the case findings, or jumps straight to implant placement without addressing the esthetic-site problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that #21 has a poor prognosis but does not clearly prioritize site optimization over tooth survival, or gives a generic extraction/replacement answer with limited reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes preservation/improvement of the future replacement site rather than definitive retention of #21, and identifies temporary retention as acceptable only if the tooth can be made biologically controlled and mechanically usable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above and clearly explains why immediate extraction is a fallback rather than the initial objective in this esthetic-zone case, while also recognizing when site conditions should take priority over implant timing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is largely unsupported by the history or fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as mobility or trauma history alone, without integrating the esthetic and radiographic implications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the history and fig_01.jpg to support the plan, including severe coronal/cervical root resorption on the radiograph, the clinical soft-tissue/recession and contour changes visible in fig_01.jpg, severe mobility/bleeding, and the high-smile-line esthetic risk.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above and explicitly explains why these combined findings imply high risk of vertical hard- and soft-tissue deficiency and papillary compromise, making definitive tooth salvage and poorly planned extraction less suitable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Management sequence is absent, unsafe, or biologically inappropriate.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a generic plan but omits key early priorities needed to make temporary retention safe, or does not state when immediate implant placement should be deferred.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Outlines a coherent sequence: debridement to sound margins, infection control with a durable seal of the defect, assessment/preservation of acceptable apical endodontic status, reinforcement/provisionalization sufficient for function and orthodontic extrusion, retention, then atraumatic extraction; states that immediate implant placement requires both socket integrity and primary stability, otherwise staging is needed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above with clear stepwise logic, including interdisciplinary coordination and an explicit staged alternative after extraction-based site development when immediate implant requirements are not met.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful reasons to stop or change the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only broad risks such as infection or mobility, without linking them to a revised management pathway.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant triggers to abandon temporary retention, such as inability to control bleeding/access well enough to obtain a durable foundation, persistent inflammation or suppuration, progressive radiographic breakdown, fracture, inadequate remaining root support, or uncontrolled mobility.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above and clearly revises the plan in both requested scenarios: early conversion to extraction-based site development when infection control/stability cannot be achieved, and delayed implant placement when post-extraction site integrity or primary stability is insufficient.

items.question_content: A 36-year-old woman presents with hypersensitivity from tooth 31. She is medically healthy. Clinical examination shows an isolated facial recession defect on 31 with probing depth 1 mm, recession depth 2 mm, recession width 3 mm, keratinized tissue width 2 mm at the recipient site, and spacing between the lower central incisors. Full-mouth plaque score is 37% and full-mouth bleeding score is 32%. Examine fig_01.jpg, including the periapical image, for the interproximal support around 31. What definitive periodontal plastic surgery plan would you recommend for this tooth, and why? In your answer, identify the recession type/classification and prognosis, justify the flap choice based on the local anatomy, describe any graft or biologic adjunct you would select in light of the patient's preference to avoid a large palatal donor graft if possible, and state the most realistic treatment goal and the main threats to long-term stability.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is not a simple RT1/Class I recession. Based on fig_01.jpg, the defect should be interpreted as an RT2 recession (approximately Miller Class III) because there is interproximal attachment/bone loss around 31. That reduces the predictability of complete root coverage compared with recession defects that have intact interproximal support. The shallow probing depth indicates the main problem is recession management rather than pocket elimination.

Management should begin with cause control: oral-hygiene instruction, reduction of plaque and bleeding scores, atraumatic brushing advice, and root surface debridement/planing of 31, followed by reassessment.

For definitive root coverage, a routine coronally advanced flap alone would not be the best first choice because the mandibular incisor area has limited coronal mobility and the recipient site has only 2 mm of keratinized tissue. Given the clinically usable adjacent keratinized tissue and spacing, a laterally positioned/repositioned pedicle flap is well justified because it transfers vascularized keratinized tissue to the defect.

An adjunct to improve tissue thickness and stability is reasonable. If the patient wishes to avoid a large palatal harvest, acceptable biologically sound options include a soft-tissue substitute or cell-based/tissue-engineering approach such as a collagen scaffold, with or without autologous fibroblast seeding where available. A connective tissue graft remains the gold standard comparator, but it is less aligned with her preference because of donor-site morbidity. The choice of adjunct should be justified by availability, biologic rationale, morbidity, and operator experience rather than by naming a single mandatory material.

The surgical approach would include recipient-site preparation and root planing, elevation of a tension-free laterally repositioned flap from the adjacent donor area, placement of the selected graft/scaffold if used, and lateral positioning of the flap to fully cover the defect and secure it without tension.

The most realistic goal is significant root coverage with reduced hypersensitivity, increased tissue thickness, and gain in keratinized tissue. Complete root coverage may occur but cannot be promised because interproximal support is reduced. The main threats to long-term stability are persistent plaque-induced inflammation, traumatic brushing, flap tension or dehiscence, relapse related to the underlying interproximal attachment loss, and recession or bone loss at the donor site of the pedicle flap. Maintenance and monitoring of both recipient and donor sites are essential.

items.question_content: A 42-year-old healthy nonsmoker woman presents with sensitivity and concern that the maxillary canine looks longer. Adjacent interproximal tissues are intact and there is no pathologic pocketing. Use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg only. Commit to one definitive plan for this exact tooth: name the specific periodontal plastic procedure you would perform, state whether the cervical wear should be restored before or after surgery in this case, and identify the single feature in fig_02.jpg that most strongly makes your plan predictable. Then state the main trade-off you are accepting with this choice and explain how your sequencing would change if, after debridement, the cervical defect proved deeper and the CEJ could not be identified reliably. Answer as what you would actually do, not as a list of all possible options.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would manage this with staged care and perform periodontal surgery first using a semilunar coronally repositioned flap (SCRF) for the maxillary canine, then reassess and place a definitive cervical composite only after soft-tissue healing and maturation if any residual noncarious cervical defect still needs contour, plaque control improvement, or sensitivity control.

Why this exact procedure: this is an isolated recession with intact interproximal tissues and no pocketing, so complete or near-complete root coverage is realistic. The single most important feature in fig_02.jpg is the broad band of attached/keratinized gingiva apical to the recession (about 3 mm), which provides the local tissue needed for a semilunar coronally repositioned pedicle approach. In this anatomy, SCRF is attractive because it uses existing keratinized tissue, preserves papillary blood supply, gives a good color/texture match, and avoids donor-site morbidity.

I would not restore first in this exact presentation because the lesion appears shallow enough that the CEJ/root contour is still clinically usable for positioning the soft tissue, and a preoperative restoration could compromise intimate flap adaptation or margin placement. The main trade-off I am accepting is less tissue-thickening/phenotype augmentation than a connective-tissue graft would provide; however, that added morbidity is not necessary here because the local tissue anatomy is already favorable.

If debridement revealed a deeper cervical defect with an indistinct CEJ, I would change the sequence: first restore the defect to an estimated anatomic CEJ/root contour with a smooth, well-finished restoration, then perform the root-coverage procedure to that reconstructed reference. If the local tissue also proved insufficient for passive, tension-free coronal positioning, I would escalate from SCRF to a more extensive coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft rather than persist with the semilunar approach.

items.question_content: A 42-year-old woman seeks relief of severe hypersensitivity at mandibular canine #43 and extraction of nonrestorable #42. Examining fig_01.jpg and the clinical data, #43 has a 5×5 mm Miller Class III, U-shaped recession with thin biotype, no keratinized tissue, shallow vestibule, early bone loss, and the tooth lies outside the alveolar housing; probing depth, mobility, and bleeding on probing are normal. She refuses orthodontic/occlusal correction and lives far away. What management would you recommend for #43 in relation to the planned #42 extraction, and why? Defend your choice against other reasonable options using the site anatomy, patient constraints, and expected short- and longer-term prognosis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would retain #43 and, after initial cause-control therapy, offer a surgical root-coverage attempt using a connective tissue graft with a tunnel/pouch-type approach, performed either with or shortly after atraumatic extraction of #42 once inflammation is controlled. The tooth is still maintainable because probing, mobility, and bleeding are normal and bone loss is only early; the main indication is severe hypersensitivity plus the mucogingival defect. A CTG-based tunnel is the best match for this site because the defect is deep/wide and U-shaped on a mandibular canine with thin tissue, no keratinized tissue, shallow vestibule, and an out-of-housing position. Preserving papillary and flap vascularity and avoiding vertical releases reduces the risk of flap shrinkage, apical relapse, and graft exposure, while CTG can thicken the biotype and increase attached/keratinized tissue. I would explicitly counsel that complete root coverage is not predictable and long-term stability is guarded because the tooth remains outside the alveolar housing and the patient declined orthodontic/occlusal correction. Reasonable alternatives include delaying definitive coverage until tooth position/occlusion is corrected, or using palliative desensitizing/restorative management alone if she declines surgery; these may be less invasive but are less likely to correct the mucogingival deficiency. Key technical priorities are passive coronal advancement after thorough tunnel release, avoiding flap perforation, using an adequately thick graft, stable coronal suturing, and strict plaque/trauma control. Follow-up should emphasize recurrence of sensitivity or recession, since short-term improvement is realistic but relapse remains possible.

items.question_content:
A 35-year-old healthy nonsmoking woman has persistent dentinal hypersensitivity and esthetic concern at 31/41 after phase I periodontal therapy. Probing depth at the involved site is 1 mm. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg only, decide whether the more defensible preoperative strategy is to attempt immediate root coverage or to stage treatment first to improve the soft-tissue environment and defer definitive coverage. Defend one strategy for this exact site.

In your answer, (1) infer the recession class/predictability from the visible soft-tissue relationships, (2) identify one figure-based feature that supports a pedicle-type root-coverage approach and one figure-based feature that makes any coronal-advancement-dependent approach less predictable, (3) explain why the strategy you did not choose is less appropriate at this time, and (4) identify the single missing or intraoperative datum that most limits confidence in your preoperative choice and how it would change your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The more defensible preoperative strategy is to proceed with immediate root coverage, specifically planning a pedicle-based approach such as a double pedicle/double papilla flap, while recognizing that the final go/no-go decision depends on intraoperative tissue adequacy.

From fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg plus the 1 mm probing depth, this appears to be an isolated recession defect with preserved interproximal soft-tissue support rather than pocket-driven periodontal breakdown. The visible interdental tissues adjacent to the exposed root look maintained, so the defect is compatible with a favorable root-coverage situation such as Miller class II.

The figure-based feature that supports immediate pedicle-type coverage is the presence of adjacent mesial and distal papillary tissue that can potentially serve as the vascularized donor tissue for coverage. The strongest figure-based feature arguing against a coronal-advancement-dependent approach is the mandibular anterior anatomy: severe crowding/labial malposition with a shallow vestibular soft-tissue environment, which makes passive broad coronal advancement less predictable and more tension-prone.

A staged augmentation-first strategy, such as first using a free gingival graft to increase attached tissue and vestibular depth and delaying definitive coverage, is less appropriate as the initial plan because it adds a second stage and donor-site morbidity, gives a less ideal color match, and may be unnecessarily invasive when the adjacent papillae appear usable and the patient wants both esthetic improvement and relief of sensitivity.

The single most important limiting datum is whether the mesial and distal papillae/pedicles are actually thick, long, and mobile enough to be approximated over the root as a well-vascularized, tension-free unit. If, intraoperatively, they are too thin, narrow, short, ischemic, or cannot meet passively without tearing or blanching, I would abandon immediate pedicle root coverage and switch to a staged soft-tissue augmentation plan first, most reasonably increasing attached tissue/vestibular depth before later attempting definitive root coverage.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old nonsmoking woman wants definitive treatment for an isolated buccal recession on #22 after a composite used for sensitivity control proved esthetically unacceptable. She is medically healthy, highly anxious about surgery, and has limited finances. Periodontal findings show a 7 mm deep, 5 mm wide Miller Class II recession, 1 mm midfacial probing depth, and essentially no attached gingiva at the recipient site. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. What definitive root-coverage strategy would you recommend for this patient, and why is it preferable in this case? Defend your plan using the local tissue conditions visible in the figures and the patient's constraints, and identify the key feasibility checks and donor-site safeguards that determine whether your plan is appropriate.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would use a staged, adjacent-tissue approach rather than immediate single-stage root coverage. The figures suggest the tissue next to #22 is initially too limited for a safe laterally positioned flap, so I would first increase the width of keratinized donor tissue with an apically repositioned split-thickness flap in the adjacent area, allow healing/maturation, and then perform a tension-free laterally positioned flap to cover #22.

This is preferable here because the defect is isolated, deep, and lacks attached gingiva, but the patient is fearful of surgery and cost-sensitive. A plan that avoids palatal harvesting or added graft materials reduces morbidity, simplifies the procedure, lowers cost, and should give a better color match from neighboring tissue. The laterally positioned flap only becomes feasible after donor-site augmentation; the progression from the limited donor tissue to a broader keratinized band in the figures is the key reason for staging.

Before starting, I would confirm excellent plaque control/no inflammation, minimal sulcus depth, and especially absence of facial bone dehiscence/adequate crestal support, because this approach depends on favorable local anatomy. At the second stage, I would remove the composite, prepare the root and recipient bed, and transfer the flap passively without tension while preserving a marginal collar of keratinized tissue at the donor tooth/teeth. That collar is important to reduce donor-site recession and attachment loss.

The main limitation is that this requires two surgeries and more treatment time, and success is technique- and case-selection dependent; if adjacent tissue cannot be made adequate, another root-coverage strategy would be needed.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old medically fit nonsmoker presents with severe isolated labial recession of the mandibular right central incisor after prolonged orthodontic treatment. She has a thin periodontal phenotype, good plaque control, probing depths under 3 mm, no interdental bone loss, and the tooth had prior root canal treatment for hypersensitivity. She refuses orthodontic retreatment. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what definitive management would you recommend for this tooth now, and why is that plan preferable in this anatomy? Explain the findings that make the plan feasible, the limits beyond which it becomes unsafe, and the main determinants of prognosis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend a tooth-preserving periodontal plastic approach, but not soft-tissue grafting alone. fig_02.jpg shows the labial root prominence extending beyond the alveolar envelope, so leaving that convexity unchanged would make root coverage less predictable because the graft/flap would have a poor recipient contour and limited vascular support over the most prominent area. Since the tooth has no interdental bone loss, shallow probing depths, no pathologic mobility, and the patient has good hygiene, a salvage approach is reasonable: perform limited odontoplasty of the protruding labial root surface only enough to reduce the prominence while preserving dentin thickness and avoiding exposure of root-filling material, then cover the defect with a connective tissue graft under a tension-free coronally advanced partial-thickness flap. This improves contour, graft adaptation, soft-tissue thickness, and vascular overlap while preserving the tooth when orthodontic repositioning is refused.

The plan is feasible only if the tooth is stable, dentin thickness is sufficient for conservative reduction, occlusal trauma is controlled, and flap design can provide stable coronal positioning and graft immobilization. It becomes unsafe if trimming risks canal/root-filling exposure, excessively weakens the root, mobility is present, traumatic loading persists, or soft tissue anatomy will not allow adequate vascularized coverage.

Prognosis is guarded but acceptable: favorable factors are isolated defect, good plaque control, no interdental bone loss, and tooth preservation; limiting factors are the thin phenotype, severe recession, narrow papillae, shallow vestibular soft tissue, and root position outside the bony housing. I would monitor graft perfusion and stability, flap tension/dehiscence, hypersensitivity or endodontic exposure, mobility/root fracture risk after odontoplasty, plaque control, increase in keratinized tissue, and recurrence over time.
