levels.description: Mentions isolated risks or benefits but does not weigh them against the proposed intervention or define when the plan should be altered.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances benefits of tooth preservation and soft-tissue improvement against the main risks: dentin over-reduction, exposure of root-filling material, graft failure, mobility, and occlusal loading.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly identifies the clinical thresholds that make the plan unsafe, such as inadequate residual dentin, pathologic mobility, uncontrolled traumatic forces, or inability to obtain adequate vascularized coverage and stable flap closure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives no prognosis or an unrealistic prognosis unsupported by case findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a generic prognosis with limited reference to patient-specific favorable and unfavorable factors.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Offers a realistic prognosis that links expected outcome to case-specific modifiers and identifies the main follow-up issues affecting stability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced prognosis distinguishing initial root coverage from long-term stability, and identifies appropriate monitoring of graft perfusion, flap tension/dehiscence, hypersensitivity or endodontic exposure, mobility/root fracture risk, plaque control, keratinized tissue gain, and recurrence.

items.question_content: A 25-year-old woman seeks correction of a gummy smile. Her upper-lip length at rest is normal, average gingival display in spontaneous smile is about 8 mm, and she refuses orthognathic surgery. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg. Assume you are seeing her twice: first at the pretreatment consultation, when she will accept only one surgical phase initially, and again at the 6-year review. Write the management decision you would defend. Identify the etiologies you can support from the figures, choose which single procedure you would perform first and why you would not start with the other plausible non-orthognathic surgery, explain how the planning records affect that choice, and interpret the 6-year records to decide whether any further periodontal surgery is justified. Finally, state how your recommendation would change if the long-term review had instead shown coronal rebound of the gingival margins and bone crest toward the CEJ rather than maintained crown proportions.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is a mixed-etiology excessive gingival display. fig_01.jpg shows normal upper-lip length at rest, so a short upper lip is not the main explanation; the marked gingival show on smiling supports a hyperactive upper lip. The amount of display is large enough to support an underlying vertical maxillary excess component. The maxillary anterior crowns also appear short/disproportionate, and the planning records in fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg imply that crown proportions can be improved surgically, supporting altered passive eruption as the dentogingival contributor. Of these factors, vertical maxillary excess is the least modifiable if orthognathic surgery is refused.

If she accepts only one initial surgery, I would perform esthetic crown lengthening with osseous recontouring first. I would not start with lip repositioning, because it does not correct the short clinical crowns and its design depends on how much gingival display remains after the dentogingival component has been corrected. Doing lip surgery first risks over- or underestimating the needed reduction. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg matter because the wax-up/mock-up let me define the intended tooth proportions, preview the esthetic endpoint with the patient, and fabricate a guide for precise soft- and hard-tissue positioning. After healing, I would remeasure the residual gingival display in spontaneous smile and only then decide whether a second-stage lip-directed procedure is justified as a compromise treatment.

At the 6-year review, I would not recommend additional periodontal surgery based on these records. fig_04.jpg shows early improvement in crown form and smile display. fig_05.jpg supports a stable periodontal/osseous result, with the crest maintained in an appropriate apical relationship to the CEJ after recontouring. fig_06.jpg shows that crown proportions remain acceptable long term even though gingival display has increased again compared with the earlier result. That pattern indicates stability of the crown-lengthening component and partial relapse of the lip-position effect over an unchanged skeletal base, not failure of the periodontal correction. Repeating periodontal surgery in this setting risks overlengthened crowns, root exposure, and sensitivity without addressing the main residual cause.

My counseling would be that non-orthognathic treatment can improve the smile, but it cannot definitively correct the skeletal component. Crown lengthening is the more predictable and durable part; lip-directed surgery is more relapse-prone. If she later wants the most definitive correction and is willing to change her preference, orthognathic management becomes the definitive pathway for the vertical maxillary excess. If she still refuses that but wants incremental improvement, repeat or modified lip repositioning could be discussed, with clear counseling about relapse and possible scar/tightness/edema/mucocele or rare sensory complications.

If the long-term review had instead shown coronal rebound of the gingival margins and bone crest toward the CEJ, my recommendation would change. In that scenario I would suspect dentogingival relapse or inadequate osseous positioning rather than attributing the residual display mainly to lip relapse. I would reassess the periodontal diagnosis and consider repeat esthetic crown lengthening/osseous correction if the biologic relationship to the CEJ had been lost, because further periodontal surgery could then be justified. Even then, I would still explain that correcting the periodontal component alone would not eliminate the underlying skeletal contribution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the problem as purely periodontal or purely lip-related, or attributes it mainly to a short upper lip despite normal lip length at rest.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes excessive gingival display and at least one plausible contributor but does not adequately identify the mixed etiology or does not distinguish hyperactive lip from short lip.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a mixed etiology including altered passive eruption/short clinical crowns, hyperactive upper lip, and vertical maxillary excess, and notes that the skeletal component remains least modifiable while orthognathic surgery is refused.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies the combined etiologies and links each to specific figure/history features, clearly separating dentogingival, dynamic lip, and skeletal contributions.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides generic management principles without meaningful use of the requested figures, or misreads the long-term findings as proof of periodontal failure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figure information but does not integrate baseline, planning, early postoperative, and long-term records into a coherent interpretation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg plus the planning records in fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg and the long-term records in fig_05.jpg/fig_06.jpg to support the initial sequencing decision and the 6-year assessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg in time sequence, showing early esthetic improvement, durable crown/crest relationships, and later residual gingival display that is better explained by lip relapse on a skeletal base than by dentogingival relapse.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses lip repositioning as the first surgery without a strong justification, or recommends additional periodontal surgery at 6 years despite stable periodontal findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a plausible plan but gives weak justification for sequencing, does not explain why not to start with the other surgery, or omits how the recommendation changes under the counterfactual long-term finding.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects esthetic crown lengthening with osseous recontouring as the first procedure, explains that reassessment should precede any later lip-directed surgery, declines further periodontal surgery at the actual 6-year review, and appropriately changes course toward periodontal re-evaluation/re-treatment if the hypothetical long-term records show coronal rebound toward the CEJ.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise, patient-centered algorithm: predictable dentogingival correction first; objective reassessment before any second-stage lip procedure; no repeat periodontal surgery when long-term figures show maintained crown proportions and apical crest position; and justified periodontal re-intervention only in the counterfactual scenario showing true dentogingival relapse.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Presents the non-orthognathic approach as predictably definitive or ignores the risks of overtreatment and relapse.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general relapse or stability concepts but does not connect them to this patient's mixed etiology and the specific long-term records.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that crown lengthening is the more durable component, that lip-directed therapy is more relapse-prone on an unchanged skeletal base, and that unnecessary repeat periodontal surgery risks overlengthening, root exposure, or sensitivity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Weighs case-specific tradeoffs in detail, including durability of periodontal correction, relapse of lip control, limitations of non-orthognathic care for vertical maxillary excess, and complications of lip surgery such as scar visibility, tightness, edema, mucocele, or rare sensory disturbance.

items.question_content: A healthy 48-year-old man had both maxillary second molars extracted because they were non-restorable. Socket preservation with deproteinized porcine bone mineral was performed at #17, while #27 healed without grafting. At 3 months, the soft tissues are healed and the patient wants implant rehabilitation. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, decide whether you would proceed with implant placement now at #17, #27, both, or neither. Give a site-specific treatment plan and justify it from the radiographic and histologic findings, including what you would still need to confirm intraoperatively before committing to implant placement.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would be prepared to place an implant at #17 now, but I would be more cautious at #27 and would only proceed there if clinical and intraoperative findings confirm that prosthetically driven placement with good primary stability is still achievable; otherwise I would augment and delay #27.

The rationale is that #17 shows better preservation of ridge form on the 3-month CBCT and better socket fill than #27. fig_03.jpg also supports biological readiness at #17: there is vital new bone with organized collagen and graft particles closely integrated with host bone, without inflammation or foreign-body reaction. Residual DPBM at 3 months is not, by itself, a reason to delay if it is incorporated and the site can provide stability.

By contrast, #27 appears more resorbed/collapsed radiographically, and the histology shows less new bone and less mature tissue than #17. That makes #27 more likely to have compromised width, less favorable 3D implant positioning, and reduced primary stability in the posterior maxilla.

Before committing surgically, I would confirm absence of active infection, adequacy of the residual walls/septal bone, buccopalatal width, apico-coronal bone relative to the sinus floor, and whether the implant can be placed in a restoratively correct position with sufficient primary stability. If #27 shows only a minor contour defect but stability is achievable, simultaneous GBR could be reasonable; if stability or bone envelope is inadequate, staged augmentation and delayed placement would be safer. Overall, #17 has the better prognosis for straightforward implant placement, while #27 has a higher likelihood of requiring additional augmentation and/or more healing time.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully, or misinterprets key findings (e.g., treats integrated graft as pathology, or ignores the difference between #17 and #27).

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that #17 appears more favorable than #27 but supports the decision with limited or generic evidence from only one data source.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the healed clinical condition with radiographic preservation at #17 versus greater collapse at #27, and uses the histology to distinguish better bone maturation/integration at #17 from less favorable regeneration at #27.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes soft tissue healing, CBCT morphology, histologic maturity, and posterior maxillary implant implications into a coherent explanation of why the two sites should not automatically be treated the same.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides an inappropriate or non-site-specific plan, such as identical management for both sites without justification, or a plan disconnected from the findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broadly reasonable direction (e.g., place at #17 or delay #27) but lacks a clear stepwise plan, contingency thinking, or intraoperative decision thresholds.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a site-specific plan: earlier/direct placement at #17 is acceptable if operative findings support it; #27 requires stricter reassessment with possible simultaneous GBR or staged augmentation if bone volume or stability is inadequate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a clear, prosthetically driven, stepwise plan for both sites, explicitly stating what would make the clinician proceed, modify, or delay treatment at each site.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks, or makes unsupported absolute claims such as assuming residual graft mandates delay or assuming both sites are equally predictable.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general risks or benefits of grafting/implant placement but does not tie them to the differences between #17 and #27.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that preserved ridge dimensions at #17 likely reduce the need for secondary augmentation and improve the chance of primary stability, while #27 carries greater risk of compromised positioning or stability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the advantage of timely implant placement against the risk of placing into inadequately matured or dimensionally deficient bone, with explicit patient- and site-specific thresholds for intervention versus delay.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major procedural risks relevant to posterior maxillary implant placement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only generic complications, such as infection, without linking them to this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant risks such as inadequate primary stability, buccal dehiscence/fenestration, need for additional GBR, and sinus-floor/anatomic limitations, with basic prevention through careful reassessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links each key risk to a preventive or management strategy, such as confirming 3D positioning on CBCT, testing stability intraoperatively, and converting to staged augmentation when stability or bone envelope is insufficient.

items.question_content: A 73-year-old woman has a mandibular canine that was avulsed and immediately self-replanted decades earlier without root canal treatment. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. The tooth is unrestored, discolored, unresponsive to electric pulp testing, and not tender to vertical percussion, with a localized gingival swelling adjacent to the tooth. What is the most likely diagnosis for the acute lesion at presentation?

question_options.text: Lateral periodontal abscess associated with periodontal breakdown
Chronic apical abscess secondary to pulpal necrosis
Internal root resorption with lateral perforation
Vertical root fracture with a draining sinus tract

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The swelling is lateral/gingival rather than apical, the tooth is unrestored, and severe periodontal support loss is evident. Lack of percussion tenderness and the long symptom-free history make a primary endodontic abscess less likely. Internal resorption would be centered on the canal space, not an obliterated canal, and a vertical root fracture is less likely in an unrestored canine without a characteristic fracture pattern.

items.answer_explanation: The swelling is lateral/gingival rather than apical, the tooth is unrestored, and severe periodontal support loss is evident. Lack of percussion tenderness and the long symptom-free history make a primary endodontic abscess less likely. Internal resorption would be centered on the canal space, not an obliterated canal, and a vertical root fracture is less likely in an unrestored canine without a characteristic fracture pattern.

items.question_content: In periodontal health communication, a communication gap occurs when essential information does not reach the patient or is not actionable. A dentist clearly explains periodontal inflammation and prevention, and the patient understands the words. However, the patient still interprets bleeding gums as normal aging and leaves unconvinced that professional care is necessary. What is this problem called?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: This is miscommunication, not a communication gap. The information reaches the patient, but it conflicts with the patient's explanatory model and normalized beliefs about bleeding gums, so the message is not accepted as intended.

items.answer_explanation: This is miscommunication, not a communication gap. The information reaches the patient, but it conflicts with the patient's explanatory model and normalized beliefs about bleeding gums, so the message is not accepted as intended.

items.question_content: A bedside oral-hygiene index records plaque as the percentage of plaque-covered tooth surfaces out of all examined surfaces. What is the name of this index?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: This definition matches the O'Leary Plaque Index, which quantifies plaque by calculating the percentage of tooth surfaces with disclosed plaque among all surfaces examined. It is an oral-hygiene measure, not a caries or gingival inflammation index.

items.answer_explanation: This definition matches the O'Leary Plaque Index, which quantifies plaque by calculating the percentage of tooth surfaces with disclosed plaque among all surfaces examined. It is an oral-hygiene measure, not a caries or gingival inflammation index.

items.question_content: A dentist is reviewing whether the periodontal impact of restorations differs by tooth surface location. In `fig_01.jpg`, panel C shows Model A stratified by surface type, comparing proximal versus non-proximal surfaces for four outcomes: bleeding on probing (BOP), probing depth (PD), PD >= 4 mm, and clinical attachment level (CAL). Based on the directions of the differences across these outcomes, what overall pattern best describes the effect modification by surface type?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The figure does not show a single directional interaction across outcomes. In panel C, restoration effects appear more pronounced on proximal surfaces for BOP and CAL, but more pronounced on non-proximal surfaces for PD outcomes. Therefore, the overall effect modification by surface type is inconsistent, and no consistent pattern emerged.

items.answer_explanation: The figure does not show a single directional interaction across outcomes. In panel C, restoration effects appear more pronounced on proximal surfaces for BOP and CAL, but more pronounced on non-proximal surfaces for PD outcomes. Therefore, the overall effect modification by surface type is inconsistent, and no consistent pattern emerged.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Because the same oral clinicopathologic pattern may also be produced by drugs, localized contactants, or graft-versus-host disease, what broader diagnostic label best describes this pattern?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The broader term is oral lichenoid tissue reaction (OLTR). Idiopathic OLP, drug-related lesions, contact reactions, and graft-versus-host disease can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable, so this label is more inclusive than naming idiopathic OLP alone.

items.answer_explanation: The broader term is oral lichenoid tissue reaction (OLTR). Idiopathic OLP, drug-related lesions, contact reactions, and graft-versus-host disease can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable, so this label is more inclusive than naming idiopathic OLP alone.

items.question_content: A 68-year-old patient with recurrent oral squamous cell carcinoma had progression after PF chemotherapy and then started nivolumab. After 6 cycles, MRI showed a partial response, with the oral lesion decreasing from 46 × 28 mm to 35 × 28 mm and previously enlarged cervical lymph nodes no longer visible. After 11 cycles, MRI showed marked enlargement of the oral/masticator-space lesion, and local stereotactic body radiotherapy was added so nivolumab could be continued. In immune-checkpoint inhibitor resistance terminology, progression after an initial documented response is most precisely classified as which type of resistance?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The patient first derived benefit from nivolumab, so later progression is acquired (secondary) resistance rather than primary resistance. Because progression was limited to a single/few sites while systemic benefit was otherwise maintained, the most precise label is oligoprogressive acquired resistance.

items.answer_explanation: The patient first derived benefit from nivolumab, so later progression is acquired (secondary) resistance rather than primary resistance. Because progression was limited to a single/few sites while systemic benefit was otherwise maintained, the most precise label is oligoprogressive acquired resistance.

items.question_content: The lesion in fig_01.jpg resolved by fig_02.jpg only after systemic cyclosporine. In the immunologic mechanism discussed for oral lichen planus, cyclosporine is noted to inhibit helper/inducer T lymphocytes and which two antigen-presenting cell marker-positive populations? Give both markers.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The discussion states that cyclosporine acts on helper/inducer T lymphocytes and inhibits CD1+ and CD14+ antigen-presenting cells. This more specific immune target profile helps explain the clinical response after systemic therapy in this recalcitrant oral lichen planus case.

items.answer_explanation: The discussion states that cyclosporine acts on helper/inducer T lymphocytes and inhibits CD1+ and CD14+ antigen-presenting cells. This more specific immune target profile helps explain the clinical response after systemic therapy in this recalcitrant oral lichen planus case.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What is the specific gingival finding shown that is most diagnostically useful in separating this presentation from common childhood viral enanthems?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Marked hemorrhagic inflammation of the marginal/attached gingiva is a classic clue to primary HSV gingivostomatitis and helps distinguish it from enteroviral enanthems, which usually do not produce this gingival pattern.

items.answer_explanation: Marked hemorrhagic inflammation of the marginal/attached gingiva is a classic clue to primary HSV gingivostomatitis and helps distinguish it from enteroviral enanthems, which usually do not produce this gingival pattern.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What histopathologic reaction pattern best describes this biopsy?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_01.jpg shows a lichenoid/interface pattern: band-like inflammatory infiltrate along the junction with apoptotic keratinocytes, fitting lichen planus rather than dysplastic epithelium or invasive SCC.

items.answer_explanation: fig_01.jpg shows a lichenoid/interface pattern: band-like inflammatory infiltrate along the junction with apoptotic keratinocytes, fitting lichen planus rather than dysplastic epithelium or invasive SCC.

items.question_content: A 4-year-old girl has the upper-lip lesion shown in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. Which findings are the strongest discriminators favoring infantile hemangioma rather than congenital hemangioma or venous malformation? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: The lesion was absent at birth and first recognized at 4 weeks of age.
It enlarged during an early proliferative phase and later stabilized.
It blanched on diascopy.
Color Doppler showed venous-type vascularity.
The child was female, premature, and of low birth weight.
The mass was soft, compressible, and reducible.
Ultrasound showed no calcification, necrosis, or invasion of adjacent structures.
The lesion became more discolored on crying with minimal bleeding.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The key discriminators are the postnatal onset and the early proliferative course followed by stabilization, which fit infantile hemangioma. Diascopy, compressibility, venous-type flow, and color change with crying support a vascular lesion but do not reliably separate infantile hemangioma from venous malformation or congenital hemangioma. Risk factors raise suspicion but are not diagnostic.

items.answer_explanation: The key discriminators are the postnatal onset and the early proliferative course followed by stabilization, which fit infantile hemangioma. Diascopy, compressibility, venous-type flow, and color change with crying support a vascular lesion but do not reliably separate infantile hemangioma from venous malformation or congenital hemangioma. Risk factors raise suspicion but are not diagnostic.

items.question_content: Using the lesion chronology (not present at birth, appeared at 4 weeks, enlarged for about 2 years, then stabilized) together with fig_01.jpg, what is the most specific short subtype designation for this vascular lesion based on both clinical behavior and vascular channel size?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Postnatal onset with an early proliferative phase followed by stabilization supports infantile hemangioma. fig_01.jpg/microscopy shows both small and large thin-walled blood-filled vascular channels, favoring a mixed subtype rather than purely capillary or cavernous.

items.answer_explanation: Postnatal onset with an early proliferative phase followed by stabilization supports infantile hemangioma. fig_01.jpg/microscopy shows both small and large thin-walled blood-filled vascular channels, favoring a mixed subtype rather than purely capillary or cavernous.

items.question_content: When a gingival giant-cell lesion is suspected to be peripheral giant-cell granuloma, which laboratory test is commonly reviewed to help exclude a brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism can resemble peripheral giant-cell granuloma histologically because both may contain multinucleated giant cells. Reviewing the parathyroid hormone level helps identify or exclude hyperparathyroidism as the underlying cause before confirming a localized reactive gingival lesion.

items.answer_explanation: Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism can resemble peripheral giant-cell granuloma histologically because both may contain multinucleated giant cells. Reviewing the parathyroid hormone level helps identify or exclude hyperparathyroidism as the underlying cause before confirming a localized reactive gingival lesion.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old woman with therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia is referred for painful oral ulcerations. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. She has persistent severe neutropenia with pancytopenia. The involved teeth are vital, and panoramic imaging shows no odontogenic source. Which findings most strongly support neutropenic ulceration as the primary diagnosis rather than plaque-related necrotizing gingivitis, leukemic gingival infiltration, classic chemotherapy mucositis, or odontogenic infection? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: The ulcers are deep and pseudomembranous with relatively little surrounding inflammatory change
The patient had documented severe neutropenia during treatment and pancytopenia at referral
Adjacent teeth were vital and imaging did not indicate a dental source
There were no visible plaque deposits despite gingival involvement
Additional ulceration was present on the tongue and in the retromolar region
The lesions appeared after azacitidine had been started
Initial viral and fungal studies were negative
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was cultured later from the oral cavity
The patient had severe thrombocytopenia, so biopsy was deferred
Tooth 46 carried an implant-supported crown

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The strongest differentiators are the ulcer morphology with minimal inflammatory halo, persistent profound neutropenia, lack of plaque despite gingival lesions, and a non-odontogenic workup (vital teeth and negative imaging). These argue against ANUG, leukemic gingival enlargement, classic diffuse mucositis, and dental infection. Negative viral/fungal studies are supportive but less discriminating, and late S. maltophilia was interpreted as secondary colonization.

items.answer_explanation: The strongest differentiators are the ulcer morphology with minimal inflammatory halo, persistent profound neutropenia, lack of plaque despite gingival lesions, and a non-odontogenic workup (vital teeth and negative imaging). These argue against ANUG, leukemic gingival enlargement, classic diffuse mucositis, and dental infection. Negative viral/fungal studies are supportive but less discriminating, and late S. maltophilia was interpreted as secondary colonization.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. No matched oral and intracranial cultures were obtained, yet severe periodontal septic foci were present and alternative causes were excluded. What is the most appropriate term for assigning the brain abscess an oral source in this situation?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Without matched oral and brain cultures, dental origin is not microbiologically proven. In this setting, severe periodontal infection plus exclusion of other causes supports an exclusion-based attribution of odontogenic origin.

items.answer_explanation: Without matched oral and brain cultures, dental origin is not microbiologically proven. In this setting, severe periodontal infection plus exclusion of other causes supports an exclusion-based attribution of odontogenic origin.

items.question_content: A child presents with severe trismus, drooling, generalized hypertonia, neck extension, rigid abdomen, and painful spasms triggered by touch and noise about once every 10 minutes, lasting 2–5 minutes each. He is alert, has preserved limb power, and has no documented respiratory distress or autonomic instability. Using the Ablett classification, what tetanus severity grade best fits this presentation?
Review fig_01.jpg. What is the specific epithelial change shown that is considered a helpful microscopic clue in establishing the diagnosis of pyostomatitis vegetans?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: A helpful histopathologic clue in PSV is intraepithelial clefting or splitting, often accompanied by eosinophil-rich pustules or microabscesses. This supports PSV in the correct clinicopathologic setting.

items.answer_explanation: A helpful histopathologic clue in PSV is intraepithelial clefting or splitting, often accompanied by eosinophil-rich pustules or microabscesses. This supports PSV in the correct clinicopathologic setting.

items.question_content: A diabetic patient has mycological cultures positive for Candida lusitaniae from the commissures, tongue, and cheeks, with erythematous crusted commissural lesions plus a mildly erythematous oral cavity and burning. What is the most specific combined oral diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The commissural lesions indicate angular cheilitis, while diffuse erythema and burning without wipeable plaques indicate erythematous candidiasis. Positive candidal cultures from commissures and oral mucosa support a combined diagnosis rather than an isolated commissural process.
objective_exact_answers: stomatitis and angular cheilitis caused by Candida lusitaniae
stomatitis and angular cheilitis caused by C. lusitaniae
Candida lusitaniae stomatitis and angular cheilitis
C. lusitaniae stomatitis and angular cheilitis

items.answer_explanation: The commissural lesions indicate angular cheilitis, while diffuse erythema and burning without wipeable plaques indicate erythematous candidiasis. Positive candidal cultures from commissures and oral mucosa support a combined diagnosis rather than an isolated commissural process.

items.question_content: A 9-year-old girl had an incidental palatal minor salivary gland tumor excised. Review fig_01.jpg. Pleomorphic adenoma may be described as myxoid (stroma-predominant), cellular (cell-predominant), or classic (mixed epithelial/myoepithelial and stromal elements). Which combined subtype pattern is most consistent with this lesion?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The lesion shows duct-like structures and myoepithelial epithelial components within fibrous stroma that has myxoid change, supporting a mixed myxoid and classic pleomorphic adenoma pattern rather than a purely cellular subtype.

items.answer_explanation: The lesion shows duct-like structures and myoepithelial epithelial components within fibrous stroma that has myxoid change, supporting a mixed myxoid and classic pleomorphic adenoma pattern rather than a purely cellular subtype.

items.question_content: A 35-year-old man repeatedly picks the gingiva around #31 with his fingernail during periods of anxiety and derives gratification from self-inflicted pain, producing the lesion seen in fig_01.jpg. In the Stewart and Kernohan classification of oral self-injurious behavior, this presentation is what type?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Type C fits best because these injuries have complex or psychologically mediated etiologies. This lesion was linked to anxiety/depression and a deliberate masochistic self-inflicting habit, not a simple superimposed lesion or ordinary habit alone.

items.answer_explanation: Type C fits best because these injuries have complex or psychologically mediated etiologies. This lesion was linked to anxiety/depression and a deliberate masochistic self-inflicting habit, not a simple superimposed lesion or ordinary habit alone.

items.question_content: A 42-year-old woman develops bruxism after starting sertraline therapy for generalized anxiety disorder. Her dentist has ruled out occlusal abnormalities and TMJ pathology. Pharmacogenetic testing reveals CYP2C19 intermediate metabolizer status and CYP2D6 normal metabolizer status. Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiology and management of this condition are correct?

question_options.text: Buspirone alleviates SSRI-induced bruxism by enhancing dopaminergic activity in the ventral tegmental area through 5-HT1A partial agonism
SSRI-induced bruxism results from increased dopaminergic activity in the mesocortical pathway
Venlafaxine is an appropriate pharmacogenetically guided alternative because it is primarily metabolized by CYP2D6
Escitalopram would be the safest alternative in this patient given her CYP2C19 intermediate metabolizer status
The serotonin-dopamine imbalance theory proposes that SSRIs suppress mesocortical dopaminergic function, leading to akathisia-like jaw movements
Norepinephrine transporter inhibition has been positively correlated with increased reporting odds of bruxism
Pharmacovigilance data estimate the prevalence of antidepressant-induced bruxism at approximately 15-20%

items.question_content: In the proposed mechanism for residual oral cenesthopathy-like sensations in burning mouth syndrome, perospirone was said to act mainly on which dopamine receptor subtype in the mesencephalon-limbic pathway?

Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A patient with pembrolizumab-associated oral erosive lichenoid disease was treated with a monoclonal antibody targeting IL-4Rα. The oral lesions improved, but new cutaneous lichenoid eruptions developed. Which inflammatory axis is thought to become relatively unopposed in this paradoxical reaction?

A child with biallelic TSPEAR variants has a phenotype limited to agenesis of permanent teeth with conical remaining teeth and taurodontism. Hearing, sweating, hair, nails, and skin are normal. Which specific named TSPEAR phenotype category best fits this dental-only pattern?

A child has recurrent mobility and loss of mandibular anterior teeth. History reveals that when unsupervised she repeatedly presses on the same teeth with her fingers over time until they avulse; laboratory evaluation is normal, and the pattern is gradual and repetitive rather than a single sudden act. In the standard classification of self-injurious behavior, which category best fits this oral presentation?
Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Using both the lesion architecture and its location, what is the most specific short diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_02.jpg shows multiple discrete tooth-like structures, indicating a compound odontoma, and fig_01.jpg shows the lesion is within bone, making it intraosseous. Combining both features gives the most specific short diagnosis: intraosseous compound odontoma.

items.answer_explanation: fig_02.jpg shows multiple discrete tooth-like structures, indicating a compound odontoma, and fig_01.jpg shows the lesion is within bone, making it intraosseous. Combining both features gives the most specific short diagnosis: intraosseous compound odontoma.

items.question_content: A 47-year-old man previously treated with allogeneic HSCT has chronic oral mucosal disease. Using the clinical history and fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, which statements are best supported? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: fig_03.jpg favors oral verruciform xanthoma because foamy macrophages are concentrated within papillary connective tissue beneath elongated rete ridges and parakeratin-filled clefts.

fig_04.jpg supports erythroplakia with high-grade epithelial dysplasia, since dysplastic change through most of the epithelial thickness with chronic inflammation does not by itself establish stromal invasion.
Despite the lichenoid-appearing background in fig_02.jpg, the dorsal tongue abnormality cannot be attributed solely to cGVHD because biopsy demonstrated a separate high-grade dysplastic process.
The multifocal yellow verrucous lesions are more specific for HPV-driven papillomatosis than for verruciform xanthoma in this setting.
Because the lesions in fig_01.jpg are asymptomatic and have a characteristic color, biopsy contributes little beyond excluding secondary infection.
A proposed link between cGVHD and verruciform xanthoma is chronic basal epithelial injury with lipid release and macrophage uptake, rather than demonstrable submucosal hyperlipidemia.
The coexistence of cGVHD and a separate dysplastic tongue lesion lowers concern for later oral carcinoma because the verruciform lesions are benign.
Color variation in oral verruciform xanthoma is independent of epithelial thickness, so a yellow-white clinical appearance strongly excludes malignant mimics.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_03.jpg shows classic OVX with xanthoma cells in papillary connective tissue. fig_04.jpg supports high-grade epithelial dysplasia on the tongue, so the tongue lesion is not explained by cGVHD alone. The proposed mechanism in cGVHD is chronic epithelial injury with lipid release and macrophage uptake; HPV causation, invasive SCC, and clinical diagnosis without biopsy are not supported.

items.answer_explanation: fig_03.jpg shows classic OVX with xanthoma cells in papillary connective tissue. fig_04.jpg supports high-grade epithelial dysplasia on the tongue, so the tongue lesion is not explained by cGVHD alone. The proposed mechanism in cGVHD is chronic epithelial injury with lipid release and macrophage uptake; HPV causation, invasive SCC, and clinical diagnosis without biopsy are not supported.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. In this patient with no recent dental procedure and no endocarditis on transesophageal echocardiography, what is the most likely mechanism by which the oral disease seeded the lumbar infection? Give the most specific short clinical phrase.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The most plausible link is spontaneous bacteremia arising from chronically infected necrotic dentition, followed by hematogenous seeding of the lumbar disc spaces/epidural tissues. The case specifically highlights distant spread without a recent dental procedure or endocarditis.
objective_exact_answers: odontogenic hematogenous seeding from spontaneous bacteremia

items.answer_explanation: The most plausible link is spontaneous bacteremia arising from chronically infected necrotic dentition, followed by hematogenous seeding of the lumbar disc spaces/epidural tissues. The case specifically highlights distant spread without a recent dental procedure or endocarditis.

items.question_content: A 62-year-old Chinese woman has had recurrent lower-lip ulceration for 1 year, usually after sun exposure. She is a nonsmoker, has poor dentition with long-standing dentures, no recent dental work, no new chronic medications, no skin or other oral lesions, and mandibular prognathism. Viral/fungal stains and direct immunofluorescence from the lip biopsy are negative. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, state your leading diagnosis and the single strongest alternative diagnosis you would still actively monitor for. Explain which findings favor one over the other, including which factors are likely causal versus incidental/aggravating. Then give your initial management plan. Finally, if after 3 months of good adherence a focal area becomes persistently indurated and nonhealing, what specific next step is required and how would that alter your working diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The leading diagnosis is isolated actinic lichen planus of the lower lip (actinic oral lichen planus), with reticular and erosive components. fig_01.jpg shows a lacy/reticulated white change on the lower lip rather than the more diffuse vermilion damage expected in straightforward actinic cheilitis, and fig_02.jpg shows a lichenoid interface pattern with band-like lymphocytic inflammation, vacuolar basal damage, and focal subepithelial clefting, which supports lichen planus. The recurrent photo-triggered course, confinement to the more exposed lower lip, and prognathism support UV as a causal factor. Poor dentition and dentures are more likely aggravating/local irritant factors than the primary diagnosis, especially as there was no recent dental work and no new chronic drug exposure to support contact or drug-induced lichenoid disease. The strongest alternative to keep under surveillance is actinic cheilitis with epithelial dysplasia/early SCC in situ, because the site is sun-exposed and lower-lip lesions can evolve atypically; HSV and autoimmune blistering disease are less likely given the chronic pattern plus negative stains and negative direct immunofluorescence. Initial management should be conservative and anti-inflammatory: strict photoprotection, topical anti-inflammatory therapy to the lip (such as a corticosteroid and/or tacrolimus), emollient/barrier care, optimization of oral hygiene and denture-related irritation, adherence counseling, and scheduled review. Immediate destructive or excisional treatment is not first choice today because the current clinicopathologic picture favors inflammatory lichenoid disease rather than proven dysplasia/carcinoma. If, despite good adherence, a focal area becomes persistently indurated and nonhealing, the next step is prompt repeat biopsy targeted to that area with specialist reassessment. At that point the priority shifts from managing known actinic lichen planus to excluding superimposed actinic cheilitis with dysplasia, early squamous malignancy, or sampling error in the original biopsy.

items.question_content: A 62-year-old woman has a recurrent lesion confined to the lower lip for 1 year. Episodes flare after sun exposure. She has mandibular prognathism, poor dentition, and background sun-related skin changes at presentation, but no other oral or cutaneous lichen planus lesions at presentation or during 2 years of follow-up. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Which findings most specifically justify classifying this lesion as isolated actinic lichen planus rather than merely a nonspecific lichenoid process of the lip? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: Sun-provoked recurrences
Mandibular prognathism increasing lower-lip sun exposure
Disease confined to the lower lip with upper-lip sparing
Reticular white change on the lip surface
Interface vacuolar change with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate
Poor dentition
No other oral or cutaneous lesions developing during follow-up
Focal subepithelial clefting on biopsy

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The actinic classification is supported by sun-triggered flares, an anatomic predisposition to greater lower-lip exposure from prognathism, and confinement to the more sun-exposed lower lip with upper-lip sparing. The isolated classification is supported by the absence of other oral or cutaneous lichen planus lesions on follow-up. Background sun-related skin changes at presentation do not contradict the isolated designation. Reticular change and lichenoid interface mucositis support lichen planus generally, but they are not specific for the actinic and isolated designation.

items.answer_explanation: The actinic classification is supported by sun-triggered flares, an anatomic predisposition to greater lower-lip exposure from prognathism, and confinement to the more sun-exposed lower lip with upper-lip sparing. The isolated classification is supported by the absence of other oral or cutaneous lichen planus lesions on follow-up. Background sun-related skin changes at presentation do not contradict the isolated designation. Reticular change and lichenoid interface mucositis support lichen planus generally, but they are not specific for the actinic and isolated designation.

items.question_content: A young patient on dialysis has progressive maxillomandibular enlargement caused by severe secondary hyperparathyroidism. Phosphate restriction, phosphate binders, vitamin D analogs, and dialysis optimization have not controlled the disease. What definitive surgery is indicated to halt further skeletal progression?

Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg: a 74-year-old man with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis on monthly secukinumab reports burning of the tongue that began 3 months after starting therapy and persists. He is a nonsmoker, has no xerostomia, and no other skin or mucosal lesions. The tongue shows bilateral, symmetrical, thick white keratotic plaques on the anterior lateral borders and mid-dorsum that are not scrapable, with fissuring and small self-inflicted erosions. Biopsy shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, dense mainly T-cell subepithelial infiltrate with focal neutrophils, scattered apoptotic bodies and basal vacuolization; DIF, p16, and EBER are negative. PAS stain and Candida culture are negative. What is the most defensible diagnosis, and what management plan would you recommend now, including whether secukinumab should be changed and how you would manage longer-term risk?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The leading diagnosis is secukinumab-associated chronic hyperplastic candidiasis (candidal leukoplakia) of the tongue, with lichenoid inflammatory features. The diagnosis is supported by the fig_01.jpg pattern of non-scrapable bilateral keratotic plaques on the dorsum and anterior lateral tongue, onset soon after IL-17 blockade, lack of common local risk factors, and exclusion of key mimics by EBER negativity, negative DIF, and nonclassic histology for OLP/OLR. Negative PAS and culture do not exclude CHC here; sampling error, patchy organisms, and chronicity can yield false-negative mycology, so clinicopathologic correlation is critical. Management should be multidisciplinary with oral medicine plus clinical immunology/dermatology/rheumatology: stop secukinumab and switch away from the IL-17 class if feasible, such as to a non-IL-17 biologic, because the drug is the likely predisposing factor. Treat the oral disease with topical antifungal therapy plus systemic antifungal therapy for this extensive lesion burden in an immunomodulated patient, along with antiseptic/oral-hygiene measures and short-interval review to confirm regression. If lesions persist, recur, or leave suspicious residual keratosis, repeat biopsy to exclude dysplasia or another diagnosis. Long-term surveillance is required because CHC is an oral potentially malignant disorder with recurrence and malignant transformation risk.

items.question_content: A 64-year-old woman has had 5 years of mostly asymptomatic raised palatal lesions. Minor irritation improves with SLS-free toothpaste; antifungal therapy was ineffective. She is a lifelong nonsmoker, does not wear dentures, swab results were negative, routine blood tests were normal, and previous biopsy reports were described only as chronic/lichenoid inflammation. She mentions a possible prior vulval lichenoid diagnosis but no current skin complaints. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg, what is the most defensible diagnosis and management strategy now, including whether further specialty involvement is warranted? Justify your choice by integrating the clinicopathologic findings and by explaining why more common causes of palatal papules are lower priority.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best diagnosis is oral lichen nitidus. The clinical pattern is of multiple persistent, discrete palatal papules that are largely asymptomatic, with no microbiologic support for candidiasis and no risk factors for smoker-related palatal change or denture-associated papillary hyperplasia. The histology is the key discriminator: a small, well-circumscribed papular lesion with dense lichenoid inflammation, lymphocytic exocytosis, and Civatte bodies, plus the characteristic architectural pattern of rete ridges/claw-like epithelial extensions embracing the inflammatory focus (“claw clutching ball”). That architecture supports lichen nitidus over oral lichen planus, which may share lichenoid inflammation but lacks this papular configuration. Current management should be conservative: explain the diagnosis, reassure, avoid irritants that provoke symptoms, and arrange open or periodic review rather than active treatment, because the disease is stable and minimally symptomatic. Escalation to topical anti-inflammatory therapy would only be reasonable if symptoms become troublesome. Further specialty involvement is not mandatory now if the oral disease is isolated and stable, but dermatology review is appropriate if skin or genital lesions/symptoms develop, if diagnostic uncertainty persists, or if the disease becomes more extensive or symptomatic.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg and the history, evaluate a healthy 14-year-old girl with abrupt recurrent tongue eruptions. Each flare lasts 1–2 weeks, resolves spontaneously, and she has had 8 episodes over 6 months. The lesions are nonpainful, magic mouthwash did not help, and she has no fever, lymphadenopathy, medications, or persistent lesion between flares. Stopping orthodontic appliances did not prevent recurrence. She later notices that outbreaks follow chewing certain flavored gums, especially cinnamon, hot mint, and pineapple. What is the most likely diagnosis, which alternative diagnoses should be considered but are less likely, and what is the most appropriate management plan, including whether biopsy is indicated and counseling about recurrence prevention?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is the nonpainful hyperkeratotic (papulokeratotic) variant of transient lingual papillitis. The image and history support this: multiple small white keratotic papules limited to fungiform-papillae-bearing anterior/dorsolateral tongue, abrupt onset, short self-limited episodes, recurrence with symptom-free intervals, and absence of systemic illness or persistent ulceration/mass. Important alternatives include classic painful transient lingual papillitis, eruptive lingual papillitis with viral/familial features, frictional/traumatic keratosis, contact hypersensitivity or irritant stomatitis from flavoring agents, candidiasis, HPV-related papillomas, geographic tongue, and less likely leukoplakia or other neoplasia because the lesions are transient, multifocal, and resolve completely. Management should be conservative: reassure that this is benign and self-limited, review a symptom/exposure diary, and identify avoidable triggers, especially flavored gums or other oral irritants. Biopsy is not routinely indicated here because the lesions are recurrent but transient and clinically characteristic; biopsy or referral becomes appropriate only if a lesion persists, enlarges, becomes painful, indurated, unilateral/fixed, ulcerated, bleeds, or is accompanied by concerning cervical nodes/systemic symptoms. Symptomatic therapy is optional and secondary; the key treatment is trigger avoidance. In this scenario, counseling to eliminate suspected gum flavors such as cinnamon, hot mint, and pineapple is the best recurrence-prevention strategy, with follow-up only if the pattern changes.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg; for fig_04.jpg, treat panel D as follow-up and not part of the baseline assessment. Three patients with psoriasis treated with IL-17-pathway inhibitors present with oral complaints. Patient 1: 22-year-old woman, mild symptoms for 1 day, last secukinumab 300 mg injection 1 week ago, no other known Candida risk noted, CBC normal 3 months earlier. Patient 2: 66-year-old woman, 5 years of fluctuating burning mouth, dysgeusia, and xerostomia, more intense since secukinumab 150 mg twice monthly; salivary flow normal, CBC normal 5 months earlier. Patient 3: 50-year-old man, burning tongue lesions for about 10 months; brodalumab was stopped 3 months ago; isoniazid had ended months before oral symptoms; CBC normal. Based on the history and figures, identify which patient most needs tissue diagnosis in addition to smear confirmation, and which patient you would prioritize for immediate systemic fluconazole if you can prescribe it to only one person today. Then give the initial management plan for each patient, including when you would escalate to biopsy or broader reassessment if lesions persist after antifungal therapy. Justify your choices using lesion pattern, microscopy, chronology, and whether Candida may be superimposed on another disorder.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Patient 1 most needs tissue diagnosis in addition to smear confirmation. fig_01.jpg shows multifocal plaque-forming white lesions on an erythematous background rather than a purely erythematous pattern, and fig_02.jpg shows tissue findings with hyperparakeratosis, acanthosis, neutrophilic microabscesses, and PAS-positive Candida hyphae in parakeratin. This supports oral candidiasis, but the fixed plaque-forming pattern means Candida could be superimposed on an underlying keratotic lesion, so biopsy is important to exclude a leukoplakic or dysplastic process.

If only one patient can receive immediate systemic fluconazole, Patient 1 is the best choice. She has multifocal plaque-forming disease, convincing mycologic support, and systemic therapy may help clear fungal overgrowth quickly so that any residual fixed plaque can be reassessed for underlying epithelial pathology. Patient 3 is a defensible second choice because of chronic symptomatic multisite disease, but Patient 2 is less compelling for initial systemic treatment.

Patient 2 is most consistent with erythematous candidiasis with angular cheilitis. fig_03.jpg shows commissural erythema, a glossy erythematous tongue, diffuse buccal erythema, palatal involvement, and Candida on cytology. Initial management can be topical antifungal therapy to the oral mucosa and commissures, short-interval review, and coordination with the dermatologist; routine discontinuation of the biologic is not required. Because symptoms fluctuated for years before worsening on secukinumab, the biologic may be a contributor or exacerbating factor rather than the sole explanation. If erythema, burning, or focal lesions persist after adequate antifungal therapy, broader reassessment is needed for another chronic burning/erythematous disorder.

Patient 3 is most consistent with erythematous candidiasis with angular cheilitis. fig_04.jpg baseline panels show scattered erythematous areas of the tongue and palate, and fig_04.jpg panel C confirms Candida on cytology. An initial plan of antifungal therapy with close review is appropriate. However, the long duration and persistence after brodalumab cessation lower confidence that the biologic fully explains the disease. If tongue or palatal lesions remain fixed or only partially improve after adequate antifungal treatment, biopsy or broader reassessment is warranted because candidiasis may be superimposed on another chronic mucosal disorder.

Chronology supports the strongest biologic contribution in Patient 1 because onset was abrupt and close to the recent secukinumab dose with no other risk factor provided. In Patient 2 and especially Patient 3, chronology is less direct, so causation should be framed more cautiously as possible contribution rather than definite primary cause.

items.question_content:
A 16-year-old otherwise healthy male has had 1 year of recurrent yellow crusting and enlargement of both lips, worse on waking. The crusts recur after removal. Prior topical corticosteroid therapy was ineffective. Review fig_01.jpg: (a,b) initial presentation and (c,d) appearance after conservative local anti-inflammatory treatment, with improved contour/crusting but mild residual diffuse erythema.

Based on the initial presentation, would you manage this first as a clinicomorphologic diagnosis or perform immediate biopsy? Commit to one position and justify it using the figure pattern, lesion distribution, chronicity, age, prior steroid failure, and the expected diagnostic yield of biopsy.

State your leading diagnosis and one important competing diagnosis that would change workup. Then name one chairside observation or maneuver you would prioritize immediately and explain how opposite findings would redirect management.

Finally, outline a morbidity-sparing 3-month management plan after failed topical corticosteroid therapy, including when you would escalate to biopsy or more invasive treatment, and why the later appearance in fig_01.jpg(c,d) would or would not change your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best initial approach is to manage this first as a clinicomorphologic diagnosis rather than perform immediate biopsy.

Leading diagnosis: cheilitis glandularis.

Why this is the leading diagnosis: The image pattern and history are most consistent with cheilitis glandularis despite the patient's young age. The important clues are chronic bilateral lip enlargement, eversion, recurrent yellow crusting, recrusting after removal, and predominance on the labial mucosal aspect rather than a primary vermilion dermatitis pattern. Morning recurrence also supports ongoing salivary secretion/inflammation with drying of secretions overnight. Failure of prior topical corticosteroid therapy does not exclude this diagnosis and is compatible with the known difficulty of controlling the condition with topical steroid alone.

Why not biopsy first: Age is atypical for cheilitis glandularis, so it should raise caution, but it does not outweigh the classic morphologic pattern. In this setting, biopsy is not the best first step because the expected histology in cheilitis glandularis is often nonspecific, such as chronic inflammation, sialadenitis, ductal ectasia, and fibrosis. Without focal red-flag features such as asymmetry, ulceration, nodularity, induration, destructive change, or suspicious surface alteration, immediate biopsy is less likely to add decisive information than careful clinicomorphologic assessment and close follow-up.

Important competing diagnosis: cheilitis granulomatosa/orofacial granulomatosis.

Why it remains plausible: A teenager with persistent lip swelling fits that differential by age better than classic cheilitis glandularis. It can also produce chronic diffuse lip enlargement and eversion.

Why cheilitis glandularis is favored over it: The recurrent yellow crusting and secretory-type pattern seen clinically are more supportive of inflamed minor salivary glands than granulomatous swelling alone. Cheilitis granulomatosa usually does not explain repeated mucous crust formation as well as cheilitis glandularis.

High-yield chairside observation/maneuver: Remove crusts, dry the lip, and inspect/palpate for dilated minor salivary duct openings and expressible thick saliva/mucin.
- If present, that strongly supports cheilitis glandularis and supports continued conservative targeted treatment.
- If absent, or if the lip feels firm, nonsecretory, asymmetric, nodular, or otherwise infiltrative, concern rises for granulomatous cheilitis or another process and biopsy becomes more appropriate.
A vermilion-dominant scaly/eczematous pattern would redirect attention toward contact cheilitis.

Morbidity-sparing 3-month management plan after failed topical corticosteroid:
1. Begin local care: gentle crust removal, hygiene, avoidance of lip trauma/manipulation, and regular reassessment.
2. Escalate to targeted local anti-inflammatory therapy rather than repeating ineffective topical steroid alone. A reasonable next step is intralesional corticosteroid treatment for the diffuse inflammatory glandular process.
3. Reassess after several weeks. If swelling/eversion improve but crusting persists, add a topical calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus while continuing local care.
4. Continue close follow-up through about 3 months, looking for improvement in contour, secretion/crusting, and symptoms.
5. Reserve more invasive treatment, such as vermilionectomy, for refractory symptomatic disease after failure of conservative therapy because of treatment morbidity.

When to escalate to biopsy: biopsy is indicated if there is persistent diagnostic uncertainty, progression despite appropriate conservative treatment, development of asymmetry, focal induration, nodularity, ulceration, bleeding, fixed plaque-like change, or persistent firm nonsecretory swelling, or if associated findings suggest granulomatous/systemic disease.

Why fig_01.jpg(c,d) would not overturn the plan: The later appearance shows overall improvement in contour/crusting after conservative anti-inflammatory management. Mild residual diffuse erythema alone is nonspecific and can be post-inflammatory. If the major secretory crusting and enlargement are improving and no new focal red-flag changes have appeared, that pattern supports continuing the conservative plan rather than switching immediately to biopsy or invasive treatment.

items.question_content: An early-60s man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and a heavy smoking history has had a painful ventral tongue ulcer for 1.5 months that did not improve with topical steroid. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide how you would manage him before any definitive cancer surgery is scheduled. Incisional biopsy from the tongue shows no epithelial atypia or invasive carcinoma, only plasma cell/lymphocyte-predominant inflammation. What is your next-step plan, and which clinical and imaging findings most strongly shift your working diagnosis and urgency?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not proceed directly to oncologic resection or neck dissection. The working diagnosis should shift from presumed oral squamous cell carcinoma with nodal metastasis toward an infectious ulcer, with primary syphilis presenting as an oral chancre high on the differential. My next step is a focused sexual history and STI risk assessment, immediate syphilis serology using both a nontreponemal and a treponemal test, and broader STI screening including HIV. I would coordinate care with oral medicine/infectious disease or an appropriate medical team, assess for secondary, ocular, or neurologic involvement by symptom review and targeted referral if indicated, stop ineffective topical steroid, and begin guideline-based systemic antisyphilitic therapy once serology strongly supports or confirms the diagnosis. I would also counsel regarding transmissibility, partner evaluation, and the need for serologic follow-up.

What shifts the diagnosis is the mismatch between cancer risk factors and the total dataset: biopsy shows no dysplasia or invasive carcinoma and instead a plasma cell-rich inflammatory pattern; fig_02.jpg shows multiple bilateral cervical nodes rather than a more typical unilateral metastatic pattern, without convincing destructive local invasion, and the tongue abnormality is relatively limited. These features make inflammatory lymphadenopathy more plausible than metastatic SCC. However, because he is older, a heavy smoker, and the lesion is an indurated nonhealing ventral tongue ulcer, I would keep malignancy in the background and arrange short-interval reassessment. If the ulcer and nodes do not regress promptly after therapy or serology is discordant, repeat biopsy and renewed cancer staging are required.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that malignancy is unproven and mentions infection/inflammation broadly, but does not specifically raise primary syphilis or an oral chancre as a leading diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies probable primary syphilis/oral chancre as the leading diagnosis while acknowledging that malignancy is not fully excluded until follow-up confirms regression or additional testing is completed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately frames the case as likely oral primary syphilis with reactive cervical lymphadenopathy, explains why SCC is now less likely, and preserves a contingency for renewed oncologic workup if the course is atypical.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores key data sources or relies mainly on smoking history/ulcer induration to justify the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one major data source well (for example, biopsy alone or clinical appearance alone) but does not coherently integrate the figures, treatment nonresponse, and biopsy findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the nonhealing indurated ulcer, lack of response to steroid, biopsy without atypia and with plasma cell/lymphocyte-predominant inflammation, and fig_02.jpg nodal/imaging pattern to argue against immediate cancer surgery and toward infectious workup.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all major findings into a clear argument: cancer risk factors justify initial concern, but the bilateral nodal distribution and limited local destructive features on imaging, combined with the biopsy pattern, make inflammatory or STI-related disease more likely than metastatic SCC.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends immediate definitive cancer surgery, or only symptomatic care such as more topical steroid, without completing appropriate diagnostic redirection.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Appropriately delays surgery but provides an incomplete plan, such as ordering a single test without addressing sexual history, STI assessment, medical coordination, or follow-up contingencies.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends focused sexual history, syphilis serology with confirmatory testing, relevant STI screening including HIV, coordination with an appropriate medical team, cessation of ineffective topical steroid, guideline-based systemic treatment if supported, and short-interval reassessment of the ulcer and lymph nodes.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, safety-oriented plan that also includes counseling about infectivity and partner management, assessment for ocular/neurologic involvement when indicated, and explicit criteria for repeat biopsy or renewed oncologic staging if clinical response is inadequate.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh the consequences of delayed cancer diagnosis against the harms of unnecessary irreversible treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either the risk of overtreatment or the risk of missed malignancy, but not both in a patient-specific way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the morbidity of unnecessary head-and-neck cancer surgery against the residual possibility of SCC, justifying a short interval for infectious workup and review rather than immediate resection.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds patient-specific nuance, such as how age, heavy smoking, and ulcer induration sustain cancer concern, while diabetes and the inflammatory pattern support careful but prompt non-surgical workup; explains why response to therapy is diagnostically informative but not a substitute for re-evaluation if atypical.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending definitive tongue resection or neck dissection before completing syphilis serology/infectious workup despite biopsy without carcinoma and an atypical bilateral nodal pattern on fig_02.jpg.

items.question_content:
Two postmenopausal women present on their first visit with recurrent oral blistering disease and normal routine blood tests. Patient A is 60 years old with 1 year of blisters that rupture into painful ulcers and gingival peeling, worse with hot/spicy foods, and no ocular, cutaneous, or genital symptoms. See fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A perilesional biopsy was taken from the left lower labial mucosa. Patient B is 67 years old, completely edentulous, with 3 months of recurrent oral blisters, painful with spicy foods; she stopped wearing complete dentures after onset and reports no extraoral symptoms. See fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg. An incisional perilesional biopsy was taken together with an intact vesicle from the left upper posterior vestibule. Direct immunofluorescence is not available today.

Using only these first-visit findings and figures, decide whether you would manage A and B under the same provisional diagnosis or under different working diagnoses. Rank your differential for each patient, explain which single feature in fig_01.jpg versus fig_03.jpg most changes your confidence, and interpret what fig_02.jpg and fig_04.jpg support but do not establish. State which biopsy would be more useful if direct immunofluorescence becomes available later, whether you would start empiric corticosteroid therapy in both or only one patient today, and the specific clinical change that would make you escalate urgency or systemic treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would manage both patients under the same leading provisional diagnosis: oral mucous membrane pemphigoid (oral-limited at presentation), while recognizing that direct immunofluorescence would still be needed for stronger confirmation and distinction from other subepithelial immunobullous disorders.

Patient A differential, ranked:
1. Oral mucous membrane pemphigoid
2. Pemphigus vulgaris
3. Erosive/bullous lichen planus or lichenoid mucositis
4. Other subepithelial immunobullous disease such as bullous pemphigoid or linear IgA disease

Patient B differential, ranked:
1. Oral mucous membrane pemphigoid
2. Traumatic or denture-associated bulla
3. Pemphigus vulgaris
4. Other immunobullous or lichenoid disease

Why both still favor MMP:
- In Patient A, the key feature in fig_01.jpg is the widespread desquamative gingival and multifocal mucosal involvement, which strongly favors an autoimmune subepithelial blistering disorder over a localized traumatic process.
- In Patient B, the key feature in fig_03.jpg is the intact vesicle with additional disease at separate oral sites rather than one isolated friction point, making pure denture trauma less convincing.

What fig_02.jpg and fig_04.jpg support, and what they do not establish:
- Both histology figures support a subepithelial blistering process because they show a subepithelial split/cleft with inflammatory infiltrate.
- This argues against pemphigus vulgaris, which would be expected to show intraepithelial or suprabasal separation with acantholysis.
- Histology alone does not definitively establish mucous membrane pemphigoid or distinguish it reliably from other subepithelial immunobullous disorders. Direct immunofluorescence remains the key confirmatory test.

Biopsy usefulness if direct immunofluorescence becomes available later:
- Patient B's specimen is more useful because it includes perilesional tissue with an intact vesicle from the posterior vestibule, which better preserves the epithelial-connective tissue junction for immunofluorescence.
- Patient A's lower labial perilesional biopsy is still acceptable, but if repeat sampling were needed, fresh perilesional non-erosive tissue adjacent to a new blister would be preferred.

Initial treatment decision:
- I would start empiric high-potency topical corticosteroid therapy in both patients today rather than wait for delayed direct immunofluorescence, because both are symptomatic and the combined clinical-histologic picture is sufficiently strong for a working diagnosis of oral MMP.
- Patient A needs closer review and broader local treatment because disease is more extensive.
- Patient B can start with topical therapy plus continued avoidance of denture trauma until healing.

Clinical change that increases urgency or need for systemic escalation:
- New ocular symptoms such as redness, pain, photophobia, grittiness, or blurred vision would increase urgency because of scarring risk.
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, breathing difficulty, ongoing new blister formation, inability to eat or maintain oral hygiene, or failure of topical therapy would lower the threshold for systemic treatment, especially in Patient A.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial
