levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Ranks plausible alternatives for each patient, including pemphigus vulgaris and other immunobullous disorders, and includes a trauma-related alternative for Patient B with appropriate caution.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-prioritized, patient-specific differential for both patients, accurately explaining why trauma may be considered in Patient B yet remains secondary to mucous membrane pemphigoid, and why histology lowers but does not eliminate competing diagnoses.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, or fig_04.jpg meaningfully, or misreads the biopsy pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the clinical figures or histology superficially, but does not connect figure-based distribution, histology, and biopsy quality to diagnostic confidence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the more extensive clinical distribution in fig_01.jpg than fig_03.jpg, correctly interprets fig_02.jpg and fig_04.jpg as subepithelial blistering patterns, and states that these findings support but do not establish mucous membrane pemphigoid without direct immunofluorescence.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes clinical distribution, dentate versus edentulous context, histology, and the stated biopsy sampling sites, and correctly judges why Patient B's perilesional biopsy with an intact vesicle is more useful for later direct immunofluorescence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management such as reassurance alone, antiseptics only, or irreversible treatment without attempting disease control.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests corticosteroid therapy or observation but does not decide whether to start treatment now versus await further confirmation, or does not tailor management between the two patients.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends appropriate empiric topical corticosteroid-based management for both patients at first visit, includes trauma reduction, and differentiates the initial treatment intensity between Patient A and Patient B.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise first-visit plan that justifies treating both patients empirically, explains why Patient A warrants broader-surface topical therapy and earlier review, and explains why Patient B can initially remain on topical therapy with denture cessation and reassessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify which patient warrants closer follow-up, and does not name a clinical change that increases urgency or need for systemic escalation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a higher-risk patient or a red-flag symptom, but the reasoning is vague or not tied to disease extent, chronicity, or functional burden.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes Patient A for closer follow-up or lower threshold for systemic escalation and identifies at least one appropriate symptom or sign that would change urgency.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes Patient A based on extent, chronicity, and functional burden, and accurately identifies urgency-changing findings such as ocular involvement or upper aerodigestive symptoms with appropriate referral implications.

items.question_content: In 181 third-trimester pregnant women, fig_01.jpg shows univariate associations between salivary immune markers and oral findings, and fig_02.jpg shows two latent immune-marker clusters (high, n=54; low, n=127). Additional reported results were as follows: married status was more common in the high cluster than the low cluster (33.33% vs 17.32%, p<0.05) on univariate comparison, but it was not significant after debiased post-selection inference (p=0.46). DMFT (6.94 vs 6.39, p=0.218) and ICDAS (3.44 vs 3.47, p=0.899) did not differ significantly between low and high clusters. After debiased post-selection inference, plaque C. albicans (coefficient -1.19, p=0.02) and plaque S. mutans (coefficient -1.01, p=0.03) showed statistically significant inverse associations with the high immune-marker cluster; salivary S. mutans was not retained as a significant variable in that debiased model. Which statements are supported? Select FOUR.

question_options.text: Women with ≥4 decayed teeth show lower salivary IFN-γ and TNF-β than women with <4 decayed teeth.
Salivary S. mutans burden ≥10^5 CFU/mL is associated with higher G-CSF despite lower FLT-3L, IL-17A, TNF-β, and VEGF-A.
Salivary S. mutans did not remain a statistically significant variable after debiased post-selection inference for the high immune-marker cluster.
Plaque C. albicans and plaque S. mutans each retained statistically significant inverse associations with the high immune-marker cluster after debiasing.
DMFT and ICDAS significantly separated the low- and high-immune-marker clusters.
Married status was more common in the high immune-marker cluster, but it was not statistically significant after debiased post-selection inference.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_01.jpg panel A supports lower IFN-γ and TNF-β in women with ≥4 decayed teeth, and fig_01.jpg panel B shows that salivary S. mutans ≥10^5 CFU/mL is associated with lower FLT-3L, IL-17A, TNF-β, and VEGF-A but higher G-CSF. Debiased post-selection inference identified plaque C. albicans and plaque S. mutans as significant inverse predictors of membership in the high immune-marker cluster. Married status differed on univariate comparison between clusters, but it was not significant after debiasing. DMFT and ICDAS did not significantly differ between clusters, and salivary S. mutans was not retained as a significant variable in the debiased model.

items.answer_explanation: fig_01.jpg panel A supports lower IFN-γ and TNF-β in women with ≥4 decayed teeth, and fig_01.jpg panel B shows that salivary S. mutans ≥10^5 CFU/mL is associated with lower FLT-3L, IL-17A, TNF-β, and VEGF-A but higher G-CSF. Debiased post-selection inference identified plaque C. albicans and plaque S. mutans as significant inverse predictors of membership in the high immune-marker cluster. Married status differed on univariate comparison between clusters, but it was not significant after debiasing. DMFT and ICDAS did not significantly differ between clusters, and salivary S. mutans was not retained as a significant variable in the debiased model.

items.question_content: In a patient undergoing microvascular decompression for hemilingual spasm, review fig_01.jpg. What intraoperative EMG finding is shown by the pretreatment tongue discharges that were synchronous with vascular pulsation and resolved after decompression?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: A discharge pattern that is synchronous with vascular pulsation and disappears after decompression is consistent with an LSR-like phenomenon. In cranial nerve compression syndromes, this supports a neurovascular mechanism and suggests that decompression was adequate.

items.answer_explanation: A discharge pattern that is synchronous with vascular pulsation and disappears after decompression is consistent with an LSR-like phenomenon. In cranial nerve compression syndromes, this supports a neurovascular mechanism and suggests that decompression was adequate.

items.question_content: A 51-year-old woman with burning mouth syndrome recorded daily 0-100 mm visual analog scale (VAS) scores before treatment, during 60 days of oral care gel use, and for 30 days after stopping the gel. Review fig_01.jpg and select ALL statements that are supported by the figure alone.

question_options.text: Resting tongue tingling is markedly variable before treatment and then remains mostly near the floor during much of treatment and follow-up.
Dry-mouth scores stay low throughout and do not parallel the larger changes seen in several other domains.
Lower scores after discontinuation are sufficient to exclude placebo response or spontaneous fluctuation.
Oral pain at mealtimes appears to have been one of the dominant baseline complaints.
Sleep disorder, depressive mood, and jitteriness all show an overall downward shift during the application period.
Taste disorder should not be counted among the fig_01.jpg outcomes because it is not one of the plotted VAS domains.
The graph pattern alone is enough to prove that the gel caused the improvement.
Breath-odor scores worsen during gel use and improve only after the gel is stopped.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: fig_01.jpg supports improvement in resting tongue tingling and in the psychosocial domains of sleep disorder, depressive mood, and jitteriness during gel use. Dry-mouth scores remain near zero throughout, and taste disorder is not one of the plotted VAS items in the figure. In contrast, oral pain at mealtimes is not a major baseline complaint on the graph, breath odor improves rather than worsens during treatment, and the figure alone cannot establish causation or rule out placebo effect or spontaneous fluctuation.

items.answer_explanation: fig_01.jpg supports improvement in resting tongue tingling and in the psychosocial domains of sleep disorder, depressive mood, and jitteriness during gel use. Dry-mouth scores remain near zero throughout, and taste disorder is not one of the plotted VAS items in the figure. In contrast, oral pain at mealtimes is not a major baseline complaint on the graph, breath odor improves rather than worsens during treatment, and the figure alone cannot establish causation or rule out placebo effect or spontaneous fluctuation.

items.question_content: A patient develops persistent mild bruxism after being switched from sertraline to venlafaxine 37.5 mg twice daily for generalized anxiety disorder. Her anxiety has remitted (HAM-A = 6) but mild teeth grinding continues. The treating clinician considers adjunctive pharmacotherapy. Which of the following correctly pairs a pharmacological agent reported as a potential treatment option for antidepressant-associated bruxism with an accurate description of its primary pharmacological mechanism?

Gabapentin — direct serotonin reuptake inhibition restoring serotonin-dopamine balance
Low-dose quetiapine — potent 5-HT2 receptor blockade with rapid dopamine receptor dissociation
Metformin — insulin-sensitizing effects reducing central inflammatory mediators
Clonazepam — GABAergic enhancement reducing masticatory muscle hyperactivity
Omeprazole — proton pump inhibition reducing gastroesophageal reflux-associated bruxism
Amitriptyline — selective dopamine D2 receptor agonism in the mesocortical pathway
Tandospirone — 5-HT1A agonism with dopaminergic modulation

items.question_content: A 27-year-old woman developed proptosis, chemosis, eye pain, and ophthalmoplegia a few hours after percutaneous balloon compression for trigeminal neuralgia. Review Figures 2 and 3. In the Barrow classification of carotid-cavernous fistulas, type A is a direct fistula between the internal carotid artery and the cavernous sinus; type B is a dural shunt between meningeal branches of the internal carotid artery and the cavernous sinus; type C is a dural shunt between meningeal branches of the external carotid artery and the cavernous sinus; and type D is a dural shunt between meningeal branches of both the internal and external carotid arteries and the cavernous sinus. Which Barrow type is shown?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: This is an indirect dural carotid-cavernous fistula supplied by meningeal branches of the internal carotid artery, without external carotid contribution. That angiographic pattern corresponds to Barrow type B. Type A is a direct ICA-cavernous sinus shunt, while types C and D include external carotid supply.

items.answer_explanation: This is an indirect dural carotid-cavernous fistula supplied by meningeal branches of the internal carotid artery, without external carotid contribution. That angiographic pattern corresponds to Barrow type B. Type A is a direct ICA-cavernous sinus shunt, while types C and D include external carotid supply.

items.question_content: A 52-year-old woman presents with 5 months of unilateral maxillary tooth pain and right facial numbness. Dental and otologic examinations are unrevealing, and pure-tone audiometry is normal. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Which diagnosis most likely explains this presentation?

question_options.text: Vestibular schwannoma arising from the internal acoustic meatus
Trigeminal schwannoma centered in Meckel cave
Cerebellopontine angle meningioma
Cerebellopontine angle epidermoid cyst

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The MRI shows a cerebellopontine angle mass with intracanalicular extension from the internal acoustic meatus, creating the classic “ice-cream cone” configuration of a vestibular schwannoma. Normal audiometry does not exclude this diagnosis. Trigeminal compression from a larger vestibular schwannoma can produce facial numbness and referred tooth pain. Trigeminal schwannomas are usually centered along Meckel cave, and meningioma or epidermoid cyst typically lack this characteristic intracanalicular origin.

items.answer_explanation: The MRI shows a cerebellopontine angle mass with intracanalicular extension from the internal acoustic meatus, creating the classic “ice-cream cone” configuration of a vestibular schwannoma. Normal audiometry does not exclude this diagnosis. Trigeminal compression from a larger vestibular schwannoma can produce facial numbness and referred tooth pain. Trigeminal schwannomas are usually centered along Meckel cave, and meningioma or epidermoid cyst typically lack this characteristic intracanalicular origin.

items.question_content: In neurovascular compression syndromes causing cranial neuralgia, what is the name of the central-to-peripheral myelin transition zone that is typically vulnerable to pulsatile vessel contact?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The root entry zone is the transition between central oligodendroglial myelin and peripheral Schwann-cell myelin. This segment is especially susceptible to focal demyelination from repetitive vascular pulsation, which can generate ectopic impulses and ephaptic transmission in cranial neuralgias.

items.answer_explanation: The root entry zone is the transition between central oligodendroglial myelin and peripheral Schwann-cell myelin. This segment is especially susceptible to focal demyelination from repetitive vascular pulsation, which can generate ectopic impulses and ephaptic transmission in cranial neuralgias.

items.question_content: A patient has years of stabbing pain confined to the infraorbital distribution, triggered by light touch and function. Imaging is normal, there is no trauma or dental cause, palpation over the infraorbital region reproduces symptoms, and lidocaine block gives complete but short-lived relief. What is the most likely diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The combination of localized infraorbital distribution pain, trigger sensitivity, normal imaging, exclusion of dental and traumatic causes, and temporary complete relief after local anesthetic block supports a primary peripheral neuropathic disorder of the infraorbital nerve. This is most consistent with idiopathic infraorbital neuropathy.

items.answer_explanation: The combination of localized infraorbital distribution pain, trigger sensitivity, normal imaging, exclusion of dental and traumatic causes, and temporary complete relief after local anesthetic block supports a primary peripheral neuropathic disorder of the infraorbital nerve. This is most consistent with idiopathic infraorbital neuropathy.

items.question_content: A 37-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset limited mouth opening and left preauricular/facial pain that was initially suspected to be a left TMJ closed lock. On examination, maximum opening is 13 mm, right lateral excursion is 3 mm, and left lateral excursion is 5 mm. Which specific excursive finding makes a true left TMJ disc displacement without reduction less likely?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: In a true left disc displacement without reduction, the left condyle cannot translate normally, so contralateral/right excursion is usually markedly limited. This patient had only mild limitation of that movement, which argued against a classic left closed lock and supported looking for a non-TMJ source.
objective_exact_answers: only mild limitation of right lateral excursion
only mild limitation of contralateral excursion

items.answer_explanation: In a true left disc displacement without reduction, the left condyle cannot translate normally, so contralateral/right excursion is usually markedly limited. items.question_content:
A 53-year-old woman presents with facial pain and headache that have recurred for more than 30 years, with troublesome episodes 1-3 times per month. She also reports awake clenching and stress-related symptom flares. She has no systemic disease, takes no medication, and does not smoke. Conservative treatments including splint therapy, NSAIDs, and a soft-food diet have not relieved the problem.

On examination, maximum mouth opening is 50 mm with normal eccentric movements. There are no TMJ sounds and no joint pain. Occlusion is stable. Palpation of the masseter and temporalis muscles reproduces familiar pain, but the pain remains localized to the palpated muscles without referral. No other local, joint, dental, or systemic disorder better explains the pain.

Using DC/TMD terminology, what is the full diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The diagnosis used in the case was chronic frequent primary myofascial orofacial pain without pain referral: chronic because it persisted for years, frequent because episodes occurred monthly, primary because no other disorder explained it, and without pain referral because palpation-induced familiar pain did not spread.
objective_exact_answers: chronic frequent primary myofascial orofacial pain without pain referral

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg together with the history, a 35-year-old man has 5 months of parotid-region pain triggered by eating, maximal at the initial mouthful and then waning during the same meal; saliva expressed from the parotid is clear but scant. He has no history of upper-neck surgery and no salivary tumor has been identified. Select all statements best supported by this presentation.

question_options.text: The key discriminator is pain that peaks at the first mouthful and attenuates during the same meal, rather than the gland enlargement itself.
Bilateral swelling in fig_03.jpg effectively excludes a first-bite pain syndrome and should redirect diagnosis to sialadenosis.
fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg being unrevealing do not prove a neuropathic diagnosis, but they do make a calculus, deep-lobe mass, or other major structural cause less likely.
Clear but scanty salivary flow on milking is less consistent with acute suppurative parotitis than with a non-suppurative disorder.
Because the pain is meal-related, obstructive sialolithiasis remains the leading diagnosis even when symptoms diminish after a few bites.
Absence of prior upper-neck surgery or a known parotid/parapharyngeal lesion shifts consideration toward an idiopathic rather than secondary form of the syndrome.
If the dominant finding had instead been persistent painless bilateral parotid enlargement, sialadenosis would be a better fit than this patient’s disorder.
The meal-related pain pattern alone is not sufficient to attribute the pain to diabetic neuropathy rather than considering a first-bite syndrome.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Support comes from the classic within-meal decay of pain, negative structural imaging, clear scant rather than purulent saliva, and lack of surgery/tumor favoring idiopathic over secondary first bite syndrome. Persistent painless bilateral enlargement would suggest sialadenosis instead. Bilaterality and diabetes do not exclude first bite syndrome, and obstructive or infective disorders fit the pattern less well.

items.answer_explanation: Support comes from the classic within-meal decay of pain, negative structural imaging, clear scant rather than purulent saliva, and lack of surgery/tumor favoring idiopathic over secondary first bite syndrome. Persistent painless bilateral enlargement would suggest sialadenosis instead. Bilaterality and diabetes do not exclude first bite syndrome, and obstructive or infective disorders fit the pattern less well.

items.question_content: A 20-year-old woman has a 5-month history of trigger-evoked right-sided facial pain with decreased sensation in V1 and V2. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg from her workup and resected trigeminal cerebellopontine angle lesion. What is the most specific WHO tumor diagnosis?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Perivascular pseudorosettes with GFAP positivity and Olig2 negativity support ependymoma. The absence of brisk mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis supports WHO grade 2 rather than a higher-grade lesion.

items.answer_explanation: Perivascular pseudorosettes with GFAP positivity and Olig2 negativity support ependymoma. The absence of brisk mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis supports WHO grade 2 rather than a higher-grade lesion.

items.question_content: A 20-year-old woman has 5 months of worsening brief electric-shock pain on the right face, triggered by talking, chewing, toothbrushing, wind, and cold, and not relieved by medication. She denies toothache. Examination shows reduced sensation in the right V1 and V2 distributions and mild ipsilateral facial weakness. Review fig_01.jpg first, then fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. From an orofacial pain perspective: (1) classify the pain syndrome and state whether this should be managed as odontogenic pain, classical trigeminal neuralgia, or a symptomatic trigeminal nerve disorder; (2) using the clinical picture plus fig_01.jpg alone, rank the 3 most plausible lesion categories and justify the ranking, including one diagnosis that becomes less likely because of the diffusion sequence; (3) explain how fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg change the final diagnosis and grade; and (4) give the safest immediate management plan, then state how your triage would change if the sensory exam were normal and fig_01.jpg were unrevealing.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
1) This is best classified as secondary trigeminal neuralgia / painful trigeminal neuropathy due to a structural trigeminal nerve lesion, not odontogenic pain and not uncomplicated classical TN. The key reasons are young age, progressive course, medication failure, objective V1/V2 sensory loss, mild additional cranial nerve involvement, and a lesion along the trigeminal nerve on fig_01.jpg.

2) Based on history plus fig_01.jpg alone, a sensible ranked differential is: 
• First: trigeminal nerve sheath or other trigeminal-associated neoplasm causing secondary TN, especially a cystic schwannoma-type process, because the lesion is centered on the pre-Meckel cave trigeminal nerve and there is objective trigeminal sensory deficit. The lack of enhancement makes a typical solid schwannoma less classic, but a nerve-related tumor remains plausible.
• Second: arachnoid/benign CSF-like cystic lesion compressing the trigeminal nerve, because the lesion is T1 low, T2 high, nonenhancing, and lacks diffusion restriction.
• Third: epidermoid cyst is less likely specifically because fig_01.jpg does not show diffusion restriction, which epidermoids usually do. Other rare CPA lesions, including extra-axial ependymoma, remain possible but would be difficult to call confidently from MRI alone.
A strong answer may swap the order of the first two categories if the MRI appearance is emphasized over the focal nerve involvement, but should still recognize a structural trigeminal lesion and use the diffusion finding to down-rank epidermoid.

3) fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg shift the final diagnosis to ependymoma, WHO grade 2. fig_02.jpg shows perivascular pseudorosettes, a classic ependymal pattern. fig_03.jpg shows GFAP positivity and Olig2 negativity, supporting ependymal/glial differentiation and arguing against an oligodendroglial mimic. The absence of high mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis supports grade 2 rather than a higher-grade ependymoma. These tissue findings also move the diagnosis away from schwannoma, which would be expected to show spindle-cell Antoni architecture/Verocay-type features rather than perivascular pseudorosettes.

4) Immediate dental/orofacial management: do not perform extraction, endodontics, or other irreversible dentoalveolar treatment; document pain distribution, trigger pattern, and baseline cranial nerve findings; explain concern for a non-dental trigeminal lesion; provide only supportive symptom management within scope; and arrange urgent neurology/neurosurgery referral for lesion-directed workup and treatment. Safety-net for worsening numbness, corneal/visual symptoms, escalating pain, or new neurologic deficits.

If the sensory exam were normal and fig_01.jpg unrevealing, urgency would decrease and the working diagnosis would move closer to classical TN, although her age would still warrant caution about secondary causes such as demyelinating disease. In that scenario, I would still avoid irreversible dental treatment without dental findings, but referral could be expedited rather than lesion-urgent, focusing on TN-oriented neurologic assessment and medical management rather than immediate neurosurgical triage for a mass lesion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all major findings, including the additional facial weakness and the patient's age, and clearly explains why uncomplicated classical TN or primary dental pain is less likely while avoiding overclaiming a specific histology from MRI alone.

levels.title: Meets

levels.description: Correctly identifies urgent referral for the actual case and explains that a normal sensory exam plus unrevealing fig_01.jpg would reduce urgency and shift consideration toward classical TN while still avoiding routine dental intervention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Calibrates urgency precisely: urgent lesion-focused referral for the actual case because of objective deficits and fig_01.jpg, but only expedited TN-oriented neurologic workup in the counterfactual; also notes that the patient's young age still argues against dismissing symptoms as routine dental pain even if imaging were unrevealing.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction, endodontic treatment, or other irreversible dentoalveolar procedures despite absent odontogenic history, objective V1/V2 sensory loss, and the trigeminal nerve lesion on fig_01.jpg

Severity Misjudged: advising routine dental follow-up or continued empiric management without prompt neurologic/neurosurgical referral despite progressive facial pain and a structural trigeminal lesion on fig_01.jpg

items.question_content: A 54-year-old man has 6 months of severe brief right cheek pain with ipsilateral hemicranial headaches, worsening on anteflexion and not relieved by daily analgesics. Examination shows no facial sensory loss, normal corneal reflexes, and no clear trigger zones. He is an active smoker with ischemic heart disease and takes anticoagulants. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what is the most likely cause of his facial pain, which imaging findings make this secondary rather than classic idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, and what is the most appropriate management strategy now? Justify your plan using lesion anatomy, hemorrhagic/procedural risk, and the patient’s comorbidities.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This is secondary trigeminal neuralgia caused by a right cerebellopontine angle arteriovenous malformation involving or tightly encompassing the cisternal segment of cranial nerve V. fig_01.jpg shows flow-void abnormal vessels around the right trigeminal nerve rather than a simple vascular loop, and fig_02.jpg shows dilated superior cerebellar and AICA feeders plus an arterialized draining vein (“red vein”), confirming an arteriovenous shunt. The associated headache and positional worsening also support an atypical secondary cause rather than classic idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. The next step is urgent multidisciplinary neurovascular management, with definitive angioarchitectural characterization and treatment planning, typically including catheter angiography if not already completed. Because the lesion is symptomatic, small, deep, and in the cerebellopontine region with deep venous drainage, endovascular embolization is a reasonable initial treatment to reduce pulsatile compression and hemorrhagic risk while avoiding the higher morbidity of open resection in this patient on anticoagulation with ischemic heart disease. The draining vein should be preserved until the nidus is controlled. Alternatives such as radiosurgery, microsurgical resection, or microvascular decompression depend on full vascular anatomy and risk profile. Close imaging follow-up is required because incomplete obliteration can leave residual hemorrhage or recurrence risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify secondary trigeminal neuralgia from an AVM; attributes the pain to odontogenic disease, primary idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, migraine, or another unsupported diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes trigeminal neuralgia or a vascular cause but misstates the lesion as a nonspecific vascular loop, tumor, or aneurysm, or fails to localize it to the right cerebellopontine/cisternal trigeminal region.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies secondary trigeminal neuralgia caused by a right cerebellopontine angle AVM compressing or involving the cisternal portion of the trigeminal nerve.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely identifies a right cerebellopontine AVM with shunting physiology involving the cisternal trigeminal nerve and explains the pain mechanism as pulsatile neurovascular irritation/demyelination.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides little or no linkage between symptoms, examination, and imaging, or ignores the figures entirely.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one data source or gives incomplete reasoning, such as citing facial pain without explaining the significance of the MRI vascular findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates unilateral paroxysmal facial pain with fig_01.jpg flow-void vessels around the trigeminal nerve and fig_02.jpg dilated feeders plus an arterialized draining vein to support an arteriovenous shunt as the cause.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes symptoms, normal sensory/corneal exam, atypical headache features, and the specific MRI/TOF findings to explain why this is secondary rather than classic idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends routine dental treatment, only symptomatic analgesics, or nonspecific follow-up without neurovascular referral or lesion-directed management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests referral or treatment but the sequence is unclear, lacks lesion-directed rationale, or proposes an option poorly matched to the anatomy and presentation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends prompt multidisciplinary management with full vascular characterization and lesion-directed therapy; identifies endovascular embolization as a reasonable current strategy for this symptomatic AVM while acknowledging other options.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan: avoid dental irreversible procedures, obtain/confirm detailed angiographic mapping, favor embolization as the initial intervention for this small symptomatic cerebellopontine AVM, preserve venous drainage until the nidus is controlled, and arrange post-treatment imaging follow-up for residual or recurrent AVM.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address hemorrhagic risk, procedural risk, or the impact of anticoagulation and ischemic heart disease.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either AVM rupture risk or treatment complications, but not both, or fails to connect those risks to this patient's anatomy and comorbidities.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Weighs the risk of future hemorrhage from a symptomatic AVM against treatment morbidity and notes that deep venous drainage, cerebellopontine location, anticoagulation, and ischemic heart disease materially affect management choice.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly compares embolization with open surgery, microvascular decompression, and radiosurgery, explaining why a less invasive endovascular approach may be preferred here despite risks such as ischemia or incomplete obliteration.

red_flags: Misattributed Etiology: Attributes the pain to odontogenic disease or uncomplicated idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia despite fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg showing a cerebellopontine arteriovenous shunt involving cranial nerve V.
Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommends tooth extraction, endodontic therapy, or a destructive trigeminal pain procedure without first addressing the MRI-demonstrated intracranial AVM.

items.question_content: A 61-year-old woman has 8 months of daily burning pain involving the tongue and anterior hard palate, present most of the day, without visible oral lesions. Symptoms began after a tooth extraction, but the site healed uneventfully. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension treated with amlodipine, and mild anxiety. Initial evaluation found poor glycemic control, which has since normalized after treatment adjustment, but the oral burning did not improve. CBC, iron/ferritin, vitamin B12, thyroid studies, renal and liver tests, ESR, albumin/total protein, oral examination, cranial MRI, and EEG are otherwise unrevealing. Duloxetine 60 mg/day has provided only partial relief. At this follow-up, you must commit to one management path rather than list options. What is the most defensible working classification now, and what exact next-step sequence would you choose today: re-open the search for a residual secondary driver before escalating symptomatic therapy, or escalate neuropathic treatment now? Defend your choice by linking the extraction history, prior hyperglycemia, amlodipine exposure, negative workup, and partial duloxetine response. State whether pregabalin should be added, substituted, or deferred, the main patient-specific harms you would monitor, and one concrete new finding that would make you change your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible working diagnosis is burning mouth syndrome with overlapping secondary contributors, best framed as secondary-type or mixed persistent neuropathic BMS rather than straightforward primary BMS. She fulfills the syndrome pattern of chronic daily intraoral burning without visible lesions and with otherwise negative investigations, but the post-extraction onset, previously uncontrolled diabetes, possible xerogenic contribution from amlodipine, and anxiety mean the case still carries plausible secondary precipitants. Persistence after HbA1c normalization does not automatically convert the case to primary BMS; it may instead reflect residual neuropathic sensitization after secondary triggers were addressed.

My next-step sequence would be a focused re-check for residual secondary drivers, not a prolonged broad re-workup. Today I would confirm that no persistent post-extraction pathology, candidiasis, salivary dysfunction/xerostomia, contact reaction, or mechanical irritation has been missed, and I would review amlodipine and other xerogenic contributors with the patient’s medical prescriber rather than stopping treatment independently. If that focused reassessment remains unrevealing, I would escalate symptomatic neuropathic management now because etiologic correction and duloxetine have already been insufficient.

Pregabalin is a reasonable next pharmacologic step in that setting. If duloxetine is tolerated and has provided some benefit, adding low-dose pregabalin with cautious titration is defensible; if adverse effects, sedation burden, or polypharmacy are concerns, substitution rather than combination is also reasonable. Counseling and monitoring should focus on dizziness, impaired balance/fall risk, somnolence, constipation, peripheral edema, and overall functional benefit, with reassessment of pain severity, sleep, anxiety, and cumulative CNS effects. A concrete finding that would change my plan would be clear medication-related xerostomia or another persistent local oral cause on repeat assessment, which should be corrected first and could justify deferring pregabalin escalation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify burning mouth syndrome, attributes the presentation to an unsupported alternate diagnosis despite the negative workup, or definitively labels the case as uncomplicated primary BMS without addressing the documented secondary contributors.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes BMS but gives a simplistic classification such as purely primary or purely secondary with limited justification and little acknowledgement of diagnostic overlap.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies BMS and classifies the case as secondary-type, overlapping, or persistent neuropathic BMS after correction of contributors, with a reasonable explanation for why the case is not straightforward primary BMS.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies BMS and explicitly explains the diagnostic tension between primary and secondary forms, showing why healed extraction and normalized glycemia do not erase plausible secondary precipitants or residual neuropathic sensitization.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses isolated facts only and does not integrate chronicity, normal oral findings, laboratory/imaging results, extraction history, comorbidities, medication exposure, and treatment response.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some relevant findings but does not connect the post-extraction onset, prior hyperglycemia, amlodipine exposure, negative workup, and partial duloxetine response into a coherent interpretation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the major data points into a coherent rationale for persistent neuropathic oral burning with unresolved secondary possibilities.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all major clinical data into a clear, internally consistent argument that distinguishes background comorbidity from plausible contributors and identifies the most important focused exclusions still worth revisiting.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not commit to a management path, gives an unprioritized list of options, or recommends immediate escalation or prolonged investigation without case-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a general direction but provides a vague or poorly sequenced plan, or fails to explain why the alternative path is less appropriate in this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a defensible next-step sequence: a focused reassessment of residual local/xerogenic contributors with coordinated medication review, followed by pregabalin escalation if no correctable cause is found and duloxetine remains insufficient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, prioritized plan that balances avoiding diagnostic drift with not overlooking a missed secondary driver, clearly justifies add-on versus substitution of pregabalin, and names a concrete new finding that would appropriately change the plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not discuss the benefits and harms of pregabalin or ignores patient-specific safety issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic adverse effects without linking them to this patient's age, current medications, or functional risks, or without explaining how they affect the add-versus-switch decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately weighs potential symptom benefit against dizziness, impaired balance/falls, somnolence, constipation, edema, and cumulative medication burden, with relevant monitoring priorities.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced benefit-risk discussion that links adverse effects to this patient's context, uses shared decision-making to justify add-on versus substitution, and specifies reassessment or de-escalation if benefit is inadequate or harms outweigh gains.

red_flags: Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Declares definitive primary BMS and escalates treatment without reconsidering persistent local, post-extraction, or xerostomic contributors despite persistent symptoms after glycemic correction.

Generic Textbook Management: Recommends a standard BMS regimen without accounting for the case-specific relevance of prior hyperglycemia, amlodipine exposure, partial duloxetine response, and the need for focused reassessment before or alongside escalation.

items.question_content:
A 19-year-old woman has disabling right-sided deep ear pain that began after a scuba-diving incident 1 year ago. The sharp pain is spontaneous, severe, brief, occurs multiple times daily, and is worsened by cold, stress, and loud noise. She also has a separate constant dull right TMJ/masticatory/cervical pain with clenching. ENT examination, otoscopy, temporal bone CT, and brain/ear MRI show no structural cause for the sharp otalgia. DC/TMD examination shows normal jaw opening and function, but familiar tenderness of the right TMJ and masticatory/cervical muscles. A diagnostic right auriculotemporal nerve block plus right masseter trigger-point injection abolishes only the dull musculoskeletal pain, not the sharp ear pain. Conservative TMD care, splint therapy, physical therapy, sleep/psychological interventions, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, and baclofen have already been tried; gabapentin was only partially helpful and caused limiting adverse effects, and the other medications were not tolerated. ENT has suggested hearing-related management and possible tympanostomy tubes/tonsillectomy, while invasive TMJ procedures are also being considered.

Using Figures 1-3, what is the single best next management step, what is the most appropriate working diagnosis classification level that justifies it, why are ENT procedures and TMJ-directed procedures lower priority, and how would the diagnosis and plan change if the sharp pain had been abolished by the auriculotemporal block?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best next step now is a carefully consented trial of adjunct botulinum toxin A, using the mixed target pattern shown in fig_03.jpg (bilateral masseter and temporalis plus peri-auricular sites), while continuing conservative TMD care and active pain-psychology/sleep management. The working diagnosis that justifies this is possible nervus intermedius neuropathy/neuralgia causing the disabling sharp deep right otalgia, coexisting with painful TMD (right TMJ arthralgia, masticatory/cervical myofascial pain, headache attributed to TMD) and mild bilateral TMJ degenerative change. It should be framed as possible rather than definite because the pain phenotype is highly compatible with nervus intermedius neuralgia, but there is no clear trigger zone on Q-tip/periauricular testing and MRI shows no neurovascular compression or other structural lesion.

Why this is the best next move: she has already had appropriate conservative care and multiple medication trials; gabapentin only partially helped and caused limiting adverse effects, and oxcarbazepine/baclofen were not tolerated. The block result is the key discriminator: local anesthetic abolished only the dull musculoskeletal pain, proving a separate TMD pain generator, but left the paroxysmal deep ear pain untouched, so TMD-directed therapy alone is insufficient. fig_02.jpg shows only mild bilateral condylar erosion and ramus asymmetry, which do not explain severe unilateral neuralgic attacks with normal jaw function. Her poor sleep, depression/anxiety/PTSD-type symptoms, and major functional impact support chronic pain amplification/central sensitization, making a multimodal but non-irreversible escalation reasonable.

ENT/TMJ procedural paths are lower priority because tympanostomy tubes and tonsillectomy do not target the demonstrated pain mechanism, and TMJ invasive procedures are not justified by the mild imaging findings, normal range/function, and failure of TMJ-related diagnostic treatment to affect the sharp otalgia. Hearing aids or audiology management may still be appropriate for hearing loss, but they are for hearing disability, not the neuralgic pain. Skull-base surgery would be premature given normal imaging and lack of a definite trigger pattern.

Botulinum toxin should be presented as an adjunct, not first-line or curative: potential benefits are reduction of both the refractory paroxysmal otalgia and the coexisting myofascial/TMD pain; risks include chewing weakness, asymmetry, local discomfort, and limited evidence base, so follow-up is required.

If the sharp pain had been abolished by the auriculotemporal block, the diagnosis would shift away from possible nervus intermedius neuropathy toward auriculotemporal neuralgia or auriculotemporal-mediated referred otalgia from TMD. In that scenario, management would pivot toward nerve-specific local treatment and musculoskeletal/TMD-focused therapy rather than prioritizing peri-auricular botulinum toxin for suspected nervus intermedius pain.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies coexisting neuropathic ear pain and painful TMD, but does not clearly justify why the neuropathic diagnosis should be framed as possible rather than definite.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies possible nervus intermedius neuropathy/neuralgia as the main source of the sharp otalgia, coexisting with painful TMD subdiagnoses and mild bilateral TMJ degenerative change, and explicitly explains why the diagnosis is possible rather than definite.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates history, exam, selective anesthetic response, and fig_02.jpg to distinguish the dull musculoskeletal pain from the sharp paroxysmal ear pain.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly contrasts the two pain generators, interprets fig_02.jpg as mild/nonspecific structural change insufficient for the chief complaint, uses the negative ENT/MRI/CT workup and negative trigger testing to narrow the diagnosis, and incorporates failed/intolerable pharmacotherapy plus psychosocial/sleep amplification into the reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers several reasonable options but does not prioritize one, or prioritizes a generic repeat-medication approach without addressing why this patient now needs a different escalation path.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes adjunct botulinum toxin now, linked to the refractory mixed neuropathic/TMD phenotype and fig_03.jpg treatment targets, while maintaining conservative care and psychosocial/sleep treatment, and explicitly de-prioritizes tympanostomy, tonsillectomy, invasive TMJ procedures, and neurosurgical escalation at this stage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not discuss treatment tradeoffs, adverse effects, or why less appropriate options should be avoided.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances prior medication benefit versus intolerability and recognizes botulinum toxin as an adjunct rather than first-line or curative therapy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why limited structural findings, normal jaw function, partial but poorly tolerated medication response, major functional burden, and limited evidence for botulinum toxin together justify cautious non-irreversible escalation; also identifies meaningful botulinum toxin risks and the weak pain rationale for ENT/TMJ procedures.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address how the diagnosis would change if the auriculotemporal block had abolished the sharp pain.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that the diagnosis would change, but does not identify the most plausible alternative or how management would shift.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly states that a positive auriculotemporal block would redirect the diagnosis toward auriculotemporal neuralgia or auriculotemporal-mediated referred otalgia and away from nervus intermedius neuropathy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately explains that abolition of the sharp pain by auriculotemporal block would substantially favor auriculotemporal neuralgia or auriculotemporal-mediated referred otalgia/TMD, and explicitly describes the corresponding change in management priority toward nerve-specific local and TMD-focused treatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits needed interdisciplinary care despite hearing loss and psychosocial/sleep comorbidity.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests referral in general terms without linking disciplines to concrete needs in this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately includes ongoing ENT/audiology and psychosocial or sleep-focused care.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Coordinates orofacial pain care with pain psychology/behavioral therapy, sleep management, ENT/audiology for hearing-related morbidity, and physical therapy for the musculoskeletal component, explaining the role of each.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommends tympanostomy, tonsillectomy, invasive TMJ procedures, or skull-base surgery as the next pain treatment despite no structural target and the discriminatory block findings.
Generic Textbook Management: Treats the presentation only as isolated TMD or only as otologic disease, ignoring the separate paroxysmal neuropathic otalgia plus psychosocial/sleep amplification.
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Gives a definitive pain-only plan while omitting ongoing ENT/audiology follow-up for the documented bilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.

items.question_content: A man in his 60s with classic left V2/V3 trigeminal neuralgia had good pain relief from carbamazepine but wanted to avoid dose escalation because of concern about driving and long-term use. MRI showed an AICA loop but no definite compression or displacement of the left trigeminal complex. He underwent percutaneous radiofrequency treatment of the gasserian ganglion. During the procedure, four cannula positions were needed before acceptable V2/V3 sensory stimulation was achieved; the final position was the most cephalad and slightly past the angle formed by the petrosal ridge and clivus. Because the sensory threshold was 0.3 V, lesioning was performed once at 70°C for 60 s rather than starting at 60°C. He was neurologically normal immediately afterward, but the next day developed binocular diplopia; monocular vision remained normal and facial pain was absent. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What cranial neuropathy/localization is most likely? Then rank the 3 most plausible mechanisms for this complication from most to least likely, using both the procedural details and figure findings. Give your first-24-hour management priorities. If trigeminal neuralgia later recurs, recommend your preferred next-step strategy and justify why the equivocal MRI should or should not move you toward microvascular decompression rather than another option. Finally, explain what additional management significance a new absent corneal reflex would have.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely deficit is an isolated left trochlear neuropathy causing superior oblique dysfunction, localizing to the extra-axial left CN IV after decussation rather than to the trochlear nucleus/fascicle. The pattern is binocular diplopia with normal monocular vision after a skull-base trigeminal procedure, without broader brainstem findings.

Most-likely mechanism ranking:
1) Procedure-related hemorrhagic compression/irritation near Meckel’s cave/cavernous-skull-base region. fig_02.jpg shows focal treated-side postprocedural signal best interpreted as a small hematoma; the next-day onset after an initially normal exam also fits a delayed mass-effect/irritative process better than an immediate fixed injury.
2) Direct mechanical injury from needle depth/trajectory. fig_01.jpg shows the steep route through foramen ovale toward the ganglion, and this case required multiple repositionings with a final cephalad tip slightly beyond the petroclival angle, making subtle malposition or local trauma plausible.
3) Secondary thermal spread from lesioning. A single lesion at 70°C for 60 s with a borderline-low sensory threshold makes heat injury possible, but it is somewhat less favored than hemorrhage because fig_02.jpg suggests focal postprocedural bleeding and the patient was initially normal.
A central ischemic event is less likely as the primary explanation for an isolated deficit temporally linked to the procedure, but it remains part of urgent reassessment if other neurologic signs appear.

First 24-hour priorities: urgent reassessment rather than routine reassurance. Perform focused cranial nerve and neuro-ophthalmic examination with ocular motility, pupils, ptosis, facial sensation, corneal reflex, and documentation of whether any additional CN deficits are present. Review the procedure details and postprocedural imaging; if symptoms worsen or the exam is not isolated/stable, obtain or repeat urgent brain/skull-base imaging to exclude enlarging hemorrhage or broader injury. If the deficit remains isolated and the patient is otherwise stable, management is mainly conservative with neuro-ophthalmology/ophthalmology input, temporary occlusion or prism if helpful, driving restriction while diplopic, and close follow-up. Escalate for reduced vision, pupillary abnormality, multiple CN palsies, severe headache, reduced consciousness, new motor/sensory deficits, or radiologic progression.

If TN recurs, this complication should reduce enthusiasm for repeating destructive percutaneous lesioning on the same side. However, the MRI did not show definite neurovascular compression, so microvascular decompression is not automatically the best next step. MRI may miss clinically relevant conflict in some patients with otherwise classic TN, so MVD can still be discussed if the patient is medically fit and willing, but it should be framed as a judgment call rather than an obvious default. Reasonable options are shared-decision re-optimization of medical therapy, a non-percutaneous option such as stereotactic radiosurgery, or MVD if the clinical phenotype strongly supports classic TN and the patient accepts the risks of craniotomy. Repeat RF-G would require especially strong justification and explicit counseling about recurrent cranial nerve injury.

If the corneal reflex is newly absent, that adds more than just “greater severity”: it implies trigeminal sensory injury with immediate risk of exposure/neurotrophic keratopathy. Acute management must add urgent ocular-surface protection (lubrication, possible shield/taping, ophthalmology follow-up), and future planning shifts even further away from repeat destructive percutaneous procedures because additional sensory loss could worsen keratopathy, numbness, or anesthesia dolorosa.

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A man in his 70s has headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and neck pain worsened by head movement. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is the eponymous syndrome name for the right internal jugular venous compression shown?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The figures show internal jugular vein compression between the styloid process and the C1 transverse process. This venous form of styloid-related compression is known as Eagle jugular syndrome, also termed styloidogenic jugular compression. The symptom cluster of headache, tinnitus, visual complaints, and positional worsening supports this diagnosis.

items.answer_explanation: The figures show internal jugular vein compression between the styloid process and the C1 transverse process. This venous form of styloid-related compression is known as Eagle jugular syndrome, also termed styloidogenic jugular compression. The symptom cluster of headache, tinnitus, visual complaints, and positional worsening supports this diagnosis.

items.question_content: A 29-year-old woman has had 3 years of disabling continuous crushing pain with electric shock-like attacks and marked static/thermal allodynia in the right labiomental region after mandibular third molar extraction. She also has a mapped area of intraoral buccal mucosal allodynia. Multiple neuropathic-pain medications were either ineffective or poorly tolerated. A long-acting mental nerve block abolished evoked labiomental pain but not spontaneous pain. She is highly concerned about treatment-induced speech impairment. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. What would be your next interventional management plan, including the anatomic target and sequencing, and why is that preferable to other reasonable next steps in this patient? Use the figures and prior block response in your justification, and state the key adverse effects/outcomes you would counsel and monitor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best next step is a conservative symptomatic trial of perineural botulinum toxin A targeted to the right mental nerve/mental foramen, using a small-volume staged approach rather than injecting at the original third-molar injury site. fig_02.jpg supports iatrogenic injury adjacent to the inferior alveolar nerve, explaining chronic post-traumatic IAN neuropathy; fig_01.jpg shows a separate buccal mucosal allodynic territory, so this is multibranch painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy rather than persistent socket pain. fig_03.jpg identifies an accessible distal terminal branch of the IAN that can be targeted with less procedural morbidity. The prior mental nerve block reducing evoked labiomental pain supports a clinically relevant peripheral target. A remote mental-nerve BTX-A approach is preferable to late surgical exploration or proximal toxin placement because the pain is chronic and refractory, late nerve surgery can worsen neuropathic pain, and proximal injections near the ramus/original injury carry greater risk of toxin spread and functional deficits. Improvement beyond the immediate mental territory would be biologically plausible through retrograde/central antinociceptive effects rather than simple local anesthesia. Because she fears speech impairment, I would begin progressively and reassess after the first injection before extending treatment. Counsel that benefit may be delayed and temporary and monitor pain intensity, trigger-evoked pain, allodynia distribution, lip competence, speech, eating, and facial symmetry.

items.question_content: A 46-year-old patient has 11 years of unilateral, electric-shock facial pain in the V2/V3 distribution, triggered by toothbrushing and chewing. Attacks last seconds, sensory exam is normal, and prior MRI plus trigeminal electrophysiology are normal. Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine-based treatment has been ineffective or poorly tolerated, and the patient wants to avoid destructive procedures if possible. What management would you recommend now, and why is it the best fit for this patient compared with other reasonable options? In your justification, address expected onset and duration of benefit, key counseling points, and what findings would make you reassess the diagnosis or escalate care.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with refractory idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia: classic unilateral brief shock-like triggerable pain in V2/V3, normal sensory exam, and normal MRI/electrophysiology arguing against secondary disease and against classical neurovascular compression. I would recommend botulinum toxin type A as the next step, ideally coordinated through an orofacial pain/neurology service, while keeping the current oral regimen stable initially if tolerated rather than stopping it abruptly. It is the best fit here because first-line sodium-channel blockers have already failed or caused intolerance, the patient prefers to avoid invasive/destructive procedures, and BoNT-A is a reversible, minimally invasive option with evidence for reducing both pain intensity and attack frequency.

I would counsel that benefit is not immediate: onset is usually about 1-2 weeks after injection, and relief is temporary, often lasting around 10-15 weeks or roughly 2-4 months, with marked individual variation, so repeat treatment may be needed and the interval should be individualized to response. It is symptomatic rather than curative, and optimal dose/interval are not fully standardized.

Compared with simply escalating oral drugs, BoNT-A may avoid further systemic adverse-effect burden in a patient already refractory or intolerant. Compared with surgical procedures, it is less invasive and generally has a lower risk of serious complications, although surgery remains appropriate if pain stays disabling despite adequate conservative treatment.

Key counseling points are transient local pain or edema, xerostomia, facial asymmetry or weakness, and possible oral incompetence; these are usually mild and self-limited, but function should be monitored. I would reassess the diagnosis or escalate care if atypical features appear, especially sensory loss, bilateral symptoms, progressive continuous pain dominating the picture, other neurologic deficits, abnormal repeat imaging, or poor response despite appropriate trials.

items.question_content: A 50-year-old man has 7 years of left electric shock-like pain limited to V3, triggered by eating and speaking. Multiple medications and prior Gamma Knife gave no durable relief; his current pain is BNI V and is making oral intake difficult. Review fig_01.jpg (MRI and 3D CTA). What definitive management would you recommend now, and why should the operative strategy be adapted from routine microvascular decompression in this anatomy? In your justification, identify which structure you would prioritize mobilizing, the most suitable surgical corridor, and the key complications that should drive counseling and postoperative surveillance.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is medically and radiosurgically refractory trigeminal neuralgia caused by neurovascular compression on fig_01.jpg, so the next step should be definitive microsurgical decompression at an experienced skull-base/neurovascular center rather than further dental or purely symptomatic treatment. The imaging shows the trigeminal nerve compressed by an AICA arising from a tortuous dolichoectatic vertebrobasilar system. Because that vessel complex is enlarged, rigid, and likely associated with critical perforators, a routine vessel-centered decompression that depends on mobilizing the artery is high risk and may still leave residual contact.

I would therefore prioritize mobilizing the trigeminal nerve rather than the dolichoectatic artery. The best corridor is an anterior transpetrosal skull-base approach because it provides working space in the direction needed for superior/rostral nerve rerouting; opening Meckel's cave to increase nerve mobility is a reasonable part of that strategy. A sling or minimal interposition can then maintain separation while avoiding aggressive basilar/AICA manipulation.

This choice is justified by the severity of pain, failure of medication and Gamma Knife, and the fact that pain is now impairing eating. The main risk avoided by a nerve-centered strategy is brainstem ischemia from stretching or injuring perforators during dolichoectatic vessel transposition. Important complications to discuss and monitor are trigeminal numbness or dysesthesia, diplopia from abducens injury, facial or cochlear nerve dysfunction including hearing loss, CSF leak, venous injury/temporal lobe complications from the petrosal route, and possible foreign-body reaction or granuloma if implanted material is used. Postoperative surveillance should include early clinical pain response plus MRI/CISS to confirm separation and diffusion imaging to exclude infarction, with longer-term follow-up for recurrence or delayed sensory symptoms.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A young woman seen in an orofacial pain clinic has hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, POTS, recurrent joint subluxations, chronic right periscapular pain with palpable trigger points, and daily occipital headaches worsened by neck movement. OTC analgesics, heat/ice, and TENS have helped little. Neurologic exam is normal. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A focal lidocaine trigger-point injection gave >50% relief of the periscapular pain for about a month, but she still reports widespread pain and frequent headaches. Based on the clinical picture and the imaging, what is the most appropriate next management strategy, and why? In your justification, make clear which pain mechanisms are most likely driving her symptoms, why the imaging changes should or should not alter your plan, and what safety precautions would be essential if you escalate treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The dominant problem is most consistent with hEDS-related chronic myofascial/cervicogenic pain with a superimposed nociplastic or central sensitization component, rather than a structural brain or cervical spine lesion that would change management. fig_01.jpg shows only minimal C5-C6 degenerative change without stenosis, and fig_02.jpg shows no cerebellar tonsillar ectopia; with a normal neurologic exam, these findings make myelopathy, radiculopathy, Chiari-related headache, or another intracranial explanation unlikely to be the main driver. The marked but localized benefit from lidocaine trigger-point injection supports a true peripheral myofascial generator, but the persistence of widespread pain and frequent headaches suggests pain amplification beyond a single trigger-point region.

The most appropriate next step is to continue multimodal care and escalate beyond purely local treatment with a monitored trial of intravenous lidocaine, while reserving repeat trigger-point injections for focal recurrences. This is justified because conservative measures have failed, symptoms are widespread, and prior response to lidocaine makes a broader sodium-channel-modulating approach more plausible. Physical therapy should be paced for hypermobility and joint instability, with behavioral support and activity modification maintained.

If treatment is escalated, key precautions are careful pre-infusion screening and monitoring: review weight-based dosing limits, cardiac history and ECG/conduction issues, liver and renal function, current medications, and autonomic symptoms given POTS. During treatment, monitor vitals and mental status for lidocaine toxicity, including perioral numbness, tinnitus, dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, bradycardia, arrhythmia, or seizures. Ongoing benefit should be judged by pain intensity, function, and headache days; if benefit is not meaningful or adverse effects occur, the infusion strategy should be modified or stopped.

items.question_content: A 56-year-old woman has reproducible jaw discomfort only during exertion, typically once her heart rate exceeds about 120 bpm, with prompt relief at rest. She has no traditional or notable nontraditional atherosclerotic risk factors and no chronic cardiac medications. Exercise testing showed ischemic ECG change without wall-motion abnormality. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is the most likely lesion-specific explanation for her symptoms? In your answer, identify the two strongest competing explanations you would still consider, explain which findings in the figures and clinical data make them less likely, and state whether you would recommend continued medical therapy or revascularization at this time. Then explain what specific change in symptoms or objective findings would make you change that recommendation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best unifying diagnosis is referred cardiac jaw pain from stable ischemia caused by a nonatheromatous structural kink/fold of the ostial-proximal left circumflex artery near the left main bifurcation, rather than a primary dental/TMD problem or routine plaque disease. The key lesion-specific point is not simply that there is a coronary narrowing, but that fig_02.jpg shows a focal geometric kink of the LCx origin and fig_01.jpg shows a narrowed eccentric orifice without plaque on intravascular imaging.

Two strong competing explanations are: (1) atherosclerotic ostial LCx stenosis and (2) vasospastic or other nonatheromatous functional ischemia. Atherosclerotic stenosis is less likely because the patient lacks risk factors, the calcium score is 0, and fig_01.jpg IVUS does not show plaque, calcification, or intramural hematoma. Vasospastic or purely microvascular ischemia is less likely because there is a discrete focal anatomic culprit on CT/3D reconstruction and IVUS. The physiology in fig_01.jpg also fits a focal geometric lesion: resting flow is relatively preserved (normal iFR), but hyperemia reveals significant limitation (abnormal FFR), consistent with a lesion that becomes hemodynamically important when demand increases.

At this time I would support conservative cardiology-led management with antianginal therapy tailored to tolerance, exercise guidance, and close follow-up rather than immediate revascularization. That choice is supported by stable, predictable exertional symptoms and the technical difficulty of intervening on an ostial/bifurcation structural lesion. Revascularization is not ruled out, but it is not the preferred first step while symptoms remain controlled and there is no instability. From an orofacial pain standpoint, this should be documented as nonodontogenic secondary jaw pain and unnecessary irreversible dental treatment should be avoided.

I would change course if symptoms became refractory despite medical therapy, occurred at lower workloads or at rest, or if repeat objective testing showed worsening ischemia. At that point, renewed heart-team discussion of revascularization would be appropriate, while acknowledging that PCI is challenging because of the ostial/bifurcation anatomy and limited landing zone, and CABG may also be less attractive if competitive native flow is substantial.

items.question_content: A 44-year-old woman has had 3–4 years of intermittent pain centered in the left maxillary facial region, with a daily background ache and severe attacks associated with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. IBS has been excluded, and a headache clinic diagnosed migraine; triptans and anti-CGRP therapy lessen but do not eliminate attacks. Neurologic and TMJ examinations are normal. Palpation tenderness of the right temporalis and left masseter does not reproduce the chief complaint. Intraorally there is generalized gingival inflammation and percussion sensitivity of the maxillary right first molar. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. The symptomatic side of the face and the tooth-specific findings do not match. What is your most defensible current dental interpretation? State whether you would intervene now, defer, or avoid irreversible treatment, and justify that choice from the figures and examination findings. Rank at least two competing explanations for the facial pain, and specify the follow-up pattern that would make you conclude the molar was only a coincidental finding rather than a contributor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible interpretation is dual pathology with uncertainty: she has a genuine migraine disorder with abdominal features, and she also has a probable odontogenic inflammatory lesion at the maxillary right first molar, most consistent with chronic apical periodontitis with symptomatic percussion tenderness. Generalized periodontal inflammation is an additional inflammatory burden, but by itself it would not explain the long-standing severe unilateral facial attacks.

I would intervene on the maxillary right first molar now, but conservatively and only after confirming concordant endodontic findings; I would avoid irreversible treatment of other teeth and would not extract this tooth as a first choice based only on the atypical facial pain pattern. fig_01.jpg supports a subtle periapical abnormality in the right first molar region, while fig_02.jpg does not reveal a more convincing alternative dental or sinus explanation. The percussion sensitivity provides tooth-specific provocation. In contrast, the facial pain is left-sided, the neurologic and TMJ examinations are normal, and muscle palpation tenderness does not reproduce the chief complaint, so the laterality mismatch creates uncertainty but does not negate the right molar as a real dental problem.

My ranked explanations are: (1) migraine disorder is the best explanation for the severe attacks with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and partial response to triptans/anti-CGRP therapy; (2) right maxillary first molar apical pathology is the strongest dental contributor or amplifier and warrants treatment; (3) myofascial/TMD pain is less likely because examination findings do not reproduce the complaint; generalized gingival inflammation alone is also less likely as the main source of this pain pattern.

The immediate plan is targeted endodontic work-up of the maxillary right first molar (pulp sensibility testing as applicable, percussion/bite testing, periodontal probing, restorability assessment, and correlation with periapical imaging; CBCT only if conventional findings remain equivocal). If findings remain concordant, proceed with tooth-preserving root canal therapy plus periodontal therapy and oral-hygiene control, while coordinating with the treating headache clinician rather than altering migraine medication independently.

The follow-up pattern that would make me conclude the molar was coincidental rather than contributory is this: the tooth becomes clinically quiet, local signs improve, and healing is proceeding, yet the patient’s typical left facial pain, abdominal symptoms, and attack burden remain essentially unchanged. In that situation, the molar was a coexisting dental disease rather than the main driver of the chief complaint, and I would shift emphasis back to non-odontogenic facial pain/migraine reassessment instead of pursuing further irreversible dental treatment.
