items.question_content: A 7-year-old girl originally presented with night pain and difficulty chewing in the lower posterior region. Teeth 74 and 85 underwent pulpectomy on separate visits and were restored with stainless steel crowns. At the 12-month review she is asymptomatic; both crowns are intact clinically, with no swelling, sinus tract, or pathologic mobility. Using the serial IOPARs in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide which tooth you would bring back sooner for the next radiographic review if the family can attend only one additional review in the coming year. Base your answer on the radiographic course over time, not on assumed material-specific behavior. In your justification, identify the main unresolved risk in each tooth, state one specific radiographic change that would make you intervene rather than continue observation in the tooth you prioritized, and explain whether the other tooth would remain under routine observation if it stayed unchanged and symptom-free.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would prioritize tooth 85 for the earlier radiographic recall, ideally sooner than tooth 74, because its unresolved concern is inside the canal system. In fig_02.jpg, the extra-radicular material clears quickly and the furcal area improves, which are favorable signs. However, later there is limited intra-radicular loss of the obturating material that appears stable by 12 months. That does not make the tooth a failure now, but if that intra-radicular loss progresses, the canal seal could be compromised and reinfection could follow.

Tooth 74 is biologically less ideal in a different way. In fig_01.jpg, the apically extruded material persists through 12 months with little or no meaningful extra-radicular resorption. That persistence warrants continued surveillance because retained extra-radicular material may remain irritating. But the intra-radicular fill appears maintained, and there is no clear radiographic progression demanding immediate intervention in an asymptomatic tooth with an intact coronal seal.

So the main unresolved risk in 85 is progressive intra-radicular loss of obturating material; the main unresolved risk in 74 is long-term persistence of extra-radicular material. Between those, I would recall 85 sooner because progression within the canal is more directly relevant to loss of seal and future endodontic failure.

A specific radiographic finding that would change me from observation to intervention in 85 would be further progressive intra-radicular resorption/loss of canal fill compared with the 12-month image, especially if accompanied by a new or enlarging furcal/periradicular radiolucency. Clinical triggers would also include pain, swelling, sinus tract, pathologic mobility, or loss of crown integrity.

If tooth 74 remained radiographically unchanged and symptom-free for another 12 months, I would usually continue observation rather than automatically retreat or extract. Persistent extra-radicular material alone is not sufficient to declare failure if the child remains asymptomatic, the SSC seal is intact, there is no enlarging radiolucency, and the developing successor shows no adverse effect. Its prognosis is more guarded than ideal, but conservative follow-up is still appropriate.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old girl with genetically confirmed congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis presents for definitive dental care. She has intellectual disability, recurrent cellulitis from dental infections, repeated self-inflicted oral injuries, and limited mouth opening from scarring. She is in permanent dentition with multiple missing mandibular teeth; the mandibular incisors are mobile, but pulp vitality testing is not feasible and pain history is unreliable. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. What is the most defensible management strategy at this stage for the mandibular anterior region and prevention of further oral injury, and why is that strategy preferable in this patient?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The priority is hazard reduction and preservation of function, not aggressive definitive reconstruction. fig_01.jpg shows active self-mutilation and scar-related morbidity; fig_02.jpg shows a compromised mandibular dentition; fig_03.jpg supports poor lower anterior prognosis with periapical change and reduced alveolar support. Because pain cannot guide diagnosis and vitality testing is not feasible, I would base decisions on mobility, radiographic support, infection risk, and whether a tooth is acting as a traumatic or aspiration hazard. Any mandibular incisor that is severely mobile or clearly contributes to repeated soft-tissue injury should be extracted selectively; the remaining lower incisors should be retained only if they are sufficiently stable, cleansable, and reviewable at short intervals. I would not remove the whole anterior segment empirically, and I would not prioritize endodontic treatment without evidence that retention is realistic. Prevention of further injury should include smoothing or covering sharp traumatic surfaces with enameloplasty/composite, intensive caregiver-led plaque control, fluoride-based prevention, and frequent recall. A removable appliance is a poor first-line choice here because absent pain perception, poor cooperation, and thin mandibular bone increase the risk of unrecognized mucosal trauma, displacement, and poor tolerance. Any invasive treatment should be coordinated carefully because CIPA increases anesthetic and perioperative risk, especially aspiration and temperature dysregulation. Overall, the best plan is selective removal of immediate hazards, conservative monitoring of salvageable teeth, and an aggressive preventive program to reduce recurrent trauma and infection.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a vague, unsafe, or clearly inappropriate plan; ignores the need to address the mobile mandibular anterior teeth and ongoing self-injury, or recommends blanket treatment without patient-specific rationale.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies either selective management of the lower incisors or injury prevention, but the plan is incomplete, poorly prioritized, or overly aggressive/conservative for the findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a coherent staged plan centered on selective extraction only for teeth with severe mobility/poor support/traumatic or aspiration risk, retention and close review of any stable remaining incisors, and active prevention of further mucosal injury.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Delivers a nuanced, stepwise plan that correctly prioritizes immediate hazards, avoids unnecessary irreversible treatment, defers nonessential reconstruction, and integrates caregiver-based prevention and specialty coordination.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh patient-specific risks, or recommends management that ignores the implications of pain insensitivity, unreliable symptoms, or self-trauma.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some risks but does not connect them convincingly to the chosen management strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why management should be guided by mobility, infection burden, traumatic potential, and aspiration risk rather than pain, and recognizes why routine removable options may be problematic.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances retention versus extraction with clear patient-specific reasoning, including absent protective pain reflex, thin mandibular support, cooperation limits, and anesthetic/autonomic risks when invasive care is needed.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the soft-tissue findings or the radiographic/dental findings, but not both, or uses them superficially.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content:
A 7-year-old girl with genetically confirmed FAM20A-related amelogenesis imperfecta with gingival fibromatosis presents in mixed dentition with marked sensitivity and poor esthetics. She also has congenital adrenal hyperplasia treated with daily corticosteroids, so you should avoid unnecessarily long or extensive surgical treatment in a single visit and favor the least invasive plan that still secures urgent dental function. The parent asks that the front teeth be improved first because of teasing at school. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

Clinical and radiographic findings include generalized thin or absent enamel, abnormal crown form, shortened clinical crowns, flat worn cusps, widespread fibrotic gingival enlargement with secondary inflammation, tooth 16 and tooth 46 fully covered by gingiva, and tooth 26 and tooth 36 partially erupted. Because of cooperation and travel limits, you can provide only one substantial nitrous oxide visit now and a shorter follow-up visit later.

State the first-phase plan you would defend. Identify the specific teeth or regions you would treat in the first operative visit and which abnormal areas you would defer, using the figures to justify why. Explain whether you would perform any soft-tissue exposure in that same visit or stage it until after initial plaque and inflammation control, given the goal of limiting operative stress while still improving access and restorability. Finally, name one clinical or radiographic finding that would make an initially selected posterior tooth a poor preservation candidate for routine protective restoration, such as definite pulpal or periapical disease, severely inadequate remaining coronal structure for coverage, or a major root abnormality, and explain how your plan would change.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The defended first phase is function-first, while still acknowledging the family’s esthetic concern. I would not use the only major visit primarily for anterior esthetic improvement. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show that the more urgent problem is posterior breakdown in erupting first permanent molars: posterior gingival obstruction, partial eruption or full coverage of molars, flat worn cusps, and generalized thin or absent enamel with abnormal crown form. These teeth are the main threat to chewing comfort, continued wear, and loss of posterior support.

In the first operative visit, I would prioritize the most strategic and restorably reachable posterior teeth, especially the partially erupted first permanent molars 26 and 36, together with whole-mouth disease-control measures such as oral-hygiene instruction, plaque reduction, fluoride or desensitizing therapy, and inflammation control. If time, bleeding control, and cooperation remain acceptable, I would extend care to a more heavily covered molar such as 16 or 46, but I would not allow a difficult exposure to consume the entire visit and prevent stabilization of the more accessible strategic teeth. I would defer anterior esthetic rehabilitation and broad nonessential restorative work because they do not best address immediate function, are more technique-sensitive in defective enamel, and are lower priority when follow-up is uncertain.

I would perform only limited soft-tissue exposure in the same visit, and only around posterior teeth that I actually intend to restore during that session. The advantage is immediate access for eruption guidance, hygiene, margin control, and durable protection of teeth that are otherwise hard to clean and highly vulnerable to further wear. However, broader soft-tissue surgery would increase chair time, bleeding, postoperative discomfort, and recurrence risk, and it would create more operative stress in a child on daily corticosteroids for CAH. Therefore, I would avoid full-mouth gingival surgery or esthetic gingival reshaping in the first phase and keep exposure targeted to teeth in which exposure directly improves restorability and short-term prognosis.

A finding that would make one of the initial posterior targets a poor preservation candidate would be definite pulpal or periapical pathology, severely inadequate remaining coronal structure for predictable coverage, or a major root abnormality that makes the tooth non-restorable. In that situation, I would not proceed as if it were a routine protective-crown tooth. I would reassess for pulp therapy, temporization, specialist input, or another strategic occlusal or space-management plan rather than automatic full coverage or automatic extraction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes comprehensive anterior esthetics, vague full-mouth care, or other lower-yield treatment without protecting strategic posterior function in this limited-access mixed-dentition case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that some care is more urgent than others, but does not clearly commit to specific first-visit targets and deferrals grounded in the case constraints.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes posterior stabilization and disease control over lower-priority esthetic work, and identifies reasonable areas to defer in light of limited visits and uncertain follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Selects specific strategic posterior teeth or regions from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg for the first operative visit, explicitly defers competing esthetic or lower-impact care, and justifies the sequence with a persuasive response to the parent's request without losing functional priorities.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or no case-specific evidence from fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, or the medical history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figure or history findings, but does not clearly connect them to access, eruption status, wear, restorability, or sequencing.

levels.title: Meets

items.question_content: A 6-year-old girl in primary dentition presents with 1 month of increasing mobility and intermittent abscess associated with the maxillary left primary central incisor. She is otherwise healthy and has a history of trauma to the same region 2 years earlier. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, identify the most likely diagnosis and state the single best management for today. Justify your answer from the figures and the clinical history. In your reasoning, address the main competing diagnosis, explain how the radiographic relationship to the adjacent primary lateral incisor and permanent successors affects management, and state the key extraction-related hazard that should modify technique.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The single best management today is extraction of the symptomatic anomalous primary incisor unit, with routine local measures for pain and infection control as needed.

The most likely diagnosis is fusion of the maxillary left primary central incisor with a supernumerary tooth. The clinical photographs support a double-tooth anomaly, and the radiograph shows separate internal canal anatomy within the enlarged tooth structure, which favors fusion rather than a routine traumatic deformity. A further associated root-level union by concrescence may be suspected in this case, especially with the trauma history, but the essential diagnosis needed for management from the provided figures is a fused primary incisor with a supernumerary component.

The main competing diagnosis is gemination. Gemination is less convincing because the radiographic appearance is more consistent with union of two tooth components rather than attempted division of a single tooth germ. Concrescence alone is also less convincing as the primary explanation because it would not account for the enlarged anomalous crown form seen clinically.

Extraction is preferred because the tooth is already symptomatic, with recurrent abscess and increasing mobility, and its anomalous anatomy makes long-term maintenance unpredictable. The panoramic radiograph shows that the adjacent primary lateral incisor is present and the permanent successors are present, so removal of this infected primary tooth is acceptable and should be followed by monitoring of healing and eruption.

The key operative hazard is difficult extraction due to abnormal union and atypical root form, with risk of fracture or trauma to adjacent structures and the developing permanent successor. Therefore, extraction should be performed carefully and atraumatically, avoiding excessive force and planning for possible unusual resistance.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Using current vascular-anomaly terminology that specifies both channel type and hemodynamic class, what is the most specific short designation for this lesion?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Bland ectatic channels contain blood in some spaces and lymph-like proteinaceous material in others, with predominant CD34 and focal D2-40 indicating combined venous and lymphatic differentiation. There is no evidence of a proliferative vascular tumor or arterial/high-flow component. The most specific modern term is a low-flow venous-lymphatic (venolymphatic) malformation.

Biopsy of one of the mucocutaneous lesions shows the histopathologic pattern classically associated with necrolytic migratory erythema. What is this pattern called?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Necrolytic migratory erythema is characterized histologically by superficial epidermal necrosis with separation of the upper epidermis, often with inflammatory infiltrates. The recognized shorthand term is epidermal laminar necrosis.

Based on the microscopic findings, which absent feature supports solid odontogenic keratocyst rather than keratoameloblastoma?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Calretinin is typically positive in stellate reticulum-like ameloblastic epithelium but not in solid odontogenic keratocyst. In this case, the absence of stellate reticulum-like change and reverse polarization, along with OKC-type corrugated parakeratinization, supports an expected negative calretinin result.

absence of stellate reticulum-like change and reverse polarization

items.question_content: A 25-year-old woman has a salivary intraductal carcinoma in the right retromolar/parapharyngeal region. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Apocrine-type intraductal carcinoma is typically androgen receptor (AR) positive, whereas intercalated-type intraductal carcinoma is typically S100 positive. In this case, the tumor shows focal apocrine and intercalated-type morphologic features, but both AR and S100 are nonreactive. What is the most appropriate subtype designation?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Apocrine-type IDC is typically AR positive, whereas intercalated-type IDC is S100 positive. This case had mixed morphologic hints but lacked both defining immunophenotypes, so the lesion should not be forced into either subtype and is best left unclassified/no subtype assigned.

items.question_content: A 67-year-old woman underwent maxillary sinus augmentation with simultaneous implant placement. Using the radiographic findings in fig_01.jpg and the histology in fig_02.jpg panel h, what is the most likely diagnosis?

This combination supports an atypical late sinus graft infection rather than a grafting void or surgical ciliated cyst.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A 13-year-old girl has recurrent, painless, multifocal exophytic lesions of the buccal mucosa and lips. She has a history of treated palmar warts and nail-biting, and biopsy confirms a low-risk HPV-associated papillary squamous proliferation. Which diagnosis is most likely?

question_options.text: Oral squamous papilloma
Condyloma acuminatum
Verruca vulgaris
Multifocal epithelial hyperplasia

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The clinical papillary exophytic morphology and histology showing a benign papillary squamous lesion with koilocytic HPV effect support oral squamous papilloma. Condyloma acuminatum is a key distractor because it is often multiple and HPV 6/11-related, but the reported pathologic interpretation here is papilloma. Verruca vulgaris and multifocal epithelial hyperplasia are plausible alternatives yet have different typical architecture and clinicopathologic patterns.

Verruca vulgaris and multifocal epithelial hyperplasia are plausible alternatives yet have different typical architecture and clinicopathologic patterns.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old boy has delayed eruption of the maxillary left central incisor with an asymptomatic anterior maxillary swelling. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Histopathology of the excised lesion showed enamel matrix, tubular dentin, primitive dental papilla, and cementum-like material, with no ghost cells and no cyst lining. Which specific differential diagnosis is most directly weakened by the absence of ghost cells?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Ghost cells are a key clue for odontogenic ghost cell lesions. Their absence makes odontogenic ghost cell tumor much less likely in this case, favoring compound-complex odontoma when integrated with the calcified mixed-pattern lesion.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. An 8-year-old boy has a year-long, painless, slow-growing submucosal swelling of the left buccal mucosa, and imaging shows no bony involvement. Which diagnosis is most likely?

question_options.text: Pleomorphic adenoma
Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Polymorphous adenocarcinoma

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The cytology and histology are classic for adenoid cystic carcinoma: basaloid cells, prominent hyaline globules, and a cribriform/tubular architecture in hyalinized stroma. Pleomorphic adenoma would be expected to show chondromyxoid stroma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma shows mucous/intermediate/epidermoid cells, and polymorphous adenocarcinoma is less characterized by the prominent hyaline globules and classic ACC-type cribriform pattern seen here.

items.question_content: A 33-year-old man presents with a recurrent mandibular swelling 10 years after conservative treatment of an ameloblastic fibroma. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Which diagnosis best fits the current lesion?

question_options.text: Odontogenic carcinosarcoma
Ameloblastic fibrosarcoma
Ameloblastic carcinoma
Ghost cell odontogenic carcinoma

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The lesion is a biphasic malignant odontogenic tumor: fig_02.jpg shows odontogenic epithelial islands with ameloblast-like peripheral cells and cytologic malignancy, along with a malignant ectomesenchymal component. Malignancy in both components defines odontogenic carcinosarcoma. Ameloblastic fibrosarcoma has malignant mesenchyme but benign epithelium, while ameloblastic carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy without a malignant mesenchymal counterpart.

items.answer_explanation: The lesion is a biphasic malignant odontogenic tumor: fig_02.jpg shows odontogenic epithelial islands with ameloblast-like peripheral cells and cytologic malignancy, along with a malignant ectomesenchymal component. Malignancy in both components defines odontogenic carcinosarcoma. Ameloblastic fibrosarcoma has malignant mesenchyme but benign epithelium, while ameloblastic carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy without a malignant mesenchymal counterpart.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What keratinization pattern best describes the cyst lining?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The lining is thin and lacks a surface keratin layer, which is characteristic of a typical dentigerous cyst. Recognizing a nonkeratinized lining helps distinguish it from keratinizing odontogenic lesions such as odontogenic keratocyst or orthokeratinized odontogenic cyst.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. When distinguishing oral focal mucinosis from irritation fibroma with myxoid degeneration, what single histologic parameter is most useful?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The key discriminator is how extensive the myxoid component is. In OFM, myxoid change is broad/extensive, whereas in irritation fibroma it is typically only focal.

items.answer_explanation: The key discriminator is how extensive the myxoid component is. In OFM, myxoid change is broad/extensive, whereas in irritation fibroma it is typically only focal.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg from the palatal lesion. What overall growth pattern is the key histologic clue in this tumor?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Infantile myofibroma characteristically shows biphasic architecture: hypercellular hemangiopericytomatous areas of primitive-appearing cells and hypocellular fascicular areas of spindle myofibroblasts. Recognizing this overall pattern is a major clue for distinguishing it from other pediatric spindle-cell tumors.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. This lesion was diagnosed as lipoma with reactive/degenerative changes. Which findings, if present instead of the current profile, would most strongly redirect the diagnosis toward dysplastic lipoma rather than either this diagnosis or atypical lipomatous tumor / well-differentiated liposarcoma? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: Nuclear MDM2 positivity in atypical adipocytic or stromal cells
Nuclear CDK4 positivity in atypical adipocytic or stromal cells
Loss of nuclear Rb expression in the atypical adipocytic cells
Diffuse p53 overexpression in most atypical cells
Numerous CD68/CD163-positive vacuolated stromal cells explaining the lipoblast-like appearance
Diffuse p16 positivity in tumor and stromal cells
A well-demarcated lesion with striking adipocyte size variation, patchy single-cell fat necrosis, and scant spindle/collagenous stroma
MDM2 amplification on FISH

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Dysplastic lipoma is supported by Rb loss, p53 overexpression, and its characteristic morphology: a well-demarcated lesion with marked adipocytic variation, patchy single-cell fat necrosis, and scant spindle/collagenous stroma. MDM2/CDK4 positivity or MDM2 amplification instead supports ALT/WDL. Histiocytic markers, p16, and similar nonspecific stains do not specifically favor dysplastic lipoma.

items.answer_explanation: Dysplastic lipoma is supported by Rb loss, p53 overexpression, and its characteristic morphology: a well-demarcated lesion with marked adipocytic variation, patchy single-cell fat necrosis, and scant spindle/collagenous stroma. MDM2/CDK4 positivity or MDM2 amplification instead supports ALT/WDL. Histiocytic markers, p16, and similar nonspecific stains do not specifically favor dysplastic lipoma.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old woman has asymptomatic bilateral posterior mandibular lesions found incidentally. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. The lesions were removed as solid non-cystic masses, and microscopy shows fibrovascular connective tissue containing irregular newly formed bony trabeculae with osteoblastic rimming. Which diagnosis best fits?

question_options.text: Conventional ossifying fibroma
Fibrous dysplasia
Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia
Odontogenic keratocyst

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The combination of a well-demarcated jaw lesion, surgical separation as a solid mass, and fibro-osseous histology with bony trabeculae and osteoblastic rimming is most consistent with conventional ossifying fibroma. Fibrous dysplasia typically blends into adjacent bone rather than shelling out. Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia is usually multifocal but is not a discrete encapsulated neoplasm. Odontogenic keratocyst is a cystic epithelial lesion, not a fibro-osseous mass.

Fibrous dysplasia typically blends into adjacent bone rather than shelling out. Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia is usually multifocal but is not a discrete encapsulated neoplasm. Odontogenic keratocyst is a cystic epithelial lesion, not a fibro-osseous mass.

items.question_content: A 13-year-old boy has a retained primary maxillary canine and failure of eruption of the permanent successor. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. Which diagnosis is most strongly supported when the radiographic and microscopic findings are correlated?

question_options.text: Central odontogenic fibroma, epithelium-rich type
Hyperplastic dental follicle
Dentigerous cyst
Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The lesion shows an enlarged asymmetric pericoronal radiolucency plus a cellular fibrous stroma containing prominent strands and nests of odontogenic epithelium with calcified material. No cystic epithelial lining is identified, arguing against a dentigerous cyst. Hyperplastic dental follicle is usually more symmetric and less convincingly neoplastic. AOT commonly occurs near impacted canines, but its characteristic duct-like epithelial pattern is not shown here. Overall, the combined clinicopathologic picture best fits epithelium-rich central odontogenic fibroma.
