items.question_content:
A publicly funded oral-health program for physically active community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older will pilot the same 3-item intake in Brazil and Portugal. Only 10% of screened participants can receive an intensive multidisciplinary review. Bite-force dynamometry is not available at intake, and the 12-month program endpoint cannot reuse the adapted frailty category because bite force was part of that frailty definition.

Use the baseline evidence below together with fig_01.jpg (Brazil) and fig_02.jpg (Portugal), which show estimated marginal means of bite force by dental prosthesis use and antidepressant use.

Given baseline facts:
- Sample: 499 physically active older adults with functional dentition; 295 in Brazil and 204 in Portugal.
- Frailty categories were non-frail (G0), pre-frail (G1), and frail (G2).
- Sex was associated with frailty in both countries and in the total sample:
  - Brazil: chi-square = 23.531, p < 0.001. Men were overrepresented in G0 and G1, while women were overrepresented in G2.
  - Portugal: chi-square = 29.654, p < 0.001. Men were overrepresented in G0, men and women were similar in G1, and women were overrepresented in G2.
  - Total sample: chi-square = 43.363, p < 0.001.
- Antidepressant use was associated with frailty in Portugal and in the total sample, but not in Brazil:
  - Brazil: chi-square = 0.173, p = 0.917.
  - Portugal: chi-square = 14.247, p < 0.001. In Portugal, non-use was more common in G0, use and non-use were similar in G1, and antidepressant use was more common in G2.
  - Total sample: chi-square = 10.806, p = 0.005.
- Dental prosthesis use was not associated with frailty:
  - Brazil: chi-square = 1.069, p = 0.586.
  - Portugal: chi-square = 1.105, p = 0.575.
  - Total sample: chi-square = 4.331, p = 0.115.
- Bite-force analysis:
  - Brazil: dental prosthesis use had a significant main effect on bite force, F(1,290) = 11.088, p < 0.001; participants without prostheses had higher bite force than those with prostheses. Antidepressant use was not significant, F(1,290) = 0.133, p = 0.716. The prosthesis-by-antidepressant interaction was not significant, F(1,290) = 0.655, p = 0.419.
  - Portugal: dental prosthesis use was not significant, F(1,200) = 0.481, p = 0.489. Antidepressant use was not significant, F(1,200) = 0.389, p = 0.534. The prosthesis-by-antidepressant interaction approached but did not reach significance, F(1,200) = 3.817, p = 0.052. Robust reanalysis also did not confirm a significant interaction.
- The evidence is cross-sectional, so associations should not be interpreted as causal.
- Denture fit, stability, and age of prosthesis were not measured.

Using only the information above and the figures:
1. Specify the 3 intake items you would use in both countries.
2. State the single referral trigger you would actually activate in Brazil.
3. State the single referral trigger you would activate in Portugal.
4. For each country, defend your chosen trigger against the strongest rejected alternative trigger.
5. Identify one misleading conclusion a naive reader could draw from fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg if the inferential results were ignored.
6. Choose one non-circular 12-month endpoint for the program.
7. Explain how your Brazil and Portugal referral rules would change if sex-based referral criteria were later prohibited.

Your justification should balance empirical enrichment, actionability for an oral-health service, equity, and statistical caution.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
A strong shared 3-item intake is: (1) biological sex, (2) current antidepressant use, and (3) a brief oral-function item such as chewing difficulty, denture instability, or perceived poor denture fit. Prosthesis presence can be recorded as context, but it should not be the sole oral item because prosthesis use itself was not associated with frailty in either country.

For Brazil, if sex-based triage is allowed, the single referral trigger I would activate is female sex. The reason is that sex was clearly associated with frailty in Brazil (p < 0.001), whereas antidepressant use was not associated with frailty there (p = 0.917), and prosthesis use was also not associated with frailty (p = 0.586). This makes female sex the strongest available frailty-enrichment signal in the Brazilian cohort under the 10% cap. I would still collect the oral-function item in everyone because it is actionable for dental care and fig_01.jpg is consistent with lower bite force among prosthesis users in Brazil.

The strongest rejected alternative trigger in Brazil is prosthesis-based triage, whether phrased as prosthesis presence alone or overinterpreting fig_01.jpg. I would reject it because the prosthesis-frailty association was not significant, and fig_01.jpg addresses bite force rather than frailty. The bite-force finding may justify closer oral assessment, but not using prosthesis presence alone as the main frailty-oriented referral trigger. I would also reject antidepressant use as the Brazil trigger because it showed no frailty association in Brazil.

For Portugal, the single referral trigger I would activate is current antidepressant use. In Portugal, antidepressant use was associated with frailty (p < 0.001), with use more common in the frail group, while prosthesis use was not associated with frailty. This trigger is also clinically actionable because it can prompt medication review, mental-health coordination, falls-risk review, xerostomia review, and oral-function follow-up.

The strongest rejected alternative trigger in Portugal is the apparent prosthesis-by-antidepressant subgroup pattern suggested by fig_02.jpg, or female sex alone. I would reject the figure-based subgroup trigger because the interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.052) and robust reanalysis did not confirm it. I would also reject prosthesis presence alone because it was not associated with frailty. Female sex is defensible because sex was associated with frailty in Portugal, but antidepressant use is more directly actionable for multidisciplinary review and remains supported by the country-specific frailty association.

A misleading conclusion would be that fig_02.jpg proves a real interaction between prosthesis use and antidepressant use in Portugal and therefore identifies a high-risk subgroup for referral. That would be incorrect because the interaction was not statistically reliable and robust methods did not confirm it. Another misleading conclusion would be that fig_01.jpg proves prosthesis use causes frailty in Brazil; the figure only shows a bite-force pattern and the evidence is cross-sectional.

A suitable non-circular 12-month endpoint is change in objectively measured maximum bite force from first definitive assessment to 12 months. This avoids reusing the adapted frailty category and is plausibly modifiable through oral rehabilitation, denture adjustment, nutritional counseling, and follow-up. It should be interpreted as a functional oral outcome, not as proof that frailty itself changed.

If sex-based referral rules are later prohibited, Brazil changes the most. I would replace female-sex referral with the oral-function item, especially chewing difficulty or denture instability/poor fit, while keeping sex only for audit and equity monitoring. Portugal would remain primarily antidepressant-triggered, with sex removed from referral but retained for monitoring disparities. In both countries, I would continue to avoid using prosthesis presence alone as the referral trigger because it was not associated with frailty in either cohort.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not provide a feasible shared 3-item intake plus country-specific trigger selection, or uses dental prosthesis presence alone as the main trigger in either country.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a plausible intake and at least one defensible trigger, but does not clearly handle the 10% referral cap, gives the same trigger to both countries without strong justification, or does not identify and reject plausible alternatives.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a feasible shared 3-item intake centered on sex, antidepressant use, and oral function or denture-related difficulty; selects a defensible Brazil trigger and Portugal trigger that fit the stated cohort results and service constraints; explicitly rejects strong alternatives for each country; and addresses how the rules change if sex-based referral is prohibited.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misstates key findings, such as claiming prosthesis use was associated with frailty, denying the Portugal antidepressant association, or treating the figure patterns as proof of statistically reliable frailty effects.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some correct findings but misses important country contrasts, omits major inferential limits, or weakly distinguishes descriptive bite-force patterns from frailty associations.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately integrates that sex was associated with frailty in both cohorts, antidepressant use was associated with frailty in Portugal but not Brazil, prosthesis use was not associated with frailty, fig_01.jpg is compatible with higher Brazilian bite force among participants without prostheses, and fig_02.jpg shows only a descriptive crossover pattern because the interaction was not statistically significant and robust checks did not confirm it; also notes the cross-sectional design and lack of denture-fit data as limitations.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores major tradeoffs, overclaims causality, or chooses a circular endpoint such as the adapted frailty category.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges some tradeoffs, but does not adequately weigh enrichment yield against actionability and equity, or proposes an endpoint weakly connected to what the program can realistically change.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly balances empirical enrichment, modifiability and actionability for oral-health services, equity concerns, and statistical caution; explains why prosthesis presence alone is a weak trigger; and chooses a non-circular 12-month endpoint that the program could plausibly improve, such as measured bite force or completion of a multidisciplinary care plan, with justification.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives conclusions with little or no logical link between the stated findings, figures, and the proposed program design.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some reasoning, but the path from evidence to trigger choice, rejected alternatives, figure caution, endpoint, or policy adaptation is incomplete or fragmented.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a clear, stepwise argument linking the stated cohort findings and figure interpretation to the 3-item intake, the selected and rejected triggers in each country, the figure-related caution, the non-circular endpoint, and the contingency plan if sex-based referral is no longer allowed.

items.question_content: A 22-year-old man has a slowly enlarging intraosseous maxillary lesion extending into the maxillary sinus. Incisional biopsy raised the differential of solid odontogenic keratocyst versus keratoameloblastoma. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Which diagnosis is best supported?

question_options.text: Solid odontogenic keratocyst
Keratoameloblastoma
Calcifying odontogenic cyst
Primary intraosseous squamous cell carcinoma

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The figures show corrugated parakeratin lining, palisaded hyperchromatic basal cells, satellite cysts, and bland solid epithelial islands with low mitotic activity. There is no stellate-reticulum-like change, reverse nuclear polarization, or dysplasia. That profile supports solid odontogenic keratocyst over keratoameloblastoma, calcifying odontogenic cyst, or primary intraosseous squamous cell carcinoma.

items.answer_explanation: The figures show corrugated parakeratin lining, palisaded hyperchromatic basal cells, satellite cysts, and bland solid epithelial islands with low mitotic activity. There is no stellate-reticulum-like change, reverse nuclear polarization, or dysplasia. That profile supports solid odontogenic keratocyst over keratoameloblastoma, calcifying odontogenic cyst, or primary intraosseous squamous cell carcinoma.

items.question_content: Your practice can intensify supportive periodontal care for only 20% of adults this year, and the software can auto-flag only one PD-based threshold at first pass. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg from a 10-year follow-up of 1887 adults with baseline and repeat PD recording. State the single rule you would implement, whether clinician override should be exceptional or routine, and one conclusion from these figures that you would not allow staff to turn into patient counseling or irreversible treatment planning.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would auto-flag the highest baseline mean-PD quintile for intensified supportive periodontal care, with clinician override kept exceptional rather than routine. The 20% capacity limit matches a top-quintile rule exactly, and mean-PD ranking is the strongest single operational choice because fig_01.jpg shows its longitudinal behavior: people starting in the first or fifth baseline quintile usually remain in the same or an adjacent follow-up quintile rather than crossing the whole distribution. That makes ranked baseline mean PD a reasonably stable first-pass marker for concentrating scarce recall capacity.

fig_01.jpg also shows that participants starting in the fifth quintile and remaining in upper follow-up quintiles carry clearly higher tooth loss than those starting in the first quintile. fig_02.jpg adds the critical nuance: the baseline curves are most clearly separated for the group that later lost 3 or more teeth, with a right shift for mean PD and for PD extent, especially PD >=4 mm. By contrast, the no-loss and 1-2-tooth-loss groups overlap much more. So the rule is defensible as a population-level way to enrich the recall pool for heavier future burden, not as a precise predictor of minor tooth loss in an individual.

Override should be exceptional because a routine override system would undermine the purpose of having one reproducible first-pass rule. Overrides can still be allowed for clearly documented chairside findings that make the automated flag misleading, but they should remain uncommon and auditable.

The conclusion I would forbid is either: 'patients in the top PD stratum are destined to lose teeth unless recall is shortened' or the mirror image 'patients below the cutoff are safe.' The figures support risk enrichment, not determinism. Tooth loss is multifactorial, separation is much stronger for >=3 teeth lost than for 1-2 teeth lost, and PD alone should not be used to justify irreversible treatment such as extraction. Staff should present the flag as a trigger for closer periodontal review and maintenance, not as a patient-level forecast or a stand-alone treatment indication.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg meaningfully, or misreads them; gives only a generic claim that deeper PD is associated with worse outcomes.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one figure well, or uses both figures only superficially; may mention higher PD and tooth loss but misses either the same/adjacent-quintile persistence in fig_01.jpg or the stronger separation of the >=3-tooth-loss group in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates both figures into the policy choice: uses fig_01.jpg to support stability of ranked mean PD over time and fig_02.jpg to show that higher baseline PD distributions are associated with greater later tooth loss, especially at the severe end.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses figure-specific patterns precisely and in a decision-relevant way: identifies the same/adjacent-quintile clustering in fig_01.jpg, distinguishes the much clearer right shift for the >=3-tooth-loss group in fig_02.jpg from the heavier overlap for 1-2 teeth lost, and ties those observations to why the chosen rule is suitable for first-pass triage rather than precise individual prognosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No clear implementable rule, or the proposal ignores the 20% capacity limit and one-threshold constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a general direction but not a usable first-pass rule; cutoff is vague, or override policy is undefined or impractically broad.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Defines a workable PD-based first-pass rule and states a clear stance on override use that fits the constrained setting.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, operational policy tailored to the constraint, including a defensible cutoff and a disciplined override policy that preserves the value of the automated first-pass triage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Treats the PD rule as deterministic, or rejects it outright without addressing the practical benefit of a simple PD-based triage tool.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either usefulness or limitations, but not both; the prohibited conclusion is generic or not well justified by the figures.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the practical value of a simple PD-based allocation rule against important limitations such as multifactorial tooth loss, imperfect individual prediction, and the danger of over- or under-reassuring patients.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies a specific tempting but invalid inference that staff should avoid, and explains from the figure patterns why it would be unsafe in counseling or treatment planning, including why PD alone should not drive irreversible decisions or label lower-ranked patients as secure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is unsupported, internally inconsistent, or disconnected from the proposed policy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Some logic is present, but the links between the figures, the chosen threshold, override policy, and prohibited conclusion are only partly developed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Reasoning is clear and coherent, showing how the figure patterns lead to the operational rule and the communication limits.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Reasoning is explicit, disciplined, and clinically coherent throughout; it clearly separates group-level triage utility from patient-level prediction and from treatment justification.

items.question_content: You are advising an NHS commissioner after the sudden loss of a 31,772-UDA practice in St Pauls, Bristol. Only one 12-month temporary NHS contract can be placed in one nearby hub, and no extra total UDAs beyond the lost contract are available. Examining fig_01.jpg, where should the replacement capacity be centred to recover access most efficiently, and what is one policy claim about access that you would explicitly avoid making from this map alone?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The first temporary contract should be centred to serve the St Pauls-Montpelier western or northwestern catchment rather than being chosen only because the closed premises sat in that locality. In fig_01.jpg, the largest deterioration after closure appears across the neighbouring west/northwest LSOAs around E01014670, E01014671, E01014563, E01014487, and E01014489, which shift into lower SPAI bands. By contrast, the LSOA containing the closed practice changes less, and the east/southeast remains relatively buffered because another provider is still present there. Under a fixed-UDA, single-site constraint, the best use of the contract is where it relieves the largest spillover competition across several adjacent neighbourhoods, not simply where the building closed.

If the former site is the only operationally viable location and still covers that degraded cluster, it could still be used, but the justification should be catchment recovery, not home-postcode replacement. One policy claim I would avoid is that this map proves residents in the most affected areas could not obtain appointments or that the closure directly worsened oral health outcomes or inequity. fig_01.jpg is a modeled, car-based spatial accessibility surface; it does not measure realized booking success, underlying need, private substitution, public-transport access, or cross-boundary care.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify a plausible priority location, treats the impact as uniform, or proposes a site unsupported by the spatial pattern in fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broad area such as St Pauls/Bristol or defaults to the former premises, but gives limited justification and does not prioritize the most affected cluster under the single-site constraint.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes a hub serving the western or northwestern St Pauls-Montpelier catchment and links the choice to wider post-closure accessibility loss rather than simple proximity to the former practice.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly argues that the first hub should target the neighbouring west/northwest cluster with the strongest deterioration, noting that the practice's own area is not the worst-hit and that some eastern areas remain comparatively buffered.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or no evidence from fig_01.jpg, or merely restates that a closure reduces access.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: References a general local decline but does not use a specific visual contrast from fig_01.jpg to support the recommendation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Cites at least one figure-specific contrast not stated in the stem, such as stronger downgrades in west/northwest LSOAs or relative preservation of access to the east/southeast.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates two or more figure-specific elements, such as named LSOAs and/or the contrasting persistence of access near the eastern provider, and correctly explains the broader spillover effect of supply competition.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the fixed-UDA, one-hub constraint or assumes extra capacity can simply be added everywhere.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges limited resources but provides little reasoning about why the proposed site would restore more access than other plausible placements.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that with only one temporary contract, the preferred location should maximize aggregate access recovery by reducing competition across several affected neighbourhoods.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances efficiency and equity under the fixed-resource constraint, and recognizes that using the former premises is acceptable only if it strategically serves the most degraded catchment rather than merely replacing capacity at the same postcode.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Makes an unsupported claim that the map proves actual appointment failure, worsened oral health outcomes, or causal inequity effects.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a vague caution that the map has limits but does not specify what claim should be avoided.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States one clear policy claim that should not be made from fig_01.jpg alone, such as direct inference about realized appointments or oral health outcomes.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: States a clear unsupported claim and explains why it is unsupported by identifying omitted factors such as private substitution, non-car travel, cross-boundary use, appointment acceptance, or underlying need.

items.question_content: A district school oral-health team is adding a sugar-reduction and activity programme in primary schools. It already collects height and weight and can fund only one additional child-reported outcome domain this year. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. The figures summarize focus-group work with 159 children aged 8–13 years from six countries: children proposed outcomes for school healthy-lifestyle programmes, then rated each outcome with a traffic-light system (green = very important, orange = important, red = not important). In fig_02.jpg, outcomes marked with an asterisk were rated overall as very important. Because participants were recruited pragmatically, some groups were online and others in person, and ratings were visible within groups, these findings should guide planning but not be treated as a universal ranking for all children. Which single child-reported domain should the team add first, and what specific overclaim should it avoid when presenting its decision?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best single additional child-reported domain is healthy diet. In fig_02.jpg, healthy diet is one of the most widely repeated outcomes across countries and is marked as overall very important. For a school oral-health programme focused on sugar reduction, it is also the most directly actionable child-reported domain and is more specific than a broad construct such as being healthy. It adds information that complements, rather than repeats, height and weight.

The team should avoid claiming that healthy diet is the single universal top priority for children in all settings or that the figures establish a definitive rank order of child priorities across countries. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show cross-country variation in reported outcomes, and the stem states that recruitment was pragmatic, delivery mode differed, and ratings were visible within groups. These data support healthy diet as a strong first choice for this programme, not a universal hierarchy of what all children value most.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses no clear domain, repeats height or weight as the added domain, or selects a domain without a defensible link to the programme aim or the one-domain constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a plausible domain but gives limited justification or does not explain why it is preferable under the single-domain budget.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses a defensible first domain—ideally healthy diet—and explains that it is child-valued, relevant to sugar reduction and oral health, actionable in schools, and not duplicative of existing anthropometry.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes healthy diet with a clear constraint-based rationale and explicitly compares it with at least one reasonable alternative such as being healthy, having fun, or feeling happy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures or misreads the displayed patterns.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only a general statement that some outcomes were rated highly, with little figure-based support.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly uses fig_02.jpg to note that the chosen domain is among the more widely repeated and overall very important outcomes, and uses fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg to recognize cross-country variation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately links specific visual patterns to the decision, such as healthy diet being one of the most widely reported starred outcomes in fig_02.jpg while fig_01.jpg shows variation across countries and little red scoring.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: States no limitation or makes an unsupported universal claim about what children value.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a vague caution but does not identify the specific overclaim that should be avoided.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Clearly states that the team should not claim a universal or definitive cross-country ranking of child priorities from these data.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: States the overclaim precisely and explains why it is unsupported using the scenario details about pragmatic recruitment, mixed online/in-person groups, visible ratings, and heterogeneity across countries.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a conclusion with little or no logical connection between the decision and the stated caution.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives some rationale, but the choice of domain and the limitation statement are weakly connected.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a coherent explanation linking the chosen domain to programme goals and linking the caution to what the figures and scenario can and cannot support.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a concise, well-integrated argument that both justifies healthy diet as the best first addition and explains why that practical choice does not justify overgeneralization.

items.question_content: As oral-health coordinator for four Palestinian refugee camps, you can fund one 12-month adolescent education program delivered through schools and primary-care teams, but you cannot increase clinic capacity or substantially expand the number of information sources available. A household cross-sectional survey of 300 adolescents aged 11–16 found mean oral-health-knowledge 5.7/7 and counted source number, not source quality. Reviewing 12903_2025_5836_Fig2_HTML.jpg, 12903_2025_5836_Fig3_HTML.jpg, and 12903_2025_5836_Fig4_HTML.jpg, which single health-literacy domain should be the first program target, and what is the most important policy claim you would refuse to make from these data?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The first target should be communication health literacy. Under a one-program constraint, it has the strongest leverage because the figure for communication shows the effect of using more information sources on oral health knowledge operating through the mediator: the indirect path is significant and the direct path is no longer significant, which is the clearest pattern of full mediation. That means simply having access to multiple sources is not enough; adolescents need the skills to ask questions, clarify messages, and discuss oral health information effectively with adults and health workers so information can be converted into knowledge. Functional health literacy is worth supporting, but it is a secondary target because its figure shows only partial mediation: basic reading/comprehension helps, yet some association remains outside that pathway. Confusion health literacy should not be the first target because its indirect effect is not significant.

The key claim to refuse is a causal one: I would not tell funders that increasing the number of sources, or even improving communication health literacy alone, will necessarily cause better oral health knowledge. These are cross-sectional mediation data, so direction cannot be established; reverse causation is plausible, and unmeasured confounding may explain part of the association. I would also avoid claiming that more sources are inherently better, because the survey counted source quantity but not source quality or reliability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not choose a health-literacy domain, or prioritizes source expansion/another action that ignores the stated one-program constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a plausible domain but not the strongest first target, or gives a mixed multi-target answer without a clear priority under the resource constraint.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects communication health literacy as the first target and explains that it is the highest-yield first focus given only one 12-month program.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Selects communication health literacy and justifies it as the first target while appropriately positioning functional literacy as supportive/secondary and confusion literacy as not first-line on the available evidence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the mediation figures or provides no figure-specific support.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses the figures in a general way but does not correctly distinguish the different mediation patterns across the three figures.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly cites the visual pattern that in 12903_2025_5836_Fig2_HTML.jpg the indirect effect is significant while the direct effect is not, indicating full mediation, and contrasts this with either 12903_2025_5836_Fig3_HTML.jpg or 12903_2025_5836_Fig4_HTML.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately contrasts all three figures: communication shows full mediation, functional shows partial mediation because both indirect and residual direct effects remain, and confusion shows no significant mediation; ties this directly to the program choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Makes or endorses a causal claim from these data, or implies the chosen program is proven to improve oral health knowledge.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that causality is limited but does not specify the main claim to avoid or the reason that claim is unsupported.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Refuses a causal policy claim and grounds that refusal in the cross-sectional design, noting reverse causation or unmeasured confounding as plausible alternatives.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Refuses the key causal claim and clearly explains that cross-sectional mediation does not establish direction; additionally notes that the survey measured number of sources rather than their quality/reliability, so one cannot claim that more sources are inherently beneficial or that the chosen mediator is the sole mechanism.

items.question_content: A health ministry expects another 6-week shutdown. It can fund one operational reform for subsidized adult dental care, cannot add treatment slots or change reimbursement, and its routine data still miss urgent non-subsidized visits. Using fig_01.jpg, argue for the single reform you would implement first; your justification should rely on the visual pattern in the figure, explain why you reject at least one plausible alternative first move, identify the one observation in fig_01.jpg that most limits any simple message that equity was preserved, and state whether your choice would change if the minister’s primary objective shifted from preserving overall continuity to specifically protecting low-income adults.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My first reform would be a system-wide continuity mechanism for clinically necessary subsidized care, such as centralized triage with protected rebooking and recall/backlog management, rather than an income-targeted allocation rule as the initial move. fig_01.jpg shows that the dominant event during lockdown is a large downward shift in subsidized care for every income decile. In the adjusted panel, the lockdown line is close to horizontal, which suggests little observable within-scheme income gradient during the shutdown itself. The unadjusted panel shows only a small irregularity around the lowest decile before and after lockdown, and that pattern weakens after adjustment. Under fixed capacity, the primary problem therefore looks like broad service interruption, not a strong income-specific skew within subsidized claims.

A plausible alternative first move would be income-targeted outreach or reserving operational attention primarily for lower-income groups. I would reject that as the first reform because fig_01.jpg does not show a large lockdown-specific income gradient within subsidized care that would justify making income-targeting the main operational response ahead of restoring continuity for everyone eligible for subsidized treatment. Targeted monitoring or outreach could still be added later as a safeguard, especially for the lowest deciles, but it is not the best first use of a single reform under these constraints.

The observation in fig_01.jpg that most limits any simple statement that equity was preserved is that the lockdown line is flat but markedly lower across all deciles. That means the figure supports a descriptive claim of broadly shared reduction in recorded subsidized use, not proof of equitable access in any comprehensive sense. The data do not capture urgent non-subsidized visits, unmet need, deferral, or outcomes, so one cannot claim that overall dental access was equal, that need was met equally, or that the shutdown itself caused fair access. Similar-looking claim patterns could still coexist with unequal hidden unmet need.

If the minister changed the objective from preserving overall continuity to specifically protecting low-income adults, I still would not switch to a purely income-targeted first reform on these data alone. I would keep the same continuity reform but modify it with targeted safeguards, such as audit-triggered follow-up for lower-income deciles or monitoring of rebooking completion by income, because fig_01.jpg suggests any income pattern is secondary to the system-wide collapse. Only if additional data showed that low-income adults were disproportionately dropping out through unmet need outside the subsidized claims system would a primarily income-targeted first reform become the better choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads fig_01.jpg, ignores the figure-dependent pattern, or claims that lockdown clearly produced a strong income gradient within subsidized care without support from the figure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that subsidized use fell during lockdown but gives an incomplete reading of the income-decile pattern, relies on only one panel, or does not distinguish adjusted from unadjusted visual information.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg to show that lockdown was associated with a marked decline in subsidized care across all income deciles and that the observed within-scheme income gradient during lockdown is small; interpretation is grounded in the visual pattern and addresses adjusted versus unadjusted information at least briefly.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately interprets both panels and adds a figure-dependent nuance not telegraphed by the stem, such as the near-horizontal adjusted lockdown line and the modest lowest-decile irregularity before or after lockdown that attenuates with adjustment, then uses that nuance to sharpen the policy conclusion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes a first reform that is inconsistent with the stated constraints, or gives no meaningful basis for why that reform should take priority over other plausible options.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a plausible reform but provides limited prioritization logic or does not clearly reject at least one reasonable alternative first move.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a feasible first reform that addresses the dominant problem shown in fig_01.jpg and explicitly explains why at least one plausible alternative would be lower priority under fixed capacity and unchanged reimbursement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear hierarchy of actions, showing why the chosen first reform is most defensible under shutdown constraints and why rejected alternatives are better treated as secondary safeguards, monitoring steps, or contingent responses.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Treats fig_01.jpg as proof of comprehensive or causal equity, or ignores the fact that urgent non-subsidized visits are not captured.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions at least one limitation or tradeoff but does not show how that limitation should change the policy recommendation or public message.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains how fixed capacity and the restricted outcome measure (subsidized claims only) shape both the recommended reform and the limits of any equity claim.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes recorded subsidized use from unmet need or overall dental access and shows why this distinction materially tempers both reform design and what can responsibly be said about equity during shutdown.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions without a logical chain from figure interpretation to reform choice, rejected alternative, limitation, and response to the changed objective.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some reasoning but leaves one or more key links underdeveloped, such as why an alternative is rejected or whether the recommendation changes when low-income protection becomes the primary objective.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a coherent argument linking the visual evidence in fig_01.jpg to the first reform, the main reporting boundary, the rejected alternative, and whether the recommendation changes under the revised objective.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a disciplined argument that explicitly states whether the reform changes under the new objective and, if not, how the design would be modified, with each step logically tied back to what fig_01.jpg does and does not show.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What tissue formation is characteristically absent in this lesion?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: A lack of bone formation is a classic microscopic clue in non-ossifying fibroma. It helps distinguish this lesion from other jaw lesions that produce osteoid or woven bone.

items.answer_explanation: A lack of bone formation is a classic microscopic clue in non-ossifying fibroma. It helps distinguish this lesion from other jaw lesions that produce osteoid or woven bone.

items.question_content: A 12-year-old boy with unremarkable medical history presents with right mandibular swelling, no pain or paraesthesia, persistence of 85, distal tipping of 44, a firm non-tender buccal bulge from 44 to 46, no lingual expansion or infection, and failure of eruption of 45. fig_01.jpg shows a 13 × 18 × 11.5 mm well-circumscribed radiopaque cluster with a radiolucent rim between 44 and 46, mild buccal cortical thinning, lingual displacement of 45, and no inferior alveolar nerve displacement. After conservative first-stage removal with extraction of 85, fig_02.jpg shows residual apical calcified tissue and 45 resting against the lingual cortical plate. At this exact decision point, would you proceed to second-stage enucleation now or observe first with orthodontic space management? Give one definitive plan and justify it from the figures and clinical findings; explain why the competing option is less appropriate here, when orthodontic traction should still be avoided, and the single follow-up change that would most strongly make you choose the opposite plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is a compound odontoma causing impaction and lingual displacement of 45. At the fig_02.jpg decision point, I would proceed with second-stage conservative enucleation now rather than observe first. The decisive finding is postoperative CBCT evidence of residual calcified tissue still in the apical/eruption pathway while 45 is already displaced against the lingual cortical plate; with retained 85 removed but 44 distally tipped, continued observation risks persistent mechanical obstruction, space loss, worsening malposition, and more difficult later orthodontics. The aim is complete but tooth-preserving clearance of the residual odontoma, preserving cortical plates, the follicle/developing 45, adjacent roots, and the inferior alveolar nerve, with all tissue sent for histopathology. After clearance, review healing and eruptive progress clinically and radiographically over the next months; orthodontics should maintain or regain space and later guide alignment. Active traction should still be avoided until the obstruction has been removed and there is either failure of spontaneous eruption despite adequate space or a planned exposure can be done safely. The competing observation-first option is less appropriate here because fig_02.jpg does not show a clear eruption path. The single change that would most strongly make observation-first preferable would be postoperative imaging showing no residual calcified tissue interposed in the eruption path together with early spontaneous eruptive movement of 45 and adequate space.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as a non-odontogenic process, routine infection, or another clearly incorrect primary diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an odontogenic lesion or odontoma but does not correctly identify compound odontoma as the leading diagnosis, or gives the wrong subtype without justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a compound odontoma obstructing eruption and displacing tooth 45.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies compound odontoma and distinguishes it from plausible alternatives using the clustered denticle-like radiopacities, radiolucent rim, patient age, and eruption disturbance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use the clinical findings or figures to justify the decision.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings or mentions fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg superficially without linking them to the treatment threshold.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the painless presentation, persistence of 85, distal tipping of 44, buccal bulge, fig_01.jpg lesion morphology, lingual displacement of 45, lack of inferior alveolar nerve displacement, and fig_02.jpg residual calcified tissue into a coherent explanation of the management problem.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why the asymptomatic presentation and preserved nerve position do not negate the importance of fig_02.jpg, and shows how the residual obstruction, lingual position of 45, and risk of space loss together change the management threshold.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives an unsafe plan, avoids choosing between re-operation and observation, or prioritizes orthodontic traction before resolving whether residual obstruction remains.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a plan but sequences the priorities unclearly, or lists both options without clearly stating which comes first and why.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a coherent first step and correctly places management of residual obstruction before active orthodontic traction.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically selects immediate second-stage conservative enucleation as the best first priority at the fig_02.jpg decision point, explains why observation-first is less appropriate in this anatomy, and names the single change that would reverse that choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not discuss meaningful risks, benefits, or alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic surgical or orthodontic risks without tying them to this child’s anatomy and postoperative CBCT findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the risks of re-entry surgery (damage to the follicle/root of 45, cortical injury, adjacent root injury, neurosensory risk) against the risks of leaving residual calcified tissue (persistent impaction, malposition, space loss, prolonged orthodontic treatment).

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly compares immediate second-stage conservative surgery with observation-first in this specific case and explains why each major risk matters given the lingual position of 45, buccal cortical thinning, and non-displaced inferior alveolar nerve.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate or incomplete plan, such as observation alone despite residual obstruction, immediate traction through residual lesion, or unnecessary extraction of 45.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests surgery or orthodontics but gives an incomplete sequence, omits histopathology or follow-up, or does not address timing of traction.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan including conservative second-stage clearance of residual tissue, preservation of tooth 45 and surrounding bone, histopathologic assessment, postoperative radiographic review, orthodontic space management/guidance, and traction only if spontaneous eruption is inadequate after clearance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise sequence with clear postoperative monitoring goals, explains why traction should be deferred until adequate space and persistent failure of eruption are demonstrated, and states that observation-first would be acceptable only if follow-up showed a clear eruption path without residual calcified obstruction.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommending extraction of the developing tooth 45 even though it remains potentially salvageable and the inferior alveolar nerve is not displaced.
Generic Textbook Management: Advising routine observation or immediate orthodontic traction despite fig_02.jpg showing residual calcified obstruction adjacent to a lingually displaced 45.
Misattributed Etiology: Treating the fig_01.jpg lesion as simple inflammatory/periapical disease and recommending endodontic or antibiotic-only management despite classic odontoma features.

items.question_content: A healthy 10-year-old boy is referred after orthodontic imaging detects a small asymptomatic defect near the mandibular left lateral incisor. The lower anterior teeth are vital. There is no swelling, dysesthesia, trauma history, or salivary-flow abnormality. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide how you would manage this lesion at this stage. State your leading diagnosis, the main competing diagnoses you must still consider, and whether you would observe, obtain further confirmation, or proceed to surgical exploration/biopsy. Justify your choice using the patient’s age, the lesion’s location/relationship to cortex and adjacent teeth, and the specific risks of under- versus overtreatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My leading diagnosis is an anterior static bone cavity (anterior lingual mandibular salivary gland depression) related to the sublingual gland. fig_01.jpg favors a small lingual cortical depression rather than a true intraosseous periapical lesion, and the lower anterior teeth are vital and asymptomatic, so inflammatory endodontic disease is unlikely. fig_02.jpg shows the sublingual gland abutting the lingual cortex, which supports a gland-related defect, but it is not definitive and does not reliably exclude a salivary neoplasm.

The critical alternatives are a sublingual gland tumor and less likely odontogenic cystic/tumorous lesions presenting near the incisor apex. Because this lesion is in the anterior mandible, the patient is unusually young, and anterior defects are harder to diagnose than classic posterior Stafne defects, I would not treat the tooth endodontically or extract it, and I would not simply dismiss the finding as a benign variant with no plan.

My management would be specialist-led confirmation while preserving the tooth and surrounding structures. Given the rare pediatric anterior location and equivocal MRI, limited lingual surgical exploration/incisional biopsy is justified to obtain histopathology and exclude a sublingual gland neoplasm. If biopsy must be deferred, only close short-interval follow-up with repeat cross-sectional imaging would be acceptable. If benign salivary tissue/static bone cavity is confirmed, no aggressive osseous treatment is needed; any soft-tissue/periosteal defect can be repaired and the area monitored radiographically for stability or bone fill.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misreads fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg, treats the lesion as a generic periapical problem, and does not use tooth vitality, asymptomatic presentation, or lingual cortical localization in the reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case data but misses a key element such as the lingual cortical defect on CT or the sublingual gland relationship on MRI; reasoning is incomplete or internally inconsistent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the asymptomatic exam, vital lower anterior teeth, normal panoramic impression, CT evidence of a localized lingual cortical defect, and MRI showing adjacent sublingual gland contact to support a likely non-odontogenic gland-related process while acknowledging residual uncertainty.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely explains why the lesion is better localized to the lingual cortex than the alveolar/apical bone, why pulpal disease is unlikely, and why the MRI finding is supportive but not definitive for benign SBC.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differential or attributes the lesion to a clearly inappropriate cause.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists possible lesions but does not prioritize them or connect them to the specific clinical and imaging findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes anterior static bone cavity/lingual mandibular salivary gland depression and considers key alternatives such as sublingual gland neoplasm and odontogenic cystic or tumorous lesions; explains why periapical inflammatory disease is less likely.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically ranks alternatives based on age, anterior location, tooth vitality, and imaging, and clearly identifies a salivary-gland neoplasm as the critical diagnosis not to miss.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends extraction, endodontic treatment, apicoectomy, or dismissal without a follow-up or diagnostic pathway.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests observation or biopsy but without a clear rationale, tooth-preservation strategy, or follow-up plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends conservative specialist management that preserves the tooth and seeks diagnostic confirmation—preferably limited lingual exploration/incisional biopsy or, if deferred, close short-interval imaging follow-up—with histopathology if tissue is obtained.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a stepwise, patient-specific plan: explain uncertainty to the family, avoid irreversible dental treatment, pursue tissue diagnosis because of the rare anterior pediatric presentation and equivocal MRI, use a lingual approach aimed at confirming benign salivary tissue versus neoplasm while minimizing morbidity, and tailor follow-up to the result.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address the consequences of missed serious disease or unnecessary intervention.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either the risk of surgery or the risk of observation, but not both in a patient-specific way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the low-probability but important risk of a salivary neoplasm against the morbidity of surgery in a child, and explains why a typical 'no treatment' approach to SBC is less secure in this unusual anterior presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced discussion of under- versus overtreatment that specifically incorporates the child’s age, anterior mandibular site, small asymptomatic nature of the defect, need for tooth preservation, and the rationale for a low-threshold tissue diagnosis despite benign-appearing features.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending root canal treatment, apicoectomy, or extraction of the vital mandibular left lateral incisor as primary management despite a lingual cortical defect and no evidence of pulpal disease

items.question_content: A 47-year-old man presents with a 2-year painless enlargement of the left cheek that is now cosmetically bothersome. He denies numbness or drainage. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg as if you are seeing the case sequentially. Before histology, state your leading diagnosis and two other clinically plausible buccal-space lesions you would still keep in mind. Then choose your preferred management pathway and surgical access, justifying why it is appropriate in this patient and naming the strongest alternative strategy you are rejecting. After reviewing fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg, explain the final diagnosis, the main reason you cannot claim a histologically margin-negative excision, and how that limitation should affect follow-up and counseling. In your reasoning, identify one figure-based feature that most lowers concern for malignancy and one preoperative finding that would have pushed you away from your chosen access or workup.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Preoperatively, the leading diagnosis is a benign lipomatous tumor arising in the buccal fat pad, most likely a lipoma/fibrolipoma of the buccal space. The strongest figure-based feature lowering concern for malignancy is the well-circumscribed fatty lesion on fig_01.jpg with fat signal/intensity behavior and no meaningful enhancement or invasive appearance. Two plausible alternatives that should still be considered are: (1) an atypical lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma, because a fatty cheek mass can rarely mimic a benign lipoma, though that is less likely here given the circumscription and lack of aggressive imaging features; and (2) a buccal-space salivary lesion or accessory parotid/minor salivary neoplasm, because cheek masses may arise from salivary tissue, although the imaging here is much more consistent with fat. Other reasonable alternatives would include buccal fat pad herniation/pseudolipoma or a vascular/soft-tissue lesion if the imaging were different.

My preferred management pathway is direct excisional biopsy with complete macroscopic removal through an intraoral approach. In this patient the lesion appears localized to the buccal fat pad, accessible from the vestibule, and benign-appearing, so transoral access gives direct entry while avoiding a facial scar and limiting unnecessary external dissection. fig_02.jpg is relevant because the parotid duct papilla must be identified and protected; dissection should proceed carefully through mucosa and buccinator with awareness of Stensen’s duct, buccal branches of the facial nerve, and nearby facial vessels. A strong rejected alternative is a transcutaneous/external approach: I would not choose it first here because the imaging does not show a large posterior, parotid-related, skin-adherent, or infiltrative lesion requiring wider exposure. I also would not insist on preoperative biopsy first in a small resectable benign-appearing fatty mass when excision will both diagnose and treat it. A preoperative finding that would push me away from this plan would be an ill-defined or enhancing non-fatty component, extension toward parotid/masticator space or skin, rapid growth, fixation, nerve deficit, or nodal disease; those would favor tissue diagnosis first and/or broader exposure.

After fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg, the final diagnosis is fibrolipoma. fig_04.jpg shows mature bland adipocytes separated by fibrous septa, without cytologic atypia, lipoblasts, pleomorphism, or mitotic activity, supporting fibrolipoma rather than atypical lipomatous tumor. The main reason I cannot claim a histologically margin-negative excision is that the specimen in fig_03.jpg was removed in multiple fragments rather than as an intact oriented specimen, so formal microscopic margin assessment is not reliable. That limitation should be discussed with the patient: prognosis is still excellent because this is a benign lesion and complete macroscopic excision is usually curative, but periodic follow-up is appropriate because fragmented excision of a multilobulated buccal fat pad lesion makes completeness of removal a clinical rather than histologic judgment. Counseling should include watching for recurrent cheek fullness/asymmetry or symptoms suggesting local recurrence, as well as postoperative ductal or facial nerve dysfunction, although neither would be expected with an uncomplicated course.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as primarily inflammatory, vascular, or clearly malignant without support, or does not provide a coherent diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign cheek mass but does not localize it well or does not distinguish the preoperative working diagnosis from the final histologic diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a benign lipomatous lesion of the buccal fat pad/buccal space preoperatively and correctly states the final diagnosis as fibrolipoma after fig_04.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies the preoperative lesion as a benign lipomatous buccal fat pad mass and the final diagnosis as fibrolipoma, while explicitly explaining that imaging supports a lipomatous lesion but histology is required to establish subtype and exclude atypical lipomatous pathology.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful differential diagnosis or lists implausible alternatives unrelated to a buccal-space mass.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists alternatives but does not explain why they are plausible or less likely in this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives at least two clinically plausible alternatives for a buccal-space lesion and uses case or figure findings to explain why they are lower priority than a benign lipomatous tumor.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically contrasts at least two strong alternatives, such as salivary neoplasm, atypical lipomatous tumor, buccal fat pad herniation, or other soft-tissue lesions, and clearly states which additional findings would have favored those diagnoses.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or makes figure-based claims that are inconsistent with the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings from either the history or one figure but does not build a sequential argument from preoperative to postoperative data.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the history with fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg for preoperative reasoning and fig_03.jpg/fig_04.jpg for postoperative reasoning, including a figure-based feature that lowers concern for malignancy and recognition that specimen fragmentation limits interpretation of margins.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the case sequentially and explicitly distinguishes what can be concluded at each stage: imaging localizes and characterizes the lesion, surgery provides definitive tissue, gross fragmentation limits margin assessment, and histology confirms fibrolipoma while arguing against malignant adipocytic tumor.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an unsafe or inappropriate plan, such as ignoring the need for definitive diagnosis, choosing an unjustified radical approach, or omitting key anatomic considerations.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends surgery or biopsy in general terms but does not justify the management pathway or access choice for this lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends direct excisional biopsy/complete macroscopic excision through an intraoral approach, justifies that choice for a localized benign-appearing buccal fat pad lesion, and identifies key structures such as Stensen’s duct and relevant nerve/vascular anatomy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, patient-specific plan for transoral excision, names and rejects a strong alternative strategy such as external exposure or biopsy-first management with sound reasoning, and identifies a specific preoperative feature that would shift management toward broader exposure and/or preoperative tissue diagnosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no prognosis or follow-up plan, or gives a prognosis inconsistent with the benign histology.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States only that prognosis is good after excision, without addressing the implications of fragmented removal.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that prognosis is excellent after complete excision of a benign fibrolipoma but that fragmented, multilobulated removal prevents formal histologic confirmation of negative margins and therefore justifies periodic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides realistic counseling that the lesion is benign and likely cured by complete macroscopic excision, but clearly explains why piecemeal removal makes completeness a clinical judgment, and outlines appropriate surveillance for recurrence, asymmetry, or local ductal/facial nerve sequelae.

items.question_content: A 67-year-old man has a 3-month history of a painless, bony-hard swelling of the mandibular anterior-left alveolar ridge with displacement of nearby teeth but no tooth mobility or mucosal ulceration. An incisional biopsy has already been performed. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, what definitive management would you recommend now? Justify your plan using the visible clinical, radiographic and histologic features, including whether you would obtain any further imaging before treatment, how extensive the surgery should be, and how you would monitor the patient afterward.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The lesion is most consistent with a benign osteochondroma of the anterior mandible. The key reasons are the hard exophytic alveolar swelling, the mixed-density bony lesion on the panoramic image in the symphysis/left parasymphysis region, and the histology showing a cartilage cap with orderly chondrocytes transitioning into bone with fibrous tissue rather than destructive atypia. Because the lesion is enlarging, sizeable, and already causing tooth displacement and lingual vestibular obliteration, definitive treatment should be surgical rather than observation.

Before surgery, I would obtain CBCT or CT to define the 3-dimensional extent, attachment to the mandible, cortical/medullary continuity, relation to roots, lingual cortex, floor of mouth, and the mental/incisive neurovascular structures. The panoramic image is insufficient for precise surgical planning.

My treatment would be conservative but complete local excision/ostectomy of the mass, removing the cartilaginous cap and its bony base to normal bone. Stable teeth should be preserved if they are not directly involved; displacement alone is not a reason for extraction. I would not choose radical resection because the figures support a benign surface osteocartilaginous lesion without clear aggressive destruction, ulceration, or mobility. If cross-sectional imaging or pathology suggested irregular destructive behavior, then I would escalate work-up and reconsider the surgical extent.

Important operative risks are injury to adjacent roots, mental/incisive nerve damage, lingual soft-tissue or floor-of-mouth injury, contour defect, and recurrence if the cap/base is incompletely removed. Follow-up should include periodic clinical review and interval imaging to detect recurrence and the very rare malignant transformation. The patient should be advised to report new pain, rapid enlargement, paresthesia, ulceration, or functional change promptly.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management such as simple observation despite progressive deformity, nonsurgical care only, or unjustified radical resection/extraction without reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that surgery is needed but gives a vague or incomplete plan; does not define the extent of excision, omits the need to remove the cartilaginous cap/base, or does not address preservation of uninvolved teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends preoperative cross-sectional imaging and conservative complete excision/ostectomy of the lesion including the cartilaginous cap and base, with preservation of stable uninvolved teeth when feasible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan: obtain CT/CBCT for extent and anatomic relations, perform complete local excision to normal bone with rationale for a conservative approach, preserve teeth unless directly involved, and state when escalation to wider surgery/work-up would be justified by aggressive features.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or misinterprets the lesion as an unrelated process without integrating clinical, radiographic, and histologic data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one data source well (for example, histology alone or radiograph alone) or gives a generic benign-lesion interpretation without linking it to the patient's presentation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the hard exophytic swelling, mixed radiographic appearance in the anterior mandible, and cartilage-to-bone histology to support a benign osteochondroma and guide management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the absence of mucosal ulceration/tooth mobility, the lesion's surface bony character and regional extent, and the orderly cartilaginous cap with bone formation to explain why the lesion behaves as a benign surface osteocartilaginous tumor and why CT is needed for definitive surgical mapping.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers no meaningful justification for the proposed intervention or ignores patient-specific risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general pros and cons of surgery but does not relate them to this lesion's size, growth, displacement of teeth, benign appearance, or surgical morbidity.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that growth, bulk, and tooth displacement favor intervention, while benign clinicopathologic features argue against unnecessarily aggressive resection.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly balances observation, limited contouring, and more aggressive surgery; justifies definitive but conservative excision by weighing symptom burden and future progression against risks to teeth, nerves, and lingual soft tissues.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits important surgical risks and provides no follow-up plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either operative complications or recurrence follow-up, but not both, or does so only superficially.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key complications such as root injury, neurovascular injury, lingual/floor-of-mouth trauma, contour defect, and recurrence from incomplete excision; recommends periodic clinical and radiographic review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds clinically important surveillance goals, including monitoring for rare malignant transformation and counseling the patient to report warning signs such as rapid enlargement, pain, paresthesia, or ulceration.

items.question_content: A 9-year-old boy presents for primary repair of an incomplete Tessier 0 cleft. He has hypertelorism, and imaging has excluded intracranial involvement. Examining fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, and knowing that a bony bridge is present across the alveolar components, what operative strategy would you choose for the lip-nasal deformity, and why do the visible facial and intraoral findings favor that plan over other reasonable repairs? In your justification, explain what you would treat now versus defer regarding the vestibule, alveolus, and supernumerary tooth.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This should be managed as an incomplete true median cleft whose anatomy is closer to a bilateral cleft lip than to a simple midline skin-mucosal gap. The key findings are hypertelorism with preserved midline tissue, a broad nasal base/alar flare on fig_01.jpg, and central vestibular deficiency with a supernumerary tooth on fig_02.jpg. My primary repair would therefore use bilateral cheilorhinoplasty principles: preserve/incorporate the available midline tissue as a philtral flap/prolabial element, reconstruct the median tubercle and central vestibule from the lateral lip elements, and perform primary nasal correction with alar-base narrowing/repositioning. The main benefit is more anatomic reconstruction of philtrum, tubercle, vestibule, and nose; the tradeoff is bilateral scarring and some risk of shortened vertical lip, but that is acceptable here because a simpler linear closure would likely leave persistent alar widening, a broad/poorly defined philtrum, and inadequate vestibular depth.

Because a bony bridge is already present across the alveolar components, I would not perform gingivoperiosteoplasty or plan alveolar bone grafting at this stage solely for the cleft. The priority now is lip-nasal repair and vestibular reconstruction. The supernumerary tooth should be assessed with pediatric dental/orthodontic follow-up and removed only if it interferes with eruption, occlusion, hygiene, or future orthodontic/alveolar management, or if it obstructs the repair or becomes symptomatic. Longitudinal follow-up should monitor lip length and scar quality, nasal symmetry and growth, dental eruption, arch development/occlusion, and whether later orthodontics, tooth removal, secondary lip-nasal revision, or delayed alveolar intervention becomes necessary.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes a non-anatomic or unsupported plan, such as vague closure without addressing lip, nose, and vestibule together, or recommends routine immediate alveolar grafting/gingivoperiosteoplasty despite the stated bony bridge. Does not appropriately address the supernumerary tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends repair of the cleft but gives only generic or incomplete planning. May mention lip repair or nasal correction but does not clearly frame the deformity as analogous to bilateral cleft lip anatomy, or is unclear about what should be done now versus deferred.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a bilateral cleft lip/cheilorhinoplasty-type repair using available midline tissue to create a philtral/prolabial element, with reconstruction of the vestibule/median tubercle and primary nasal/alar base correction. Correctly defers alveolar grafting or gingivoperiosteoplasty because of the bony bridge and does not advocate routine immediate removal of the supernumerary tooth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent stepwise operative strategy that clearly separates immediate goals from deferred care, including vestibular reconstruction now, no alveolar graft because of bony continuity, and tooth management based on eruption/orthodontic indications. Explicitly tailors the plan to this child's anatomy rather than giving a standard protocol.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets the visual and clinical data, or does not connect the findings to the chosen plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings from the stem or figures but with weak synthesis; reasoning is largely descriptive rather than explanatory.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the major case-specific findings—hypertelorism, broad nasal base, incomplete midline soft-tissue cleft, preserved midline tissue, vestibular deficiency, supernumerary tooth, and absent intracranial involvement—into a coherent justification for the selected repair.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Demonstrates high-level synthesis by explaining why these findings support a true/incomplete median cleft pattern amenable to bilateral-cleft-like reconstruction and why vestibular/nasal correction is a higher priority than alveolar intervention in the presence of a bony bridge.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No meaningful discussion of benefits, drawbacks, or patient-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros or cons of surgery but not the tradeoffs relevant to this anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains the main benefits of the chosen approach—more anatomic philtrum, tubercle, vestibule, and alar-base correction—and the main drawbacks, such as bilateral scarring, possible shortened vertical lip, and the possibility of future revision with growth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances benefits and drawbacks in a patient-specific way and explains why less comprehensive closure would risk under-correction of the nose and vestibule despite potentially simpler scarring.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes secondary dentoalveolar procedures over primary functional/anatomic repair or does not distinguish urgent from deferred issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that primary repair is important but is unclear about which dentoalveolar issues should be deferred.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes lip-nasal and vestibular reconstruction now, while deferring alveolar grafting and most supernumerary-tooth decisions to follow-up unless there is obstruction, symptoms, or eruption interference.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides clear follow-up priorities and intervention triggers, such as eruption disturbance, occlusal/arch-development problems, persistent vestibular deficiency, or growth-related lip-nasal asymmetry.

items.question_content: In an oncocytic salivary neoplasm like the one in fig_01.jpg, positivity for which marker would favor acinic cell carcinoma over oncocytic carcinoma?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Acinic cell carcinoma may enter the differential diagnosis of an oncocytic salivary tumor because it can show oncocytoid change. SOX10 positivity supports acinar/intercalated duct differentiation and therefore favors acinic cell carcinoma rather than oncocytic carcinoma.
