items.question_content:
Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

Patient 1 is a 9-year-old girl who had avulsion of mandibular left lateral incisor (#32). The tooth was reimplanted within 20 minutes, splinted, and endodontic treatment was started 1 week later with canal debridement and calcium hydroxide dressing. The splint was removed after 2 weeks, but she did not return for the planned completion of endodontic follow-up. She presents 3.5 years later with pain in #32.

Patient 2 is an 18-year-old woman who had avulsion of all four mandibular incisors (#31, #32, #41, #42) after a seizure-related fall. The teeth remained dry extraorally for about 36 hours before delayed reimplantation. Extraoral root canal treatment was completed before reimplantation, and the teeth were splinted. She missed scheduled follow-up and presents 7 months later.

Using the figures and this history, decide for each remaining reimplanted tooth whether retention/retreatment is defensible or whether extraction is indicated at these review visits. Justify your management based on prognosis, resorption pattern, periodontal and alveolar support, missed follow-up, age, and initial extraoral dry time.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: At these late review visits, none of the affected reimplanted teeth has a realistic long-term prognosis. In Case I, #32 is essentially hopeless at 3.5 years because the radiograph and working-length loss show severe communicating internal and external inflammatory resorption with periodontal communication, plus pain, mobility, pockets, and gingival inflammation. Definitive recommendation is extraction to limit further alveolar destruction, with informed discussion if the family refuses; short-term observation would be only a reluctant compromise, not a curative plan. Earlier completion of endodontic therapy after calcium hydroxide might have improved survival, but at this presentation retreatment is unlikely to arrest the process predictably. In Case II, #31 is already lost, and #32, #41, and #42 should be extracted because 36 hours of dry time implies non-viable PDL, and the current grade III mobility, deep pockets, severe inflammatory root resorption, marked alveolar bone loss, and failed prolonged splinting indicate treatment failure. Delayed reimplantation here served at best as a temporary alveolar-preservation measure, not a durable tooth-saving strategy. Immediate priorities are removal of hopeless teeth, management of infection/inflammation, counseling on prognosis and bone loss, oral-hygiene instruction, and rehabilitation planning. For the 9-year-old, replacement must be growth-conscious and interim; for the 18-year-old, provisional replacement can be followed by definitive prosthetic rehabilitation after healing and assessment of bone support. Medical follow-up for seizure evaluation is also important in Case II.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misreads major findings in fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg, such as periodontal communication, re-avulsion, grade III mobility, or alveolar bone loss, and does not connect them to prognosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical or radiographic findings but reasoning is fragmented, case-specific details are missed, or the significance of missed follow-up and dry time is underdeveloped.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly synthesizes the clinical and radiographic data in both cases, linking resorption pattern, mobility, pockets, bone loss, and follow-up failure to current status.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all key findings and clearly contrasts why Case I initially had salvage potential whereas Case II began with a far worse biologic prognosis, yet both are now failures for different reasons.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides an inappropriate or unsafe plan, such as routine retreatment, prolonged splinting, or indefinite retention of clearly hopeless teeth without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes need for intervention but gives an incomplete, inconsistent, or poorly prioritized plan, or addresses only one case adequately.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends extraction of hopeless teeth at these review visits, addresses immediate management of pain/inflammation, and proposes age-appropriate rehabilitation and follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a precise stepwise plan for both cases, including why retreatment is no longer defensible, what earlier endodontic completion might have offered in Case I, and why delayed reimplantation in Case II was mainly temporary alveolar preservation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misjudges prognosis as favorable or uncertain despite advanced inflammatory resorption, mobility, and alveolar support loss.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States prognosis is poor but gives limited explanation or does not distinguish between the biologic circumstances of the two cases.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that all affected teeth are hopeless at re-presentation and that Case II predictably fails faster because of prolonged dry time, non-viable PDL, and splint-related plaque retention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nuanced prognosis, including that Case I might have enjoyed longer survival with timely endodontic completion, while continued retention now risks further bone loss without meaningful salvage benefit.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh the risks of continued retention versus extraction, or ignores patient-specific rehabilitation constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either benefits of retaining teeth or risks of extraction, but not both, or applies the same reasoning to child and adult without adaptation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances temporary function/alveolar preservation against ongoing inflammatory destruction, mobility, pain, plaque retention, and future restorative needs; adapts rehabilitation to age and bone status.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly justifies why aggressive salvage has low expected benefit relative to harm and incorporates seizure-related medical follow-up in the adult as part of comprehensive risk management.

items.question_content: A 24-year-old systemically healthy man is referred after an unsuccessful attempt to treat the left maxillary first molar because of complex anatomy. The tooth is temporized, unresponsive to pulp and periapical tests, and has asymptomatic apical periodontitis associated with the prior incomplete treatment. Review fig_01.jpg panel A-D for the anatomy and imaging findings. Assuming the tooth is restorable, identify the anatomic anomaly and the pulpal/periapical status, then give the best definitive management. Explain the key technical modifications you would make for access, canal location, cleaning/shaping, irrigation, and obturation, emphasizing how this anatomy changes retreatment strategy and which iatrogenic risks must be actively prevented.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is a hypertaurodontic maxillary first molar, evidenced radiographically by the enlarged elongated pulp chamber, apically displaced pulpal floor/furcation, and relatively short roots. In the clinical context, the most consistent diagnosis is failed or incomplete prior endodontic treatment of a nonvital/previously treated tooth with asymptomatic apical periodontitis. The best management is nonsurgical orthograde root canal retreatment, not extraction or surgery, because the source of disease is intraradicular and the tooth is restorable.

Retreatment should be planned with the CBCT findings in mind and performed under rubber dam and a dental operating microscope. Access must be cautious because the pulpal floor is deeper than usual; remove only minimal cervical dentin to gain straight-line access and avoid perforation or unnecessary weakening. Deeply placed canal orifices should be searched for under magnification and negotiated first with small hand files. Canal anatomy and working length should be confirmed with an apex locator and radiographs correlated with the CBCT.

Because taurodont teeth have a large chamber and potentially thin dentinal walls, debridement should rely more on chemical cleaning than aggressive enlargement: copious sodium hypochlorite irrigation, ideally activated ultrasonically, with recapitulation and conservative rotary shaping rather than excessive flaring. The main risks are missed canals, inadequate debridement of the long chamber, strip perforation/transportation from over-instrumentation, and poor filling of the enlarged chamber. Obturation is best done with a warm vertical or other thermoplasticized technique to adapt filling material to the irregular chamber and canal system. A sound definitive coronal seal is essential, and post placement should generally be avoided if possible in a taurodont tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not recognize taurodontism or gives an incorrect pulpal/periapical diagnosis unrelated to prior failed treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an anatomic abnormality or prior treatment failure, but misclassifies the anomaly or gives only a vague/incomplete endodontic diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies taurodontic anatomy and links the case to failed/incomplete prior treatment with apical disease, but does not clearly characterize the severity as hypertaurodontic or is imprecise about pulpal status.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies a hypertaurodontic maxillary first molar and a failed/incomplete prior endodontic treatment with asymptomatic apical periodontitis, using the imaging and history coherently.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides generic statements without connecting history, testing, and fig_01.jpg findings to the management plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case details but misses important implications of the elongated chamber, apically displaced floor/furcation, or short roots.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Adequately synthesizes the failed prior attempt, nonresponse to testing, and radiographic/CBCT anatomy to explain why this tooth is unusually difficult and why standard molar tactics are insufficient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly integrates the imaging features with the clinical history to justify retreatment, conservative access, enhanced visualization, careful canal search, and a chemistry-heavy debridement strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe management approach, or gives only a generic endodontic protocol with no taurodont-specific modifications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses retreatment but omits several critical steps such as magnification/CBCT-guided planning, careful orifice location, conservative shaping, activated irrigation, or appropriate obturation technique.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends nonsurgical orthograde retreatment with a reasonable sequence: isolation, careful re-entry, small-file negotiation, working-length control, conservative shaping, copious irrigant use, and thermoplastic/warm obturation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise, case-specific plan: CBCT-informed orthograde retreatment under microscope and rubber dam; minimal cervical dentin removal; deep-orifice location with small files; apex locator plus radiographic confirmation; emphasis on irrigation over aggressive enlargement; warm vertical/thermoplastic obturation; and prompt definitive coronal seal with avoidance of unnecessary post placement.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not recognize major anatomy-related risks or proposes actions that increase them.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one risk, such as missed canals or perforation, but does not explain prevention in this anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies multiple relevant risks—missed deeply placed orifices, inadequate debridement of the enlarged chamber, over-instrumentation/perforation, or poor obturation—and gives basic prevention strategies.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates the key taurodont-specific hazards and matches each with preventive measures: magnification and CBCT to avoid missed canals, minimal dentin removal to reduce perforation/weakening, conservative shaping to protect thin walls/short roots, activated irrigation for chamber debridement, and warm obturation plus coronal seal to reduce persistent infection.

items.question_content: Based on fig_01.jpg, a 15-year-old girl presents 1 week after motorcycle trauma with persistent throbbing pain from the left maxillary incisors. Medical history is noncontributory; she has an upper-lip laceration/swelling, TMJ findings are unremarkable, occlusion is stable, oral hygiene is fair, and the clinical crown height is minimal. Tooth 21 shows an oblique palatal crown-root fracture extending ~3 mm subgingivally; tooth 22 shows a more horizontal fracture ~2 mm subgingivally. The coronal fragments are mobile but soft-tissue attached, both teeth are tender to vertical percussion, and radiographs show cervical/coronal-root fracture lines with PDL widening. Give one definitive tooth-preserving plan from fragment removal to definitive restoration. In the same answer, justify your endodontic timing after repositioning against the main competing timing strategy, identify the single early failure pattern you would fear most in a still-growing 15-year-old and how you would distinguish it from inflammatory resorption, and explain exactly how your plan would change if tooth 21 had the same 3 mm subgingival extension on the labial rather than palatal aspect.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best definitive tooth-preserving plan is surgical extrusion of both incisors, but with different maneuvers. After removing the mobile coronal fragments and confirming restorability, both teeth should be atraumatically extracted with maximal preservation of the periodontal ligament and minimal extraoral time. Tooth 21 should be immediately replanted in a slightly more coronal position with 180° rotation because its fracture is oblique and deepest on the palatal aspect. Rotation exploits the labial-palatal CEJ/cervical contour asymmetry so the deepest palatal subgingival margin becomes more accessible and functionally supragingival, improving ferrule and biologic width without labial bone reduction. Tooth 22 should undergo simple coronal surgical extrusion of about 2 mm without rotation because the fracture is more horizontal; rotation adds PDL trauma without improving margin exposure. Repositioning should be checked for occlusal clearance, then stabilized with a short passive flexible splint for about 2 weeks.

For pulpal management, I would extirpate the pulp immediately at the surgical visit or as soon as possible after repositioning rather than waiting 7-10 days. These are symptomatic complicated crown-root fractures in likely closed-apex teeth that have also undergone intentional replantation; early canal disinfection reduces the risk of infection-driven inflammatory resorption. Calcium hydroxide dressing should be placed, with canal completion/obturation after initial stabilization, then bonded reinforcement/composite build-up. Definitive full-coverage crowns should be staged rather than placed immediately, so periodontal healing, mobility, probing, and early radiographic changes can be reassessed first.

The early failure pattern I would fear most in a still-growing 15-year-old is ankylosis/replacement resorption because it can progress to infraocclusion and compromise alveolar development even if the tooth is asymptomatic. I would distinguish it from inflammatory resorption by serial standardized periapical radiographs plus clinical percussion and mobility testing: ankylosis shows a high metallic percussion note, reduced physiologic mobility, and progressive loss of a distinct PDL space/root-bone continuity, later with infraocclusion; inflammatory resorption shows irregular progressive root surface radiolucencies with adjacent bone loss and is more closely linked to intracanal infection.

If tooth 21 had the same 3 mm subgingival extension on the labial rather than palatal aspect, routine 180° rotation would lose its biologic advantage and could worsen the labial emergence profile or merely move the problem palatally. I would instead favor simple coronal surgical extrusion without rotation if adequate ferrule and biologic width could be obtained, or orthodontic extrusion if more controlled coronal movement were needed. Labial osseous crown lengthening would remain a less attractive option in this 15-year-old esthetic-zone patient unless conservative options failed or the tooth proved nonrestorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not provide a viable tooth-preserving plan, or recommends the same maneuver for both teeth, or omits a coherent sequence from repositioning to restoration.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that extrusion/repositioning is needed but gives an incomplete or generic plan, such as recommending surgical extrusion without clearly assigning 180° rotation to tooth 21 and non-rotational coronal extrusion to tooth 22, or omitting splinting/endodontic/restorative sequencing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends surgical extrusion for both teeth with 180° rotation plus coronal repositioning for tooth 21, simple coronal surgical extrusion for tooth 22, short passive flexible splinting, and staged endodontic/restorative management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise stepwise plan linking fragment removal, atraumatic extraction, minimal extraoral time, immediate replantation/repositioning, occlusal clearance, tooth-specific use of rotation, short passive flexible splinting, intracanal medication, completion of endodontics, interim reinforcement/build-up, and delayed definitive full-coverage restoration after periodontal reassessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning ignores key clinical or radiographic findings, or does not connect them to the chosen plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts, but the connection between fracture geometry, minimal clinical crown, adolescent esthetic-zone considerations, and treatment choice is incomplete.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates age, esthetic zone, minimal clinical crown height, fracture depth/orientation, PDL widening, tenderness, and stable occlusion to justify tooth preservation and different maneuvers for the two incisors.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains how the palatal obliquity and labial-palatal cervical/CEJ asymmetry make 180° rotation biologically useful for tooth 21, why the more horizontal fracture of tooth 22 does not benefit from rotation, and why that logic would change if the 21 defect were labial instead of palatal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not commit to an endodontic timing strategy after repositioning, or proposes a sequence that leaves pulpal management unjustifiably unaddressed.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a timing preference for root canal treatment but gives limited case-specific reasoning or does not address the competing timing strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a defensible timing strategy for pulpal management after repositioning and supports it with case-based reasoning, while appropriately staging definitive restoration rather than collapsing all treatment into one visit.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes the sequence of surgery, pulpal disinfection, splinting, reassessment, and definitive restoration; explicitly contrasts the chosen endodontic timing with the main alternative strategy; and explains why that prioritization best manages biologic risk in this symptomatic 1-week intentional replantation case.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major foreseeable complications, selects an implausible main threat, or cannot distinguish between ankylosis/replacement resorption and inflammatory resorption.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists complications but does not prioritize the one most threatening here, or gives vague surveillance, or provides only one nonspecific differentiating feature.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies ankylosis/replacement resorption or inflammatory resorption as a principal concern, gives appropriate prevention/surveillance measures, and distinguishes it from the other process using at least one specific clinical or radiographic feature.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes a single most consequential early failure pattern for this 15-year-old, explains why it matters in this age group, and distinguishes it from the competing complication using a targeted monitoring plan with specific clinical and radiographic markers.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions without a clear logical link from findings to decisions, or does not address how the plan would change in the labial-fracture counterfactual.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some logic but leaves important transitions unexplained, such as why rotation is surface-dependent or why the restoration sequence is staged.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a clear chain of reasoning from the case findings to the chosen maneuvers, endodontic timing, complication surveillance, and the modified plan for a labial 21 fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows a fully coherent, case-anchored argument that not only states what to do but explains why each decision follows from fracture orientation, biologic width, periodontal preservation, adolescent growth considerations, and the labial-versus-palatal counterfactual.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommending extraction of either incisor or routine osseous crown lengthening as first-line management without first using a tooth-preserving extrusion strategy in this 15-year-old esthetic-zone case.
Generic Textbook Management: Giving both incisors the same maneuver or applying 180° rotation without linking it to the palatal oblique fracture geometry of tooth 21.
Severity Misjudged: Advising prolonged observation without timely canal disinfection after intentional replantation of these symptomatic complicated crown-root fractures.

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide what the first irreversible intervention, if any, should be today for this 13-year-old boy in mixed dentition who presented with noneruption of the maxillary canines. He has a prominent palatal talon cusp on the permanent maxillary left lateral incisor, enlarged mesiodistal width of that lateral incisor (10 mm versus 7.5 mm for the adjacent central incisor), radiographic pulp extension into the cusp, and panoramic evidence of canine impaction tendency. Give your next three management steps in priority order. You must explicitly state whether, at this stage, you would or would not: extract the primary canine(s), reduce the talon cusp, or begin endodontic treatment. Justify each decision from the case findings and name one specific clinical or radiographic change that would make you change your sequence.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: No irreversible treatment of the lateral incisor should be the first step today. The immediate priority is to recognize the eruption problem and preserve the lateral incisor because the radiograph shows pulpal tissue extending well into the talon cusp. A strong answer prioritizes: (1) clinical and radiographic assessment of the talon cusp and canine region in view of the noneruption of the canines and the panoramic tendency toward impaction; (2) observation and conservative management of the talon cusp if it is not currently causing a significant problem; (3) management planning for the canine eruption disturbance based on the clinical and radiographic findings. Extraction of the primary canine(s) should not be the automatic first step from the panoramic finding alone. Talon cusp reduction should not be done routinely or in one visit because the pulp extends into the cusp; reduction is indicated if the cusp is causing functional or clinical problems. Endodontic treatment is not indicated now; it becomes relevant if pulp exposure occurs during treatment or if the tooth later shows pulpal involvement. A valid trigger to change the sequence would be clear evidence that the talon cusp is causing occlusal interference or that the canine impaction tendency is progressing on further assessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses an inappropriate invasive first step, such as immediate full cusp reduction, routine endodontic treatment, or extraction without prioritizing the competing eruption and pulp-preservation issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides some ordering of care, but the sequence is incomplete, does not clearly distinguish what should be done now versus later, or gives unsupported priority to one problem.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes conservative assessment/prevention first, defers irreversible treatment of the talon cusp, and recognizes that the canine eruption problem requires separate interceptive/orthodontic planning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Ranks the next three steps clearly, states that no immediate irreversible treatment of the lateral incisor is the best initial choice, and justifies why irreversible procedures are deferred despite the canine eruption concern.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets key case findings from fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, or the stem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings but does not integrate the mixed dentition stage, enlarged lateral incisor width, pulpal extension into the cusp, and canine impaction tendency into one coherent plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly synthesizes the age, mixed dentition, talon cusp anatomy, pulp extension, and eruption disturbance into a management approach.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses the figures and stem to distinguish the talon-cusp problem from the canine eruption-space problem, showing how each finding changes sequencing and choice of intervention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not recognize the major risks of pulp exposure from aggressive reduction or the consequences of poorly timed canine intervention.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions pulp risk or impaction risk, but does not clearly explain how those risks alter the treatment sequence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that pulpal extension makes immediate complete reduction hazardous and that canine management should not be reduced to cusp treatment alone.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the benefits and harms of observation, staged reduction, interceptive extraction of primary canine(s), and deferred endodontics, and identifies a concrete trigger that would justify changing the sequence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not give a workable plan or fails to answer whether to extract the primary canine(s), reduce the cusp, or start endodontic treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a generic plan but omits at least one of the required yes/no decisions or lacks a clear trigger for escalation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a coherent plan with explicit current decisions on primary canine extraction, cusp reduction, and endodontic treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides explicit current decisions on all three interventions, a stepwise management pathway, and a specific clinical or radiographic change that would alter the plan.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommending immediate one-visit complete reduction, extraction of the permanent lateral incisor, or routine endodontic therapy despite radiographic pulp extension into the talon cusp.
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Recommending automatic primary canine extraction or surgical exposure without acknowledging the need for eruption localization/space analysis and interceptive planning.
Generic Textbook Management: Giving a standard talon-cusp or impacted-canine protocol without committing to which intervention, if any, should occur first in this specific mixed-dentition case.

items.question_content: Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, a 37-year-old woman reports 1 week of spontaneous nocturnal pain from tooth 27. The tooth is tender to percussion, non-responsive to cold, and has no caries, mobility, or periodontal disease. IOPA is inconclusive except for a suspicious apical radiolucency. She recently had thyroid surgery and is currently receiving radioactive iodine (I-131) for papillary thyroid carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis and the best definitive management for tooth 27? Justify why this approach is preferred over endodontic salvage by integrating the CBCT findings, likely prognosis, key differentials, and any precautions or follow-up needed because of her oncologic treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is radicular dens invaginatus (radicular variant of dens in dente) in tooth 27, specifically an enamel-lined intraradicular invagination opening on the root, associated with loss of vitality, symptomatic apical periodontitis/periapical osteolytic change, and a transverse fracture of the palatal root. fig_01.jpg supports a root-based invagination rather than coronal dens invaginatus, and fig_02.jpg shows the palatal root fracture, which markedly worsens restorability and endodontic prognosis. Definitive management is extraction of 27 with curettage of the periapical lesion rather than nonsurgical or surgical endodontic treatment. Endodontic salvage is unfavorable because molar RDinD has highly complex anatomy, the lesion is already established, and the fractured palatal root makes long-term retention poor even if canals were treated. Key differentials are coronal dens invaginatus type III, enamel pearl, and painful endodontic entities such as irreversible pulpitis or phoenix abscess; these are less likely because the anomaly is confined to the root, appears as an internal invagination rather than an external radiopaque pearl, and the structural CBCT findings explain the symptoms. Because she is receiving I-131, management should include coordination with her oncology/nuclear medicine team, careful timing and atraumatic surgery, informed consent, analgesia, chlorhexidine rinse, and close follow-up to monitor socket healing and regression of the osteolytic area.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as routine caries-related pulpitis, simple periapical disease, or another unrelated condition; does not recognize a radicular invagination or the prognostic importance of the fracture.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an anomalous tooth or apical pathology but misclassifies it, omits that it is radicular rather than coronal, or misses the palatal root fracture.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies radicular dens invaginatus/radicular variant of dens in dente with pulpal necrosis or symptomatic apical pathology and notes the fracture or otherwise states that the tooth has poor structural prognosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely identifies an enamel-lined radicular invagination opening on the root in tooth 27, with non-vital pulp, apical osteolytic change/symptomatic apical periodontitis, and a transverse palatal root fracture.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions without linking them to the history, examination, and imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant findings but misses important links, such as the significance of the negative cold test, percussion pain, inconclusive IOPA, or why CBCT is decisive.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the clinical findings with fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to explain why a developmental root anomaly with apical disease is the best explanation for the presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all major data sources coherently, including why conventional radiography was insufficient, how CBCT distinguishes the anomaly from mimics, and why the fracture changes prognosis and treatment choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends symptomatic treatment alone, watchful waiting, or routine root canal treatment without addressing the structural/anatomic barriers to success.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects extraction or endodontic therapy but with weak justification, no consideration of prognosis, or no mention of managing the periapical lesion/follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends extraction of tooth 27 with curettage because the combination of molar RDinD, apical lesion, and palatal root fracture makes endodontic salvage unfavorable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, well-justified plan: extract 27, curette the lesion, explain why nonsurgical/surgical endodontics or intentional replantation carry poor prognosis here, and include postoperative surveillance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the current I-131 therapy or dismisses all systemic implications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions the oncologic history but does not translate it into practical perioperative considerations.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recognizes that active radioiodine treatment warrants coordination with the medical team, careful surgical planning, and close healing follow-up while still addressing the dental source of pain/infection.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the need for definitive infection control against potential healing concerns during I-131 therapy, and proposes sensible modifications such as atraumatic technique, informed consent, analgesia, chlorhexidine, and monitoring for delayed healing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differentials or lists diagnoses that are not clinically reasonable for this presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names one or more plausible differentials but does not explain why they are less likely.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Considers key alternatives such as coronal dens invaginatus type III, enamel pearl, and painful pulpal/periapical entities, with brief rationale for exclusion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically rules out the main mimics by contrasting root-only involvement versus crown-plus-root involvement, internal invagination versus external radiopaque enamel pearl, and structural CBCT findings versus symptom-only endodontic diagnoses.

items.question_content: A 22-year-old woman presents with 5 days of intermittent pain from tooth 45, worsened by cold and lingering after the stimulus. A deep disto-occlusal carious lesion is present; pulp testing is exaggerated/lingering and apical tissues are clinically normal. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, the mandibular second premolar shows unusual root and canal morphology. What is the most likely canal configuration, and what is your stepwise endodontic plan from diagnosis through obturation? Explain how the imaging findings change access design, canal location/negotiation, shaping, and irrigation, and identify the main procedural risk that must be actively prevented.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues in tooth 45. The anatomy is a two-rooted mandibular second premolar with separate buccal and lingual roots; the lingual root has one canal, while the buccal root begins as one canal and bifurcates in the middle third into two separate canals with separate exits, giving three canals overall. The key clues are two distinct root outlines with separate PDL spaces, an off-centered/disappearing buccal canal trace on angled radiographs, and CBCT confirmation of a mid-root buccal split.

Management should be modified from a routine premolar RCT. First, confirm anatomy with straight and mesial/distal angled periapicals plus an apex locator; if 2D findings are equivocal, limited-FOV CBCT is justified because it changes treatment strategy. Prepare a buccolingually extended access for straight-line entry to both roots and improved visualization of the buccal split. Use DOM magnification, DG16 exploration, and selective ultrasonic troughing to uncover the bifurcation rather than cutting blindly.

Negotiate first with precurved small hand files (#6, #8, #10) to establish patency of each path and determine separate working lengths for all three canals. Create a conservative manual glide path before rotary shaping. Use flexible small-taper NiTi cautiously and only after the file is already in the canal; do not force instruments into the bifurcation. Irrigate copiously with sodium hypochlorite, activate irrigant ultrasonically, remove smear layer with EDTA, and consider interappointment calcium hydroxide if using a two-visit approach. Obturate only after confirming three negotiable canals and tug-back/fit in each, using a technique that seals each canal individually with an adequate coronal seal.

The main procedural risk is missing the bifurcated buccal canal or causing ledging, transportation, perforation, or instrument separation at the split. Prevention depends on early recognition of the anatomy, magnification, careful troughing, precurved hand-file negotiation, conservative shaping, and radiographic/EAL verification of each canal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the tooth as routine single-root/single-canal anatomy, or gives an implausible diagnosis that ignores the clinical and imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an anatomic variation but misstates the number/location of roots or canals, or fails to identify the buccal canal bifurcation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies two roots and three canals overall, with a single lingual canal and a buccal canal system that divides into two separate canals; pulpal/apical diagnosis is essentially correct.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely identifies symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues and accurately describes a two-rooted mandibular second premolar in which the buccal root shows a mid-root 1-to-2 split with separate exits, while the lingual root contains one canal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic answer without using the clinical tests or the radiographic/CBCT clues shown in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one source of information, such as symptoms alone or a vague statement about unusual anatomy, without explaining the specific image features.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates symptoms, sensibility findings, angled radiographic signs, and/or CBCT evidence to justify the diagnosis and the need for altered treatment strategy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly synthesizes the lingering cold response, normal apical status, two distinct root outlines/separate PDL spaces, off-centered or disappearing buccal canal trace, and CBCT demonstration of the buccal split to support both diagnosis and management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Suggests routine premolar root canal treatment without meaningful modification for the aberrant anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some appropriate measures, such as magnification or altered access, but omits key steps in canal localization, negotiation, conservative shaping, or irrigation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides an appropriate stepwise plan including confirmation of anatomy with angled radiographs/EAL and possible CBCT, buccolingual access modification, magnification and ultrasonic troughing, precurved small-file negotiation, conservative glide path and flexible NiTi shaping, copious NaOCl with EDTA, and obturation of all three canals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a coherent, prioritized plan from diagnosis to obturation, with explicit rationale for each modification: why access must be extended, how the split should be negotiated before rotary use, how working length/patency should be verified for each canal, and how irrigation and obturation should be adapted to a bifurcating buccal root.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify any important risk, or suggests management that would predictably increase harm in this anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists only generic endodontic complications without linking them to the buccal bifurcation and two-rooted anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the major risks of missing the bifurcated canal and procedural errors such as ledging, transportation, perforation, or file separation, with at least one appropriate preventive measure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately prioritizes the greatest case-specific hazard as failure to locate/negotiate the buccal split and explains concrete prevention: early recognition of radiographic clues, DOM/ultrasonic troughing, precurved hand files, conservative shaping, and verification of separate canal paths and exits.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is the most specific classification of the two additional anterior maxillary teeth?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The extra teeth are bilateral, located in the maxillary lateral incisor region, and closely resemble normal lateral incisors in morphology. That makes them supplemental/supplementary rather than rudimentary.

items.answer_explanation: The extra teeth are bilateral, located in the maxillary lateral incisor region, and closely resemble normal lateral incisors in morphology. That makes them supplemental/supplementary rather than rudimentary.

items.question_content: A 44-year-old woman had a CBCT scan for a periapical lesion on tooth #3. Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, tooth #2 shows an incidental anatomic variant. If primary root canal treatment of #2 becomes indicated and the tooth is restorable, what is the most appropriate endodontic management plan? In your answer, identify the root/canal configuration and furcation finding, explain why the panoramic-like view is insufficient, and describe how these findings should change access design, canal-location strategy, and risk management.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show a five-rooted maxillary second molar with five separate canals: MB1, MB2, DB, MP, and DP, giving a 3-buccal/2-palatal configuration. A small enamel pearl is present in the furcation between the MP and DP roots. fig_03.jpg shows why a panoramic-like 2D image is inadequate: superimposition obscures the extra roots/canals and the enamel pearl, so routine imaging could underestimate the anatomy. If #2 requires root canal treatment, I would use the existing CBCT as the preoperative map, supplement with angled periapicals as needed, and treat under rubber dam with magnification/illumination; referral to an endodontist is appropriate if experience is limited. Access should be modified from a routine maxillary second molar outline to allow systematic exploration for two mesiobuccal orifices, one distobuccal orifice, and two separate palatal orifices. Ultrasonic troughing and small precurved files would help locate and negotiate the canals, especially MB2, which is harder to visualize apically. Each canal should be treated as independent unless proven otherwise, with separate working lengths, glide paths, cleaning/shaping, and obturation. Main risks are missing MB2 or an additional palatal canal, excessive dentin removal or perforation during access/troughing, negotiation errors in poorly visible apical anatomy, and failure from incomplete debridement/obturation. The enamel pearl should be documented because it can favor plaque retention and furcation periodontal involvement, so periodontal assessment and preventive advice are warranted.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not recognize the tooth as having five separate roots/canals, or describes it as routine maxillary second molar anatomy. Misses the enamel pearl or materially mislabels the root pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an unusual anatomy with extra roots/canals but gives an incorrect number or incomplete localization (for example, notes only four roots or mentions extra canals without identifying the buccal/palatal distribution). Furcation finding is omitted or vague.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies five roots with five canals in tooth #2: MB1, MB2, DB, MP, and DP, with a 3-buccal/2-palatal configuration, and notes the enamel pearl in the palatal furcation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies the full five-root/five-canal configuration and enamel pearl, and adds clinically relevant image-based detail such as the poorer apical visibility of MB2 and the relative prominence of the DP root/canal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes routine three-canal management, gives no meaningful modification for the documented anatomy, or recommends extraction solely because the anatomy is unusual.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that extra canals should be sought but gives a vague or incomplete plan, with little detail on access modification, canal-location strategy, or separate management of the canals.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides an appropriate CBCT-guided endodontic plan: use the CBCT as a map, treat under magnification and isolation, modify access to locate all five orifices, negotiate with fine instruments, establish separate working lengths/glide paths, and clean, shape, and obturate all canals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a clear stepwise plan tailored to this tooth, including mesio-buccal and palatal access modification, adjunctive use of angled periapicals/ultrasonics/precurved files, explicit attention to the difficult MB2 canal, conservative dentin removal, and referral when operator skill or equipment is insufficient.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major risks or suggests unsafe management that increases the chance of perforation, missed anatomy, or treatment failure.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic endodontic risks without linking them to this anatomy, or identifies one major risk but ignores others.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key case-specific risks: missed MB2 or additional palatal canal, perforation or excessive dentin removal during access/troughing, negotiation problems in poorly visualized apical anatomy, and failure from incomplete debridement/obturation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the major endodontic risks and also explains the clinical significance of the enamel pearl as a furcation plaque-retentive factor with potential periodontal involvement, including the need to document and monitor it.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is largely unsupported by the provided figures or ignores the imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figure information but does not clearly connect the CBCT findings to the treatment implications or does not explain the limitation of the panoramic-like image.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to define the external and internal anatomy and uses fig_03.jpg to justify why panoramic-like imaging is insufficient for treatment planning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses the contrast between the 3D/axial CBCT views and the panoramic-like reconstruction to build a coherent management rationale, showing exactly how image interpretation changes access design, canal search strategy, and risk control.

items.question_content: When periapical radiographs are inconclusive because a suspected root perforation lies on the buccal or palatal surface, what imaging modality is most appropriate?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: A small or limited field-of-view CBCT is preferred because it overcomes the superimposition that can hide buccal or palatal perforations on 2D periapical images. It provides 3D localization of the perforation site and extent, improving diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning while limiting the scanned volume.

items.answer_explanation: A small or limited field-of-view CBCT is preferred because it overcomes the superimposition that can hide buccal or palatal perforations on 2D periapical images. It provides 3D localization of the perforation site and extent, improving diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning while limiting the scanned volume.

items.question_content: During gentle sodium hypochlorite irrigation, the patient repeatedly felt mild pain. Review fig_01.jpg. What anatomic finding most plausibly explains this?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The pain was most consistent with irrigant extrusion through EIRR defects that communicated with the canal. In this case, CBCT later confirmed three perforating/canal-communicating lesions, explaining discomfort despite gentle irrigation.

items.answer_explanation: The pain was most consistent with irrigant extrusion through EIRR defects that communicated with the canal. In this case, CBCT later confirmed three perforating/canal-communicating lesions, explaining discomfort despite gentle irrigation.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg panel c. What type of resorption is most evident in the replanted mandibular second molar?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The 2.5-year radiograph shows irregular loss of the external root structure and contour, which is characteristic of external root resorption rather than internal resorption. This is a recognized late complication after intentional replantation and, when extensive, usually indicates poor long-term prognosis for the replanted tooth.

items.answer_explanation: The 2.5-year radiograph shows irregular loss of the external root structure and contour, which is characteristic of external root resorption rather than internal resorption. This is a recognized late complication after intentional replantation and, when extensive, usually indicates poor long-term prognosis for the replanted tooth.

items.question_content: Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, a 5-year-old boy presents the same day after a bike fall with a chin bruise, anterior open bite, deranged occlusion, a left mandibular step deformity, deviation to the right, and limited mouth opening. The OPG shows a right condylar fracture and a left parasymphysis fracture. He is in primary dentition, and the limited opening makes impression-based cap-splint fabrication difficult. What is the most appropriate definitive management plan, and why is it preferable to ORIF and conventional closed-reduction methods in this child? Include the intended duration of fixation, what should follow immediately after release, and the main complications this plan is designed to prevent.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best plan is early closed reduction with orthodontic appliance-assisted immobilization rather than ORIF. In this 5-year-old, the combined condylar and parasymphysis fractures explain the open bite, malocclusion, step deformity, deviation, and restricted opening, but because he is in primary dentition, ORIF is relatively undesirable unless absolutely necessary: plates and screws can injure developing tooth buds, disturb mandibular growth centers/periosteum, and add scarring. Conventional arch bars or eyelet wiring are also less suitable because primary teeth have poorer anchorage, conical crowns, and physiologic root resorption, increasing the risk of loosening or avulsion; a cap splint is impractical here because limited opening makes impressions difficult.

I would band the second primary molars, bond brackets, place light archwires to stabilize the arches, and use intermaxillary elastic traction/MMF to reduce the parasymphyseal step and re-establish occlusion. Fixation should be brief, about 1 week, because the condylar component should not be immobilized for long. After release, use guiding elastics and begin jaw-opening/functional exercises, with liquid then semisolid diet and close follow-up of occlusion, mouth opening, deviation, and radiographic healing.

This approach aims to prevent tooth-bud injury, growth disturbance, persistent malocclusion, restricted opening, deviation, and especially TMJ ankylosis from prolonged immobilization.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully connect the clinical findings and radiograph to the fracture pattern, or ignores key facts such as primary dentition, condylar involvement, or limited mouth opening.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes mandibular fractures but integrates the case incompletely; misses one or more major features influencing management, such as the parasymphysis step deformity, condylar fracture, or impracticality of cap-splint fabrication.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly synthesizes the symptoms and OPG findings into a combined right condylar and left parasymphysis fracture requiring conservative reduction with restoration of occlusion in a young child.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly links each key finding (open bite, deviation, step deformity, limited opening, primary dentition) to both the diagnosis and the practical choice of closed orthodontic-assisted fixation over other options.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate definitive treatment, or gives only vague supportive measures without a clear reduction and fixation strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses closed reduction in general terms but omits major elements such as appliance-based stabilization, brief MMF duration, post-release guiding elastics, exercises, or follow-up priorities.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends closed reduction using bonded/banded orthodontic stabilization with archwires and intermaxillary elastics/MMF for about 1 week, followed by guiding elastics, diet modification, jaw exercises, and follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise plan tailored to this child: early reduction; banding/bonding for primary-dentition anchorage; brief elastic MMF to restore occlusion and reduce the parasymphyseal step; immediate transition to functional rehabilitation and serial clinical/radiographic review.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare options or ignores child-specific risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that surgery should be avoided but gives limited or generic justification, or fails to explain why other closed methods are less suitable here.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately weighs avoidance of ORIF because of tooth-bud, periosteal, and growth-center injury against the limitations of arch bars/eyelets in primary teeth and the impracticality of a cap splint with restricted opening.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances risks and benefits comprehensively, including why short-duration orthodontic-assisted MMF is acceptable despite temporary diet restriction and possible minor transient tooth movement, because it minimizes more consequential growth and surgical harms.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify important complications relevant to this fracture pattern and treatment choice.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic healing problems or names complications without linking them to prevention or monitoring.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies major complications such as TMJ ankylosis, persistent malocclusion, deviation, restricted mouth opening, growth disturbance, or injury to developing teeth, and notes that brief fixation plus exercises and follow-up help prevent them.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows strong foresight by tying complications to management details: brief immobilization to reduce ankylosis risk, functional rehab to recover opening, nutritional/diet support during fixation, and serial occlusal/radiographic review to detect malreduction or delayed functional problems.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. What is the most likely periapical diagnosis affecting the mandibular incisors? Provide a short term only.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The lower anterior periapical image shows periapical radiolucent change around the mandibular incisor apices, which is most consistent with inflammatory apical disease. The key radiographic inference is a periapical lesion centered at the root apices rather than a normal variant or purely coronal pathology.

items.answer_explanation: The lower anterior periapical image shows periapical radiolucent change around the mandibular incisor apices, which is most consistent with inflammatory apical disease. The key radiographic inference is a periapical lesion centered at the root apices rather than a normal variant or purely coronal pathology.

items.question_content: A 25-year-old woman presents for root canal treatment of a restorable right mandibular first molar with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis and acute apical periodontitis. The tooth has a leaking resin restoration, no periapical radiolucency, and no relevant medical history. At the first visit, four canals have been negotiated. Using only the diagnostic and working-length information in fig_01.jpg panel A and fig_01.jpg panel B, decide whether the canal system is sufficiently defined to complete treatment today. Defend that decision from the images rather than from textbook prevalence. Then explain where you would search next on the chamber floor, what specific finding would make you stop further troughing and instead stage the case or escalate to CBCT/referral, and how that threshold changes if an operating microscope is not available at this visit.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not regard the canal system as adequately characterized for completion today. fig_01.jpg panel A shows a separate distolingual extra root consistent with radix entomolaris, so the distal anatomy is already non-routine. fig_01.jpg panel B confirms a complex distal root configuration at working length rather than a straightforward single distal canal pattern. In a mandibular first molar with that radiographic appearance, four negotiated canals are not enough to assume that no further anatomy is present. The two structures I would still actively try to rule in or out are a middle mesial canal between the mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canals and an additional canal within the distal complex, most plausibly between the main distal canal and the radix entomolaris canal.

My next step would be targeted conventional re-exploration under magnification rather than immediate obturation and rather than routine CBCT as the first move. I would refine visualization of the chamber floor, then conservatively trough the developmental groove between MB and ML and the distal groove between the principal distal orifice and the radix orifice. I would use a DG16 or similar explorer, look for a reproducible catch, hemorrhagic point, or developmental line angle, and negotiate any suspect point with precurved #06-#10 hand files. Any newly negotiated path would then be verified with an apex locator and, if needed, an angled working-length radiograph before shaping.

I would stop further troughing when continued dentin removal begins to threaten the furcal danger zone or strip-risk area, or when careful magnified exploration has failed to produce a reproducible catch or negotiable path. At that point the correct move is to stage the case with intracanal medication and a good coronal seal, or escalate to CBCT/referral if the anatomy remains clinically important but cannot be defined safely. Blind deepening of the chamber floor is not justified.

If no operating microscope were available, my threshold for stopping would be lower. Without magnified visualization, the risk-benefit balance shifts away from further troughing and toward staging, limited-FOV CBCT, or referral to an endodontist, because the chance of missed anatomy still matters but the risk of furcal or strip perforation from unguided dentin removal becomes less acceptable. Key risks in this tooth are missed canals, strip or furcal perforation during mesial troughing, and transportation or file separation in the narrow, curved radix entomolaris.

levels.description: Ignores fig_01.jpg panel A and fig_01.jpg panel B, misreads the radiographs, or concludes from the stem alone that four negotiated canals are sufficient for completion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes unusual anatomy in general terms but does not use specific image-based clues from fig_01.jpg panel A and fig_01.jpg panel B to justify ongoing concern about uncharacterized canal anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly uses fig_01.jpg panel A to identify a separate distolingual extra root consistent with radix entomolaris and uses fig_01.jpg panel B to explain why the distal anatomy is non-routine, supporting a continued search for additional untreated anatomy before obturation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the radiographic clues from fig_01.jpg panel A and fig_01.jpg panel B into a coherent judgment about what anatomy still most plausibly remains uncharacterized, and explains why those images support targeted chairside re-exploration before routine obturation or automatic CBCT.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes obturation or another definitive step without adequately addressing unresolved anatomy, or gives no clear management decision.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that more evaluation is needed but does not clearly prioritize between further exploration, staging, CBCT, or referral.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes further conventional re-exploration and/or staging over immediate completion, with a clinically defensible explanation of why the anatomy is not yet sufficiently defined.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes the first-line action now, the circumstances that justify staging, and the situations in which lack of safe visualization or persistent uncertainty should shift the case to CBCT or referral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a vague, unsafe, or impractical plan for further exploration.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests additional searching but does not specify where on the chamber floor to explore or how new anatomy would be confirmed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Describes a workable search strategy that includes the mesial groove between MB and ML and the distal groove related to the distal complex/radix entomolaris, conservative troughing, small precurved hand files, and confirmation with apex locator and/or angled radiography.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, stepwise plan plus a defensible stopping rule for when further troughing is no longer justified, and explains how interim disinfection and temporary sealing would be used if the anatomy cannot be safely finalized in the same visit.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh relevant risks and benefits, or recommends a course that ignores major case-specific hazards.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic endodontic risks but does not relate them to the mesial danger zone, the extra distal root, or the decision to keep searching versus stop.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefit of finding missed anatomy against the risks of perforation, over-troughing, transportation, or file separation, and gives a reasonable explanation for not making CBCT the automatic first step when conventional methods remain informative.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows nuanced case-specific tradeoff analysis, including the curved and potentially narrow radix entomolaris, mesial strip/furcal risk, and the lower threshold for staging or referral when a microscope is unavailable.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old girl has pain and recurrent labial swelling related to tooth 22 for 6 months despite endodontic treatment started 1 month earlier. Medical history is noncontributory. Tooth 22 is tender to percussion, non-responsive to electric pulp testing, has normal probing depths with slight mobility, and adjacent teeth test normal. Examine fig_01.jpg. What is your working diagnosis and your preferred tooth-preserving management sequence at this stage? Justify the sequence from the anatomy and pattern of destruction visible in fig_01.jpg, and explain why at least two other reasonable approaches would be less suitable for this patient. Then assume an intervention directed mainly at the apical exit has been completed, but 6 months later the patient is pain-free and develops a new sinus tract. Examine fig_02.jpg. What does the new localization imply about the missed source of infection, and how should your plan change now? Include the main long-term complications you would monitor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The working diagnosis is Oehlers type IIIb dens invaginatus in tooth 22 with pulpal necrosis and a large chronic apical periodontitis/periradicular lesion. fig_01.jpg supports this because the invagination extends through the root to the apex, the main canal anatomy is distorted/separated by the invaginated space, there is a large periradicular radiolucency, and the labial cortical plate is deficient. Those features make complete orthograde cleaning and sealing unpredictable, especially after a recent failed endodontic attempt.

My preferred tooth-preserving sequence is staged. If access is possible, I would first use orthograde re-entry for disinfection and intracanal medication as an interim measure, but I would not rely on nonsurgical retreatment alone as the definitive solution. Because the anatomy is type IIIb, prior treatment has already failed, and the apical anatomy is inaccessible to predictable orthograde sealing, I would move to direct management of the apical anatomy, with intentional replantation being the preferred definitive option in this case because it allows visual control of the complex apical exit while preserving the tooth. I would avoid extensive removal/merging of the invagination because that could leave very thin dentinal walls and increase fracture risk. Extraction is also less suitable because she is 15 years old, the tooth is strategically important esthetically, and retaining it preserves bone during growth. Conventional orthograde retreatment alone is less suitable because it is unlikely to disinfect and seal all portals of exit in this anatomy.

fig_02.jpg changes the interpretation. The recurrent sinus is now localized to the mesial mid-root region, and gutta-percha tracing/radiographic localization indicates that the persistent disease is centered at the middle third of the root rather than the resected apex. This implies a missed lateral canal/lateral foramen on the mesial mid-root surface, not merely failure of the apical seal.

The plan should therefore change to targeted endodontic microsurgery: raise a flap over the involved mesial aspect, curette the lesion, identify the lateral communication under magnification and staining, conservatively prepare it, and seal it with a biocompatible root-repair material. Extraction should be reserved only if a crack, non-restorability, or uncontrollable periodontal defect is found.

Long-term monitoring should include closure of the sinus tract, reduction and resolution of the mid-root and apical radiolucency, periodontal ligament continuity, bone fill, mobility, and periodontal attachment at the surgical site. Important failure modes are persistent leakage or missed anatomy, external inflammatory root resorption, replacement resorption/ankylosis after replantation, apicomarginal or mid-root periodontal breakdown, and root fracture.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies tooth 22 as Oehlers type IIIb dens invaginatus with pulpal necrosis and chronic apical periodontitis/periradicular disease, and later recognizes persistent infection from a lateral communication rather than isolated apical failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately defines both stages of the problem: initial type IIIb dens invaginatus with complex apical disease, then a missed mesial middle-third lateral canal/lateral foramen as the specific source of recurrence shown in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figure findings or treatment history meaningfully.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings from fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg but does not connect them to the change in management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the prior failed endodontic treatment with key fig_01.jpg findings such as invagination extending to the apex, distorted/separate canal anatomy, and extensive periradicular destruction to justify why orthograde treatment alone is unreliable; also uses fig_02.jpg localization of the sinus tract/radiolucency to infer a mid-root source.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes both figures and the chronology coherently, distinguishing what fig_01.jpg explains about the initial anatomic treatment limits from what fig_02.jpg newly reveals about a second portal of exit at the mesial mid-root.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation, antibiotics alone, extraction without conservative consideration, or repeats nonspecific retreatment that does not address the anatomic source.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a partly appropriate intervention but gives no clear sequence, does not account for the type IIIb anatomy, or fails to modify the plan after fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a tooth-preserving plan that recognizes orthograde retreatment alone is unlikely to predictably disinfect/seal this anatomy and recommends direct management of the apical anatomy; after fig_02.jpg, appropriately changes to targeted endodontic microsurgery to identify, debride, and seal the mid-root lateral communication.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Lays out a clear staged sequence: interim orthograde disinfection/medication if accessible, definitive intentional replantation or an equivalently well-justified direct visual approach to manage the apical anatomy because of prior failure and type IIIb complexity, then focused microsurgical treatment of the mesial middle-third communication when fig_02.jpg localizes persistent disease; reserves extraction for fracture or non-restorability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives no meaningful justification or ignores patient-specific factors.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only generic comments about preserving the tooth or about surgical risk.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefits of retaining a restorable maxillary lateral incisor in a 15-year-old against the limitations of purely orthograde treatment and the risks of invasive management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly compares at least two reasonable alternatives not chosen and explains why they are less suitable here, using patient age, esthetics/growth, thin residual dentin if the invagination is aggressively removed, and inaccessible anatomy after failed treatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic postoperative issues such as pain or infection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant long-term concerns including persistent sinus or radiolucency, periodontal attachment loss, mobility changes, root resorption, ankylosis, and fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: An 11-year-old girl presents with intermittent moderate pain from the left mandible. The mandibular first molar is carious, and there is no swelling, sinus tract, trauma history, or systemic disease. Examine fig_01.jpg (tooth radiographs) and fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg (parental panoramics). What is the most likely underlying dentin disorder in this child, and what definitive management would you choose for the symptomatic molar? Defend your plan by linking the imaging and family pattern to the diagnosis, explaining why this tooth should or should not be retained, and identifying the main technical and biologic risks that must shape treatment and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is dentin dysplasia type II (DD-II) with pulpal necrosis/infected pulp and chronic apical periodontitis of the mandibular first molar. fig_01.jpg supports DD-II because the permanent molar shows essentially normal root development but abnormal pulp morphology with marked chamber constriction/calcification, pulp stones, narrow canals, and a periapical radiolucency. fig_02.jpg shows similar pulpal abnormalities in the mother, while fig_03.jpg is unaffected, supporting a familial autosomal dominant pattern. DD-I is less likely because the roots are not short or rudimentary; dentinogenesis imperfecta is less likely because the key pattern here is pulpal calcification in permanent teeth rather than generalized crown discoloration/bulbous crowns.

The tooth should be retained with nonsurgical root canal treatment if it is restorable and periodontally sound. In an 11-year-old, a first permanent molar is strategically important, and DD-II usually preserves root length and overall tooth support, so endodontic treatment can have a reasonable prognosis if the canals are negotiable. Extraction would be a fallback only if the tooth were non-restorable or canal negotiation proved impossible.

Treatment must be planned as a complex calcified-canal case: careful preoperative radiographic assessment, rubber dam isolation, magnification and illumination, conservative access, ultrasonic removal of pulp stones/calcified obstructions, small hand-file scouting with electronic and radiographic working-length confirmation, cautious shaping to avoid iatrogenic damage, copious irrigation, obturation once canals are negotiated, and a durable coronal seal. Major risks are failure to locate or negotiate canals, perforation during access, ledging/transportation, instrument separation, missed canals, and persistent apical disease. Follow-up should confirm healing of the apical lesion and include periodic surveillance of the remaining dentition plus family counseling because DD-II is generalized and inherited.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe definitive plan, or gives no clear plan for the symptomatic molar. Does not justify whether the tooth should be retained.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broadly plausible plan but with weak justification, minimal tailoring to calcified canals/DD-II, or poor reasoning about retention versus loss of the tooth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately recommends tooth retention with nonsurgical root canal treatment if restorable, gives a reasonable rationale based on strategic value and preserved roots, and mentions key technical adaptations for a calcified canal case.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise, case-specific plan: retain the tooth with nonsurgical endodontic treatment because it is a strategic first permanent molar with acceptable root support in DD-II; explains conditions that would change the plan; and tailors access, canal negotiation, obturation, coronal seal, and follow-up to the abnormal pulp anatomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misreads the figures and family information; reasoning is unsupported by the available data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the tooth radiograph or the family pattern superficially, but does not synthesize them with the clinical presentation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the key radiographic features in fig_01.jpg with the maternal/paternal imaging pattern and the clinical context to support the diagnosis and treatment choice.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and the history into a coherent argument: permanent tooth with normal roots but abnormal pulp morphology and apical disease, plus a maternal-only pattern consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, directly informing prognosis and management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Incorrectly identifies the underlying disorder or attributes the presentation only to routine caries/trauma without recognizing a hereditary dentin anomaly.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a hereditary dentin abnormality but misclassifies it or does not connect it to the pulpal/periapical diagnosis of the symptomatic molar.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies DD-II as the most likely disorder and recognizes that the symptomatic tooth has pulpal necrosis/infection with apical pathology.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies DD-II and accurately distinguishes it from major alternatives such as DD-I and dentinogenesis imperfecta using the preserved root form, pulp changes, and family pattern.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify important risks or follow-up needs for this endodontic case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic endodontic risks or only postoperative review, without linking them to calcified/anomalous pulp anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies several relevant risks, such as difficulty locating canals, perforation, instrument separation, missed canals, or persistent apical disease, and notes the need for follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates both technical and biologic complications specific to DD-II/calcified canals, explains how they influence treatment execution, and includes lesion-healing review plus ongoing surveillance of the remaining dentition and family counseling.

items.question_content: A 38-year-old woman has spontaneous lingering heat pain from tooth 46 and is diagnosed with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with apical periodontitis. After rubber-dam access you identify MB, ML, and one distal orifice. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg; CBCT is not available.
