levels.description: Does not recommend a defensible management plan, or recommends a clearly unsuitable approach without justification; omits how the tooth would be managed endodontically.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests retreatment or another option but gives a vague, incomplete, or poorly sequenced plan; may mention disinfection or revascularization without detailing key steps.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends repeat regenerative endodontic treatment and outlines an appropriate sequence: re-entry, removal of the existing coronal barrier, renewed canal disinfection, intracanal calcium hydroxide, EDTA rinse, reinduction of bleeding, matrix placement, new bioceramic seal, and coronal restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a high-quality repeat RET plan with preservation-focused details appropriate to a fractured immature tooth: limited instrumentation, disinfection focused on the coronal fragment to the fracture line, activated/ultrasonic irrigation for biofilm control, preservation of apical vitality, attention to coronal seal, and explicit follow-up strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets major case data or figures; does not connect the recurrent radiolucency to the prior treatment context.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but misses important interactions, such as the significance of the immature thin-walled coronal fragment, horizontal root fracture, or likely retained vitality of the apical fragment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates age, immature root anatomy, dens invaginatus, horizontal root fracture, prior apparent healing, and recurrent radiolucency to conclude that the coronal fragment likely has recurrent/persistent infection while the apical fragment may still support healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the imaging and clinical course at a nuanced level, including the relevance of the incisal fracture in fig_02.jpg as evidence of recurrent trauma, the widened interfragment gap in fig_03.jpg, and the limited value of negative sensibility alone after RET.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare management options or makes trade-offs that are clearly inappropriate for this tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives such as extraction, apexification, or conventional root canal treatment but gives only superficial or generic reasons.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why repeat RET is preferable to apexification or conventional root canal treatment in a young patient with a short, thin-walled coronal fragment and residual healing potential, while recognizing extraction as a legitimate backup if salvage fails.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances prognosis realistically: acknowledges poor crown-to-root ratio, risk of persistent infection or re-trauma, and uncertainty of success, yet justifies salvage because repeat RET can preserve structure and permit continued apical maturation/calcified healing that other options cannot.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits relevant complications, monitoring, or reasons the plan could fail.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Notes a need for review but does not identify specific complications or meaningful follow-up targets.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important concerns such as persistent/recurrent infection, mobility, reinjury, and the need for long-term radiographic follow-up to assess lesion resolution and healing between fragments.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds nuanced follow-up points: negative sensibility may persist despite success, healing may occur by calcified or other tissue interposition, and retreatment should be abandoned for extraction only if symptoms, radiolucency, mobility, or restorability worsen.

items.question_content:
A 20-year-old man presents shortly after a fall with trauma to maxillary right central incisor (11) and mild dull pain. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg only.

The patient wants the most conservative option possible and asks whether the fractured fragment is worth preserving and whether treatment can realistically be completed in one visit. Write the decision note you would give a senior clinician before starting treatment. Commit to one primary tooth-preserving pathway for the first visit and justify it from the figures and history. Explain why at least two other reasonable pathways are less suitable in this specific tooth at presentation, identify the single unresolved factor that prevents you from promising definitive success on day 1, and state how your plan and prognosis would change if flap reflection later showed the palatal fracture margin to be at or slightly below the crestal bone.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My working diagnosis is a recent complicated oblique crown-root fracture of 11 involving enamel, dentin, and pulp in a mature permanent tooth. fig_01.jpg suggests a displaced/mobile coronal fragment with partial palatal attachment and loss of part of the crown. fig_02.jpg shows an oblique fracture line extending cervically/subgingivally, a closed apex, preserved root length and periodontal support, and no clear separate root fracture.

The most defensible first-visit pathway is staged tooth preservation with provisional fragment preservation, pulpal control, and deferred commitment to definitive reattachment until direct inspection confirms restorability. I would not promise completion in one visit. The fracture appears to extend subgingivally and the hidden palatal extent relative to the crestal bone cannot be judged reliably from presentation alone; that uncertainty determines whether predictable isolation, bonding, and maintenance of periodontal health are possible.

For pulpal management, I would favor root canal treatment in this specific case because the tooth is mature, the pulp is exposed in a displaced/mobile crown-root fracture, the fragment is unstable, and the tooth will likely undergo repeated manipulation and subgingival assessment before a predictable definitive coronal seal is achieved. After stabilization/protection and trauma documentation, the fragment should be handled carefully and preserved hydrated if removed, followed by flap reflection to inspect the fracture margin directly.

If inspection shows only minimal subgingival extension with maintainable supracrestal tissue attachment and adequate access/isolation, I would keep fragment reattachment as the definitive intent because it is the most conservative way to preserve natural contour, translucency, surface texture, and tooth structure. Because some coronal tooth structure is missing, adjunctive composite completion may still be required.

Two or more other reasonable pathways are less suitable at presentation:
1. Vital pulp therapy/partial pulpotomy is biologically plausible after fresh trauma, but here it is less attractive because the tooth is mature, the fragment is mobile, the fracture is crown-root rather than a simple coronal exposure, and definitive sealing conditions are uncertain.
2. Immediate full-coverage restorative replacement of the crown or a post-core-crown approach without trying to preserve the fragment is too invasive and premature before restorability is clarified.
3. Immediate orthodontic or surgical extrusion is not my first move at presentation because the tooth may still be restorable with a less invasive adhesive pathway; however, those options become more relevant if the fracture is deeper than expected.
4. Extraction is not justified at this stage because the root appears intact and periodontal support is present.

The single unresolved factor preventing a definitive day-1 promise is the true apical extent of the palatal/proximal fracture margin in relation to the gingival margin and crestal bone. If flap reflection later shows that margin at or slightly below the crestal bone, direct adhesive reattachment becomes substantially less predictable. My plan would then shift away from same-pathway definitive reattachment toward exposing a maintainable restorative margin, most often with orthodontic extrusion in the esthetic zone; surgical extrusion may be considered depending on urgency and root form. Crown lengthening is generally less attractive for a maxillary central incisor because of esthetic and attachment loss tradeoffs.

With crestal involvement, prognosis becomes more guarded: periodontal inflammation risk rises if the attachment apparatus is violated, isolation becomes harder, ferrule and crown-root ratio may become limiting, and long-term debonding or refracture risk increases. The tooth may still be salvageable, but success is less predictable and treatment becomes longer and more invasive than when the fracture margin is only minimally subgingival.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the injury, for example as an uncomplicated crown fracture, denies pulpal involvement, or asserts a definite root fracture not supported by fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes traumatic fracture of 11 but incompletely characterizes the crown-root pattern, pulpal involvement, root maturity, or displacement/mobility of the coronal segment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a complicated oblique crown-root fracture of 11 with pulpal involvement in a mature tooth, with a displaced/mobile coronal fragment and no clear radiographic root fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies the injury and explicitly links the diagnosis to conditional restorability and the need for staged reassessment rather than immediate definitive coronal repair.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic trauma answer with little or no meaningful use of fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical or radiographic data, but the connection between specific figure findings and the chosen pathway is incomplete or superficial.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses specific findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to justify the pulpal approach, fragment preservation, and why definitive treatment cannot be promised at presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately interprets the fracture orientation and fragment relationship from the figures and identifies the hidden fracture-margin relation to the crestal bone/supracrestal tissue attachment as the key unresolved determinant of restorability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Presents an unsafe or illogical sequence, such as definitive bonding before assessing restorability, or irreversible treatment without adequate evaluation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests a generally plausible plan but does not clearly distinguish what should be done on the first visit from what depends on later direct inspection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes first-visit stabilization/protection, trauma assessment, pulpal control, fragment preservation, and direct reassessment of the fracture margin before definitive commitment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly separates immediate from conditional decisions and explicitly justifies why same-day definitive success should not be promised before flap-based inspection of the fracture extent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan, such as extraction without considering conservative options, definitive reattachment without reassessment, or a plan that ignores subgingival restorability issues.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a plausible tooth-preserving plan but does not commit to a primary pathway, omits major steps, or does not explain how the plan would change with crestal involvement.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a coherent primary tooth-preserving pathway for the first visit, with justified pulpal management, fragment preservation, conditional reattachment, and an appropriate contingency if the fracture is at or below the crestal bone.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides an adaptive, case-specific plan that favors the most conservative viable pathway at presentation and appropriately pivots to margin-exposing tooth-preserving strategies when direct adhesive rehabilitation becomes unpredictable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives a one-sided recommendation with no meaningful comparison of alternatives or prognosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives or prognosis change only generically, without case-specific reasons why those alternatives are less suitable now.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares at least two reasonable alternative pathways not chosen and explains relevant tradeoffs such as conservation, esthetics, seal predictability, periodontal impact, invasiveness, and treatment time.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced comparison of alternatives that explains why an option may be less suitable at presentation yet become appropriate if crestal involvement is confirmed, with a realistic prognosis that reflects ferrule, periodontal, and long-term adhesive risks.

red_flags: Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Promising definitive adhesive reattachment without direct assessment of the fracture margin after fragment removal and flap reflection
Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommending extraction or another irreversible option without first considering viable tooth-preserving strategies
Generic Textbook Management: Providing a standard trauma protocol that ignores the figure-based fracture configuration and restorability constraints

items.question_content: A 44-year-old woman has a restorable maxillary left second molar (#15) with spontaneous pain, lingering cold pain, and marked percussion tenderness; periodontal findings are normal. After access under a dental operating microscope, the chamber-floor view is shown in fig_01.jpg. Before committing to definitive shaping or obturation, CBCT slices are obtained (fig_02.jpg). Using the figures, identify the most likely canal configuration and the main alternative interpretation you would want to exclude. Then state whether you would have completed treatment before reviewing fig_02.jpg, justify that decision, and give a prioritized plan from access refinement to obturation that addresses the single greatest technical failure risk in this tooth. Finally, explain how your plan would change if CBCT were unavailable after the fig_01.jpg finding.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg together support a fused-root maxillary second molar with a type 1-3 configuration in the buccal root and a type 1-1 configuration in the palatal root. The chamber-floor image suggests a shared or elongated buccal orifice/C-shaped buccal entry rather than separate conventional mesiobuccal and distobuccal orifices, and the CBCT slice progression shows one buccal coronal pathway that divides in the middle third into three buccal canals with separate apical exits. The main alternative interpretation to exclude is a routine maxillary molar pattern with separate buccal canals or an MB2-type assumption, because treating it that way could miss additional buccal divisions inside a fused root.

I would not complete definitive shaping or obturation before reviewing fig_02.jpg. After the fig_01.jpg finding, the priority is anatomic mapping rather than enlargement. I would refine access conservatively under the microscope, remove only enough dentin to expose the buccal groove/common entry, scout with small precurved hand files, and determine whether multiple buccal limbs are negotiable. If the canal map remained uncertain, I would stop short of definitive instrumentation until 3D imaging clarified the anatomy.

Once fig_02.jpg confirms the configuration, my plan is to negotiate each of the three buccal branches separately plus the palatal canal, obtain individual working lengths with apex locator and radiographic correlation, and shape conservatively with modest taper and dentin preservation because the fused buccal root and shared coronal segment increase the risk of thinning, transportation, or strip perforation. Because the common buccal segment and fins will not be fully instrumented mechanically, I would rely heavily on sodium hypochlorite, EDTA, recapitulation, and activated irrigation for disinfection. Obturation should be done only after all branches are confirmed patent, clean, and dry, and the method chosen must allow predictable sealing of the three buccal branches and the palatal canal without blocking one buccal branch while filling another.

The single greatest technical failure risk is missing one or more buccal divisions and therefore undercleaning and underfilling part of the system. If CBCT were unavailable after the fig_01.jpg finding, I would be even more conservative: microscope-guided exploration, multiple angled radiographs with files placed in different buccal limbs, apex locator correlation, and no blind enlargement. If the anatomy still could not be mapped confidently, I would place an intracanal medicament, temporize, and refer or reassess rather than complete the case as though it were a routine molar.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg meaningfully, or interprets the tooth as a routine maxillary second molar without resolving the buccal anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes unusual buccal anatomy but incompletely describes the figure findings, or does not distinguish the case from a routine separate-buccal-canal pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to identify a shared buccal coronal path/common buccal entry that divides into three buccal canals, with a separate single palatal canal, and states that a routine buccal-canal interpretation must be excluded.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately synthesizes the figure progression from the chamber-floor appearance to the CBCT levels, explains the type 1-3 buccal configuration and type 1-1 palatal canal, and clearly justifies why a routine maxillary molar interpretation is less likely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Would proceed to routine definitive shaping or obturation before the anatomy is adequately mapped, or gives no clear sequence of priorities.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some caution but does not clearly decide whether to pause treatment, obtain more information, or reorder the treatment sequence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that after the fig_01.jpg finding definitive shaping or obturation should be deferred until the anatomy is mapped, with priorities of conservative access refinement, scouting, and separate working-length control before enlargement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear staged decision: limited exploration and mapping after fig_01.jpg, CBCT review before committing to full instrumentation, and a defined fallback if the anatomy remains uncertain, such as temporization or referral rather than blind completion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan, or describes routine endodontic treatment without adapting to the shared-entry trifurcating buccal system.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses tooth-preserving root canal treatment but gives only a general plan, with limited adaptation of access, canal negotiation, disinfection, or obturation to the anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a stepwise plan that includes conservative microscope-guided access, separate negotiation and working-length control for the three buccal branches and palatal canal, conservative shaping, strong emphasis on chemical disinfection and irrigant activation, and obturation of all mapped canals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a logically ordered plan specifically tailored to the common buccal coronal segment and deeper trifurcation, including how to avoid blocking sibling branches during obturation and how the plan changes when CBCT is unavailable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits the major risks created by the anatomy or identifies the wrong primary risk.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic endodontic complications, or lists risks without linking them to this tooth's anatomy or to prevention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the main technical failure risk as missed buccal division(s) and also notes important related risks such as dentin over-removal, strip perforation, transportation, or incomplete debridement, with basic mitigation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how the anatomy creates distinct risks at access, scouting, shaping, irrigation, and obturation, and gives practical prevention strategies such as conservative troughing, dentin preservation, staged decision-making, and reliance on chemical disinfection for uninstrumented areas.

items.question_content: An 18-year-old woman presents 5 days after a bicycle fall with trauma to #21 and #22. Both teeth are painful to percussion and grade II mobile. A careful hand attempt to reseat them does not succeed. Using only the pretreatment clinical view in fig_01.jpg and the preoperative periapical image in fig_02.jpg, decide the best tooth-preserving management for today's visit and justify it. In your justification, identify the injury pattern and salvageability, compare your chosen approach with at least two other plausible tooth-preserving options that you generate yourself, explain which specific pretreatment findings make one plan biologically preferable at this delay, outline the key priorities for stabilization and pulpal/periodontal management during the first month, and name the single patient or tooth factor that would most strongly push you to a different plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This is delayed extrusive luxation of mature permanent incisors #21 and #22. fig_01.jpg shows coronal displacement/elongation with associated soft-tissue injury, and fig_02.jpg shows widened periodontal ligament spaces with intact roots and no obvious root fracture, so the teeth are still salvageable. The 5-day delay plus failed hand reseating suggests organized clot or early socket healing that makes repeated forceful closed repositioning less biologically sound. If the roots appear favorable for atraumatic removal, the best tooth-preserving option at this visit is intentional replantation, meaning very atraumatic extraction followed by controlled repositioning into the original sockets. The priorities are to protect cementum and periodontal ligament, minimize extraoral time, keep the teeth moist in saline while out of the mouth, remove only the obstructing clot from socket and root surface so the teeth can fully seat, verify alignment, adjust occlusion, and place a short passive flexible splint for about 10 to 14 days; the existing orthodontic brackets visible in fig_01.jpg can help with stabilization. Because these are closed-apex teeth in an 18-year-old after severe luxation, pulpal necrosis is highly likely, so endodontic treatment should begin after initial stabilization, around 7 to 10 days, with calcium hydroxide as an intracanal medicament before later obturation, followed by close clinical and radiographic follow-up for inflammatory resorption, ankylosis, and periodontal healing. Two reasonable alternatives are orthodontic repositioning and another assisted closed or limited surgical repositioning attempt without deliberate extraction. Orthodontic repositioning is more conservative regarding extraction trauma but is slower, leaves the teeth displaced longer, and does not address the likely socket obstruction causing failure of reseating. Another forceful closed attempt risks additional periodontal ligament and socket-wall damage after resistance has already been demonstrated. Observation alone is inappropriate, and extraction with replacement is disproportionate in a salvageable 18-year-old. The single factor that would most strongly push me away from intentional replantation is any tooth anatomy or condition predicting traumatic extraction, especially unfavorable root form, because that would undermine the biologic premise of the procedure; in that setting I would favor a non-extractive tooth-preserving approach such as orthodontic repositioning. A major systemic infection-healing risk such as immunosuppression would also lower the threshold to avoid replantation and would require medical coordination.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the injury or treats the case as avulsion, intrusion, lateral luxation without justification, uncomplicated mobility, or a non-salvageable situation unsupported by the pretreatment findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a displacement injury but does not clearly identify delayed extrusive luxation of mature permanent incisors, or is unclear about salvageability and root status.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies delayed extrusive luxation of #21 and #22 in mature permanent teeth and recognizes that the pretreatment radiograph does not show an obvious root fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly distinguishes extrusion from other traumatic displacement injuries using pretreatment clinical and radiographic features and frames the case as salvageable but biologically time-sensitive.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use the pretreatment figures or the stated clinical history to support the management decision.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings or only one data source, without integrating fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and the delayed failed reseating into a coherent explanation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses at least one pretreatment finding from fig_01.jpg and one from fig_02.jpg, together with the 5-day delay and failed hand reseating, to justify the chosen plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the pretreatment displacement and soft-tissue injury seen in fig_01.jpg, the widened periodontal ligament space and intact roots seen in fig_02.jpg, and the delayed failed reseating into a biologically coherent explanation for why simple closed repositioning is now less suitable while tooth preservation remains reasonable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses an inappropriate plan such as observation alone, repeated forceful blind repositioning, extraction without a preservation rationale, or replacement-focused treatment despite a salvageable presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects a generally tooth-preserving plan but gives an incomplete immediate sequence, does not address first-month management, or omits major biologic priorities.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses intentional replantation only if atraumatic extraction is feasible and outlines the key priorities: periodontal ligament and root-surface protection, very short moist extraoral time, limited clot removal to permit seating, accurate repositioning, occlusal adjustment, flexible splinting, and early endodontic treatment in mature luxated teeth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a prioritized plan for today's visit and the first month that includes atraumatic handling, confirmation of seating, a short passive flexible splint of about 10 to 14 days, endodontic initiation at about 7 to 10 days with calcium hydroxide before later obturation, and explicit monitoring for ankylosis and inflammatory resorption.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare reasonable alternatives or rejects them without case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only one alternative or gives generic pros and cons that are not tied to the delay, failed reseating, or figure findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the preferred plan with at least two plausible tooth-preserving alternatives generated by the respondent and rejects them using case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances immediate correction of displacement, occlusion, and aesthetics against periodontal ligament trauma, ankylosis, inflammatory resorption, treatment duration, and proportionality, while making clear why extraction and replacement would be excessive in this salvageable 18-year-old.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify any tooth or patient factor that should change the plan, or still recommends intentional replantation despite a clear reason it would be biologically unsound.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a relevant factor, such as unfavorable root form or major immunosuppression, but does not clearly explain why it alters the indication or what alternative would follow.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a high-impact factor that would shift management away from intentional replantation, most defensibly extraction expected to be traumatic because of unfavorable root form, or alternatively a major systemic infection-healing risk such as immunosuppression, and proposes a reasonable non-replantation tooth-preserving alternative with rationale.

items.question_content: A 51-year-old woman with crowned maxillary central incisors reports upper anterior discomfort and wishes to keep the teeth if feasible. Tooth 21 is non-responsive to cold/EPT, tender to percussion and bite, with no mobility or deep probing. Tooth 11 is slightly tender to percussion, normal to palpation, and also has no mobility or deep probing. Review fig_01.jpg, but base your diagnostic reasoning on the preoperative radiograph in panel A. Argue for your preferred first-visit strategy and overall plan: identify the most likely diagnosis for each tooth, decide whether tooth 21 should undergo definitive treatment immediately or only after further imaging, name the strongest competing diagnosis for tooth 21 that would materially alter management, state the finding that would make you abandon tooth-preserving treatment of 21, and place tooth 11 appropriately in the sequence. Briefly justify prognosis for both teeth.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis for tooth 21 is internal root resorption in a tooth that is now non-vital/infected, presenting clinically as necrotic pulp with symptomatic apical periodontitis. On fig_01.jpg panel A the defect is canal-centered, with smooth ballooning enlargement continuous with the canal space, which favors internal rather than external resorption. The absence of deep probing or mobility does not suggest an obvious periodontal communication or a clearly hopeless fracture. Tooth 11 is best interpreted from fig_01.jpg panel A as a previously treated tooth with a short/inadequate root filling; with percussion tenderness, it is most consistent with symptomatic apical periodontitis/persistent post-treatment apical disease and is a retreatment case.

My preferred first-visit strategy is to prioritize tooth 21 and obtain a limited-field CBCT before definitive treatment if it is readily available, because the lesion is large and a single periapical film cannot reliably show perforation status, remaining dentin thickness, or external communication. That said, if CBCT cannot be obtained immediately and the tooth appears clinically restorable, proceeding with carefully consented nonsurgical treatment of 21 is still defensible; immediate extraction would be premature on the current data.

The strongest competing diagnosis for tooth 21 is a management-altering perforating/external resorptive defect; in a crowned tooth, vertical root fracture is a less likely but important alternative. Current findings still favor internal resorption because of the centered radiographic appearance and lack of isolated deep probing. The finding that would make me stop pursuing tooth preservation would be confirmation of hopeless structural compromise, such as severe perforation/external communication with very thin residual dentin making predictable repair impossible, clear vertical root fracture, or non-restorability.

If tooth 21 is salvageable, treat it first with isolation and magnification, conservative chemomechanical debridement, avoidance of aggressive enlargement of already thinned walls, obturation of the canal, repair/sealing of the resorptive cavity with a biocompatible material suitable for irregular defects, and a sound coronal seal/final restoration. Tooth 11 should then undergo orthograde nonsurgical retreatment.

Prognosis for 21 is guarded initially because of lesion size and uncertainty about perforation/remaining dentin, but becomes more favorable if the defect is contained or repairable, periodontal support remains intact, infection is controlled, and the coronal seal is adequate. Prognosis for 11 is generally favorable after proper retreatment if healing is seen clinically and radiographically on follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misdiagnoses tooth 21 as a routine apical lesion only, misses the resorptive nature of the defect on fig_01.jpg panel A, or fails to recognize tooth 11 as an endodontically treated tooth with persistent disease.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Correctly identifies endodontic pathology in one or both teeth but incompletely characterizes tooth 21 or tooth 11, or gives an imprecise diagnosis without linking it to the preoperative radiograph.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies tooth 21 as internal root resorption in a now non-vital/infected tooth with symptomatic apical periodontitis, and tooth 11 as a previously treated tooth with symptomatic/persistent apical periodontitis requiring retreatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully integrate fig_01.jpg panel A with the clinical tests, or ignores key findings such as the absence of deep probing and mobility.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical and radiographic findings but does not clearly explain why the appearance on fig_01.jpg panel A favors one diagnosis over another, or does not use the periodontal findings appropriately.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg panel A and the examination findings coherently: recognizes the canal-centered, smooth/symmetrical ballooning enlargement on tooth 21, incorporates the non-response to sensibility testing and percussion/bite tenderness, and uses the lack of deep probing/mobility to support salvageability unless further imaging proves otherwise.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible alternative diagnosis for tooth 21 that would change management, or proposes an implausible alternative.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a plausible competing diagnosis such as external resorption, perforating defect, or vertical root fracture, but does not explain why it is less likely on current evidence or what would confirm it.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a credible management-altering alternative diagnosis for tooth 21 and explains why the present data still favor internal resorption; specifies the added clinical or CBCT finding(s) that would shift the diagnosis and plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent plan, recommends observation/restorative-only care, or fails to address both teeth and the sequence of care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends endodontic treatment in general terms but without a clear first-visit decision, without a conditional plan based on additional imaging/restorability, or without addressing repair of the resorptive defect and later management of tooth 11.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a tooth-specific, stepwise plan: prioritizes tooth 21, justifies either limited-field CBCT first or immediate carefully consented nonsurgical treatment if appropriate, includes conservative disinfection and sealing/repair of the resorptive defect with a biocompatible material plus coronal seal, and then places tooth 11 in appropriate orthograde retreatment sequence. Clearly states how proof of severe perforation, fracture, or non-restorability would change the plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the main risks and benefits relevant to tooth retention versus non-retention.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some risks or benefits but does not tie them closely to lesion size, structural compromise, patient preference, or the value of further imaging.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefit of attempting conservative retention against risks from lesion size, thin remaining dentin, possible perforation or fracture, and explains why extraction would be premature unless hopeless non-restorability is demonstrated.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits prognosis or gives a clearly unrealistic prognosis unrelated to the case findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only a generic prognosis with limited connection to perforation status, remaining dentin, restorability, or retreatment outcome.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that tooth 21 has an initially guarded prognosis that improves if the defect is sealable/repairable, sufficient dentin remains, periodontal support is intact, infection is controlled, and the restoration seals well; states that tooth 11 is generally favorable after proper retreatment with follow-up confirmation of healing.

items.question_content:
A 39-year-old man is reviewed 6 weeks after orthograde treatment of #13-23 for pulpal necrosis with chronic apical disease. Two anterior sinus tracts persist and mild percussion tenderness has developed. Cast post-and-core restorations are already cemented for #13-23, and the same maxillary anterior segment is expected to need surgical crown lengthening before definitive crowns.

Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, write your management recommendation for the next visit. Commit to the surgical field you would plan before raising a flap, and identify the radiographic feature or clinical-radiographic combination on each included tooth that supports including it rather than leaving it to observation. Explain how the existing posts change your choice compared with the same case before post cementation. Finally, name one preoperative or intraoperative finding that would most strongly overturn your plan, and state exactly how your management would change.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My recommendation for the next visit is periapical surgery combined with the planned surgical crown lengthening, with the pre-flap surgical field including #12, #11, #21, and #22.

That field matches the symptomatic and radiographic pattern in the anterior segment. Clinically, the persistent sinus tracts are in the #12 and #22 region, which makes the lateral incisors the clearest active source teeth. Radiographically, #12 and #22 also have the most unfavorable apical anatomy: both show apical external root resorption and open apices, and #12 also shows internal root resorption. Those features make spontaneous resolution after recent orthograde treatment less predictable and support definite inclusion in surgery.

I would also include #11 and #21 rather than limiting surgery to the laterals alone. fig_01.jpg shows a broad periapical radiolucent lesion involving the maxillary anterior teeth, and fig_02.jpg shows that the centrals lie within the same diseased anterior periapical field between the two symptomatic laterals. In the reported management, surgery was planned and carried out on #12, #11, #21, and #22 together, which is reasonable because the lesion spans that central anterior region and the same segment also requires crown lengthening. Including the centrals addresses the involved periapical area as a unit rather than assuming the lesion is confined to the laterals only.

I would not pre-plan surgery for #13 or #23. Although they were part of the original orthograde treatment and are adjacent to the lesion, the surgical plan in this case did not include them. Their apical configuration was more favorable clinically during treatment, with good apical constrictions, and they were managed orthogradely without being selected for the periapical surgical procedure.

The cemented cast posts shift the balance toward surgery. Once the posts are already in place, orthograde retreatment becomes more destructive and less practical because post removal risks root damage, perforation, fracture, and loss of remaining tooth structure in teeth that are already being restored. In this situation, targeted periapical surgery is the more appropriate tooth-preserving way to manage persistent disease.

Before post cementation, I would be more willing to consider further orthograde revision or a delay for reassessment, because access for retreatment would be less destructive. Even then, the persistent sinus tracts and the unfavorable apical anatomy of #12 and #22 would still keep surgery high on the list, but the threshold to re-enter the canals would be lower before posts were placed.

The finding most likely to overturn this plan would be a vertical root fracture or a tooth being judged non-restorable, especially in one of the planned surgical teeth. If that were found preoperatively or after flap reflection, I would abandon root-end surgery for that tooth and change management to extraction with restorative redesign for the segment rather than proceed with apical surgery on a hopeless tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use fig_01.jpg or fig_02.jpg, or gives no tooth-specific or region-specific basis for the recommendation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses general radiographic impressions but does not correctly identify the planned surgical field, or does not connect the persistent sinus tracts and anterior radiolucency to the included teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to support surgery on #12, #11, #21, and #22, correctly citing the stronger anatomic disease features of #12 and #22 and the shared anterior periapical lesion involving the centrals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figures and clinical findings tooth by tooth: identifies #12 and #22 as the most clearly pathologic because of persistent sinus tracts plus open/resorbed apical anatomy, recognizes internal root resorption in #12, explains why the broad anterior periapical lesion justifies including #11 and #21 in the same surgical field, and excludes #13 and #23 with case-supported reasoning.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no clear plan, recommends observation alone despite persistent disease, or proposes an unsupported surgical field.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends surgery but does not commit to the planned pre-flap field, or includes/excludes teeth without clear case-based boundaries.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a pre-flap surgical field of #12, #11, #21, and #22, and leaves #13 and #23 out of the planned periapical surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Defines the planned field as periapical surgery on #12, #11, #21, and #22 in conjunction with crown lengthening, clearly distinguishes these teeth from #13 and #23, and ties the field to the combined clinical and radiographic pattern rather than to unsupported preferences.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not explain how the posted restorative situation changes management, or gives only generic comments about surgery versus retreatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that posts make retreatment harder but gives limited case-specific reasoning or does not address how the decision would differ before post cementation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that existing posts shift the balance toward surgery because post removal risks structural damage and restorative compromise, and states that orthograde revision would be more plausible before post cementation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison showing why the current posted/restorative context favors periapical surgery now, while also explaining how the balance would shift before post cementation and why the persistent disease pattern would still keep surgery under strong consideration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not name a plan-changing finding, or names one without stating how management would change.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a plausible finding such as fracture or non-restorability, but the effect on management is vague or incomplete.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a major finding that would overturn the plan and states the corresponding change in treatment, such as abandoning salvage for a fractured or non-restorable tooth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the single most decisive finding and links it to an exact management change, for example abandoning root-end salvage and moving to extraction with restorative redesign for a fractured or non-restorable planned tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Lists conclusions without a logical link between the figures, clinical findings, restorative constraints, and management choice.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides some rationale but leaves important steps in the argument implicit or internally inconsistent.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows a clear, coherent chain of reasoning from the persistent sinus tracts, the radiographic lesion pattern, the involved teeth selected for surgery, and the impact of existing posts to the final surgical plan and contingency change.

items.question_content: A 45-year-old non-smoker reports slight pain on chewing on the lower right. Oral hygiene is good. Probing shows an isolated 10 mm narrow pocket with bleeding at the mesial root of #47 and a 6 mm bleeding pocket only on the distal root of #46; the mesial root of #46 probes 4 mm without bleeding, with grade I furcation and no mobility. The patient wants to avoid implants if a predictable tooth-preserving plan exists. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, recommend the definitive management for this posterior segment. State which tooth/root(s), if any, you would retain, the treatment sequence, and why your plan is more appropriate than other reasonable options in this patient.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would give #47 a hopeless prognosis and recommend extraction of that tooth. The combination of an isolated deep narrow periodontal pocket and the radiographic pattern on fig_02.jpg is highly suggestive of vertical root fracture involving the mesial root; in an already heavily restored molar with limited remaining tooth structure, this is not predictably salvageable. For #46, I would make a root-specific decision rather than extract the whole tooth: the distal root is compromised, but the mesial root appears potentially retainable because its probing is comparatively favorable, there is no mobility, and support is better than for the distal root. If removal of the existing splinted restoration confirms that the mesial root is restorable with an acceptable crown-root ratio, I would retain only the mesial root of #46.

Sequence: first stabilize periodontal inflammation and reinforce plaque control; then remove the existing restoration and reassess caries extent/restorability. Perform endodontic retreatment of the retained root of #46 if required to ensure a sound seal and post/core plan. Next, extract #47 and resect/remove the distal root of #46. After healing, restore the retained mesial root of #46 with a definitive full-coverage restoration designed to direct forces axially, minimize lateral loading, and keep margins cleansable. Replacement of the #47 space can be deferred and reconsidered later based on healing, function, and patient preference.

This is more appropriate than removing both teeth because pathology is localized and #46 still has one root with salvage potential in a motivated patient who prefers tooth preservation. It is also more predictable than trying to retain the fractured/root-compromised portions. The main risks are fracture of the retained root, unfavorable crown-root ratio, secondary caries, plaque retention, and occlusal overload, so long-term maintenance and careful prosthetic design are essential. Prognosis is hopeless for #47 and guarded-to-fair for the retained mesial root of #46 if restorable and properly restored.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe definitive plan, such as attempting to retain the likely fractured #47, offering only vague therapy, or extracting/retaining teeth without root-specific justification or sequence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that definitive treatment is needed but gives an incomplete or weakly justified plan; may identify one tooth correctly yet miss the root-specific strategy for #46, omit sequencing, or ignore restorative/endodontic requirements.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends extraction of #47 and conservative retention of the salvageable part of #46, with a generally appropriate sequence that includes reassessment, surgical removal of the diseased root/tooth, and definitive restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent interdisciplinary plan: periodontal stabilization, restoration removal and restorbility reassessment, endodontic retreatment of the retained root if needed, extraction of #47, resection/removal of the distal root of #46, healing, and full-coverage restoration of the retained mesial root with cleansable margins and controlled occlusion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the clinical and radiographic data meaningfully or ignores major case factors visible in fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Cites some isolated findings but does not synthesize them into a coherent justification for the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates key findings from history, probing, and radiographs to support differential prognosis of #46 and #47.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the deep isolated pocket at #47, the radiographic fracture-type pattern, the extensive splinted post-crown restorations and subgingival caries on fig_02.jpg, the better mesial-root periodontal status of #46, absence of mobility, and the patient's preference to justify a root-specific conservative approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misattributes the problem to generalized periodontitis, a routine endodontic lesion, or another diagnosis that does not fit the root-specific pattern.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suspects localized root pathology but is uncertain or inaccurate about which tooth/root is likely fractured or which part remains potentially retainable.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies #47 as highly suspicious for vertical root fracture with poor prognosis and recognizes localized distal-root compromise of #46 with better prospects for the mesial root.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies likely vertical root fracture of #47 from the combined probing/radiographic pattern and clearly distinguishes the hopeless prognosis of #47 from the guarded but potentially favorable prognosis of the mesial root of #46 if restorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison of risks, benefits, or patient-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons but does not tie them to this patient's anatomy, restorability, or preferences.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why conservation of a salvageable root may be preferable to more extensive tooth loss in this patient while acknowledging limitations and need for maintenance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances conservative retention against complete extraction/replacement by discussing patient preference, remaining bone support, restorbility, crown-root ratio, occlusal loading, hygiene access, risk of fracture/secondary caries, and the conditions under which the retained root would or would not remain a predictable choice.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old boy with Noonan syndrome presents with pain from the left side of the jaws. He has severe caries, multiple teeth absent without extraction history, narrow crowded arches with a high palate, mild congenital cardiac disease for which his cardiologist advised that infective endocarditis prophylaxis is not required, LABA use, and previous prolonged bleeding after extraction despite normal PT/PTT/INR/BT. On testing, teeth #16, 25, 27, 36, and 37 are hyper-responsive to thermal stimuli and tender to percussion; the remaining teeth respond within normal limits. An incisional biopsy from the mandibular enlargement has been reported as a giant cell lesion compatible with aneurysmal bone cyst. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. For the symptomatic tooth complex shown in fig_04.jpg, state your most likely tooth-level diagnosis and your definitive management. Justify that choice against the main reasonable alternatives by integrating the figures, the overall dentition, and the medical history. Include how the mandibular lesion changes sequencing of care, the key technical modifications for this tooth, and the specific finding that would make you abandon tooth preservation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The tooth complex in fig_04.jpg is the priority symptomatic maxillary posterior unit, corresponding to #27 with an anomalous mesiopalatal supernumerary/fused component. The pulpal/periapical diagnosis is most consistent with chronic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis. fig_04.jpg also suggests nonstandard canal anatomy with mixed apical maturity, including open-apex canal(s), so definitive treatment should be preservation-based nonsurgical endodontic therapy if the unit is restorable and periodontally maintainable.

My plan would be: caries removal and access under magnification, careful mapping of every canal in the main tooth and anomalous segment, working-length confirmation with angled radiographs and CBCT only if conventional imaging does not clarify the anatomy, chemomechanical preparation of all negotiable canals, apical barrier/fill with MTA or equivalent bioceramic material in open-apex canal(s), conventional obturation in mature canals, then a durable coronal seal and definitive restoration. Isolation and clamp choice may need modification because of the high palate, narrow arches, and severe crowding. Tissue handling should be atraumatic, and if any surgical step becomes necessary, local hemostatic planning matters because Noonan syndrome can be associated with bleeding tendency even when basic coagulation screening is normal. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated because cardiology has already advised against it.

Preservation is preferred over extraction or removal of the anomalous segment because this patient already has multiple missing teeth and severe arch discrepancy, so retaining a functional posterior tooth is strategically valuable. Removing only the anomalous component risks creating a nonrepairable periodontal defect, and full extraction adds surgical bleeding risk and further compromises an already reduced dentition. Palliative care or temporary measures alone would not be definitive for a tooth with this pulpal/periapical picture.

The mandibular lesion does change sequencing, but mainly by requiring interdisciplinary planning rather than by making endodontic treatment inappropriate. Because the lesion is already biopsied as a giant cell lesion compatible with aneurysmal bone cyst and the patient’s current odontogenic symptoms need relief, I would proceed with disease control and definitive management of symptomatic teeth while coordinating timely surgical follow-up for the mandibular lesion. I would not ignore the lesion, but I also would not delay all dental treatment solely because it is present.

I would abandon tooth preservation if the tooth proved non-restorable, if the anomalous component had a non-maintainable periodontal communication/defect, if there were structural fracture or hopeless periodontal support, or if the canal anatomy could not be predictably disinfected and sealed. In that event, a surgical option could become the better choice, with additional hemostatic planning because of the bleeding history.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the tooth/process, gives no tooth-level diagnosis, or proposes management inconsistent with the symptomatic tooth shown in fig_04.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either the endodontic nature of the problem or the anomalous anatomy, but not both, or gives an incomplete tooth-level diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the fig_04.jpg tooth as an anomalous maxillary posterior tooth complex requiring definitive endodontic management, with a diagnosis consistent with irreversible pulpitis and symptomatic apical periodontitis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above diagnosis and explicitly notes that fig_04.jpg suggests mixed apical maturity/open-apex canal(s), which materially affects canal management and obturation strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses generic reasoning and does not meaningfully incorporate the figures or relevant medical history.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Incorporates some case facts, but does not clearly connect the figures, dentition, and systemic history to the treatment choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the figure-based tooth anatomy, overall dentition in fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg, the biopsy-reported mandibular lesion, and the medical history into a coherent rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows clearly how each major datum changes treatment choice, sequencing, and technique, including why bleeding history still matters despite normal screening tests and why cardiology guidance means routine antibiotic prophylaxis is unnecessary.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no definitive plan or recommends clearly inappropriate or unsafe management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a broadly plausible plan but omits essential execution details for the anomalous tooth or does not distinguish management of open-apex versus mature canals.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends preservation-based nonsurgical endodontic treatment if restorable, including identification and treatment of all canals, apical barrier/fill for open-apex canal(s), conventional obturation for mature canal(s), and definitive coronal sealing/restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above plan with clear sequencing, technique modifications for access/isolation in this anatomy, and explicit contingencies for when further imaging or a change in treatment direction would be required.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Prioritizes care in a clinically unsound way or ignores the impact of the mandibular lesion on sequencing.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges both the symptomatic tooth and the mandibular lesion but gives vague or weak sequencing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately prioritizes definitive management of symptomatic odontogenic disease while arranging timely referral/follow-up for the mandibular lesion rather than allowing one problem to obscure the other.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds a well-ordered sequence that includes immediate disease control, coordination with surgical care for the lesion, and realistic staging of broader restorative/maintenance needs in this dentition.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare reasonable alternatives or favors an irreversible option without patient-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives superficially but does not weigh them using this patient's anatomy, dentition, and medical context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why tooth preservation is favored over extraction, removal of the anomalous segment, or palliative management by using strategic tooth value, risk of periodontal defect, reduced dentition, and bleeding history.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the alternatives in a nuanced way, states the specific clinical findings that would shift the decision toward surgery, and outlines the main precautions if that surgical threshold is reached.

items.question_content: A 41-year-old healthy woman has 1 week of dull continuous pain from both maxillary first molars, worse at night and with thermal stimuli. Teeth 16 and 26 are carious, tender to percussion, restorable, and periodontally sound; the pulpal diagnosis is symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis. Examine fig_01.jpg carefully. What definitive management would you choose for these teeth, and how should the anatomy visible in fig_01.jpg change your access, canal negotiation, and obturation strategy compared with a routine maxillary first molar? Justify your plan from the clinical findings and imaging.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The best definitive treatment is nonsurgical root canal therapy for both 16 and 26 because both teeth are restorable, periodontally stable, and have pulpal/apical findings consistent with endodontic disease rather than a need for extraction or primary surgery. fig_01.jpg should not be managed as a simple single-canal molar: the 3D imaging shows a single root with one main canal coronally that divides in the middle third and exits as three separate canals. That finding should change the plan from a routine maxillary first molar approach to a conservative but carefully extended access that allows deep inspection of the chamber floor and the coronal third of the canal under strong illumination/magnification. After initial entry into the apparent single canal, small precurved files should be used to scout for the split, and each branch should be confirmed as a separate path with electronic length determination and angled radiographic/3D correlation before shaping. Instrumentation and irrigation must be directed to all three branches while preserving dentin and avoiding apical extrusion, because the division zone is at risk for blockage, ledging, and incomplete debridement. Obturation should seal all three apical canals and the divided segment, using a technique that adapts well to complex anatomy rather than treating the tooth as one straight canal. Key risks are missed branches, perforation from over-searching coronally, procedural errors at the point of division, and inadequate cleaning or filling of the separated canals.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores fig_01.jpg or misreads it as either routine three-root anatomy or a simple single straight canal; does not connect the clinical findings to an endodontic diagnosis and management need.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical or imaging findings but incompletely; recognizes an anatomic variation without clearly explaining its treatment implications, or identifies the need for endodontic care without showing why the imaging changes the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates symptoms, percussion tenderness, restorable/periodontally sound status, and fig_01.jpg to conclude that the teeth need definitive endodontic treatment and that the canal system divides into three separate paths that require individualized management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the deceptive 2D appearance with the 3D anatomy in fig_01.jpg, explicitly explaining why routine assumptions about maxillary first molars would be unsafe here and how the imaging findings materially alter technical planning.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate definitive management, such as extraction without justification, no endodontic treatment, or a one-canal treatment plan that does not address the canal division.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends root canal treatment but provides a mostly generic plan, with limited adaptation of access, canal location, working-length confirmation, shaping, or obturation to the divided canal anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends nonsurgical root canal therapy with a coherent stepwise plan: modified access, careful scouting of the deeper split, confirmation of separate branches, individual cleaning/shaping, and obturation of all three apical canals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, conservative, and technically sound strategy that balances canal discovery with dentin preservation, explains how to negotiate the division zone, and links obturation choice to the need to seal the full split anatomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful risks of this anatomy or lists complications unrelated to the scenario.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic risks such as failure or infection, with little connection to the specific anatomy or how those risks would be prevented.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies major anatomy-related risks such as missed branches, perforation from excessive searching, blockage/ledging at the split, and inadequate cleaning or obturation, with reasonable preventive measures.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how each key complication arises from the single-root canal division pattern and gives practical prevention or mitigation strategies tied to access design, scouting, irrigation, and obturation.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of either maxillary first molar despite both being restorable and periodontally sound without first pursuing conservative endodontic management
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: planning to instrument or obturate these teeth as a single straight canal based on the 2D appearance while ignoring the canal division visible on fig_01.jpg

items.question_content: A 12-year-old boy seeks correction of poor esthetics and Class II division 1 malocclusion. Clinical exam shows a maxillary left “double tooth” formed by fusion of the central incisor with a mesiodens; both are clinically healthy. Study fig_01.jpg carefully. Before any treatment is started, what definitive management strategy would you choose to preserve function and esthetics while still allowing orthodontic correction? Justify your choice from the anatomy visible on imaging rather than from the crown appearance alone, explain why less invasive or more radical paths would be less favorable in this patient, and state the single most important long-term complication you would actively monitor for after treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would aim to preserve the permanent maxillary central incisor and remove the supernumerary portion by a CBCT-guided hemisection/separation plan, rather than extract the whole double tooth or simply reshape/observe it. The key reason is the internal anatomy on fig_01.jpg: this is not just a large crown problem. The fusion extends through the root, with a shared canal system coronally and in the middle third, then a complex apical relationship with separation/rejoining and a labially positioned apical exit. That makes simple surgical separation with an attempt to keep the pulp vital highly unpredictable, because sectioning is likely to violate a shared pulp space and compromise the retained incisor. I would therefore include definitive endodontic management of the fused canal system before or as part of separation, then surgically remove the mesiodens portion along a CBCT-defined plane that protects the incisor, smooth the retained root surface, and manage the expected socket/periodontal defect to preserve support. Orthodontic movement should begin only after healing is stable and then with light forces.

This is preferable because the central incisor is a strategic anterior tooth in a 12-year-old: retaining it preserves esthetics, alveolar bone, and future orthodontic options. Observation or crown recontouring alone would not solve the malalignment/proclination and leaves a plaque-retentive fusion line. Extracting the whole fused unit would create a difficult anterior replacement problem in a growing patient.

The main long-term complication I would monitor is periodontal-apical breakdown on the mesial aspect of the retained incisor: a deep vertical pocket/osseous defect with possible sinus tract and later periapical radiolucency, especially if a small apical remnant or leakage persists. Follow-up should include probing depths, mobility, sinus tract assessment, and serial periapical imaging, with CBCT if clinical signs develop or worsen.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation/cosmetic reshaping only, extraction of the entire fused unit/permanent incisor, or surgical separation without addressing the shared endodontic anatomy; no coherent sequencing with orthodontic treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the supernumerary portion should be addressed or that the incisor should be retained, but the plan is incomplete, poorly sequenced, or omits a major component such as endodontic control of the shared canal system, CBCT-guided surgery, or management of the post-separation defect.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends preserving the central incisor via planned hemisection/removal of the mesiodens, with definitive management of the shared canal system and surgery guided by CBCT; delays orthodontics until initial healing/stability is achieved.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced interdisciplinary plan that includes preservation of the incisor, endodontic management of the complex fused system, careful surgical separation along an imaging-defined plane, root-surface finishing/defect management, and cautious later orthodontic movement with gentle forces.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Bases management mainly on esthetics or crown size/shape and does not use the imaging anatomy in the reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses one imaging feature but misses the critical internal root/canal configuration or does not explain how the anatomy changes treatment choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the imaging to identify that fusion extends through the root with a shared canal relationship and clinically important proclination, and connects these findings to the need for a preservation-focused endodontic-surgical plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes multiple fig_01.jpg findings—root-level fusion, shared coronal/midroot canal anatomy, complex apical relationship/labial apical exit, and severe labial proclination—into a coherent justification for why simple separation or purely restorative management is biologically unreliable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful patient-specific trade-off analysis, or offers reasoning that ignores growth, esthetics, and orthodontic implications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general pros and cons but only superficially, without tying them to this 12-year-old patient and the anterior tooth’s strategic value.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why preserving the central incisor is preferable to removing the whole fused unit in a growing patient, and why simple monitoring/recontouring or separation without endodontic control is less favorable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances esthetics, alveolar preservation, growth-related concerns, orthodontic feasibility, and biologic/endodontic-periodontal risks across reasonable options, with clear patient-specific justification for retaining the central incisor.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits likely complications or lists only vague generic risks.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions failure, infection, or root resorption generically, but does not identify the most relevant long-term complication for this anatomy or how it should be monitored.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies periodontal/apical breakdown as the main long-term concern, such as a deep mesial pocket/vertical defect, sinus tract, retained apical fragment, labial bone loss, or periapical lesion, and proposes follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes periodontal-apical failure over less critical issues and gives a concrete surveillance strategy (probing, mobility, sinus tract checks, serial radiographs/CBCT as indicated) with recognition that worsening findings would trigger re-intervention.

items.question_content:
A 34-year-old woman returns 9 months after removal of IMF screws placed during repair of a left mandibular fracture; the surgical field included the #33-34 region. She reports pain on chewing and intermittent localized swelling adjacent to #34. Tooth #34 is non-responsive to sensibility testing and tender to percussion. During access under rubber dam, size 8 and 10 K-files meet a firm stop short of the radiographic apex. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg.

You must give the patient one definitive recommendation today. Commit to a primary management pathway rather than listing a menu. Justify it using the figures and the canal-access finding, explain why this is not a routine necrotic premolar, identify the strongest competing approach you considered and why you rejected it here, state the circumstance most likely to make you change course, and include the main site-specific consent issue and your prognosis for tooth retention.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The working diagnosis is iatrogenic IMF screw-related root perforation of #34 with loss of canal continuity, resulting in pulp necrosis and symptomatic apical periodontitis with recurrent localized swelling. The key imaging feature is on fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg: the defect is in the middle third of the root, begins buccally, and traverses through the canal space toward the lingual side. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg support a root-centered/periradicular pathosis rather than a routine apical lesion from an otherwise intact canal.

Because the canal cannot be negotiated to full working length, this is not a standard necrotic premolar that can predictably be managed orthogradely alone. The combination of a buccolingually traversing mid-root defect and a firm stop short of the apex means the apical segment is unlikely to be adequately cleaned and sealed from a coronal approach.

For a restorable, periodontally supportable tooth, my definitive recommendation would be a planned combined tooth-preserving strategy: orthograde chemomechanical management of the accessible coronal segment under rubber dam, sealing the accessible canal/perforation portion with a calcium-silicate repair/filling material, then endodontic microsurgery/apicectomy to manage the inaccessible apical segment with root-end preparation and retrograde sealing, followed by definitive coronal restoration and follow-up.

The strongest competing approach is nonsurgical root canal treatment alone. I would reject it as the definitive plan here because the decisive problem is not just infection, but the inability to predictably treat the apical segment through the canal. Primary extraction is not my first choice if the tooth is otherwise maintainable, since this is a localized iatrogenic injury and retention remains feasible. However, extraction becomes the better option if new information shows a vertical root fracture/crack, nonrestorable tooth structure, periodontal communication or hopeless support, inadequate residual root after resection, inability to obtain a predictable seal, unsafe surgical access, or persistent disease after adequate combined treatment.

The circumstance most likely to change my plan would be proof that the apical segment is fully negotiable to working length and canal continuity is functionally restorable; in that scenario, conventional nonsurgical root canal treatment alone would become first-line and surgery would be reserved for failure.

The main site-specific consent issue is the mental foramen/mental nerve region in mandibular premolar surgery. CBCT-based localization should guide flap design, osteotomy position and size, and retraction, with counseling about possible lower-lip/chin paresthesia.

Prognosis for tooth retention is guarded to fair/favorable rather than excellent. It depends on restorability, periodontal support, ability to obtain both orthograde and root-end seals, and adequate remaining root after resection; it is worsened by the middle-third transradicular defect and the need to treat an apically inaccessible segment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the problem, such as calling the tooth vital/reversibly inflamed, a primary periodontal lesion, or a routine necrotic tooth without meaningful structural injury.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either prior screw-related injury or endodontic disease, but not the full causal diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies IMF screw-related root perforation of #34 associated with pulp necrosis and apical inflammatory disease requiring active treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies a middle-third canal-traversing perforation/root disruption from IMF screw placement and links it to pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis/recurrent localized swelling.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or misinterprets the imaging/access findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either clinical findings or imaging, but does not connect them coherently to treatment feasibility.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates symptoms, sensibility/percussion findings, the short file stop, and the radiographic/CBCT findings to explain why this is not routine orthograde endodontic disease.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically interprets fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg as a buccal-to-lingual middle-third defect through the canal space, uses fig_01.jpg and/or fig_02.jpg (and/or fig_05.jpg) to support root-centered/periradicular pathosis, and explicitly links this anatomy to likely orthograde inaccessibility of the apical segment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation alone despite current disease, a generic RCT plan that ignores the inaccessible apical segment, or extraction without sufficient case-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends intervention but provides an incomplete, weakly justified, or poorly sequenced plan.

levels.title: Meets
