levels.description: Provides an appropriate retention-oriented plan for a restorable tooth that manages the accessible canal orthogradely and recognizes that surgical management of the apical segment may be necessary.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Recommends a definitive, stepwise combined strategy for a restorable tooth: orthograde management/sealing of the accessible segment plus planned apical surgery with root-end management, definitive restoration, and follow-up; also states that full working-length negotiability would shift first-line care to nonsurgical RCT alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison of benefits, risks, and alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers generic pros and cons with limited case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen pathway with at least one plausible competing approach using predictability, morbidity, and tooth-preservation considerations.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why orthograde-only care is not sufficiently definitive in this anatomy, why extraction is not first choice if the tooth is maintainable, and gives objective thresholds that would shift to extraction or abandonment of retention (for example crack/vertical root fracture, nonrestorability, periodontal communication/hopeless support, unsafe surgical access, inadequate residual root after resection, inability to seal, or persistent disease after adequate treatment).

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify a relevant site-specific hazard or discusses only vague generic postoperative risks.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a local surgical risk but does not connect it to planning or consent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the mental foramen/mental nerve region as the principal local hazard and recommends CBCT-based localization/counseling.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how mental nerve risk changes flap design, osteotomy position/size, retraction, and consent, and also identifies at least one plausible post-treatment failure mode requiring monitoring, such as persistent leakage, infection, delayed healing, or ongoing symptoms.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits prognosis or gives an unrealistic prognosis unsupported by the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only a vague prognosis without relating it to anatomy or treatment feasibility.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a realistic guarded/fair prognosis for retention and relates it to the need to manage an apically inaccessible segment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Ties prognosis explicitly to perforation location and extent, ability to achieve orthograde and retrograde seals, residual root adequacy after resection, restorative/periodontal status, and follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Lists multiple options without prioritizing one primary pathway.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a preferred option but with substantial hedging or without a clear trigger for changing course.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to one primary recommendation and identifies a plausible circumstance that would change the plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes one definitive pathway over plausible alternatives and identifies the single most important finding that would reverse or restage management, with reasoning tied to this case.

items.question_content:
A healthy 32-year-old woman reports spontaneous pain and lingering cold pain from a restorable mandibular first molar; the tooth is tender to percussion and periodontal probing is normal. Under rubber dam, caries excavation creates a large pulpal exposure. One canal orifice becomes visible, while part of the chamber remains protected by dentin. After removing only the obviously diseased coronal tissue, hemorrhage is still brisk despite brief chlorhexidine and 5.25% NaOCl attempts. She wants the least invasive definitive treatment that is still biologically sound.

Using fig_01.jpg panel A first, decide whether you would still complete definitive vital pulp therapy today or convert to canal treatment, and justify the minimum extent of further tissue removal you would choose. Your reasoning should integrate the preoperative radiographic pattern, the fact that some chamber tissue is still dentin-covered, and the meaning of persistent bleeding. State the specific intraoperative finding that would make you abandon your initial plan. Then use fig_01.jpg panel B and fig_01.jpg panel C to identify 2 imaging findings that retrospectively support your decision and 1 imaging or clinical finding that would have shown it was the wrong choice. Finally, explain briefly whether your threshold for VPT would change if the previously dentin-covered chamber area had also been directly exposed and bleeding diffusely.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would still attempt definitive VPT the same visit, but only in the most conservative form that remains biologically defensible: a localized/selective tampon pulpotomy at the exposed site rather than immediate full canal treatment. fig_01.jpg panel A shows apical involvement associated with a deep carious/restorable tooth, but this does not by itself prove total pulpal necrosis. The lingering cold response, normal probing, and intraoperative bleeding all support that at least part of the pulp is still vital. The key anatomic point is that one exposed area is involved while pulp over the remaining chamber is still protected by dentin, so I would not remove uninvolved tissue simply because bleeding is delayed.

The minimum further tissue removal would be limited to the exposed/inflamed site only. I would preserve the dentin-covered mesial chamber tissue, clean the wound, and place a hydraulic calcium-silicate material directly over the bleeding pulp with gentle pressure from a dry pellet to obtain a tampon effect, followed by an immediate well-sealed definitive restoration. A limited deeper amputation could be considered only within the already exposed site if needed, but not by extending into the previously protected area without evidence it is involved.

Persistent bleeding weakens the prognosis but is not an automatic indication for pulpectomy if the bleeding is still from vital tissue and can be controlled mechanically while a tight coronal seal is achieved. The intraoperative finding that would make me abandon VPT is persistent uncontrolled diffuse hemorrhage or other evidence that a stable biologic seal cannot be achieved despite site-directed management; purulence/necrotic tissue or loss of restorability would also shift me to canal treatment.

Retrospective support from fig_01.jpg panel B and fig_01.jpg panel C would include: (1) postoperative imaging consistent with a conservative coronal biomaterial placement beneath the restoration rather than full canal obturation, showing radicular pulp was intentionally preserved; and (2) 1-year resolution of the apical/PDL changes with re-establishment of normal periapical architecture, plus a hard-tissue bridge adjacent to the capping material. Findings that would have shown the original choice was wrong include persistent/recurrent spontaneous pain, loss of vitality, swelling or sinus tract, increasing percussion tenderness, or radiographic enlargement/nonhealing of the apical lesion, new furcal disease, or resorption.

If the previously dentin-covered chamber area had also been directly exposed and bleeding diffusely, my threshold for VPT would become higher because the disease would appear less localized. I would only continue with VPT if a more extensive but still controlled pulpotomy produced manageable bleeding and a sealable wound. If bleeding remained diffuse and uncontrollable across the chamber, same-visit canal treatment would be more appropriate.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets the case data or ignores major findings. Treats the preoperative apical changes as automatic proof of total necrosis, or ignores the significance of vitality signs, normal probing, or the localized dentin-covered anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant information but incompletely or inconsistently. Recognizes either vitality preservation or the apical changes, but does not clearly reconcile fig_01.jpg panel A, the clinical findings, and the bleeding pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg panel A with symptoms, percussion tenderness, normal probing, restorability, localized exposure, and persistent bleeding into a coherent biologic explanation for why VPT can still remain on the table in a mature molar despite apical change.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains why the radiographic pattern in fig_01.jpg panel A does not by itself mandate canal treatment, and shows how the combination of localized exposure plus dentin-protected remaining chamber tissue narrows the defensible extent of pulp removal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan, or gives no clear definitive same-visit management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broadly plausible plan but the extent of tissue removal is unclear, or abandons conservative treatment without sufficient case-based justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects a defensible same-visit plan that preserves viable pulp when possible, limits tissue removal to involved areas, uses an appropriate bioactive pulp-covering material, and emphasizes the need for an immediate coronal seal, while allowing escalation to canal treatment if biologic criteria are not met.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, site-directed plan consistent with localized/selective tampon pulpotomy: preserves the dentin-protected chamber tissue, explains why unnecessary extension into uninvolved pulp is not indicated, and clearly describes the role of mechanical tamponade plus definitive restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not state when the initial plan should be abandoned, or gives a threshold that is unsafe or unrelated to the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a vague stopping rule or does not meaningfully address how management would change if the previously protected chamber tissue were also exposed and bleeding diffusely.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States a clear intraoperative threshold for abandoning VPT, such as persistent uncontrolled diffuse bleeding, purulence/necrosis, or inability to obtain a seal, and appropriately explains that diffuse exposure would make VPT less favorable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows stepwise prioritization: preserves tissue when disease appears localized, escalates only when biologic or restorative conditions fail, and clearly distinguishes the significance of localized versus diffuse bleeding in determining how far treatment should proceed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not interpret fig_01.jpg panel B/fig_01.jpg panel C or gives inaccurate success/failure markers.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic follow-up endpoints with limited use of the postoperative and recall images.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies 2 retrospective findings supporting the decision, such as conservative postoperative material placement and 1-year healing/re-establishment of normal periapical structures or hard-tissue barrier formation, and identifies at least 1 meaningful finding that would indicate failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses fig_01.jpg panel B and fig_01.jpg panel C specifically to justify why the original plan was validated, and links concrete clinical and radiographic failure triggers to why that initial decision would then be judged incorrect.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old girl presents 2-3 months after trauma with fractured maxillary central incisors. Tooth 11 has localized labial swelling in the apical region, no sinus tract or mobility, and both 11 and 21 do not respond to cold or EPT. Examine fig_01.jpg; the radiograph for 11 shows a horizontal root fracture with apical periodontal widening/loss of lamina dura. For tooth 11, what definitive management would you choose now, and why? Base your justification on the fracture level and pulpal/periapical status, explain which other reasonable management paths you considered but would not select first, and state the follow-up findings that would make you judge the tooth as healing versus failing.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would retain tooth 11 and manage it conservatively with nonsurgical endodontic treatment as the first-line approach. fig_01.jpg shows the fracture is toward the middle/apical part of the root, which generally carries a better prognosis than a cervical fracture, and the tooth has no mobility or obvious displacement, so immediate splinting is not the priority. However, this is not a case for observation alone: the delayed presentation, lack of sensibility together with localized apical swelling, and the apical PDL/lamina dura disruption indicate pulpal necrosis with periapical infection. Because the clinical and radiographic signs suggest disease beyond a purely coronal-fragment problem, I would disinfect and obturate to the apex, treating both fragments rather than limiting treatment to the coronal fragment only. A well-sealed definitive coronal restoration is also necessary once the tooth is controlled endodontically.

Reasonable alternatives include observation, coronal-fragment-only root canal treatment, and surgical apical management or extraction. Observation is inappropriate because there are active signs of infection. Treating only the coronal fragment would be less suitable here because the apical region is clinically involved. Surgical removal/apicectomy or extraction should be reserved for persistent non-healing, inability to control infection nonsurgically, or loss of restorability—not as first choice in a restorable adolescent incisor with a favorable fracture level.

Follow-up should check pain/tenderness, swelling, sinus tract, mobility or depressibility, and occlusion. Radiographically, success would be shown by resolution of periapical changes, re-establishment of a normal PDL space and lamina dura, reduction/closure or hard-tissue healing of the interfragmentary space, and no internal or external root resorption. Persistent symptoms, enlarging radiolucency, resorption, or continued non-healing at the fracture line would indicate failure and the need to reconsider treatment, including possible surgical salvage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully integrate the history, clinical findings, and fig_01.jpg; misses the significance of swelling and apical radiographic change, or misinterprets the fracture in a way that leads to an implausible conclusion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a horizontal root fracture and pulpal compromise but links the findings incompletely; may rely on non-response to sensibility testing alone or underuse the apical swelling/radiographic findings in the reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates delayed trauma, apical swelling, negative sensibility tests, fracture level on fig_01.jpg, and apical PDL/lamina dura disruption to conclude that tooth 11 has a favorable fracture location but active pulpal/periapical infection requiring treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced synthesis: explains why the fracture level supports retention, why lack of mobility/displacement matters, and why swelling plus apical radiographic change makes simple observation or limited treatment less suitable despite the generally good prognosis of more apical fractures.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no clear definitive plan, recommends observation despite active infection, or proposes an inappropriate first-line surgical/irreversible approach without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses tooth retention and endodontic treatment in general terms but does not clearly state whether the apical fragment should be included, or omits key elements such as need for coronal seal/restoration and structured follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends conservative nonsurgical endodontic management of tooth 11 with disinfection and obturation to the apex, effectively treating both fragments because the findings suggest infection is not confined to the coronal fragment; also notes that the tooth should be definitively restored and monitored.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a coherent, stepwise plan that prioritizes retention, explains why splinting is not indicated from the presented findings, includes endodontic control of both fragments, definitive coronal sealing, and reserves surgery only as a contingency for persistent non-healing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare reasonable alternatives or compares them incorrectly, showing little awareness of patient-specific risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one alternative strategy but gives superficial or generic reasons that are not well tied to this patient’s fracture location, age, or infection status.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Weighs observation, coronal-fragment-only treatment, and surgical approaches against the chosen plan; explains that observation is unsafe with swelling/apical changes, coronal-only treatment is less convincing with apical involvement, and surgery should be reserved for failure of conservative therapy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances options in a patient-specific way, highlighting the value of preserving a restorable adolescent maxillary incisor, the comparatively favorable prognosis of an apical/middle-apical fracture, and the lower morbidity of a tooth-retaining nonsurgical approach when feasible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful follow-up parameters or misses major failure signs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives only generic follow-up statements such as 'review clinically and radiographically' without specifying what would indicate healing or failure.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant clinical signs (pain, tenderness, swelling/sinus tract, mobility/depressibility) and radiographic signs (normalizing lamina dura/PDL, reduction or closure of fracture space, absence of periapical radiolucency and resorption) to judge healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes healing from failure, including persistent or enlarging radiolucency, non-healing at the fracture line, internal/external resorption, or renewed symptoms as triggers for reassessment and possible surgical salvage.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of tooth 11 at presentation despite a restorable adolescent maxillary incisor with a favorable middle/apical root fracture and viable conservative endodontic options

items.question_content: A 19-year-old woman presents 22 months after maxillary trauma. Forty-five days ago a painful palatal swelling in the left anterior maxilla was incised and drained; she is now asymptomatic. Tooth #21 is grossly destructed and submerged. Tooth #22 is labially displaced, restored, nonmobile, and gives no thermal/EPT response. Examine fig_01.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend for the left maxillary incisor region, particularly tooth #22, and why? Base your justification on the likely status of #22, the source and extent of the periapical lesion, and the anatomic risks visible on imaging that should shape access strategy, lesion management, and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Tooth #21 is hopeless and should be removed. Tooth #22 should not be merely observed. In a tooth with pulp canal obliteration after trauma, a negative sensibility test alone is not enough to diagnose necrosis, but here the combination of trauma history, prior palatal abscess, periapical radiolucency, widened PDL/loss of lamina dura, deep restoration/previous attempted access, and CBCT evidence of complete coronal obliteration strongly supports pulpal necrosis/infection associated with calcific metamorphosis. The lesion may involve both incisors, so definitive treatment should eliminate the unrestorable source (#21) and retain #22 with orthograde root canal treatment.

For #22, I would use CBCT-based guided access rather than freehand access, because the remaining canal is likely only apical and conventional scouting carries a high risk of gouging, perforation, and unnecessary loss of peri-cervical dentin. Initial lesion management should be conservative: disinfect #22 orthogradely and remove/curette pathologic tissue through the extraction socket or another conservative route if needed. Because fig_01.jpg shows palatal cortical perforation and limited remaining support, a buccal surgical approach could further weaken support for #22 and should be avoided unless healing fails.

The prognosis for retaining #22 is fair to good if the canal can be predictably reached, disinfected, and sealed and the lesion resolves, but it is guarded by complete obliteration, large lesion size, prior infection, risk of access deviation/perforation, incomplete debridement, and reduced supporting bone. Follow with clinical and radiographic review for pain, swelling, sinus tract, mobility, percussion/palpation tenderness, and reduction of the radiolucency; persistent disease would justify surgical endodontic reassessment or escalation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends monitoring/bleaching only for #22, extraction of both teeth without conservative justification, or a plan that does not definitively address the lesion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that active treatment is needed but gives an incomplete or poorly sequenced plan; may treat #22 endodontically yet ignore the hopeless status of #21, or propose surgery/access without explaining why this anatomy changes the approach.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends extraction of unrestorable #21 and orthograde root canal treatment for restorable #22; selects a controlled guided access approach for #22 because of severe obliteration and manages the lesion initially conservatively with review of healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent stepwise plan that preserves #22 while removing the hopeless tooth, uses CBCT-based guided access to the apical canal remnant, explains why nonsurgical disinfection is first-line for #22, and reserves more invasive surgery or extraction of #22 only for failure or non-navigable anatomy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Bases the decision on a single datum or misreads fig_01.jpg; does not connect trauma history, sensibility testing, and imaging.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant findings but misses key synthesis, such as relying on negative sensibility alone or ignoring the prior swelling or CBCT extent of disease.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates trauma history, prior palatal swelling/incision and drainage, absent sensibility, radiolucency, and fig_01.jpg evidence of calcific obliteration to support apical disease associated with #22, while recognizing that #21 may also contribute because it is grossly destructed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly notes that sensibility tests can be unreliable in PCO, but the combined history and imaging make intervention indicated; incorporates image-based features such as complete obliteration, loss of lamina dura/widened PDL, and palatal cortical perforation in the reasoning.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful comparison of risks and benefits, or the reasoning is unsafe.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons only, without tying them to this tooth and lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that guided access improves precision, conserves tooth structure, and reduces perforation/gouging risk in a severely calcified anterior tooth, while acknowledging added CBCT exposure, cost, planning time, and technical dependence.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also weighs lesion-management routes against support for #22, explaining why a buccal surgical approach could be disadvantageous given the palatal perforation and limited remaining support, and why surgery is better reserved for nonhealing or failure of orthograde management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores complications and follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists vague complications without prevention or case-specific monitoring.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies likely complications such as access deviation/perforation, excessive dentin loss, inability to negotiate or clean the apical canal, and persistent apical disease, and recommends clinical and radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Ties complications to this case by discussing compromised bone around #22, possible persistence from dual-tooth pathology, and specific follow-up markers such as symptoms, sinus tract, mobility, percussion/palpation, and radiographic reduction of the lesion.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old girl presents with an esthetic concern in the maxillary anterior region. Clinical examination shows a conical supernumerary structure fused to the labial surface of the maxillary left central incisor. Both structures are asymptomatic, respond positively to pulp testing, and have normal mobility and probing depths. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, which demonstrate fusion with a communication path between the pulp spaces. During flap elevation, the radicular portion of the supernumerary structure is found to be covered by only a thin layer of labial alveolar bone (fig_04.jpg). What definitive management is most appropriate, and why? In your answer, explain how the positive vitality tests influence management, outline the treatment sequence, and state how far the anomalous structure should be resected.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The appropriate management is a conservative multidisciplinary plan: perform endodontic treatment of both communicating canal systems first, then carry out limited surgical recontouring, and finally restore the tooth esthetically.

Although both structures test vital and are asymptomatic, the CBCT demonstrates pulpal communication between the fused central incisor and the supernumerary tooth. Therefore, vitality does not support simple cosmetic reduction, separation alone, or observation, because trimming or surgically removing the labial component could expose or contaminate the shared canal space and lead to pulpal necrosis, infection, or an endodontic-periodontal complication.

The sequence should be:
1. CBCT-guided root canal treatment of both communicating dental structures, with a sound seal up to the level of the coronal communication.
2. Surgical flap elevation and conservative recontouring/removal of the labial supernumerary crown.
3. Seal any exposed coronal internal space.
4. Complete the final esthetic restoration, typically with adhesive composite recontouring/restoration.

The supernumerary structure should be resected only coronally, not completely removed to the root. Because the radicular portion is covered by only a thin layer of labial bone, complete root removal would risk loss of facial osseous support, gingival recession, pocket formation, and poor esthetic outcome. Preserving the radicular portion helps maintain labial bone and soft-tissue support while allowing correction of the visible deformity.

Follow-up should assess symptoms, periapical healing, probing depths, mobility, gingival contour or recession, restoration seal, and discoloration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation only, simple cosmetic reduction/restoration, orthodontics alone, or extraction/complete excision without a tooth-preserving rationale; does not provide a coherent sequence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that intervention is needed but gives an incomplete or poorly sequenced plan, such as surgery before addressing pulpal communication, or vague multidisciplinary management without defining the key steps.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a conservative tooth-preserving plan that includes endodontic treatment before surgical reshaping and esthetic restoration; the general sequence is appropriate but the extent of resection or rationale is not fully developed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly recommends treating both communicating canal systems first, then conservative surgical recontouring with preservation of the radicular portion/facial support, sealing exposed internal space, and final esthetic restoration, with a well-justified sequence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figures or bases the decision only on esthetics or current vitality testing.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions fusion or a supernumerary tooth but does not adequately integrate the imaging with the clinical findings; misses either the communicating canal anatomy or the surgical/anatomic limitation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the clinical findings together with fig_01.jpg-fig_03.jpg to recognize fused anatomy with pulpal communication and explains why this changes management despite positive vitality.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all relevant data: asymptomatic but vital teeth, normal periodontal findings, fused labial supernumerary anatomy on fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg, pulpal communication on fig_03.jpg, and the thin labial bone over the radicular portion shown in fig_04.jpg to justify limiting resection.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful risk-benefit reasoning or substantially misjudges the trade-offs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only one major risk or gives generic discussion of risks and benefits without applying them to this anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances esthetic benefit against the risks of pulpal exposure/contamination and periodontal damage, and explains why a purely cosmetic or observational approach is insufficient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly contrasts the chosen conservative plan with more aggressive removal, explaining why complete root excision or loss of the central incisor would create unnecessary periodontal and esthetic harm given the possibility of preservation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify relevant complications or need for follow-up.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic infection risk or generic recall without case-specific complications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant complications such as persistent endodontic infection, labial bone loss, gingival recession or pocketing, restoration leakage, or discoloration, and recommends clinical/radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links prevention to the plan itself: pre-emptive sealing of communicating canals before recontouring, preservation of radicular support to protect facial bone and gingiva, and targeted monitoring of probing depth, mobility, periapical status, gingival contour, and esthetics.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old healthy man presents with a fractured maxillary left central incisor and wants to keep the tooth if feasible. He is asymptomatic, with normal probing and mobility. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. What is the most appropriate definitive management strategy for this tooth? Justify your choice using the tooth’s endodontic, periodontal, restorative, and imaging findings, explaining why it is preferable to other reasonable options in this patient. Also explain how the deviation seen during guided drilling should affect your intraoperative decisions and which guide-design or clinical safeguards are most important to prevent a serious iatrogenic error.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best option is to retain the tooth and perform orthograde nonsurgical endodontic retreatment, using a static CBCT/STL-guided approach to remove the fractured fiber post and re-enter the canal, then complete cleaning, shaping, obturation, and provide a definitive coronal restoration if restorability is maintained.

This choice is supported by the case findings. The tooth is strategically important in the esthetic zone, the patient is young and wishes to keep it, and the clinical exam does not suggest hopeless periodontal or structural status: probing and mobility are normal, and there is no percussion tenderness. fig_01.jpg shows a failed prior root canal with a fractured post and a periapical radiolucency; the CBCT shows preserved buccal and palatal plates, which supports a treatable lesion of endodontic origin rather than a non-restorable periodontal problem. The likely diagnosis is previous endodontic treatment with asymptomatic apical periodontitis. Because the disease source is intracanal, orthograde retreatment addresses the cause directly.

A guided approach is justified because freehand post removal in this situation has high risk of deviation, perforation, and unnecessary dentin loss. fig_02.jpg shows that the drill path can be planned along the post/canal axis, making treatment more conservative and predictable. Other pathways are less attractive here: extraction would be premature in a restorable anterior tooth, and a surgical-only approach would not first eliminate the intracanal cause and does not solve the need for internal retention in a heavily damaged crown.

The deviation seen in fig_03.jpg should trigger reassessment, not automatic abandonment or blind continuation. I would stop, inspect under magnification, confirm whether the canal is still accessible, verify patency/working length with a file and apex locator, and evaluate whether there is perforation or dangerous dentin thinning. If the canal remains negotiable and root integrity is acceptable, I would proceed cautiously with retreatment; if not, I would change the plan.

Key safeguards are accurate limited-FOV CBCT and high-quality intraoral scan, reliable DICOM-STL registration, no change in tooth morphology between scanning and treatment, a rigid guide with stable seating and verification windows, no rocking during use, proper drill-sleeve compatibility with minimal tolerance, adequate sleeve design/material, staged drilling with irrigation and debris removal, and repeated microscopic/radiographic verification during access.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends no viable definitive plan, or chooses extraction, surgical-only management, or blind/freehand post removal as first-line care without defensible case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects retention or retreatment in general terms but omits the need for guided access/post management, gives an incomplete sequence, or does not justify why this is the best option for this tooth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends tooth preservation by orthograde nonsurgical retreatment with guided access for post removal, followed by disinfection, obturation, and definitive coronal restoration; justification is generally appropriate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan and explicitly explains why this conservative approach is superior to other reasonable options for this patient, using esthetic-zone value, restorability, intracanal etiology, and avoidance of unnecessary dentin loss/iatrogenic damage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets major clinical or imaging findings; reasoning is inconsistent with the figures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant findings but leaves important figure-based evidence unaddressed or links the findings to the plan weakly.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates symptoms, periodontal stability, preoperative imaging, and intraoperative findings into a coherent rationale for management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely links the figure-based findings—fractured fiber post, failed prior treatment, periapical lesion, preserved surrounding plates, planned drill trajectory, and deviation with maintained canal access—to feasibility, prognosis, and next steps.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully weigh risks and benefits; ignores iatrogenic risk or the burdens of guided treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons but not why they matter in this specific tooth or patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the advantages of guided retreatment—greater precision, dentin conservation, lower perforation risk—against disadvantages such as CBCT exposure, cost, and technique sensitivity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why those trade-offs favor guided orthograde retreatment in this young anterior tooth with restorative value and an intracanal source of disease, while recognizing why more invasive or more destructive pathways carry greater biological or restorative cost.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address deviation/perforation risk, or would continue drilling blindly despite loss of accuracy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that deviation is a problem but gives vague or incomplete prevention and management steps.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that deviation requires immediate reassessment and continuation only if no perforation or critical thinning is evident and canal access is confirmed; includes several practical safeguards.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies multiple specific sources of error and prevention measures, including registration quality, guide seating and stability, verification windows, avoiding rocking, proper sleeve/drill compatibility and sleeve design, staged drilling with irrigation/cleaning, and magnified plus radiographic/apex-locator verification.

items.question_content: A 34-year-old man with pulpal necrosis and symptomatic apical periodontitis in maxillary left second molar undergoes access. Under magnification, the chamber floor shows MB and palatal orifices plus a third orifice almost adjacent to the palatal one; searching for the distobuccal canal in its expected position has already produced gouging. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide how you would map this tooth’s canal anatomy and proceed from this point. Explain why your plan is safer and more predictable than continuing treatment based on routine maxillary second molar anatomy, and state the main complication or prognostic issue you would monitor.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg support a three-canal maxillary second molar with altered coronal anatomy: the orifice near the palatal canal is the distobuccal canal, not a second palatal canal. The CBCT shows partial fusion of the roots in the coronal and middle thirds, with separation apically, so I would treat MB, DB, and palatal canals as separate canals that happen to have an eccentric coronal map.

The safest next step is to stop any further blind troughing in the usual DB area, reassess the gouged chamber floor for possible perforation, and use the CBCT map to negotiate the three canals separately under magnification. Working length should be established for each canal with an apex locator and radiographic confirmation. Instrumentation should stay conservative in the fused coronal portion because the canals are close together there, while still achieving full cleaning, shaping, irrigation, and obturation of all three separate canals. An interappointment calcium hydroxide dressing is reasonable if infection control or symptoms warrant, followed by obturation and a sound coronal seal once the tooth is asymptomatic.

This approach is safer than relying on routine maxillary second molar anatomy because the major risks now are iatrogenic perforation or further floor weakening from continued searching in the expected DB position, and missing the true DB canal by mislabeling it as an extra palatal canal. fig_02.jpg also shows early periapical change associated with the palatal root that was not obvious on the periapical film; this does not change the indication for nonsurgical endodontic treatment but should be part of follow-up. Prognosis is favorable if no perforation exists and all three canals are disinfected and sealed; it becomes more guarded if the gouging communicates with the furcation or if any canal is missed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg coherently; assumes routine maxillary second molar anatomy or misreads the third orifice as straightforwardly conventional without explaining the imaging.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an anatomic variation but incompletely or incorrectly interprets it, such as noting fusion without correctly identifying the eccentric distobuccal canal or missing the implication of apical separation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly interprets the third orifice near the palatal canal as the distobuccal canal and recognizes partial coronal/middle root fusion with separate apical canals/roots.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the full imaging picture: eccentric distobuccal orifice, fused coronal/middle root configuration with apical separation, existing chamber-floor gouging, and the early palatal-root periapical change, and uses these findings to justify management.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends management that is inappropriate or unsafe for the anatomy shown, such as continuing treatment without altering strategy, or offering an unjustified irreversible/surgical approach.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses nonsurgical root canal treatment but gives a generic plan with little adaptation to the eccentric orifice position, fused-root anatomy, or existing gouging.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides an appropriate CBCT-guided nonsurgical plan: stop further blind searching, treat MB/DB/palatal as three separate canals, confirm working length individually, and complete careful cleaning, shaping, obturation, and coronal sealing while respecting the altered anatomy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a clear stepwise plan that also includes reassessment of the gouged floor for perforation, use of magnification/localization aids, conservative preparation in the fused coronal portion, and rationale for staged disinfection/interappointment medication when indicated.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits the major procedural risks or proposes actions that would increase them.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only one generic complication or gives limited prevention/management detail.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the key risks in this case—missed canal, further pulpal-floor/furcal damage from continued gouging, and difficulty cleaning closely positioned canals in fused anatomy—and explains how the plan reduces those risks.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also explains how management would change if the gouging proves to be a true perforation and links prevention directly to the CBCT-guided anatomical map.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No prognosis is given, or the prognosis is clearly inconsistent with the findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a vague prognosis without relating it to the anatomy, gouging, or periapical status.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States a realistic prognosis that is generally favorable if all three canals are adequately treated and no perforation is present, with recall to assess healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically notes the need to monitor healing associated with the palatal root and explains why prognosis becomes more guarded if chamber-floor gouging communicates with the furcation or if canal misidentification leads to a missed canal.

items.question_content: A healthy 6-year-old boy with complete primary dentition has occasional thermal and sweet sensitivity from the upper left anterior teeth. fig_01.jpg shows an enlarged clefted crown of #61 with carious developmental grooves and caries in #62. fig_02.jpg shows #61 has a single enlarged root and root canal, and both lesions are close to the pulp. fig_03.jpg shows developing permanent incisors, with altered development/position of #22. What is the most appropriate management strategy now, and why? Base your answer on the findings in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, and include the key follow-up priorities for the permanent dentition.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The enlarged bifid #61 is most consistent with gemination rather than fusion or simple macrodontia because the primary tooth count is complete and fig_02.jpg shows one enlarged root/canal rather than two separate dental units. fig_01.jpg also shows a clefted crown with plaque-retentive grooves, explaining the caries risk. My management would be conservative retention with definitive caries control, not immediate extraction. Both #61 and #62 need operative treatment because the lesions are already deep and symptomatic to provocation; preventive sealing alone would be insufficient. Caries should be removed and both teeth restored, with reshaping/sealing of the developmental grooves on #61 to improve cleansability and esthetics. For #61, if excavation results in carious pulp exposure but the tooth is still restorable, the radicular pulp appears vital, and hemostasis is achievable, vital pulp therapy such as pulpotomy is appropriate. Extraction would be reserved for a nonrestorable tooth or evidence of pulpal necrosis/infection, pathologic mobility, or unfavorable root resorption. This conservative approach preserves anterior esthetics, function, and arch integrity while the permanent incisors continue to develop. Follow-up should be close and periodic, with clinical and radiographic review of pain, swelling/fistula, restoration seal, recurrent caries, pulpal failure, and physiologic resorption/exfoliation. fig_03.jpg also makes monitoring of the eruption path, rotation, and developmental progress of #22 a priority, with orthodontic surveillance if the disturbance persists.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads or ignores key figure-based findings; does not use the enlarged clefted crown, single root/canal, caries depth, or the altered development/position of #22 in the reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely or inaccurately; relies mainly on either the clinical appearance or the radiograph without integrating both into management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg to identify a double primary tooth most consistent with gemination of #61, deep caries in #61/#62 near the pulp, and a permanent successor that needs surveillance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes crown morphology, tooth count, single enlarged canal/root, symptoms, and dentition stage into a coherent explanation of why the anomaly is gemination rather than fusion or macrodontia, and shows how those findings change treatment and follow-up priorities.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no definitive plan for the active disease, or recommends clearly inappropriate care that does not address the caries/pulpal risk.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests restoration or observation but omits management of likely pulpal involvement, or treats the anomalous tooth generically without considering its unusual anatomy and restoratability.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends conservative retention of the restorable geminated #61, operative treatment of both #61 and #62, vital pulp therapy for #61 if carious exposure is encountered in an otherwise vital restorable tooth, and definitive restoration with improvement of plaque-retentive grooves.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a clear stepwise plan: preserve if restorable, remove caries under appropriate isolation, assess pulp status intraoperatively, select pulpotomy rather than more aggressive or insufficient care when indicated, restore anatomy to improve function/esthetics/hygiene, and schedule structured review.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers little or no patient-specific justification, or does not weigh reasonable alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides generic pros and cons but weakly links them to the child's age, dentition stage, symptoms, tooth anatomy, or eruption considerations.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why conservative management is favored over extraction or purely preventive care: the tooth appears restorable, there are no signs of infection or pathologic resorption in the stem/figures, the caries is too advanced for sealants alone, and retention supports esthetics, function, and eruption guidance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances immediate disease control with future eruption needs and explicitly states when the plan would change, such as nonrestorability, necrosis, swelling/fistula, abnormal mobility, or pathologic resorption.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits follow-up needs or relevant complications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions follow-up only in vague terms without identifying what specifically must be monitored.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the need to monitor restoration integrity, recurrent caries in grooves, pulpal failure/infection, resorption/exfoliation pattern, and the development/eruption of #22.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links periodic clinical and radiographic surveillance to specific escalation triggers, including persistent delay or malposition of #22 and the need for orthodontic assessment if eruption guidance becomes problematic.

items.question_content: A 17-year-old male presents 6 years after trauma with fractured #9 and #10, both non-responsive to thermal and electric pulp testing and currently asymptomatic. Periapical radiographs and CBCT are provided in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. He wants to preserve the teeth and regain esthetics. Based on the imaging and clinical context, what definitive management would you choose now for #9 and #10? Justify your plan by identifying the key anatomic findings that should change access, debridement/obturation, and post-endodontic reinforcement, explain why this route is preferable to other reasonable options at this stage, and give a realistic prognosis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best initial approach is tooth-preserving nonsurgical endodontic treatment of both teeth, followed by reassessment and definitive adhesive restoration if they are restorable. The clinical picture is of traumatized, nonvital anterior teeth with apical disease of endodontic origin, so elimination of intracanal infection should be attempted before moving to more invasive options.

fig_01.jpg and fig_03.jpg indicate that #9 is not a routine central incisor: it has two separate roots/canals and marked crown-root angulation/dilaceration. Therefore access must be modified to follow the altered long axis and deliberately locate two distinct canal orifices; shaping should be cautious, conservative, and well controlled to avoid transportation, ledging, perforation, or instrument separation in the curved anatomy. Each canal must be cleaned and obturated as a separate system.

fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show that #10 has a developmental groove and a C-shaped canal configuration. That means routine round-canal preparation is inadequate; debridement must emphasize circumferential instrumentation and copious irrigation to address fins/isthmuses, with obturation adapted to the irregular canal space.

Because both teeth have major coronal loss, post-endodontic rehabilitation should be adhesive and fiber-based only after confirming adequate remaining tooth structure/ferrule. Aggressive post preparation should be avoided because these roots are atypical and likely thin. Definitive esthetic crowns can be considered after a sound seal and core are achieved.

This conservative route is preferable now because the teeth appear retainable, the patient is young, and even a relatively large lesion with cortical involvement can heal after adequate canal disinfection and sealing. Surgical treatment should be reserved for persistent disease, inability to disinfect nonsurgically, or non-restorability.

Prognosis is fair to guarded rather than excellent: healing potential is reasonable, but the outlook is limited by unusual anatomy, root curvature, the developmental groove acting as a plaque/bacterial niche, trauma history, substantial structural loss, and the size/cortical extension of the periapical lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No coherent plan, or proposes a clearly inappropriate pathway that does not prioritize controlling the endodontic source of disease in these retainable teeth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses endodontic retention but gives a generic protocol. Limited or no anatomy-specific modification for #9 and #10, weak sequencing of restoration, or unclear criteria for when to reassess/escalate care.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends initial nonsurgical endodontic treatment of both teeth with a stepwise plan: modified access and separate treatment of both canals in #9, tailored cleaning/obturation for the irregular canal in #10, then post-endodontic reinforcement and definitive restoration if restorable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, patient-specific sequence that integrates conservative nonsurgical treatment, anatomy-guided access and shaping, cautious post-space strategy in compromised anterior teeth, and clear triggers for moving to surgery or other options only after reassessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figure-based findings or treats the case as a routine single-canal trauma case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some data, such as trauma history or non-vital status, but misses major imaging findings or links them poorly to management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the key data: delayed trauma history, negative sensibility, apical lesion involving both teeth, anomalous two-root/two-canal and curved anatomy of #9, and irregular C-shaped anatomy with groove in #10.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the full clinical-radiographic picture, including structural compromise and cortical/periapical extent visible on CBCT, and explicitly shows how those findings alter the management choice and technical approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful justification for the chosen route or bases the decision on a single factor such as lesion size alone.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that tooth preservation has advantages but does not adequately weigh it against case-specific complexity or other reasonable options.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why conservative retention is reasonable now despite the lesion and anatomic complexity: young patient, endodontic etiology, apparent restoratability, and potential for healing after adequate disinfection and seal.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances biologic healing potential, structural preservation, esthetic value, morbidity of more invasive pathways, and the conditions that would justify changing course if nonsurgical treatment fails.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify the major technical hazards created by the anomalous anatomy and structural loss.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic risks such as fracture or reinfection, without linking them to the actual anatomy of #9 and #10.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important case-specific risks such as missing a second canal in #9, transportation/ledging/perforation or instrument separation in curved canals, incomplete debridement or obturation of the C-shaped space in #10, and weakening the roots during post preparation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies the key risks and links them to prevention strategies, such as anatomy-guided access, careful working-length control, conservative shaping, enhanced irrigation focus in irregular spaces, and cautious adhesive reinforcement rather than aggressive root enlargement.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No prognosis is given, or the prognosis is clearly incompatible with the findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a prognosis but offers little or no justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Gives a fair or guarded prognosis and supports it with relevant factors such as unusual anatomy, trauma history, structural loss, developmental groove, and extent of periapical disease.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced prognosis that distinguishes likely biologic healing after adequate endodontic therapy from the ongoing restorative and structural risks that limit long-term certainty.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of #9 and/or #10 as first-line management despite a plausible conservative endodontic retention pathway in this 17-year-old with apparently restorable teeth

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. A healthy 17-year-old male first presented 6 months after trauma to tooth #9 after incomplete emergency care elsewhere; extraction had been advised, but he strongly wished to retain the tooth. He was later lost to follow-up and re-presented at age 25 with mild labial vestibular tenderness at #9. Write the age-25 specialist decision note. Make one management recommendation and justify it from the serial radiographs/photographs, identifying the imaging change that most alters the biologic objective and what objective remains realistically achievable now. Also explain why the main alternative is less suitable in this patient, what minimum same-day findings you would need before committing to retention if CBCT is unavailable today, which single new finding would end a tooth-preserving plan, and how the radiopaque material beyond the canal in fig_02.jpg and its later appearance in fig_03.jpg should affect urgency, intervention, and follow-up. Close with one modern protocol change you would use only if a maturation strategy were still biologically plausible.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Age-25 endodontic decision note: The figure finding that most changes the biologic objective is the interval change from fig_01.jpg to fig_02.jpg panel A: the apical fragment/root end visible at baseline is no longer present as a usable root end and is best interpreted as having been resorbed and replaced by bone. fig_02.jpg panel B and fig_03.jpg panel F also show persistent coronal structural compromise with a longitudinal crack, while the remaining coronal root segment is short. Taken together, the realistic objective now is not further root maturation or meaningful root-length gain, but control of infection and provision of a durable apical and coronal seal in a tooth that is retained only if it remains restorable.

My management recommendation is orthograde tooth-preserving salvage only if the crack/restorability assessment is favorable. In practical terms, that means reassessing restorability, disinfecting the coronal canal space, using an interappointment calcium hydroxide dressing if infection control is incomplete or exudate persists, then placing an orthograde MTA/bioceramic apical barrier/seal as indicated, followed by a durable coronal restoration and occlusal management, with long-term review. If the extent of the crack or root support remains uncertain without additional imaging, I would avoid an irreversible commitment that day, stabilize/temporize as needed, and obtain further imaging before definitive treatment. Surgical intervention is not first-line here; it becomes a backup only if orthograde management fails or healing does not occur.

The main alternative is extraction with site-preserving and esthetic replacement planning. It is more defensible at age 25 than it was at 17 because growth-related implant timing concerns are much less important now. However, if the tooth is restorable, retention is still preferable because it preserves a natural tooth with PDL proprioception, helps maintain anterior soft tissue and ridge architecture, and avoids committing a young patient to a prosthetic lifetime. Prior non-attendance also argues against another staged biologic maturation approach that depends on strict recall; it does not automatically make extraction superior, but it favors the simplest durable retention strategy over a complex regenerative one.

Minimum same-day findings needed before committing to retention, if CBCT is unavailable, are: circumferential periodontal probing to look for an isolated narrow deep defect; crack mapping with magnification/transillumination and bite testing; direct assessment of restorability and ferrule; mobility, percussion, and palpation; and occlusal evaluation. The single finding that would end a tooth-preserving plan is confirmation that the crack represents a vertical/rootward fracture or extends subcrestally so that the tooth is nonrestorable, especially if associated with an isolated deep periodontal pocket. In that situation, the recommendation should shift to extraction, site preservation when appropriate, and replacement planning/referral.

The radiopaque material beyond the canal in fig_02.jpg is most consistent with extruded MTA/bioceramic. Its later appearance in fig_03.jpg is important: one component persists in a stable way and is surrounded by bone, while a smaller component diminishes/disappears. That pattern supports biocompatibility and healing rather than automatic failure. Therefore it should not raise urgency or trigger surgical retrieval by itself when the patient is asymptomatic and the periapical condition is improving. It should be documented and followed clinically and radiographically. Intervention is reserved for persistent or worsening symptoms, nonhealing or enlarging radiolucency, sinus tract/foreign-body reaction, or involvement of adjacent structures.

If a maturation strategy were still biologically plausible, one modern protocol change would be to avoid older full-strength regenerative protocols and instead use lower-concentration sodium hypochlorite with a final 17% EDTA rinse at the scaffold-induction visit; acceptable related updates include avoiding stem-cell-toxic full-strength triple antibiotic paste and using local anesthetic without vasoconstrictor to facilitate bleeding induction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not base the recommendation on the serial figures, or misses the key structural evolution that changes the treatment objective.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes trauma/fracture or apical disease but gives a largely static reading of the case, without identifying the decisive time-dependent change in the root/apical anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies that the apical fragment/root end seen in fig_01.jpg is no longer present as a usable root end in fig_02.jpg panel A, consistent with resorption and bony replacement, and integrates the short remaining coronal root plus visible coronal structural compromise to conclude that further root maturation is no longer realistic while infection control/apical sealing may still be.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a coherent prognosis from specific figure findings across fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, explicitly linking the loss of the apical fragment, the persistent crack/structural compromise, and later healing behavior to the shift from a maturation goal to a structural/restorative retention decision.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsupported plan, such as default extraction without restorability assessment, routine retreatment without addressing the altered apical anatomy, or a renewed maturation strategy as the obvious choice.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broadly reasonable direction but gives a vague or incomplete plan, with limited sequencing, contingencies, or attention to coronal seal/restorative support.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends orthograde tooth-preserving salvage only if the tooth is restorable, with infection control, apical barrier/seal, definitive coronal restoration, and follow-up; identifies extraction/replacement as the main alternative when restorability is lost.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, conditional plan: recognizes when to defer definitive treatment pending clarification, when interim calcium hydroxide is appropriate, when surgery is only a backup after orthograde failure/nonhealing, and why a renewed maturation attempt ranks below simpler salvage options in this anatomy and follow-up context.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully compare the chosen recommendation with a plausible alternative, or ignores patient-specific trade-offs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative but compares options only superficially, with limited use of age, esthetic-zone, compliance, or replacement considerations.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why the chosen recommendation is preferable to the main alternative using case-specific factors such as age 25 versus adolescence, anterior esthetics/soft-tissue preservation, prior non-attendance, and the burden of long-term replacement therapy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides balanced consent-style reasoning that shows why the recommendation is appropriate now, why the threshold differs from the adolescent setting, and under what clinical circumstances the alternative would become preferable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify the minimum same-day workup before retention, or fails to name a decisive finding that would end the tooth-preserving plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic tests or concerns but does not prioritize the minimum same-day findings needed when CBCT is unavailable, or gives an imprecise reversal finding.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes the essential same-day checks without CBCT, including circumferential probing, crack assessment under magnification/transillumination or bite testing, restorability/ferrule, mobility/percussion/palpation, and occlusal assessment; identifies a decisive reversal finding such as subcrestal/rootward fracture extension with an isolated deep pocket or clear nonrestorability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how to proceed if findings remain equivocal without CBCT that day, and clearly states the immediate next step once the reversal finding is present, such as extraction planning, site preservation consideration, and replacement referral/discussion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the radiopaque material beyond the canal or treats it as automatic failure requiring removal.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the material as relevant but gives vague or incomplete interpretation of its significance or follow-up implications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Interprets the material beyond the canal as likely extruded MTA/bioceramic and explains that observation is appropriate when symptoms are absent and healing is occurring, with documentation and clinical/radiographic monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Uses the serial behavior in fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg to explain why urgency and intervention thresholds remain low despite persistent material beyond the canal, and states clear triggers for intervention such as persistent symptoms, nonhealing/enlarging radiolucency, sinus tract/foreign-body reaction, or threat to adjacent structures.

items.question_content: A 32-year-old woman has 4 months of pain and recurrent swelling from the mandibular anterior region. Zirconia crowns splint the lower anterior teeth from canine to canine, so tooth-specific sensibility and percussion testing cannot be done until the crowns are removed; she is initially reluctant. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, decide whether the right mandibular canine should currently be managed as a tooth to preserve or excluded from the future prosthetic plan. Justify your decision from the imaging, state the minimum diagnostic work-up that is still mandatory after crown removal before any definitive treatment, describe your first-line definitive management if the tooth proves restorable, and name one post-removal finding that would make you change course. Also explain how the presence of multiple mandibular anterior lesions affects what you do before remaking the prosthesis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would keep the right mandibular canine in the treatment plan provisionally rather than exclude it now. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg support a mandibular canine with two roots and two canals with a very apical bifurcation, so this is better treated as an anatomic variant than as a routine single-canal canine. fig_01.jpg also shows multiple mandibular anterior periradicular radiolucencies, which means the canine may be involved but cannot be assumed to be the only source of pain and swelling.

The next mandatory step is removal of the splinted mandibular crowns, with provisionalization as needed, followed by tooth-specific reassessment of all mandibular anterior teeth: sensibility testing, percussion/palpation, periodontal probing, mobility, restorability and crack assessment, and targeted periapical radiographs; sinus-tract tracing is appropriate if present. Only after that work-up can the right canine be assigned a definitive pulpal and periapical diagnosis.

If the right canine is restorable and is confirmed as a non-vital source tooth with apical disease, first-line definitive management is orthograde nonsurgical root canal treatment of both canals/roots, guided by the CBCT findings. Because the bifurcation is very apical, access should be conservative but sufficient, ideally with magnification, and each canal requires separate working-length determination, careful cleaning/shaping, irrigation, obturation, and a durable coronal seal. Treat any other diseased mandibular anterior teeth identified during reassessment before final prosthodontic reconstruction.

I would not remake the definitive prosthesis until the entire mandibular anterior segment has been diagnosed, necessary endodontic treatment completed, symptoms controlled, and early radiographic healing demonstrated. A finding that would make me abandon orthograde preservation would be a vertical root fracture or other non-restorable structural loss after crown removal; confirmed destructive external root resorption with poor prognosis would also justify changing to extraction or another non-preservation approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not correctly use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, or fig_03.jpg, or assumes the right canine has routine anatomy while ignoring the multiple anterior lesions and the current inability to test teeth individually.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either unusual canine anatomy or the presence of multiple lesions, but does not integrate both with the testing limitation to justify the provisional management decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg to identify a two-root/two-canal right mandibular canine with apical bifurcation and uses fig_01.jpg to recognize multiple mandibular anterior periradicular lesions, supporting provisional preservation pending direct diagnosis.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also explains why the imaging favors an anatomic variant rather than assuming external resorption or routine morphology, and why the canine cannot be diagnosed in isolation because several anterior teeth may contribute to symptoms.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Commits to immediate extraction, definitive recrowning, or other irreversible treatment without first obtaining tooth-specific diagnosis after crown removal.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a preference for conservative care or extraction but gives only generic reasons and does not compare the risks of preserving versus excluding the canine in this prosthetic situation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Weighs salvage against exclusion and supports orthograde preservation first if the tooth is restorable, while recognizing that blind treatment and premature prosthetic replacement both carry significant risk.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly balances abutment value, complex apical bifurcation and missed-canal risk, diagnostic uncertainty under the splinted crowns, and the restorative consequences of losing the canine or remaking the prosthesis too early.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent sequence, omits mandatory post-removal work-up, or manages the tooth as if it were a routine single-canal canine.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives some correct steps but with weak sequencing, incomplete reassessment, or no meaningful adaptation of the endodontic plan to the anatomy shown in fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a clear sequence: remove the splinted crowns and provisionalize as needed, perform tooth-specific reassessment of the mandibular anteriors, carry out nonsurgical root canal treatment of both canals if the right canine is restorable and implicated, provide coronal seal, and delay definitive prosthodontics until review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also adds anatomy-specific technical planning, including magnification, conservative but adequate access, separate working-length control and shaping for each canal, and careful instrumentation because the very apical bifurcation increases iatrogenic risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Focuses only on the right canine or gives no valid finding that would change the proposed plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges that more information is needed but does not clearly prioritize diagnosis of the whole mandibular anterior segment or identify a defensible trigger for changing course.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes full mandibular anterior reassessment after crown removal before definitive prosthetic replacement and gives at least one valid post-removal finding that would change management, such as vertical root fracture, non-restorability, or confirmed destructive external resorption.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly links that finding to a different management direction and explains how it changes sequencing for the future prosthesis and the treatment of the remaining mandibular anterior teeth.

items.question_content: A 27-year-old woman wants to retain tooth #9 if that is still a reasonable option. The tooth had root canal treatment and a full crown several years ago. She now has a 2-month labial sinus tract, percussion sensitivity, no thermal response, and an 8-10 mm narrow isolated pocket on the palatal side. Based on fig_01.jpg, what definitive management would you recommend, and why? Explain which findings most strongly drive your decision, why more limited endodontic or periodontal measures are unlikely to resolve this problem, and what technical priorities and follow-up findings would determine whether a tooth-preserving attempt is succeeding or failing.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This is a vertical root fracture of an endodontically treated maxillary central incisor with periodontal communication. My recommendation would be to discuss extraction as the most predictable standard option, but because the patient is young, the tooth is in the esthetic zone, and she wishes to retain it, I would offer intentional replantation with extraoral repair of the fracture as a last-resort tooth-preserving treatment, with a guarded prognosis. The key findings are the isolated deep narrow palatal pocket, sinus tract, prior RCT, and the CBCT appearance in fig_01.jpg showing a fracture line on the palatal aspect extending from the cervical region toward the apex with associated palatal/apical bone loss. Together these are much more consistent with VRF than with persistent intracanal infection alone. Orthograde retreatment, apical surgery, or periodontal debridement alone are unlikely to succeed because they do not eliminate or seal the fracture line or allow direct debridement of the contaminated external root surface and granulation tissue. If retention is attempted, the critical priorities are atraumatic extraction, preservation of periodontal ligament vitality, keeping extraoral time short and the root moist, thorough debridement of infected tissue, secure sealing/repair of the fracture with adequate mechanical stability and a biologically acceptable external surface for periodontal healing, correction of occlusal overload, and short-term stabilization after replantation. Prognosis remains guarded because the fracture is extensive and communicates with the periodontium. Success in the first year would be resolution of the sinus tract, normalizing probing depth and mobility, absence of percussion pain, and radiographic/CBCT bone fill. Failure would be recurrence of the isolated pocket or sinus tract, persistent tenderness, increasing radiolucency, mobility, ankylosis or external resorption, or refracture.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends management that does not address the fracture as the primary problem, or gives no coherent definitive plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Offers a plan but it is incomplete, overly generic, or does not clearly justify why a tooth-preserving attempt would require direct fracture management; may default to extraction without meaningful consideration of patient-specific retention factors.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a defensible definitive plan and recognizes that successful retention would require direct management of the fractured root rather than routine retreatment alone; includes key procedural priorities in broad terms.

levels.title: Exceeds
