levels.description: Selects intentional replantation with extraoral fracture repair as a conditional, last-resort retention strategy while acknowledging extraction as the more predictable alternative; clearly explains why this sequence best fits the tooth, patient preference, and lesion pattern, and identifies the main technical priorities for success.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the case or ignores major clinical or imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but misses the importance of the combined pattern, such as the isolated palatal pocket or the cervico-apical fracture with surrounding bone loss.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly links the history, examination, and CBCT findings to a vertical root fracture with periodontal communication.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates the sinus tract, prior RCT, isolated narrow pocket, percussion findings, and fig_01.jpg fracture/bone-loss pattern into a clear explanation of why the lesion reflects VRF rather than a problem confined to the canal or apex.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh prognosis, patient preference, or the tradeoff between retention and replacement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions prognosis or patient wishes but gives a superficial or one-sided analysis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that prognosis is guarded and balances the esthetic/strategic value of the tooth against the lower predictability of salvage.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced appraisal: extraction is more predictable, but a carefully selected retention attempt is reasonable in this young, healthy patient in the esthetic zone if she accepts uncertainty and follow-up needs.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful failure modes or postoperative risks.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists nonspecific complications without tying them to this procedure or fracture pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important risks such as recurrent periodontal breakdown, persistent infection, or loss of stability, and names relevant follow-up findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically links success and failure to preservation of PDL vitality and short extraoral time, plus monitoring for recurrence of the sinus tract or isolated pocket, mobility, radiolucency, ankylosis, external resorption, and refracture.

items.question_content: An 18-year-old man presents 2 days after a sports injury with intermittent pain and a mobile coronal fragment involving tooth 21. Medical history is noncontributory. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg, decide the single tooth-preserving strategy you would recommend today. Your answer must identify the diagnosis and justify why vital pulp therapy or root canal treatment is the better pulpal approach; cite the figure-based findings that make immediate fragment reuse biologically reasonable here and the one finding that still makes it risky; state whether any intraradicular reinforcement belongs in the initial visit and why; justify your plan against the next two plausible alternatives you considered for this patient; and explain exactly how your plan would change if surgical exposure showed the deepest palatal fracture margin to be intraosseous rather than supraosseous.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend same-visit conservative management with definitive-intent fragment reattachment only if biologic and restorative thresholds are met after exposure. The diagnosis is a complicated oblique crown-root fracture of mature tooth 21 with pulp exposure and symptoms consistent with irreversible pulpitis; fig_02.jpg does not suggest separate root fracture or periapical pathosis. Although vital pulp therapy can be appropriate after some traumatic exposures, it is less suitable here because the tooth is mature, the exposure is already 2 days old, the coronal fragment is highly mobile, and the subgingival fracture makes predictable sealing during fragment management difficult. Root canal treatment is therefore the better pulpal approach.

The figure-based findings favoring immediate fragment reuse are: fig_01.jpg and fig_03.jpg show a large single fragment rather than comminution; fig_02.jpg shows an oblique crown-root fracture with deeper palatal extension rather than an obvious vertical root split; fig_04.jpg shows the fragment is available and protected from dehydration; and fig_05.jpg shows that flap reflection can expose the deepest palatal margin, making direct assessment of margin position, isolation, and finishing possible. The main remaining risk is the palatal subgingival margin itself, because even with an intact fragment, biologic width violation and poor cleansability could make the restoration periodontally unacceptable.

My plan would be to preserve the fragment in saline, complete endodontic treatment, reflect the flap to inspect the deepest palatal margin, and proceed to immediate reattachment only if the fragment seats precisely and the exposed margin is maintainable without leaving the restoration within the supracrestal attached tissues. Intraradicular reinforcement can belong in the initial visit, but only after restorability is confirmed; a fiber post is reasonable in an endodontically treated reattached incisor to improve retention and stress distribution, not to compensate for an unfavorable margin.

The two strongest alternatives are orthodontic extrusion and surgical crown lengthening. Orthodontic extrusion is conservative and useful if more sound tooth structure must be brought coronally, but it is slower and does not provide immediate esthetic rehabilitation when a fitting fragment is available. Surgical crown lengthening provides faster exposure but sacrifices supporting tissue and can worsen esthetics and crown-root ratio in a maxillary central incisor, so it is less attractive when invasion appears minimal and localized. If surgical exposure instead showed the deepest palatal margin to be intraosseous, I would abandon definitive same-day reattachment, complete pulpal stabilization/RCT, provide provisional esthetics, and shift to an exposure strategy such as orthodontic extrusion, with surgical extrusion as a faster alternative if necessary, before definitive restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the injury, recommends a pulpal approach incompatible with the findings, or ignores the crown-root nature of the fracture.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes traumatic fracture of tooth 21 with pulpal involvement but incompletely characterizes the oblique subgingival pattern, pulpal status, or maturity-related implications.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a complicated oblique crown-root fracture of mature tooth 21 with pulpal involvement and no evident separate root fracture or apical pathosis, and selects an appropriate pulpal strategy for this presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the correct diagnosis and pulpal diagnosis, and clearly distinguishes what is established from the preoperative figures from what still depends on direct surgical/restorative assessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg meaningfully, or relies on generic trauma rules instead of case-specific figure interpretation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figures correctly but misses important implications of fragment integrity, hydration/recoverability, fracture orientation, or exposed margin assessment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the figures to support why fragment reuse is feasible to consider, identifies the subgingival palatal margin as the biologic risk, and links flap exposure to the ability to inspect, isolate, and finish the margin.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a threshold-based argument from the figures, including fragment condition, oblique fracture direction, recoverability/rehydration, and fig_05.jpg-based interpretation of whether the deep margin appears surgically exposable without obvious need for more aggressive tissue removal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Chooses an inappropriate management plan, omits essential pulpal or restorative steps, or commits to definitive reattachment regardless of biologic/restorative constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a broadly plausible plan but does not define the conditions required for immediate reattachment, or does not address whether intraradicular reinforcement belongs in the initial visit.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends an appropriate same-visit tooth-preserving plan that includes endodontic management, fragment preservation, flap-based margin assessment/exposure, and conditional immediate reattachment, with intraradicular reinforcement used only if restorability is confirmed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan with explicit biologic and restorative stop thresholds, correctly frames intraradicular reinforcement as conditional rather than routine, and shows how the same-visit sequence serves immediate esthetic rehabilitation while preserving tooth structure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives a one-sided recommendation without weighing biologic, periodontal, or restorative risks, or does not compare plausible alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general pros and cons but does not compare the chosen plan against at least two realistic alternatives for this specific patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the chosen plan with at least two plausible alternatives and appropriately weighs immediate esthetics, conservation, treatment duration, periodontal sacrifice, and long-term restorability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced patient-specific trade-off analysis showing why the chosen plan is preferable now, while explaining precisely when the balance would shift toward an alternative approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not explain how management changes if the deepest margin is intraosseous, or continues with definitive reattachment despite loss of biologic/restorative acceptability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that an intraosseous margin is problematic but gives an incomplete or poorly sequenced change in management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly states that discovery of an intraosseous deepest palatal margin should stop definitive same-day reattachment and redirect treatment toward stabilization/provisionalization plus a more appropriate exposure strategy.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes long-term biologic/restorative success over immediate esthetics, specifies the altered sequence of care after the intraosseous finding, and selects a coherent next-step strategy consistent with this patient's age and goals.

items.question_content: A 27-year-old ASA I woman presents with a recurrent draining opening in the right submandibular region that has persisted for 6 years despite chlorhexidine, 6 months of doxycycline, two neck operations, and a negative tuberculosis workup. On dental review, the mandibular right first and second molars do not respond to pulp vitality testing; neither is tender to percussion or mobile. Using fig_01.jpg, decide what you would do at this visit before any further cervical procedure is considered. Give your working diagnosis, identify which tooth is the most likely principal source and whether the adjacent molar should be included in the first phase of care, and justify why a conservative dental approach is or is not appropriate despite the extent of the bony change. Then state what specific lack of response after initial treatment would make you change your plan and how you would escalate the workup.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The working diagnosis is an extraoral sinus tract of odontogenic origin, most consistent with a chronic apical abscess/chronic apical periodontitis draining through the skin. fig_01.jpg makes the mandibular right second molar (#31) the most likely principal source because the periapical destruction is centered more severely there, and the CBCT shows extensive bony loss in continuity with the posterior mandibular apical region. The adjacent first molar (#30) is not innocent, however: it is also non-vital and shows apical PDL change, so it may be a secondary contributor or part of a combined endodontic source.

My first-line management is elimination of the dental source with nonsurgical endodontic treatment, not more neck surgery, empiric antibiotics, or primary excision of the tract. I would prioritize #31 first because fig_01.jpg shows the larger destructive lesion around that tooth, but because both molars are non-vital and adjacent, I would either treat both in the initial phase or confirm the tract path with gutta-percha tracing/repeat correlation if there is any doubt before limiting treatment to one tooth. If the teeth are restorable and periodontal support is acceptable, retention with endodontic treatment is preferable to extraction or extraoral surgery. The extent of bone loss alone does not justify neck surgery when the patient is systemically well, the teeth are not mobile, and the draining tract suggests a chronic decompressed process rather than uncontrolled spreading infection.

What would make me change course is failure of the tract to show early improvement after adequate canal disinfection of the tooth or teeth selected—persistent drainage, failure of the cutaneous opening to begin closing within about 1 to 2 weeks, or later absence of radiographic osseous healing. That would trigger re-evaluation of source control: confirm whether #30 also needs treatment if not already addressed, repeat imaging or trace the tract, and look for missed anatomy, persistent intraradicular infection, vertical root fracture, endo-perio disease, osteomyelitis, actinomycosis, or a non-odontogenic lesion. If the healing pattern remains inconsistent with an odontogenic sinus tract, biopsy or appropriate referral would then be warranted.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify an odontogenic source or attributes the lesion primarily to a cervical/dermatologic condition.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a possible dental origin but does not clearly diagnose an odontogenic cutaneous sinus tract/chronic apical abscess, or misidentifies the likely principal tooth source from fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies an odontogenic cutaneous sinus tract from chronic apical infection and correctly interprets fig_01.jpg to make tooth #31 the most likely primary source while recognizing that tooth #30 may also contribute.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately diagnoses the lesion, justifies the source assignment from the fig_01.jpg radiographic pattern, and explains why the distant neck opening is still compatible with posterior mandibular apical disease; mentions tract tracing only when source correlation remains uncertain.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Bases the answer on a single finding or ignores the figure when reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some of the history, clinical tests, or imaging but leaves major gaps in linking the recurrent neck drainage, failed prior care, pulp findings, and fig_01.jpg bony changes.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the 6-year recurrent drainage, failed antibiotics/surgeries, non-responsive molars, lack of percussion pain or mobility, and fig_01.jpg periapical/CBCT findings into a coherent odontogenic explanation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all data sources and explicitly explains why chronic drainage can coexist with minimal dental symptoms and why extensive bone loss in fig_01.jpg does not by itself mandate extraoral surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends further antibiotics, repeat neck surgery, observation alone, or unsupported extraction as the primary next step.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses dental treatment but gives an incomplete sequence, does not justify which tooth to prioritize, or ignores the decision about whether to include the adjacent molar in the first phase.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends nonsurgical endodontic source control, prioritizes #31 because of greater fig_01.jpg destruction, and appropriately includes #30 in the first phase or after source confirmation because it is also non-vital and radiographically suspicious; defers extraoral surgery if the teeth are restorable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, defensible plan that balances tooth preservation with source certainty, states when tract tracing or additional correlation is needed before limiting treatment to one tooth, and defines when conservative care should convert to retreatment, surgery, extraction, biopsy, or referral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful follow-up target or contingency plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions follow-up or possible failure in general terms without stating what specific non-response would change management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States concrete failure triggers such as persistent drainage, lack of early tract closure, or absent later radiographic healing, and lists plausible causes including missed anatomy, persistent infection, untreated adjacent tooth, root fracture, endo-perio disease, or non-odontogenic pathology.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds an appropriate escalation pathway, including repeat imaging or tract tracing and biopsy/referral when the healing pattern is inconsistent with an odontogenic sinus tract or suggests osteomyelitis/actinomycosis or another non-endodontic process.

items.question_content: A 24-year-old woman is referred after 2 weeks of persistent pain and intermittent swelling in the left maxillary canine-premolar region despite recent treatment elsewhere. Teeth 23-25 are non-responsive to sensibility testing and mildly tender to percussion/palpation; probing depths and mobility are normal. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, defend a region-wide management plan at presentation. Commit to which teeth you would treat immediately, which image finding most changes your plan, and the minimum access strategy you believe is sufficient for tooth 23 while preserving structure. Your justification must come from the figure-based anatomy and lesion pattern, not from a generic CDI protocol. Then state how you would respond if, after technically acceptable orthograde treatment, the patient later re-presents with renewed swelling/pain and CBCT shows the radiolucency is smaller but still present.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The principal disease source is tooth 23: Oehlers type II coronal dens invaginatus with pulpal infection/necrosis involving a highly distorted canal system and associated apical periodontitis. The regional radiolucency is most consistent with endodontic inflammatory disease; cystic change is possible, but lesion size alone does not justify primary surgery. I would not manage this as a 23-only problem, because fig_01.jpg also shows an independent adjacent-tooth finding that materially changes the plan: a mesial-wall perforation of tooth 24. Tooth 25 is less specifically localizable than 23 or 24, but with loss of sensibility, recent treatment elsewhere, and inclusion within the same periapical complex, it should not be assumed uninvolved.

The key figure-based reason to avoid routine access is the changing 3D relationship between the invagination and the true canal in tooth 23. In the coronal/upper portion, a tooth-shaped invagination compresses the true canal into a crescent. More apically, the invagination becomes more cylindrical and the true canal becomes ring-shaped around it. Because these spaces shift through the root, a single freehand palatal access is likely to miss infected anatomy, and wholesale removal of the invagination would be unnecessarily destructive and increase perforation/fracture risk.

The smallest defensible access strategy is a CBCT-planned, minimally invasive guided approach with three targeted straight-line trajectories for tooth 23. Fewer routes would risk leaving inaccessible infected spaces unreached; more are not justified initially if three paths provide adequate rectilinear access to the true canal and invaginated component while preserving dentine. The goal is not to remove the entire invagination, but to create enough preplanned access for effective debridement and irrigation.

At presentation, I would pursue orthograde source control rather than primary surgery: treat tooth 23 with guided/preplanned access, activated irrigation, intracanal medicament if needed, and obturation once infection is controlled; treat tooth 24 endodontically and repair the perforation after disinfection/localization with a bioceramic material such as MTA; and include tooth 25 in the overall orthograde plan because it is clinically non-vital and part of the same symptomatic region after recent intervention. Blind hunting or aggressive troughing in tooth 23 should be avoided.

If symptoms recur later despite technically acceptable orthograde treatment and the radiolucency is smaller but persistent, partial shrinkage should not be mistaken for cure. The next step would be endodontic microsurgery with curettage and biopsy/histopathology, while reassessing the adjacent treated teeth rather than automatically blaming 23 alone. The rationale is persistent disease after adequate orthograde care, raising concern for residual apical/extraradicular infection or an inflammatory odontogenic cyst.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses dens invaginatus as the principal problem, or treats the case as a routine single-tooth apical lesion without recognizing clinically relevant adjacent-tooth disease.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes tooth 23 as the main diseased tooth but incompletely characterizes the case, such as omitting the independent significance of tooth 24 or oversimplifying the regional lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies tooth 23 as type II coronal dens invaginatus with endodontic infection/apical periodontitis and recognizes that adjacent teeth in the 23-25 region cannot be assumed uninvolved.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: In addition to the above, explicitly identifies the mesial-wall perforation of tooth 24 as a management-changing finding and characterizes the radiolucency as most consistent with endodontic inflammatory disease, with cystic change remaining possible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions with little or no use of fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated figure findings but does not integrate the 3D anatomy of tooth 23 with the lesion pattern and adjacent-tooth finding.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the figures to explain that the invagination distorts and changes the course of the true canal, making routine access unreliable and supporting a preplanned minimally invasive approach.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically interprets the figure-based anatomic transition in tooth 23 (coronal tooth-shaped invagination with crescent-shaped true canal; deeper more cylindrical invagination with ring-shaped true canal), links this to the need for multiple targeted straight-line paths, and incorporates the tooth 24 perforation into the reasoning.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends extraction, primary surgery alone, or a generic single-access RCT plan that ignores the CDI anatomy or the adjacent-tooth issue.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends orthograde treatment but gives a generic or incomplete plan, such as focusing only on tooth 23, not addressing how access will be designed, or not accounting for the perforation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends orthograde source control with conservative CBCT-informed access planning for tooth 23, coherent management of teeth 23-25, and appropriate handling of the tooth 24 perforation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent region-wide plan that commits to the minimum sufficient access strategy for tooth 23 as three targeted preplanned trajectories, avoids unnecessary removal of the invagination, sequences tooth 24 disinfection before definitive perforation repair, and justifies how tooth 25 will be managed rather than ignored.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Shows poor prioritization, such as jumping to surgery because of lesion size, or performing blind high-risk exploration first.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a general sequence but does not clearly justify why certain actions should occur before others.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes orthograde source control at presentation and avoids blind exploration in tooth 23 until access is precisely planned.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: At recurrence after technically acceptable orthograde treatment and partial radiographic improvement, appropriately escalates to endodontic microsurgery with tissue diagnosis while reassessing adjacent treated teeth rather than attributing failure to tooth 23 by default.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not explain why the proposed approach is safer or more appropriate than alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that conservative treatment is preferable but gives only general reasons.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that blind conventional access or broad removal of the invagination risks missed anatomy, perforation, and structural weakening, and that lesion size alone does not mandate surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances dentine preservation against debridement completeness, justifies the extra planning burden of guided targeted access, and explains why symptomatic recurrence with a smaller persistent lesion shifts the balance toward surgery because persistent apical/extraradicular infection or cystic pathology becomes more likely than simple delayed healing.

items.question_content: A 21-year-old man presents 9 years after trauma with a fractured, discolored maxillary central incisor. The tooth is asymptomatic, nonmobile, not tender to percussion, and gives no response to electric pulp testing. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Before treatment is started, what definitive management would you choose for this tooth, and why is it preferable to other reasonable options in this patient? Base your justification on the clinical and radiographic findings, and include the main technical risks that should shape execution and follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The preferred plan is orthograde endodontic treatment with apexification using a bioactive apical barrier, followed by a strong coronal seal and definitive esthetic restoration. The key findings are a long-standing traumatic crown fracture/discoloration, no EPT response, and fig_02.jpg showing an immature root with an open apex and periapical radiolucency. Together these support pulp necrosis with apical periodontitis in an immature permanent incisor.

Apexification with an apical plug is preferable here because the tooth is restorable, the patient is already 21, and the necrosis has been present for many years, so predictable continued root development is unlikely compared with younger, more recently infected cases. Long-term calcium hydroxide apexification is less favorable because it delays rehabilitation, needs multiple visits, and may further weaken already thin dentinal walls. Extraction or surgical treatment is not first-line because the lesion can be managed orthogradely and the tooth has strategic and esthetic value.

Execution should prioritize disinfection while preserving fragile root walls: minimal instrumentation, careful working-length control, cautious irrigation to avoid extrusion through the wide apex, and short-term intracanal medicament if needed to reduce bacterial load. Then place a 4-5 mm bioactive apical plug to create an apical stop, complete obturation, and restore coronally promptly.

Main risks are irrigant or filling-material extrusion, inadequate apical seal/microleakage, persistent infection, and later cervical or root fracture because of thin walls. Follow clinically and radiographically for symptom resolution and reduction/healing of the periapical radiolucency, while monitoring the integrity of the restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate definitive plan such as vital pulp therapy, routine obturation without addressing the open apex, or first-line extraction/surgery; or provides no coherent sequence of care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for endodontic retention but proposes a vague or weakly justified plan that is not clearly adapted to an immature open apex, or omits key sequencing elements.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects orthograde apexification with a bioactive apical barrier and subsequent obturation/coronal restoration, with a reasonable stepwise rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced, tooth-preserving plan tailored to the open apex and esthetic need, including conservative disinfection, apical barrier creation, prompt coronal seal, and appropriate review strategy.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

items.question_content: Tooth #3 in a healthy 20-year-old man has deep occlusal caries, lingering thermal pain, nocturnal radiating pain, percussion tenderness, normal probing/mobility, and a vital response. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Use fig_02.jpg to infer the actual canal anatomy, then use fig_01.jpg to judge what a clinician could reasonably suspect before 3-D confirmation. If no operating microscope were available and the patient would accept CBCT only if it changed same-day management, would you continue clinically, obtain limited-FOV CBCT before further dentin removal, or refer? Defend one approach by linking the figure findings to the probable canal pattern in each root, your stopping point for further troughing/search, and the resulting strategy for working-length confirmation and shaping/obturation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The pulpal/apical diagnosis is symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis in a restorable tooth, so the overall goal remains nonsurgical root canal treatment. fig_02.jpg retrospectively shows the true anatomy: three roots with three canals in the mesiobuccal root, two in the distobuccal root, and one in the palatal root. The mesiobuccal root appears to maintain three distinct canals to separate exits, whereas the distobuccal root most likely shows two canals that converge before one apical exit; the palatal root has a single large canal.

Using only what could reasonably be inferred during treatment, fig_01.jpg should already raise strong suspicion that this is not a routine 3- or 4-canal maxillary first molar: the preoperative image suggests complex buccal-root anatomy, the access view shows additional buccal-root orifices rather than a simple MB1/DB1/palatal pattern, and the angled working-length films suggest multiple negotiable buccal canals. On that basis, the most defensible first-visit choice is to continue clinically with a careful, conservative search rather than order routine preoperative CBCT for every suspected extra canal. However, because no microscope is available, the threshold to stop and escalate is lower.

I would proceed only while the chamber-floor map, file negotiation, apex-locator readings, and angled radiographs remain mutually consistent and additional dentin removal is modest and targeted. I would refine access only enough to obtain straight-line visualization of the buccal developmental grooves, use DG16, small precurved #6-10 files, and conservative ultrasonic troughing. I would stop further troughing and either obtain limited-FOV CBCT or refer if: suspected canals cannot be reproducibly negotiated; radiographic and chamber-floor findings conflict; working-length readings are unstable; or further troughing would risk furcal/strip perforation or unnecessary loss of pericervical dentin.

The anatomy changes the technical plan. Working length should be confirmed with separate small files and mesial/distal angulated radiographs to separate overlapping buccal canals. The MB canals should be treated as three independent canals unless confluence is clearly demonstrated. In the DB root, both canals still require separate negotiation, cleaning, and shaping even if they merge apically. The palatal canal can generally accept a larger preparation than the narrow buccal canals. Because complex buccal roots may contain fins, isthmuses, and difficult-to-clean recesses, irrigation with NaOCl, EDTA, and irrigant activation is especially important. Prognosis is good if all canals are located, disinfected, and sealed; the major causes of failure would be missed buccal canals or iatrogenic damage from overaggressive troughing while chasing anatomy without adequate confirmation.

A well-justified alternative answer could favor earlier CBCT or referral, but only if it explicitly ties that decision to the absence of magnification and a rising risk of structural damage or unresolved anatomy.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg panel a. What obturation technique is represented by the dense material placed only at the apical end of the canal before coronal backfilling? Answer with the technique name only.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The radiograph shows a short, dense apical barrier occupying only the terminal portion of the canal, with the remaining canal backfilled separately. That configuration is characteristic of an apical plug technique, commonly used when a conventional apical stop is inadequate.

items.answer_explanation: The radiograph shows a short, dense apical barrier occupying only the terminal portion of the canal, with the remaining canal backfilled separately. That configuration is characteristic of an apical plug technique, commonly used when a conventional apical stop is inadequate.

items.question_content: A 35-year-old healthy woman has pain on chewing from a previously treated mandibular left first molar restored with a PFM crown and an intracanal post. The tooth is slightly tender to percussion, with normal periodontal findings. Examine fig_01.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend, and how would you sequence the major steps to maximize tooth retention while minimizing iatrogenic damage? Justify your plan from the findings, including any part of the previous endodontic treatment you would intentionally leave undisturbed and the prognosis you would communicate.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend conservative nonsurgical retreatment as the first-line approach, but only after explaining that the prognosis is guarded because fig_01.jpg shows combined iatrogenic/biologic problems: a furcal perforation, a separated instrument in the mesiolingual canal extending beyond the apex, existing post-crown complexity, and loss of tooth structure. The normal periodontal status and localized disease still make retention reasonable.

My sequence would be: gain adequate access by modifying/removing the existing coronal restoration and removing the post only as needed for straight-line access; work under a microscope; identify and seal the furcal perforation early with a bioceramic/MTA-type repair because it is a major pathway for contamination and further periodontal breakdown; then selectively retreat the diseased mesial root system. I would attempt conservative orthograde management of the separated instrument only after creating straight-line access and exposing a short coronal segment, using limited ultrasonics and/or a retrieval device. If retrieval requires excessive dentin removal or risks another perforation, I would stop and consider bypass or later surgical options rather than over-enlarge the root.

I would intentionally leave the distal canals undisturbed if, as suggested by fig_01.jpg, their obturation appears acceptable and there is no distal apical disease or coronal leakage. Retreatment there would add risk without clear benefit. After mesial disinfection, I would obturate, ensure a definitive coronal seal, and review radiographically. The prognosis is fair-to-poor overall, but better if the perforation can be sealed well, the mesial infection controlled, and the tooth restored with a durable coronal seal.

items.question_content: A mandibular left lateral incisor is planned for primary nonsurgical root canal treatment. No CBCT is available at the first visit. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg. Based only on these figures, state the canal configuration you think is most likely and distinguish what is radiographically certain from what is still inferential. Then give a prioritized first-visit plan that is intentionally conservative but still addresses the highest-risk part of the anatomy: access design, canal scouting, working-length strategy, shaping limits, irrigation emphasis, and obturation concept. Finally, if during treatment one negotiated path repeatedly reaches patency but the second file binds about 3 mm short with an apex-locator reading suggesting confluence, explain whether you would continue to pursue two separate apical endpoints or accept a single endpoint, and justify how you would avoid a false working length, blockage, or apical transportation.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely configuration is a Vertucci Type VII pattern (1-2-1-2): a single canal coronally, separation into buccal and lingual canals, reunion in the apical third, then redivision into two apical exits. What is radiographically certain from the figures is that this is not a routine single-canal incisor: fig_02.jpg shows buccolingual canal separation best on the angled views, fig_03.jpg demonstrates two distinct apical exits with retrograde file placement, and fig_01.jpg suggests that crown position does not guarantee a straight coronal access path. fig_04.jpg and fig_05.jpg strongly support a midroot separation and an apical reconvergence/redivision, and they also suggest a lingual lateral/apical accessory opening. What remains partly inferential in a clinical first visit is the exact negotiable course through the merged segment and whether the accessory/lateral anatomy is instrumentable; that anatomy is mainly something to clean chemically and seal, not to chase mechanically.

My first-visit plan would be conservative but anatomy-specific. Access should be modified to follow the root/canal axis rather than assuming a routine centered incisor access; I would extend sufficiently lingually/incisally to inspect the buccolingual extent of the chamber under magnification without excessive dentin removal. I would scout early with small precurved hand files in both suspected pathways, establish a reproducible glide path by hand, and use the apex locator early but not in isolation. Working length should be confirmed with angled radiographs because straight projection risks superimposition and a false impression of one canal or one terminus. Shaping should remain small and conservative, especially near the apical third, because the highest-risk segment is the confluence/redivision zone; aggressive taper could straighten the path, create blockage, or transport one limb of the apical anatomy. Cleaning should rely heavily on irrigation and chelation with activation rather than large apical enlargement. For obturation, I would treat the case as requiring sealing of two main apical exits, not as a simple single-terminal canal. Master cone fit should be checked so one cone does not obstruct the other pathway at the merged segment.

If one file repeatedly reaches patency but the second binds about 3 mm short with an apex-locator reading suggesting confluence, I would not automatically accept a single endpoint. In this tooth, a short electronic endpoint could represent the point where canals join, a ledge, debris accumulation, or an inability to re-enter the redividing apical segment, not the true final terminus of that canal. I would first recapitulate, irrigate, use lubricant/EDTA, re-establish the glide path with smaller precurved files, and reassess with angled radiography and repeat apex-locator readings from both paths. My default aim would remain two separate apical objectives because the figures support two foramina. I would accept a single endpoint only if repeated careful reassessment showed reproducible evidence that the second path truly shares one common apical terminus and that further pursuit would create more risk than benefit. The main technical errors to prevent are false working length at the confluence, blockage of one limb by dentin mud or a master cone, ledging/transportation during attempts to force the apical redivision, short filling of one exit, or extrusion through a separate foramen or accessory opening.

items.question_content: A healthy 15-year-old boy presents 18 months after extrusive luxation and repositioning of tooth #21. The tooth is asymptomatic, shows no pink discoloration or crown color change, but is non-responsive to cold testing. Periapical radiography and CBCT are shown in fig_01.jpg, and invasive cervical resorption has already been confirmed. Based on the history and fig_01.jpg, what definitive management would you choose for tooth #21 now, and why? Justify your choice using the lesion’s location/accessibility, the pulpal status, and this patient’s age and esthetic risk; then state the key procedural priorities needed to preserve prognosis and the main late complications you would monitor for.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would attempt to retain tooth #21 with intentional replantation, complete extraoral debridement of the cervical resorptive defect, restoration of the defect under direct vision, and root canal treatment because the tooth is necrotic. The trauma history is a strong predisposing factor for ICR, and the negative cold test indicates pulpal necrosis, so endodontic treatment is required in addition to treating the resorption.

fig_01.jpg supports a cervical external resorptive defect in a distal/subgingival position that is difficult to access predictably from within the canal. A purely internal endodontic approach would disinfect the canal but would not reliably eliminate the fibrovascular resorptive tissue on the external cervical surface. A conventional flap/osteotomy approach is a reasonable alternative, but in this maxillary anterior esthetic zone it risks loss of papilla/crestal support and visible periodontal defects. Immediate extraction and replacement would be unnecessarily aggressive in a 15-year-old if the tooth remains restorable.

Intentional replantation is justified here because it gives 360-degree access to the lesion for complete debridement and controlled restoration while avoiding a periodontal flap in the esthetic zone. The prognosis depends on respecting periodontal ligament biology: atraumatic extraction, handling only the crown, keeping the root surface moist and clean, minimizing extraoral time, complete removal/inactivation of resorptive tissue, smooth well-adapted restoration, prompt replantation into the socket, and short-term flexible splinting. Endodontic disinfection and obturation should follow as part of the plan, with calcium hydroxide as an interim medicament being reasonable in a trauma-associated necrotic tooth.

Follow-up should monitor probing depth and attachment, gingival/papillary esthetics, mobility, percussion changes, and radiographic/CBCT signs of periodontal ligament healing. The main late complications are recurrence/progression of cervical resorption, inflammatory root resorption, replacement resorption/ankylosis, loss of PDL space, and apical pathology. Overall prognosis is guarded but acceptable if the lesion can be fully accessed and extraoral handling is biologically controlled.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why an internal-only approach risks incomplete debridement and why a flap/osteotomy approach risks esthetic periodontal damage; recognizes that removal/replacement is undesirable in a 15-year-old if retention is feasible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the benefits of intentional replantation (complete access, tooth retention, esthetic preservation) against its biologic risks (PDL damage, ankylosis/resorption) and gives a realistic prognosis contingent on careful execution and follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits follow-up needs or fails to identify meaningful complications.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key late risks such as recurrence/progression of resorption, inflammatory root resorption, ankylosis/replacement resorption, periodontal attachment loss or increased probing depth, and periapical pathology; recommends clinical and radiographic monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds procedure-specific surveillance details such as percussion changes, mobility, PDL-space assessment, papillary/gingival esthetics, and long-term review because complications may emerge after initially satisfactory healing.

items.question_content: A 22-year-old man with Ellis class II fractures of both maxillary central incisors has no response to cold testing. He wants the teeth retained with as little dentin loss as possible, but he cannot commit to frequent recall visits. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What overall management strategy would you choose from access through definitive restoration, and why is it the best fit for this patient? Base your justification on the apical anatomy and canal path visible on imaging, the restorative/occlusal situation, and the main risks that should change your sequencing or follow-up.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with traumatized, nonvital immature permanent maxillary central incisors with open apices. I would retain both teeth and perform nonsurgical root canal treatment. For access, I would use a highly conservative approach; guided access is especially reasonable here if the guide seats accurately, because fig_01.jpg shows a straight coronal-to-apical path and preserving pericervical/pericingulum dentin is valuable in structurally compromised anterior teeth that will need definitive restoration. If guide fit or angulation is uncertain, I would switch to conventional access under magnification rather than force a guided path.

Because the teeth are nonvital, apexogenesis is not indicated. The key apical decision is between regenerative treatment and creating an artificial apical stop. In this 22-year-old who cannot attend frequent recalls, I would favor apical-barrier apexification with a calcium-silicate material, using an internal matrix/barrier if needed to control placement and reduce extrusion through the open apex, followed by obturation and an adhesive coronal seal.

Definitive crowns should not be rushed. fig_02.jpg shows an occlusal situation consistent with deep bite that would compromise space and longevity of anterior full-coverage restorations. I would therefore coordinate orthodontic bite opening first, then proceed to definitive crowns only after symptoms have resolved, the endodontic result is stable, and adequate clearance is achieved.

Main risks to monitor are guide misfit or bur deviation causing perforation or excess dentin loss, irrigant or bioceramic extrusion through the open apex, inadequate disinfection because the access is small, cervical/root weakening from over-instrumentation, and restorative failure if the deep bite is left uncorrected. Follow-up should include clinical symptoms, percussion/palpation, restoration integrity, occlusion, and radiographic review of periapical healing and apical barrier stability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic plan that does not use the case data or figures meaningfully; ignores either the apical anatomy, the occlusal/restorative constraint, or the limited follow-up context.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts but incompletely. May recognize pulpal necrosis or trauma yet misses key figure-derived implications such as open apices/straight path in fig_01.jpg or the occlusal limitation in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the main data sources into a coherent rationale: nonvital traumatized incisors, immature/open apices and favorable straight path on fig_01.jpg, limited follow-up, and the deep-bite restorative issue visible on fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all relevant findings into a patient-specific plan and clearly explains how the imaging and occlusion directly influence access design, apical management choice, and timing of definitive restoration.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe overall plan, such as vital pulp therapy/apexogenesis for nonvital teeth, immediate definitive crowns without managing the endodontic and occlusal problems, or no clear definitive treatment pathway.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes endodontic treatment but with an incomplete or poorly sequenced plan; may omit how to manage the open apex, ignore the need for dentin-preserving access strategy, or fail to coordinate occlusal correction before final restoration.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents an appropriate stepwise plan: retain the teeth, perform conservative access (guided or equivalently justified minimally invasive access), disinfect the canals, manage the open apex with an apical barrier approach appropriate to this patient, seal the teeth, address the deep bite before final full-coverage restoration, and review healing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a strong, nuanced sequence with contingencies: conservative guided access if seating/path are reliable, conversion to conventional access if not; clear rationale for apical-barrier apexification over follow-up-intensive options; delay of definitive crowns until occlusal clearance and endodontic stability are confirmed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh reasonable options or misjudges the patient-specific trade-offs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions advantages of one approach but gives little comparison or weak justification for why it fits this patient better than other plausible strategies.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why dentin-preserving access is beneficial here and why a faster, more predictable apical-barrier strategy is preferable to options that depend on repeated visits or greater biologic uncertainty in this adult patient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances trade-offs in detail, including technique sensitivity, cost/time and availability of guided access, preservation of tooth structure, predictability of apical management, and the restorative consequences of delaying or ignoring bite correction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits relevant complications or gives no monitoring/prevention strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists only general endodontic complications without linking them to the open apex, guided access, or occlusal/restorative context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies several case-specific risks, such as guide misfit/deviation, perforation or excess dentin removal, irrigant/material extrusion through the open apex, inadequate disinfection through a small access, fracture risk, or restorative failure if the deep bite is untreated.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links the major risks to prevention and follow-up, for example verifying guide seating, using an internal barrier for the open apex, careful irrigation/instrumentation, reassessing occlusion before crowns, and monitoring radiographic healing and apical barrier integrity.

items.question_content: An 8-year-old girl underwent delayed replantation of avulsed 11 after approximately 2 hours of dry extraoral time. At later review, fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg were obtained; the tooth was subsequently extracted after a new unfavorable crown-root fracture, allowing assessment in fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg. Using these figures, argue for the single biologic interpretation of healing you find most defensible for 11. In your reasoning, indicate which findings are strongest, which are weakest, what alternative interpretations a cautious examiner should still consider, and what would and would not be justified if only fig_01.jpg were available.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible interpretation is not simple apexification and not replacement-resorptive healing, but regeneration/repair of vascularized pulp-like and dentin-forming radicular tissue within an immature previously nonvital replanted tooth. I would still use cautious language: the evidence supports a pulp-dentin-like regenerative outcome rather than proof of a completely normal pulp.

fig_01.jpg supports continued root maturation: increased root length, more anatomic root form, and apical closure rather than only a short apical stop. That makes a mere apical barrier less convincing. However, fig_01.jpg alone cannot prove tissue identity, vitality, or true pulp regeneration; radiographs show form, not histologic nature.

fig_02.jpg adds supportive but indirect evidence of vascularized tissue, because contrast appears to track toward/into the canal space through the apex. This is important because it argues against a purely inert calcific barrier. Its weakness is that angiography is still indirect and cannot by itself define whether the intraradicular tissue is normal pulp, pulp-like connective tissue, or another reparative tissue.

The strongest evidence comes from fig_04.jpg and fig_05.jpg. fig_04.jpg shows dentinal tubules in the apical third, indicating organized dentin formation rather than a nonspecific apical calcific plug. fig_05.jpg shows palisaded peripheral cells resembling odontoblasts adjacent to dentinal tubules and connective tissue architecture resembling pulp with fibroblast-like cells. Together these findings are much more consistent with pulp-like connective tissue plus dentin deposition than with simple apexification.

A cautious differential should still consider: (1) apexification-like healing with an apical hard tissue barrier, and (2) tissue ingrowth/repair related to periodontal or osseous tissues, including ankylotic-replacement phenomena. Apexification is less likely because the evidence is not limited to apical closure; there is continued root development with dentin-like tubules and odontoblast-like lining. Replacement resorption/ankylosis is less likely as the main explanation because that would favor root substitution by bone and loss of normal radicular structure, not intraradicular pulp-like tissue with dentinal tubules and odontoblast-like cells. Periodontal/bone ingrowth repair is also less satisfactory because it does not explain the combined radiographic maturation, angiographic vascular entry, and pulp-like histology as well as the regenerative interpretation does.

fig_03.jpg mainly explains why the tooth was eventually lost: a later unfavorable crown-root fracture. It does not by itself negate the biologic evidence of radicular maturation; it highlights that structural/restorative prognosis can still be poor even when biologic healing is favorable.

If only fig_01.jpg were available, the reasonable clinical conclusion would be that continued root maturation/apical closure occurred and that healing was compatible with a regenerative or maturogenesis-type outcome. But it would be an overclaim to say true pulp regeneration, vascularized intracanalar tissue, or a pulp-dentin complex had been proven. Those stronger claims depend on the added angiographic and especially histologic evidence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the healing pattern or makes a clearly unsupported conclusion, such as calling the outcome straightforward apexification or normal periodontal healing without addressing contrary figure evidence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes root maturation/apical closure but is vague or inconsistent about the biologic meaning, or overstates certainty without distinguishing repair from true regeneration.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly concludes that the figures best support regeneration/repair of pulp-dentin-like radicular tissue rather than a mere apical barrier, with generally appropriate caution about the limits of proof.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies regeneration/repair of vascularized pulp-like and dentin-forming radicular tissue as the best-supported interpretation and explicitly distinguishes this from proof of a completely normal pulp.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not consider plausible alternative interpretations or discusses alternatives that are not clinically relevant to the figures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one plausible alternative interpretation but does not meaningfully compare it with the preferred conclusion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Addresses at least two plausible competing interpretations, such as simple apical barrier formation and ankylotic/replacement or periodontal tissue ingrowth, and uses figure findings to argue against them.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically compares multiple plausible alternatives and explains why none account for the combined radiographic, angiographic, and histologic findings as well as the chosen interpretation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Relies on one modality alone or ignores the figures' differing evidentiary strengths and limitations.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses more than one modality but without clear synthesis, or treats indirect evidence as definitive without acknowledging limitations.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_04.jpg/fig_05.jpg appropriately; recognizes histology as strongest, angiography as supportive but indirect, and explains what fig_01.jpg alone can and cannot establish.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Ranks the evidentiary value of the modalities coherently, identifies a valid limitation for each major modality, and gives a precise counterfactual explanation of what would remain unproven if only fig_01.jpg were available.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides assertions without a clear chain from observed findings to conclusion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Shows some logical progression but leaves major inferential gaps or does not resolve conflicting possibilities.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a clear, logically ordered argument from figure findings to final interpretation, including appropriate caveats.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a concise but highly coherent argument that balances supportive evidence, counterarguments, and uncertainty without overclaiming.

items.question_content: An 8-year-old boy with untreated intrusion of primary tooth #61 at age 2 returns 6 months after extraction of over-retained #61 and mobile #62. The permanent #21 and #22 still have not erupted; #22 is palpable buccally but #21 is not. Examine fig_01.jpg. What is the most appropriate management strategy now? Justify your choice from the trauma history, eruption pattern, and radiographic findings, and explain the main problems your plan is intended to prevent and the key follow-up priorities after intervention.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This is a localized post-traumatic eruption disturbance of #21/#22, most likely related to displacement/scarring after intrusion of #61. Because eruption has not resumed 6 months after removal of the retained primary teeth, and fig_01.jpg shows an immature/open-root #21 with disturbed sequence (#22 more advanced than #21) plus mesial displacement of #23, passive observation alone is no longer the best option. I would arrange interceptive multidisciplinary management: orthodontic assessment of space and canine path, then surgical exposure of #21/#22 with a tissue-preserving approach that maintains attached gingiva where possible, followed by a period of spontaneous eruption rather than immediate traction because the incisors still have eruptive potential. The aim is to remove soft-tissue obstruction/deflection early and reduce later ectopia, crossbite, need for more complex orthodontic extrusion, and possible canine impaction. Follow-up should monitor eruption progress and position of #21/#22, space and #23 trajectory, periodontal/gingival health, root maturation and later vitality, and developmental defects such as enamel hypoplasia; orthodontic traction is added only if eruption stalls or malposition persists.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not propose a credible next step for persistent eruption failure; defaults to vague recall only or gives an inappropriate, non-interceptive plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that specialist input or surgery may be needed but provides an incomplete plan, omitting space/orthodontic assessment, timing, or the intended eruption strategy after exposure.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends timely interceptive management with orthodontic evaluation of space/canine path and surgical exposure of #21/#22 to facilitate eruption, followed by monitoring for spontaneous eruption.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: As above, and specifies a tissue-preserving exposure that protects attached gingiva when feasible, clearly sequencing pediatric, orthodontic, and surgical roles and reserving orthodontic traction for failed spontaneous eruption or persistent malposition.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Bases the plan on a single isolated finding or ignores the relevance of the trauma history and imaging.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the trauma history or the delayed eruption but misses key radiographic or clinical clues that change management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates prior intrusion of #61, failure of eruption despite extraction of #61/#62, buccal palpability asymmetry, and fig_01.jpg evidence of immature #21 and disturbed eruption sequence with #22 ahead of #21.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also identifies the mesial position of #23 in fig_01.jpg as a time-sensitive warning for future orthodontic complications and frames the problem as localized post-traumatic eruption disturbance rather than generalized delay.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides little or no rationale for timing, or misjudges the balance between continued observation and active intervention.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States generic benefits of treatment, such as improved esthetics, without explaining why action is needed now for this child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that immature/open roots preserve eruptive potential, but prolonged delay increases risk of ectopic eruption, more difficult future orthodontics, and worsening arch problems.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances early exposure against surgical/periodontal burden, explaining why minimal tissue-preserving exposure with initial passive eruption is preferable to either prolonged waiting or immediate forceful traction at this stage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful postoperative or developmental follow-up concerns.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only routine healing or a single complication without a structured follow-up focus.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Plans follow-up for eruption progress and position, periodontal/gingival status, and root development of the erupting incisors.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also monitors malposition/crossbite, #23 trajectory and space, and post-traumatic developmental sequelae such as enamel hypoplasia or later vitality issues, with escalation to orthodontic traction if eruption stalls.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of unerupted #21 or #22 despite open apices and preserved eruptive potential on fig_01.jpg.

items.question_content:
A healthy 14-year-old boy presents with recurrent submental swelling and a draining lesion on the right side of the chin. Review fig_01.jpg panel A-I before any treatment is started.

What is your definitive diagnosis and first-line management for the responsible tooth? In your answer, use the figures to:
1. Identify the offending tooth and both developmental anomalies, including the specific dens invagination subtype and the imaging feature that supports it.
2. State the pulpal and periapical diagnoses, and explain why the drainage site does not rule out this tooth as the source.
3. Give at least one realistic alternative diagnosis you considered and why it is less likely.
4. Justify your initial treatment choice over another reasonable management option of your choice, specifically addressing the patient's age, restorability, cortical perforation, and the canal configuration.
5. Explain whether the invaginated tract, the main canal, or both should be treated in this case, and what diagnostic change would make you preserve the main pulp instead of completing full root canal treatment.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The responsible tooth is the left mandibular lateral incisor. fig_01.jpg shows two developmental anomalies in the same tooth: a lingual talon cusp/dens evaginatus and dens invaginatus. The invagination is Oehlers type III-B because the CBCT demonstrates a canal-like invagination extending through the root and communicating with the periodontium at the apical foramen, separate from the main canal space.

The pulpal diagnosis is pulpal necrosis. The periapical diagnosis is chronic apical abscess with an odontogenic cutaneous sinus tract; the CBCT also shows a large periradicular lesion with buccal cortical perforation. The right-sided chin drainage does not exclude this left mandibular incisor because odontogenic infection can track along cancellous bone and soft-tissue/fascial planes and emerge at a distant cutaneous site, especially in younger patients.

Plausible alternatives include a primary periodontal lesion and a nonodontogenic skin infection/dermatologic sinus. A primary periodontal source is less likely because the lesion is centered apically and the probing pattern is normal rather than showing a deep isolated periodontal defect. A nonodontogenic skin lesion is less likely because the imaging identifies a clear dental source with complex infected endodontic anatomy.

The preferred first-line management is tooth-preserving nonsurgical orthograde endodontic treatment, guided by the CBCT anatomy. This is justified because the patient is young, the tooth is restorable, and source control is feasible even though there is a large lesion, cortical perforation, and extraoral drainage. Those findings alone do not make extraction or immediate periradicular surgery the best initial option. Skin treatment alone or antibiotics alone would not remove the source. Surgery or extraction would be reserved for nonrestorability, inability to disinfect/seal the anatomy adequately, or failure of properly executed orthograde treatment.

In this case, both the invaginated tract and the main canal should be treated because the tooth is necrotic and the CBCT shows separate spaces with apical communication and complex anatomy that can both harbor infection. Management should therefore differ from a routine mandibular incisor root canal by using anatomy-driven access, careful location/negotiation of the separate spaces, enhanced disinfection of irregular areas, and apical barrier management if apical constriction is compromised by resorption/destruction, followed by a sound coronal seal.

I would preserve the main pulp instead of completing full root canal treatment only if new diagnostic evidence showed that the main pulp remained vital and was separate from the infected invagination. In that scenario, selective treatment or sealing/disinfection of the invaginated tract with close follow-up would be preferred over treating the entire tooth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the source tooth or gives a nonodontogenic primary diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes an endodontic source in the mandibular incisor region but incompletely identifies the anomalies or pulpal/periapical diagnosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the left mandibular lateral incisor with dens evaginatus/talon cusp and dens invaginatus, with pulpal necrosis and chronic apical abscess/cutaneous sinus tract.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies combined dens evaginatus and Oehlers type III-B dens invaginatus, explicitly citing apical communication with the periodontium and relating that anatomy to the disease process.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use figure-based or clinical evidence to support conclusions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings from fig_01.jpg but does not connect them into a coherent explanation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the crown anomaly, periradicular lesion, CBCT anatomy, and distant cutaneous drainage into a coherent endodontic explanation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically uses fig_01.jpg findings to explain the separate invaginated tract, apical periodontal communication, and cortical perforation, and connects these with the distant sinus location and the endodontic—not primary periodontal—origin.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differential diagnosis or lists alternatives without case-based reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions at least one plausible alternative diagnosis but gives limited or generic reasons against it.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Considers at least one realistic alternative diagnosis, such as a primary periodontal lesion or nonodontogenic cutaneous lesion, and rules it out using case-specific findings.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends skin treatment alone, antibiotics alone, immediate extraction/surgery without adequate justification, or a generic single-canal root canal plan that ignores the anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a conservative endodontic approach but provides a generic plan with limited adaptation to the invagination, separate spaces, or apical destruction.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends CBCT-guided nonsurgical orthograde treatment with modified access, disinfection of the complex anatomy, appropriate sealing/obturation strategy, and restoration/follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly states that in this necrotic case the invaginated tract and main canal should be managed as distinct spaces when indicated, and correctly changes strategy in the vital-main-pulp scenario toward preserving the main pulp while selectively treating/sealing the invagination.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful justification for the chosen intervention or ignores key patient/anatomic factors.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives only generic reasons for tooth preservation or only generic warnings about complexity.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Justifies orthograde tooth-preserving care based on age, restorability, and feasibility of source control despite the large lesion and cortical perforation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains why cortical perforation and an extraoral sinus tract do not by themselves mandate surgery or extraction when orthograde treatment is feasible, and identifies appropriate triggers for escalation if healing fails.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old woman near completion of orthodontic treatment wants esthetic correction of her maxillary anterior teeth, but Tooth 12 remains painful after prior root canal treatment and has a joined-crown anomaly. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management approach would you choose for Tooth 12 before any periodontal or restorative smile rehabilitation, and justify your choice and sequence using the anatomy and periapical findings visible in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, including implications for prognosis?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would prioritize tooth-preserving endodontic management of Tooth 12 before any esthetic phase. The anomaly is most consistent with fusion rather than gemination because the crown is joined but separate canal systems are visible. The previous treatment likely failed because only one canal was treated; fig_01.jpg shows an untreated canal associated with persistent apical radiolucency. fig_02.jpg adds critical 3D information: complex apical anatomy with bifurcation/isthmus and a large well-defined unilocular periapical lesion, so infection may persist in areas that are difficult to disinfect orthogradely.

My plan would be to retain the tooth if it is restorable and periodontally supportable, then perform CBCT-guided orthograde retreatment first to locate, disinfect, shape, and obturate both canals and re-establish an adequate coronal seal. Because the CBCT shows complex apical anatomy and an extensive lesion, I would have a low threshold for adjunctive periradicular surgery if complete orthograde control is unlikely or if healing is uncertain/persistent. Surgical management should include apical management, curettage of the lesion, tissue submission for histopathology, and retrograde sealing as indicated.

I would delay gingival recontouring and any restorative camouflage until the tooth is asymptomatic and early clinical/radiographic stability is demonstrated. The main risks are missed anatomy, perforation or inadequate debridement in the anomalous canal system, persistent apical disease, and soft-tissue/esthetic compromise from surgery in the anterior maxilla. Prognosis is fair to good if both canals are properly treated, apical pathology is addressed when indicated, and the tooth is followed clinically and radiographically over time.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the primary problem or attributes the pain/radiolucency to a non-endodontic cause without support; does not recognize the significance of the untreated canal/anomalous anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes failed root canal treatment or apical pathology but incompletely identifies the anomaly, or misclassifies the developmental defect without linking it to the canal configuration and treatment failure.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies persistent post-treatment apical disease associated with an anomalous joined crown and a previously untreated canal; appropriately keeps the diagnosis at a working clinical level.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately explains that the anomaly is more consistent with fusion than gemination because separate canals are present, and identifies the periapical lesion as chronic apical pathology that may be cystic but is not overcalled histologically.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives a generic answer with little or no use of the symptoms, prior treatment history, or imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as the missed canal or the radiolucency, but does not synthesize fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg into a coherent explanation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the persistent symptoms, prior incomplete treatment, fig_01.jpg evidence of an untreated canal, and fig_02.jpg evidence of lesion extent and apical complexity to justify management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows why the 3D findings in fig_02.jpg materially change decision-making by demonstrating apical bifurcation/isthmus and lesion extent that reduce the predictability of orthograde treatment alone and require careful sequencing before esthetic care.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation alone, immediate esthetic treatment before infection control, or another clearly inappropriate plan; does not provide a defendable sequence of care.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests retreatment or surgery but the plan is incomplete, poorly sequenced, or does not clearly prioritize elimination of endodontic infection before periodontal/restorative rehabilitation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes tooth preservation with orthograde retreatment of both canals first, re-establishment of a coronal seal, delay of esthetic treatment, and recognition that surgery may be required because of the apical anatomy and lesion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise plan: confirm restoratability/periodontal support, perform CBCT-guided orthograde retreatment of both canals, then use periradicular surgery with lesion curettage/biopsy and retrograde apical management when indicated by the complex apical anatomy and large lesion, followed only later by periodontal and restorative smile rehabilitation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks, or presents an unrealistic prognosis unsupported by the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic risks or benefits and gives little case-specific discussion of prognosis or follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefits of retaining a young anterior tooth against the morbidity and limits of retreatment/surgery, and notes the need for clinical and radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically discusses the risks of missed anatomy, iatrogenic damage during retreatment, persistent apical disease, and anterior soft-tissue/esthetic effects of surgery, while giving a realistic fair-to-good prognosis contingent on infection control, coronal seal, healing, and maintenance.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of Tooth 12 without first considering tooth-preserving retreatment/surgical management despite a restorable young anterior tooth and an identifiable untreated canal on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg

items.question_content: A 58-year-old woman has 1 week of pain from tooth 37 after endodontic access was started elsewhere.
