The tooth remains responsive to cold/EPT and is mildly tender to percussion, with no swelling or mobility. Examine fig_01.jpg. State your definitive management plan and justify it from the imaging and clinical findings. Your reasoning should explain why the tooth is or is not suitable for conservative retention, how the distal-root defect and the mesio-cervical access-related weakening should each influence your endodontic and restorative choices, and what specific imaging finding would most change the plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is internal inflammatory root resorption in the distal canal/root of 37, with a separate iatrogenic mesio-cervical access gouge causing marked thinning of dentin. Conservative retention is appropriate because fig_01.jpg supports a lesion that is contained within and continuous with the canal, without root-surface perforation, and clinically there is no swelling or mobility, so the tooth is still restorable. Vitality does not argue for observation here; in internal resorption, vital inflamed pulp can sustain clastic activity, and the symptoms/tenderness suggest active pulpal disease that should be removed.

My plan is nonsurgical orthograde root canal treatment under rubber dam with careful refinement of the access, controlled working length, and thorough chemical debridement because the resorptive lacuna is irregular and difficult to instrument directly. Activated NaOCl and EDTA are important, and an interappointment calcium-hydroxide dressing is reasonable if multi-visit disinfection is chosen. For the distal canal, the resorptive cavity should be obturated with a warm/thermoplasticized gutta-percha technique plus sealer so the material can adapt to the internal defect. The mesio-cervical thinned area from access error should be reinforced/sealed with a bioactive repair material such as MTA/bioceramic before the definitive coronal restoration, followed by a durable bonded coronal seal.

I would not choose monitoring alone because the tooth is symptomatic and the lesion is active, and I would not move first to extraction or surgery because the defect is nonperforating and the tooth appears salvageable. The imaging finding that would most change the plan is root-surface perforation or structural loss so extensive that predictable restoration is not possible; that would worsen prognosis and shift management toward perforation repair with a bioactive material if localized, or extraction if the tooth is structurally hopeless. Follow-up should assess symptom resolution, arrest of resorption, healing, and any signs of leakage or fracture.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion or treats it as simple caries/apical disease only; does not recognize the access-related structural defect.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a resorptive process but does not clearly identify it as internal and nonperforating, or misses the separate mesio-cervical iatrogenic thinning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies nonperforating internal inflammatory root resorption in the distal root/canal and recognizes a separate access-related mesio-cervical weakening defect.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately distinguishes the lesion from external cervical resorption/perforation using fig_01.jpg and the clinical findings, and states that the tooth is currently restorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a plan with little or no use of the clinical findings or fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely; may mention symptoms or CBCT, but does not connect them coherently to salvageability and treatment choice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates vitality, percussion tenderness, absence of swelling/mobility, the contained CBCT lesion, and the access-related thinning into a coherent justification for management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains how each finding affects diagnosis, urgency, retention potential, and the specific obturation/restorative strategy, including why vitality does not justify observation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan, omits definitive endodontic treatment for active internal resorption, or ignores the structural defect.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests root canal treatment but gives a generic or incomplete plan, fails to tailor filling to the internal defect, or does not address the mesio-cervical weakening.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends orthograde nonsurgical root canal treatment with careful access refinement and isolation, thorough chemical debridement of the irregular defect (with irrigant activation and, if multi-visit, intracanal medicament), warm/thermoplastic obturation of the nonperforating resorptive cavity, repair/reinforcement of the thinned mesio-cervical area with a bioactive material, and definitive coronal seal.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise sequence tailored to fig_01.jpg and correctly states how the plan would change if perforation or non-restorable structural loss were present.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not justify the choice of conservative care or ignores major risks and alternative pathways.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a preference for retention but offers limited reasoning, or does not define when prognosis would worsen enough to change treatment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Justifies conservative retention over monitoring or more invasive options because the lesion is contained and the tooth appears restorable, while recognizing risks such as missed perforation, inadequate sealing of the resorptive cavity, and cervical fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances benefits and risks in patient-specific terms and identifies a clear imaging trigger for changing course: root-surface perforation or structural compromise that makes predictable restoration impossible.

items.question_content: A 12-year-old boy presents 1 year after trauma with a fractured maxillary left central incisor. The tooth is non-vital, not tender to percussion, has normal mobility and sulcular depth, and the gingiva is healthy. Examine fig_01.jpg and the 12-month review image in fig_02.jpg. If your goal is to preserve the tooth and alveolar contour during growth whenever reasonably possible, what definitive management would you recommend, and why is it the best choice in this patient? Justify your decision from the clinical and radiographic findings, outline the key technical priorities that will determine success, and state which follow-up findings would make you regard healing as acceptable versus failure.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend intentional replantation as a tooth-preserving option for 21, with extraoral management of the fracture and endodontic treatment, followed by prompt replantation and semi-rigid splinting. The main reasons are the patient’s age, anterior esthetic importance, need to preserve alveolar bone during growth, non-vital status, normal periodontal probing and mobility, absence of acute infection, and the longitudinal crown-root fracture pattern seen on fig_01.jpg, which makes simple restoration or routine endodontic treatment alone unlikely to succeed. Compared with other reasonable options, this approach offers a chance of retaining the natural tooth and ridge when implant placement is unsuitable in a growing child, although the prognosis remains guarded.

Critical technical priorities are atraumatic extraction, maintaining a moist root surface and minimizing extraoral time to protect the periodontal ligament, adapting/sealing the fracture line, completing canal management, accurate repositioning, stabilization with a flexible or semi-rigid splint, plaque control, and definitive restoration once stability is confirmed.

Acceptable healing would be an asymptomatic tooth with healthy gingiva, normal probing depth, stable or normal mobility, no tenderness, maintained position, and no progressive inflammatory resorption or periapical pathology radiographically. On fig_02.jpg, limited partial periodontal-space obliteration can be acceptable if it is localized and non-progressive, but it should be monitored because it may herald ankylosis or replacement resorption. Failure would include recurrent pain or infection, deep isolated periodontal pocket, increasing mobility or infraocclusion, progressive periodontal-space loss with ankylosis features, or progressive external/replacement resorption.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends a clearly unsuitable plan for this presentation, such as routine restoration/endodontics alone despite the root-extending fracture, or gives no coherent definitive plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for definitive management but proposes preservation vaguely or with major omissions in sequence and rationale.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends intentional replantation or an equivalent tooth-preserving plan appropriate to this case, with a generally correct stepwise rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced, case-specific plan centered on intentional replantation, including atraumatic extraction, extraoral fracture/canal management, prompt replantation, stabilization, and restoration/follow-up priorities.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or no relevant evidence from the history, examination, or figures, or misinterprets the findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some key findings but links them weakly to the management decision.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the child’s age/growth, non-vitality, lack of percussion pain, normal mobility, normal sulcular depth/gingiva, and the fracture pattern on fig_01.jpg into a coherent justification.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the clinical and radiographic findings into a persuasive explanation of why this tooth is damaged yet still a defensible candidate for preservation rather than being automatically deemed hopeless.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores patient-specific consequences of the chosen plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons with limited relevance to this child.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances preservation benefits against realistic risks, and explains why retention has value in a growing child with an anterior tooth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly compares reasonable options generated from the case, emphasizing alveolar/esthetic preservation during growth while acknowledging the guarded prognosis and circumstances that would shift the decision away from replantation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications or demonstrates unsafe unawareness of them.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists complications but does not relate them to prevention or follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key risks such as periodontal ligament injury from desiccation/extraoral delay, inflammatory or replacement resorption, ankylosis, infection, and periodontal breakdown.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links the major complications to preventive technique and monitoring strategy, including moisture control, minimal extraoral time, splinting, hygiene, and serial clinical-radiographic review.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives an unsupported prognosis or misclassifies obvious healing/failure features.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a generic prognosis with limited discussion of follow-up indicators.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States a guarded but reasonable prognosis and identifies core success indicators: asymptomatic function, healthy probing/gingiva, stable mobility, and no progressive radiographic pathology.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Distinguishes acceptable healing from failure in a nuanced way, including cautious interpretation of localized non-progressive periodontal-space obliteration on fig_02.jpg versus progressive ankylosis/resorption or periodontal breakdown.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old woman presents 1 week after attempted root canal treatment on tooth #31 with persistent pain. Exam shows a fractured temporary restoration, tenderness to percussion, distal gingival overgrowth, and residual subgingival distal caries. Review fig_01.jpg. Assuming the tooth is otherwise restorable, what is the best management plan at this visit? Defend your choice using the fragment position and access visible in the figure, explain how you would localize and remove it or decide not to, and state how you would sequence the subsequent endodontic and restorative steps.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would aim to retain tooth #31 and remove the separated instrument before completing endodontic treatment. fig_01.jpg indicates this is not a routine intracanal separation: the fragment is extra-radicular, lodged distal to the tooth in the bony/periodontal region, with limited direct access and subgingival distal destruction. Leaving it in place risks persistent foreign-body inflammation and continued symptoms.

Management should begin with removal of the temporary and residual caries, reassessment of restorability, anesthesia, magnification, and protection of canal orifices. The critical step is localization: use a probe under the microscope and angulated radiographs to determine the fragment's buccolingual position and whether limited periodontal/flap access is required for safe visualization. If the fragment head can be identified and engaged, retrieve it with a loop-type device using gentle coronal traction after hemostasis. I would avoid blind ultrasonic troughing or aggressive bone removal, because with an extra-radicular fragment this can push it deeper, fracture it, increase bone loss, or move it toward vital structures.

If localization remains uncertain, the fragment cannot be safely engaged, or retrieval would require excessive bone removal or create risk to adjacent anatomy, I would stop and refer for advanced/surgical management rather than continue blindly.

After retrieval, irrigate the site, manage the deep distal margin with preendodontic build-up/deep margin elevation to create a sealable margin and allow proper isolation, then complete root canal treatment. Definitive full-coverage restoration should follow after soft-tissue healing. Follow-up should assess pain resolution, soft-tissue/probing improvement, and radiographic healing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unsafe plan such as blind intracanal management of the fragment, immediate obturation without addressing the extra-radicular foreign body, or extraction without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that intervention is needed but gives an incomplete or poorly sequenced plan; may mention retrieval or RCT completion without clear localization strategy, access management, or restorative sequencing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes conservative tooth retention with retrieval of the extra-radicular fragment before canal completion, followed by management of the subgingival margin/build-up and then endodontic completion and definitive restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent stepwise plan: reassess restorability after caries removal, protect canal orifices, localize under magnification with radiographic guidance, gain soft-tissue access if needed, retrieve with controlled traction, then perform margin relocation/preendodontic build-up, complete RCT under proper isolation, and delay final cuspal coverage until periodontal healing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets the case or ignores the figure; treats the problem as a routine intracanal file separation or does not use the clinical context in reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely links symptoms, restorative breakdown, and figure-based fragment location/access limitations to the chosen management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the patient's pain, percussion tenderness, residual subgingival caries/gingival overgrowth, and the figure-based impression of an extra-radicular fragment with limited access to justify the plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly interprets the figure as showing extra-radicular distal bony involvement requiring buccolingual localization and altered access, and explains why this changes management compared with routine intracanal retrieval.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh risks and benefits, or endorses a clearly disproportionate approach without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic pros/cons or fails to connect them to this case's extra-radicular location and restorability.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Justifies conservative retention because the tooth is restorable and the fragment may perpetuate inflammation, while acknowledging the need to minimize additional hard- and soft-tissue damage.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the benefits of retaining the tooth and removing the foreign body against case-specific risks such as deeper displacement, further fracture, excess bone removal, or proximity to vital structures, and defines a reasonable threshold for stopping and referring.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications or proposes maneuvers likely to worsen them.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies few or only generic complications, with limited prevention or monitoring strategies.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant complications such as bleeding, fragment displacement, additional bone loss, inability to visualize/engage the fragment, or persistent periodontal inflammation, and gives reasonable preventive steps.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates and manages case-specific hazards: need for hemostasis and magnification, protection of canal orifices, avoidance of blind ultrasonic manipulation, criteria for abandoning retrieval, and follow-up for pain, soft-tissue healing, probing changes, and radiographic resolution.

items.question_content: A 46-year-old woman wants to retain tooth #44 after failure of prior root-canal treatment. The tooth is clinically restorable. Use the pretreatment view in fig_01.jpg panel A only, and answer as you would at the consultation before any intervention. Give a ranked definitive management strategy for this tooth. In your justification, identify the provisional diagnosis and most likely cause of failure; cite the specific radiographic findings in fig_01.jpg panel A that support salvage rather than immediate removal; state the single most important 3-D anatomic question that additional imaging must answer before you commit to re-access; and define the stop/go criteria that would make you continue, stage, redirect to another definitive approach, or declare the tooth non-salvageable. Finally, name one other plausible definitive pathway that some clinicians might choose first here and explain specifically why you would rank it lower for this premolar.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The provisional diagnosis is previously treated tooth #44 with post-treatment apical periodontitis, most likely driven by persistent intraradicular infection apical to an iatrogenic mechanical obstruction. On fig_01.jpg panel A the canal appears blocked by a separated bur/instrument, and there is associated periapical pathosis with apical/root-end compromise consistent with external apical resorptive change. Even so, immediate extraction is not the first choice because the tooth is restorable and the pretreatment image does not by itself show a hopeless periodontal condition or definite vertical root fracture.

My ranked definitive strategy is:
1) Orthograde retreatment first, but only if safe re-access appears feasible after further imaging and magnified assessment.
2) Surgical endodontic management if orthograde recovery of the canal would require destructive dentin removal yet the tooth still has adequate remaining root length, no vertical root fracture, and acceptable restorative/surgical prognosis.
3) Extraction only if the tooth proves non-salvageable because of vertical root fracture, non-restorability, unreparable perforation, inadequate residual root length/support, or if neither orthograde nor surgical treatment can predictably control the disease without unacceptable structural damage.

The specific pretreatment findings supporting salvage are the localized apical lesion, the obstructing metallic fragment within the canal, and altered apical anatomy rather than generalized hopeless support. These suggest a potentially treatable technical failure rather than a tooth that is automatically hopeless.

The single most important unanswered 3-D question is the exact buccolingual relationship between the obstructing fragment, the true canal path, and the external root surface—essentially whether a safe dentin corridor exists to remove or bypass the obstruction without perforation or critical thinning of this premolar root. Limited-FOV CBCT and/or angled radiographs are justified to assess remaining dentin thickness, eccentricity of the fragment, transportation, perforation, and whether apical anatomy remains negotiable.

Stop/go criteria: continue orthograde treatment only if conservative access under microscope control allows centered troughing or bypass while preserving radicular dentin, with recovery of the original canal path or safe access to the infected apical segment. Stage the case if access is regained but persistent exudation/infection control requires intracanal medication before obturation. Redirect away from orthograde treatment if the fragment is eccentrically positioned and retrieval/bypass would require unsafe dentin sacrifice, risks perforation, or still would not permit meaningful apical disinfection. Declare the tooth non-salvageable if additional imaging or intraoperative findings reveal vertical root fracture, inadequate root structure for either orthograde or surgical management, non-restorability, or irreparable perforation.

A plausible alternative that some clinicians might rank first is immediate apical surgery. I would rank it lower initially because the primary suspected cause is intracanal infection blocked off by the obstruction; if orthograde access can be regained safely, it addresses the full canal system and preserves root length better than jumping directly to root-end surgery. For this premolar, the key principle is dentin preservation with infection control—not heroic fragment retrieval at any cost.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the main problem or gives a diagnosis/etiology inconsistent with fig_01.jpg panel A.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes prior endodontic failure and apical disease but does not clearly identify the intracanal mechanical obstruction or its significance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies post-treatment apical periodontitis associated with an obstructing separated bur/instrument and apical/root-end compromise visible on fig_01.jpg panel A.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies post-treatment apical periodontitis caused by persistent infection apical to a separated bur/instrument, notes apical external/root-end compromise, and explains why the tooth is compromised but not automatically hopeless.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg panel A meaningfully or ignores the need for additional imaging.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some pretreatment findings but only loosely links them to the treatment ranking, or asks for more imaging without defining what it must clarify.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Cites specific fig_01.jpg panel A findings that support salvage and correctly identifies the decisive unresolved 3-D issue as the relation of the obstruction to the true canal, remaining dentin, and external root surface.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the pretreatment radiographic findings into a coherent justification for the management ranking, explicitly explaining how additional imaging would assess fragment position, remaining dentin thickness, transportation/perforation risk, and feasibility of orthograde versus alternative treatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides an inappropriate or generic plan, or does not rank definitive options.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a broadly reasonable first choice but lacks a clear decision tree, weakly defines sequencing, or does not state when to redirect or abandon treatment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a ranked definitive plan with orthograde retreatment first if safe, a credible second-line definitive alternative if orthograde access is unsafe or inadequate, and extraction/non-salvage criteria. Includes core operative priorities such as conservative re-access, dentin preservation, disinfection, and appropriate obturation/coronal seal.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, stepwise decision tree that distinguishes when to proceed immediately, when to stage treatment, when to redirect to surgery, and when to declare the tooth non-salvageable, with each branch tied to specific radiographic or intraoperative findings.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh case-specific risks and benefits of competing definitive options.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general risks or benefits but does not define meaningful case-specific thresholds.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why salvage is reasonable initially, why aggressive orthograde retrieval at all costs is inappropriate, and why at least one plausible alternative is ranked lower in this specific premolar.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Defines explicit case-specific thresholds such as unsafe dentin sacrifice, inability to regain/disinfect the apical canal, perforation/transportation risk, inadequate residual root length for surgery, vertical root fracture, or non-restorability, and uses them to justify the ranking of orthograde treatment, surgery, and extraction.

items.question_content: A 27-year-old man reports mild bite pain on both maxillary second molars. Thermal tests are normal, probing depths are <3 mm, and there is no caries or gingival inflammation. CBCT and the relationships visible in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show mesio-inclined impacted maxillary third molars causing severe distal external root resorption of the adjacent second molars with communication to the canal. Assume that on one side the defect is positioned mainly palatally, so after third-molar removal you cannot directly visualize or reliably seal the resorptive exposure from a standard buccal microsurgical approach. What definitive management would you choose for that second molar, and why is it preferable to the other reasonable options in this patient?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would still remove the impacted third molar because it is the cause, but for the second molar I would not attempt a blind retrograde vitality-preserving procedure if the palatal resorptive communication cannot be directly accessed and sealed. My preferred plan would be to retain the second molar if it is restorable and periodontally supportable, and manage it with conventional orthograde root canal treatment. The tooth currently shows a normal/reversibly affected pulp clinically, but the CBCT shows severe external resorption reaching the canal; once direct visualization and sealing are not achievable, the key prerequisite for retrograde vital pulp treatment is lost. In that setting, trying to preserve vitality surgically carries a high risk of incomplete cleaning, microleakage, persistent inflammation, and later necrosis. Observation after third-molar extraction alone is less appropriate here than in a non-communicating defect because the canal is already exposed and the patient is symptomatic, so contamination risk is real. Extraction of the second molar would be a fallback only if CBCT or intraoperative findings show inadequate remaining root structure, poor periodontal support, or an overall non-restorable prognosis. I would explain these trade-offs to the patient, obtain consent, and follow the retained tooth with clinical and radiographic review for healing and absence of further resorption or apical disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate definitive plan, such as blind retrograde treatment despite inaccessible sealing, ignores removal of the causative impacted third molar, or chooses second-molar extraction as routine first-line management without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that treatment is needed but gives a vague or weakly justified plan for the second molar, or names RCT/extraction without clear indications or sequencing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends removal of the impacted third molar and orthograde RCT for a restorable second molar because reliable retrograde access/sealing is not possible; reserves extraction for clearly non-restorable or poor-support cases.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above plan with clear sequencing logic, explicitly states that rVPT depends on direct visualization and sealing, and frames retention of the second molar as preferred when prognosis remains acceptable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets key findings, such as the normal sensibility tests, lack of periodontal/caries pathology, or CBCT evidence that resorption reaches the canal.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings correctly but misses the importance of canal communication and the changed access constraint, or overstates pulpal disease despite the presented testing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the patient's age, mild bite symptoms, normal thermal response, shallow probing, absence of caries/gingival inflammation, and CBCT/figure findings of third-molar-induced distal resorption reaching the canal into a coherent plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all available clinical and imaging evidence and clearly explains why the palatal/inaccessible location changes the suitability of a vitality-preserving retrograde approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides little or no comparison of reasonable options, or advocates an option without addressing patient-specific risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists alternatives but discusses trade-offs superficially or generically.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that observation is less predictable because the canal is already involved, inaccessible rVPT risks leakage and failure, orthograde RCT sacrifices vitality but improves contamination control and sealing, and extraction should be reserved for poor-restorability scenarios.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a nuanced, patient-specific justification balancing biologic preservation, technical feasibility, long-term seal, and tooth retention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits important risks or follow-up considerations.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one complication or generic review but without case-specific relevance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant complications such as sealing failure, persistent contamination/infection, later pulp necrosis or apical disease, and proposes clinical and radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also specifies triggers for changing the plan, such as non-restorable remaining root structure, poor periodontal support, or inability to achieve predictable conventional endodontic treatment.

items.question_content: An 8-year-old boy presents about 1 year after a fall with persistent mobility of both maxillary central incisors. Exam shows mild coronal extrusion, grade III mobility, plaque-induced gingival inflammation, no tenderness to percussion or palpation, no discoloration, and positive EPT responses in both teeth. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is your definitive management now, and why is it the best choice in this child? Include whether endodontic treatment is indicated at this visit and what follow-up changes would make you alter the plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The priority is to preserve both incisors conservatively. fig_02.jpg shows horizontal root fractures in the apical third with immature roots, wide canals, and open apices; combined with positive sensibility, no discoloration, no tenderness, and no radiographic inflammatory change, this supports likely maintained vitality of the coronal fragments and good healing potential. Because presentation is delayed by about a year, immediate forceful manual repositioning is less favorable: clot/healing at the fracture site and socket may resist relocation, and sudden movement could further injure the PDL or pulp. I would first control the gingival inflammation and plaque burden with careful debridement, chlorhexidine/oral-hygiene reinforcement, and soft-diet advice, because sulcular infection could jeopardize healing at the fracture level. Then I would use gentle orthodontic repositioning of the extruded coronal fragments with light continuous forces and stabilize them as needed. Root canal treatment is not indicated now. In an immature tooth, EPT alone is not definitive, but serial positive responses plus the absence of symptoms and radiographic pathology justify observation rather than prophylactic endodontics. Follow-up should be close initially, then long-term annually for at least 5 years, monitoring position, mobility, percussion sound, crown color, periodontal health, sensibility, and radiographic signs of fracture healing, apical radiolucency, or resorption. If evidence of coronal-fragment necrosis or inflammatory resorption appears, endodontic treatment should be limited to the coronal segment up to the fracture line; the apical fragment is usually left untreated unless it becomes independently diseased.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate overall plan such as routine extraction, immediate prophylactic root canal treatment, or ignores the need to reposition/stabilize and review the traumatized teeth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a broadly conservative approach but with major omissions or poor sequencing, such as ignoring periodontal decontamination, not addressing stabilization/repositioning strategy, or giving an unclear pulp management plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends retention of both incisors, periodontal inflammation control, gentle orthodontic repositioning of the coronal fragments with stabilization/light forces, and no root canal treatment at this stage, with planned review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced conservative plan that explicitly prioritizes infection control, atraumatic orthodontic repositioning for the delayed presentation, avoidance of immediate endodontics, and explains that future treatment would target only the coronal segment if necrosis develops.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully use the clinical and imaging findings, or bases the plan on unsupported assumptions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but misses important interactions, such as the significance of delayed presentation, immature roots/open apices, or the fracture level seen on fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly links the delayed presentation, positive sensibility/no symptoms, and fig_02.jpg findings of apical-third horizontal fractures with immature open apices to a conservative vitality-preserving approach.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg with the clinical exam in a nuanced way, noting that sensibility testing is supportive rather than absolute in immature teeth, that apical-third fractures/open apices favor healing, and that plaque-induced gingival inflammation increases risk of bacterial contamination of the fracture environment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful justification for the chosen intervention or misstates the main risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions general advantages of conservative care but does not explain why this is preferable in a delayed, root-fractured immature dentition.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that gradual orthodontic movement is less traumatic than forceful late repositioning and better preserves pulp/PDL healing potential, while acknowledging the need for compliance and monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the benefits of retaining vital immature incisors against the burdens of longer treatment and follow-up, and clearly reserves invasive measures for failure signs rather than using them routinely.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits relevant complications or follow-up triggers.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic review without specifying what complications are important in this trauma scenario.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the need to monitor mobility, tooth position, percussion, color, periodontal status, sensibility, and radiographic signs of healing, apical inflammation, or root resorption.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifies actionable triggers for changing the plan, such as signs consistent with coronal-fragment necrosis or inflammatory resorption, and states that endodontic treatment should be confined to the coronal segment to the fracture line if needed.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of either maxillary central incisor at this stage despite positive sensibility, immature open apices, and no clinical or radiographic evidence of necrosis or resorption

items.question_content: This patient has known relapsing chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis of the left mandible. Nearly 8 years after the initial mandibular treatment, she develops new pain localized around the left mandibular second molar. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What is the most defensible management at this visit, and why? Base your reasoning on the imaging pattern, the possibility of tooth-specific disease, and the background mandibular process.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not assume the new pain is either purely a CNO flare or a routine periapical infection. The figure pattern should be interpreted as atypical for simple apical periodontitis: the radiolucency is not a classic well-circumscribed round periapical lesion and appears to sit within a jaw that already shows broader osseous change. Even so, the symptoms are localized to a specific tooth, so a superimposed odontogenic source must be actively investigated rather than dismissed.

My immediate plan would be a focused endodontic work-up of the second molar: vitality testing, percussion/palpation, periodontal probing, restorability assessment, and correlation with the periapical findings. If the tooth is restorable and the pulp is partially necrotic or non-vital, the most defensible treatment is conservative root canal therapy. That removes a possible dental driver of pain while preserving the tooth and avoids unnecessary extraction or further jaw surgery in a mandible already altered by CNO.

I would not use empiric antibiotics unless there are objective signs of acute bacterial infection such as pus, cellulitis, or systemic illness. Steroid-only management would also be insufficient if tooth-specific necrosis is identified. Follow-up should be coordinated with the team monitoring the mandibular disease: assess symptom resolution and repeat imaging. Improvement around the tooth after RCT would support a superimposed endodontic component; persistent or progressive changes elsewhere would indicate ongoing CNO activity.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Attributes the problem entirely to a routine dental abscess or entirely to CNO without considering overlap or other plausible causes.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions both a tooth-related source and CNO activity but does not distinguish their relative likelihood or explain how they would be separated clinically.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recognizes that a superimposed endodontic problem and the underlying mandibular disease are both plausible, and explains why pure acute bacterial osteomyelitis is less supported without clear infection features.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes a combined interpretation: underlying CNO with a possible tooth-specific pulpal/periapical contributor, and explains why the radiographic pattern is atypical for ordinary apical periodontitis yet too localized to ignore as purely mandibular disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figures or bases the answer on only one datum, such as pain location alone.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the history of CNO or the tooth symptoms, but shows limited integration of the imaging pattern with the clinical context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the localized second-molar symptoms with the long-standing relapsing unilateral mandibular disease and recognizes that the figure-based radiolucency is not a straightforward routine periapical presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly connects the image pattern to broader mandibular osseous involvement while also using the tooth-focused symptoms to justify targeted pulp assessment before assigning the lesion wholly to either CNO or endodontic infection.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends immediate extraction, additional mandibular surgery, or empiric prolonged drug treatment without a targeted dental assessment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests only observation or symptomatic medication, or proposes dental treatment vaguely without specifying tooth-preserving endodontic evaluation and criteria for intervention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends focused endodontic evaluation and, if the second molar is restorable and shows partial necrosis or non-vital pulp, root canal treatment; avoids routine antibiotics unless infection signs emerge; includes follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan: immediate tooth-specific testing and radiographic correlation, conservative RCT if indicated, preservation of the tooth, coordination with the team following the mandibular disease, and predefined reassessment if symptoms or radiographic change do not improve.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address the consequences of under- or over-treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes either the value of tooth preservation or the need to control a possible dental source, but not both.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains the need to avoid both missing a true odontogenic source and performing unnecessary irreversible treatment in a jaw already affected by CNO.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly justifies conservative endodontic management as the best balance of diagnostic clarification, symptom relief, tooth preservation, and avoidance of unnecessary surgical morbidity or misdirected escalation of CNO treatment.

items.question_content: A 71-year-old woman has spontaneous pain and percussion sensitivity from a restorable mandibular left second molar. Maximum mouth opening is about 32 mm. A CBCT and surface scan have already been used to fabricate a tooth-supported guide. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg carefully. You are treating today with the printed guide and standard ultrasonic/endodontic instruments available chairside. Based on the figures, what is the most feasible way to gain access to the calcified canal system, which canal region would you use the guide-derived path for first, and how would you execute access while minimizing furcal/perforation risk? Justify your choice with specific figure findings, name one reasonable alternative you would reject and why, and give two concrete intraoperative findings that would make you stop and change plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The key figure-based problem is geometric, not diagnostic: the guide appears to seat, but the posterior interocclusal clearance is insufficient for the sleeve-plus-bur-plus-handpiece assembly. fig_01.jpg shows severe canal obliteration with a preplanned drill trajectory to remaining canal space, and fig_02.jpg panel A shows that the guide can be positioned even though a conventional guided bur approach is not practically insertable in this limited opening. Therefore, I would keep the existing guide as a trajectory-transfer device rather than a drilling guide.

I would use the guide-derived path for the mesial canal system first. fig_01.jpg panel B-F specifically maps the mesiobuccal/mesiolingual region and the virtual path to the residual apical canal space beyond the calcified segment, which is the area most in need of guided localization and carries greater risk of furcal strip/perforation if approached freehand.

Execution: isolate, verify stable guide seating, then pass a visible marker through the guide sleeve to transfer the planned path onto dentin (in this case, graphite marking is appropriate). Remove the guide and advance a short, fine ultrasonic tip under the microscope along that mark in very small increments, approximately 1-2 mm at a time, with irrigation/cooling and no lateral sweeping. Re-seat the guide repeatedly to refresh and verify the trajectory, and relate depth/orientation to the CBCT plan until the mesial canal is located. Once a lumen is found, establish working length, negotiate, shape, irrigate, and obturate conventionally; any more accessible canal can then be managed by standard endodontic steps once the chamber anatomy is clarified.

A reasonable alternative to reject is standard static guided bur access. It is attractive because the 3D plan already exists, but in this patient it is not feasible because the limiting factor is vertical posterior clearance, not planning accuracy. I would also reject blind freehand troughing as the primary strategy because a heavily calcified mandibular second molar with limited opening, posterior access, and thinner danger zones has a higher risk of excessive dentin removal, furcal drift, and perforation.

I would stop and change plan if: (1) the guide no longer seats reproducibly/stably, so the transferred path can no longer be trusted; (2) the trough begins to deviate eccentrically toward the furcation or external root surface, or dentin becomes dangerously thin; and also if the planned depth is reached without any canal sign or a perforation is suspected. In those situations I would stop, obtain reassessment imaging or re-plan, and avoid continuing blindly.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures or misreads the main constraint.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies either calcification or limited opening, but does not connect the figure findings to why the existing guide cannot be used conventionally.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates that severe pulp canal obliteration is present, a preplanned guided path exists on fig_01.jpg, the guide can seat, and the posterior vertical clearance shown across fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg prevents routine bur/handpiece use.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly interprets the geometry in fig_01.jpg panel G/H and fig_02.jpg panel A, explains that guidance remains useful even though guided drilling is infeasible, and identifies from fig_01.jpg panel B-F that the planned path is directed to the mesial system.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an unsafe or impractical plan, such as forcing conventional guided drilling, blind deep freehand access, or extraction without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests a conservative or guide-assisted approach, but the access sequence is vague, the target region is not identified, or the use of the existing guide is not operationalized.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the existing guide to transfer the planned trajectory to dentin, then uses short ultrasonics incrementally under magnification to locate the canal system before completing conventional root canal treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, stepwise rescue plan: stable guide seating, trajectory transfer/marking, repeated guide re-seating for verification, small incremental ultrasonic advancement with depth control, and prioritization of the mesial system for guided localization.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare reasonable alternatives or ignores patient-specific feasibility constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that the chosen plan is safer or more conservative, but gives only generic reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Rejects at least one plausible alternative and explains, using this patient's limited opening and posterior calcified anatomy, why the chosen approach is more feasible or safer.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison of feasibility, dentin preservation, and iatrogenic risk across plausible alternatives such as standard static guided bur access and blind freehand troughing, tied directly to the figure-based constraints.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications and provides no stopping criteria.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one major risk, usually perforation, but gives limited prevention or unclear indications to stop.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important risks such as furcal/lateral perforation, deviation, excessive dentin removal, or overheating, and gives at least two concrete stop-and-change-plan findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds specific preventive measures and clear next steps after stopping, such as reassessment imaging, re-planning, or referral, rather than continuing blindly.

items.question_content: A healthy 16-year-old girl presents with tooth #47: deep occlusal caries, pain on biting, percussion tenderness, Grade I mobility, no response to cold/heat/EPT, and a single 7-mm mid-buccal probing defect; adjacent teeth test normal. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. At the stage when you are deciding whether to complete treatment orthogradely, state your working diagnosis, defend your preferred management pathway, and say whether CBCT is needed before finishing. Then answer this variation: if at 3 months the tooth is asymptomatic and the periapical radiolucency is shrinking but the 7-mm buccal pocket is unchanged, how would that alter your diagnosis, prognosis, and next step?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My working diagnosis is pulpal necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis in tooth #47, with a primary endodontic lesion causing a secondary periodontal communication, in a mandibular second molar with likely C-shaped/fused-root anatomy. fig_01.jpg supports this by showing fused roots/ribbon-like canal morphology and a large periapical radiolucency. fig_02.jpg shows the key feature that changes completion of treatment: the distal root does not have a reliable apical stop because of inflammatory external resorption/open apex, so conventional cone-fit obturation to a normal constriction is inappropriate.

Therefore I would complete treatment with nonsurgical orthograde endodontics rather than primary periodontal therapy, surgery, or extraction, provided the tooth is restorable. The plan is conservative cleaning/shaping because C-shaped roots are thin and prone to strip perforation, heavy reliance on irrigant disinfection and activation to reach fins/isthmuses, calcium hydroxide if exudation or canal wetness persists, then placement of a 4-5 mm MTA/bioceramic apical plug in the resorbed distal apex before backfilling the remaining irregular canal system with a technique that adapts to webs and isthmuses, followed by a good coronal seal/restoration and review. I would not require CBCT routinely before finishing if the anatomy has been negotiated and the 2D films are adequate; I would obtain CBCT if crack/VRF is suspected, if the extent of resorption/anatomy remains unclear, or if healing is unsatisfactory.

Why the pocket should not be assumed to be primary periodontal disease: the patient is young, adjacent teeth are normal, the defect is isolated to one mid-buccal site, the tooth is non-vital, and the radiographic/percussion findings point to an endodontic source. A pure periodontal lesion is less likely initially. A serious alternative diagnosis to keep in mind is a crack/vertical root fracture or a true combined endo-perio lesion.

If after 3 months the tooth is comfortable and the periapical radiolucency is decreasing but the 7-mm pocket is unchanged, I would revise my interpretation. That pattern means the apical endodontic disease is healing, but the pocket is probably not just a secondary drainage tract. My differential would shift toward a crack/vertical root fracture, a primary periodontal defect, or a true combined lesion. Prognosis becomes more guarded. The next step is targeted reassessment: repeat full periodontal charting, inspect for crack lines/transilluminate and perform bite testing, evaluate restorability, consider CBCT, and involve periodontics if indicated. Periodontal or surgical treatment may then be needed depending on the cause; extraction becomes reasonable only if a fracture, non-restorability, or persistent untreatable combined disease is confirmed.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misdiagnoses the case as primary periodontal disease, a routine mature-apex endodontic case, or another diagnosis that does not account for both the pulpal findings and the atypical apical anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes endodontic disease but incompletely characterizes it; misses either the likely C-shaped/fused-root anatomy, the endodontic-periodontal communication, or the resorptive/open-apex component.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies pulpal necrosis with apical periodontitis in tooth #47 and correctly interprets the isolated probing defect as most consistent initially with a primary endodontic lesion and secondary periodontal communication; recognizes likely C-shaped/fused-root morphology and loss of a normal apical stop from resorption/open apex.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the full working diagnosis above and also states an appropriate initial prognosis (guarded but reasonable) based on the combination of complex anatomy, resorption, and favorable age/healing potential.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures or key clinical findings coherently.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings correctly but does not connect the isolated pocket, non-vital tests, and radiographic anatomy/apical changes into a coherent argument.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the non-response to sensibility tests, pain on biting/percussion tenderness, isolated 7-mm mid-buccal probing defect, normal adjacent teeth, fig_01.jpg evidence of fused/C-shaped anatomy with periapical radiolucency, and fig_02.jpg evidence of absent or unreliable apical stop into a consistent management rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all of the above and explicitly explains why the pattern favors an endodontic source over primary periodontal disease at presentation, while acknowledging the specific findings that would reopen the differential later.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate primary approach such as periodontal therapy alone, immediate extraction, or routine obturation without apical management.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses nonsurgical endodontic treatment but gives a generic or incomplete plan, omitting either conservative management of thin C-shaped roots, strong disinfection strategy, interappointment medicament when needed, apical barrier creation, or definitive restoration/follow-up.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends tooth-preserving nonsurgical orthograde treatment with a sound sequence: conservative cleaning/shaping, irrigation-centered disinfection for the irregular canal system, calcium hydroxide if needed, apical plug/barrier for the resorbed open apex, obturation adapted to the irregular canal anatomy, coronal seal, and review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above sequence and clearly justifies why completion with an MTA/bioceramic apical barrier is the preferred way to finish this case, while appropriately reserving surgery/extraction for confirmed failure, fracture, or non-restorability.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers no plausible alternative diagnosis or gives alternatives unrelated to the presented findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a plausible alternative, such as periodontal disease or crack/vertical root fracture, but does not explain why it is less likely initially or how later findings would change the differential.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Considers at least one clinically plausible alternative diagnosis—such as a true combined endo-perio lesion, primary periodontal lesion, or crack/vertical root fracture—and explains why it is not the leading diagnosis at presentation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly explains that a persistently unchanged isolated deep pocket despite symptom resolution and radiographic apical healing would shift the differential away from a pure endodontic drainage tract toward crack/vertical root fracture or true periodontal/combined disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not prioritize next steps appropriately or proposes escalation without a case-based trigger.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives vague follow-up or CBCT advice without linking it to the changing clinical picture.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately prioritizes intracanal infection control and orthograde completion first, defers CBCT unless anatomy/diagnosis remains unclear or healing deviates, and provides a reasonable follow-up plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly states that if the radiolucency is shrinking but the 7-mm pocket persists unchanged, the next priority is re-evaluation for fracture/true periodontal involvement with targeted tests, possible CBCT, and periodontal input, with prognosis downgraded accordingly.

items.question_content:
A 19-year-old woman returns 3 years after severe bicycle-related dental trauma with persistent pain from tooth 22 on biting, worse with heat and at night. Tooth 22 is now non-responsive to electric pulp testing and tender to vertical percussion; buccal mucosa and palpation are unremarkable. A prior emergency access attempt did not locate the canal. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

You must choose the next definitive management for tooth 22 today. Commit to one pathway and justify it by identifying: (1) the single imaging finding that most argues against retention, (2) the single finding that still makes a conservative attempt biologically reasonable, and (3) how those findings change both your access strategy and your consent discussion. Then state the strongest reasonable alternative you are rejecting, why it is less appropriate at this stage, one intraoperative endpoint that would make you stop pursuing retention, and one follow-up change that would convert a guarded prognosis into failure.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My next definitive step would be a conditional attempt to retain tooth 22 with CBCT-based guided orthograde endodontic access, but with a clearly guarded prognosis and explicit consent that extraction may still become necessary.

The imaging finding that most argues against retention is the complex root fracture pattern on fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg: a double fracture line creating two root fragments. That markedly worsens structural prognosis, raises concern about long-term stability, and increases the risk that further dentin removal or instrumentation could compromise the tooth.

The finding that still makes a conservative attempt biologically reasonable is that, despite the fracture and severe canal obliteration, the figures do not show obvious destructive apical breakdown or progressive resorptive change that would make the tooth immediately hopeless, and the CBCT anatomy is sufficient to plan a controlled path toward the residual canal space. Clinically, the tooth is symptomatic and non-responsive, so the endodontic component still needs definitive treatment; lack of swelling or obvious periodontal breakdown does not rule that out.

Those two findings change the access strategy decisively: I would avoid any further blind/freehand trephination because the tooth is both obliterated and structurally compromised. The access must be minimally invasive, preplanned from CBCT, and aimed at preserving cervical/root dentin while verifying canal direction and working length. They also change the consent discussion: I would tell the patient that the goal is tooth preservation in a 19-year-old, but the fracture pattern makes prognosis poor-to-guarded, and success means symptom resolution plus radiographic stability of the fractured root, not merely getting into the canal.

The strongest reasonable alternative I would reject at this stage is immediate extraction. It is reasonable because the fracture morphology is unfavorable, but I would reject it for now because the patient is young, the tooth is anterior and valuable to preserve, and the current imaging does not show a biologic situation that clearly precludes a conservative attempt. Another nonguided orthograde attempt would be less appropriate still because it adds iatrogenic risk without solving the access problem.

The intraoperative endpoint that would make me stop pursuing retention is inability to establish and verify a safe canal path without perforation, major deviation, or excessive dentin sacrifice, or discovery that the fracture pattern is mechanically unstable during treatment.

A follow-up change that would convert the prognosis from guarded to failed would be progressive mobility or new/progressive radiographic inflammatory change around the fractured root fragments (for example increasing radiolucency or resorption), especially if accompanied by recurrent symptoms. Overall, this is a tooth worth a conservative attempt, but only under image-guided, minimally invasive conditions and with clear criteria for abandonment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets or ignores major clinical/imaging findings, or does not meaningfully use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses symptoms/history or a single imaging feature only, but does not integrate both the canal obliteration/access difficulty and the fracture-related structural problem.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the trauma history, current symptoms, loss of sensibility, failed prior access, and the figure-based findings of severe canal obliteration with a complex root fracture in tooth 22.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all key findings and explicitly explains the competing implications of fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg: endodontic disease requiring treatment versus structurally compromised root morphology that makes prognosis guarded but not necessarily hopeless at presentation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management such as observation alone, repeat blind access, or a plan that does not address the obliteration/fracture complexity.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a definitive pathway but gives an incomplete or weakly justified plan, or does not adapt the access strategy to the imaging findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to a coherent definitive pathway and explains how the next step should be adapted to the calcified canal and fractured root; if retaining the tooth, proposes image-based minimally invasive orthograde access with a backup if safe canal treatment proves infeasible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes guided orthograde access as the preferred next step after failed conventional access, clearly linking that choice to dentin preservation, perforation avoidance, and the need to manage a structurally compromised lateral incisor with predefined stopping rules.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully discuss patient-specific risks, benefits, alternatives, or consent.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic failure risk or generic benefit of retention without tying them to the fracture pattern, age, or access difficulty.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefits of preserving a young patient's anterior tooth against patient-specific risks such as perforation, excessive dentin loss, persistent infection, and fracture-related instability/propagation, and identifies a reasonable alternative pathway.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison between the chosen plan and the strongest rejected alternative, and shows how the imaging findings specifically alter the consent discussion and the threshold for abandoning retention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives no meaningful prognosis or stop/failure criteria.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that prognosis is uncertain or guarded but gives vague or non-case-specific endpoints.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a guarded/conditional prognosis and identifies one appropriate intraoperative stop point and one clinically meaningful follow-up change that would indicate failure of retention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Defines prognosis in biologically specific terms tied to the fracture/obliteration problem, such as inability to reach a verifiable canal safely without destructive iatrogenic damage intraoperatively, and later development of increasing mobility, progressive radiolucency/resorption, or recurrent symptoms around the root fragments.

items.question_content: A 40-year-old woman returns with acute pain and localized soft-tissue redness adjacent to a previously root-treated mandibular left second molar. Nine years earlier the tooth had been found to have a severe strip perforation with extruded obturation material but was asymptomatic, so she chose review rather than intervention and was later lost to follow-up. Examine the serial periapical radiographs in fig_01.jpg. If she now wants to retain the tooth, what definitive management would you recommend at this visit, and why? Base your answer on the radiographic evolution and the anatomic/structural limitations of the tooth, and identify the technical priorities and main complications that would govern success.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The tooth has progressed from a monitored iatrogenic perforation to biologic failure. fig_01.jpg shows a persistent mesial-root strip perforation with extruded gutta-percha, later a new large periradicular radiolucency when symptoms developed. The gradual resorption of the extruded material did not mean healing of the perforation. Continued observation is no longer appropriate.

If the patient wishes to retain the tooth, the best tooth-preserving salvage option is intentional replantation. Orthograde retreatment alone is unlikely to predictably manage a midroot strip perforation in the thin mesial root and may worsen the defect or fail to obtain a seal. Conventional periradicular surgery is less favorable because access to a mandibular second molar mesial root is limited and the defect is not merely apical.

The key steps are atraumatic extraction with maximal periodontal-ligament preservation, keeping the tooth moist and minimizing extraoral time, extraoral resection/removal of the structurally compromised perforated part of the mesial root, root-end cavity preparation, placement of a biocompatible root-end filling material, and immediate replantation with stable passive seating. The prognosis is guarded but reasonable as a last-resort retention strategy if the patient is informed that extraction remains an alternative.

Main risks are root or socket damage during extraction, prolonged extraoral time causing PDL injury, persistent leakage/infection, external inflammatory resorption, ankylosis/replacement resorption, mobility/periodontal breakdown, and eventual failure requiring extraction. Prevention depends on atraumatic handling, rapid extraoral repair, good seal, and close clinical/radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends continued observation only, gives no definitive management, or proposes a plan that does not address the perforation and current disease process.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that active treatment is required but proposes a vague or incomplete plan, or names a plausible intervention without explaining how it would manage the perforation and lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends intentional replantation as a tooth-preserving salvage approach and outlines the essential sequence: atraumatic extraction, extraoral management of the compromised root/perforation, root-end sealing, and immediate replantation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent, stepwise intentional replantation plan, clearly framing it as a last-resort retention strategy and accurately identifying the critical technical priorities that make it feasible.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores the tooth's structural/anatomic limitations and the patient's wish to retain the tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives generic pros and cons but weakly links them to this molar's midroot strip perforation, thin mesial root, or current symptomatic lesion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why simpler options are less favorable in this case, weighing retention against feasibility and prognosis, and acknowledges extraction as a fallback if salvage is not possible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nuanced comparison of realistic options using patient-specific anatomy, structural compromise, and current disease status, with clear justification for choosing intentional replantation now.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads or ignores the serial radiographic course and does not connect symptoms with the imaging findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies either the perforation or the later radiolucency, but does not meaningfully use the serial evolution in fig_01.jpg to support the plan.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the key data: persistent strip perforation, extruded material, apparent radiographic resorption over time, then development of a large symptomatic periradicular lesion indicating treatment failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes history, symptoms, and the full serial radiographic evolution to show why earlier apparent stability did not equal biologic resolution and why intervention is now indicated.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications or mentions only trivial postoperative discomfort.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists some complications but without relating them to intentional replantation or without prevention/monitoring strategies.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies major risks such as extraction damage, prolonged extraoral time with PDL injury, persistent infection/leakage, resorption, ankylosis, or periodontal instability, and mentions follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies the key complications and links them to specific preventive measures such as atraumatic extraction, moisture control, brief extraoral time, careful sealing, and serial clinical/radiographic review.

items.question_content: A 20-year-old man with dental phobia presents with pain on mastication and recurrent labial swelling at previously treated maxillary left central incisor (#21). Probing is normal, sensibility is negative, a sinus tract is present, and no root surface is exposed intraorally. After access, removal of prior filling, irrigation, and 2 weeks of calcium hydroxide, the sinus tract persists with serous canal exudate. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend now, and why? Justify your choice using the tooth anatomy and cortical plate findings, explain why it is preferable to other reasonable options in this patient, and state the clinical or imaging findings that would make you change to a more invasive plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would continue with orthograde non-surgical retreatment as the primary strategy rather than moving directly to surgery or extraction. fig_01.jpg supports a previously treated immature central incisor with an open apex, short root, and thin dentinal walls, so aggressive shaping would further weaken the tooth and conventional apical stop-dependent obturation is unreliable. fig_02.jpg shows a facial apical fenestration with preservation of the palatal cortical plate, which is consistent with an endodontic lesion that has perforated the labial cortex rather than a periodontal defect; this is reinforced by normal probing and the sinus tract.

The immediate priority is infection control: repeat copious disinfection, keep or renew intracanal calcium hydroxide until the canal becomes dry and the sinus tract resolves, then create an apical barrier with a calcium-silicate material and complete obturation with a good coronal seal, using minimal instrumentation because of the fragile root walls. This approach addresses the likely cause, which is persistent intraradicular infection, while preserving a restorable tooth.

I would not choose surgery first because the presence of a fenestration alone does not prove that the defect requires surgical correction, especially when there is no intraoral root exposure and the palatal plate is intact. Surgery adds morbidity and should be reserved if orthograde treatment cannot eliminate the disease. Extraction is least desirable because it is irreversible in a young patient when the tooth is still potentially maintainable.

I would escalate to a more invasive plan if, after adequate orthograde disinfection, there is persistent pain, swelling, sinus tract or exudate, inability to obtain a dry canal, radiographic or CBCT enlargement/non-healing, development of mucosal/root exposure, symptomatic material extrusion or evidence of persistent extraradicular pathology, vertical root fracture, or the tooth becomes non-restorable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No coherent definitive plan, or recommends immediate extraction/surgery as the default approach without addressing intraradicular infection and the open apex.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a conservative direction but is vague or incomplete; does not clearly include continued disinfection/medication followed by a definitive open-apex sealing strategy, or proposes a standard obturation approach unsuited to this anatomy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends orthograde non-surgical retreatment first, with further disinfection and intracanal medicament until the canal is dry/asymptomatic, then apexification or an apical barrier with calcium-silicate material and definitive obturation/coronal seal; reserves surgery for failure.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the stepwise plan above and explicitly adapts technique to thin root walls/open apex, such as minimal instrumentation and controlled irrigation to reduce weakening and extrusion risk, with practical patient-centered execution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Reasoning is disconnected from the case data or misinterprets the radiographic/CBCT findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as symptoms or apical radiolucency, with limited integration of fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and the periodontal findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the endodontic symptoms, normal probing, fig_01.jpg features of open apex/short root/thin walls/inadequate prior treatment, and fig_02.jpg facial cortical fenestration with intact palatal plate to support a primarily endodontic process suitable for orthograde management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly distinguishes apical fenestration from marginal periodontal dehiscence or primary periodontal disease and explains why the combined imaging and clinical findings favor conservative endodontic source control.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare reasonable options or provides a clearly distorted comparison of risks and benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives but the comparison is superficial or not tailored to this patient's anatomy and presentation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that tooth preservation and orthograde source control are favored over the morbidity of surgery and the irreversibility of extraction, while acknowledging the technical risks created by the open apex and thin walls.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison showing why fenestration alone does not mandate surgery, why extraction is disproportionate in a young patient with a restorable tooth, and when the balance would shift toward invasive care.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores important complications or gives no meaningful triggers for reassessment/escalation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic endodontic complications but not the key risks created by this open apex and cortical defect.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant risks such as persistent infection/exudate or sinus tract, extrusion of irrigant or filling material through the open apex/fenestration, root fracture due to thin dentinal walls, and radiographic non-healing; states that these would prompt escalation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds a focused follow-up strategy with clinical and radiographic review and includes development of intraoral root exposure, persistent extraradicular pathology, or loss of restorability as specific triggers for invasive management.
