items.question_content: A 27-year-old ASA I woman re-presents with a draining sinus in the anterior maxilla 1 year after root canal treatment of the maxillary right central incisor and subsequent definitive restoration. The right lateral incisor responds to sensibility testing; the canine had prior root canal treatment years earlier and has no current clinical pathosis. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, but basing your answer only on information available at the recurrence visit (not the later healing shown in follow-up panels), identify the most likely tooth and mechanism responsible for the recurrent sinus tract. Provide a ranked differential diagnosis, explain why the tracing result and CBCT should be interpreted together rather than separately, and outline your management sequence. Include one additional finding that would make you abandon conservative orthograde management and explain how it would change your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely source is tooth #8 (maxillary right central incisor), not #7 or #6. The most likely mechanism is reinfection through disruption of the main root-canal seal at the level of a previously involved lateral canal after post-space preparation/restorative treatment, rather than primary apical failure.

Ranked differential:
1) Tooth #8: loss of main-canal seal with persistent/recurrent infection communicating through a lateral canal in the distal midroot.
2) Tooth #8: post-related complication such as lateral perforation or vertical root fracture.
3) Persistent extraradicular or untreated intraradicular infection of #8 unrelated to the restoration, but this is less likely.
4) Adjacent-tooth source (#6 or #7), least likely given the available findings.

Why the figures matter together: fig_01.jpg panel B shows the sinus-tract tracing is misleading/inconclusive because it stops between #7 and #6, but sinus tracts can follow the path of least resistance and may not point directly to the diseased root surface. fig_01.jpg panel C localizes the lesion three-dimensionally to the distal midroot of #8 at the level of the previously suspected lateral canal. fig_02.jpg panel A shows no apical radiolucency, which argues against apical endodontic failure as the main problem and supports a lateral midroot source instead. The timing after definitive restoration further supports disturbance of the existing seal rather than a new disease process in a neighboring tooth.

Management sequence:
- First, reassess #8 for restorability and for findings that would suggest fracture or perforation: periodontal probing, mobility, transillumination/crack assessment, and careful radiographic/CBCT correlation.
- If no evidence of fracture, perforation, or non-restorability is found, the preferred treatment is conservative orthograde retreatment of #8: remove the post/restorative interference, re-clean and disinfect the main canal, and re-obturate/reseal the canal and coronal access. Direct negotiation of the lateral canal is not required initially.
- Do not treat the vital lateral incisor or the asymptomatic canine based only on the tracing result.
- Do not proceed immediately to surgery if orthograde correction of the likely cause is feasible.
- Review clinically and radiographically because sinus-tract closure can be delayed; persistence over a short early interval alone does not prove failure.

A finding that would change the plan: an isolated narrow deep periodontal pocket or other convincing evidence of vertical root fracture in #8 would shift management away from simple orthograde retreatment toward surgical assessment or extraction depending on restorability. Likewise, a confirmed lateral perforation could favor repair with a different approach rather than routine retreatment alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg coherently, or misidentifies the source as an adjacent tooth or as apical disease without addressing the figure findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical facts correctly but incompletely; may mention recurrence after restoration or neighboring tooth status, yet does not clearly interpret the tracing as potentially misleading and/or does not use the CBCT and apical findings together.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the misleading/non-localizing tracing in fig_01.jpg, the CBCT localization of a lateral midroot lesion on #8 in fig_01.jpg panel C, the absence of apical pathosis in fig_02.jpg panel A, and the adjacent-tooth findings to identify #8 as the source.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the recurrence-visit evidence into a coherent mechanism, explicitly explaining why sinus-tract tracing alone should not determine tooth selection and why the combined 2D/3D imaging pattern supports disruption of the main-canal seal with lateral communication rather than primary apical failure or adjacent-tooth disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible differential, or lists implausible causes without ranking or case-based reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names the likely tooth or mechanism but gives little structured differential reasoning, or omits major plausible alternatives such as vertical root fracture, post-related perforation, or adjacent-tooth disease.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a ranked differential in which #8 with recurrent lateral-canal-related infection from compromised main-canal seal is most likely, while appropriately lowering alternatives such as perforation, fracture, persistent apical disease, and adjacent-tooth sources.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-ranked differential that distinguishes tooth source from pathogenic mechanism and identifies concrete discriminating findings that would move fracture, perforation, or another source higher or lower in the ranking.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends management that does not appropriately address the likely source, such as treating the wrong tooth, antibiotics alone, observation alone, or immediate extraction without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests retreatment or surgery but with weak sequencing, limited rationale, or no attention to excluding fracture/perforation/restorability before definitive treatment.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Prioritizes reassessment of #8 and, if no fracture/perforation/non-restorability is found, recommends conservative orthograde retreatment of #8 to restore disinfection and seal; does not initially treat adjacent teeth or jump straight to surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan: confirm restorability and exclude competing structural causes, remove post/restorative interference if present, re-clean and re-obturate the main canal, re-establish the coronal seal, and reserve surgery for failure of adequate orthograde management or for findings that make orthograde care inappropriate.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify any finding that would alter the plan, or proposes a plan change unrelated to the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names a finding that might change management but does not clearly explain why it matters or what the new plan would be.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a specific additional finding such as an isolated deep narrow periodontal defect, confirmed perforation, progressive nonhealing after adequate retreatment, or non-restorability, and explains an appropriate change in management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links the additional finding to a clear shift in decision-making, explaining why that new information would outweigh conservative orthograde management and support a different strategy such as surgical repair, fracture-directed extraction, or another targeted intervention.

red_flags: Misattributed Etiology: initiating endodontic treatment on the vital lateral incisor or the asymptomatic canine despite recurrence-visit evidence localizing the lesion to the maxillary right central incisor

Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending extraction of the maxillary right central incisor before assessing restorability and the feasibility of correcting the likely disrupted canal seal orthogradely

items.question_content: An 11-year-old boy returns 4 years after regenerative endodontic therapy for a traumatized immature maxillary right central incisor. The tooth is functional, asymptomatic, and the coronal restoration appears intact. Compare the earlier and later images in fig_01.jpg: the tooth had previously shown healing and root maturation, but now there is a new periapical radiolucency with irregular incomplete apical formation and persistent empty canal space coronally/midroot. What is your preferred management now, and why? In your justification, explain the most likely source of the recurrence, what biologic outcome is still realistic for this tooth, and what prognosis and surveillance plan you would present to the parents.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My preferred management is conservative endodontic retreatment with a second regenerative approach rather than immediate irreversible treatment. This tooth is still restorable and functional, and its root remains vulnerable because development was incomplete and the walls were previously thin. The earlier images in fig_01.jpg show that the first RET initially achieved healing and further maturation, so the tooth has already demonstrated reparative potential. The new lesion despite an apparently adequate coronal seal makes recurrent post-treatment apical periodontitis most likely, with persistent intraradicular infection being more likely than obvious coronal leakage.

The retreatment objective is to eliminate or suppress infection while preserving the tooth and any remaining reparative potential. I would re-enter the canal, remove the existing coronal barrier if needed, avoid aggressive instrumentation that could weaken the root, disinfect in a RET-compatible and relatively low-cytotoxic manner, recreate an intracanal scaffold from induced apical bleeding, and place a bacteria-tight coronal barrier/restoration.

Because the apex is now irregular and closer to closure than at the start, I would not promise true pulp-dentin regeneration or major additional root lengthening. The realistic biologic goal is healing of the periapical lesion, continued retention of the tooth, and possible formation of an apical hard-tissue/mineralized barrier, with at most limited further wall thickening.

I would explain that prognosis for retention is reasonable but guarded: success means no symptoms and radiographic healing, not necessarily return of normal pulp function or indefinite cure. Main risks are another recurrence, reduced stem-cell contribution after partial apical maturation, and future cervical/root fracture because this tooth began with thin dentinal walls. Long-term follow-up is essential to monitor symptoms, sinus tract, percussion/palpation findings, restoration integrity, and radiographic or CBCT evidence of periapical healing and apical hard-tissue formation. If disease persists or recurs again, the plan should shift to a non-regenerative apical barrier/definitive root canal strategy, with extraction reserved for an unrestorable tooth or uncontrolled disease.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes no definitive management, only observation, or an inappropriate irreversible approach without addressing the endodontic source of disease; does not account for the immature/restorable tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests retreatment or another endodontic option but gives an incomplete or weakly justified plan; limited attention to preserving a thin-walled immature tooth or to how retreatment should differ from routine root canal management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses conservative endodontic retreatment with a second RET as the preferred next step and explains the main principles: regain canal access, conservative disinfection with minimal instrumentation, re-establish a scaffold, and reseal coronally to control infection while preserving the tooth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a coherent, stepwise second-RET strategy tied to this anatomy and history, explicitly balancing infection control with preservation of residual reparative potential and noting an appropriate fallback to a non-regenerative apical barrier/definitive root canal approach if healing fails again.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads or ignores fig_01.jpg and does not connect the imaging/history to the current problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated facts from the stem or figure but does not integrate the prior healing, current recurrence, and intact restoration into a coherent explanation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the asymptomatic clinical status, intact coronal restoration, earlier healing/root maturation on fig_01.jpg, and later recurrent radiolucency with irregular incomplete apex/empty canal space to identify recurrent post-treatment apical periodontitis and likely persistent intraradicular infection.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the serial imaging and clinical course to explain both the likely source of recurrence and why the current anatomy changes the biologic expectations of retreatment compared with the original RET.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and harms, or recommends a plan that ignores major case-specific risks.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides generic pros and cons but does not meaningfully apply them to this child's tooth, prior RET response, or current apical status.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a second RET offers tooth retention and potential further healing without unnecessary weakening of the root, while acknowledging risks such as persistent infection, reduced regenerative potential after partial apical maturation, and future fracture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a nuanced, patient-specific comparison of benefits, limitations, and next-step thresholds, including why immediate irreversible treatment is not the best first choice here and when escalation would become appropriate.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: States an unsupported hopeless or guaranteed prognosis, or omits follow-up entirely.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a vague prognosis with minimal justification and limited follow-up advice.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that prognosis is reasonable but guarded for tooth retention and periapical healing, with limited expectation for true regeneration or major additional root development, and recommends long-term clinical/radiographic review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a realistic prognosis plus a specific surveillance plan focused on symptoms, sinus tract, percussion/palpation, restoration integrity, and serial imaging signs of healing or hard-tissue barrier formation, while emphasizing that apparent healing does not guarantee definitive success.

items.question_content:
A 6-year-old girl with genetically confirmed keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome is referred for gingival bleeding and oral discomfort. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. She is in early mixed dentition and has carious primary maxillary first molars (54 and 64). Oral mucosal biopsy shows no dysplasia, and fungal and microbiologic tests are negative. Dental treatment will be completed under general anesthesia. After extraction, histologic examination of the removed teeth confirmed enamel mineralization defects, supporting concern that restorative durability may be reduced.

Based on the figures and this clinical information, what is one defensible initial operative philosophy? In your answer, identify the key tooth-preservation mistake to avoid when interpreting fig_02.jpg, explain how the negative mucosal workup should affect management and surveillance, and state the single later radiographic finding that would most change your retention/space-management plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible first-GA philosophy is selective preservation with definitive disease elimination, not blanket conservation and not indiscriminate retention of all primary molars. fig_03.jpg does not make the original extraction choice wrong in hindsight; it mainly shows that intensive prevention, moisture support, and close follow-up can normalize plaque-driven inflammation in KID syndrome.

fig_02.jpg in a 6-year-old with genetically confirmed KID should be managed as likely syndromic agenesis rather than simple delay. The likely absent permanent teeth are 15, 25, 17, 27, 37, and 47. The key planning error to avoid is treating mandibular second primary molars as “no-successor” teeth because 37 and 47 are absent. Second permanent molars have no primary predecessors, so 75 and 85 do not gain special long-term value from second-molar agenesis. The truly strategic teeth are 55 and 65, because they are the predecessors of the likely absent 15 and 25 and may preserve space, function, and alveolar support if sound/restorable. By contrast, 54 and 64 are not strategic because 14 and 24 are present.

Therefore, if 54 and 64 were carious with compromised prognosis, extracting them under the same GA was justified despite KID mucosal fragility. A restore-everything approach overvalues avoidance of surgery and undervalues the biologic cost of retaining plaque-retentive diseased teeth in a child with severe gingival/mucosal inflammation, poor hygiene, and dryness. The better plan is limited but definitive surgery plus aggressive prevention: debridement, sealants on permanent molars, caregiver-assisted plaque control, fluoride, and oral/labial moisture support, followed by close recall. The later confirmation of enamel mineralization defects further supports caution about long-term restorative predictability.

The negative biopsy and negative fungal/microbiologic tests change surveillance more than treatment labeling. They argue against reflexively labeling the condition candidiasis, bacterial infection, or dysplasia at baseline, and against routine empiric antimicrobial management. However, they do not justify discharge or relaxed follow-up because KID syndrome carries increased risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma. Persistent or focal ulceration, induration, leukoplakic or erythroplakic change, verrucous change, asymmetry, enlarging lesions, or non-healing sites should trigger prompt reassessment and low-threshold repeat biopsy or referral.

The single later radiographic finding that would most alter retention and space-management logic would be late development of 15 and 25. If those maxillary second premolars appeared later, 55 and 65 would cease to be long-term surrogate teeth and would be retained only temporarily to guide eruption and space. Persistent absence of 17, 27, 37, and 47 still would not create primary predecessor teeth to preserve, so long-term management there remains orthodontic/prosthetic, with strong protection of the first permanent molars.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads fig_02.jpg, treats the missing pattern as simple delay without using age and syndrome context, or confuses which absent permanent teeth do and do not have primary predecessors.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes probable agenesis or identifies some correct tooth-preservation logic, but incompletely maps the missing teeth or does not clearly distinguish absent maxillary second premolars from absent second permanent molars.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly integrates the age, KID syndrome, and panoramic pattern to identify likely absence of 15, 25, 17, 27, 37, and 47; explains that 55/65 are strategic because 15/25 are likely absent; and explicitly states that absent second permanent molars have no primary predecessors, so 75/85 are not special no-successor teeth.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Avoids a definitive first-GA philosophy, or recommends blanket restore-all or extract-all management without tooth-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses a generally appropriate approach but does not clearly justify which teeth should be preserved versus removed, or does not address the retrospective challenge posed by fig_03.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Defends a clear first-GA plan of selective disease elimination with preservation of truly strategic teeth, supports extraction of compromised 54/64 while prioritizing retention of sound/restorable 55/65, rejects the false strategic status of mandibular second primary molars, and explains why later clinical improvement does not retroactively invalidate the original tooth-specific decisions.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the trade-offs between avoiding surgery, eliminating disease, restoration longevity, and preserving future posterior support.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions some pros and cons but incompletely weighs KID mucosal fragility, poor hygiene, single-GA opportunity, enamel mineralization defects, and the strategic value of specific primary teeth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly weighs the competing restore-everything argument against selective extraction, addressing mucosal fragility, inflammatory burden, plaque retention, restorative durability in enamel mineralization defects, the advantage of definitive care in one GA, and the difference between strategic and non-strategic primary molars.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Treats the negative biopsy and microbiology as grounds to stop surveillance, or recommends routine empiric antimicrobial treatment despite the negative workup.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges that negative tests affect management, but does not clearly connect them to ongoing KID-specific surveillance or gives vague triggers for reassessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains that negative biopsy and microbiology shift the case away from infectious or dysplastic labeling at baseline while maintaining low-threshold surveillance because of KID-associated oral cancer risk, and specifies concrete triggers for reassessment or repeat biopsy/referral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no adaptive plan if later radiographs change the developmental interpretation, or changes management based on incorrect tooth mapping.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that later tooth development would alter the plan, but does not clearly identify which finding matters most or how retention logic would change.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies late development of 15/25 as the single most important later radiographic finding, explains that 55/65 would then shift from potential long-term surrogate teeth to temporary teeth managed around eruption, and notes that persistent absence of second permanent molars still requires later orthodontic/prosthetic planning rather than predecessor-tooth retention.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: Recommends extraction of sound/restorable 55/65 despite likely absence of 15/25, sacrificing the only truly strategic primary predecessors without justification.

Misidentified Strategic Teeth: Treats 54/64 or 75/85 as the key no-successor teeth because fig_02.jpg shows absent second permanent molars, demonstrating incorrect interpretation of primary-successor relationships.

Generic Textbook Management: Recommends routine empiric antifungal/antibiotic treatment or relaxed long-interval follow-up despite negative tests and the ongoing KID-associated need for close mucosal surveillance.
Incomplete Diagnostic Workup: Dismisses the bilateral age-inappropriate absence on fig_02.jpg as simple delayed development and makes no plan for serial radiographic confirmation of likely agenesis.

items.question_content: A 38-year-old healthy woman presents with pain on chewing, apical swelling, negative vitality tests, and a mandibular right first molar with an extensive restoration and incomplete prior root canal filling. During orthograde retreatment, the mesial canals were negotiated to working length, then shaped, cleaned, and medicated, but the distal canal could not be reached because of severe apical calcification, and a small hand file fractured during negotiation. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What would be the most appropriate next step in management, and why? Justify your decision from the clinical findings and the information visible in the figures, including the factors that most affect safety and prognosis.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most appropriate next step is to obtain CBCT-based treatment planning and proceed with guided nonsurgical retreatment to conservatively re-establish access to the calcified distal canal system. The clinical findings of swelling, pain on chewing, tenderness to percussion/palpation, negative vitality testing, and the periradicular radiolucency support persistent apical disease associated with an incompletely treated tooth. Because the mesial canals have already been negotiated, cleaned, and medicated, the remaining priority is safe access to the obstructed distal canal anatomy so the full root canal system can be disinfected and obturated.

fig_01.jpg shows incomplete prior obturation, severe distal canal obliteration, and periapical disease. The CBCT information is important because it demonstrates distal root anatomy not fully defined on periapical radiography alone, including two distal canals, and helps localize the obliterated segment. After file separation, further blind troughing would carry substantial risk of perforation, deviation, transportation, and unnecessary dentin removal. fig_02.jpg shows how CBCT and surface scan data can be merged to plan a precise drill path and fabricate a guide, improving the likelihood of reaching working length in the distal canals while limiting structural damage.

Once guided access is achieved, the distal canals should be negotiated, the obstructing fragment managed if removable or bypassable, and chemomechanical preparation completed, followed by intracanal medication as needed, obturation of all canals, and definitive coronal restoration. Prognosis is favorable if distal patency is regained and the canal system is fully disinfected and sealed. Key determinants of safety and prognosis are preservation of root structure, avoidance of perforation, recognition and treatment of both distal canals, management of the separated instrument, and confirmation of healing on follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores key clinical or imaging findings, or misinterprets the figures. Does not connect symptoms and swelling with persistent endodontic disease related to incomplete prior treatment and calcified canal anatomy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but incompletely. May note incomplete prior treatment or calcification, yet misses the significance of the periradicular lesion, separated file, or distal root anatomy visible in fig_01.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the symptoms, failed distal negotiation with file fracture, incomplete prior obturation, and fig_01.jpg evidence of distal obliteration/periradicular disease to justify further management.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all major findings and explicitly uses the figures to recognize the clinical implication of complex distal anatomy, including the value of fig_02.jpg planning data in improving feasibility and precision of nonsurgical treatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent definitive plan, recommends only symptomatic care/observation, or proposes a plan unrelated to the endodontic source of disease.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests retreatment or another intervention but without a clear rationale, sequencing, or explanation of how the distal root problem should be addressed safely.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends CBCT-based planning with guided nonsurgical retreatment to regain distal canal access/patency, complete disinfection and obturation of the full canal system, and restore the tooth with a sound coronal seal, reserving more invasive options for failure or poor restorability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a clear, stepwise, evidence-based plan: CBCT evaluation and guide planning for the calcified distal root, management of the obstructing fragment by bypass/removal if feasible, completion of orthograde chemomechanical treatment of all canals, and integration of definitive restorative follow-up into the plan.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores the tooth-preservation value of a conservative option in this restorable, systemically healthy patient.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions advantages of one option but gives little comparison with other reasonable pathways or does not relate the choice to the imaging findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a conservative orthograde approach supported by CBCT-based planning offers the best initial balance of source control and tooth preservation compared with more invasive options, given the treatable anatomy and absence of systemic limitations.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly relates the improved risk-benefit to CBCT-derived trajectory planning and remaining root structure, while acknowledging when escalation to surgical treatment or extraction would become reasonable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Identifies no relevant complications or presents an unsafe, overly optimistic plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Notes only generic failure risk without case-specific hazards.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies major case-specific risks such as perforation/transportation, excessive dentin removal or root weakening, missing distal anatomy, inability to manage the separated file, and persistent disease if apical patency/disinfection is not achieved.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds practical prevention or monitoring points, such as guide verification, confirming trajectory/working length, securing definitive coronal restoration, and long-term radiographic follow-up to assess healing.

items.question_content: Based on fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, what healing outcome is most strongly supported for the replanted immature maxillary central incisor?

Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, a maxillary central incisor is fractured and discolored, is nonresponsive to electric pulp testing, and shows an incompletely formed root with a periapical radiolucency. If definitive coronal restoration is needed without prolonged interim treatment, what endodontic procedure is most appropriate?
In fig_01.jpg, the apical third of the root has irregular external contours rather than a smooth tapering apex. What specific resorptive diagnosis does this finding indicate?

Inspect the follow-up radiographs in fig_01.jpg. Tooth #21 remained asymptomatic and responsive to cold and electric pulp testing, but the 1-year image showed localized reduction in pulp-space visibility rather than periapical disease or root resorption. Name this specific post-luxation sequela.
For the 55° canal curvature shown in fig_01.jpg C, what pre-bent instrument type was used to establish the glide path before rotary NiTi preparation?

A patient presents with a maxillary anterior tooth initially thought to have an isolated endodontic lesion. Review fig_01.jpg. What radiographic finding demonstrated communication between the root canal and the mesial periodontium, leading to a revised diagnosis of a combined endodontic-periodontal lesion?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The master-cone radiograph showed calcium hydroxide beyond the canal in the mesial periodontal tissues. That demonstrated canal-periodontal communication, changing the case from an apparently isolated endodontic lesion to a combined endodontic-periodontal lesion and supporting intentional replantation.
objective_exact_answers: calcium hydroxide spillage into the mesial periodontal tissue

items.answer_explanation: The master-cone radiograph showed calcium hydroxide beyond the canal in the mesial periodontal tissues. That demonstrated canal-periodontal communication, changing the case from an apparently isolated endodontic lesion to a combined endodontic-periodontal lesion and supporting intentional replantation.

items.question_content: A 30-year-old woman is undergoing endodontic retreatment of a maxillary right first premolar with a separated instrument in the palatal canal. In fig_01.jpg(c) and fig_01.jpg(d), identify the modified instrument used to create a staging platform for straight-line access before ultrasonic troughing.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The platform was created by modifying a No. 2 Gates-Glidden drill. In this case, its tip was cut to make a flat internal platform that improved straight-line access and allowed controlled ultrasonic dentin removal around the coronal part of the fragment.

items.answer_explanation: The platform was created by modifying a No. 2 Gates-Glidden drill. In this case, its tip was cut to make a flat internal platform that improved straight-line access and allowed controlled ultrasonic dentin removal around the coronal part of the fragment.

items.question_content: Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, which statements best justify the specific sequence used: short-term calcium hydroxide dressing, Biodentine apical plug, then obturation in the same treatment phase? Select all that apply.

question_options.text: The interim calcium hydroxide dressing was used mainly to reduce the intracanal bacterial load in a necrotic canal before definitive apical sealing.
The high pH of calcium hydroxide was cited as creating favorable conditions for Biodentine curing.
The Biodentine plug was chosen primarily to preserve pulp vitality and stimulate continued root wall thickening in this tooth.
Biodentine’s handling and faster setting made delayed second-stage obturation unnecessary in this case.

items.question_content: A 27-year-old woman with insulin-treated type 1 diabetes has 1 month of left-sided foreign body sensation and intermittent foul-smelling unilateral nasal discharge. Intraoral exam shows a normal maxillary dentition with no missing or supernumerary teeth. Examining fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, there is a tooth-density structure arising from the floor of the left nasal cavity; the crown projects into the nasal lumen lateral to the septum, the root is minimally anchored to the posterosuperior hard palate, the lesion is closely related to the inferior turbinate, and there is no septal penetration, turbinate erosion, cortical disruption, sinonasal mass, or surrounding inflammatory change. What is the most appropriate management plan, including the most likely diagnosis, the preferred surgical route, why the main alternative approach is less suitable in this anatomy, and the key perioperative risks/precautions?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This is a symptomatic ectopic intranasal supernumerary tooth. Management should be definitive surgical removal rather than observation because the patient is symptomatic and the tooth is acting as a persistent intranasal irritant with infection risk. Based on the CT anatomy, the preferred approach is a transoral sublabial/vestibular approach under general anesthesia. The rationale is that the tooth is inferiorly positioned, projects into the nasal cavity, and has its implantation/minimal osseous anchorage at the posterosuperior hard palate/nasal floor, so a transoral corridor gives better control for exposure, luxation, and en bloc removal while protecting the nasal mucosa. Although endoscopic transnasal extraction is often minimally invasive, it is less suitable here because the working space is limited and the tooth is close to the inferior turbinate and nasal mucosa; traction from above risks mucosal injury, fragmentation, and incomplete removal. Preoperatively, confirm and optimize glycemic control because type 1 diabetes increases infection and delayed-healing risk. Intraoperatively, elevate a careful subperiosteal flap, dissect parallel to the mucosal plane, shield the nasal mucosa, remove the tooth gently en bloc, inspect for any perforation, irrigate, and close without tension. Main complications to anticipate and prevent are nasal mucosal perforation, bleeding, tooth fragmentation with retained pieces, postoperative infection/delayed healing, persistent nasal symptoms, and oronasal fistula.

A 5-year-old boy presents with a 2-year history of clear fluid leaking from his left neck whenever he drinks liquids. At age 1, a painless left lateral neck swelling without an external opening was noted, which periodically enlarged during upper respiratory tract infections. He underwent multiple incision and drainage (I&D) procedures and one attempted surgical excision, after which the leakage began. Examination reveals a cutaneous opening at the lower third of the left anterior sternocleidomastoid border, as shown in the clinical photograph (fig_01.jpg), with clear fluid extruding during swallowing. No tenderness, additional masses, or respiratory distress is present. The family has significant financial constraints limiting access to advanced imaging. Based on the clinical photograph and history, discuss: the most likely diagnosis including the specific branchial cleft of origin, explain the pathomechanism by which repeated I&D transformed the original anomaly, and outline the optimal stepwise management plan — including how you would confirm the internal opening and what acute infection management you would recommend to preserve anatomy for definitive surgery.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is a third branchial cleft fistula. The clinical photograph demonstrates an external cutaneous opening at the lower third of the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle with fluid extravasation during swallowing, which is pathognomonic for a branchial cleft fistula communicating with the pharynx. The left-sided predominance and the location of the external opening along the lower anterior SCM border, combined with the age of presentation, are characteristic of third branchial cleft anomalies.

The original anomaly was most likely a branchial cleft sinus (internal sinus communicating with the pyriform sinus) or cyst, as no external opening was present initially. Repeated I&D procedures caused chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and disruption of tissue planes. Each I&D episode promoted epithelialization of the drainage tract, creating an acquired external opening. This iatrogenic process transformed a sinus into a complete fistula — a tract now communicating between the pyriform sinus internally and the skin externally. Studies have shown that none of the third/fourth branchial cleft fistulae in large series were true congenital fistulae; rather, they were acquired secondary to recurrent infections or multiple I&D procedures.

Optimal stepwise management:
1. Acute infection control: When infection is present, treat with appropriate antibiotics. Crucially, if drainage is needed, needle aspiration should be used instead of I&D to preserve tissue planes and minimize further scarring.
2. Allow inflammation to subside completely before planning definitive surgery.
3. Confirmation of internal opening: Under general anesthesia, perform endoscopic evaluation of the pharynx using methylene blue dye instilled through the external opening to identify the internal opening, which for a third BCA is expected at or near the pyriform sinus. This avoids the cost of CT imaging and is diagnostically reliable.
4. Definitive surgical excision: Via an external transverse cervical incision at the mid-jugular level, the entire fistula tract is excised. The tract courses medial to the SCM and lateral to the common carotid artery. Intraoperative endoscopic assistance helps ensure complete excision of the internal opening. Fibrosis from prior I&D complicates dissection and increases risk of recurrence and injury to adjacent structures (carotid artery, vagus nerve, recurrent laryngeal nerve).
5. Postoperative care: Place a drain (remove at 24 hours), monitor for wound dehiscence, and follow up at 1 month, 6 months, and annually for at least 4 years given the 3.4-fold increased recurrence risk associated with prior I&D.
6. Address psychosocial morbidity: Acknowledge the child's distress from visible discharge and peer ridicule; consider supportive counseling.

A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents for a 7-month history of painless, progressive right-sided mandibular swelling. There is no paresthesia, no mucosal inflammation, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, buccal cortical expansion extends from the right first molar to the retromolar region. An incisional biopsy performed previously was reported as fibrous dysplasia. Panoramic radiography shows an amorphous radiolucent lesion in the right mandible associated with multiple unerupted permanent tooth germs. CT demonstrates a well-defined expansile mass measuring 37.3 × 45.7 mm with cystic components but no cortical destruction. A skeletal survey is unremarkable. Differential diagnoses include ameloblastoma and odontogenic myxoma.

Based on the clinical photograph and imaging provided, formulate the definitive surgical management plan for this child. Justify why your chosen approach is preferred over alternative options, and explain how the patient's age, the location of the lesion, and the presence of unerupted permanent teeth influence your decision.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The appropriate management is conservative bone contouring/recontouring (osteoplasty/shaving) of the right mandible using fissure and carbide burs through an intraoral approach, with preservation of the inferior alveolar nerve and the unerupted permanent tooth germs, followed by long-term clinical and radiographic follow-up. Radical en bloc segmental resection is not indicated. Rationale: (1) Fibrous dysplasia is a benign, self-limiting developmental lesion driven by a postzygotic GNAS mutation; complete excision is neither curative nor necessary, and recurrence after conservative debulking in young patients is acceptable given the morbidity of resection. (2) The patient is 4 years old and in active craniofacial growth — segmental mandibulectomy would cause severe functional and aesthetic deformity, disturb mandibular growth centers, and sacrifice multiple unerupted permanent tooth germs visible on the OPG. (3) Reconstruction with vascularized free flaps or reconstruction plates in a 4-year-old carries high morbidity, growth disturbance, and hardware failure risk. (4) Because lesional activity typically slows after skeletal maturity, the goal at this age is to restore facial symmetry and function while deferring any more aggressive intervention until growth is complete, and only if symptoms (pain, rapid growth, rising alkaline phosphatase, functional compromise) recur. (5) Pre-operatively, the differential (ameloblastoma, odontogenic myxoma) has already been excluded by histopathology, so re-biopsy is not required, but ongoing surveillance for the rare (<1%) malignant transformation is warranted. Bisphosphonates are not first-line and have no established role in asymptomatic pediatric craniofacial FD.

items.question_content: A 60-year-old man is brought after assault. He was unconscious at the scene, has already been orotracheally intubated, and is currently haemodynamically stable. Before anyone manipulates the retained objects, you are asked to brief the trauma team using fig_01.jpg. Explain the injury pattern you infer, which problem should drive the first operative episode, and the safest overall extraction strategy. Include which specialty support is required for removal and the key intraoperative priorities. Finally, if over the next 72 hours sedation is reduced, the subarachnoid blood is decreasing on serial CT, but the patient still fails to awaken and the ventricles progressively enlarge, explain your leading diagnosis, the key alternatives you would still consider, and the form of CSF diversion you would discuss with neurosurgery.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
fig_01.jpg implies two separate penetrating tracts. The harpoon is the dominant injury: it enters through the oral cavity/oropharynx, crosses the skull base just above the atlas in the right paramedian/clival region, traverses the posterior fossa through the right cerebellar hemisphere, breaches the occipital bone, and ends in the occipital scalp soft tissues. The knife is a distinct transmidfacial injury running from the right cheek through the right maxillary sinus and hard palate, across the left maxillary sinus, toward the left zygomatic side. The harpoon therefore controls management because it is an intracranial skull-base/posterior-fossa injury with haemorrhagic and infectious risk; the facial knife is important but secondary until intracranial control is achieved.

Both objects should remain in situ until controlled operative removal. This should be a combined neurosurgical and OMFS case, with ICU-level support and no blind traction. The first operative episode should be driven by the posterior-fossa/skull-base harpoon injury rather than the facial knife.

The safest extraction strategy for the harpoon is controlled exposure of the distal intracranial/occipital end, not transoral withdrawal. The shaft can be shortened intraorally to improve access, then a posterior cranial exposure with a craniotomy fashioned around the occipital exit so the distal end and surrounding dura can be visualized. Removal should be anterograde, along the original tract, under direct vision. After removal: copious irrigation and debridement, inspection of the posterior-fossa/skull-base tract, watertight dural closure to reduce CSF leak and meningitis risk, and avoidance of replacing contaminated bone because of contamination from the aerodigestive tract and paranasal sinuses. Only after intracranial control should the knife be exposed and withdrawn under direct vision along its tract, followed by repair of palatal, sinus, facial soft-tissue, and bony injuries as indicated.

At 72 hours, failure to awaken despite decreasing subarachnoid blood but progressive ventriculomegaly most strongly suggests post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Alternatives still to consider include residual sedative effect, primary posterior-fossa/cerebellar injury or oedema, delayed rebleeding, and less likely metabolic causes, but the imaging trend makes hydrocephalus the leading treatable explanation. I would discuss neurosurgical CSF diversion. An external ventricular drain is a reasonable acute temporizing option if immediate CSF diversion or ICP control is needed; if ventriculomegaly and impaired consciousness persist, ventriculo-peritoneal shunting becomes appropriate.

items.question_content: A 56-year-old man with painful unresectable locally recurrent right maxillary sinus squamous cell carcinoma previously received cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy. The recurrence tracked to the cranial base through the maxillary nerve/foramen rotundum and was judged unresectable. Pembrolizumab led to progressive disease, followed by progression on cetuximab/paclitaxel/carboplatin. PD-L1 CPS is 80. Four sessions of NIR-PIT reduced tumor bulk but caused a maxillary sinus-cutaneous fistula. Two months later his performance status remains acceptable, albumin is 3.1 g/dL, and current disease extent is shown in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. At this point, what is your immediate management priority: further local salvage, systemic salvage, or symptom-directed palliation? State the specific treatment you would start first and justify it using the figures and treatment history. Also identify at least two plausible alternatives you are not choosing and one concrete change in the patient’s condition that would make you revise your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My immediate priority would be systemic salvage, not another local-only intervention and not palliative-only care at this moment. I would start anti-PD-1 rechallenge, preferably with an anti-PD-1 agent such as nivolumab, within multidisciplinary head-and-neck oncology follow-up.

Why this is most defensible:
1) The figures argue that repeated local treatment has not achieved durable control. fig_02.jpg shows residual disease after four NIR-PIT sessions at the treatment margins, including periocular/nasal and lateral maxillary regions, and fig_03.jpg shows rapid visible regrowth within 2 months. That pattern suggests marginal escape after local therapy rather than stable local control.
2) The prior history narrows alternatives. He already progressed on pembrolizumab and then on cetuximab/paclitaxel/carboplatin, so repeating the same cytotoxic strategy has low expected value. The tumor was previously judged unresectable because of cranial-base extension, and fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg/fig_03.jpg together suggest anatomically difficult periocular/maxillofacial disease in a previously irradiated field.
3) Another local escalation is unattractive. Further NIR-PIT would be questionable after four sessions with residual marginal disease and an existing maxillary sinus-cutaneous fistula. Re-irradiation after prior definitive chemoradiotherapy would carry substantial morbidity. Extirpative salvage surgery would likely be high morbidity and still of doubtful feasibility given unresectability and disease distribution.
4) Palliative-only care is not yet the best first choice because the performance status is preserved and there is still a reasonable active salvage option.

Why anti-PD-1 rechallenge is reasonable despite prior pembrolizumab failure: NIR-PIT can produce immunogenic cell death, antigen release, and host immune activation that may re-prime response to checkpoint blockade. The very high PD-L1 CPS supports biologic plausibility, although the evidence base is limited and the low albumin adds some uncertainty rather than ruling it out.

Alternatives I am not choosing: (a) further NIR-PIT/local-only salvage, because prior local control was incomplete and complicated by fistula; (b) re-irradiation, because of prior definitive RT and morbidity risk; (c) repeat cytotoxic chemotherapy, because the recent regimen already failed; (d) immediate palliation alone, because the patient remains fit enough for another active attempt.

Monitoring and revision trigger: I would reassess early with short-interval clinical and imaging review, while monitoring for immune-related adverse events, wound/fistula deterioration, infection, bleeding, pain, and orbital/skull-base symptoms. I would revise the plan if there were no early objective response or if he developed substantial performance-status decline, uncontrolled wound infection/bleeding, or vision-threatening/orbital progression; at that point I would shift toward symptom-directed palliation or another noncurative supportive strategy.

items.question_content:
A 61-year-old woman with a history of resected cutaneous microcystic adnexal carcinoma of the eyelid and forehead presents with asymptomatic bilateral floor-of-mouth nodules. Orthopantomogram and routine laboratory results are unremarkable. MRI shows a 10-mm left sublingual lesion and a 7-mm right sublingual lesion. On prior MRI obtained 7 years earlier, both lesions were already present without appreciable interval enlargement. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg.

The patient will agree to only one initial operation because she wants to minimize the risk of bilateral tongue sensory and speech dysfunction. Write the recommendation you would send the surgeon: state your leading diagnosis and most likely tissue of origin; choose which side to operate on first and whether that first procedure should be diagnostic sampling or margin-oriented excision; and decide whether the opposite side should be treated in the same sitting, delayed pending final pathology, or initially observed.

Your justification must explicitly compare fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg and explain what fig_04.jpg supports diagnostically and what it does not establish by itself. End by naming the single alternative diagnosis or disease process that, if true, would most alter surgical planning, and explain how your recommendation changes if the long-term stability history were unavailable and the chosen side had new ipsilateral tongue numbness.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis is bilateral primary sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma (SMA) of salivary origin, most likely arising in the bilateral sublingual/floor-of-mouth salivary tissue rather than representing metastatic cutaneous MAC.

Why this is favored:
- fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show paired lesions centered in the sublingual/floor-of-mouth salivary territory rather than a skin-bearing adnexal site or nodal pattern.
- Both lesions share the same malignant fibrous/cellular MRI pattern: low or relatively low T2 signal, restricted diffusion/low ADC, and uniform enhancement with rapid early enhancement followed by persistence/plateau.
- The left lesion is relatively more ill-defined/heterogeneous and shows a persistent delayed rise rather than a cleaner plateau, making it the more concerning side for infiltrative interface and difficult clearance.
- fig_04.jpg shows infiltrative cords/strands with tiny ducts and microcysts in dense sclerotic stroma, which is classic for SMA/MAC-spectrum morphology. CK7, CEA, and EMA support ductal differentiation, but these immunostains are not specific enough by themselves to prove SMA over all salivary mimics; morphology plus site are what make SMA the preferred diagnosis.

If the patient will accept only one initial operation, I would prioritize the left side first. Because the lesion is small, accessible, and already highly suspicious for an infiltrative salivary malignancy, my preferred first procedure would be margin-oriented excision of the left sublingual/floor-of-mouth lesion rather than limited sampling alone. A small biopsy could establish malignancy, but it may underrepresent infiltrative extent and does not solve the local-control problem. If preoperative uncertainty remained unusually high or major functional sacrifice seemed likely, a staged diagnostic biopsy could still be defended, but simple observation or shelling out the mass would not be appropriate.

I would not treat the opposite side in the same sitting under this patient-specific constraint. Staging the contralateral side after final pathology and margin review better protects bilateral tongue sensation, ductal function, and floor-of-mouth mobility. Structures that must be anticipated because of the lesion location and infiltrative/perineural behavior include the lingual nerve, Wharton duct/sublingual gland complex, mylohyoid, and adjacent floor-of-mouth/tongue musculature.

The single alternative process that would most alter surgical planning is metastatic/recurrent cutaneous MAC. If that were true, the emphasis would shift toward confirming metastatic disease and broader staging rather than assuming paired primary salivary tumors. The strongest argument against it is the bilateral mirror-image sublingual-centered distribution in a nonadnexal mucosal site together with the very long stability history; bilateral sublingual metastases would be extraordinarily unusual.

If the stability history were unavailable and the chosen side had new ipsilateral tongue numbness, I would still favor an SMA-spectrum salivary malignancy based on site and histomorphology, but concern for active perineural spread would rise substantially. That would lower my threshold for definitive treatment of the symptomatic side, more aggressive assessment of local extent, and postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy if margins were close/positive or perineural invasion proved significant. It would also make same-day contralateral surgery even less attractive, because preserving the opposite side becomes more important.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misclassifies the lesions as benign/inflammatory, gives an implausible diagnosis, or treats the lesions as metastatic cutaneous MAC without reconciling the salivary-site evidence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a malignant SMA/MAC-spectrum or other low-grade salivary carcinoma process but is nonspecific about the preferred diagnosis and/or tissue of origin.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies primary sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma (or SMA-spectrum adenocarcinoma strongly consistent with SMA) arising in bilateral sublingual/floor-of-mouth salivary tissue and explains why this is favored over metastatic cutaneous MAC.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures appropriately or substantially misstates the imaging/pathology findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some of the clinical, imaging, or histologic evidence correctly but does not synthesize them into a coherent argument, or omits meaningful comparison between fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, or overstates what the immunostains prove.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the clinical, imaging, and histologic data: compares fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg as paired sublingual-centered lesions with low/relatively low T2 signal, restricted diffusion/low ADC, uniform enhancement, and rapid early enhancement with persistence/plateau; identifies the left side as relatively more ill-defined/heterogeneous or potentially more infiltrative; and interprets fig_04.jpg as infiltrative cords/strands with tiny ducts/microcysts in dense sclerotic stroma while correctly stating that CK7/CEA/EMA are supportive but not specific.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation alone, simple enucleation, or another plan that ignores the likely infiltrative malignant nature of the lesions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Chooses an initial side or procedure but gives limited case-specific rationale, or does not clearly address whether the opposite side should be treated the same day, delayed, or observed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Selects and justifies an initial side to treat (typically the more concerning left-sided lesion based on the figures), chooses an oncologically coherent first-step procedure such as margin-oriented excision or a clearly justified diagnostic biopsy strategy, and gives a reasoned plan for the contralateral side consistent with the patient’s constraint.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address the tradeoff between local control and bilateral functional morbidity.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either oncologic control or functional morbidity but does not balance them in a case-specific way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances local control against bilateral tongue/floor-of-mouth functional risk, explains why same-day bilateral surgery may be undesirable under the patient’s preference, and identifies structures or functions at risk such as the lingual nerve, Wharton duct/sublingual gland complex, mylohyoid, and adjacent floor-of-mouth/tongue musculature.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible alternative diagnosis or disease process that would alter planning.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a plausible alternative but with limited explanation of why it is less likely or why it would change management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a clinically plausible alternative that would materially alter surgical planning—most strongly metastatic/recurrent cutaneous MAC—and gives a specific case-based argument against it using site, imaging pattern, and/or long-term course.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully change the interpretation or management threshold in the counterfactual scenario.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes increased concern with loss of stability history and new tongue numbness but does not clearly state how that changes confidence or management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that removal of the reassuring stability history plus new ipsilateral tongue numbness raises concern for active perineural spread and a less indolent course, lowering the threshold for more aggressive extent-of-disease assessment, definitive treatment of the symptomatic side, and postoperative adjuvant therapy while still grounding the diagnosis in site and morphology.

items.question_content: A 45-year-old man developed a rapidly enlarging painful right maxillary mass after molar extraction, with cheek swelling, epistaxis, nasal symptoms, and facial numbness. The provided clinical photos, CT images, and histology are shown in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what management strategy would you choose to achieve definitive control while minimizing recurrence and morbidity?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is a peripheral giant cell granuloma arising at a post-extraction site, with aggressive extension into the maxillary sinus and infratemporal fossa. Management should be complete surgical excision with removal of the lesion to healthy underlying bone, using an approach that provides full access to the sinonasal and lateral extension; in this case, an endoscopic transnasal maxillary sinus approach is appropriate, with reconstruction/closure of the residual bony defect as needed. The specimen should be sent for histopathologic confirmation, and the local traumatic trigger should be addressed. Close follow-up is needed because superficial or incomplete removal carries a significant recurrence risk, especially with this degree of bone erosion and extension.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses only one clue, misreads the lesion, or gives an incoherent interpretation of the clinical, imaging, and histologic data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a giant-cell/maxillary lesion but omits major elements such as the post-extraction setting, destructive extension, or histologic support.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Synthesizes the history, exam, imaging, and histology into a coherent working diagnosis and management direction.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates all modalities smoothly and explains how the combined findings justify definitive surgery rather than a limited or purely symptomatic approach.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not consider relevant mimics or assigns an unrelated diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names one or two alternatives but does not explain why they are less likely in this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately distinguishes peripheral giant cell granuloma from key mimics such as central giant cell lesion, brown tumor, pyogenic granuloma, or metastatic disease using the available findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically rules out the important differentials and shows why histology and lesion location strongly favor a peripheral reactive giant-cell lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation, incomplete treatment, or a plan that would leave gross disease behind.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests surgery but does not specify complete removal, adequate access, or defect management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends complete excision to healthy bone with appropriate access to the maxillary sinus/infratemporal extension, histologic confirmation, and closure or reconstruction when needed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a stepwise, anatomy-aware operative plan that prioritizes full clearance, hemostasis, defect repair, and structured follow-up to reduce recurrence and morbidity.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses the need for follow-up or ignores the risk of recurrence and adjacent-structure involvement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions recurrence in general terms but does not connect it to incomplete excision or the lesion’s extent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies recurrence risk from superficial/incomplete excision and notes the need to monitor for bleeding, sinus, orbital, or neurologic issues.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates practical postoperative surveillance needs and case-specific complications related to bone erosion, sinonasal extension, and facial nerve/sensory symptoms.

items.question_content:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging right submandibular swelling. A “mixed tumor” was excised from the same region 10 years earlier, and regrowth was first noticed 5 years ago. Examination shows a healed scar, a firm mobile 3.0 x 2.0 cm mass, and several small ipsilateral level II/III nodes. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

Provide a ranked differential diagnosis for this postoperative submandibular-bed lesion, but commit to the single most likely diagnosis. Identify the one imaging feature that most supports your leading diagnosis and the one feature that most prevents you from managing this as a straightforward benign recurrence. Then choose your preoperative decision pathway: what tissue would you sample first, and why is that target more informative than the strongest competing target? If that result supports your leading diagnosis, define the extent of first surgery, whether the neck should be included at that stage, and the operative principle most important for reducing future recurrence. Finally, state one concrete finding that would make you escalate beyond surgery alone and explain how management would change.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis is multifocal recurrent pleomorphic adenoma in the postoperative right submandibular gland bed. The strongest single imaging feature supporting this is the clustered multinodular pattern in a prior operative bed after excision of a “mixed tumor,” which is much more typical of recurrent pleomorphic adenoma than of a de novo solitary salivary malignancy or primary nodal disease. The single feature that most prevents this from being treated as a routine benign recurrence is the partly indistinct interface of some nodules with the gland bed/adjacent tissue, especially when considered together with heterogeneous enhancement, central non-enhancing areas, fascial thickening, and enhancing cervical nodes; these do not prove malignancy, but they raise concern for atypia, malignant transformation, or another aggressive process.

A ranked differential would be: (1) recurrent pleomorphic adenoma, (2) carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma or another malignant salivary neoplasm such as adenoid cystic or lymphoepithelial carcinoma, and (3) primary nodal disease such as lymphoma or tuberculous lymphadenitis. The malignant salivary alternatives remain plausible because of the partially ill-defined margins and suspicious nodal/fascial findings, but they are less favored because the lesion is multinodular and centered in the postoperative submandibular bed. Lymphoma or tuberculosis are lower because the dominant abnormality appears bed-centered rather than purely nodal, and the overall pattern fits recurrent salivary neoplasia better.

The preferred preoperative pathway is to treat this as a recurrent salivary gland neoplasm while selectively excluding malignancy. The first tissue target should usually be the dominant submandibular-bed lesion by image-guided FNAC or core biopsy, because the main unresolved question is the biology of the recurrent bed mass itself and that result most directly determines the required extent of gland-bed surgery. Sampling a cervical node first is a reasonable competing option only if a node is morphologically more suspicious than the primary bed lesion, but in this case the nodes are indeterminate rather than definitively metastatic.

If sampling supports recurrent pleomorphic adenoma, the first operation should be revision excision of the involved submandibular bed/residual gland with removal of all detectable nodules in one operative field. The neck should not be routinely added as an elective neck dissection on the basis of these small enhancing nodes alone; nodal surgery should be selective and driven by proven metastatic disease, convincing direct nodal involvement, lymphoma, or another specific diagnosis. The operative principle most important for reducing another recurrence is meticulous en bloc removal without enucleation, capsular rupture, or tumor spillage, because recurrent pleomorphic adenoma is often multinodular and can reseed.

Management should escalate beyond surgery alone if there is a concrete sign of more aggressive biology, such as biopsy or final pathology showing carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma/malignant transformation, a cytology-positive cervical node, unresectable residual multifocal disease, or margins that cannot be safely cleared. In that setting, treatment would broaden to appropriately more aggressive resection and therapeutic neck management when indicated, with postoperative radiotherapy considered for malignant transformation, residual disease, or repeated multifocal recurrence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misses recurrent salivary neoplasia as the main problem or interprets the lesion primarily as a simple inflammatory/reactive process.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a recurrent submandibular tumor but does not specifically identify recurrent pleomorphic adenoma as the leading diagnosis, or treats the cervical nodes as definitively metastatic without adequate support.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies recurrent pleomorphic adenoma in the postoperative right submandibular bed as the leading diagnosis and acknowledges that malignant transformation or another aggressive salivary neoplasm still requires exclusion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely identifies multifocal recurrent pleomorphic adenoma as the leading diagnosis, correctly frames the cervical nodes as indeterminate rather than proven metastatic disease, and anchors the interpretation to the prior same-site mixed tumor history.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg coherently or misreads the imaging in a way that undermines the conclusion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses the history and a few generic imaging observations but omits important figure-based findings or does not distinguish reassuring from concerning features.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates multiple case-specific findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, including the postoperative bed location, multinodular/clustered appearance, enhancement pattern, and at least one concerning feature such as central non-enhancing areas, partly indistinct margins, fascial thickening, or enhancing nodes.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Directly identifies the single most supportive and the single most concerning imaging feature, and explains how specific findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg shift confidence toward recurrent pleomorphic adenoma while preserving concern for more aggressive biology.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no plausible serious alternatives or lists alternatives that are not clinically credible in this setting.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists alternatives but does not rank them or connect them to the postoperative bed pattern and imaging findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Ranks at least two serious alternatives and gives case-based reasons they remain possible yet less likely than recurrent pleomorphic adenoma.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a prioritized differential that includes both a malignant salivary neoplasm and a primary nodal process, and clearly explains why each is less favored based on lesion-centered postoperative bed disease and the specific imaging behavior.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate sequence, such as immediate empiric treatment or definitive neck management without adequate tissue diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests tissue diagnosis or surgery but does not justify which target should be sampled first or why that choice best answers the central clinical question.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses a rational first tissue target, usually the dominant submandibular-bed lesion with selective node sampling when warranted, and explains why it is more informative than proceeding directly to a competing approach.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly compares the chosen first sampling target with the strongest competing target, shows how that choice resolves the main diagnostic uncertainty, and links the result to the next management step.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends clearly inappropriate management such as observation alone, enucleation/shelling out, routine elective neck dissection for indeterminate nodes, or automatic radiotherapy for presumed benign disease.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests surgery but does not adequately define the extent of gland-bed resection, the role of the neck, or the principle for minimizing further recurrence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends revision excision of the involved submandibular bed/residual gland with removal of all detectable nodules, emphasizes avoidance of capsular rupture/tumor spillage, and does not include the neck routinely without stronger evidence.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear operative plan, correctly limits neck treatment to diagnosis-driven or therapeutic indications, and identifies a concrete trigger for escalation beyond surgery alone with an appropriate change in management such as therapeutic neck treatment and/or postoperative radiotherapy.

items.question_content: A 72-year-old woman with no relevant medical history and no medications reports dysarthria and difficulty eating. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, and use fig_03.jpg as needed, to decide the next management step now. What is the most likely diagnosis, which image- or function-based clue makes the lesion clinically significant rather than incidental, and what would change your recommendation if she later wanted future dentures? Briefly state the postoperative change you would use to judge success.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The most likely diagnosis is symptomatic giant torus involving the maxilla and mandible (torus palatinus and torus mandibularis). The case is clinically significant because the bony overgrowths are associated with dysarthria and difficulty eating, and fig_03.jpg supports impaired tongue motion / reduced tongue space as the mechanism of functional limitation. The next management step is surgical excision or recontouring after image-based operative planning, with histopathologic confirmation of the removed tissue as benign bone. If she later wanted future dentures, the indication for resection would become stronger because tori can interfere with prosthetic fabrication and retention. If she were asymptomatic and had no prosthodontic problem, observation would be reasonable. Postoperative success would be judged by improved tongue mobility, better speech intelligibility and oral intake, healed mucosa, and no clinical or radiographic recurrence on follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion or gives no specific diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign oral bony lesion but not the specific torus diagnosis, or identifies only one site.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies a symptomatic torus / giant torus involving the maxilla and mandible.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies symptomatic giant torus involving both maxilla and mandible and explicitly frames it as benign but functionally significant.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not connect the symptoms with the figures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only the symptoms or only the images.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates dysarthria and eating difficulty with the visible bony overgrowths to explain why the case matters.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically ties fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to lesion extent and fig_03.jpg to tongue-motion limitation, using both to justify the management choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an unrelated or unsupported approach.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States that treatment may be needed but does not clearly choose a next step or explain timing.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends surgical excision or recontouring now because the lesion is symptomatic and functionally limiting, with imaging used for planning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds a stepwise plan: image-based operative planning, resection or recontouring now, histopathologic confirmation of excised tissue, and a different recommendation if she were asymptomatic unless denture fabrication or other functional problems were expected.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare benefits and harms.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions benefits or risks in generic terms.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances expected improvement in speech, eating, and tongue mobility against operative morbidity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly explains why surgery is proportionate in the current symptomatic patient, while observation would be reasonable in asymptomatic disease without prosthodontic need.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits postoperative monitoring.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists only nonspecific surgical risks.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Mentions wound healing, pain or swelling, oral intake, tongue mobility, and recurrence monitoring.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds objective functional follow-up and notes that persistent or recurrent symptoms should prompt clinical reassessment and imaging if needed.

items.question_content: A 73-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with a 2-month painless right preauricular mass measuring about 2.5 cm clinically. Head and neck examination is otherwise unremarkable, and no cervical lymph nodes are palpable. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. First, using only the history/exam plus the preoperative information in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, provide a ranked differential diagnosis and state which single operative approach is most justified before final paraffin histology.
