If bleeding remains active or the collection enlarges, surgical control or angiographic embolization is indicated. For future surgery in a similarly atrophic anterior mandible, I would obtain preoperative CT/CBCT, treat the site as high risk because resorption brings vessels closer, use a broad reflected field, control buccolingual drill angulation, avoid unnecessarily long implants, consider shorter implants when appropriate, and perform meticulous hemostasis at both buccal and lingual periosteal-release sites. Postoperatively, observe the patient for a period rather than immediate discharge and give explicit instructions about tongue swelling, bleeding, or breathing difficulty. I would also monitor for delayed infection of residual hematoma and graft/membrane material.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the clinical course and figures coherently; gives an unrelated cause or ignores the imaging distribution of the hematoma.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes postoperative hemorrhage but attributes it vaguely or to lingual cortical perforation without reconciling the acute imaging findings in fig_01.jpg and the later clinical evolution shown in fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses the delayed onset, the acute fig_01.jpg pattern, and the later fig_02.jpg evolution to support soft-tissue arterial injury associated with the augmentation/flap procedure rather than drill perforation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifically identifies periosteal releasing-incision injury of a buccal vessel, most plausibly the ascending mental/submental terminal branch, with secondary spread into the floor of mouth, while correctly recognizing that fig_02.jpg is a later postoperative image rather than the immediate emergency presentation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Treats the problem as routine postoperative swelling or proposes outpatient observation without airway-focused escalation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes urgency but does not clearly prioritize airway protection over local wound management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that airway security is the immediate priority and recommends urgent hospital management with compression and escalation to intubation if obstruction progresses.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the correct sequence: immediate compression, emergency transfer, airway protection before definitive hemostasis, then reassessment/imaging for ongoing bleeding.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends no meaningful plan or advocates routine immediate drainage/exploration of the stable hematoma.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides only a partial acute plan or only prevention steps, or omits thresholds for escalation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: After airway control, recommends observation when the hematoma is stable and bleeding has ceased, with escalation to surgical control or embolization if bleeding persists or the collection enlarges; includes reasonable preventive steps for future surgery.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds case-specific prevention: preoperative CT/CBCT, recognition of atrophic interforaminal risk, careful buccolingual angulation, avoidance of unnecessarily long implants, wide flap reflection, meticulous hemostasis of periosteal-release sites, and short postoperative observation with warning instructions.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no rationale for management choices or ignores major risks created by the proposed intervention.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either airway risk or bleeding risk but does not weigh the consequences of intervention versus observation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that airway obstruction is the dominant immediate threat and that decompression of a stable hematoma can worsen bleeding by removing tamponade.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also recognizes delayed rebleeding after local anesthetic vasoconstriction wears off and the later risk of infection involving residual hematoma and graft/membrane material.

red_flags: Severity Misjudged: recommending discharge or office-only observation despite progressive tongue elevation and dyspnea from floor-of-mouth swelling after anterior mandibular implant/GBR surgery

items.question_content: A 1-year-old boy from a consanguineous family has had multiple painless tongue masses since birth that have slowly enlarged and now interfere with mastication. Exam shows intact mucosa and no cervical lymphadenopathy; see fig_01.jpg. Fiberoptic assessment shows additional pharyngeal nodules (fig_02.jpg). Histology from a representative tongue lesion is shown in fig_03.jpg. The parents ask whether these findings should simply be observed because he is so young, or whether treatment is indicated now, and whether a possible genetic basis would change your plan. What definitive management would you recommend, and why?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would recommend definitive treatment now rather than simple observation: planned surgical excision of the symptomatic tongue lesions under general anesthesia, with careful preservation of tongue bulk and mobility, and submission of all tissue for histopathologic confirmation. The leading diagnosis is a multifocal benign lipomatous lesion, most consistent with fibrolipoma, because the lesions have been present since birth, are slowly enlarging, painless, covered by intact mucosa, and fig_03.jpg shows a benign lobulated adipocytic pattern rather than an aggressive infiltrative process. The child already has functional compromise with mastication, so waiting offers little benefit and risks further feeding and speech-related problems as growth continues. At the same time, radical ablative surgery is not justified because the lesions appear localized and clinically benign. Histology remains essential to exclude reasonable mimics such as lymphangioma or hemangioma, neurofibroma or schwannoma, salivary lesions, and rare liposarcoma. Because fig_02.jpg shows additional pharyngeal nodules in an infant, ENT collaboration and preoperative airway assessment are important, and the pharyngeal lesions need parallel evaluation and management. Follow-up should monitor healing, feeding, tongue function and future speech, recurrence, and progression of pharyngeal disease. A possible genetic contribution may justify counseling or later testing, but it does not replace tissue diagnosis and should not alter the need for symptom-directed local treatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as primarily infectious, inflammatory, or clearly malignant, or does not recognize a benign lipomatous process.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign soft-tissue mass but does not prioritize a lipomatous/fibrolipomatous diagnosis or provides an unfocused differential without hierarchy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a multifocal benign lipomatous lesion, with fibrolipoma as the leading diagnosis, and mentions key alternative diagnoses that still require histologic exclusion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly prioritizes multifocal fibrolipoma or equivalent benign lipomatous diagnosis and explains why vascular, neural, salivary, and malignant mimics are less likely based on the case and figures while still requiring pathology confirmation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores major clinical or figure-based information, or bases reasoning on unsupported assumptions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings only, such as symptoms or histology alone, without integrating onset, growth pattern, distribution, and pharyngeal involvement.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates congenital onset, slow enlargement, functional impact, intact mucosa, absent cervical nodes, fig_01.jpg lesion pattern, fig_02.jpg pharyngeal disease, and fig_03.jpg benign adipocytic features into a coherent interpretation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes all available clinical and figure findings into a clear, internally consistent explanation that directly supports the proposed management and limits overcalling malignancy or underestimating airway-related burden.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management such as observation alone despite current functional impairment, nonspecific drug therapy, or unjustified radical resection.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests surgery but without explaining timing, need for tissue submission, preservation of tongue function, or handling of the pharyngeal lesions.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends definitive surgical excision of the symptomatic tongue lesions under general anesthesia, with histopathologic confirmation, conservative preservation of tongue function, and parallel ENT management of pharyngeal lesions.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan that includes preoperative airway consideration, targeted excision of localized lesions, routine pathology for all excised tissue, postoperative functional surveillance, and coordinated management of the pharyngeal component.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits, risks, or alternatives, or gives a one-sided recommendation with no case-specific justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either symptom relief or surgical risk, but not both, and does not explain why the chosen plan is preferable to reasonable alternatives.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the benefits of excision against anesthesia and surgical morbidity in an infant, and explains why observation is weak given progressive enlargement and mastication difficulty.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison of observation, conservative excision, and more extensive surgery, addressing infant airway risk, feeding and speech implications, recurrence surveillance, and why a possible genetic basis is adjunctive rather than plan-determining.

items.question_content: A 19-year-old healthy man presents with a 7-month gradually enlarging painless swelling in the left posterior mandible. He reports no fever, pus discharge, pain, or paresthesia. Use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg together with the history to identify the most likely diagnosis and justify it against at least two plausible alternatives. Then outline the definitive management you would choose at this stage, including how the lesion’s relationship to the mandibular canal affects the operation and what additional pathology workup is needed before you finalize prognosis. Finally, explain how your diagnosis, urgency, and treatment extent would change if the same patient instead developed new lower-lip numbness and the lesion appeared poorly defined and destructive.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The leading diagnosis is intraosseous schwannoma (neurilemmoma) of the left mandible, most likely arising in relation to the inferior alveolar nerve. This is supported by the patient’s age, slow painless enlargement, the benign-appearing expansile posterior mandibular lesion in fig_01.jpg with cortical expansion/root effects rather than infiltrative destruction, the apparent canal relationship/intraoperative nerve association, and the spindle-cell fascicular pattern in fig_02.jpg. H&E suggests a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor but is not definitive by itself.

Plausible alternatives include intraosseous neurofibroma and an odontogenic radiolucent lesion such as odontogenic keratocyst or unicystic ameloblastoma. Neurofibroma remains a close neural differential because it can also be an intraosseous spindle-cell lesion related to a nerve, but schwannoma is favored by the circumscribed behavior and typical encapsulated benign presentation; intratumoral axons would support neurofibroma rather than schwannoma. Odontogenic lesions are reasonable radiographic mimics because of the unilocular expansile mandibular radiolucency and root resorption, but they are less consistent with the spindle-cell neural histology and nerve-related operative findings.

At this stage, the appropriate treatment is conservative complete excision/enucleation with curettage or local excision because the lesion is enlarging but clinically and radiographically benign, and these tumors are usually well circumscribed and treatable without mandibular resection. Surgical planning should prioritize identifying the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle and preserving it if the tumor can be separated safely. Observation is not ideal because the lesion is growing and expanding bone. Segmental or wider resection, or planned nerve sacrifice, is not first-line for the current presentation unless the lesion is inseparable, recurrent, or shows malignant/aggressive features.

Definitive pathology requires immunohistochemistry. Strong diffuse S-100 and Sox-10 positivity with no malignant features supports schwannoma. Additional markers may be used if needed to distinguish from other spindle-cell lesions; demonstration of intratumoral axons would favor neurofibroma. Prognosis is generally good after adequate excision, with low recurrence, but follow-up should include clinical and radiographic review for bony healing, recurrence, and neurosensory status.

If the patient instead had new lower-lip numbness and the lesion became poorly defined and destructive, the case would no longer be managed as a routine benign encapsulated lesion. Concern would rise for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor or another aggressive/malignant jaw lesion. Urgency increases, and the plan should shift to expedited imaging review, biopsy or pathology reassessment before definitive surgery, and referral/management in an oncologic or tertiary setting as needed. The surgical extent would likely escalate from simple nerve-sparing excision to wider resection if infiltrative or malignant disease were confirmed.

items.question_content: A 42-year-old woman with mild mental deficit presents with a painless gingival mass in the left mandible that has enlarged slowly for more than 2 years and now causes facial asymmetry and occlusal interference. Oral hygiene is poor; there is no cervical lymphadenopathy or sensory deficit. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. An incisional biopsy from the pedunculated part is reported as peripheral myxoma. Based on the clinical course and the imaging, what definitive management would you choose now, and how would you justify the extent of surgery, any dental extractions, and the surveillance plan despite the biopsy result?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would proceed with definitive local management of a peripheral soft-tissue lesion rather than radical bony surgery. The key reason is the clinicoradiographic pattern: this is a long-standing, painless gingival mass with occlusal imprinting and tooth displacement, and fig_02.jpg shows mineralized content within the soft tissue but no destructive intraosseous lesion. Together with the absence of paresthesia or cervical nodes, that makes an aggressive intraosseous or malignant process less likely. The biopsy result should be treated cautiously because it came from a limited pedunculated area of a heterogeneous lesion; sampling error is plausible, so the whole specimen is needed for final diagnosis.

My plan would be to first control local irritants as much as possible, then excise the lesion completely with adequate peripheral and deep margins down to the periosteum/periodontal ligament, curetting the base and submitting the entire lesion, including calcified areas, for thorough histopathology. I would preserve teeth if they are maintainable, but extract teeth only if they have hopeless prognosis, are severely displaced or engulfed, or prevent complete excision and hygienic rehabilitation. Mild cognitive impairment alone does not mandate general anesthesia; if cooperation is adequate, local anesthesia with behavioral support is reasonable and avoids unnecessary anesthetic risk.

Follow-up should be structured and longer than routine wound review because recurrence is meaningful in peripheral ossifying-type lesions, especially if irritants persist or excision is incomplete. Early visits should assess healing, plaque control, function, and residual tooth stability; longer surveillance should look for regrowth at the surgical base and recurrent occlusal problems. If final histology or postoperative behavior is inconsistent with a benign peripheral lesion, I would then escalate the workup and referral.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate definitive plan, such as observation alone, superficial removal only, or treatment that does not address the need for complete lesion management and full-specimen histopathology.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends excision in general terms but gives limited rationale, omits the need for deep/peripheral margins or full-lesion histology, or gives poorly justified extraction decisions.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends complete local excision of the peripheral lesion with appropriate margins and submission of the full specimen, with selective rather than routine extraction of involved teeth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise, patient-specific plan: preoperative irritant control, definitive excision to periosteum/periodontal ligament with representative sampling of calcified areas, selective extractions only when prognosis or access requires, and a clear justification for the operative setting.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the clinical course or imaging to justify management, or ignores the mismatch between biopsy and overall presentation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated facts from the stem or figures; recognizes either the peripheral soft-tissue nature or the biopsy limitation, but not both in a coherent argument.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links recurrence to incomplete excision and persistent local irritants, and outlines practical surveillance targets such as regrowth at the base, tooth stability, occlusion, and the need to escalate if behavior becomes atypical.

red_flags: Premature Irreversible Treatment: recommending mandibular resection for this lesion despite fig_02.jpg showing a peripheral soft-tissue process without osseous destruction

items.question_content:
A 54-year-old man with a 2-year history of left preauricular discomfort/swelling underwent open surgery 7 months ago for an intra-articular left TMJ lesion. He has no history of TMJ trauma or known systemic joint disease. At review he reports only mild discomfort, function is preserved, and WBC is 9000/ul without a convincing acute inflammatory pattern. MRI is repeated again at 22 months because the postoperative lesion persists. You are given the serial MRI (fig_01.jpg), the first operative specimen (fig_02.jpg), and the later operative specimen (fig_03.jpg).

From the standpoint of the 7-month review, what is the most defensible management and why? Identify the leading diagnosis and one competing explanation, but defend your choice by citing what the figures show and what they do not allow you to conclude in a previously operated TMJ. Then, after incorporating fig_03.jpg, explain whether the later lesion is better understood as missed disease, true recurrence, or a new postoperative process, and give the single strongest figure-based argument for that conclusion. Finally, if at 22 months the patient insisted on the least invasive diagnostic step before another operation, explain what you would recommend or decline first and why.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
At 7 months, the most defensible choice is active surveillance with a short-interval reassessment plan rather than immediate re-operation. The leading diagnosis at that stage is residual or recurrent synovial chondromatosis, because fig_02.jpg shows immature cartilaginous/fibrous nodules from the first operation without a crystal-rich pattern, substantial calcification, or ossification. A reasonable competing explanation is postoperative synovitis/scar-related nodular change; an early crystal deposition process is possible but would not be the leading call from the 7-month data alone.

The figures support caution but not certainty. fig_01.jpg shows a persistent postoperative lesion in the lower joint space and later interval enlargement, so this is not a trivial normal postoperative appearance. However, MRI in a previously operated TMJ is nonspecific: scar tissue, postoperative synovitis, recurrent cartilaginous disease, and crystal deposition may all appear as heterogeneous soft-tissue signal abnormalities. Thus, at 7 months, MRI alone cannot prove recurrence, nor can it exclude a new postoperative process. Because symptoms are minimal, function is preserved, and there is no convincing acute inflammatory pattern, a monitored surveillance strategy is acceptable at that time, but only as structured follow-up, not reassurance.

After incorporating fig_03.jpg, the later lesion is best understood as a new postoperative CPPD process rather than missed disease or simple recurrence of the original lesion. The single strongest figure-based argument is the discordance between the two specimens: fig_02.jpg shows the original lesion as cartilaginous/fibrous nodules without crystal deposition, whereas fig_03.jpg shows rectangular to needle-like basophilic crystals with partial birefringence under polarized light, which is characteristic of CPPD. That makes missed pre-existing CPPD unlikely. Pure recurrence of synovial chondromatosis is also less convincing, because the later specimen is dominated by crystal deposition rather than the original histologic pattern.

At 22 months, if the patient insisted on the least invasive diagnostic step before another operation, I would not rely on TMJ aspiration as the first or sole test, even though crystal analysis is the general gold standard for CPPD. In this case the joint is small, previously operated, and scarred; the compartments are altered, the lesion is mass-like, and sampling may be technically difficult and low yield. A negative aspirate would not reliably exclude recurrent intra-articular pathology. If there were a safely accessible target, image-guided tissue sampling could be discussed, but the most definitive and practical approach remains targeted repeat exploration/excision because it both establishes diagnosis and removes the enlarging lesion.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly contrasts missed initial disease, true recurrence, and a new postoperative process, then uses the serial and histologic evidence to justify why surgery-induced CPPD is the strongest final interpretation.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Supports structured surveillance at 7 months in the minimally symptomatic patient and then supports tissue acquisition once persistent enlargement and later pathology shift the interpretation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise plan that is internally consistent at both time points, including how follow-up should be structured and why targeted re-exploration/excision remains the most definitive approach for an enlarging scarred intra-articular lesion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh the morbidity of repeat TMJ surgery against the risk of delayed diagnosis, or ignores the limitations of less invasive testing.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

items.question_content: A 28-year-old man seeks correction of spacing and flaring of the maxillary anterior teeth. He reports no pain or thermal sensitivity. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. What would you recommend as the next definitive management before any esthetic correction, and why is that the correct sequence in this patient? Base your answer on the visible findings, include the key confirmation step for the lesion, and state the main follow-up issues that would determine when anterior rehabilitation can proceed.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not proceed directly to cosmetic alignment or restorative closure of the spacing. The most likely diagnosis is a compound odontoma (or composite compound odontoma) in the anterior maxilla. This is supported by the clustered tooth-like radiopaque structures with a surrounding radiolucent rim on the radiographs, plus the palpable/visible hard buccal protuberance and flaring of the incisors in an otherwise asymptomatic adult.

The next definitive step is planned conservative surgical exposure and enucleation/removal of the lesion before esthetic treatment. Before surgery I would document the adjacent anterior teeth clinically, including vitality, mobility, periodontal condition, and baseline occlusion/esthetic concerns. If the relation of the lesion to adjacent roots is still uncertain after the available views, further cross-sectional imaging can be considered, but the current films already strongly support a localized odontogenic hard-tissue lesion. The removed specimen should be submitted for histopathologic confirmation.

This sequence is best because the lesion is the likely cause of the tooth displacement, is typically encapsulated and amenable to removal, and leaving it in place could maintain or worsen malposition, interfere with stable esthetic correction, and potentially permit cystic change. After healing, I would reassess wound healing, soft-tissue contour, radiographic resolution/bone fill, and especially the vitality and position of the adjacent incisors before planning orthodontic or restorative anterior rehabilitation. The impacted canine and third molars are additional findings to document, but they are not the first priority for the presenting complaint unless they change the broader treatment plan.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not prioritize the causative anterior lesion or focuses first on incidental findings unrelated to the chief complaint.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not mention postoperative monitoring or possible adverse effects relevant to this case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic pain or infection without linking follow-up to adjacent teeth or later rehabilitation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Includes follow-up of wound healing and adjacent incisor vitality/mobility, periodontal or gingival contour, and need for radiographic review before esthetic treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Also recognizes risks such as root injury, loss of vitality, residual contour defect, or unexpected histopathology, and explains how these findings would modify subsequent anterior rehabilitation.

items.question_content: A 58-year-old edentulous man has worn the same complete dentures for 4 years and now reports masticatory difficulty. He has a broad mandibular vestibular fibrous enlargement; the lesion is firm, non-hemorrhagic, and neither ulcerated nor indurated. Extra-orally, the occlusal vertical dimension is reduced. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what management pathway would you choose from initial visit to definitive prosthetic rehabilitation, and why is that pathway most appropriate for this patient’s future denture retention and stability? Base your justification on the visible tissue conditions and the main problems a less thoughtful approach could create.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is most consistent with denture-induced inflammatory fibrous hyperplasia (epulis fissuratum) from chronic trauma by an ill-fitting denture, with concomitant denture stomatitis/candidiasis on the palate. The management should be staged, not limited to removing the fold alone. First, eliminate the active inflammatory/infective burden and the traumatic cause: reinforce denture hygiene and night removal, treat the palatal candidal erythema with topical antifungal therapy plus chlorhexidine, and condition or adjust the existing prosthesis so the tissues can settle. Once the palatal erythema resolves, proceed to definitive surgery for the mandibular lesion.

Because fig_01.jpg shows a large anterior vestibular fold on a severely resorbed mandibular ridge with a shallow vestibule and little keratinized tissue, simple excision with primary closure would be a poor choice: it would further reduce vestibular depth, roll the lip inward, leave inadequate keratinized mucosa, and worsen future mandibular denture retention and stability. Definitive treatment should therefore be excision combined with vestibular deepening and soft-tissue augmentation, preferably with an autogenous free gingival/mucosal graft, to maintain or increase sulcus depth and create a more durable denture-bearing surface.

The excised tissue should still be sent for histopathology to confirm the reactive diagnosis. During healing, use a tissue-conditioned/relined transitional prosthesis rather than deliver the final denture immediately. After soft-tissue maturation, fabricate a new properly extended complete denture that also corrects the reduced vertical dimension. Follow-up should monitor graft take, donor-site pain, infection, relapse or recurrent hyperplasia, persistent palatal inflammation, and recurrence if the prosthesis remains ill fitting.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends observation alone, medication alone, or simple excision without correcting the denture-related cause or planning for prosthetic rehabilitation despite the anatomic problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies some appropriate elements but the sequence is incomplete or mismatched; may treat candidiasis or excise the lesion, yet omits vestibular management, temporary prosthetic conditioning, or delayed definitive prosthesis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a coherent staged plan: control denture-related inflammation/candidiasis and traumatic factors first, then definitive excision with vestibular deepening and soft-tissue augmentation, followed by healing and fabrication of a new denture.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the full staged plan and clearly justifies why combined excision plus vestibular-deepening grafting is preferred here because the lesion is extensive on a resorbed ridge with shallow vestibule and inadequate keratinized tissue; includes transitional relining/tissue conditioning and pathology submission.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the clinical findings or figures to support the plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as naming denture trauma, but does not connect the visible mandibular anatomy and palatal mucosal changes to the treatment sequence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the major data: fig_01.jpg supports extensive fibrous hyperplasia on an atrophic ridge with shallow vestibule/limited keratinized tissue, fig_02.jpg supports denture stomatitis/candidiasis, and reduced vertical dimension supports the need for new prosthetic rehabilitation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figures and examination findings into a clear rationale for staging, explaining how the mandibular soft-tissue deficiency drives the surgical design and how the palatal inflammation changes timing before definitive surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh risks and benefits, or recommends a plan that predictably worsens the prosthetic foundation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros or cons but misses the case-specific consequences of inadequate vestibular preservation or ongoing prosthetic trauma.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that a simpler approach risks loss of vestibular depth, insufficient keratinized mucosa, poorer mandibular denture retention/stability, and recurrence if the traumatic denture is not corrected; also recognizes the trade-off of added surgical morbidity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances the prosthetic gains of vestibular-deepening grafting against donor-site morbidity and treatment time, and explains why immediate definitive prosthesis or nonsurgical-only management is less suitable in a large fibrotic lesion on an atrophic ridge.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits important complications or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only nonspecific postoperative issues such as pain or infection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key complications or monitoring points: graft take, donor-site discomfort, relapse/shallowing of the vestibule, recurrent hyperplasia, persistent palatal inflammation, and the need for postoperative denture and hygiene control.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Includes the major postoperative risks and also notes the need for histopathologic confirmation and reassessment if healing is atypical or the lesion persists after removal of the traumatic source.

items.question_content: A 6-year-old girl presents with failure of eruption of the maxillary anterior teeth. Teeth 51 and 61 are retained, tooth 62 has never erupted, and a supernumerary tooth in the anterior maxilla was identified several years earlier. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. Give a ranked preoperative differential for the pericoronal lesion and name the specific imaging feature that makes you less comfortable treating it as a routine dentigerous cyst. Then state your initial operative plan, including whether you would preserve or remove impacted 62 and why, and how you would protect the adjacent developing permanent teeth. After reviewing fig_03.jpg, identify the final diagnosis from the histologic pattern and explain how that diagnosis changes surveillance and your threshold to escalate treatment if the lesion later recurs or shows cortical destruction.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Preoperatively, a dentigerous cyst is a strong clinical possibility because the lesion is pericoronal to an unerupted tooth, but ameloblastic fibroma should also be high on the differential. Other less likely considerations are a developing odontoma/other mixed odontogenic lesion, odontogenic fibroma, or ameloblastoma. The imaging detail that makes this less comfortable as a routine dentigerous cyst is that the radiolucency around the crown of impacted 62 is well defined but not smoothly corticated; in fig_02.jpg its outline is irregular/lace-like rather than a simple symmetric follicular enlargement. Together with years of eruption delay and the associated supernumerary tooth, that warrants definitive tissue diagnosis.

My initial treatment would be conservative but complete surgical excision/enucleation of the lesion with full histopathologic examination, plus removal of the supernumerary tooth. I would remove impacted 62 as well, because the lesion surrounds its crown and it is a primary tooth with limited strategic value compared with the adjacent permanent incisors. I would preserve 11, 21, and 22 and protect their follicles/PDL/supporting bone with careful access, minimal bone removal, and atraumatic dissection. Observation or simple decompression alone would risk leaving an odontogenic tumor undiagnosed; radical resection would be overtreatment for a small, localized first presentation without destructive imaging.

fig_03.jpg is diagnostic of ameloblastic fibroma: cords and islands of odontogenic epithelium with peripheral cuboidal/columnar ameloblast-like cells and central stellate-reticulum-like cells in a primitive spindle-cell ectomesenchymal stroma, without enamel or dentin formation. Supportive immunoprofile includes epithelial CK positivity and mesenchymal vimentin positivity with low Ki-67.

Once ameloblastic fibroma is confirmed, follow-up must be much more intensive and prolonged than for a routine cyst: long-term, ideally lifelong, clinical and radiographic surveillance for recurrence, while also monitoring eruption and root development of adjacent permanent teeth. If recurrence occurs, or if later imaging shows cortical destruction or other aggressive behavior, the threshold to escalate from repeat conservative removal to wider resection becomes substantially lower.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful differential, or gives a single unsupported diagnosis that omits both dentigerous cyst and ameloblastic fibroma.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one of the key possibilities or lists alternatives without ranking or case-specific reasoning.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Places dentigerous cyst and ameloblastic fibroma among the leading preoperative possibilities and mentions at least one other plausible odontogenic alternative, with rationale based on the child's age, delayed eruption, and pericoronal relationship.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clearly ranked differential and explains why dentigerous cyst is a strong mimic yet insufficiently secure, while more aggressive alternatives are less likely given the lesion's small, localized appearance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the figures meaningfully or misinterprets the lesion-to-tooth relationship.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses generic findings such as delayed eruption or supernumerary tooth but does not identify a figure-based reason the lesion is atypical for a routine dentigerous cyst.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the key figure-based suspicious feature—such as the clear but irregular, non-smooth, or lace-like pericoronal border around impacted 62 in fig_02.jpg—and integrates it with the prolonged eruption disturbance and associated supernumerary tooth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figure findings and clinical history into a nuanced argument: suspicious enough to require definitive tissue diagnosis, yet not radiographically destructive enough to justify initial radical surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management such as observation alone, purely orthodontic management, or immediate radical resection without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for surgery or biopsy but gives a vague plan, or does not clearly address management of the supernumerary tooth, impacted 62, and adjacent permanent teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends conservative complete excision/enucleation/curettage with full histopathology, removal of the supernumerary tooth, removal of impacted 62 because the lesion involves a primary tooth, and preservation of adjacent developing permanent teeth and supporting structures.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise operative plan, explicitly justifies why observation/marsupialization is insufficient and why radical surgery is excessive at first presentation, and describes atraumatic protection of the adjacent permanent tooth germs and supporting tissues.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify the final diagnosis from fig_03.jpg or gives an incorrect histopathologic interpretation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a benign odontogenic or mixed odontogenic lesion but does not correctly specify the diagnostic histologic pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies ameloblastic fibroma and supports it with the characteristic pattern of odontogenic epithelial cords/islands with peripheral ameloblast-like cells and central stellate-reticulum-like cells in primitive ectomesenchymal stroma, with no hard tissue formation.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately identifies ameloblastic fibroma and distinguishes it from key mimics such as odontoma, ameloblastoma, and odontogenic fibroma using the histologic pattern and, when cited, the supportive immunohistochemical profile.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful follow-up plan or suggests only routine short-term review.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends follow-up in generic terms but does not link it to recurrence risk, adjacent tooth development, or triggers for treatment escalation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that confirmation of ameloblastic fibroma requires prolonged clinical and radiographic surveillance for recurrence and monitoring of eruption/root development of adjacent permanent teeth, with prompt reassessment if new radiolucency or eruption disturbance appears.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds that surveillance should be very long-term or lifelong and clearly explains that recurrence or later cortical destruction lowers the threshold for wider resection because recurrent disease carries a higher risk profile, including rare malignant transformation after multiple recurrences.

items.question_content: A 48-year-old man presented with 6 months of painful jaw swelling and tooth mobility. Prior incisional biopsy with immunohistochemistry established Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and he had declined ablative surgery. Review the baseline findings in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, the interval follow-up in fig_03.jpg, and the 1-year image in fig_04.jpg. How do you interpret the disease course at this stage, and what would you do next? Defend your plan by explaining how the serial figures affect your view of disease extent, whether management should proceed with or without repeat tissue sampling, and what minimum re-staging and surveillance are required before keeping treatment jaw-directed rather than broadening to more intensive therapy.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The serial record is most consistent with osseous LCH that initially responded to conservative treatment and then showed localized reactivation/relapse at 1 year, rather than uninterrupted diffuse progression or complete cure. fig_01.jpg shows extensive destructive jaw disease at baseline. fig_03.jpg shows interval improvement with bone fill/remineralization and better clinical appearance in previously involved areas. fig_04.jpg then shows a new or renewed focal destructive mandibular lesion, while much of the prior disease burden appears more sclerotic/healed. 

Therapeutically, I would treat this as single-system osseous LCH still apparently confined to the jaws unless re-staging proves otherwise. Because both maxilla and mandible have been involved, it is more appropriately thought of as multifocal disease within one system rather than a trivial solitary lesion, so the decision to remain local must be justified by repeat staging.

I would not jump straight to mandibular resection or empiric systemic therapy. If the current radiographic pattern is concordant with prior LCH and there are no new atypical clinical features, repeat biopsy is not automatically required before retreatment because the original tissue diagnosis was secure and the serial response/relapse pattern is plausible for LCH. However, I would have a low threshold to re-biopsy if the lesion has atypical imaging features, associated soft-tissue mass, suspected superimposed infection, new neurosensory change, unexpectedly aggressive behavior, poor response to another local attempt, or if re-staging reveals discordant disease that raises diagnostic doubt.

Minimum work-up before committing to local-only care should include full head-and-neck and systemic review for additional bone pain, skin lesions, pulmonary symptoms, and endocrine symptoms such as polyuria/polydipsia; clinical examination; baseline laboratory assessment such as CBC and liver profile; chest assessment; and whole-body skeletal/systemic staging imaging such as PET-CT or an equivalent survey based on availability, ideally with hematology/oncology input.

If re-staging remains negative outside the jaws, I would favor another conservative jaw-directed treatment to the active mandibular site. In this case, repeat intralesional corticosteroid is the most directly supported choice because there was prior radiographic response and surgery had been declined; limited curettage or carefully selected low-dose radiotherapy are reasonable alternatives if access, tissue uncertainty, or failure of injection changes the balance. Follow-up should be close with repeat panoramic or sectional imaging and long-term surveillance because relapse can occur after apparent healing.

I would broaden beyond local therapy if re-staging shows additional skeletal sites or extraskeletal/risk-organ involvement, if there is progressive enlargement despite local control attempts, impending or actual pathologic fracture, worsening function or tooth support, soft-tissue extension, new neurosensory deficit, or persistent uncertainty about the diagnosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the condition or misreads the serial course, for example calling the case healed, generalized uncontrolled progression, or a non-LCH process without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes LCH and some ongoing disease activity but does not correctly characterize the 1-year pattern from the serial figures.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly interprets the course as interval response/partial remission followed by localized recurrent osseous activity at 1 year, not complete resolution.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately interprets fig_01.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg as multifocal jaw LCH with substantial healing/remodeling of prior sites and a focal renewed mandibular lesion at 1 year, and classifies the working problem as jaw-confined single-system osseous disease pending re-staging.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figures or prior pathology, or bases the plan on a single data point.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the pathology/history or the imaging, but does not synthesize them into a coherent interpretation of the disease course.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates prior tissue confirmation of LCH with the serial radiographic changes and clinical context to justify the current working diagnosis and management direction.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg with the clinical history to explain why relapse/reactivation is favored, while also recognizing why the pattern still requires re-staging and why severe dental disease alone does not adequately explain the full jaw distribution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Offers no alternative explanation for the 1-year lesion or treats the diagnosis as beyond question despite new activity.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a generic alternative diagnosis but does not relate it to the figures or to the decision about repeat biopsy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Considers at least one clinically plausible alternative explanation for the new destructive focus, such as superimposed infection/osteomyelitis or another destructive lesion, and links that reasoning to whether re-biopsy is needed.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically weighs relapse of LCH against plausible alternatives and gives a defensible threshold for repeat biopsy based on atypical imaging, soft-tissue component, neurosensory change, discordant staging, or poor response to retreatment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent next-step plan, or recommends clearly mismatched care such as observation alone despite active disease or immediate radical treatment without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests treatment in broad terms but does not tailor it to the serial response, the 1-year finding, or the need to confirm disease extent before local-only management.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a stepwise plan that includes re-staging and, if disease remains localized, a conservative jaw-directed retreatment with appropriate follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a patient-specific, evidence-based plan that addresses whether repeat biopsy is needed, justifies a conservative local retreatment pathway if re-staging is negative, acknowledges other reasonable local options, includes multidisciplinary input and surveillance, and states clear triggers for escalation beyond local therapy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh the risks and benefits of local versus broader treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives generic pros and cons but does not connect them to this patient's jaw involvement, prior response, or relapse pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a conservative jaw-directed approach can be reasonable if re-staging is negative, while acknowledging the risks of missed systemic disease and structural mandibular complications.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced comparison of conservative retreatment versus more invasive or systemic approaches, explicitly addressing preservation of teeth/jaw form and function, morbidity of resection, recurrence risk, diagnostic uncertainty, and the danger of undertreating disseminated disease.

items.question_content: A 10-year-old girl has 1 week of progressive left maxillary swelling and delayed eruption of the permanent canine. Aspiration yields straw-colored fluid. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management would you recommend for this lesion and the associated unerupted canine, and why is that plan preferable to other reasonable options in this patient? Include the key elements of postoperative surveillance.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: This should be managed as a benign but neoplastic pericoronal odontogenic lesion, most consistent with a follicular adenomatoid odontogenic tumor arising in association with a dentigerous cyst. I would recommend complete surgical enucleation/curettage of the lesion with removal of the associated unerupted canine and histopathologic examination of the entire specimen. In this patient, tooth preservation is less favorable because fig_01.jpg shows an extensive lesion around the canine with superior extension toward the maxillary sinus/lateral nasal wall, buccal cortical expansion/erosion, and an unfavorable displaced canine position, so orthodontic salvage would be unpredictable and could compromise complete removal. More conservative approaches may be reasonable for smaller lesions with a favorably positioned tooth, but here the anatomy and mixed cystic-neoplastic features support definitive excision. Surgery should protect adjacent teeth and avoid creating oroantral or oronasal communication. Prognosis after complete removal is excellent and recurrence is rare, but follow-up should be long-term with clinical and radiographic review to confirm bone regeneration, resolution of swelling, no recurrence, and normal development/eruption of adjacent teeth and occlusion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends inappropriate management such as observation alone, repeated aspiration, antibiotics alone, or a vague plan that does not definitively address the lesion or associated tooth.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests surgery but the plan is incomplete, non-definitive, or poorly matched to this case; tooth management is omitted or unjustified, and follow-up is minimal.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends definitive excision/enucleation of the lesion with an appropriate plan for the associated canine and histopathologic assessment, with generally sound rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly recommends complete enucleation/curettage with a well-justified decision to remove the unerupted canine in this specific patient, explains why selected conservative options are less suitable here, and includes practical surveillance priorities.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides generic management with little or no use of the clinical history, fig_01.jpg, or fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only isolated findings, such as cystic aspirate or impaction, without integrating imaging extent and histologic pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates major data sources, including the pericoronal cystic relationship and either the radiographic extent or the odontogenic epithelial tumor features, into a coherent management rationale.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the short symptomatic course, straw-colored aspirate, impacted canine relationship, extension toward sinus/nasal structures, cortical expansion/erosion on fig_01.jpg, and AOT-like ductal/whorled epithelial features on fig_02.jpg into a clear explanation of why definitive excision is indicated.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or materially misjudges the balance of benefit and harm.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions pros and cons superficially but without linking them to the child's anatomy, eruption status, or lesion behavior.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Reasonably compares definitive excision with more conservative possibilities and links the preferred plan to case-specific factors such as extent and tooth position.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly weighs the low recurrence and curative potential of complete excision against the costs of canine loss, explains why tooth preservation/eruption would be unpredictable here, and shows awareness of future orthodontic implications.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits relevant complications and surveillance needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists only generic surgical risks such as pain, bleeding, or infection without case-specific concerns.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies important case-specific risks such as injury to adjacent teeth, sinus or nasal communication, and the need for radiographic follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates sinus/nasal communication risk, adjacent tooth effects, need to verify bone fill and absence of recurrence, and monitors eruption/developmental consequences for the remaining dentition and occlusion.

items.question_content: A 29-year-old woman presented 5 days after a dog-bite injury involving the philtrum and upper lip. The philtrum was reconstructed with a full-thickness skin graft and the upper lip with a mucosal V-Y advancement flap. About 10 months later, the philtral scar became symptomatic and was revised with a second full-thickness graft from the opposite retroauricular side. After that revision, tender/pruritic nodules developed in the philtral graft, did not improve with intralesional steroid therapy, and recurred after local excision. You are now seeing her at the recurrence shown in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what operation would you offer now? Defend your choice by integrating the traumatic wound pattern, later scar behavior, and the clinical/histologic appearance in the figures. In your justification, explain the recurrence mechanism you think is most plausible in this patient, why at least two other reasonable management strategies are less appropriate, and the single new finding that would most strongly make you switch to broader philtral re-reconstruction rather than another focal procedure.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is recurrent secondary milia, i.e., keratin-filled squamous-lined epithelial cysts/implantation-type cysts arising within the philtral full-thickness skin graft and adjacent scar. At this recurrence, I would offer complete lesion-directed excision of all clinically evident nodules with removal of the entire cyst wall and any immediately involved scar, while preserving the remainder of the philtral reconstruction. All excised tissue should again go for histopathologic confirmation, and I would not continue steroid injections as definitive treatment because they do not eliminate an epithelial cyst lining.

The reasoning is figure-based and multimodal. fig_01.jpg shows an irregular traumatic defect with partial epithelialization, which raises the possibility that microscopic epidermal remnants remained in the recipient bed despite wound preparation. fig_02.jpg shows later hypertrophic scar and contracture of the philtrum, indicating a fibrotic, high-tension environment. fig_03.jpg shows recurrent, discrete lesions centered in the grafted philtral region and histology consistent with a keratin-filled cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium. That pattern supports a localized epithelial cyst process rather than diffuse failure of the whole philtral subunit.

The recurrence mechanism is most plausibly multifactorial: retroauricular full-thickness graft skin transfers adnexal structures such as pilosebaceous units and eccrine ducts; the irregular, partly epithelialized bite wound may have left epidermal remnants in the recipient bed; and later hypertrophic scarring/tension in the dynamic perioral region may have promoted duct obstruction and keratin retention. The interaction of donor-site adnexal density and recipient-site fibrosis best explains repeated recurrence.

Two or more alternative strategies are less appropriate. Continued steroid injections or observation are poor choices because the lesions recurred despite steroid therapy and histology indicates a structural epithelial cyst, not just inflammatory scar activity. Immediate broad philtral scar/graft re-revision is also less appropriate now because the disease appears focal and graft-centered rather than a diffuse subunit failure; broader revision would increase donor-site morbidity, risk new scarring, and could recreate the same problem if the wound bed and tissue choice were not changed. Empiric antibiotics or simple drainage would also be inappropriate because the course and histology do not support suppurative infection.

If further philtral reconstruction later became necessary, I would change the wound-bed preparation first: sharply excise epithelialized or unstable scar margins to create a uniform, well-vascularized recipient bed rather than relying on curettage alone. If reconstructive options allowed, I would also consider tissue with lower adnexal density or local tissue rather than repeating the same donor-site strategy.

The single finding that would most strongly make me switch from another focal excision to broader philtral re-reconstruction would be extension of similar lesions beyond the graft margins into adjacent native philtral or upper-lip tissue. That would suggest the problem is no longer a localized graft-contained cystic process, but a broader scar-field/subunit problem requiring more extensive resection and reconstruction.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the recurrence as keloid, hypertrophic scar alone, infection alone, or another diagnosis that does not fit the clinical and histologic findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a recurrent postoperative epithelial/adnexal/implantation cyst process but does not clearly identify secondary milia or equivalent keratin-filled squamous-lined cysts in the grafted philtrum.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies recurrent secondary milia, or an equivalent epidermal inclusion/keratin cyst process, arising within the grafted philtral scar and distinguishes it from diffuse philtral subunit failure.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case details or one figure but does not clearly connect the initial traumatic wound, later scar evolution, and recurrent clinical-histologic pattern.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg with the timeline: the irregular/partly epithelialized traumatic wound, subsequent hypertrophic scar/contracture, recurrent graft-centered lesions, histology showing a keratin-filled squamous-lined cyst, and lack of response to steroid therapy, and uses these data to justify both diagnosis and the limited extent of surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or non-definitive plan such as observation alone, antibiotics/drainage for presumed infection, or immediate broad re-reconstruction without adequate case-based justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recommends local excision but does not specify complete removal of the lesion/cyst wall, preservation of uninvolved philtrum, histopathologic confirmation, or the need to stop relying on steroid injections as definitive treatment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Recommends complete lesion-directed excision of all recurrent nodules/cyst walls within the involved scar, preservation of the salvageable philtral reconstruction, histopathologic confirmation, discontinuation of steroid injections as primary treatment for the nodules, and appropriate recurrence follow-up; if further reconstruction became necessary, proposes a concrete change in wound-bed preparation and/or tissue choice.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not meaningfully compare the chosen plan with plausible alternatives.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions one or more alternatives but gives limited case-specific reasoning for why they are less appropriate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Compares the chosen operation against at least two plausible alternatives generated from the case, such as continued steroid treatment/observation, broad philtral scar-graft re-revision, or empiric infection management, and weighs recurrence control against morbidity, preservation of philtral contour, and the localized nature of the pathology.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no credible threshold for changing from focal treatment to broader re-reconstruction, or gives a threshold inconsistent with the case.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a generic escalation trigger without clearly linking it to a change from localized cystic disease to broader subunit failure or alternative pathology.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies a specific new finding that would justify abandoning another focal procedure for broader philtral re-reconstruction, such as extension of similar lesions beyond the graft-native border, and clearly explains why that would imply a field/subunit-level problem rather than a localized graft-contained cystic recurrence.

items.question_content: A 68-year-old woman is referred 8 hours after a bear attack. She is alert and hemodynamically stable after transfer, with no airway compromise. Based on Figures 1 and 2, what should the initial operative management be at this stage, and why is this the most appropriate approach?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The appropriate first operation is urgent debridement and staged reconstruction rather than extensive definitive reconstruction in a single sitting. In this stable patient, management should focus first on trauma principles, contamination control, and preservation of viable tissue.

The wound should undergo copious irrigation and meticulous debridement of soil, debris, and clearly nonviable tissue while preserving salvageable avulsed facial soft tissue for anatomical repositioning. Because the ocular injury is nonsalvageable, the destroyed orbital contents should be managed with ophthalmology involvement and exenteration rather than attempted globe salvage in a heavily contaminated field.

The facial fractures should then be reduced selectively to restore facial buttress support and allow soft-tissue redraping. Because the midfacial fractures are comminuted and fragile, limited semirigid stabilization with wire fixation is preferred for key segments; aggressive plating of multiple small fragments should be avoided because it may further fragment bone, increase devascularization, and raise infection risk in a contaminated delayed-presenting injury.

After skeletal support is re-established, the viable avulsed hemifacial tissues should be re-approximated anatomically in layers to preserve native tissue, restore facial contour, and optimize later function and appearance. Definitive secondary procedures, such as orbital prosthetic rehabilitation, scar revision, and other refinements, should be staged after infection risk is controlled and healing is established.

Adjunctive care includes broad-spectrum antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, and close postoperative surveillance for infection, necrosis, wound breakdown, and fixation failure.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an unsafe or inappropriate plan, such as simple closure, no meaningful debridement, no management of the nonsalvageable orbit, or immediate extensive definitive reconstruction despite contamination and comminution.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes the need for surgery and mentions debridement or closure, but the sequence is incomplete or omits major elements such as orbital management, selective skeletal stabilization, tissue preservation, or staged reconstruction.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends urgent operative debridement, appropriate management of the nonsalvageable orbital injury, selective reduction/stabilization of the midface, layered re-approximation of viable avulsed tissue, and delayed secondary reconstruction once healing permits.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear first-stage operative sequence that prioritizes contamination control, preservation of viable tissue, restoration of facial support with selective semirigid stabilization, and staged later rehabilitation, with rationale matched to the figures and presentation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh risks and benefits, or recommends choices that ignore major hazards of gross contamination, delayed transfer, or fragile comminuted bone.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions infection or instability in general terms but does not connect these risks to the proposed operative choices.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a conservative first-stage approach is preferred: delayed contaminated injury increases infection risk, fragile comminuted bones may not tolerate aggressive hardware, and preserving native soft tissue supports later function and aesthetics.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Gives a nuanced comparison of options, balancing stability versus implant burden, debridement versus tissue preservation, and immediate versus staged reconstruction in this specific patient.

items.question_content: A 48-year-old woman has a 3-year enlarging painful left cheek/maxillary mass with recent 23-kg weight loss, epiphora, exophthalmos, blurred vision, rhinitis, and an ulcerated intraoral gingival component. She has had no prior surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy, and no cervical nodes are palpable clinically. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg. A prior CT report also mentioned small submandibular/cervical nodes despite the clinically N0 neck. Ignoring the postoperative figures, answer three parts: (1) What is the most likely diagnosis and what is the single strongest competing diagnosis? (2) Would you commit to definitive resection on the present work-up, or first obtain additional study/tissue—and why? (3) State the specific finding that would make you preserve the orbit versus include orbital sacrifice, and explain how you would manage the radiologically noted neck.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most likely diagnosis is a primary malignant maxillary bone tumor, most likely osteosarcoma. The strongest competing diagnosis is chondrosarcoma. Preoperatively, fig_02.jpg favors osteosarcoma because the lesion is aggressively destructive with a broad zone of transition, bone-forming/periosteal reaction, and mineralized matrix rather than a purely lytic or purely cartilaginous pattern. fig_03.jpg shows locally advanced maxillary disease extending toward the orbit and sinonasal region. fig_01.jpg supports a large invasive lesion with intraoral breakthrough and orbital/nasolacrimal symptoms. fig_05.jpg confirms malignancy and matrix production, but FNAB is limited for architectural subtype definition. fig_04.jpg shows no obvious pulmonary metastasis on plain film, but that is less sensitive than chest CT.

I would not make the orbit/no-orbit decision on FNAB plus CT alone if a prompt incisional or core biopsy from the intraoral component and MRI of the maxilla/orbit/skull base can be obtained without major delay. The key issue is not whether this is malignant—it almost certainly is—but whether tissue architecture and soft-tissue extent are sufficiently defined to plan margin-driven surgery, especially around the orbit/skull base. So the best pathway is urgent sarcoma-capable MDT review, rapid definitive tissue sampling, MRI for orbital/periorbital/skull-base extent, and preferably chest CT for staging; then proceed without unnecessary delay to wide en bloc resection.

Orbit preservation is reasonable if MRI and intraoperative assessment show that the tumor remains confined to maxillary bone/adjacent walls and negative margins can be achieved without invasion of orbital fat, extraocular muscles, globe, or orbital apex. If the periorbita/orbital contents are breached, or a clear margin cannot otherwise be achieved, orbital sacrifice/exenteration is justified. Ocular symptoms alone are not enough; the deciding factor is demonstrated invasion or inability to obtain oncologic margins.

For the neck, this remains clinically N0. Small radiologic nodes should not trigger routine elective neck dissection in suspected osteosarcoma. They should be correlated with targeted ultrasound-guided FNA/core if truly suspicious or progressive. Neck dissection is reserved for proven nodal disease. Overall, the correct balance is short, targeted completion of work-up followed by definitive resection, not prolonged delay and not blind radical surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misidentifies the lesion as benign, inflammatory, odontogenic infection, or primarily sinus disease, or does not recognize a malignant maxillary bone process.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes malignancy but gives a vague diagnosis or an unsupported diagnosis that does not fit the radiographic and cytologic pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies an aggressive primary maxillary bone malignancy and appropriately favors osteosarcoma, while acknowledging that FNAB alone is limited for final subtype definition.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Correctly identifies probable maxillary osteosarcoma and explicitly justifies it from figure-based destructive bone changes, mineralized/periosteal pattern, and malignant matrix-producing cytology, while keeping the preoperative diagnosis appropriately qualified.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful differential diagnosis or lists implausible alternatives only.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative diagnosis but does not compare it with the leading diagnosis using case evidence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies chondrosarcoma as the strongest competing diagnosis and gives at least one case-based reason it is less favored than osteosarcoma.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically compares osteosarcoma with the strongest alternative diagnosis, using the figures and FNAB limitations to explain why one is more likely preoperatively while acknowledging residual uncertainty.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or none of the provided history, figures, or pathology to support the answer.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions isolated findings but does not synthesize them into a coherent assessment of diagnosis, extent, and staging.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg-fig_05.jpg with the history to describe locally advanced malignant maxillary bone disease, orbital/sinonasal risk, FNAB limitations, clinically N0 versus radiologically small nodes, and the limited reassurance of negative chest plain film.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Precisely synthesizes the clinical presentation and each relevant figure into a unified argument for probable osteosarcoma, current resectability, need for targeted additional work-up, and the distinction between local extent, nodal uncertainty, and distant staging.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

items.question_content: Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. A 10-year-old boy presents soon after a bite from a known but unvaccinated dog with a severely contaminated right lower-lip avulsion involving about half of the lower lip and extending across the vermilion into the cutaneous lip. He is hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and routine laboratory results are normal. What definitive first-stage reconstructive strategy would you choose at the initial operation, and how would you justify that choice based on the goals of preserving lip function and the likely medium-term esthetic trade-offs visible on follow-up?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This should be managed as an urgent operative reconstruction rather than a simple laceration repair. Initial management should include copious irrigation of the contaminated bite wound, sharp debridement of clearly nonviable tissue, assessment and repair of deeper structural support such as fascia/orbicularis as needed, and immediate definitive reconstruction in the same operation if a viable vascularized bed is present. For the defect shown, the best first-stage choice is limited edge regularization and approximation followed by a full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) inset over the repaired bed and secured with firm immobilization, such as a bolster or compression dressing.

The main justification is functional priority. In a child with a large lower-lip avulsive defect crossing vermilion and cutaneous lip, the immediate goal is to preserve oral aperture, lip competence, mobility, speech, and overall contour while avoiding commissural distortion and microstomia. An immobilized FTSG can resurface a broad defect in one stage without adding bulk. It is therefore a defensible option in an acutely contaminated injury with substantial tissue loss. Mucosal grafts or small local advancement procedures are better suited to smaller vermilion defects. Larger local, lip-switch, or regional flaps may improve color and texture match but may also require staged surgery and can increase bulk, donor morbidity, commissure distortion, or risk of microstomia in a small growing mouth.

Perioperative care should also include bite-wound antibiotic coverage, tetanus review, and rabies risk assessment based on local public-health guidance and observation of the dog. If the known dog remains well during a 10-day observation period, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis may not be required.

Follow-up should monitor early graft take, infection, necrosis, dehiscence, edema, salivary contamination, and oral competence. Medium-term follow-up should assess contraction with growth, partial vermilion-border effacement, contour irregularity or shallow indentation, dyschromia, hair-bearing skin or fine vellus hairs on the graft, scar firmness, speech, symmetry, and psychosocial impact. The likely trade-off is that stable function can be preserved despite moderate esthetic sequelae such as color mismatch, border irregularity, and fine hairs. If function remains intact and the child and family are satisfied, conservative scar care and observation are appropriate, with elective secondary refinement reserved for later if priorities change.

items.question_content: A 53-year-old woman undergoes radical resection of recurrent right cheek squamous cell carcinoma with total parotidectomy, resection to mandibular periosteum including zygomatic arch/coronoid process, sacrifice of frontal-temporal and buccal facial nerve branches, and supraomohyoid neck dissection. TMJ capsule has already been covered separately, and a lower-cheek local flap has been rotated to restore the superior cheek. fig_01.jpg shows the remaining contiguous donor-site/neck skin defect with exposed deep tissues and relatively stiff surrounding skin. What reconstruction would you choose for the remaining cutaneous defect, and why is it better suited than other reasonable options here? Base your answer on the defect geometry visible in fig_01.jpg and explain the key design, harvest, inset, and early postoperative decisions needed to maximize flap survival and preserve neck function.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would choose a thin pedicled fasciocutaneous internal mammary artery perforator flap, ideally planned on the dominant perforator after perforator mapping, and modify it into a bilobed/"shark" design with a smaller perpendicular random-pattern extension. The main axial paddle would resurface the lateral neck, while the small superior lobe would fill the medial submandibular gap left between the rotated cheek flap and the neck wound. This is better suited to fig_01.jpg than a skin graft or primary closure because deep tissues are exposed and the wound is large, stiff, and multi-vector. It is preferable to a bulky muscle flap because neck contour and mobility matter, and to a free flap because a reliable local-regional thin flap can provide color/texture match with less operative burden and donor morbidity. A submental flap is less attractive in a recurrent oncologic case with neck dissection, and a single-paddle supraclavicular-type flap may be less adaptable to the under-chin/medial gap geometry.

Key technical points are: map the perforator preoperatively; design the axial skin island along the perforator course with the secondary lobe directed to where the residual medial defect sits; elevate in a suprafascial plane; protect the pedicle by preserving soft tissue around it rather than skeletonizing it; rotate in the direction with least torsion; inset the lobe under the chin to achieve tension-free closure and avoid a tight cervical band. Postoperatively I would closely monitor for venous congestion, pedicle kinking/twisting, distal ischemia of the random extension, dehiscence, and later scar contracture limiting neck motion. Early management should include temporary limitation of neck movement, slight extension, then gradual mobilization once viability is secure.
