items.question_content: A man in his 70s presents to an oral and maxillofacial clinic with 10 years of right tonsillar fossa/upper neck pain, dysphagia, foreign-body sensation, and voice change, now worsened by head turning and accompanied by severe unilateral headache, dizziness, intermittent diplopia, tinnitus, and eye congestion. Brain MRI has been unrevealing, inflammatory markers are normal, and a short steroid course did not resolve symptoms. Examining fig_01.jpg, what is the most appropriate definitive management pathway now, and why is that pathway preferable to other reasonable options in this patient?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is symptomatic vascular Eagle syndrome with combined carotid and jugular involvement: an elongated/mineralized stylohyoid complex is mechanically injuring the right extracranial ICA, producing a pseudoaneurysm, while also contributing to right IJV compression against C1. The symptom pattern fits both arterial/sympathetic irritation (neck pain, dizziness, diplopia) and venous outflow obstruction (headache, tinnitus, eye congestion), and the normal inflammatory workup plus failure of steroids make isolated carotidynia/TIPIC unlikely.

Management should be urgent referral to a multidisciplinary vascular/head-and-neck surgical team for definitive decompression of the causative stylohyoid complex through a controlled cervical approach, combined with assessment and repair/reconstruction of the ICA pseudoaneurysm as needed. The key principle is that the external mechanical cause must be removed; otherwise the artery and vein remain at risk.

This is preferable to conservative or symptom-only care because a symptomatic extracranial ICA pseudoaneurysm carries risk of thromboembolism, stroke/TIA, rupture, and continued local neurovascular compression, while persistent IJV compression can sustain intracranial venous hypertension symptoms. Isolated endovascular treatment would be less suitable if the vessel is markedly looped/tortuous and still externally compressed; venous stenting or medical therapy alone would also fail to address the osseoligamentous entrapment. Avoid provocative tonsillar/styloid manipulation. Post-treatment surveillance should include vascular imaging such as duplex ultrasound and/or CTA to confirm ICA patency and relief of jugular compression, with monitoring for neurologic and cranial nerve complications.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends only symptomatic dental/medical care, reassurance, or nonspecific referral; does not propose definitive management of the vascular lesion.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes need for referral or surgery but gives an incomplete plan, such as styloid treatment without addressing the ICA pseudoaneurysm, or vascular repair without relieving the external compression.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends urgent multidisciplinary operative management with cervical decompression of the stylohyoid complex and vascular surgical assessment/repair of the ICA pseudoaneurysm.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides the above plan and clearly justifies why definitive treatment must remove the external compressive cause and address the arterial injury; includes appropriate postoperative vascular surveillance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores key symptoms or fig_01.jpg and does not connect the presentation to a combined neurovascular compression syndrome.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies Eagle syndrome or a vascular abnormality but does not integrate both the arterial and venous components or the significance of positional worsening and failed inflammatory treatment.

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly correlates arterial/sympathetic symptoms with the ICA lesion and venous symptoms with jugular outflow obstruction, while using the normal inflammatory workup and steroid failure to argue against a purely inflammatory diagnosis.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances operative risks against the greater danger of persistent mechanical arterial and venous compression, and explains why isolated endovascular or conservative options may be inadequate in a tortuous externally compressed vessel.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Treats the problem as routine or elective without urgent escalation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests expedited referral but underestimates the significance of the symptomatic pseudoaneurysm and neuro-ophthalmic symptoms.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies the need for urgent vascular/head-and-neck evaluation because of symptomatic extracranial ICA pseudoaneurysm with concurrent IJV compression.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly triages as urgent and advises avoidance of provocative office manipulation because of immediate risk of embolic or other neurovascular complications.

Generic Textbook Management: treating this only as uncomplicated neuralgia/TMD/Eagle pain with analgesics, steroids, splints, or other conservative care while ignoring the combined carotid pseudoaneurysm and jugular compression on fig_01.jpg.

items.question_content: A 47-year-old woman presents with acute right periorbital swelling and pain with eye movements 2 months after maxillary molar extraction. Review fig_01.jpg. Using the Chandler classification—stage I: preseptal cellulitis; stage II: orbital cellulitis; stage III: subperiosteal abscess; stage IV: orbital abscess; stage V: cavernous sinus thrombosis—which stage best fits this orbital infection?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: Chandler stage II corresponds to orbital cellulitis: infection posterior to the orbital septum without formation of a subperiosteal or orbital abscess. The described post-septal fat stranding places the process beyond simple preseptal cellulitis, while the absence of a drainable collection excludes stages III and IV.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. Select all findings that directly support active iatrogenic displacement of tooth 41 as the dominant mechanism of recession, rather than background mucogingival susceptibility alone.

Marked labiolingual torque discrepancy of tooth 41 relative to adjacent incisors

Absence of attached gingiva at tooth 41

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The decisive finding was preserved eruptive capacity without a normal eruption trajectory. In other words, the canine lacked a physiologic eruptive path, indicating ectopic positioning and explaining why active surgical-orthodontic guidance was needed rather than observation alone.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. Which pretreatment findings most strongly argue that this was a growth-modifiable skeletal/airway problem rather than isolated dental crowding? Select all that apply.

Narrow maxillary arch with a high palatal vault
Failed water-holding test
Normal number and eruption sequence of teeth
Caries in 55, 54, 74, 84, and 85
3-mm mandibular midline deviation to the right
Periapical lesion of 74

items.question_content: A 21-year-old man seeks right posterior mandibular bone grafting and implant rehabilitation after prior gunshot-related reconstruction. He also reports numbness and pressure pain on the inner aspect of the left mandible. Panoramic imaging is atypical, and CBCT/3D views are provided in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg. Based on these figures, outline the operative plan you would adopt before any mandibular surgery in this patient and justify how the imaging should change your approach. Focus on which sites you would treat as high risk, whether the planned rehabilitation can proceed now, and the key modifications to access, anesthesia, fixation or osteotomy planning, and counseling needed to avoid neurovascular or midline lingual complications.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The CBCT makes the left anterior mandible a high-risk zone. The normal buccal mental foramen is absent on the left; instead, the main mental foramen exits lingually, the mandibular canal then courses forward along a lingual groove, and a second anterior labial exit is present between the left canine and first premolar. Therefore I would not use routine mental foramen landmarks for any left-sided flap design, implant planning, apical surgery, bone harvest, or trans-cortical fixation. The left canine-premolar region and adjacent lingual cortex must be treated as a neurovascular danger area because both the lingual exit and anterior labial exit are vulnerable.

The planned right posterior grafting and implant rehabilitation can proceed only with standard site-specific CBCT planning of the right side, because the variation is unilateral and there is no reason to delay all treatment solely because of the left-sided anomaly. However, before any additional surgery I would document baseline neurosensory status on the left and warn the patient that prior symptoms increase the importance of avoiding further nerve trauma.

Operatively, if treatment is required near the left anterior mandible, I would use limited exposure, avoid vertical releases or osteotomies across the anomalous canal pathway, avoid bicortical screws or fixation that could cross the lingual groove or anterior exit, and plan any osteotomy trajectory only after tracing the canal in all planes. Mental nerve infiltration based on expected buccal foramen position may be unreliable or hazardous on the left, so anesthesia should be planned from the proximal inferior alveolar nerve course with supplemental techniques as needed rather than assuming normal mental nerve anatomy.

The enlarged, atypical genial tubercles create a second hazard at the lingual midline. Retraction, graft fixation, or osteotomy in that region should protect the prominent tubercles and attached genioglossus/geniohyoid muscles to avoid fracture, bleeding, or functional morbidity. Counseling should specifically cover persistent or worsened paresthesia, bleeding, traumatic neuroma risk, anesthesia difficulty, and possible lingual midline complications.

items.question_content:
A 55-year-old woman with progressive systemic sclerosis reports intermittent dry mouth and wants a fixed maxillary rehabilitation. She declines the initially proposed option of fixed anterior crowns with a removable posterior prosthesis. In patients with sclerosis and xerostomia, reducing broad prosthesis-mucosa contact may be advantageous. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg.

Based on the clinical findings and figures, outline the maxillary treatment plan you would offer. Your answer should: (1) identify the anatomic obstacle affecting conventional implant placement, (2) explain why a fixed solution may be favored in this patient, (3) describe the planned role of digital guidance and why the anterior osteotomies would not be completed as a routine fully guided sequence, and (4) state the main complications that must be minimized during transcanine implant site preparation. Finally, explain how your recommendation would change if the patient later accepted a removable posterior component.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The maxillary plan would be a prosthetically driven fixed rehabilitation that uses carefully planned implant placement despite the impacted canines, rather than defaulting to a removable posterior design. The key anatomic obstacle is the presence of bilateral horizontally impacted maxillary canines occupying the usual anterior implant pathway, as seen on the panoramic image and planning views.

A fixed solution is reasonable here because the patient specifically declines a removable posterior prosthesis, and progressive systemic sclerosis with xerostomia makes broad mucosal coverage less desirable and may complicate tolerance and hygiene with removable appliances.

Digital planning should be used to position the implants according to the intended prosthetic outcome while selecting a trajectory through the canine regions that attempts to avoid enamel. The anterior transcanine sites should not be treated as a routine fully guided drilling sequence because the guide can limit irrigation at the osteotomy and drilling through dense tooth structure raises concern for frictional heat. A suitable approach is guided pilot drilling to establish the trajectory, followed by completion of the osteotomy without the full guide and with additional copious saline irrigation/cooling.

The main complications to minimize during transcanine preparation are thermal injury to bone from inadequate cooling, which could impair osseointegration, and injury to the impacted canine tissues, especially pulpal involvement that could lead to postoperative pain. The procedure also aims to avoid hard enamel during drilling because it can complicate the osteotomy path.

If the patient later accepted a removable posterior component, the plan could become more conservative: fixed crowns could be used in the anterior region and a removable prosthesis in the posterior maxilla, reducing the need to place implants through the impacted canine regions.

items.question_content: Examining fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, a 16-year-old girl presents with poor smile esthetics, severely broken-down maxillary incisors, enamel chipping with dentin exposure in 11, 12, 21, 22, 34, and 44, generalized enamel opacities, and congenital absence of 31, 32, 33, 41, 42, and 43. IOPA findings show radiolucency involving enamel, dentin, and pulp with widened PDL spaces for 11, 12, 21, and 22; 34 and 44 show enamel-dentin radiolucency without periapical change. Cold and electric pulp tests are negative for 11, 12, 21, and 22, but positive for 34 and 44. There are no hair or skin abnormalities, and family history is noncontributory. What is the most appropriate staged management plan, including the working diagnosis, restoration strategy for the maxillary anterior teeth, management of the mandibular anterior edentulous space at this age, and why two plausible alternatives would be inappropriate?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The working diagnosis is localized enamel hypoplasia affecting 11, 12, 21, 22, 34, and 44, associated with nonsyndromic oligodontia of the mandibular anterior segment. Amelogenesis imperfecta and ectodermal dysplasia are less likely because the defect is not a generalized inherited ectodermal pattern and there are no extraoral ectodermal findings; rampant caries is less consistent with the developmental pattern and congenital agenesis. Management should be staged and tooth-preserving: first disease control and diagnosis confirmation, then conventional root canal treatment for 11, 12, 21, and 22 because they are nonvital with pulpal involvement, followed by post-endodontic composite core build-up using fiber posts to improve stress distribution in structurally compromised roots. If ferrule is inadequate, perform crown lengthening before definitive preparation. Definitive esthetic rehabilitation of the maxillary anteriors can then be completed with full-coverage crowns such as lithium disilicate, ideally guided by diagnostic smile design/wax-up. Teeth 34 and 44 should be restored conservatively with direct composite because they are still vital and show no periapical disease. For the mandibular anterior agenesis, the appropriate option at age 16 is an interim removable partial denture with an acrylic base, with periodic review and modification during growth; definitive implant or fixed prosthetic replacement should be deferred until skeletal growth is complete and space/occlusion are stable. Two inappropriate alternatives are extracting the maxillary incisors instead of restoring them, and placing immediate implants or a definitive fixed bridge in the mandibular anterior region now; both are unnecessarily irreversible, and the latter is particularly problematic in an actively growing patient.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. A 29-year-old medically fit nonsmoker presents with a fractured, root-canal-treated maxillary right lateral incisor (#12) in the esthetic zone. Periodontal probing is 3 mm or less, the tooth is non-mobile and non-tender, oral hygiene is acceptable, and the gingival biotype is thin. What definitive surgical-restorative approach would you choose for replacing #12, and why is it the best fit for this patient? Justify your plan using the preoperative clinical and CBCT findings in fig_01.jpg, outline the key sequencing and 3-dimensional positioning principles needed to preserve the facial tissues, and state the intraoperative findings that should make you change course.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best plan is partial extraction therapy with a socket-shield and immediate implant placement, with immediate provisionalization only if primary stability is achieved and the provisional can be kept out of occlusion. This patient is a strong candidate because the tooth is in the maxillary esthetic zone, the soft tissue biotype and facial plate are thin, and full extraction would risk facial collapse and recession. fig_01.jpg also supports feasibility: the root appears straight and the socket anatomy is favorable for palatal implant positioning, while the absence of tenderness, mobility, deep pockets, or periapical pathology lowers concern for active infection.

The sequence is: atraumatically section the root, remove only the palatal portion, preserve a stable buccal root fragment, reduce and smooth it just below the gingival margin, then prepare the osteotomy palatal to that fragment so the implant gains palatal/apical bone support without displacing the facial tissues. The implant must be positioned prosthetically and palatally, not against the facial plate or the retained fragment, and provisionalization should be non-functional.

I would abandon or modify the plan if the buccal fragment becomes mobile or fractures, if a crack extends into the retained portion, if the facial plate is damaged, if unexpected infection or granulation tissue suggests the retained segment is not maintainable, or if correct 3-D implant position and primary stability cannot be obtained. In those situations I would convert to complete extraction and a more conventional staged or site-preservation approach.

items.question_content: A 13-year-old girl requires uprighting of a severely mesially tipped, deeply impacted mandibular left first molar. Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. It converts the force system into near-pure bodily distalization with minimal vertical effect on the first molar.
A retromolar miniscrew would be less suitable because distal traction on this deeply impacted first molar could be unfavorable.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: For a deeply impacted, severely mesially tipped mandibular first molar, the cantilever must deliver a strong uprighting moment while also allowing eruption. An anterior miniscrew increases cantilever length, so the needed moment can be produced with less extrusive force. Retromolar anchorage would tend to apply distal traction, which was considered unfavorable for this first molar position.

items.question_content: An 8.9-year-old girl in mixed dentition with a skeletal Class III is being considered for early treatment. Examine fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. Would the appliance shown in fig_01.jpg be an appropriate first-phase choice for this patient? Defend your decision using the facial, occlusal, and cephalometric pattern visible, explain the biomechanical goals you would prioritize, and state the main next-step and prognosis issues you would discuss with the family.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Yes. A PS3-type full-coverage intraoral pushing-splint is an appropriate first phase here because the records show more than a simple dental anterior crossbite: the patient has a skeletal Class III pattern in mixed dentition with negative overjet/open-bite tendency, bilateral posterior crossbite, and a markedly hyperdivergent vertical pattern on cephalometric tracing. The key objective is therefore sagittal improvement without worsening lower facial height.

The main biomechanical priority is vertical control while correcting the Class III relationship. A pushing-splint that covers the dentition and applies forward force to the maxilla and backward force to the mandible is well suited to a child whose severe vertical pattern makes bite-opening side effects especially undesirable. Compared with generic Class III traction approaches that can extrude posterior teeth and rotate the mandible clockwise, this choice is better matched to the need to limit further vertical opening.

My plan would be an interceptive orthopedic phase now, while growth remains modifiable, with close monitoring of compliance and of overjet, overbite, molar/canine relationship, transverse fit, and vertical cephalometric response. I would aim for a clearly positive overjet, even mild sagittal overcorrection, before transitioning later to comprehensive fixed appliances to align the arches, refine intercuspation, and address any residual open-bite or transverse problems as the permanent dentition erupts.

Counseling should be guarded but positive: early treatment can improve the sagittal jaw relationship and may reduce the severity of later treatment needs, but the severe structural hyperdivergent pattern makes long-term vertical control and facial esthetics less predictable. Continued growth could limit stability, so long-term follow-up is essential and future camouflage or orthognathic correction may still be needed if skeletal or profile concerns remain.

items.question_content: An 11-year-old boy with clinical features of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia presents because the appearance of his teeth has led to bullying at school. He has asthma but is otherwise healthy. All erupted teeth are vital; plaque score is 29%, and BPE shows no pockets deeper than 3 mm. Use fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg for the dentofacial, occlusal, and radiographic findings. If your goal over the next 18 months is to achieve the greatest functional and psychosocial benefit without compromising definitive rehabilitation in late adolescence, formulate a phased management strategy. Decide which single dental site you would actively preserve or create space for, and which single site you would deliberately avoid setting up as a definitive replacement space at this age. Justify both decisions from the figures. Then explain what clinical or radiographic changes would make you move from observation to surgical exposure or active orthodontic traction at the preserved-space site, and how your plan would differ if the patient were already skeletally mature.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The plan should be interceptive and multidisciplinary, with prevention first: reinforce plaque control, fluoride-based prevention, and restore active disease before prolonged orthodontic treatment.

The site I would actively preserve/create space for is the maxillary left posterior segment. fig_03.jpg shows an unerupted/displaced 25 with space loss, and in a child with ectodermal dysplasia every present permanent tooth is strategically valuable. Recovering space here can save a permanent tooth, preserve posterior support, and reduce later prosthetic burden. Management would be to regain and maintain space orthodontically, typically by uprighting/distalizing the adjacent teeth and monitoring eruption once adequate space exists. In the same quadrant, I would be cautious about sacrificing retained primary teeth that may temporarily support aesthetics or function unless they obstruct the eruption path or compromise the plan.

The site I would avoid setting up as definitive replacement space now is the mandibular incisor segment. fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg show severe lower anterior tooth-size deficiency with absent lower central incisors and small/conical remaining incisors. In an 11-year-old, creating or preserving two ideal lower incisor implant spaces is usually a poor interceptive goal because growth is ongoing and the lower anterior segment is biologically and prosthetically unfavorable for definitive replacement at this stage. Instead, I would align the lower incisors, remove the retained primary incisor when appropriate, centralize and consolidate the space into a simplified restorable arrangement, improve tooth form with additive composite, and if replacement is needed use a minimally invasive interim option such as a resin-bonded approach rather than definitive implants.

I would escalate the maxillary left site from observation to exposure/traction when: sufficient space has been created clinically and confirmed radiographically; the path of eruption remains unfavorable or eruption does not progress after a reasonable review period; root development and position suggest the tooth is still salvageable; and there is no sign of ankylosis or another obstruction that makes spontaneous eruption unlikely. If these milestones are not met, continued monitoring after space recovery is reasonable.

If the patient were already skeletally mature, the principle of saving 25 would remain, but the restorative planning could become more definitive. Space and root positions could be set up more deliberately for final prosthetic solutions where needed, such as resin-bonded bridgework or implants if anatomy permits. In the lower incisor region, definitive replacement would become a more realistic option only after confirming adequate alveolar width, root divergence, occlusion, and long-term maintenance prognosis.

items.question_content: A 13-year-old girl has left posterior bite collapse, delayed eruption of the mandibular left first molar, and pain where the opposing maxillary molar is biting into mandibular soft tissue. Examine fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. If the goal is to preserve both mandibular molars, what staged orthodontic strategy is most defensible? Specify which problem you would address first, what type of force system you would choose for the mandibular second molar and for the mandibular first molar, and where you would place mandibular skeletal anchorage. Justify the sequence and mechanics from the tooth positions in the figures, especially the differing need for distalization versus eruption, and explain how your plan reduces the main unwanted effects during uprighting.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The first priority is to create vertical clearance by intruding the over-erupted maxillary left first molar, because it is traumatically contacting the mandibular gingiva and would block safe uprighting/extrusion of the mandibular molars. After clearance is gained, I would treat the mandibular second molar before the first molar. On fig_02.jpg, the second molar is mesially tipped and overhangs the first-molar space, so it is the immediate obstacle to eruption of the first molar. Its main requirement is distalization with uprighting, not major eruption. Therefore I would use a compression-based uprighting/distalizing system on the lower arch that produces a distal force and uprighting moment with minimal extrusion, ideally with the active wire segment kept inferior to avoid occlusal interference.

Only after space has been recovered and the first molar crown is accessible would I surgically expose the mandibular first molar and upright it with a cantilever system. This tooth is much more deeply impacted and severely mesially tipped, so it needs a large uprighting moment plus eruption/extrusion to reach occlusion; a cantilever is appropriate because it can deliver both. Mandibular skeletal anchorage should be placed anterior to the molars, preferably between the canine and first premolar, to provide a long cantilever arm and a larger uprighting moment for a given vertical force. An anterior TAD is preferable to retromolar anchorage here because distal traction from behind could be unfavorable for a deeply impacted first molar whose center of resistance is positioned distally relative to its final position. Hooking the cantilever to the TAD, rather than the main archwire, also avoids intrusive side effects on the rest of the dentition.

Key unwanted effects to control are occlusal interference from extrusion, intrusive reaction on anchor teeth, unwanted arch distortion, tube debonding, and TAD soft-tissue/loosening problems. My plan limits these by intruding the opposing maxillary molar first, using a low-extrusion distalizing system for the second molar, reserving the extrusive cantilever for the first molar only when clearance and space exist, and using anterior skeletal anchorage to reduce adverse reactions elsewhere in the arch.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links complications directly to preventive design choices in this case: gain vertical clearance first, select minimal-extrusion mechanics for the second molar, use TAD-supported cantilever rather than the main archwire for the first molar, and choose a longer anterior cantilever to achieve the needed moment with less harmful side effect.

items.question_content: A healthy 10-year-old boy in early mixed dentition is distressed by the appearance of his upper front teeth. There is no trauma history, and the overall tooth count is normal. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg, determine the most likely anomaly affecting each maxillary central incisor and formulate the best management strategy at this stage. State whether you would intervene now or defer, what tooth mass you would remove or preserve, and whether movement of a maxillary incisor across the midpalatal suture is justified here. Defend your choice by integrating figure-based anatomy, space analysis, skeletal pattern/growth, and long-term restorative implications. Also give one reasonable alternative plan you would reject, explain why, and state how your recommendation would change if the same anatomy presented after skeletal maturity. Conclude with the main complications that would require active monitoring if your preferred plan were used.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
This is bilateral double-tooth anomaly, but the two centrals are not the same. With a normal tooth count, the right maxillary central (#11) is most consistent with fusion to a supernumerary tooth, while the left central (#21) is more consistent with incomplete gemination. fig_02.jpg is the key: #11 shows two distinct roots with individualized pulp spaces, whereas #21 shows a single enlarged root/common pulp configuration. fig_01.jpg supports abnormal enlarged crowns with notching, and fig_04.jpg shows major arch-length deficiency; fig_03.jpg suggests a skeletal Class I pattern with slight vertical tendency, so treatment should ideally relieve crowding without worsening profile.

I would intervene now rather than defer, because the child has an active esthetic complaint and is still growing, making orthodontic movement across the midpalatal suture biologically more acceptable than after maturation. My preferred plan would be to extract #21 and preserve #11, then mesialize the retained fused #11 across the midpalatal suture as part of comprehensive orthodontic treatment. I would use #11 as the tooth mass occupying the two central-incisor positions rather than routinely performing immediate hemisection/separation, because preserving vitality and avoiding extra surgical/endodontic/restorative burden is more conservative at this age. Later, minor recontouring/restorative refinement can improve tooth form if needed.

Why this is the best fit here: #11 has greater usable dental mass and two rooted components, making it the more serviceable tooth to keep. Removing #21 reduces anterior tooth mass and helps space management in a patient who already has severe upper and lower crowding visible on fig_04.jpg. This also preserves a natural tooth and alveolar support, avoids committing a 10-year-old to prosthetic replacement, and is compatible with maintaining the facial profile in a Class I skeletal pattern.

A reasonable alternative would be to defer definitive anterior management until skeletal maturity and later use hemisection/restorative reconstruction or extraction with prosthetic replacement. I would reject that now because it prolongs the psychosocial burden, misses the biologic advantage of treatment during growth, and increases future surgical/endodontic/prosthetic complexity. Extracting both anomalous incisors with later implants would be especially inappropriate in a growing child.

If the same anatomy presented after skeletal maturity, I would be more cautious about planned movement across the midpalatal suture because of a more ossified suture and higher concern for root resorption and periodontal compromise. My threshold to choose restorative-surgical options, hemisection, or a different space-management strategy would therefore be lower in the adult.

Main complications to monitor are external root resorption during cross-suture movement, pulpal vitality and periodontal status of the retained tooth, frenum stretching/inflammation and relapse tendency, adjacent root proximity and torque control because of the divergent roots, and decalcification/white-spot lesions during prolonged treatment.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old girl requests orthodontic treatment. From fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, she has bilateral ~90° rotation of the maxillary second premolars, prior loss of the maxillary and mandibular first premolars, mild crowding in both arches, a 4-mm deep bite, Class II subdivision, skeletal Class I, a hypodivergent pattern, and proclined upper incisors. What initial orthodontic biomechanics and anchorage strategy would you choose for the maxillary premolars, and why is it the best fit for this patient? Explain how your plan would control unwanted reciprocal or vertical effects during derotation and how you would reduce long-term relapse risk.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would use direct skeletal anchorage for the maxillary second premolars rather than relying on adjacent teeth or a continuous base arch as the main anchorage. The key is to create a true rotational couple on each rotated premolar, ideally from buccal and palatal attachments supported by TADs, so the tooth rotates with minimal translation. This is the best fit here because the rotations are severe and bilateral, first premolars are already missing, and conventional tooth-borne mechanics would risk reciprocal movement of canines/molars, anchorage loss, and slower correction while the patient still needs crowding relief and bite correction.

I would start derotation early and simultaneously align the rest of the arches with light wires, then fully engage the premolars once they are sufficiently derotated. Because she has a deep bite and hypodivergent pattern, vertical side effects matter: the force vector should be kept as close to the occlusal plane as practical to minimize unwanted intrusion or tipping of the premolars and avoid worsening the bite; screw stability, soft-tissue irritation, and root clearance should be monitored. After derotation, residual space can be used strategically during space closure and bite correction.

Relapse risk is high after derotating premolars, so I would plan prolonged retention, preferably bonded retention with a removable overlay retainer as needed, and add circumferential supracrestal fiberotomy once final tooth position is stable to reduce supracrestal fiber rebound.

items.question_content: A 10-year-old boy presents 6 years after trauma to the primary maxillary incisors; CBCT is declined. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg and fig_06.jpg. You are taking over the case at the stage shown in fig_06.jpg panel A-B. Based on the evolution visible across the figures, what should be done next for the left anterior maxilla? Defend your decision against the other reasonable paths suggested by the case, rather than simply naming a technique. Explain which tooth you would prioritize now, the surgical-orthodontic design you would use to obtain eruption while preserving the gingival outcome of 2.1, and one specific finding that would make you change to a different plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The next step at the fig_06.jpg stage is not mere continuation of the original approach unchanged and not a shift in priority to the canine. The best next intervention is a modified interdisciplinary orthodontic-periodontal step focused on 2.1: surgically re-expose the central incisor and provide/transpose keratinized tissue to it, then continue light orthodontic traction and later derotation.

The figure sequence supports this. fig_01.jpg shows trauma-related sequelae with a large lesion around the primary incisors and displacement of the permanent anterior teeth. fig_02.jpg shows that after removal of the primary obstruction/infection, 2.2 regained eruptive progress, which argues for preserving and guiding the permanent teeth rather than extracting them. fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg show that despite space control and orthodontic setup, 2.1 still has not erupted, so further passive observation is no longer the most defensible choice. fig_05.jpg shows why simple waiting is inadequate: 2.1 is submucosal, positioned apically to the crest, horizontal in the sagittal plane, and rotated. By fig_06.jpg it is closer to eruption, but it is still emerging in a mucogingival situation where periodontal quality is now the key issue.

Therefore, I would still prioritize 2.1 before the canine. Central incisor position determines anterior esthetics, midline control, and safe root relationships for later movements. At this stage I would use a tissue-preserving exposure that places keratinized tissue on the labial aspect of 2.1, such as a laterally positioned pedicle flap from the adjacent keratinized tissue, while keeping orthodontic forces light and directed to bring the tooth through the center of the alveolar ridge rather than labially through thin mucosa. This is preferable to continuing the initial closed traction alone, because once the crown is near eruption but still in alveolar mucosa, unchanged traction risks inadequate keratinized tissue and later recession. It is also preferable to a wide open-window exposure, which would worsen soft-tissue loss, and to prioritizing canine traction first, which would compete for space/anchorage and increase risk to adjacent roots before the central incisor path is secured.

The canine should remain secondary until 2.1 is brought into a favorable position and the periodontal envelope is protected; 2.2 can be aligned conservatively as indicated by its spontaneous improvement. Because CBCT is unavailable, serial 2D radiographic and clinical reassessment is important during movement.

A finding that would make me change plan would be evidence suggesting that orthodontic eruption is not biologically feasible, especially suspected ankylosis: no movement over time despite appropriate force, metallic percussion sound, or radiographic signs inconsistent with normal movement. In that situation I would reassess the diagnosis and prognosis rather than simply increasing traction. If, conversely, the crown were already emerging through adequate attached gingiva, a second mucogingival procedure might be unnecessary and I would continue conservative traction/alignment only.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg panel g. A 60-year-old woman received natural tooth pontics in a fiber-reinforced composite bridge after extraction of hopeless maxillary lateral incisors. The pontic tissue surface was shaped to lightly contact the ridge while remaining floss-cleansable. What is this tissue-side pontic form called?

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The case described the tissue surface as a sanitary ovate form. It combines esthetic ridge contact with embrasure access for flossing and avoids the hygiene limitations of a broad ridge-lap design.

This differs from erosion, which is chemically driven and often shows smooth cupping, and from abrasion, which is usually linked to an external mechanical habit.

items.question_content: A healthy 40-year-old man requires implant placement in the posterior maxilla with only 4 mm of residual subantral bone. The panoramic radiograph in fig_01.jpg appears to show no relevant sinus abnormality, but during a lateral-window sinus augmentation the anatomy in fig_02.jpg is encountered; fig_03.jpg later clarifies its full extent. Based on these figures, what is the most appropriate diagnosis of this anatomic variant, how should the sinus lift be modified intraoperatively, and what preoperative imaging and risk-control changes are essential in similar future cases?

golden_answer.subjective_answer: The key finding is a rare complete horizontal maxillary sinus septum dividing the sinus into superior and inferior compartments. The panoramic image failed to show it, and the cross-sectional image demonstrates both its extent and an additional septal anatomy, confirming that panoramic imaging alone is inadequate for surgical planning. With only 4 mm of residual bone, a lateral sinus augmentation is still appropriate, but a standard single hinge-door/window should not be forced upward and medially because that greatly increases Schneiderian membrane perforation risk. The safest modification is to create separate smaller lateral access windows/osteotomies above and below the septum, or otherwise access each compartment separately, then elevate the membrane compartment by compartment and graft both spaces. The septum should be preserved if it does not interfere with implant trajectory, because it can serve as a tenting support for the graft; septum removal should be reserved only for a low or obstructive septum that prevents adequate augmentation or implant placement after careful membrane dissection. For similar future cases, preoperative CBCT/CT should be obtained routinely for posterior maxillary sinus augmentation, especially when residual bone is limited, to identify septal number, orientation, height, and relationship to the implant site so window design and staging can be planned. Main risks to anticipate and prevent are membrane perforation, incomplete sinus elevation, graft displacement, postoperative sinusitis, and implant malposition.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Fails

items.question_content: Four years after a regenerative endodontic procedure on tooth 2.2 for pulp necrosis/chronic apical abscess associated with dens invaginatus, the patient returns with mild relapse in the maxillary anterior segment and wants the quickest correction. Assume this could be managed either by full engagement of all four maxillary incisors or by a more limited plan that accepts a small residual discrepancy to reduce movement of one tooth. Tooth 2.2 is asymptomatic, has physiologic mobility, probing depths ≤3 mm, mild discoloration, and a delayed cold response. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, decide whether 2.2 should be actively moved, mainly passively engaged/bypassed, or excluded from retreatment. Identify which maxillary incisor you would protect most from further mechanics, explain how the CBCT/panoramic findings support that choice, and state what planned movement or follow-up change would make you switch to the more conservative option.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would not automatically exclude or bypass 2.2. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, I would allow only limited active movement of 2.2 if it is necessary for relapse correction, but I would design the retreatment around protecting the maxillary incisor(s) that already show more apical shortening—most clearly 1.2 on fig_02.jpg, and likely the other incisors with moderate remodeling.

Why: fig_01.jpg supports endodontic stability of 2.2: the previous periapical disease has resolved, surrounding bone appears healed, and there is no sign of recurrent apical pathology. fig_01.jpg also shows intracanalar hard-tissue change after REP (dentin bridge/mineralized tissue with coronal calcific change), which suggests healing but also means this is not a normal pulp space and future endodontic access could be more difficult if problems arise later. fig_02.jpg is the key comparative image: 2.2 shows only minimal apical remodeling, whereas 1.2 and the adjacent maxillary incisors show greater shortening/remodeling. So REP history alone does not make 2.2 the tooth I would protect most; radiographically, 1.2 is more vulnerable.

Plan: if the relapse can be corrected with small alignment changes, I would include 2.2 with very light, well-controlled forces and small activations, while avoiding making any already shortened incisor the high-demand tooth. I would avoid aggressive continuous mechanics, especially significant intrusion, marked palatal root torque, large bodily movement, or using 2.2 as a major anchorage/force-delivery tooth. Baseline periapical imaging before retreatment is reasonable; follow with clinical review and limited conventional radiographic reassessment if the movement is more than trivial or if symptoms/signs change. CBCT should be reserved for uncertainty or new pathology, not routine monitoring.

I would switch to the more conservative option—accepting some residual discrepancy or bypassing 2.2—if the planned correction requires high-risk movements such as substantial intrusion or root torque of 2.2, or if follow-up shows pain, percussion tenderness, increasing mobility, probing changes, recurrent periapical radiolucency, or progressive apical shortening. In summary, 2.2 can be moved cautiously, but the imaging suggests the tooth to protect most is not the REP-treated lateral incisor; it is the incisor(s) with greater existing apical resorption, especially 1.2.

items.question_content: A 12-year-old girl presents because of a convex profile and prominent maxillary incisors. Cephalometry shows ANB 5°, SNB 75°, U1/NA 42°, with a mild hyperdivergent tendency. Study fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg only. Before any treatment is started, formulate the most defensible strategy for the first 6–9 months. Do not just list appliances. Your answer should: (1) state your primary objective in order of priority; (2) identify the single pretreatment feature in the figures that most changes your biomechanics from a routine Class II division 1 case, and explain why; (3) define your space-management philosophy for this patient and justify it; (4) give one reasonable competing strategy you rejected and why; (5) specify two review findings that would make you continue your plan and two that would make you change it; and (6) explain how poor compliance with elastics/removable appliances would alter your mechanics while preserving your goals.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The priorities should be: first, control the vertical/posterior occlusal environment; second, use remaining growth to favor a more forward mandibular response without increasing lower facial height; third, reduce maxillary incisor protrusion/overjet and coordinate the constricted maxillary arch; fourth, finish the Class II correction with minimal lower-incisor compensation.

The pretreatment feature that most changes the biomechanics is the posterior eruption relationship visible on fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg: the maxillary second molars are still erupting and appear to have inadequate vertical room, while the lower posterior segment is relatively more erupted, creating an unfavorable steep posterior occlusal relationship in a mildly hyperdivergent Class II patient. That makes this different from a routine overjet-reduction case, because mechanics that add posterior vertical dimension or extrude upper incisors/lower molars risk clockwise mandibular rotation and worsening facial balance.

My space philosophy would be a staged nonextraction approach initially, not a reflex extraction plan. The skeletal discrepancy is mild, growth remains, lower crowding is limited, and the maxillary arch is constricted rather than massively tooth-size deficient. Space can be sought through arch coordination/expansion, posterior development/distalization potential, and conservative lower-arch management rather than relying on uncontrolled lower-incisor flaring. Limited interproximal reduction in the lower incisors is acceptable if needed to protect incisor position.

A reasonable competing strategy is premolar-extraction camouflage, especially because the overjet is large and the upper incisors are markedly proclined. I would not begin there because it does not address the posterior vertical/eruption problem that appears to be influencing mandibular posture, and the patient still has growth that may be harnessed. However, extraction remains a fallback if early treatment fails to improve the posterior vertical relationship or if lower-incisor compensation becomes excessive.

The first 6–9 months should focus on posterior disclusion/vertical reorganization to create room for eruption/uprighting of the maxillary terminal molars and reduce posterior interference, while simultaneously leveling the lower arch and flattening the curve of Spee with torque control. After that, align the upper arch, coordinate/expand the narrow maxillary arch, retract and torque-control the upper incisors, and use sagittal correction mechanics chosen to minimize extrusion of upper incisors and lower molars. Conventional long Class II elastics should not be the main engine of correction.

Findings that would support continuing the plan include: (1) increasing vertical room or eruption/uprighting of the maxillary second molars with a flatter posterior occlusal relationship, and (2) improvement in overjet/Class II relationship without clockwise mandibular opening or unacceptable lower-incisor flaring. Findings that would make me change course include: (1) persistent lack of posterior eruption/vertical improvement or ongoing terminal-molar space impasse, and (2) worsening lower-incisor proclination, open-bite tendency, or failure of vertical control. Clear compliance failure is another strong reason to alter the plan.

If compliance with elastics or removable appliances is poor, the goals do not change: vertical control and favorable posterior occlusal reorganization remain central. What changes is the delivery system: I would shift toward less compliance-dependent fixed biomechanics for anchorage/vertical control and be quicker to reconsider camouflage with tooth removal if the same goals cannot be achieved predictably without overcompensation.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. A 16-year-old male who is still growing seeks the most durable rehabilitation for severely compromised posterior dentition. Using only the pretreatment information, formulate the one management strategy you would present as your primary recommendation. Defend it by stating which posterior teeth you would attempt to save and which you would sacrifice, identifying the single pretreatment finding that most limits your orthodontic mechanics, and explaining how that finding changes your anchorage/force design. Also name the strongest plausible competing strategy you would reject for this patient and why. Finally, give a contingency if one maxillary right premolar later proves non-restorable after initial disease control.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
My primary recommendation would be definitive rehabilitation by infection control and selective extractions followed by comprehensive orthodontic space closure, rather than a plan that mainly preserves spaces for later prosthetic replacement.

Tooth-by-tooth, UR6 and LL6 are hopeless residual roots and should be removed. UL5 is also the maxillary left tooth I would sacrifice because of its severe structural/periapical compromise and because that space can be used strategically. In contrast, UR4 and UR5 should not be extracted automatically; if they are structurally restorable after endodontic assessment, I would try to retain them with endodontic treatment and coronal protection because keeping these teeth reduces unnecessary loss of dental units on the maxillary right while still allowing posterior rehabilitation. All third molars should be preserved if feasible, with LL8 uprighted and incorporated into the mandibular left posterior replacement sequence.

The single pretreatment finding that most constrains mechanics is the CBCT evidence that the maxillary incisor roots are already against the labial cortical plate in a Class II division 2 pattern. That means anchorage cannot rely on reciprocal anterior effects. I would use skeletal anchorage, ideally anterior palatal indirect anchorage for the maxillary arch, to stabilize the anterior segment and permit posterior mesialization with controlled 3D force vectors close to the posterior segment center of resistance. The aim is to protract posterior teeth without further compromising incisor root position, without lingual collapse of the maxillary incisors, and without unwanted lower anterior displacement during mandibular left protraction. In the mandible, anchorage reinforcement is also needed while LL7 is mesialized and LL8 is uprighted/protracted.

The strongest competing strategy I would reject is interim space maintenance with removable/fixed prosthetic replacement while waiting for implants after growth. It is simpler in the short term, but in this specific patient it does not solve the malocclusion, does not preserve posterior alveolar bone as effectively, leaves a long period of prosthetic dependence during adolescence, and wastes the opportunity created by available second/third molars for biologic space closure. Autotransplantation is less attractive here because it depends on donor/root anatomy and carries ankylosis and resorption risk.

If one maxillary right premolar later proves non-restorable after initial disease control, I would convert that tooth into an additional strategic extraction site and re-evaluate the right-side space-closure plan, anchorage demand, and final occlusal goals. If controlled protraction of UR7/UR8 can still create a functional posterior result without overcompromising symmetry or treatment burden, I would continue orthodontic closure. If not, then limited temporization of the residual space until skeletal maturity becomes a reasonable backup. Key monitoring throughout would include incisor root/cortical safety, root resorption, periodontal status during protraction across atrophic sites, and the endodontic prognosis of retained premolars.

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets

levels.title: Exceeds

levels.description: Anticipates the major case-specific complications and surveillance points, including incisor root/cortical risk, periodontal and alveolar response during long-distance protraction, prognosis of retained UR4/UR5, LL8 integration, and the need to revise the plan if a retained premolar later becomes non-restorable.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old girl with genetically confirmed Freeman–Sheldon syndrome presents for correction of crowding. She has marked microstomia with limited oral access, declines commissuroplasty, and her parents will not consent to extraction of the lingually displaced mandibular second premolars. Tooth 46 is restorable. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, formulate the orthodontic plan you would actually consent this patient for. Focus on decision-making rather than wire sequence: identify the figure-derived finding that most determines your space-management choice; state which problem you would deliberately defer or accept at the finish; define a realistic treatment end point; explain the strongest reasonable alternative plan you would reject in this patient and why; and describe the retention burden you would warn the family about. Finally, if commissuroplasty later became acceptable but lower-premolar extraction still did not, what part of your plan would change, and what part would remain the same?

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most defensible plan is a compromise, non-surgical orthodontic approach after disease control, not an attempt at ideal full correction. First, tooth 46 should be restored and oral-hygiene optimization completed before fixed appliances, because limited opening increases plaque retention and makes restorative access and orthodontic maintenance harder.

The figure-derived finding that most drives space management is the ectopically erupted maxillary canine seen in fig_01.jpg in the setting of severe maxillary crowding. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg also show that the patient otherwise has preserved Class I relationships and a Class I skeletal pattern, so the aim should be to relieve crowding and establish functional overjet/overbite while preserving the existing jaw and molar relationships rather than destabilizing them. In this context, extraction of the ectopic maxillary canine is the most pragmatic space-creating decision: it avoids a prolonged, technically difficult attempt to recover a poorly positioned canine through marked microstomia. By contrast, tooth 46 is restorable and should not be extracted for orthodontic convenience, and lower second-premolar extraction is unavailable because consent is refused.

The problem I would intentionally defer or accept is the lower premolar-related discrepancy: because of the parental refusal, the lingually displaced mandibular second premolars may remain incompletely corrected or be left for later surgical/extraction management. I would also accept that the maxillary midline may shift and canine substitution may be necessary after extraction of 23. My realistic end point is functional alignment with acceptable overjet and overbite, improved anterior aesthetics and hygiene access, and maintenance of the existing Class I framework, not perfect symmetry or complete ideal detailing of every tooth.

The strongest reasonable alternative plan I would reject is comprehensive idealized correction with surgical access improvement and full recovery/alignment of all displaced teeth, or nonsurgical attempts to gain space mainly by expansion/proclination. In this patient, those approaches carry a poor cost-benefit balance: they increase treatment complexity, chair time, hygiene difficulty, and relapse risk in the setting of microstomia and a tight perioral envelope. Even if one considered other maxillary extractions, a plan that preserves the ectopic canine would require more demanding mechanics than this patient’s access and circumstances favor.

Retention must be more intensive than routine because of the strong relapse tendency from the perioral musculature. I would use combined retention: fixed anterior lingual retention plus removable clear retainers, with the maxillary retainer designed with anterior palatal coverage to help preserve the gained transverse dimension. Full-time wear initially, then prolonged night wear, with close long-term review for hygiene, caries, retainer failure, and relapse. Prognosis is good for functional improvement, but guarded for perfect long-term stability.

If commissuroplasty later became acceptable but lower-premolar extraction still did not, the main thing that would change is access: bonding, finishing, and possibly the degree of detailing achievable would improve, and I could reconsider whether any difficult tooth movement is now worth attempting. What would remain the same is the need for a compromise endpoint, the limited value of chasing complete lower idealization while lower extractions remain refused, the importance of preserving the basic Class I framework, and the need for robust long-term retention. Commissuroplasty would make delivery easier, but it would not by itself remove the lower-arch consent constraint or the syndrome-related relapse risk.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides generic orthodontic advice with little or no use of fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg or misreads the major findings.

levels.title: Partial

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates the important findings from fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg and history, including severe crowding with an ectopic maxillary canine, restricted oral access from microstomia, preserved Class I occlusal/skeletal relationships, and lower premolar-related anomaly/complexity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figures and history into a coherent rationale showing why the ectopic maxillary canine is the key space-management issue, why existing Class I relationships should be preserved, and why lower-arch idealization is less attractive under the observed lower premolar anatomy and consent limits.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Plan is unsafe, impractical, or ignores the refusal of commissuroplasty/lower-premolar extraction; or recommends extraction of restorable 46 for orthodontic space without convincing justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests a compromise approach but is vague, poorly sequenced, or does not define a realistic end point or intentionally accepted residual problem.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a feasible compromise plan with disease control first, then limited-access fixed appliance therapy aimed at functional alignment, acceptable overjet/overbite, and preservation of the existing Class I framework; supports extraction of the ectopic maxillary canine or a comparably well-justified alternative; accepts a residual mandibular premolar-related discrepancy and/or upper midline consequence; includes appropriate retention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear stepwise plan the clinician could realistically consent: restoration/hygiene first, practical mechanics compatible with microstomia, explicit space-management decision tied to the figures, clearly stated deferred/accepted problem, realistic finish, and retention tailored to the final occlusal goals.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or ignores the implications of access limitation, consent refusal, and stability.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Acknowledges that treatment is a compromise but does not clearly explain why a plausible alternative should be rejected or how the plan would adapt if circumstances changed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why a conservative compromise plan offers better value than more invasive, prolonged, or unstable alternatives in this patient, and discusses the trade-off between functional improvement and nonideal symmetry/detailing.

levels.title: Exceeds
