levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits major complications or gives no meaningful retention/monitoring strategy.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions relapse or retention in general terms but with limited case-specific detail.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies the major case-specific risks, including relapse from the tight perioral envelope and hygiene/caries challenges from limited oral access, and recommends long-term combined fixed and removable retention with follow-up.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Anticipates relapse, hygiene/caries burden, retainer failure, and persistence of lower premolar-related issues; explains the rationale for maxillary palatal coverage in retention and gives a realistic, guarded stability assessment with structured long-term review.

items.question_content:
A 25-year-old woman is being treated with clear aligners for skeletal Class II division 2 malocclusion. She has a 7 mm deep overbite, 5 mm overjet, a unilateral right Class II molar relationship, and porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns on Teeth 12-22 and 36; difficulty bonding to Teeth 12-22 and Tooth 46 also makes conventional fixed appliance therapy undesirable. She also reports painless bilateral TMJ clicking. Tooth 45 was extracted so the right mandibular posterior segment could be mesialized to obtain a Class I molar relationship. The treatment goals are to correct the deep bite and overjet without clockwise mandibular rotation, maintain vertical control to support profile improvement, and avoid worsening TMJ symptoms.

Review fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. During right mandibular molar mesialization, Tooth 46 is no longer following the planned movement.

What biomechanical modification would you institute now, and why is it preferable to continuing the current aligners unchanged? Base your answer on the figures and the stated treatment goals. Include what you would monitor at subsequent visits.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would change the mechanics rather than continue the aligners unchanged. The appropriate modification is to add power/cantilever arms to Tooth 46 on both the buccal and lingual sides and use elastic traction to maxillary anchorage under the aligner to generate an uprighting moment while continuing controlled mesialization.

The problem shown in the figures is uncontrolled mesial tipping of Tooth 46 during mesial movement. Aligners alone are less effective for bodily mesial movement of mandibular molars because the line of force is not expressed close enough to the center of resistance, so the crown tips mesially instead of translating. By raising the point of force application and using buccal and lingual traction, the force system adds a couple that uprights Tooth 46 and makes the movement closer to bodily mesialization into the 45 extraction space. If buccolingual roll develops, the elastic vector should be re-directed to add a transverse corrective moment rather than simply increasing force.

This is preferable to continuing the current trays unchanged because persistent tipping would compromise space closure, root position, occlusal stability, and the final molar relationship. It is also preferable to shifting to more conventional bonded fixed mechanics in this patient because multiple porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns are present and bonding is specifically problematic on Teeth 12-22 and Tooth 46. The aligner-assisted auxiliary mechanics also preserve vertical control, which is critical here: the treatment aims to open the deep bite without posterior extrusion and clockwise mandibular rotation, so maintaining control of the occlusal plane supports counterclockwise mandibular rotation and facial improvement. In addition, Class II traction can help the sagittal correction without unnecessarily flaring the maxillary incisors. Because she has TMJ clicking, traction should be used carefully and reduced or paused if symptoms worsen.

At follow-up visits, I would monitor aligner tracking and compliance, the crown-root inclination and rotation of Tooth 46, whether 47 is following bodily mesially, any buccolingual roll, unwanted posterior extrusion or bite opening, side effects on maxillary anchorage teeth, incisor torque/proclination, occlusal contacts and midline, rate of space closure, and TMJ symptoms such as pain, locking, or reduced opening.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not modify the mechanics appropriately, or recommends simply continuing unchanged without addressing the mesial tipping problem. Offers no actionable force-system correction.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that auxiliaries or elastics are needed but gives a vague or partially incorrect plan, such as nonspecific 'add elastics/attachments' without explaining how tipping would be corrected or how mesialization would be controlled.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Proposes a workable correction using power/cantilever arms and elastic traction to upright Tooth 46 and continue mesialization with clearer control of the line of force. Explains that the aim is to convert uncontrolled tipping toward bodily movement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise biomechanical plan: dual buccal/lingual power-arm traction or equivalent moment control, sequencing to regain uprighting before or while advancing mesialization, and adjustment of the vector if buccolingual roll appears. Clearly links the mechanics to bodily molar movement into the extraction space.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives a generic answer that does not use the clinical details or the figures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some case facts but incompletely; may mention clear aligners or deep bite without integrating the figure-based tipping, unilateral extraction space, or the crown/TMJ context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the observed mesial tipping in fig_01.jpg with the traction options in fig_02.jpg and connects the plan to unilateral molar correction, clear aligner limitations for posterior mesialization, and the presence of multiple porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns including the bonding difficulty on Teeth 12-22 and Tooth 46.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figures and clinical context into a coherent rationale that also incorporates the stated vertical, sagittal, facial, and TMJ goals.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks, or proposes mechanics that ignore the patient's major constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either benefits or risks but not both, or discusses them only generically.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why the modified aligner-assisted traction is preferable to doing nothing: it improves control of molar movement while maintaining vertical control and avoiding unnecessary reliance on difficult bonding to crowned teeth, especially Teeth 12-22 and Tooth 46.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced analysis of trade-offs, including control of posterior extrusion and clockwise mandibular rotation, possible incisor proclination, anchorage side effects, and the need to modulate traction if TMJ symptoms worsen.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits meaningful follow-up concerns or monitoring.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists only generic monitoring items such as 'check progress' without identifying the likely side effects of this force system.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key issues to monitor: aligner tracking/compliance, 46 inclination/rotation, space closure progress, vertical side effects, anchorage effects, occlusal contacts, and TMJ symptoms.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds how monitoring would change management, such as re-vectoring elastics if buccolingual roll appears or reducing/pausing traction if TMJ symptoms, pain, or functional limitation develop.

items.question_content: A 26-year-old woman with McCune-Albright syndrome is referred for orthodontic preparation to address facial asymmetry and maxillary overgrowth. Since childhood she has required optic nerve decompression and repeated nasal surgery for obstruction; she now reports intermittent maxillary pain and remains under endocrine follow-up. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, state your management stance at this visit regarding orthodontic treatment and any later orthognathic surgery. Justify it from the serial imaging and current craniofacial findings, and outline a concise plan that addresses timing, why this case should not be managed as routine malocclusion, and the key monitoring or specialty input needed before irreversible intervention.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would support cautious orthodontic treatment now, but only as a staged, closely monitored plan and not as routine orthodontics. fig_01.jpg suggests the skeletal disease is relatively stable by adulthood: the scan at 26 is essentially unchanged from 22, with no new sites of uptake. That makes treatment more defensible now than during childhood/adolescence, when fibrous dysplasia is more active. However, fig_02.jpg shows extensive craniofacial involvement, especially severe maxillary disease with major anatomic distortion, so any future orthognathic surgery remains higher risk and should not be automatic.

My sequence would be: confirm current multidisciplinary clearance, document baseline symptoms/occlusion/photographs, begin conservative orthodontic decompensation only if goals are functional and realistic, and reassess response before committing to surgery. If orthognathic correction is still needed, it should be planned only after stability is reconfirmed and with full informed consent about unpredictability.

This is non-routine because tooth movement and bone response in dysplastic bone may be atypical, relapse risk is higher, anatomy is distorted, and the maxillary/sinonasal involvement plus prior airway surgery increase operative complexity. Benefits of proceeding are improved occlusion, facial balance, and possibly function; risks include relapse, pain, difficulty operating in abnormal bone, and worsening of airway/nasal issues if poorly planned. I would involve orthodontics, oral and maxillofacial surgery, endocrinology, and ENT, with repeat imaging/clinical review if pain, asymmetry, or other signs suggest renewed activity. If new progression appears, I would defer irreversible surgery.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends routine treatment or blanket avoidance without a defensible plan; does not address staging, timing, or the special constraints of craniofacial fibrous dysplasia.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Takes a general position on treatment but gives incomplete sequencing or weak justification; limited recognition that orthodontics and surgery require modification from standard care.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a cautious staged approach, typically allowing orthodontic treatment now because the patient is an adult with apparently stable disease, while reserving orthognathic surgery for later coordinated planning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, individualized sequence: verify stability and baseline status, start conservative orthodontic treatment only with defined goals, reassess response, and consider orthognathic surgery only after renewed confirmation of stability and informed consent.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores the figures or bases the decision on a single isolated fact.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either age/history or one imaging modality, but does not integrate serial disease activity with current craniofacial extent.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the serial scintigraphy as evidence of relative stability and the CBCT as evidence of extensive craniofacial involvement affecting treatment complexity.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes serial stability on fig_01.jpg, extensive maxillary/craniofacial distortion on fig_02.jpg, adult age, prior optic/airway surgeries, and current pain into a coherent justification for cautious intervention rather than routine care.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Presents a one-sided recommendation with no meaningful weighing of benefits and harms.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic risks or benefits but not those most relevant to this patient.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances benefits of treating malocclusion/asymmetry and function against patient-specific risks such as atypical bone response, relapse, surgical complexity, and sinonasal/airway concerns.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explains why stability favors proceeding now more than earlier in life, while also defining circumstances that would favor deferral, such as new progression, worsening symptoms, or poor systemic/airway readiness.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify important complications or gives only vague statements.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies one complication, such as relapse or pain, but gives little prevention or monitoring strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies multiple relevant concerns, such as relapse, unpredictable tooth movement/bone response, anatomic distortion affecting surgery, and the need to monitor for reactivation or symptom worsening.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Links each major complication to practical mitigation, such as conservative mechanics, prolonged retention, careful surgical planning, and stopping or revising the plan if clinical or imaging signs of renewed activity appear.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No referral or multidisciplinary coordination is proposed.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions referral in generic terms without connecting it to the clinical issues in this case.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately involves oral and maxillofacial surgery, endocrinology, and ENT/airway evaluation before irreversible intervention.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifies coordinated longitudinal follow-up among orthodontics, oral and maxillofacial surgery, endocrinology, ENT, and imaging review to guide timing and safety of treatment.

items.question_content: A 10-year-old child in mixed dentition presents for routine review. Premature loss of 74, 75, and 85 is present. Huckaba analysis shows a 3.8 mm deficiency in the mandibular right premolar region for eruption of 45, whereas Moyers analysis does not indicate a need for active space regaining in the left mandibular quadrant. The molar relationship is Class I bilaterally. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, formulate your preferred lower-arch management plan for this child. Do not just name the appliance: justify, from the figure layout and space analyses, which tooth you intend to move to create room for 45, how the anchorage unit should be organized to protect 46 and the opposite side, and what clinical/radiographic findings would make you stop active regaining and convert to passive maintenance. Include one important complication specific to this force system and how you would monitor or limit it. Finally, explain whether the same design would still be your first choice if an equivalent space deficiency were also present on the left, and why.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The preferred approach is a mandibular lingual-arch-supported open-coil space regainer on the right, functioning at the same time as a lower lingual holding arch. This is justified because the right side has a true 3.8 mm space deficiency for eruption of 45, while the left side needs maintenance rather than active regaining.

The key figure-based point is the direction of intended tooth movement. fig_01.jpg panel C shows inadequate space for 45 between 44 and 46. In fig_02.jpg panel A and fig_02.jpg panel D, the open-coil assembly is supported from the tube on 46 and the U-shaped wire contacts the tooth anterior to the deficient space, namely 44. Therefore the active goal is mesial movement/uprighting of 44 to recreate the lost space distal to 44 for 45. The appliance is not primarily chosen to distalize 46.

Anchorage should be cross-arch and bilateral: the lingual arch soldered to both molar bands turns the lower arch into the anchorage unit and acts as a space maintainer for the rest of the arch. This helps resist distal movement of 46, preserves the bilateral Class I molar relationship, and avoids losing space on the left while right-sided regaining is carried out.

Active regaining should stop when review shows that the required space for 45 has been recovered clinically and radiographically and the eruption path appears adequate. At that stage the spring should be neutralized and the appliance left passive as a lingual arch space maintainer.

An important limitation is poor axial control of the moved tooth, so 44 may tip rather than translate bodily. Additional risks are plaque accumulation, gingival inflammation, and decalcification/caries around bands. Monitoring should include review of tooth angulation, space gained, eruption progress of 45, band integrity, and oral hygiene; overactivation should be avoided and the spring locked once the target space is reached.

If the same degree of deficiency were also present on the left, this unilateral design would not be the best standalone choice in its current form. The case would then require bilateral active space regaining or a modified bilateral cross-arch design, because a right-sided active unit with passive left maintenance would not address both deficiencies.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not integrate the history, space analysis, and figures into a coherent rationale, or misstates which side needs active space regaining.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that the right side needs active management and the left mainly needs maintenance, but gives limited or incomplete linkage to the figures and/or space analyses.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates Huckaba and Moyers findings with fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg to justify unilateral active space regaining for 45 with simultaneous passive maintenance elsewhere in the mandibular arch.

levels.title: Fails

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a fixed regaining approach with some anchorage support, but incompletely or incorrectly explains the intended tooth movement, the anchorage design, or the treatment endpoint.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a lingual-arch-supported open-coil space regainer or equivalent cross-arch fixed design; correctly states that the active objective is to regain space for 45 by moving/uprighting 44 mesially while the lingual arch serves as bilateral anchorage and space maintenance; and states that active treatment should stop once adequate clinical and radiographic space and eruption path for 45 are established, after which the appliance is maintained passively.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not explain why the selected anchorage strategy is preferable in this child, or ignores the bilateral hypothetical.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions a general anchorage or maintenance advantage but does not clearly relate it to preserving 46, the contralateral quadrant, or the bilateral hypothetical scenario.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that cross-arch anchorage is preferred because it resists distal movement of 46, helps preserve the Class I molar relationship, and maintains left-side space; and correctly states that if an equivalent deficiency were also present on the left, a bilateral active regaining approach or modified bilateral design would be needed rather than the same unilateral setup alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify a relevant complication or follow-up issue.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies a relevant complication but gives little or no case-specific monitoring or prevention strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies at least one important complication specific to this force system or appliance, such as tipping/poor axial control of 44, overactivation/relapse, or band-related gingival/plaque/caries risk, and describes an appropriate monitoring or prevention step.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides conclusions with little or no logical explanation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Reasoning is present but incomplete, loosely organized, or not clearly tied to figure-derived features.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Shows a clear stepwise explanation from findings to plan, explicitly using figure-derived features such as the open-coil/U-wire relation to 44 and the lingual arch spanning the molar bands.

items.question_content: A 28-year-old woman presents 1 year after bilateral sagittal split mandibular setback surgery, stating that her bite opened immediately after surgery and has progressively worsened. She refuses another operation. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg as your main evidence, decide whether camouflage should prioritize correction of the sagittal discrepancy or the vertical discrepancy first, and justify that priority from the records. Then outline a stepwise orthodontic plan and defend it against one other reasonable non-surgical approach that you think is less suitable here. Your answer must cite specific findings visible in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, identify one finding that argues against using anterior extrusion as the main method of bite closure, and name one additional diagnostic assessment or records review you would obtain before committing to definitive mechanics because of the postsurgical progression. Explain how an abnormal or unstable result on that assessment would change prognosis or treatment goals.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Camouflage should prioritize sagittal correction first, then final vertical correction. fig_01.jpg shows a true anterior open bite extending through the anterior teeth and first premolars, while the posterior teeth are in centric occlusion and the posterior relationship is Class II. This means the case is not just an isolated vertical problem; the dental Class II relationship must be corrected to create a favorable occlusal platform before finishing the bite vertically. fig_01.jpg also shows a relatively flat profile and slightly increased lower anterior facial height, so treatment should preserve facial esthetics and maintain vertical control.

fig_02.jpg supports a camouflage approach by showing postoperative fixation plates, all teeth present including third molars, and a cephalometric pattern described for this patient as skeletal Class I with hyperdivergence rather than a marked residual skeletal Class III. Therefore, the records support managing the dental Class II discrepancy and open bite orthodontically rather than assuming that a major residual skeletal anteroposterior discrepancy is the dominant problem.

Stepwise plan:
1. Review full pretreatment and postsurgical records, confirm the history of immediate postoperative open bite with later worsening, and counsel the patient that this is non-surgical correction after an adverse surgical outcome, with possible need for future surgery if orthodontic correction proves insufficient.
2. Bond both arches and perform initial leveling/alignment conservatively, avoiding mechanics that worsen the vertical dimension.
3. Correct the Class II relationship first by distalizing the entire maxillary arch with skeletal anchorage, preferably palatal mini-screws, because the posterior relationship in fig_01.jpg is Class II and the profile is already acceptable.
4. After achieving a Class I or near-Class I posterior relationship, intrude the maxillary molars with skeletal anchorage to close the open bite through posterior vertical control and mandibular autorotation.
5. Use only limited anterior extrusion and incisor detailing during finishing; anterior extrusion should not be the primary mechanism of bite closure.
6. Retain with fixed lingual retainers and clear night-time retainers, with follow-up of vertical stability.

A reasonable but less suitable non-surgical alternative would be extraction camouflage or primarily closing the bite by anterior extrusion. Extraction camouflage is less suitable because crowding is mild, the profile is relatively balanced, and extraction does not directly address the posterior Class II relationship together with the vertical problem. Primary anterior extrusion is also less suitable because this patient already has increased lower anterior facial height and a hyperdivergent pattern, and the records show the posterior teeth are in occlusion; closing the bite mainly by extruding incisors would be less favorable biomechanically and potentially less stable than posterior intrusion with vertical control.

The additional assessment I would obtain is a careful review of any available serial postsurgical records or repeat baseline records to verify whether the occlusion and jaw relationship are still changing after surgery, since the patient reports progressive worsening. This could include comparison with prior photographs, cephalometric radiographs, occlusal records, and clinical follow-up examinations. If those records show ongoing change or instability, the prognosis for stable orthodontic correction becomes more guarded, treatment goals may need to be more conservative, and the patient should be counseled more strongly about the possibility that orthodontics alone may not provide a definitive long-term solution.

levels.description: Does not decide whether sagittal or vertical correction should be prioritized first, or gives a priority that is unsupported and inconsistent with the records.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: States a priority but gives only generic open-bite reasoning, with little case-specific justification from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly prioritizes sagittal correction before final vertical correction and links that decision to the posterior Class II relationship in fig_01.jpg together with the later need for vertical control.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a clear, case-specific rationale for why correcting the AP discrepancy first creates a more favorable occlusal platform for subsequent posterior intrusion and overbite correction, while also explaining why reversing the sequence would be less efficient or less controlled in this patient.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg accurately or bases the answer mainly on unsupported assumptions.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses only one or two isolated findings from the figures, such as the open bite alone, without integrating facial, occlusal, and radiographic information.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly integrates several visible pretreatment findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, such as anterior open bite with posterior occlusion, posterior Class II relationship, relatively acceptable/flat profile, and radiographic or cephalometric information consistent with orthodontic camouflage.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the figures into a coherent biomechanical argument, explicitly showing how the occlusion, facial appearance, and radiographic pattern together support whole-arch distalization plus posterior vertical control and argue against less suitable alternatives, without overclaiming from the images alone.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no coherent plan, ignores the patient's refusal of surgery, or proposes mechanics centered mainly on anterior extrusion or other poorly matched treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes camouflage but with incomplete sequencing, vague anchorage strategy, or mechanics that do not adequately address both AP and vertical components.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Outlines a stepwise non-surgical plan with alignment, maxillary whole-arch distalization under skeletal anchorage, subsequent posterior intrusion for open-bite closure, and limited anterior finishing rather than major anterior extrusion.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a precise, biomechanically sound plan that explains anchorage requirements, sequencing, and finishing, while preserving facial esthetics and controlling vertical side effects.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare the chosen plan with any plausible alternative or ignores patient-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Names an alternative but discusses tradeoffs only in generic terms.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Defends the chosen plan against a reasonable non-surgical alternative, such as extraction camouflage or primary anterior extrusion, using patient-specific concerns including facial esthetics, mild crowding, vertical control, and stability.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced comparison of alternatives, weighing esthetic, biomechanical, and stability consequences in this exact postsurgical adult case and clearly justifying why the selected plan offers the best balance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits additional assessment despite the progressive postsurgical course, or claims a predictable stable result without qualification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests follow-up or records review vaguely but does not explain how abnormal findings would alter management or prognosis.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies an appropriate added assessment, such as serial postsurgical records review or repeat baseline documentation to evaluate ongoing change, and explains that instability would worsen prognosis and require more guarded counseling or modified goals.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly connects the progressive postsurgical history to the need for targeted verification of stability over time, and explains how continued change would affect timing, goals, stability expectations, and the possibility that orthodontics alone may not provide a definitive solution.

items.question_content: A 19-year-old man presents with chewing difficulty, midfacial depression, and a prognathic mandibular appearance. In infancy he underwent right-eye enucleation and radiotherapy to the left eye for bilateral retinoblastoma, and at age 11 he received additional treatment for nasopharyngeal cancer. Using fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, write a pretreatment conference note for definitive oral rehabilitation. Identify whether the skeletal Class III deformity reflects mainly maxillary/midface deficiency, mandibular prognathism, or both, and justify your answer from the records. The pretreatment panoramic and intraoral records show multiple missing maxillary permanent teeth, retained maxillary primary central incisors and right primary canine, an upper right primary molar root rest, and impacted lower right second and third molars. State which teeth you would plan to retain as part of rehabilitation versus extract at treatment initiation, with reasons. Then outline a staged interdisciplinary plan from presurgical orthodontics through definitive prosthetic rehabilitation, including a brief note on why prior childhood irradiation warrants cautious staging and coordination for grafting and implants.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The pretreatment records show a severe skeletal Class III deformity due to both marked maxillary/midface growth deficiency and mandibular prognathism, with the maxillary deficiency being especially prominent. fig_01.jpg shows midfacial depression, reverse incisor relationship, severe anterior and posterior crossbite, and posterior openbite. fig_02.jpg supports a severe sagittal discrepancy with maxillary retrusion and a mandibular component, so this is not an isolated dentoalveolar problem and not a purely mandibular excess case.

Teeth to retain as part of rehabilitation: the retained maxillary primary central incisors can be preserved if serviceable because they help maintain the anterior segment and may be restored as part of the final rehabilitation. 

Teeth to extract at treatment initiation: the retained upper right primary canine and the upper right primary molar root rest should be removed to regain prosthetic/implant space and eliminate poor-prognosis obstructive remnants. The impacted lower right second and third molars should also be extracted because they are nonfunctional and complicate orthodontic-surgical planning.

Staged plan: obtain multidisciplinary assessment and confirm prior oncology/radiation history; perform presurgical orthodontic decompensation, alignment, and space management; carry out the indicated extractions above; correct the skeletal discrepancy with two-jaw orthognathic surgery, addressing both maxillary deficiency and mandibular prognathism; continue postsurgical orthodontic finishing; then place implants and provide definitive prosthetic rehabilitation after skeletal and occlusal stabilization. Prior childhood irradiation warrants cautious, staged coordination for bone healing, augmentation, and implant timing, without assuming specific dose data not provided.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misclassifies the deformity as primarily dental or as an isolated maxillary or mandibular problem without recognizing the combined skeletal Class III pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a severe skeletal Class III pattern with marked maxillary/midface deficiency and a mandibular prognathic contribution, supported by the records.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic answer with little or no use of findings from the figures or stem.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Uses relevant pretreatment findings such as midfacial depression, reverse incisor relationship, crossbite/openbite pattern, missing maxillary teeth, retained primary teeth/root rest, or impacted lower right molars.

criteria.name: Management of retained and impacted teeth

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not distinguish teeth to preserve from teeth to extract, or recommends unsupported retention/extraction.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Appropriately preserves the retained maxillary primary central incisors if serviceable, and recommends extraction at treatment initiation of the upper right primary canine, upper right primary molar root rest, and impacted lower right second and third molars, with reasons.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Suggests camouflage or definitive prosthetic rehabilitation before skeletal correction, or gives a disordered sequence.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Presents a logical sequence of presurgical orthodontics and space management, indicated extractions, two-jaw orthognathic correction, postsurgical finishing, and delayed implant-prosthetic rehabilitation.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores prior irradiation or recommends routine grafting/implant placement without caution.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Notes that prior childhood irradiation warrants cautious staging and interdisciplinary coordination for healing, augmentation, and implant timing, without adding unsupported dose or field assumptions.

items.question_content: A 35-year-old man with cleidocranial dysplasia returns after 12 years without treatment, still complaining that his permanent teeth failed to erupt. Compare fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg. What definitive management strategy would you recommend now, and why? Base your answer on the interval radiographic findings, explain the sequence of care you would prioritize, and state what makes the prognosis better or worse in this adult patient.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would recommend active, staged recovery of strategically useful impacted permanent teeth rather than continued observation. Comparing fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, the dentition is largely unchanged over 12 years: multiple permanent teeth remain impacted, many deciduous teeth are still retained, supernumerary teeth remain, and fig_02.jpg shows dense/sclerotic alveolar bone in the premolar regions. This indicates that spontaneous eruption is unreliable in this adult CCD patient and that both mechanical obstruction and abnormal eruption biology are contributing.

Management should begin with comprehensive orthodontic, periodontal, and radiographic assessment, ideally with CBCT localization and space analysis. Next, remove retained deciduous teeth and supernumerary teeth that block eruption pathways. Then surgically expose selected impacted permanent teeth with favorable position and periodontal support, followed by orthodontic traction and space management. Teeth with very poor position, no movement, suspected ankylosis, or inadequate periodontal support should not be pursued aggressively at first and can be considered later for prosthetic replacement.

The prognosis is guarded overall because of adult age, long-standing impaction, periodontal bone loss, and sclerotic alveolar bone, all of which may slow or limit movement. However, it is not hopeless: the radiographs show failure of untreated eruption, not proof that orthodontically assisted eruption cannot work. A tooth-by-tooth salvage approach is justified before irreversible removal.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not use the interval imaging meaningfully, or misreads the case as routine delayed eruption. Omits key radiographic factors such as persistent impaction, retained deciduous teeth, supernumerary teeth, or alveolar sclerosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies some relevant findings but links them weakly to the management choice. Uses only isolated features and misses the importance of the 12-year interval or the significance of dense/sclerotic alveolar bone.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the major radiographic findings into coherent reasoning: long-standing failure of spontaneous eruption, persistent impacted permanent teeth, retained deciduous teeth, supernumerary obstruction, and dense/sclerotic premolar-region bone; may also note periodontal bone loss.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the interval comparison at a high level, recognizing that apparent minor eruption may not represent healthy eruptive capacity and that the imaging supports both mechanical obstruction and abnormal eruption biology in CCD.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no clear plan, recommends passive observation as definitive care, or offers a generic answer without sequencing.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests extraction or orthodontic treatment but without a staged rationale, without selecting which teeth should be addressed first, or without addressing obstructing retained/supernumerary teeth.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a staged plan: full assessment, selective removal of retained deciduous and supernumerary teeth blocking eruption, surgical exposure of salvageable impacted teeth, orthodontic traction/space management, and later prosthetic replacement only for teeth that are not realistically recoverable.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-prioritized, interdisciplinary plan that starts with periodontal and imaging workup, selects teeth strategically for recovery, explains when to stop pursuing eruption, and reserves prosthetic options for non-salvageable teeth rather than as the first-line response.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not discuss patient-specific risks, burdens, or tradeoffs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only one generic risk such as age or treatment duration, with little balancing against benefits of tooth preservation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the main risks and benefits: slower movement and surgical difficulty in an adult with sclerotic bone and periodontal compromise versus the benefit of preserving permanent teeth and reducing premature reliance on prosthetic replacement.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows nuanced judgment by rejecting age-only nihilism, recognizing that dense alveolar bone may hinder but not preclude movement, and explaining why a conservative salvage attempt is preferable before irreversible treatment if teeth are strategically recoverable.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no prognosis or an unrealistic prognosis unsupported by the findings.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a vague prognosis such as 'guarded' without linking it to the imaging or clinical context.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: States that spontaneous eruption prognosis is poor without intervention, while active treatment offers a meaningful but guarded chance of success because of age, chronic impaction, and periodontal/alveolar factors.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Distinguishes overall guarded case prognosis from tooth-specific variability, correctly noting that non-treatment prognosis is poor but selected teeth may still respond favorably to properly sequenced orthodontic-surgical management.

items.question_content: A 15-year-old boy presents mainly because of severe lower anterior crowding. Review the pretreatment records in fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg. What treatment strategy would you commit to at the outset, and why? Base your justification on the biologic source of the space deficiency and the patient’s facial/dental findings, not just the amount of crowding. Also state which developments during treatment would make you abandon your original plan and switch to a different space-gaining approach.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would begin with a non-extraction, transverse-correction strategy, specifically skeletal maxillary expansion first, ideally with a bone-anchored expander, then comprehensive fixed appliances. The key reason is that the records suggest the crowding is not simply a tooth-size problem: the pretreatment records show a transverse maxillary deficiency with a constricted upper arch, and the mandibular crowding appears secondary to reduced arch perimeter and collapsed posterior segments rather than excess lower incisor mass alone. In a 15-year-old, I would prefer skeletal anchorage over a tooth-borne expander to maximize orthopedic change and reduce unwanted buccal tipping.

The rest of the records support avoiding routine extraction as the initial choice. The upper incisors are retroclined, the overbite is deep and impinging, overjet is increased, and the soft-tissue profile is convex with reduced incisal display. Removing teeth and retracting anterior segments risks worsening smile fullness and incisal show, while simply aligning by further proclining the lower incisors would be undesirable because they are already proclined. After expansion, I would coordinate both arches, upright the mandibular posterior teeth, control lower incisor position, procline the upper incisors appropriately, level the curve of Spee/deep bite, and finish the canine relationship and overjet/overbite.

I would reconsider this plan if expansion fails to produce a meaningful skeletal response, if the correction is mainly dental tipping, if periodontal support becomes compromised, if lower incisors would need excessive further proclination to relieve residual crowding, or if significant space deficiency persists after transverse correction. Those findings would justify changing to another space-gaining strategy, including extraction if needed. Because expanded arches relapse more easily, long-term retention would be important.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate or poorly sequenced plan that does not address the transverse problem; relies on vague alignment alone or commits to irreversible space reduction without rationale from the records.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes a need for space gain but gives an incomplete plan or weak sequencing; may mention expansion or orthodontics generally without prioritizing initial transverse correction or explaining how the remainder of treatment would be managed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a coherent initial strategy centered on transverse correction first, followed by comprehensive alignment/arch coordination and bite correction; includes a reasonable contingency if space remains inadequate.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-sequenced, patient-specific plan: initial skeletal expansion before lower alignment, then coordination of both arches, uprighting of posterior segments, control of incisor position, and deep-bite/occlusal correction, with clear thresholds for changing strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses isolated findings or misreads the records; attributes the problem mainly to tooth-size excess or ignores the figure-based transverse diagnosis.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical or radiographic findings but misses key links between the transverse discrepancy, mandibular crowding, incisor inclinations, and soft-tissue findings.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Synthesizes the pretreatment records to explain that the space deficiency is largely arch-width/perimeter related, supported by transverse narrowing plus the dental and facial findings.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates nearly all relevant findings from fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg into a coherent biologic explanation, including why the lower crowding is secondary to transverse restriction and why the incisor/profile findings shape the space-gaining strategy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: No meaningful weighing of options, or risk-benefit reasoning is clinically unsound.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives generic pros and cons but little case-specific analysis of why one pathway is preferable here.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains case-specific benefits of initial skeletal expansion and the disadvantages of relying on other space-gaining methods in this patient, including lower incisor position and facial esthetics.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Nuanced comparison of benefits and tradeoffs, including age-related limits of expansion, risk of dental tipping, periodontal or stability concerns, and why some alternatives could worsen the patient’s profile, bite, or incisor inclinations.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits monitoring needs or fails to recognize important reasons the original plan might fail.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic follow-up or relapse without specific treatment-changing triggers.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies plausible complications or failure signals such as inadequate skeletal response, excessive dental tipping, loss of lower incisor control, periodontal problems, or residual space deficiency.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly links specific complications/failure signals to how management would change and includes realistic attention to long-term retention for stability.

items.question_content: A 14-year-old in late mixed dentition has a left posterior lingual crossbite, a markedly mesially tipped 46, an over-retained but sound 75, and no clinical 85. Based on fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, the mandibular right posterior segment shows severe infraocclusion/ankylosis with displacement of the successor, while the cephalometric pattern and soft-tissue profile are favorable and should ideally be preserved. What is the most predictable definitive treatment strategy for this patient? Justify your plan by stating which teeth you would aim to retain or remove, how you would manage the mandibular spaces and anchorage, and why your approach is preferable to other reasonable options in this specific patient.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The most predictable plan is comprehensive orthodontic treatment with early correction of the transverse discrepancy, combined with surgical-orthodontic management of the mandibular posterior problems. I would correct the left posterior crossbite first, then surgically remove the severely ankylosed/submerged 85. I would also remove the impacted 45, because its position relative to the ankylosed 85 makes successful exposure/traction prolonged and less predictable, and the tooth is at risk of damage during removal of the ankylosed primary molar. Because 35 is absent and 75 is only a retained primary tooth with limited long-term longevity, I would also remove 75 and close both mandibular spaces orthodontically rather than plan lifelong prosthetic replacement.

Space closure should be TAD-assisted. Skeletal anchorage is needed to upright the mesially tipped 46 and then mesialize the mandibular molars bilaterally while minimizing reciprocal anterior retraction. That is important because the cephalometric and soft-tissue findings are already favorable, so uncontrolled anchorage loss or incisor retraction would be undesirable. This approach also helps restore arch symmetry and uses orthodontic tooth movement to promote bone and soft-tissue regeneration in the deficient posterior mandibular sites.

This plan is preferable because it avoids dependence on retained primary teeth and future implants in a growing adolescent, reduces long-term restorative burden, preserves the favorable incisor position/profile, and may create space for more favorable eruption of the mandibular third molars. Key risks to monitor are anchorage loss, unwanted anterior movement, root resorption/root parallelism during molar mesialization, periodontal health and bone fill in the extraction sites, stability of the transverse correction, and the eruption path of the third molars.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides observation only, a vague orthodontic plan, or a plan that does not definitively address the ankylosed/submerged primary molar, displaced successor, and bilateral mandibular space problem.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Addresses some elements but lacks a coherent definitive strategy; for example, treats the crossbite only, removes 85 without a clear plan for the right posterior space, or proposes mandibular management without adequate anchorage strategy.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends a coherent definitive plan centered on crossbite correction, surgical management of the ankylosed/submerged 85 and the compromised 45, removal of 75 because of 35 absence and primary-tooth longevity concerns, and orthodontic bilateral mandibular space closure with molar uprighting/mesialization using skeletal anchorage.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents the above plan with clear sequencing, interdisciplinary coordination, and explicit rationale for preserving anterior position/profile while correcting asymmetry and posterior arch distortion.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Gives little or no justification, or recommends a plan without weighing predictability, restorative burden, growth status, or biologic cost.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros/cons but incompletely relates them to this patient; may note that treatment is difficult without explaining why one strategy is more predictable here.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why rescuing the displaced 45 is less predictable in the setting of severe ankylosis/submergence, why relying on the retained 75 or future prosthetic replacement is less favorable in this adolescent, and why space closure offers biologic and long-term advantages.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances short-term difficulty against long-term benefits with patient-specific nuance, including preservation of favorable facial/incisor relationships, avoidance of future implant dependence, improvement of posterior alveolar deficiency, and possible benefit for third-molar eruption.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores or misinterprets key findings from the figures and scenario.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some findings but misses important relationships such as the absent 35, tipped 46, status of 75, or the favorable skeletal/incisor pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the essential findings: severe infraocclusion/ankylosis in the 85 region with successor displacement, congenitally missing 35, mesially tipped 46, over-retained but sound 75, transverse discrepancy, and favorable cephalometric/soft-tissue features.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the clinical and radiographic findings into a persuasive explanation of why bilateral mandibular space closure with controlled anchorage best fits this specific occlusal, skeletal, and restorative context.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify meaningful risks or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic risks such as root resorption without linking them to the planned mechanics or sites involved.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies relevant risks and monitoring points, including anchorage loss/unwanted anterior retraction, difficulty of molar uprighting and mesialization, root parallelism or resorption, periodontal/bone response in extraction sites, and monitoring of third-molar eruption.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Adds thoughtful preventive or follow-up considerations such as maintaining transverse correction stability, monitoring occlusal settling and posterior function, and recognizing the need to reassess if eruption or periodontal response is not proceeding favorably.

items.question_content: A 24-year-old woman seeks correction of “sticking-out” upper front teeth after two prior orthodontic courses. She is missing one premolar in each quadrant and one mandibular incisor, so additional extraction space is effectively exhausted. Clinically she has 9.5 mm overjet, slight anterior open bite with traumatic contact, and a mild skeletal Class III tendency; fig_01.jpg also raises concern for a CO-CR discrepancy. Examining fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, what definitive management pathway would you recommend if the goal is to preserve the maxillary anterior teeth? Justify your plan from the imaging and clinical findings, and explain the sequencing and monitoring decisions most critical to staying within biologic and anatomic limits.

golden_answer.subjective_answer: I would pursue a tooth-preserving orthodontic camouflage plan rather than routine alignment or more extractions. fig_02.jpg shows severely shortened maxillary anterior roots with loss of normal palatal bony housing, so the aim is not just to tip crowns back but to create posterior space and carefully reposition the roots toward the alveolar envelope. Because premolar extraction space is already exhausted, space should be generated with absolute skeletal anchorage, preferably palatal for maxillary total-arch distalization, using very light, controlled forces for en-mass anterior retraction with torque control and some intrusion as needed. I would first open/deprogram the bite to eliminate anterior trauma and clarify centric relation because fig_01.jpg suggests a CO-CR discrepancy; only then would I continue retraction/distalization and later coordinate the mandibular arch and restorative space once stable posterior contacts are established. Prognosis is guarded, so explicit informed consent is essential. Monitoring must be close: serial radiographs or limited-field CBCT when justified, mobility, vitality, periodontal support, TMJ symptoms, and root position relative to cortical boundaries. I would reduce forces, pause, or revise the plan if there is progressive root resorption, worsening dehiscence/periodontal support, instability, or no remaining distal bone for safe movement.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes routine braces, further extractions, or surgery without a coherent preservation-focused orthodontic plan; ignores the need to create posterior space and control anterior root movement.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes that anchorage or space creation is needed but gives a generic or poorly sequenced plan; may mention retraction or distalization without showing how root position, bite opening, or force control will be managed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends tooth-preserving orthodontic management using skeletal anchorage to create posterior space, with light-force controlled retraction/torque of the maxillary anterior segment and early bite opening/deprogramming before settling and finishing.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: As above, and clearly explains why total-arch distalization with root repositioning into the alveolar housing is preferable in this reduced dentition, emphasizing controlled bodily/torque correction rather than simple crown tipping and adapting later finishing/restorative decisions to anatomic limits.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets or ignores fig_01.jpg/fig_02.jpg and does not recognize that the anterior roots and surrounding alveolar support are severely compromised.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some clinical information but incompletely links it; may note the overjet or missing teeth while missing the significance of the CBCT findings or the dentoalveolar-versus-skeletal balance.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the adult status, prior extraction pattern exhausting easy space, large overjet with anterior trauma, mild skeletal Class III tendency, and the CBCT evidence of markedly shortened anterior roots with cortical/alveolar boundary problems.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Additionally incorporates the possible CO-CR discrepancy/TMJ implications from fig_01.jpg and clearly explains that the dominant challenge is dentoalveolar movement within hard anatomic limits rather than a purely skeletal discrepancy.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful discussion of trade-offs, prognosis, or consent.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions root resorption risk only in general terms, without balancing it against benefits or patient-specific alternatives.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains the guarded but reasonable rationale for preserving the incisors: potential esthetic, functional, and periodontal benefit versus risks of further resorption, long treatment time, periodontal damage, and distalization limits; includes informed consent.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Compares why other plausible pathways are less favorable in this specific reduced dentition or may carry greater biologic cost, while still acknowledging that prognosis may force revision if risk escalates.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not identify major complications or monitoring needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic orthodontic risks without case-specific triggers for intervention.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies likely complications such as progressive root resorption, dehiscence or periodontal support loss, unresolved occlusal trauma/CR instability, and running out of distal bone, and calls for periodic imaging and clinical review.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Specifies actionable modify/stop triggers such as worsening resorption or mobility, deterioration in periodontal support or vitality, inability to continue movement within alveolar boundaries, or new TMJ/occlusal symptoms requiring force reduction, re-imaging, or plan revision.

items.question_content: A 14-year-old boy with Class II malocclusion is in bilateral maxillary first-premolar extraction space closure on a 0.019 × 0.025-in stainless-steel archwire with 100 g closed-coil springs, without TADs or posterior segment consolidation. Only the right extraction site received six MOPs every 4 weeks for 3 months. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg and fig_03.jpg, decide how you would manage the next 8 weeks of space closure. Do not answer only “continue” or “stop” MOPs: identify the clinically important movement pattern on each side (sagittal and any transverse/rotational component that changes your decision), state whether the anchorage objective is actually being achieved efficiently, and name the single first change you would make to the mechanics/adjunctive strategy. Justify why that choice is better in this patient than simply repeating the same unilateral protocol. Then state how your plan would change if, at the next review, the left canine were still clearly lagging but the right canine showed greater apical blunting than the left.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The figures suggest the right intervention side has already expressed the intended biologic effect: the right canine moved farther distally than the left, and the right first molar showed less mesial drift, so anchorage preservation was better on the MOP side rather than worse. The movement is not purely a sagittal story, however. The right canine also shows a palatal component while the left canine shows buccal drift, and the canine rotational change is not meaningfully different between sides. fig_03.jpg shows slight apical shortening/narrowing on both sides without a clinically important excess on the right at this stage.

So the anchorage objective is being achieved on the right, but not in a way that should simply be repeated uncritically, because further unilateral acceleration risks increasing side-to-side discrepancy in space closure and transverse/root control. My first change would be to stop repeating right-sided MOPs for the next interval and continue controlled conventional space closure on the rigid rectangular wire, remeasuring remaining space and canine root position before adding any further adjunct. If a meaningful asymmetry remains, any future adjunctive acceleration should be directed selectively to the lagging side only, provided radiographic root clearance and periodontal health are acceptable. I would not make routine posterior anchorage reinforcement or TAD placement the first change, because the current records do not show anchorage failure; they show better anchorage preservation on the MOP side.

This is preferable to repeating the same unilateral protocol because the right side has already gained the biologic advantage, and further right-only MOPs would offer diminishing benefit while increasing the chance of asymmetric canine position, transverse discrepancy, and cumulative root/soft-tissue burden.

Counterfactual: if the left canine were still clearly lagging at the next review but the right canine then showed greater apical blunting than the left, I would avoid any further right-sided MOPs and prioritize protection of the right canine root. Space closure on the right would continue conventionally, or be slowed if needed, while any consideration of acceleration would shift—cautiously—to the left side only after confirming safe root position radiographically and acceptable periodontal status.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the figures, does not distinguish right and left side behavior, or makes claims inconsistent with the records.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings only, such as saying one side moved faster or that roots look acceptable, without integrating anchorage and movement pattern.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly identifies that the intervention side shows greater distal canine movement and less mesial molar movement than the control side, and includes at least one clinically relevant non-sagittal or root-safety observation from fig_02.jpg or fig_03.jpg.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately synthesizes the figure-based pattern: greater distal canine movement on the right, less right molar mesialization, clinically relevant transverse difference between canines and/or molars, no meaningful canine rotational advantage, and only slight comparable apical changes on fig_03.jpg; explicitly connects these findings to the management decision.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes an inappropriate plan, such as repeating unilateral right-sided MOPs unchanged despite the current side-to-side discrepancy, or recommends major changes without case-based justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives a generic plan to continue, stop, or monitor treatment, but does not specify the first modification to mechanics/adjuncts or does not address bilateral coordination.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides a defensible next-step plan that avoids unchanged right-only repetition, continues controlled space closure, and reserves any further adjunctive acceleration for a clearly lagging side only after reassessment.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a sequenced, patient-specific plan that clearly identifies the first change, explains why routine anchorage reinforcement is not the first response to these records, and defines when selective adjunctive use would become appropriate based on reassessment.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks, or treats MOPs as automatically indicated or risk-free.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions either the benefit of faster movement/anchorage preservation or the risks of asymmetry/root effects, but not both in a patient-specific way.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances the observed benefit of faster right canine distalization and reduced right molar mesialization against risks of continued unilateral acceleration, including side-to-side discrepancy, transverse control issues, and cumulative hard-tissue burden.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows clear prioritization of benefit versus harm both for the current decision and for the counterfactual scenario, including why new right-sided apical blunting would change the threshold for further adjunctive intervention.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not prioritize actions or gives an internally inconsistent sequence.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists several possible actions but does not identify which should be done first or why.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies one immediate first change and gives a coherent reason for sequencing it before any further MOP use.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the immediate step clearly and also adapts that priority appropriately in the counterfactual scenario, with root protection taking precedence over further acceleration on the right.

items.question_content:
A 13-year-old girl in active growth presents with chewing difficulty and anterior spacing. She has no significant medical history, no obvious syndromic features, no family history of unerupted teeth, and genetic testing is unavailable. Use only the pretreatment records in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

Before any irreversible treatment, write the management note you would present at a case conference. Decide whether the posterior eruption disturbance should be provisionally managed as one biologic pattern or whether one posterior region should be separated from the rest at baseline; only separate a region if the figures truly justify it. Support your judgment with specific tooth- and quadrant-level findings from the images, including what keeps you from overcalling ankylosis.

Then commit to the single highest-yield action for the next 12 months of growth and explain why it should take priority over other reasonable moves now. State which teeth you would deliberately keep out of active force systems or anchorage, what follow-up information would be decisive before any irreversible step, and the one later finding that would most change your plan.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
Pretreatment conference note:

Working interpretation
- The posterior problem should not be treated as a simple single-site mechanical impaction pattern. The strongest baseline reading is a predominantly biologic posterior eruption-failure pattern involving multiple first-molar-centered units, but not every site should automatically be grouped together.
- The upper-left second-premolar/retained deciduous molar region should be provisionally separated from the rest because it has the clearest local confounder.

Why
- fig_01.jpg shows a bilateral posterior open bite with several infraoccluded/submerged posterior teeth rather than one isolated impacted tooth. Multiquadrant first-molar involvement is difficult to explain by one local obstruction alone.
- The upper-left posterior segment is different: the pretreatment radiograph suggests a retained deciduous molar in the path of the unerupted upper-left second premolar, so that region has a plausible local mechanical component.
- fig_02.jpg shows complete root formation and preserved periodontal ligament space around the infraoccluded/impacted teeth, with no obvious baseline bony pathology. That argues against simple delayed eruption and means radiographic ankylosis is not established at baseline, even though it cannot be excluded with absolute certainty.
- Confidence is moderate, not absolute: the multiquadrant pattern points toward suspected PFE/indeterminate eruption failure, but the upper-left local obstacle muddies the picture and genetic confirmation is unavailable.

Most important alternative explanations
- Local mechanical obstruction fits the upper-left second-premolar region but does not explain the wider first-molar pattern.
- Ankylosis/secondary retention remains in the differential for any infraoccluded tooth, but preserved PDL spaces on fig_02.jpg make blanket baseline ankylosis a weaker explanation for all quadrants.
- Constitutional delay is less convincing because roots appear complete and the pattern is selective and posterior.

Single highest-yield action for the next 12 months
- Highest priority: conservative diagnostic-phase management, with limited site-specific interception of the upper-left obstructive region if confirmed, while otherwise avoiding active loading of the suspect posterior units.
- In practice, the best-supported action is to clear the apparent upper-left local obstacle and observe whether that site erupts, because this is the only posterior step that both helps the patient and tests whether one region is mechanically different from the others.
- This outranks broader posterior orthodontic mechanics during growth because if the multiquadrant first-molar units represent PFE, eruptive traction is unlikely to work and may worsen the posterior open bite or create unfavorable anchorage effects. It also outranks irreversible posterior treatment at this age because diagnosis and vertical growth are not settled.
- A closely monitored observation-first approach could still be defended if the clinician felt the local obstruction was not yet sufficiently certain, but broad posterior extrusion/protraction would be a poorer baseline choice.

Teeth/segments to keep out of active force systems or anchorage
- Do not routinely load the infraoccluded first molars or other posterior teeth suspected of being within the eruption-failure pattern.
- Do not use those suspect molars as major anchorage units.
- Manage only clearly responsive segments, such as the anterior teeth, if treatment is needed during growth.

Decisive follow-up before any irreversible step
- Serial clinical photographs or models/scans and repeat radiographs to document whether the upper-left second premolar erupts after path clearance.
- Comparison of vertical change over time in the first-molar-centered posterior units.
- Percussion/mobility findings and further imaging only if a specific site remains ambiguous.
- The key question is whether any suspect posterior unit demonstrates genuine eruptive response once a clear path exists.

Single later finding most likely to change the plan
- The most plan-changing later finding would be spontaneous eruption or clear vertical movement of the upper-left second premolar after removal of the retained deciduous tooth. That would strongly support a site-specific mechanical component in that quadrant and justify localized orthodontic management there, while leaving the remaining multiquadrant first-molar pattern under continued suspicion for biologic eruption failure.
- By contrast, if multiple posterior units remain vertically static despite a clear path, confidence in PFE becomes stronger and long-term care should shift toward supportive/restorative planning rather than active eruptive mechanics.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misreads the pretreatment problem as simple delayed eruption, a uniform single-site mechanical impaction pattern, or definite ankylosis/PFE without acknowledging baseline uncertainty.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Recognizes eruption failure but gives an overly uniform diagnosis, or separates the wrong region, or does not identify the upper-left posterior region as the main locally confounded site.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a likely multiquadrant biologic eruption-failure pattern centered on the posterior first-molar units and provisionally keeps the upper-left second-premolar/retained deciduous molar region separate because of possible local obstruction.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Accurately frames the baseline picture as suspected PFE/indeterminate biologic eruption failure affecting multiple first-molar-centered posterior units, while correctly separating the upper-left second-premolar region as the major local mechanical confounder and avoiding overcalling baseline ankylosis.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides no meaningful alternative explanations or rules out plausible alternatives incorrectly.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions alternatives such as obstruction, ankylosis, or delayed eruption, but without case-specific comparison.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Compares the leading alternatives using pretreatment evidence, typically local obstruction, ankylosis/secondary retention, and delayed eruption.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Systematically explains why a local obstacle is plausible mainly in the upper-left region, why multiquadrant first-molar involvement argues against a purely mechanical whole-mouth explanation, and why preserved PDL/complete roots make simple delay or blanket baseline ankylosis less convincing.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Uses little or no information from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some figure findings but relies mainly on general knowledge or misses the tooth- and quadrant-level asymmetry.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates key pretreatment findings from fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, including bilateral posterior open bite, multiquadrant infraoccluded posterior teeth/first-molar involvement, the upper-left locally confounded region, and preserved PDL space with complete roots.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Builds a coherent baseline argument from specific sides/teeth in fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg, clearly distinguishing what supports a biologic pattern from what creates local uncertainty, and explicitly notes why ankylosis is not proven by these baseline images.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not commit to a priority, or prioritizes broad posterior traction/protraction or another aggressive irreversible step during baseline uncertainty.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Suggests caution but does not clearly rank actions or explain why the chosen step is the highest-yield move now.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Commits to one appropriate 12-month priority, such as conservative management with targeted upper-left interception if justified or carefully justified observation-first, and explains why this outranks broader posterior mechanics during growth.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a well-justified priority that tests the locally confounded upper-left region while protecting the remaining posterior units, and explicitly states why both full posterior orthodontic mechanics and irreversible posterior treatment are lower-priority choices at this stage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Would include suspect posterior teeth in active force systems or anchorage, or omits necessary follow-up before irreversible treatment.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a cautious plan but is vague about which teeth to exclude, how to preserve function, or what serial information is still needed.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies which teeth/segments should stay out of active loading or anchorage, preserves function/esthetics with reversible measures, and names appropriate serial observations or imaging before irreversible steps.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a stepwise 12-month plan with tooth-specific exclusions, reversible interim support, targeted follow-up after any local interception, and clear thresholds for when later irreversible treatment could be reconsidered.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not address case-specific risks or benefits.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Gives only generic caution without linking risk to this patient's growth stage and diagnostic uncertainty.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that loading suspect posterior units may bring nonresponse, worsening open bite, or anchorage-related harm, while conservative or site-specific management preserves later options.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Balances growth, uncertainty, and long-term treatment flexibility, and correctly identifies one later finding that would materially redirect the plan.

red_flags: Generic Textbook Management: recommending broad posterior extrusion/protraction or routine use of the infraoccluded posterior teeth as anchorage during growth despite pretreatment evidence suggesting biologic eruption failure with a locally confounded upper-left site

items.question_content: A 25-year-old woman seeks alignment of crowded teeth. She reports no prior extractions, no family history of missing teeth, and no relevant medical problems. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg, identify the exact anomaly pattern and propose a definitive management plan. Do not assume impaction versus agenesis without justifying it from the records. Explain why your chosen space-management strategy fits this patient better than the strongest competing approach you considered. In your answer, specify the intended final role of the teeth adjacent to the absent sites, the functional finishing scheme you would accept in excursions, and one additional clinical or radiographic finding that—if present instead—would materially change your plan, with the revised approach.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The records support isolated/non-syndromic bilateral agenesis of the permanent canines in both the maxilla and mandible—all four permanent canines are absent.
