levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the main cross-figure findings: prior post-related structural compromise, recent retreatment need in 21/22, limited coronal dentin/core retention, remaining facial enamel, and favorable anterior loading pattern.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg into a tooth- and segment-level rationale that explains why the case is a conservative candidate despite substantial structural risk, and uses the figures to justify the post decision rather than relying on a rote rule.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an unsuitable definitive strategy, ignores sequencing after retreatment, or gives no defensible tooth-by-tooth foundation plan.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Proposes a plausible overall restoration but gives weak reasoning for post use/avoidance or treats the four incisors identically without figure-based justification.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Provides an appropriate definitive plan after endodontic stabilization and gives a coherent rationale for post placement decisions based on available retention and structural loss.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Presents a well-prioritized, clinically coherent plan that correctly explains the role of posts as core-retentive rather than root-strengthening, and defends the selected restoration against the best alternative in this specific anatomy and occlusal context.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not compare a credible alternative or does not explain how a changed occlusal scheme would alter treatment choice.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions pros and cons in general terms but does not clearly weigh conservation against masking/retention/loading or gives an implausible adaptation to the altered occlusion.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a credible alternative, compares it case-specifically with the chosen plan, and appropriately changes the plan when edge-to-edge incisal function with working-side contacts is introduced.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Shows nuanced judgment about why the chosen plan wins under the actual low-loading conditions yet would reasonably lose under the altered functional scheme, with clear patient-specific tradeoffs.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits restoration-specific early failure risks or gives only vague complications.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Lists generic risks without identifying the most likely early failure mode in this case or linking it to the mixed substrate and structural compromise.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies a plausible main early failure mode such as adhesive/marginal failure, debonding, ceramic chipping/fracture, or endodontic persistence, and links it to the actual case features.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the most likely early failure mode for this specific case and explains why it outranks other risks, while also noting appropriate follow-up of periapical healing and occlusal stability.

items.question_content: A 57-year-old woman with stage 4 grade C periodontitis, crowding, and hopeless maxillary central incisors from root fractures is planned for extraction and implant replacement. The adjacent lateral incisors have reduced periodontal bone support, with a crown-root ratio of less than 1:1, and further loss of support was expected after central incisor extraction. She also desired orthodontic correction, and the team used digital set-up to plan implant placement before orthodontic treatment so the implants could later serve as anterior anchorage after osseointegration. She had no history of smoking or systemic disease. Review fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg. Which considerations supported connecting the implant-supported maxillary central incisors to the adjacent lateral incisors? Select ALL that apply.

question_options.text: The lateral incisors had such reduced periodontal support that, after extraction-related bone loss beside the central incisors, they were unlikely to remain functionally reliable as independent units.
The connection was intended to reproduce periodontal-ligament behavior by increasing implant mobility and equalizing tooth and implant displacement under load.
Digital set-up allowed implants to be placed before orthodontics and later used as stable anterior anchorage after osseointegration.

By preserving function of the compromised lateral incisors, the connection was expected to help maintain surrounding hard and soft tissues and reduce the need for more extensive tissue reconstruction.
A history of periodontitis was treated as an absolute contraindication to independent anterior implant crowns, leaving connection as the only implant-based option.
Because the connection was in the anterior region, the clinicians considered load-related interface problems less likely than they would be in a molar tooth-implant connection.
The definitive superstructure was screw retained specifically to simplify management of future intrusion or abutment complications.
Active smoking and diabetes increased expected peri-implant breakdown, so splinting was selected to compensate for those systemic risks.

golden_answer.subjective_directions: The report justified connection because the laterals had poor support and doubtful independent function, the implants were incorporated into the pre-orthodontic anchorage plan, splinting was expected to help preserve hard and soft tissues around the compromised laterals, and the anterior region was judged less load-challenging than posterior connections. The case did not claim restored PDL-like mobility, absolute contraindication from periodontitis, screw-retained definitive restoration, or systemic risk from smoking/diabetes.

items.answer_explanation: The report justified connection because the laterals had poor support and doubtful independent function, the implants were incorporated into the pre-orthodontic anchorage plan, splinting was expected to help preserve hard and soft tissues around the compromised laterals, and the anterior region was judged less load-challenging than posterior connections. The case did not claim restored PDL-like mobility, absolute contraindication from periodontitis, screw-retained definitive restoration, or systemic risk from smoking/diabetes.

items.question_content: A 45-year-old woman seeks definitive restoration of four maxillary implants after dissatisfaction with her interim prosthesis. She has a high smile line, well-controlled hypertension, medication-related xerostomia, and a natural mandibular dentition. After correcting the interim prosthesis to an acceptable occlusal vertical dimension, only about 6 mm of restorative space remains. Review the attached figures. A final impression has been made using the adjusted interim denture, the corrected OVD has been recorded, the denture surfaces/opposing arch/bite have been digitally scanned, and a prototype has been tried in and approved. Based on this case, what definitive maxillary prosthetic design is most appropriate, and why is it preferable to a conventional implant overdenture or a fixed full-arch restoration in this patient? Include the key design and workflow decisions required for success in this limited space and the main biologic and prosthetic risks that should be discussed and monitored.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
The best choice is a CAD/CAM-milled monolithic PMMA maxillary implant-retained overdenture, preferably palateless, retained on the four implants with low-profile attachments such as Locators. The decisive issue is the severe lack of restorative space: a conventional overdenture with separate denture teeth, base, and housings usually needs more vertical height and would likely reproduce the excess base show seen in fig_02.jpg, while a fixed full-arch restoration is also less forgiving in this space and more difficult to optimize esthetically and hygienically in a xerostomic patient with a high smile line. A monolithic milled design integrates teeth and base, reduces required thickness, improves strength compared with conventional processed acrylic at minimal thickness, and avoids tooth debonding from the base. A palateless design is reasonable because four implants can provide retention while improving comfort, taste, and speech.

Key decisions are to first re-establish an appropriate OVD from the interim prosthesis by removing reline material and adjusting base and tooth contours; make a precise final impression and record the corrected OVD; digitally scan the intaglio, polished, and tooth surfaces plus the opposing arch and bite; use a facially driven digital setup to reposition tooth size, alignment, lip support, and smile display; verify esthetics, phonetics, and OVD with a printed prototype before milling; and at insertion verify passive fit radiographically, accurately pick up the housings, and refine occlusion to stable posterior centric contacts with anterior disclusion and controlled excursive balance.

The main risks to discuss and monitor are peri-implant mucositis/peri-implantitis from plaque accumulation, attachment wear and loss of retention requiring maintenance, prosthesis or housing fracture if thickness or fit is inadequate, wear against the opposing natural dentition, and mucosal soreness worsened by xerostomia. Close recall, hygiene instruction, and periodic occlusal and attachment maintenance are essential.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Selects an inappropriate definitive option, does not address the limited restorative space, or proposes a plan incompatible with the esthetic and functional constraints.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies an implant overdenture or CAD/CAM approach but does not clearly justify a monolithic design, omits the palateless/attachment rationale, or fails to compare meaningfully with conventional overdenture and fixed full-arch alternatives.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Chooses a CAD/CAM monolithic implant-retained overdenture and explains that limited space, excessive base display, and esthetic demands make it preferable to a conventional overdenture and generally more suitable than fixed full-arch treatment in this patient.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a well-prioritized plan specifying a palateless monolithic CAD/CAM maxillary overdenture on four implants with low-profile attachments, and links the decision to restorative space, high smile line, corrected OVD, opposing natural dentition, hygiene, and long-term maintenance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Ignores key clinical and figure-based findings or bases the answer on generic overdenture principles without using the case details.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses some relevant findings but misses major constraints such as the approximately 6 mm space, high smile line, excessive denture-base display, xerostomia, or opposing natural dentition.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates the main findings from fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, and fig_04.jpg with the history to justify the prosthetic choice and workflow.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Synthesizes the clinical, digital, and figure-based information into a coherent chain of reasoning from problem definition to definitive design, prototype verification, insertion, and follow-up.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh alternatives or presents risks and benefits inaccurately.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons but does not connect them to this patient's limited space, esthetic demands, xerostomia, or implant configuration.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains why monolithic CAD/CAM and palateless design offer better space efficiency, esthetic control, and maintenance than conventional overdenture or fixed full-arch alternatives while acknowledging tradeoffs.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides nuanced patient-specific tradeoff analysis, including retention dependence on four implants, hygiene demands in xerostomia, wear against natural teeth, and why the selected design still offers the best overall balance.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits important complications or follow-up needs.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Identifies only one or two generic complications without prevention or monitoring strategies.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies key biologic and prosthetic risks such as peri-implant disease, attachment wear/retention loss, fracture or fit problems, occlusal wear, and mucosal soreness, with basic follow-up recommendations.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies the major complications and pairs them with practical prevention and monitoring steps such as hygiene instruction, recall intervals, passive-fit verification, attachment maintenance, and occlusal review.

items.question_content: A 69-year-old ASA I patient with no regular medication presents with a fistulous 45 and will only accept extraction if he can leave the appointment with a fixed replacement; he refuses a removable provisional. A pre-extraction digital scan is available. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and fig_06.jpg, infer the retention and load-bearing concept of the fixed interim that was designed for this posterior site, then decide whether you would reproduce that concept for this patient or alter it. Anchor your reasoning to the figures: identify the substrate you would rely on, the surface/unit you would intentionally avoid recruiting, and why the shown posterior design is defensible only as an interim despite the usual preference for simpler resin-bonded designs. Finally, state the two most important delivery-stage precautions to avoid harming socket healing, and explain how your plan would change if the mesial enamel surface you intended to bond to proved unusable on the day of extraction.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would broadly reproduce the mesial-only adhesive concept shown in the figures, with the understanding that it is a temporary, non-functional fixed provisional rather than a definitive posterior resin-bonded bridge.

Figure interpretation is central. fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg show that the distal unit, 46, is an implant-supported crown. That is the unit I would intentionally avoid recruiting. It offers no enamel for predictable adhesive bonding, and linking a tooth-supported provisional across a fresh socket to an implant-supported restoration is biomechanically unfavorable because of differential mobility and stress concentration. The design figures, especially fig_03.jpg and fig_04.jpg, show a custom printed provisional replacing 45 with a primary retentive wing on the lingual surface of 43 and a mesial extension/support arm carried over 44 along the prosthetic equator; fig_05.jpg shows the printed restoration and fig_06.jpg confirms the same intraorally. So the load path is intentionally mesial, not distal.

I would therefore use the same basic strategy: a prefabricated printed adhesive interim supported from the mesial natural teeth, preserving future implant options and avoiding irreversible preparation of adjacent teeth. I would not convert this to a conventional FDP and I would not splint to 46.

Why this design is acceptable only as an interim: permanent resin-bonded bridges often favor simpler single-retainer concepts because multiple retainers or multi-tooth blocking can create unfavorable stress patterns and debonding behavior. Here, however, the service goal is different: same-day fixed replacement after extraction in a posterior site, with minimal biological cost, no removable denture, and maintenance of the socket for later definitive treatment. Using 43 as the main bonded retainer with 44 as auxiliary support reduces lever arm demands compared with trying to involve the distal implant unit, and the limited temporary duration makes this compromise more defensible than it would be for a definitive prosthesis.

The two most important delivery-stage precautions are:
1. Protect the fresh socket from contamination: complete extraction, debridement, hemostasis, and wound closure first, then isolate carefully so etchant, adhesive, cement excess, and finishing debris do not enter the socket. Most finishing should be done extraorally, with minimal intraoral adjustment near the wound.
2. Protect the clot from pressure and function: the pontic tissue surface should be smooth, highly polished, and passive or only very lightly supportive, and the pontic should be kept out of occlusion in centric and excursions.

If the mesial enamel surface I planned to bond to were unusable at the appointment, I would not rescue the case by bonding to 46 or by creating a tooth-implant splint. If 44 still provided reliable enamel, the best fixed fallback would be a more conventional single-retainer cantilever bonded from 44 only, while accepting higher posterior debond risk. If neither 43 nor 44 offered dependable enamel, a predictable fixed adhesive interim would no longer be available; I would re-consent the patient rather than force an unreliable or unnecessarily irreversible solution.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Provides a generic posterior Maryland-bridge answer, or misreads the figures in a way that drives the plan away from the actual anatomy/design.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses either the radiographic figures or the design figures, but not both coherently. Recognizes a mesial bonded concept or concern about the distal side, but misses the key figure-based reason.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Correctly interprets either the distal implant-supported unit or the mesial design geometry and links that observation to a conservative fixed interim plan.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg and fig_02.jpg with fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, fig_05.jpg, and/or fig_06.jpg: identifies 46 as an implant-supported crown that should not be recruited, and identifies the printed mesial-only design as a lingual wing on 43 with an extension/support over 44 replacing 45, then ties those observations directly to the final decision.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Recommends an inappropriate or unnecessarily irreversible plan, or does not answer whether the shown concept should be reproduced or altered.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Selects a reasonable fixed provisional but does not clearly justify the chosen design for this dentition or gives a weak contingency if the intended bonding substrate is unavailable.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Endorses or appropriately modifies a mesial adhesive interim that preserves future definitive options, and provides a plausible fallback plan if the intended mesial bonding surface cannot be used.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly supports the shown mesial-only temporary concept (or a justified minor modification), explains why it is acceptable only as an interim in a posterior site, and states that if 43 cannot be used, a 44-only cantilever is the only reasonable fixed adhesive fallback if enamel is adequate; otherwise a same-day fixed bonded solution should not be forced.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh relevant trade-offs or ignores the biomechanical implications of the actual adjacent structures.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic pros and cons of fixed provisionals but does not connect them to this posterior implant-adjacent situation.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Balances minimal invasiveness and same-day fixed replacement against posterior loading, debonding risk, and limited interim longevity, using case-based reasoning.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Explicitly rejects recruiting 46 or creating a tooth-implant splint across the fresh socket, and clearly explains why preserving natural-tooth enamel support and future implant options outweighs more aggressive or less predictable fixed alternatives.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits key delivery-stage risks to wound healing or proposes steps likely to contaminate or overload the fresh socket.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only one relevant precaution or gives vague postoperative advice without linking it to socket protection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies two relevant delivery-stage precautions such as wound protection during bonding, passive pontic contour, occlusal unloading, or minimizing intraoral grinding.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Identifies two or more precise precautions and explains why they matter next to a fresh socket: achieve hemostasis/closure before bonding, keep etchant/adhesive/cement and grinding debris out of the wound, finish largely extraorally, maintain a smooth passive or lightly supportive tissue surface, and eliminate pontic contacts in centric and excursions.

items.question_content: A 57-year-old nonsmoking woman with no systemic disease has stage IV grade C periodontitis, anterior crowding, reduced posterior occlusal support, and hopeless maxillary central incisors with root fractures. After initial periodontal therapy, she requests an esthetic fixed solution and orthodontic correction. The adjacent lateral incisors are retainable but have markedly reduced periodontal support and an unfavorable crown-root relationship likely to worsen after central incisor extraction. Using fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, fig_03.jpg, fig_04.jpg, and fig_05.jpg, state your definitive rehabilitation strategy and justify why it is the best choice for this patient. Include the key sequencing decisions and the main long-term risks that should drive maintenance.

golden_answer.subjective_answer:
I would replace the two maxillary central incisors with prosthetically driven implants and connect/splint the anterior restoration to the retainable lateral incisors after periodontal stabilization. In this patient, the lateral incisors should not be expected to function independently after extraction because their periodontal support is already reduced and the crown-root relationship is unfavorable; additional crestal loss could leave them unstable and compromise the gingival architecture. A tooth-preserving fixed solution also avoids sacrificing more adjacent teeth and better supports anterior hard and soft tissues. Although implant-tooth connection is not routine, here it is justified as an exceptional, patient-specific strategy because it preserves the compromised laterals and supports the planned orthodontic phase by providing stable implant anchorage.

Sequence: first complete inflammation control and supportive periodontal therapy, then restore/reinforce posterior occlusal support. Next, extract the fractured centrals atraumatically and place implants according to cephalometric and digital setup guidance so the final incisal edge position and anteroposterior tooth position are prosthetically correct. Perform hard/soft tissue augmentation if needed for contour stability in the esthetic zone. After osseointegration, place a provisional connected to the lateral incisors, begin orthodontics with the implants serving as anchorage, and deliver the definitive prosthesis once tooth positions are stable.

The main long-term risks are recurrent periodontitis around the lateral incisors, peri-implant mucositis/peri-implantitis, natural-tooth intrusion or mobility because teeth and implants move differently under load, prosthetic complications, and crestal bone loss if hygiene or occlusal control deteriorates. Prognosis is acceptable only with strict supportive care, low plaque levels, and regular periodontal/radiographic review; her nonsmoking, systemically healthy status improves the outlook.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Proposes a plan that is not viable for this case or omits major phases, such as bypassing periodontal stabilization, ignoring posterior support and orthodontic needs, or leaving the compromised lateral incisors to function independently without justification.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Provides a broadly fixed replacement plan but sequencing is generic or incomplete. Rationale for retaining and splinting the lateral incisors is weak, and periodontal, surgical, orthodontic, and prosthetic steps are not well integrated.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Recommends implant replacement of the maxillary central incisors after disease control and posterior support improvement, with connection/splinting to the compromised lateral incisors and prosthetically driven planning. Gives a sensible sequence from stabilization to surgery, provisionalization, orthodontics, and definitive restoration.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Clearly presents implant-tooth connection as an exceptional patient-specific solution, explains why it best addresses the compromised lateral incisors plus orthodontic goals, and includes atraumatic extraction and hard/soft tissue augmentation as indicated, with orthodontics timed after osseointegration so implants can serve as anchorage.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Does not weigh benefits and risks in a patient-specific way, or ignores the reduced support and unfavorable crown-root relationship of the lateral incisors.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions generic esthetic or functional advantages but does not meaningfully balance trade-offs or acknowledge the controversy and biomechanical implications of implant-tooth connection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Explains that independent function of the lateral incisors is risky, that preserving them avoids unnecessary sacrifice of additional teeth and can better preserve tissues, and that the implants can aid orthodontic anchorage while requiring careful long-term surveillance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Provides a nuanced balance of tissue preservation, invasiveness, esthetics, treatment duration, orthodontic efficiency, and long-term uncertainty, and notes that the patient's nonsmoking, systemically healthy status improves the risk profile.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Misinterprets or ignores the figures and key clinical data.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Uses isolated findings, such as the hopeless central incisors, but does not integrate the broader periodontal, occlusal, and planning information.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Integrates fig_01.jpg, fig_02.jpg, and fig_03.jpg findings of poor anterior condition, generalized periodontal compromise, reduced posterior support, and weakened lateral incisors with fig_04.jpg and fig_05.jpg planning information.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Coherently links the clinical photographs, radiographs, periodontal chart, and cephalometric/digital planning figures to the proposed implant position, support strategy, and treatment sequence.

levels.title: Fails
levels.description: Omits or misidentifies major complications relevant to this rehabilitation.

levels.title: Partial
levels.description: Mentions only generic implant failure or infection without addressing the specific risks created by periodontitis, compromised lateral incisors, or implant-tooth connection.

levels.title: Meets
levels.description: Identifies at least three relevant risks, such as recurrent periodontitis around the lateral incisors, peri-implant mucositis/peri-implantitis, natural-tooth intrusion or mobility, prosthetic complications, or crestal bone loss, and recommends regular maintenance.

levels.title: Exceeds
levels.description: Prioritizes the complications appropriately and proposes focused surveillance, including close recall, plaque control, periodontal charting, occlusal review, and radiographic bone monitoring.

items.question_content: Review fig_01.jpg. In an edentulous patient with persistent nodular ridge enlargement after extraction, biopsy shows hyperplastic squamous epithelium with elongated rete ridges over dense fibrous connective tissue with abundant collagen and only low-grade inflammation. What specific pathologic diagnosis was reported?
items.answer_explanation: The biopsy was reported as fibrous epulis. The combination of hyperplastic epithelium, elongated rete ridges, collagen-rich fibrous connective tissue, and only mild inflammation fits a fibrous epulis–type lesion rather than a purely inflammatory postextraction swelling.
